en: Oṃ, may there be well-being!
Homage to the sandals of Śrīnātha. Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
The First Bliss in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa of the Manthānabhairavatantra.
Within the circle of Saṃvatī, the power of bliss (Ānanda-śakti) is established in the sequential steps; she is most formidable.
For the purpose of emanation (sṛṣṭi), there is a group of four, then Akula and Kula, another group of five, and a group of six.
There are four, then another group of five, again four, and the sixteen-fold consecration of the Command (ājñā).
In the midst of the eight divine forms are the syllables Ha, Sa, Kha, Pha, and Ra; the digit is the flower-bindu, and the mudrā is space.
The Bāla, Kaumāra, Vṛddha, and Paramaśiva-kalās, as well as Vakradevī and the Kramas,
are the essence consisting of the ninefold division and the distinction of the Couple (yugma) within the City of the Moon (Candrapurya) of Śrīnātha.
There are three descents of the Siddhas in the first Kali Age, and their authority resides in Koṅkaṇa.
Among those indeed, in the lineage of nine persons consisting of sons and disciples, there were sixteen from their midst.

The continuum, the lineage, the aggregate, the sequence of steps, the entirety up to the sixteenth [stage], and the end of the sequence; these are indeed the remaining mandalas, the pure assembly of the venerable true natures.
First, the entire lineage-sequence up to the eighteenth, arising from the mandala.
The purification of the body (piṇḍaśuddhi), which effects the destruction of the impurities of the bound soul (paśu) through the threefold sequence of ritual acts, [is performed] in the fire of Śiva.

Bow down to that most excellent Guru, the venerable Kulīśa Bhairava, by whom the stage of rest in the center, the expansion, experience, conviction, and one's own authority have been brought into union.

In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: the meaning of the sequence (*krama*), consisting of three and a half verses, composed as an experience preceded by the form of Khañjinī; then again, another [sequence] called the Divine (*divya*) and the Human (*mānava*), which is the flood of the triple transmission (*trikramaugha*).
The mandala, divided by many distinctions, consisting of the sequence of all words, possessing the sixfold convention beginning with *ka*, endowed with all qualities— that is Bhairava.
Śrīnātha said: Who is at the end of the mandala, and how many are there? How does the mandala come to be? And how is that power of bliss (ānanda-śakti), and how is that power so terrifying?
Having taken up its obscuration, what indeed is the sequence of its steps?
And how does the tetrad according to the principle of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāya) become Akula?
What indeed is called "Kula," and what is the nature of Kula conduct?
What is the pentad in brief, as well as the hexad and the tetrad?
"Regarding the group of five: how can one who has four become more than sixteen-fold?
Where is the initial consecration? Tell me, [how] the eight deities come to be."
How does that [reality] exist within the embodied form, and what kind of mudrā is it therein?
Furthermore, how do the stages of childhood, youth, and likewise old age occur?
What is the supreme art (kalā) of Śarva, the sequential deity of the sequences?
How is Candrapurya described, O Śrīnātha, and what is its essential nature?

How does the conclusion of the flood of disciples consisting of sixteen [parts] come about? What is the lineage, the clan, and the entire collection of words and their sequence? In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
what is the end of the sixteen, the end of the sequence, and who indeed are the remaining mandalas?
I did not know of its wandering, nor especially of its stainless nature.
All this, in brief, is the determination of the true nature of the object of worship;
how will my sons understand its eighteen divisions?
How is the division of the couple the essence within the teaching of the three Siddhas?
Who would have authority in the South, and what is the nature of the group of nine?
Likewise, O Goddess, how is it known that the circle of the hermitage (āśramapūrvamaṇḍala) has eighteen divisions according to the threefold sequence of consecrations?
Briefly, who is the sacrificial animal here, and how does the mandala come to be?
By what means and in what essential form does the destruction of impurity itself occur?
First, what is this "piṇḍa" said to be, which is established within every body?
And how is it that the one named Śiva is the ground of rest in the midst of fire?
O Goddess, what is its essential nature, and what is the conviction regarding its own authority?
By whom was it created, who indeed is he here, and how does one become Bhairava?
"What is meant by the name Kaulīśa? Everything follows the *anupaddhati*. Tell me out of grace, O Vakrikā, if you are pleased.
Thus begins [the section] in the descent of the Great Sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage measuring seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru.

In the *Ājñāpārameśvara*, known as the *Svāminīmata*, a compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the tradition of the Mother (*avvākrama*), which exceeds one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the first seat (*ādyapīṭha*), belonging to the division beginning with the letter *ka* within the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimalaṣaṭkanirṇaya*) of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*),
[this is] the chapter concerning the Question of the Holy Lord (*śrīnātha*).
The first chapter is named Ānanda.
The venerable Vakrā said:
"Listen, O Lord of great wisdom, you who are the vessel of Kulakaula, to the second bliss."
By the mere knowledge of which, clear consciousness arises.
Therefore, I shall fully proclaim Vakrikā, the Supreme Goddess,
whom they call Śāvara and so forth, who has become manifold though being one.
"Constantly abiding at the edge of the mandala, he is the agent of creation and destruction;
resembling the flax flower, he is eternally risen and undivided."
Omnipresent and eternally peaceful is that mandala in your lineage;
situated in the midst of the staff of the skull-bowl, it pervades the subtle particles of the atoms.
Dissolved within the interval between prāṇa and apāna, she is called the power of bliss (ānanda-śakti).
With limbs variegated by the divisions of time, slender, and absorbed in the state of supreme, immutable terror, she is dissolved in the ground of blissless awakening to reality.
In the sixteen-fold expansion of the quarters, the form of the Goddess is threefold.
Established through the divisions of words by means of the limbs, sub-limbs, and faces,
that which is the sequence beginning with Bharga is situated in its reverse portion;
the sequence is divided ninefold as the Old, the Youthful, and the Child.
Will, knowledge, action, and intellect—this group of four is that which has manifested power;
the five subtle elements beginning with sound constitute the pentad preceded by knowledge.
The sixfold group consisting of skin, eye, nose, tongue, ear, and mind is called action.
The fourfold state consists of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the other, which is the fourth (turya).
Water, fire, earth, wind, and space—this pentad beginning with "jewel" (ratna);
the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* joined with the three gunas; the Lord of Trees (*Vṛkṣanātha*);
the illustrious Kubjī in her sixfold form; and the digit *Ha-Sa-Kha-Pha-Ra*, known as the *bhaga*, which pervades all.
At its end, when it has been stirred, having entered the power of Rudra, which is a treasury of supreme bliss;

Absorbed within the Root Lord, there are again six types of concealers by means of the sixfold seats and so forth; then, through their churning, the divine liṅga is divided. Therein resides she whose nature is the bliss of command, who is pure with the delight of pleasure, the creator of the universe, and the destroyer.
She whose form is consciousness, known as Vakrikā, has attained the supreme state; she bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Taking the vessel for the sake of drinking, one should flood oneself with the supreme nectar from the uvula; by that very act, this consecration occurs.
The Mālinī and the mass of sounds (śabdarāśi) abide pervading the lineage (gotra).
That lineage is the creator of emanation; the world is enveloped by Śiva and Śakti. [It is] endowed with the group of houses and accompanied by the eight Kulas. *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
It is joined with eight wheels and has Brahmāṇī as its eight deities.
The power of the mudrā is fully described as that by which this world is sealed;
that fourfold creation exists within the fourfold collection of beings.
The stages of childhood, youth, and likewise old age,
are established in their respective order along the path of the equinoctial station within the three paths.

At the end of the full moon, when it has reached the new moon, that digit is established as the "space-digit" (khakalā); that digit should be known as the space-digit, and it is complete, abiding in the heart.
And the goddess named Śrīmatā is the one who wanders through the three worlds;
she is declared according to the sequence of the sixty-four, as the goddess of the Krama and Vakrikā.
In the midst of the union of emission, however, is situated Candrapurī;
it is the support of the sphere of Sūṣman, carrying the nectar of the waves.
The supreme reality, the universal form, is established at the end of *unmanā*;
that is Śrīnātha, the support of the *kula*, the Lord of Kujī, the leader of the Siddhas.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
O Lord of the Gods, I shall now declare the eighteen divine divisions,
the tradition of the eighteen lineages which has emerged from the command of Unmanā.
The first is the Tradition of the Transmental (Unmanāmnāya), joined with four modes and consisting of five, six, and threefold; the second is the Transmental-Mind (Manonmana).
The third is the pervasion of Samanā; the fourth belongs to Vyāpinī;
the fifth, O Śambhu, is the Unmanifest (Avyakta); and the sixth is said to belong to Nandinī.
Manthāna is the seventh in the mouth; Pheruka shall be the eighth;
the ninth is called Samaya, and Jambhala is remembered as the tenth.
The tenth is Kālasaṃkarṣa, the twelfth is Caṇḍanirṇaya,
the thirteenth is Aghorīśa, and the fourteenth is Trailokya.
The Vinaya is said to be the fifteenth; Kamala would be the sixteenth.
Carcikā Devī is the seventeenth, and Śrīnātha would be the eighteenth.
Thus, there are eighteen divisions that have come down through the lineage of succession;
they have arrived according to the sequence of the divine tradition by way of the various streams.
They know the union of Śiva and Śakti as *sāmarasya* (equilibrium);
the meeting of both sides is remembered as this "division of the couple" (*yugmabheda*).
The three Siddhas—Candra, Arka, and Agni—are considered to be Mi, Ṣa, and O in the Trika;
they are Siddhas established in their offices of authority and lords of the three worlds.

O Lord Vṛkṣanātha, the digit of consciousness (citkalā), situated between the moon, sun, and fire, is like nectar; it consists of the self whose nature is the purified reality of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) and resides in the south.
The Lord of Gods, Navātmanānanda, endowed with the nine powers, having arrived at the ninefold state, is established in the sequence beginning with the letter *ga* within the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
The sixteen maṇḍalas of the foundational supports, beginning with Bharga-sthāna and the others,
are the cause of great prosperity for the multitude of disciples born from the unerring source.
The *piṇḍa* is said to be Kuṇḍalinī, conjoined with the bliss of the ninefold self (*navātmānanda*).
In her progression through the various divisions of the sequence, she resides in the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) in the form of the *piṇḍa*.
By the very sequence of descent, she is established at the *dvādaśānta*;
and through the distinction between the lower and the higher, she has descended as Vakrikā.
The flood of the stream of the mental continuum is that aspect which is devoid of bliss;
it exists within saṃsāra, whereas the supreme aspect is like a river.
The auspicious *kalā*, though appearing as a single mass, is divided by the fifty *gotras*;
Śiva, however, is indeed changeless, the medicine that transcends *saṃsāra*.
Furthermore, that which is neutral and nameless is called Śiva;
therefore, between the Iḍā and Piṅgalā, there is the crooked ground of rest.
Arising from the cause, she should always abide following the path of Śiva;
resembling the flax flower, she is six-faced and the supreme digit (kalā).
The supreme power (parā kalā), whose form is knowledge, should abide accompanied by consciousness;
its cognition is manifold, following after both discernment and ignorance.
The Lord of the World: "She is indeed Vakrikā, whose form is the Kula;

she is well-known in her office and presided over by the five principles (pañcatattva). In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, she is celebrated as the Mistress of the Transmission (Kramanāyikā) within the Śāmbhava office."
The pervasion of the fifty worlds extends from Kālāgni up to Śiva.
Therein, in the center, I created the fourfold world of moving and non-moving beings;
she, consisting of the three qualities and the three measures, remained established as the form of creation.
Bhairava is of a pervasive form, great and without beginning or end;
he sustains all in the form of nectar, his body being the void, stainless and untainted.
Because he resounds with the true existence of knowledge, he is the Lord Bhairava;
inexhaustible and devoid of decay, he is celebrated as Bhairava.
The name Īśa is established as residing at the end, middle, and beginning of Kula and Kaula;
he is the Lord (Īśvara) of all gods, celebrated as Kaulīśa.
The group of four consists of four divisions, and that power is likewise fourfold;
these are well-known as *mi*, *ṣa*, *ca*, and *o*, and the ritual manual (*paddhati*) has been demonstrated by them.
Thus [ends] the introduction in the Great Sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, within the lineage measuring seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru.

In the *Śrīcaturviṃśatisahasrasaṃhitā*, spoken in the tradition of the Mother (*avvākrama*), belonging to the *Kādivibheda*, the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimalaṣaṭka*), brought down to the first seat (*ādyapīṭha*) along the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), within the *Svāminīmata* which is the supreme command of the Lord, in the description of the chapter on Questions and Answers exceeding one hundred thousand quarters.
The second [chapter], named the Joy of the Arising of the Sequence.
The illustrious Vakrā said: "The third bliss is on the supreme form of Kailāsa, at the summit of the Meru temple."
And in the great and delightful Mahārāma grove, [he reached] the silent hermitage of the Lord’s cave.
The Triratra is surrounded by seven mountain ranges and eight regions;
in its center is the Triratra itself, extending for a hundred yojanas.
That stone was like a moonstone, yet possessed a luster equal to molten gold;
it was beautifully adorned with jewels, pearls, and corals, and was most enchanting to behold.
She is perfectly clear and greatly radiant, with a splendor equal to ten million moons;
she is endowed with seven coils and possesses five seats.
In its center is a circular region eighty-six yojanas in extent,
both in width and depth, as pure and stainless as clear crystal.
It was joined by two gateways, adorned with eight walls,
inhabited by eight deities, and both formidable and terrifying.
It is adorned with the lion’s roar of the abode of the unbroken mandala;
it effects great presence and is joined with the letters beginning with *Ā* and *Ka*. In the center of that, within the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, is that triangle measuring fifty yojanas.
The subterranean chamber, joined with three girdles, is the abode of the deity.
Slightly reddish, silvery, and brilliantly white, possessing a splendor like that of a hundred suns,
it is an unbroken orb measuring exactly twenty-five yojanas in its center.
Within the belly of the half-moon, in its center, is Kulakālikā;
her own body is a solar disc measuring fifty yojanas.
In the midst of that is the Kramamudrā, the Command (ājñā), and the Guru of the three lineages (oli);
it is the divine Khecarakrama consisting of the elder, the middle, and the child.
This is indeed the western chamber, known by the name Candrapurī;
it is the first maṇḍala, the domain of the mantra-practitioners.
It consists of one foot, possesses the three powers (triśakti), and is differentiated by the triad of vidyās.
And in the midst of that, by means of an easy method, the Kaulinī [is attained] by the qualified practitioner.
Established in the form of a *liṅga*, she is lion-shaped and faces downward;
the Blessed Lord Rudra, Śrīkaṇṭha, the husband of Umā, questioned her.
Śrīkaṇṭha said: In this Śākta house of the Guru, within the central liṅga arisen from the bhaga,
whose authority prevails, and who stands as the teacher for men?
Śrīkaulinī said:
"In the past, my Guru indeed granted me authority here over the Sadyojāta lineage and the Western House."
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
That power which is called the Yoni (Bhaga), the Mother of the World, consisting of three syllables,
is indeed the Command (Ājñā), Kaulinī, and she abides as the Neuter (Napuṃsaka).
Śrīkaṇṭha said: "O Bhairava, you are the womb, the supreme space, the divine liṅga, and the neuter; O best of inner sanctums, you are the embryo within the bliss of the bhaga."
Established through three divisions as the triple-formed Kaulinī,
you alone are the singular deity of the Kula by means of the sequence of manifold forms.
O Goddess, you are the mother of the worlds, the universal womb, O Grandmother;
by you and by me, O Queen of Gods, the three worlds are woven like warp and woof.
"O Goddess, I am generally not your disciple, but have come to you as a friend; out of the force of our former affection, I have come for the sake of the knowledge of worship."
"O Umā, since he has arrived desiring knowledge, explain it to him;
for I have already declared to you many times my unsurpassed knowledge."
Indeed, you yourself previously explained that to me in its entirety;
therefore, O Supreme One, there exists no broken state of discipleship between us, but only pure friendship, O Blessed Lady. Thus, speak without hesitation.
For this reason, I desire that Kaula knowledge which consists of direct realization.
Śrīkaulinī said:
"In human form, why are you called Śrīkaṇṭha?
Having come as a divine nature, you are certainly the Lord of Umā."
O Śambhu, the wise hunter, though disguised by a magical illusion, was recognized by me through his own voice; he was deluded by the net of my magic.
"O Great Śambhu, O Maheśvara, I have understood that you have come for the purpose of destroying darkness; for what reason is this, O Lord?"
You surely conceal yourself for some reason; from what refuge do you do so?
I shall tell you exactly what has happened, for you are exceedingly dear to me.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Listen likewise, O Lord, to the supreme cause of yoga;
I shall describe in detail that which was previously indicated by me.
On the western reflection of Kailāsa, at the summit of the Meru palace,
in a great and delightful grove, lies the hermitage of the cave-dwelling Lord Tūṣṇīnātha.
It is triangular, resembling seven mountain ranges, surrounded by the eight families,
measuring three hundred yojanas, and encircled by twelve verses.
Fifty accomplished yoginīs were born by the will of Śrīkulīśa;
they are the stone [of realization] consisting of three types: beginning with the vowels (ādi), the consonants (kādi), and the letter *tha* (thakārādi).
The mother of the lineage-holders and the bestowers of liberation upon the Siddhas,
she emerged from her dwelling in the cave into the three lineages of mantra and mudrā.
By the nature of passion (rajas), form is proclaimed to be like a flower;
that stone is the moonstone (candrakānti), possessing a luster equal to molten gold.
Extremely clear, situated between *ha* and *kṣa*, pierced in the middle by *ama*;
she resides in power (*śakti*), stands in the midst of power, and spreads across both *ha* and *kṣa*.
In the fiery *yonimaṇḍala*, which is the support for the triangular world,
there is a solar disc outside of that, slightly reddish and of great brilliance.
Extending for one hundred and fifty yojanas all around,
that delightful realm of all yogins is of the form of an unbroken mandala.
From the midst of that, however, there emerged the lineage of seventy million,
as well as the terrible Bhairava known as the Thirty-two Lions.
Abiding in the seed-syllable, she exists in five states;
abiding in power, she is established in five ways.
And in his lap is that Vidyā, raining down the nectar of the subtle breath.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Bhairavī Kālikānandā is the agitator of the three worlds;
she whose belly is half-moon-shaped sits upon a yellow seat.
Resembling well-refined gold, eighty-four *yojanas* in extent, it lies flat on its back;
situated beneath that, in its center, is the Neuter (*napuṃsaka*).
Resembling pure crystal, it is a circular solar mandala;
that is the Self of that wheel, differentiated by the moon, the sun, and fire.
In the midst of that, however, is the goddess Amā, who obstructs both the fortnight and the non-fortnight;
she is then born in the Lion-gait (siṃhakrama) as the goddess Vakrā within the three groups (trivarga).
Having the appearance of moonlight rays, she has five locations and is adorned with five ornaments;
she is also completely filled by the sequence of five times five, and is clothed in nakedness.
The maiden, through her celibacy, is the glorious goddess whose womb is the Bhaga;
she exercises her will at the edge of the continents, having manifested her authority in three ways.
She is neither female nor male in form; that bliss is the neuter.
It has the form of a *liṅga* with a substratum, and likewise without a substratum.
Abiding in the void, its form withdrawn, unmanifest and of the nature of Bhairava—
such is the power of bliss (ānanda-śakti), the divine liṅga that arises in due sequence.
The external field of both is divided by the three mudrās;
it is the mass of letters abiding in the peak, residing in the triangular cave.
The house named Candrapura is situated in the west and faces downward;
it has one leg and three arms, and is adorned with the tree of the three powers (triśakti).
In the midst of that, within the great city of Manthāna, resides the authority;
the power is Manthānabhairavī, the Kulakaulinī of all divisions.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: Vakradevī indeed stands in the form of a *liṅga*, facing downwards;
and one should contemplate the Self (*ātman*) situated in the heart as Śvetapiṅgalanāyaka.
Circular and exceedingly rich in splendor, it is sung as the syllable Oṃ.
Situated there, within the midst of light, is the primordial seat (ādyapīṭha), which maintains its own essential nature; it has the form of a jewel-liṅga, intensely red and of great brilliance.
It is the terrible [mantra] that causes immediate possession, situated above Aghora.
His command resides eternally within his own mouth; through its twenty-seven divisions, according to the sequence of six types, it constitutes the oral tradition of the Āmnāya.
Childhood, youth, and old age—these three stages are established in sequence;
and the eldest, the middle, and the youngest are adorned by the three lineages (oli).
This is indeed the western chamber, known by the name Candrapurī;
it is the grasping of the threefold reality for the lineages of the Krama-maṇḍala.
In the section on the Krama-mudrā, it is marked by the seat of the mudrā;
the city situated in the middle of the half-moon is joined with the Praṇava.
In reverse order, beginning with the letter *ca*, [one should worship] in the Maṇipūra; then again, in the western lotus-foot of the glorious Rudra, the sequence of desire.
Śrīkaṇṭha said: "In the house at Candrapura, within the Śākta tradition, in the central liṅga arisen from the womb— what teacher and mantra-master resides there of the Western Krama?"
The venerable Vakrā said: "O Maheśvara, of the palace of Candrapurya and of Aghora,
I am the Guru, I am the Mantrin, established in the state of the Neuter."
Through the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader, she is the omniscient Unmanā, the Supreme;
having emerged from her dwelling among the Siddhas, she exists in the nature of the Śāmbhava command.
Therefore, the Western Śāmbhava [tradition] stands above all others;
this is eternally distinguished as the present state of the Multiformed One.
That power which is called Bhaga, who rests upon the lap of Śambhu, is Kaulinī;
by means of celibacy (brahmacarya), she is the illustrious Goddess Napuṃsakā.
The ground of Nirvāṇa has been attained, and the imperishable command of the Siddhas is established in the sky.
Thus spoke Śrīkaṇṭha; this is the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
The venerable Vakrā said:
"Tell me the true essence of the Kaula, which was spoken in the Western House."
"O Mother, tell me how one who is veiled by illusion can attain immediate liberation;
for you are not veiled by illusion, but are indeed the manifest, stainless God."
Īśvara: "You are five-faced, seeking knowledge, known by the name Rudra;
you are the teacher in the three worlds, the creator and the destroyer again and again. You alone are the sole agent of creation and destruction within the earthly lineage."
Therefore, O Lord of the World, for what purpose do you desire the command of Śambhu?
For you are generally a seeker of desire and never a seeker of our command;
you have come here, O Rudra, for the purpose of tormenting us.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
"In former times, I abandoned both womanhood and likewise manhood; by the power of the knowledge of the planes (bhūmikā), I have become manifest age after age."
I am the supreme divine body in the form of emptiness;
I am that goddess Mālinī, I am that Siddhayoginī.
I am that Kālikā, indeed I am the mistress of the lineage-sacrifice (kulayāgeśvarī);
I am that goddess Carcikā, and I am Kubjikā in my sixfold form.
I was indeed bestowed by Dakṣa within the firmament for the sake of creation;
thus, in the Kali age, she manifests her descent for the liberation of those seeking release who are terrified by the fear of saṃsāra.
Formerly, I was Bhadrakālikā, the daughter of Dakṣa;
exceedingly beautiful and large-eyed, I was wedded by Śambhu.
At the time of her season, the queen entered into the presence of the god with full ceremony.
I, Līnā, who am supreme bliss, have attained a subtle state of bliss;
the pure Prajāpati, though lacking skill, performs the sacrifice.
On the banks of the Gaṅgā at Māyāpurī is the means for accomplishing dharma, kāma, and artha;
there dwell all the hosts of gods and asuras, including Vāsudeva and others, in their entirety.
Those who were established throughout the three worlds were invited by Dakṣa;
however, I was not there at first, nor was the five-faced Lord.
Out of fear of disturbing the sacrifice and apprehension regarding the sages,
Dakṣa, being terrified, did not invite the two Lords to the assembly; consequently, a great and most dreadful wrath was then ignited by them.
For the purpose of destroying the sacrifice, a curse was unleashed upon Dakṣa.
Vīrabhadra, intent on conquering the three worlds, was dispatched along with his hosts;
that great hero, surrounded by a multitude of attendants,
began the destruction of the sacrifice which was provided with a vast array of materials.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
everything without exception has been utterly destroyed, and the eradication of both beginning and end has been accomplished.
All the deities, terrified, fled in the ten directions;
some, intent on saving their lives, sought refuge there.
Some entered the openings of the netherworld; some came to the deep abysses;
some perished while traveling through the sky; and some arrived in the heavens.
Some entered Pātāla, while Dakṣa fell into a state of agitation;
with a joyful heart, he propitiated the one seated upon a lotus-throne.
Dakṣa said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, you who bestow grace upon the worlds;
O Unmanifest One, O Bhagavān Śambhu, O Sadāśiva whose form is the Liṅga!"
In the midst of the great forest, in this Nandana grove,
I have recited the mantra and performed sacrifice with devotion many times in such a manner.
"Be gracious, O Blessed Lord Śambhu; bring the sacrifice to completion.
Having thus petitioned him, Dakṣa stood with his palms joined in reverence.
Endowed with great power, he praises [the Lord] with the King of Hymns.
Dakṣa said:
"Homage to you, the Lord of the Kula, the bestower of the Kaula attainments!"
Obeisance to you, Śrī Śrīnātha, whose form consists of primordial wisdom and discerning consciousness,
who resides within the center of the heart-lotus in the orb of the rising sun.
I pay homage to the Great Vow of Knowledge (vidyā-mahāvrata), whose light is eternally risen, and from whom,
by the will of Śiva, there has arisen the assembly of fifty wheels.
I pay homage to the lineage of the Siddhas and the tradition of the deities, the great ocean of knowledge,
which brings about the awakening to the true meaning of the reality of mantra upon the mountain ranges of the six cakras.
I praise the Sun of Consciousness, from whom everything has emerged by his will—
the fivefold sequence of Nāda, Bindu, Kalā, Jyotis, and Ānanda. (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)

I bow to that which has reached the five stages, the object of knowledge, both supreme and non-supreme; having abandoned the thicket of ignorance—mind, intellect, and ego—I behold the true essence of mantra; I bow to the ocean of primordial wisdom.
It extends as far as the seven oceans, encompassing the domain of the ocean of saṃsāra.
I pay homage to the one beyond conceptual proliferation, without support, both supreme and non-supreme within the void;
the all-pervading Lord who dwells upon the three peaks, abides in the five principles, and is present in the five states.
I praise the flawless Kula, the true essence of both Akula and Kula, the division of the Trika, the supreme and the non-supreme, the support of the arts of the mantra-wheel.
I praise the foundation mandala, the wheel at the lower Brahma-aperture, endowed with four petals, red in color, and greatly radiant.
Above that, at the base of the navel, is a five-petalled wheel;
I worship the vajra resembling a ruby, the city of the full jewel.
I bow to the god Anāhata, who has a five-spoked wheel in the city of the heart, whose vehicle is the dark blue cloud, and who blazes with great radiance.
Thus, I praise that which possesses five petals, is situated in the pure throat, resembles the luster of molten gold, and has the nectar as its domain.
I bow to the supreme and non-supreme Command (ājñā), which resides in the fourth state, exists as the fivefold drop at the summit of the head, and resembles pure crystal.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
I salute the divine and flawless Great Wheel, which is the form of light, the stainless sixteen-spoked [mandala] of the Great Sound located in the middle of the palate.
I immediately salute Him who is conjoined with the syllable *ya* and the rest, who upholds the Brahma-mantra, who is as white as snow, jasmine, and the moon, and who is Śiva himself.
Then, Janārdana, who is differentiated by the distinctions of the [vowels] beginning with *a*, I praise him who resembles a ruby and is adorned with red ornaments.
I pay homage to the third Rudra, who is endowed with the five beginning with *ṭa*, who is worshipped,
who blazes like crushed collyrium, and who is formidable yet free from affliction.
And that which is the Lord, fivefold in the nature of the letter *ca* and others,
resembling a firebrand-circle (*alāta-cakra*) and radiant as a *liṅga*, I praise him.
Above that, conjoined with the five powers through the divisions beginning with *ka*,
I praise Īśānabhairava in the form of pure crystal;
and [I praise] Sadāśiva with the sixteen vowels from *a* to the visarga.
I always salute the one whose form is light, who awakens the command of the Kaula.
There, I praise Kuladāmarī, who resides within the support, who is distinguished in the midst by mantra and mudrā, and who is renowned as the Mistress of the Wheel.
I bow to the Goddess in the city of Uḍḍāmarī, who resides in the Maṇipūra, who illumines the supreme reality, and who is renowned as the Mistress of the Wheel.
In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:
I praise Jvālinī in that city— she who resides in the center of the heart-lotus, who awakens the wheel of the Siddhas,
and who is renowned as the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakranāyikī*).
I pay homage to the messenger Śākinī, who resides in the center of the Viśuddha-cakra, who is the Śavarī who pierces through gnosis, and who is renowned as the mistress of the wheel.
I bow to her whose form is space, who resides at the crown of the head upon the wheel, who is endowed with the perfected reality, and who is renowned as the Mistress of the Wheel.
I bow to Khecarī in the City, who stands in the center of the Wheel of Names, endowed with the perfected reality, and renowned as the Mistress of the Wheel.
I worship her who is shaped like a *kadamba* bud, established at the end of the sixteen [fingers], known as Pūrṇā, whose form is nectar during the bright fortnight;
in her center is the orb of Kālikā, whose lap holds the lioness of nectar.
I bow to the Goddess, whose form has the appearance of moonlight.
I bow to that goddess Kulamālinī, who is the supreme nectar of the left, who is most excellent and gladdened by the sacrificial pap (caru), and who, as Vāmā, brings about emanation.
I bow to Siddhadivākara in the south, who is the supreme state of splendor, who has fully embraced the essence of reality, and who is exalted by her brilliance.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Within the midst of the triad of powers (śakti) resides the deity in the form of a sprout;
I bow to her whose body is the shape of the womb (bhaga), situated upon the triangular seat (pīṭha).
I bow to the circle of the navel, the great jewel situated at the place of sound, blazing with the digestive fire, and the support for the state of ultimate reality.
The deity named Kuṇḍalī, who is the perfected limb that removes its veil, who dwells in three places and has the form of three coils— I bow to Siddhakuṇḍalī.
I salute that which is infinite, whose form is the splendor of mantra consisting of nine aspects, established as the immutable peak-syllable (kūṭa) in the supreme ether, just like the Guru.
I bow to her who abides in the Nameless, who resides in the supreme abode, who manifests as the triad of powers,
who is established in the single reality, and who strikes the blow of pure consciousness.
I bow to that which, divided by the distinctions of will, knowledge, and action, resides at the moon-crested peak,
within the range of the ultimate power, through the very sequence of going and coming.
O support of the five kalās of the void, through the reverse process of Māyā and by means of the nocturnal practice, I perceive [Thee]; I salute Ghaṭa according to the tradition.
I praise the Bindu, the wish-fulfilling gem, which resides in the Fourth State, is immortal and white, has emerged from the mouth of ultimate reality, and flows by taking refuge in gnosis.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Above that, there is mere light, the sustainer of what remains of the *kalās*.
It is perceived through the piercing of the *bindu*; I salute that imperishable cavity.
I salute the unbroken Maṇḍala, the great jewel that is the support of living beings, which removes the impurities of the fetters of the bound souls, and which is stainless and circular in form.
I salute Śiva, the great nectar, the god who pervades all limbs, adorned with mudrās and mantras, and established in the light of the nature of consciousness.
I praise that which transcends the *laya* of mantras at the end of the sixteen,
the reversal at the end of the twelve, the supreme state, and that which rests upon the end of *nāda*.
I bow to the supreme Kālikā, who is the Great Lakṣmī residing within, and who, for the sake of revealing the ultimate reality, is more weighty than the reality of the self.
Having ascended to the deity by means of the resonance of the sound of the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*),
I bow to her who bestows the boons of sustenance and fearlessness within the form, at the external focal point.
I bow to the digit consisting of Śiva, the intermediate Vidyā who has gone to the supreme sky of Śiva’s side, mounted upon the chariot of the fourth wheel.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
having fixed the mind in the center of Śakti, one should contemplate the mass of consciousness in the void;
I salute that which is tranquil, stainless, and completely free from all dualities.
Meditating upon the Greatly Terrible One, who resides in the region of the navel and is supported by the space of the King of Space, and grasping the root, I pay homage to the beginningless Sky.
Having made the void within the city of the heart and the wind within the womb of space,
and recollecting the primordial cause, I pay homage to Jyotirmaheśvara.
"Residing in the middle of the throat like the tide of the great ocean,
I salute the ocean of the digits of space in the form of the supreme void (*paravyoman*).
The void situated in the middle of the palate is turned upward, struck by lightning.
I salute the Supreme Goddess, who is mounted upon the chariot of the sound of Brahman and resides in the sky.
But by means of the sequence of the fifty phonemes of the Kula-consciousness,
this King of Hymns is the great secret, the Great Consciousness-Bhairava.

Praised by Dakṣa with a focused mind, this is the internal sacrifice of meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*). He who remembers it before the sequence (*krama*), or remembers it at the three times of day—[attains success]. *From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.*
By means of constant devotion, one shall attain equality with Bhairava;
freed from old age and disease, and abandoned by the snare of enjoyments, liberated from suffering and poverty, one may wander at ease.
The person who possesses liberation while living remains for a very long time.
One shall not be afflicted by untimely death and will be freed from the web of obstacles;
by the power of this King of Hymns, this comes to pass—of this there is no doubt.
One should conceal [this] from the disciples of others; it must not be given to just anyone.
It should never be given even to one's own son if he is devoid of devotion.
One should never bestow this upon those whose conduct has fallen away from their family traditions;
it must not be given to Tantrikas, but should be protected like one's own body. It is the knowledge of the true nature of liberation that illuminates the knowledge of the Self.
Furthermore, whoever, having risen in the morning, should call to mind this determination of the body;
He knows self-knowledge as having the nature of the understanding of the hymn;
having completed it according to this rite, the skillful one should ask for forgiveness.
The Supreme Lord, being pleased and gratified by the King of Hymns, spoke thus, supremely tranquil: "Tell me the ultimate truth."
"For what purpose have you praised [him] with this great king of hymns?
Dakṣa said:
"O Lord, that auspicious sacrifice which was commenced by me on the banks of the Gaṅgā—"
For the sake of attaining dharma, kama, and artha, I, being of dull intellect, did not succeed;
I did not invoke the God, and consequently, the sacrifice was destroyed.
And through your anger, I have fallen from my curse once again,
as well as causing distress and bondage for those priests present at the sacrifice.
O Great Lord, forgive that which has arisen from the god’s anger;
show your grace toward those who have departed, those who have perished, and those who are bound within the great belly, so that they may no longer come into existence.
Śrīnātha said:
Thus he spoke with favor: "Arise, O son of a seer! (Kumārikākhaṇḍa).
For those who are lost, those who are ruined, and those who are bound, I have secured their liberation; this is the truth, O observer of pure vows.
"O wise one, by my grace, perform the commencement of the sacrifice which bestows success;
there is no doubt in this matter. This is a great boon resulting from the curse.
Having understood this, the Goddess then related this account that had occurred.
And because of my connection with Dakṣa, I am that evildoer.
"My father's sacrifice has been destroyed by me; now I shall purify myself by kindling the supreme fire, which resembles surging waves of blazing flames."

one should then assume the vajra-posture (vajrāsana) and remember the portion of Aghoreśvarī.
Consumed by the fire of time itself, she became smokeless embers;
the virtuous woman, having died and turned to ashes, has crossed over from the world of mortals.

indeed, I was born during his eighth great birth.

Now,
within this lineage, there has arisen a certain great instruction;
indeed, in the midst of the Cave-Dweller, the state of Śambhu exists.
Having gone there, I shall now bestow my grace upon you;
for the Goddess, having known this previously, has been born in your western house.
And the family goddess Kauleśī is established in her office;
in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the Lord of the God of Gods, the Great Master, has arrived seeking to bestow grace.
By her, through the very sequence of tradition, grace was bestowed upon him by means of that descent of power (śaktipāta); thus his latent impressions (vāsanā) became completely purified.
The goddess Carcikā was born from the command within the lineage of Mālinī;
she is the supreme, divine, and unbroken Command of Śambhu.
By the power of the Command, the goddess is filled with hundreds of masses of lightning.
Intensely illuminated by rays of splendor, it attained the state of a divine linga.
Thus, in the Kali age, that Carcikā exists in the form of a *liṅga*,

Thus, in the primordial descent (*ādyāvatāra*) of the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) measuring seventy million [verses], emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the first sacred seat (*ādyapīṭha*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimalaṣaṭka*),
in the *Kādi* division, in the *Svāminīmata*, the supreme command of the Lord, the glorious twenty-four thousand [verse scripture]...
In the *Avvākrama-bhāṣita* of the *Saṃhitā*, this is the bliss titled "The Chapter on Dakṣa’s Curse and Grace."
Śrīkaṇṭha said:
"Thus, by your very nature, the state of the Śāmbhava command has been attained. This is the Fourth Bliss.
Through the relinquishing of all dualities, it is peaceful, transcendent, and beyond both the supreme and the non-supreme.
Therefore, you are my guru and mother; forgive me by right.
Among all mothers and Siddha-Rudras, you alone are the deity dwelling in my heart.
"You are my power, O Mother Rudrā, in the western house;
for I am here seeking desire, not seeking a command, being one who longs for the Krama."
I am indeed your disciple, having properly approached you with a clear mind, for the sake of the great arising of the lineage of the stream of the divine and non-divine stages.

O Goddess, tell me the family tradition (kulāmnāya) that has come down through the sequence of succession, as well as the eight signs of realization (pratyaya), and my own doctrine concerning the division beginning with *ka*.

thus [is it] the sequence of written syllables found in the Vāyupurāṇa and other texts."
For the God of gods, who is devoid of the conviction of command, there arises a sense of deficiency; therefore, I entreat you for your command in the future.
Furthermore, his command, beginning with the syllable Śrī, proceeds through the lineage (gum-nāya);
therein, in the Kali age, Śrīnātha receives that command of Śambhu.
For the sake of the liberation of all living beings, he will manifest an incarnation;
this truth concerning the Purāṇa is also due to your devoted service.
The Śrīmata, the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), descended through the lineage of the Root Transmission (Mūlānvaya);
it is the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, free from the dust of the maṇḍala and devoid of caste and the sacred syllable (praṇava).
"Speak the sequence of the Kaulika tradition and the lineage of the Gurus, which is throbbing with life.

[grant] devotion in the disciple, the command of the Guru, and the attainment of both.

this Linga is its hermitage, the embodiment of your Śakti-family.
