Haiṃ, O Rudrasaṃmohani! [From] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Shmlkryūṃ, you who have taken your seat upon the lap of the god Navātmānanda.
You are worshipped by those following the path of mantra, by the Mothers who delight in the drinking of heroes, and by those possessed of excellent devotion.
O Goddess, you are worshipped with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the festivals of divine drinks. Aṃ Aḥ.

Ha He Aiṃ Hauṃ! You are propitiated by those various auspicious waters arising from one birth, two births, three births, four, five, six, or seven births, as well as by the waters of the Phalgutīrtha; Svauṃ! O Beloved of the honey and the Phalgutīrtha! ( ) Svauṃ! O Beloved of the honey and the Phalgutīrtha! ( )
*Saum*, hail to you in your true form!
*Kām*, O wearer of the shaven head!
*Mlūm*, O you who shine with the vows of mantra and vidyā! You are worshipped by those established in divine conduct—by skull-bearers, skeletons, and holders of begging bowls.
Rūḥ!
O you who bear the skull-staff and the Ruru deer!
Klīṃ! O you who cause the agitation of the three worlds!
Klūṃ! O Kaulamātaṅginī!
Klūḥ! O you who are adorned with a serpent as a sacred thread and a girdle!
Āṃ! O bestower of supreme bliss!
"Oṃ Aiṃ! You are worshipped as being complete and transcending these classes of mantra-syllables: *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *svadhākāra*, *vauṣaṭ*, *vaṣaṭkāra*, *hūṃ*, and *phaṭkāra*.
Thaṃ! O Supreme Bhairavī of the thirty-two [syllables], you who abide within the union of the two pentads."
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:

You are the series of seed-syllables of speech (Vāgbīja), consisting of forty-two letters; you are worshipped by practitioners, sons, and mothers who hold rosaries in their left hands and recite them within the maṇḍala. O Hasū! You are praised.
O you who abide within the *saṃvarta* maṇḍala with initiated yogis and assemblies of yoginīs, you who look upon [us] with grace;
(*khphreṃ*), O leader of the *khecarī* wheel! (*khphreṃ*)
Ṛ ṝ ṝ auṃ auṃ, O you who perform the gathering of the wheels (*cakramelāpakāriṇī*).
Lūṃ, you are worshipped by those devoted to the play of Rudra.
Bhṛṃ, O Bhṛkuṭī, O Karālabhairavī, O beloved of Bhairava!
BŪM. O you who are praised by heroes, great heroes, and the assembly of heroes!
BHAṂ. O you who are languid with the play of a madwoman!
YŪM. O bestower of the yogic accomplishments of the yoginīs!

O Goddess Mlāṃ! For whomsoever you look upon with eyes like lotus petals, filled with affection, *khaṃ*, for him there exists the unimpeded attainment of the celestial, atmospheric, and subterranean *khecarī-siddhis* throughout the seven netherworlds.
*Hūṃ*! Whoever recites this Great Daṇḍaka with devotion once or twice a day...
That man who, being pure, should constantly and at the three times of day remember the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, he too is protected from thieves, fire, weapons, the ocean, and even mountains.
Phai~ phai~ phai~! O Goddess Mahālakṣmī, those who are thieves of gold, those who are attached to the wives of others,
and those defiled by the great sins of killing a Brahmin or a cow— by recollecting your face, which resembles the full moon, they are all liberated.

Even those whose cheeks are illuminated by shimmering divine *māṇikya* earrings, and whose arms and feet are secured by firm bonds and serpent-nooses as door-bolts—they too are liberated from their bondage. Those who are seized by planets (*graha*) and tormented by many *bhūtas*, *vetālas*, and *rākṣasas*—they too [are freed] by the chanting of your name. *Phreṃ*. Those who are swallowed by the planets and oppressed by many *bhūtas*, *vetālas*, and *rakṣasas*—they too [are freed] by the proclamation of your name.
O Goddess, by recollecting your two lotus feet, they are liberated from terrible and great diseases:

*Hūṃ Mahākāli, you whose splendor is like the fire of cosmic destruction!* [Salutation] to her whose crown is adorned with Skanda, Govinda, Brahmā, Indra, Candra, and Arka; and who is golden-hued like the filaments of a beautiful lotus surrounded by bees and garlands of flowers.
Who shines? Śrūau~! O garland of the lords of the Karavīra cremation grounds!
Glauṃ! O Mother Kadambāmbikā, adorned with caves, forests, mountains, gardens, and groves;
Ha! O dweller in the Karavīra cave;
Cchauṃ! O dweller in the garden of the fourteen worlds!

Kṛkarāṭ: O you who resound through the three worlds! Ḍāṃ ḍāṃ, O Mother Ḍāmarā! Jyūṃ kuṃ hskṣmlvryūṃ! At the end of the power (śakti) arisen from the sequence of the sandals and the liṅga is the great cause, the state of Śambhu.
This is the manuscript of the Great Knowledge of the Kādimata-Ḍākinī-maṇḍala-stream; therein shines the mass of sounds known as the Vīrāvalī, radiant with light:
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Phaṭ Hrasūauṃ—the divine liṅga-throne, by means of the powers of the Nirvāṇayogāvalī, which is preeminent within the maṇḍala. *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*
Hkṣauṃ! Salutation to the one who resembles pure crystal, who is endowed with the five great arrows of supreme nirvāṇa in the sky,

who is the state of ultimate repose in the authority of the command, who has become the intoxication of all aesthetic arts (kalās), who is the transmission of Madana, who is accomplished by the Yoginīs, who is constantly saluted and celebrated by the streams of the tradition of knowledge through prose and verse, and who is the awakening that realizes all objects contemplated in the four quarters.
O Mother of all heroes, you awaken!
Bhaṃ bhaṃ bhai! O Bhairavī, I have come to you for refuge, O Bhairavī of the Linga and the Sky; I am here seeking your command.
"Forgive my transgression, O Śivā, O Umā, Mother of the World! O Kālikā, who dwells in the depths of the cave that is the lotus-heart of the Kula!
Through this hymn of praise to Mālinī, I am one who rejoices in the covenant; I bow at Your feet. Out of compassion, have mercy upon me! ()
The Mālinīstavarāja was brought down by Ādinātha;
the Great Voice, impelled by his command and urged forth by bliss, was set in motion.
For the sake of receiving the command and for the purpose of attaining authority,
whoever recites this at the beginning of the sequence during the observance of the Youthful Sequence (Bālakrama), [attains the goal].
Then, through that sequence, his perfection arises— the eightfold qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā)—
and the touch of the state of bliss is born from the very act of utterance (uccāra).
Whether three times a day or once, with a single-minded and concentrated focus,
divine possession proceeds by means of the application of the enumeration of seed-syllables.
Blessed is the favor of the command; there is no doubt that the perfection of speech [is attained].
Thus, in this sequence, his tradition of mantras is indeed manifold.
One shall attain the state within the peaceful supreme reality, whose form is invisible;
by remembering it even once, one shall obtain the entire sequence of mantras and vidyās.
O Mother, one should obtain thorough knowledge in two ways and in three ways;
one should conceal [this teaching] from the disciples of others who are devoid of the lineage transmission.
One should not cause those who are arrogant and deceitful to give [the offering].
Thus was the Great Goddess praised by the high-souled Bhairava.
Then, having burst through the *liṅga*, the Supreme Goddess emerged;
remaining within the *liṅga* and taking the form of the *liṅga*, she spoke to Siddhanātha.

O Śambhu, because of our former affection and because of my cultivation of a friendly disposition, I grant you this certainty: the Kula, which is the Kaula, is to be grasped through meditative realization.
Out of affection, he designated him as a Mahākaulika in thought and word;
when he was thus addressed by the Goddess, he attained the state of friendship.
Therefore, this Siddhanātha became renowned here by the name Mitra.
O Kaulikī, from this first beginning, sovereignty over my portion belongs to you.

The minister who upholds the command of Bhairava and Kaulīśa, the authorities— thus, in the primordial descent of the Great Manthānabhairava Sacrifice, in the lineage measuring seventy million verses emerged from the path of Meru,
exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the first seat (pīṭha), in the determination of the Pure Sixfold Division within the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha).

In the *Kādibheda*, within the *Ājñāpārameśvara* according to the system of the Master (*svāminmata*), in the venerable *Caturviṃśatisahasrasaṃhitā* spoken in the *Avvākrama*, this is the bliss (*ānanda*) named the chapter on the *Mālinīstavarāja*.
The Fifth Bliss.
The venerable Vakrā said:
"This Kaula knowledge is the city of the intellect of the Krama-maṇḍala."
O Lord, it is not ordained that one should give out of devotion, attachment, or desire.
"O Śūlapāṇi, because of the affection from former times, how can this disciple be dear to me? O wielder of the trident, the reversal of the roles of teacher and disciple is improper."
O Lord of Gods, even when [the practice] has been performed, derision arises;
there is great danger from both the path that follows the natural order and that which goes against it.
Loss of intelligence and mental exhaustion arise from improper conduct;
as long as there is no relationship of teacher and disciple, there will be suffering like that of a slave.
"In that case, how can there be accomplishment for the practitioner through family lineage?
I shall not speak of disciples, nor am I a guru."
From here, O Śambhu, the sequence of the Sūtra is given as that Kula-transmission;
you are a man of knowledge and a great scholar, yet she is not at all wise enough for discipleship.
When there is devotion in the disciple and knowledge in the guru, and when both possess this realization, then that initiation is truly born; otherwise, it is a mere mockery.
Śrīnātha said:
"In the past you were my wife, and I was Manmatha; both of us, under the power of love, experienced bliss until the end of desire, just as we do now."
In that way, you would become another embodied being, and I would become a mortal body; through our exchange, there would be saṃsāra, and that is what one desires.
Likewise, in due course, the conceptualization that "I am the disciple" and "you are the mother" does not constitute a fault here; this is the ascetic practice of the mantra-convention.
When [the transmission] reached you with the words "of yours," you were established in the lineage of the Siddhas;
thus, in this sequence, I remain as your disciple according to the previous compendium, [as taught in] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Before the lineage, before the mandala, and before you, with a serene mind,
transform [this] into its true nature for yourself and for me according to reality.
Therefore, out of affection for me, grant the illumination of knowledge;
I am your disciple, O auspicious one, and you are my mother—act accordingly.
Thus, we have reached this state, having transcended our former associations;
therefore, out of affection, you look upon me for the sake of showing favor.
There is no accomplishment in the *tantra* during the fourth great age, the Kali;
yet here, in the house of the glorious Candrapura, accomplishments are certainly attained.
"May I be attentive within the maṇḍala in birth after birth;
thus, speak the sequence of the command, the compendium of the meaning of the Saṃhitā."
Tell me the instruction regarding that supreme Kaulika knowledge by which the cage of the body is moved by mere consciousness alone.
You alone are the sign of space, while this earth is the seat;
the moving and the unmoving are dissolved within you, and for that reason you possess the form of the *liṅga*.
You are the mantra, you are the supreme knowledge (*parā-vidyā*), you are the command (*ājñā*), and you are both the transcendent and the immanent (*parāparā*).
You are accomplishment (*siddhi*), and you are power (*śakti*), O you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge!
Impelled by your power, may I be born again and again in this world;
I am a mortal of blessed body, for I am capable of worshipping you.
The specialized sequential cognition is considered to bestow accomplishment;
it is attained through discipline by means of the unity of the stages of accomplishment.
That very [reality] belongs to the ascetic endowed with austerity, to the one who moves through the sky,
to the manifest and unmanifest, to the pure, and to that which abides from the letter *Na* to the letter *Pha*.
Having first performed prostration with the eight limbs, I have offered myself to the one whose body is the lion-signal, from within the sequence of Mālinī.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
O Goddess, this hermitage of devotion has been offered here to you;
of this there is no doubt, for there is no wealth greater than you.
"You shall attain success; there is no doubt in this. A devotee shall clearly receive the Command (ājñā).
Devotion toward the disciple, knowledge of the Guru, and the Kula tradition received through the Command."
O Mudrā, who art the probe of gnosis, who manifests for one endowed with devotion— be gracious, O Goddess of gods, and grant me your vision now!
The venerable Vakrā said:
"I have not seen a body; only a linga is seen, divine and made of pure gold, whirling like a fire-lamp."
Therefore, manifest yourself within my deluded mind;
having burst open the seal, appear before me directly, O Lord!
O Śambhu, I have emerged from the bursting of the *liṅga* with great splendor,
possessing a crooked form and a terrifying face that is triangular in shape.
I am Śyāmā, red in color, three-eyed, and possessing a radiance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction; because I am endowed with the gaze of a lion, I am known as Siṃhāvalokinī.
O Bhairavānanda, having seen you, I became contracted with shame;
for that reason, I became Vakrikā, adorned by the eight limbs. At that time, I was born as Vakrā, possessing a divine body and great power.
"You have been pierced by me merely at the sight; this truth has been accomplished by me."
Śrīnātha said:
"I have been pierced by you with your power; indeed, I am overwhelmed by the mere sight of you. I did not see your body, for I had fallen under the sway of sleep and exhaustion."
"O Goddess, my mind having been stolen away by another, I neither hear nor see; at that time, I was pierced by you with a glance."
When these conditions have been attained, the initiation by piercing (vedhadīkṣā) occurs in the Kula tradition:
namely, hearing, thought, mental vision, consciousness, fortitude, and patience.
The body, pierced by the penetration of power, has entered into another mind;
the command of the sign has been attained in its true nature by means of the probe of knowledge.
Among the Siddhas, I am the first Siddha, known by the name Mitra;
for I am your devotee and servant, and you are my goal and supreme refuge.
This prostration with eight limbs has been performed by me three times like a staff; you, O Guru, are my sole sovereign command and all-pervading teacher.
For I alone have been born as a disciple through the lineage and conduct of the wise one; O Goddess of the lords of gods, forgive me for having received the transmitted command through your grace.
"O Vakrikā, you are my sovereign mother, the goddess who is the ground of rest; you are my refuge and you are my lord—I have come to you for shelter.
O Goddess, you alone are the source of both heaven and liberation, O Mother!"
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my ascetic practice has become fruitful.
Today I have attained sovereignty; today my command has been transmitted to me.
Today, O Bhairavī, by your grace I am a yogin;
please tell me now the instruction, the ritual action, and the training.
Having heard these words of the Siddha, the Goddess spoke this speech:
The illustrious Vakrā said:
"Out of affection from former times, I have declared my friendship for you;
O god Mitra, great Siddha, this is proclaimed as the name of the Command."
Puṣpā is to be propitiated as the seventeenth, and likewise the self as the eighteenth; O you of noble vows, Jyeṣṭhā is to be propitiated by me in the sequence of seventeen and ten.
These followers of Śambhu, the leaders of the Siddhas, are to be worshipped by you in the sequence beginning with Unmanā and ending with the venerable Nātha and Ciñciṇī.
O Śambhu, without knowing the convention of the flowers, one does not possess liberation;
likewise, O God, [one must know] the Bālakrama, the sacred seats (pīṭhas), and the deities within those seats.

Externally, however, there are eight deities; the Kaulikī consists of the letters from *na* to *pha*. "Arise! O Maheśvara, you who are joined to the Krama, you alone are the lineage and the clan; today I have made this manifest."
This knowledge, which has come down through the succession of the lineage, must be protected.
Emerging from the mouth of the Yoginī, having issued forth through the path of Meru,
[it is] the devotion to the Kumārī-Yoginīs and the subjugation of those who violate the samaya.
And my command must be carried out: you may wander at will and live happily;
wherever people are devoted to me, there reveal the knowledge. (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
O Khaga, having accomplished all things by his command, he who seeks the Moon should bestow the pill that causes falling [of the semen] merely by his glance.
Thus, O Bhairava, this power of your knowledge has indeed been described;
it is certain that you possess the capacity for both restraint and grace.
Having gone to the world of mortals, perform your play as you desire;
liberated from old age and death, your movement shall be eternal in the sky.
For you are indeed liberated from all sins, like pure gold;
whereas those who commit sins such as the killing of a Brahmin day after day [remain bound].
By the mere remembrance of you, they perish; there is no doubt about this.
They meditate upon you constantly, even through remembering you at the three times of day.
They are perfected ones; there is no doubt in this— they are liberated from the bonds of fetters—
those who revile you, O friend, or even those who defame you.
They die and go to an evil rebirth; they are destroyers of liberation, of this there is no doubt.
They go to the Raurava hell; how could there be liberation for them?
Having spoken thus, the beautiful Siddha remained prostrate before the Goddess and, with supreme devotion, spoke as Śrīnātha.
O Great Goddess, you are the guide; grant me initiation. Bestow upon me the power of prosperity and the grace of initiation, exposition, and other such favors.
Then, O Ācārya, I wandered in the midst of the Yogīsīs;
having heard these words of the Siddhas, she was pleased with the Mother of Yoga (Yogamātṛ).
O friend of Siddhanātha, O Lord of the world,
this is that consecration which arises from the vision at the end of the sixteen.
The goddess Pūrṇā, complete with the sixteen digits (kalās), should be uttered;
raining down a flood of nectar, she is Amā, the seventeenth digit.
The consecration of the Lord was bestowed by the Goddess Avalokita;
today I grant you the state of a sky-walker (*khecaratva*), provided you grasp the *liṅga* according to its true meaning.
"The capacity for initiation, exposition, and mastery—this is the command that bestows liberation.
This very consecration, O beloved, has now been granted by me to you."
The supreme moon, having restored life, should split the vajra-linga within the Kula-abode.
In whatever place this [liṅga] may be— whether born of mantra, innate, or even artificial—
it should always be worshipped; indeed,
it should be worshipped especially so.
Having bathed and being pure, one should with devotion pay homage to the Śrī-liṅga facing west;
then, on the day of the Liṅga-pūjā, the consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed by the Ācārya.
For those who have been consecrated by a family preceptor (kulācārya) but are devoid of the worship of the Liṅga, there is no attainment of accomplishment; otherwise, their downfall will occur.
Having spoken thus to the Siddha, the Goddess of the lords of gods, her family and form unseen, appeared and gazed upon the circle like a lion.
Then the Siddha, greatly delighted, himself assumed the form of a lion;
with prostrations of the eight limbs, the Siddha asked forgiveness of Bhairavī.
With twelve divine verses, they praise the divine teaching:
[She who] is mounted upon the seat of the syllable Aiṃ, seated upon a vajra-lotus— *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
I bow to her known as Śrī Kujā, who constantly bestows accomplishment upon me—
the Great Māyā of the power of knowledge, who illumines divine wisdom.
I bow to the goddess named Śrīkujā, who has entered into invisibility,
residing in the center of the four seats (catuḥpīṭhaka) through the power of her divine energy.
I bow to the one named Śrī Kuja, who is endowed with six aspects;
she is the goddess known as Menā, established in the fourth station.
I bow to her who is named Śrīkujā, who dwells eternally at the end of the *liṅga*,
who is accompanied by the Bālakrama, and who is Ciñciṇī through the bliss of the vulva (*bhaga*).
I bow to the one named Śrī Kujā, who is Aghorā consisting of the vowels from *na* to *pha*;
formerly, the pure stone on Candradvīpa was worshipped by me.
I bow to her named Śrīkujā, who has emerged from seven births;
I bow to her named Śrīkujā, who is fierce, more fierce than the fierce, who relies upon non-fierce knowledge, who is eternally disciplined, and who abides in her own wheel.
The divine Rudra-śakti, possessing the luster of the rising sun, should always be worshipped in the form of the Command (ājñā), situated between the two Trikoṇas of birth.
I bow to her named Śrīkujā, who clearly bestows spiritual accomplishment; I bow to her named Śrīkujā,
even by the mere recitation of her names and sacred seats (pīṭhas).
She is constantly worshipped by the deities who are devoted to the practice of celibacy.
I bow to her known as Siddhayogeśvarī, the illustrious one called Kujā.
[From] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: [She is surrounded] by hosts of Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, and groups of Yoginīs.
I bow to the goddess known as Śrīkujā, who delights in instrumental music and dance; she is full,
formidable, fierce,
and she dwells in the state beyond the measurable.
"I bow to the sovereign goddess named Śrīkujā. Thus,

in the primordial descent (*ādyāvatāra*) of the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) measuring seventy million verses, emerged from the Path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters,
on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimala-ṣaṭka*), in the *Kādi* division.

In the *Ājñāpārameśvara*, the *Svāminīmata*, the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the tradition of the Mother (*avvākrama*), this is the bliss titled "The Chapter on the Empowerment of the Command of Śrīnātha. Śrīnātha said:
Furthermore, O Bhairavī, tell me that very descent of the sacred seats (pīṭha) as it occurs,
O Goddess, by which living beings are agitated.
The venerable Vakrā said: Regarding the sixth bliss—
that power which was previously called the *bhaga* and described as the perfected one (*siddhā*).
In some places, she entered a hermitage of mudrās together with the deities.
Having become silent, she entered the middle of the cave, absorbed in ascetic contemplation,
having assumed a dark form as a wandering mendicant through her ecstatic practice of celibacy.
The knower of Brahman constantly caused it to fly upward by means of his night-walking power;
thereupon, a great sound arose throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
By the power of divine knowledge, having attained a perfected form and being preeminent in strength,
she came through the air by means of her celibacy, sporting in the midst of the sky.
By entering both [the gates], the ritual of the seat (pīṭha) and the garden is performed;
there the Lord of Birds (Khageśa), having attained perfection, is capable of attracting the three worlds.
This is from the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Having reached the hermitage of the Goddess, he worships the sandals with devotion;
thus worshipped according to his desire, the Goddess is the supreme command of the Krama.
Prostrating with the eight-limbed salutation and with eyes full of tears, one should ask for forgiveness; thus, the divine command of the Lord of Siddhas will arise within the noble-born woman.
Then, having been saluted, Oḍīśa, the leader of the Siddhas,
a knower of the Kaula tradition who moves by night, departed as a perfected one into the midst of the trees.
Because it wanders from tree to tree like a *kadamba* flower, it is therefore called *kadambaka*;
because it has assumed the form of a lion, it is thus known as *saṃketasiṃhaka*.
Therefore, this Lion-knowledge bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
then the fifty Rudras, having become silent, assembled together.
The goddess Kubjikā, worshipped and praised by all the gods and others, being pleased, grants a boon: "Wander about as you please."

Having heard this, they were indeed satisfied and worshipped the Goddess with the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra-pūjā*); at that time, the attendants mentioned were Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣmīśa, and Trimūrtika. (From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*)
Likewise, Amarīśa, Arṣīśa, Bhārabhūti, and Atithīśvara.
Sthāṇu, Hara, Jhaṇṭīśa, and likewise Bhautika; Sadyojāta, Anugrahīśa, and after that Aṅkurīśa.
Mahāsena, Krodhīśa, Caṇḍīśa, Pracaṇḍarā, the one named Krūra, Ekarudra, Kūrma, and likewise Ekanetraka.
Caturmukha, Ajeśa, Śyena, Someśvara,
Lāṅguli, Dārukeśa, and likewise Ardhanārīśvara.
Likewise Umākānta, Āṣāḍī, Ḍiṇḍina, Dhātṛrudraka, as well as Mīna, Meṣa, and Lohita.
Likewise, there is Śikhivāhin, and another, Chagalaṇḍa;
and Dviraṇḍa, Mahākāla, Bālīśa, and Bhujaṅgama.
Pinākīśa, Khaḍga, Bakānanda, Śvetaka, Lakulin, Bhṛgudeveśa, and after that Saṃvartaka.
In this way, there are fifty Rudras who are always intent upon service,
as well as seven other deities who are the primary attendants of Sumūla.
All of them were obedient to her command and devoted to the worship of the Goddess's feet;
likewise, the trees are said to be three, as are the three types of creepers.
Kharara, Garara, and Rara were his female attendants;
Kubera was his mount, and Karbura was his attendant.
All those other Bhairavas themselves are obedient to his command;
they are the attendants of other goddesses and Gandharva women.
There is no counting the number of yogis, yoginīs, and vīras;
thus, through their sequential union, the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and pleasure groves (udyānas) are illustrated.
The Karavīra cremation ground is presided over by Karapuṣpa;
there is the wheel of the Rudras known by the name Kaṅkālabhairava.
Fierce, more fierce than the fiercest, intense, agitated by beasts of prey, and terrifying—
she constantly protects her devotees in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, yet in an instant she slays those who are bound in ignorance (paśus).
There, in that lineage, the guardian of the cremation ground is named Yogeśvara;
thus this sacred seat (pīṭha) is proclaimed, situated within three types [of divisions].
The mudrā that is established without support and for which no binding exists—
that mudrā is the bestower of liberation, conceived as being in the center of the sacred seat (pīṭha).
Manifested in the form of the moon, she is united with the Mother of the Seat (Pīṭhāmbā);
in that state, she becomes the Mistress of the Seat (Pīṭheśī), known by the name Khecarī.
There the goddess Khageśī is renowned as Kubjikā, and likewise the Siddha Uḍīśa; the others are her attendants.
Thus has been declared the means for attaining accomplishment, which has emerged from Oḍiyāna;
there the Goddess resides for three hundred divine years.
Filled with the bliss of Bhairava, she traveled through the sky on the path of Śiva;
twenty sages also arrived there in haste.
For the sake of acquiring the Command, those wise ones who were true devotees were initiated by Siddhanātha after twelve years had passed. They were initiated.
Kaśyapa, Mārkaṇḍa, Vasiṣṭha, Gotama, Māṇḍava, Śambhu, Saṃvarta, Āpastamba, and Parāśara.
Yājñavalkya, Vyāsa, Durvāsas, Āsurī, Hārīta, Nīlakaṇṭha, and Viśvāmitra the archer;
They know Ṛṣiśṛṅga, Śaktiputra, and Dakṣa as the twentieth;
this is the descent of the Jyeṣṭha-pīṭha, remembered as the first Oṃkāra.
Now I shall describe the second [site], situated to the south of the Lord;
it is located on that very northern path and is known by the name Vīrakṣetra.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
The goddess who is remembered as Khageśī by name, the affectionate one, resides in the syllable Oṃ;
she alone enters there in another form for the knower of yoga.
Cāmuṇḍā, in her red form, stands upon that bilva tree in the shade,
mounted in yoga and surrounded by seven maidens.
Thus, O beloved, having reached the stage of practice in the form of a youth,
the accomplished Bhairava entered upon the ground before the feet of the Goddess.
The divine mandala has been prepared as described in the Western Lineage;
the goddesses of the sacred seats have been worshipped, and one's own body is offered.
Having performed a prostration with joined palms and being filled with tears, one should ask for forgiveness;
then that goddess, being pleased, shall grant the auspicious sign of accomplishment.
"O Lord of Conduct, arise! Your command shines forth spontaneously. There, he who was faithful and pure in his vows became engaged in the conduct.
He who sees a pleasant place always sports there;
in this way, those fifty heroes, being terrified, arrived there.
Because they have ascended [to this path], those heroes are remembered on earth as "Vīras";
having entered the Vīra-path, they are entirely free from deficiency and are devoted to the worship of the Goddess's feet.
Worshipped by all those fifty heroic leaders,
they were all honored and praised individually within the field of heroes.
Satisfied, that heroine of heroes grants a boon to all:
"Freed from old age and death, wander as you please."
Delighting in service, all were intent on hearing his commands. [From] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Kamaṇḍalu, Naṭa, Dhūrta, Soma, Ṭaṅkaṭa, and Śūlin.
The shaven-headed bearer, the spark, the protection, the vigor honored by the gods,
the mirror, the churner of the immortals, the life-force, beautiful in every limb.
Śivottama, Mahārāva, Nandivīra, Kapardin, Someśvara, Śambhu, Ekanetra, and Vṛṣadhvaja.
Mātaṅga, Candranāga, Mohana, Kamaleśvara, Ḍambara,
Lohita, Dhūmra, Kāmada, and Ghoradaṃṣṭrin.
Saṃvara, Śarvara, Candra, Aṭṭahāsa, Kapīśvara,
Dīrghatanu, Mahārāva, Bhṛṅgirāva, and Vṛkodara.
Markaṭa, Lambakarṇa, Jīmūta who has the roar of a cloud,
Dāmodara, Karāla, and likewise Mahodadhi and Aneka.
By the power of the accomplishment of heroes, fifty heroes bestow success;
the prostitute, Muṇḍinī, and the fisherwoman—these three are the attendants.
Lolādevī, Vicitrā, and Bhābhūtī as the third—
these three, known as the group beginning with the courtesan, are established in the ritual service (parikarma).
There are three male attendants, each with his own distinct name:
Kallola, Kṛkara, and Kāmeśvara as the third.
Likewise, there is another, Siddhanātha, the lord and master of all;
and the remaining ones are declared to be the servants (kiṅkara) who stand at the gateway.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Thus, the Southern Seat has emerged from Oḍḍiyāṇa;
there is a cremation ground there, a terrifying grove named Lakuṭa.
The wheel of yoga is situated there, joined with divine yoginīs;
the guardian of the cremation ground is there, bearing a severed head and a skull-cup.
Like the edge of a razor, that intense and perilous sphere of the Kaulas may,
in a mere moment, kill those fools who merely bear the name.
One must never destroy trust in the auspicious seat of Jālandhara;
nor should one harbor pride there, even if it were Sadāśiva himself in person.
Such is the Jālandhara-pīṭha; there, the one renowned as Jālāvvā resides.
Karālā is established as the Mudrā, and Raktajā is the shadow of the pīṭha.
Furthermore, Rakta is accomplished by heroes and is worshipped by the best of gods;
the sacred seat (pīṭha) shall be known by the name Puṣpa, and its presiding deity is named Kumāra.
There, she is known as Śavarī because of her Śavara form;
she is also named Siddhayoginī, and she possesses great power through the accomplishment of conduct (caryāsiddhi).
The remaining others are attendants who follow in sequence along the paths of ritual action (kriyāmārga).
And the Supreme Goddess remained there for the duration of one hundred divine years.
Assuming many forms and exceedingly fierce, she leapt into the midst of the sky;
there, twelve sages arrived, seeking her command.
Initiated by Siddhanātha in years past,
those true devotees who have sacrificed their lives become recipients of accomplishment within the lineage.
Kapila, Vālmīki, Bhṛgu, Śrīvatsa, Bhṛṅgirāja, Ṛṣabha, Timira, Gālava, Sūryaraśmi,
Kumāra, Candramas, Jyotis, and Śakra as the twelfth.
Thus has been declared the descent at Dakṣapīṭha during the Tretā Yuga.
Emerging from Oḍiyāṇa is the second leader of the sacred seats (pīṭhanāyaka).
Now I shall speak of the third; listen to how it is. From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
In a certain region, there is a delightful place, the supreme treasure among lands,
located in the southern direction within the circle of the Deccan; and right there dwell the most excellent people, devoted and firm in their vows.
In this region, in Mahādeśa, there is indeed the hermitage of Bhairava.
Filled with the nectar of Bhairava, it shines in the center of the mountain;
the Lord, who awakens one to the stainless reality, is established there as before.
There, fifty Bhairavas sport again and again;
having arrived at the Mahāyāna, they sport, being intent on devotion.
Filled with nectar by the gaze of the full moon, Śavarī assumed a divine form.
And she is called Samarī because of the equality of all beings;
having become a full moon in its digits, she has arisen from the netherworld (pātāla).
Yellow in color, richly endowed with great beauty, and adorned with divine garlands; there,
in that hermitage of Kumārikākhaṇḍa, she fixed her mind steadily and established unwavering contemplation.
By that, the immovable *akṣaciñciṇī* of Bhairava is declared;
thus the supreme latent impression (*vāsanā*) stands as the one named *samarikā*.
The seventh is endowed with the seven born of noble lineage, while the eighth is of the nature of Śiva;
having understood this, that perfected one, whose body is yellow, entered.
Having become one whose form was invisible, he went down to the ground at the tips of his feet out of devotion to the mandala, as prescribed in the Kula scripture.
The worship was performed as prescribed in the western house of the Yoginīs,
while Rativigraha praised him with various prostrations.
She floats up again and again in the form of the surging power;
by performing prostrations with the staff-like arms, Bhairavī was thus gratified by him.
"Being satisfied, they grant their command: 'Go yourself to the Vīracakra;
O Lord of the Gods, fetch the great *mahāphalgu* from the Vīracakra.
Having heard this, the Siddha went there and disappeared somewhere within it.
He entered the circle of heroes (vīracakra), indeed into the midst of the earth-dwelling women (bhūcarīs).
One who seeks food remains there for five days and nights;
then, those stationed within report that he is seeking food.
That wheel was agitated, and a great agitation arose within him;
impelled by those stationed on the wheel, the Siddha churned it and produced the [elixir] in the vessel.
Thrust from the center of the dispersion and well-sealed by the space-mudrā,
it remains within the vessel for as long as five nights.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
By the power of the Goddess’s command, having burst open the jar, he emerges in an instant; he remains there and then takes the sacrificial meat.
That wheel was terrified by him; having employed a stratagem, he himself departed.
Upon reaching the site of the Goddess’s hermitage, he prostrated at her lotus feet.
Seeing that Bhairavānanda, the joyful Bhairavī says:
"O Lord of the Gods, a second substance has been brought from the circle of yogis."
Having heard that a great service had been performed for those engaged in the yoga of the three principles (*tritattva*),
he became joyful in mind and addressed the circle of yogis.
At your command, I went to the assembly of the circle of sky-farers;
having entered that circle, I made a request to one who was seeking meat.
Having heard this, those of great strength, who were agitated and stationed upon the wheel,
churned me and then threw me into the interior of a jar of wine.
Having remained for five nights within the center of the jar of distraction,
one then [proceeds] solely by the power of the command through the recollection of the feet and the tips of the toes of the Goddess.
Having shattered that jar, I emerged by means of a stratagem;
having heard this, she was then pleased and again gave me an auspicious command.
The great jewel named Mahādeva, the great guru, was given;
there, attendants stood present, endowed with the contemplation of yoga.
Fifty Bhairavas gathered there at Pūrṇagiri;
therefore, that is the field of Bhairava, which bestows the siddhis of the Bhairavīs.
They all arrived there, intent on worshipping the feet of the Goddess with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra) accompanied by wine and meat, according to the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
She was worshipped by the goddess of the sacred seat (pīṭhadevī) with manifold hymns and praises;
[the lords of the cremation grounds were] Asitāṅga, Sitāṅga, Kāpālī, and Bhṛkuṭīkṛta.
They know Krodha, as well as Unmatta, Karāla, Bhīṣaṇa, Maheśvara, Mahākāya, Aṭṭahāsa, and Tumburu.
Mahākāya, Nṛsiṃha, Vijaya, Paśupati, Khaṭvāṅgin, Ḍāmara, Ṭaṅka, Caṇḍīśa, and Pracaṇḍavān.
Muṇḍadhārī, Śiva, Śambhu, Uḍḍāma, Ḍāmara,
Ardhanārī, Vṛddhaśukra, Kāla, Caṇḍa, and Kuleśvara.
Long-lipped, gurgling, and terrible, with the fierce form of Kāladaṃṣṭra,
possessing a fearsome nose, a vajra-body, the Lord of the Kaulas, whose banner is the bull.
Bhṛgu is the wielder of the trident, intent and fierce, tawny-hued, wearing red garments, and radiant throughout the three worlds; thus there are fifty Bhairavas.

"These [mantras] have been taught in due order; when remembered, they always bestow accomplishment. One should pronounce all of them preceded by 'Śrī', and they should be worshipped with great effort."
All those who are obedient to the command and worship the lotus feet of the Goddess are to be known as her attendants, O Pūrṇagiri of great fame.
Likewise, O Śambhu, the three beginning with Khaṭṭikī are remembered as the Kuladevis;
these three, in their service, are likewise known by the name Trika.
Vijayā, Damanā, and Mahimā as the third;
these are indeed the three types of *khaṭṭikī* and so forth, namely the *cellakas*.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the wise know three designations;
they have been thus declared.
For these are known as attendants for the service of others— attendants upon the women of the gods and gandharvas;
their number is beyond reckoning at the edge of the mandala, O fair-faced one.
Vikrama and Ḍobika are immediately [manifest] as the very form of the Goddess; thus Pūrṇapīṭha is proclaimed.
Pūrṇāvvā is to be known as the manifest (prakaṭā); now hear of the secret seat (guptapīṭha).
The sacred seat named Khecara is the abode of the goddess Śavarī;
its mother is Maṅgalāvvā, and the sixth deity is the Lord himself.
Furthermore, the lotus mudrā there is declared to be the seat of meditation;
likewise, I shall describe to you the Bhairava seat, which is the cremation ground.
Known by the name Uḍḍāmara, it is both fearful and fearless for yoginīs; established there according to the observance (*samaya*), it is a division of the Kaula on this earth.
By that [means], the most difficult and fierce time established there becomes a vessel for the accomplishments of heroes and an awakener of the knowledge of yoga.
He grants success to yogins, but never to others;
there he is the guardian of the cremation ground, known by the name Vikṛtānana.
And thus, having remained for one hundred and fifty divine years seated upon the southern lion-throne at the northern seat (uttarapīṭha), she departed into the sky.

And likewise Varuṇa, Agastya, Vṛddhaśukra, and Janārdana.
Yama, Nārada, Ketu, and Rāhu—
these five were born as the incarnations of Pūrṇapīṭha in the Dvāpara Yuga.
The third leader of the sacred seats has emerged from Jālandhara;
I shall now fully describe the fourth incarnation as it occurred.
At the edge of the continent, there exists a great and divine place called Siddhāśrama;
it is a certain region that is exceedingly beautiful, celestial, and most enchanting.
The presence of the Yoginīs is found there in every house;
this scripture is the covenant of all beings,
and there Kāmeśvarī resides in Kāmarūpa in the form of Bhaga.
The doctrine of Śrī Kujā.
But the fifty who have attained perfection in the *rasas* are completely absorbed in the play of desire and longing.
Therefore, Śavarī of firm youth is said to have attained perfection at Siddhāśrama;
she herself conquers on the ground to the north of a deserted temple.
Accompanied by the seven Mothers, the eighth deity there is the goddess [Kālarātri].
O Three-eyed One, one should constantly wander in the temple of the god; therefore, that tree is known as the Kadamba in Kāmarūpaka. [From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa]
And the Blessed One is capable of assuming any form at will; he is great, wearing a white form.
Mitradeva: He is self-perfected and the bestower of curses and favors;
out of devotion to his master, he takes an incarnation there.
Having prostrated before the lotus-like sandals, he entered the house of the Yoginī;
from the mere remembrance of the tips of the Goddess’s feet, he let out a cry of joy—
yes, from the mere remembrance of the tips of her feet!
One should establish the divine maṇḍala as prescribed in one's own lineage;
with great cintāmaṇi flowers, there is the auspicious liquor kadambarī.
Śāvarī, by whom the moving and unmoving universe was created, was worshipped by the Siddhas;
she emerged as a divine meteor from the mouth of Siddhanātha in the west.
Having thus offered his family lineage, his knowledge, his vital breath, and his very self,
he should perform a hundred circumambulations and prostrate with the eight limbs.
Śavarī, being pleased with him, grants him abundant commands.
O Lord of Mitra, speak! Arise, O savior of the world!
Reflect upon this according to your capacity in Kāmarūpa during the Kali age:
"In the Kula teaching, you alone are the agent of creation and destruction."
"The perfection of the pill has been granted to you; wander at your pleasure.
Having worshipped and paid homage, all who had gathered there departed.
Then, becoming joyful in mind, the goddess spoke these words:
"O one of great renown, whatever pill or other [substance] has been acquired by you shall all become fruitful through my grace."
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Having thus obtained the boon, they remained stationed right there within.
All fifty attendants are remembered as being obedient to the command;
the yogi [attains] the stainless Akula, bliss, and the Lord of the Lotus.
Bahula, Pulina, Bhūti, Madana, Kaṅkarāṭ,
Śiśu, Kumuda, Capala, Śyāma, Tamāla, Gada, and Koṅkaṇa.
Kaulīśa, Kamala, Kāntida, Damatha, Aṭavīmukha, Amṛta, Kumbhakeśa, and Ghughura, who bears the name Kāla.
Amogha, Sundara, Saṃvarta, the Lord Avyaya,
Kadhiśa, Nayanam, Kānti, Ākāśa, and Parama-Śaśi.
They know Kaubera, Kulavāgīśa, Kubera, and Viraja;
likewise Nityānanda, Śveta, Yogeśvara, and Gaṇeśvara.
Someśvara is the support of the Kula; Nakta is Dhūrjaṭi by number.
Thus, there are fifty Siddhas in the sequence beginning with Mātṛkā.
O Lord, the Siddhā Rasakṛṣā is stationed in the assembly pavilion, and likewise the seven attendants are established in that very place;
three are designated as being outside: Śilpinī and the pair of Cakriṇīs.
And Mātaṅginī is the third; these are her attendants.
Their secret designations, as they are declared in the scripture,
are Sunandinī, Bhadrā, and the third is the goddess Chiñchā.
The *cellakas* and attendants belong to the family of Vajradhara, O Tāra; those who are remembered there as attendants, O Bhairava, belong to the *kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
Thus, by the power of the command of the fierce Goddess, Siddhāśrama became known as the sacred seat (pīṭha) named Kāmarūpaka.
When the deity is in the state of desire, that is called Kāmarūpa;
in that [state], the color should be white, and the leader [Nāyakī] is in white form.
Through the state of union of both, the young girl is the deity of the sacred seat (pīṭha);
one should know that at the front of the vulva (bhaga) is this Kāmarūpa seat.
I shall declare the secret pair joined for the sake of desire.
O lady of excellent hips, on the Ucchuṣma-pīṭha there is a Śāvarī by name; that goddess Koṅkaṇā has emerged from Koṅkaṇa.
And thus you have become a perfected one (siddha) known by the name Mitradeva.
One should understand the *yonimudrā* in the circle of the Mothers at the tip of the womb; right there, situated on the inner path, is the cremation ground with its forest entrance,
where the leader known as Śaṅkhapāla resides like the Lord of Death.
Rākṣasas as well as the leaders of the sky attend upon him.
At night, when the lamp is lit, the host of yoginīs plays;
there stands the wheel of Yama, the assembly of yoginīs and heroes.
Then, on a fierce day and under an auspicious constellation, there occurs a union;
in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa region, this is the Kulakaula, the meeting of the Yoginīs and the Heroes.
Siddhanātha, the great lord, remained there in invisibility;
thus is that foremost seat (agrapīṭha), accompanied by the goddess of the seat.
Abiding in a divine form and delighting in the pleasures of sensual enjoyment,
she gave the seat (*pīṭha*) to the Siddha and departed by way of the *khecarī* path.
Then, many born of the lineage of the Siddhas were initiated there:
Citrasena, Nāsika, Śuka, and Trailokyapālaka.
Kapālī, Ḍāmara, Vighneśa, and Kālapāśaka—
these eight are remembered as the Ṛṣis who have been initiated as the leaders of the Siddhas.
This descent to Kāmarūpa has occurred in the Kali age;
it has emerged from Pūrṇapīṭha and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus, he who knows the fourfold tradition of the sacred seats (pīṭha-āmnāya) beginning from the Kṛta Age is indeed one who possesses the tradition; otherwise, he is merely a bearer of the name.
At the end of that Kali age, in the illustrious region of Kāmākhyā,
in that eastern Siddhāśrama within the forest, there is the place known as Tisra.
In the midst of the three river currents, that place where Vighneśa and Kṣetrapālaka reside as deities is indicated as the Tisrapīṭha.
In a world devoid of devotion and full of deceit, the Command becomes weak;
this occurs at the edge of the island in the northern region and within the worlds of Trikūṭa. —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Māyā, in the form of a Mātaṅgī, from among the three streams,
reached the place of the three rivers and arrived at the Yakṣa cave.
Having made his descent there, he established the seat known as Tisra,
which was concealed from the world of mortals.
O God, the previous body was created;
then, O God, the fifth [body] becomes manifest at the increase of the digits (kalā).
Starting from that point, it proceeds in succession; from there, the Saṃvartaka [wind] arises.
Having attained the cessation of further command from the world of mortals,
I have previously performed spiritual practice together with you.
And you, O Lord of Mataṅgī, having been born there in the final age,
though born from the lineage of the lowest castes, are nevertheless worthy of progeny.

Again, taking up the sequence of the stations (*sthiti-krama*), O God, the *ughā* has emerged from the Tisra-pīṭha; it is the mandala of the sequence of the oil-presser woman (*tailikā*) in the house of the Guru.
That shall become manifest, immediate knowledge arises;
thus there shall be the peerless great presence within the lineage of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
In that age, O tree, you indeed [resided] in the cave of Akula;
this is the final seat of the age, the fifth leader of the seats.
When the fourth age, the Kali Yuga, has arrived, and the northern region is under the rule of barbarians,
while other teachers and disciples have fallen under the sway of greed and delusion.
When the penetration of my command has faded and authority has come to an end, when the violation of the samaya occurs and the guru’s command is transgressed,
I shall again bring about creation through a fifth incarnation.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
within the great sacred seat (pīṭha) called Tisra, which is surrounded by all other sacred seats.
Since it is superior to all, terrible, and brings about immediate restraint,
the stability of the current of the transmission (*kramaugha*) arises once again from that fifth sacred seat (*pīṭha*).
And that twenty-eighth division shall be honored;

Kucandra and Pīṭhasiddha, as well as the Mother Vakrikā herself;

From striking it, the *tāḍī* tree will then become ablaze;

Beginning from Tisrapīṭha, the performance of worship proceeds.

There is no doubt that [these] will exist in Tisra, the leader of the *pīṭhas*,

The leader named Ghora, together with the Siddhas, is worshipped by the immortals;
the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Ardhacandrottara has emerged from the top of the vulva.

Residing there is the supreme Kālī, who illuminates divine knowledge; she is the lineage of the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the tradition of the transmission, and the pure wisdom considered authoritative in the scriptures.
O Lord, you will manifest in the future during the latter half of the Kali age; of this there is no doubt.
O handsome one, this descent of the sacred seats has thus been told to you.
And the future is discerned as the fifth, Tisrapīṭha;

Kaumāra is at Pūrṇapīṭha, while Vṛddhaka is at Oḍiyāṇa;
having thus understood this sequence of the pīṭhas as it has come down through the lineage of oral tradition.
But he who constantly worships [it] is Bhairava himself in person;
whether he be a teacher or even a practitioner, he indeed wanders through the sacred seats (pīṭhas).
He is liberated, he is Śiva manifest, the possessor of the sacred tradition, the supreme teacher;
[he is freed from] even a thousand killings of Brahmins and ten million killings of cows.
All innumerable sins are destroyed by serving the sacred seats (pīṭha);
therefore, one should indeed always and constantly worship the four sacred seats.
His wish shall become an accomplishment, and he shall become beloved by the Yoginīs;
he should address all those preceded by "Śrī" who are established at the end of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
Having obtained a boon from them, he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
yet, the hero who enters Oḍḍiyāna and acts with pride [shall suffer].
He shall live for only one month in poverty and death;
he who is arrogant and deluded in soul shall do so in Jālandhara within the Kumārikā-khaṇḍa.
A thief will strike him, or a river, or a terrible disease;
his life lasts but six months, and he dies along with his kinsmen.
Alternatively, he who at the Pūrṇapīṭha cultivates egoism and harbors hatred toward others;
It perishes by fire or burning.
Alternatively, one dies in a battle involving poison in the fifth month;
or one withers away with one's own body and dies within a fortnight.
O fortunate one, having become arrogant, that guru shall go to hell;
for someone, sitting comfortably in Kāmarūpa, will surely act with pride.
The blow of a hammer unseen falls upon his head;
through discipline comes worldly enjoyment, and through discipline liberation shall arise.
Therefore, this Vinayakaula should practice discipline;
otherwise, he shall have no enjoyment in this world, nor will it exist for him in the next.
Therefore, one should not harbor pride nor practice hatred.
One should perform the *vīrabhojya* feast during the fourfold cycle of *O*, *JĀ*, *PŪ*, and *KĀ*.
Having performed worship according to one's ability, one should then worship those born of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*).
The practitioner attains accomplishment both in this world and in the next.
The Rudras, Bhairavas, Vīras, and Siddhas are to be worshipped in the fourfold [arrangement];
this descent of the four seats (catuṣpīṭha) has been determined for the four ages. Indeed, he who wanders according to truth shall be a teacher within the Kula.
Three measures in size, resembling light, it is situated in the center of the mandala of fire.
I praise the Great Festival of the Glorious Garden (Śrī Udyānamaha), which sets in motion the command of the Kaulas;
it is the supreme, intense [syllable] of two morae, situated in the right corner. —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
I pay homage to the great one named Śrījāla, the restrainer of the net of māyā,
who is the singular, supreme, and subtle, bestowing the attainment of supreme knowledge.
I bow to the one named Pūrṇa, situated in the left corner, difficult for even the gods to attain,
consisting of half a mora, exceedingly subtle, and having the nature of supreme bliss.
I bow to that divine one named Śrīkāma, who stands before him,
situated within the city of Śrīcandradvīpa, and who flows forth through three streams.
"I bow to the one who has reached the end of the twelve and who sets in motion the command of the Kaula.
Having spoken thus, the Goddess quickly departed for the pilgrimage seats (*pīṭhas*).
In Kāmarūpa, Vārāṇasī, Nepāla, Pūrṇavardhana,
Purastīra, Kanyākubja, Pūrṇagiri, Āmrātakeśvara, Ekāmra, Trisrotas, and Kāmakoṭṭaka;
Likewise,
[it is found] on Kailāsa, in Bhṛgunagara, at Kedāra, and in Candrapuraka.
In the Śrīpīṭha, in Ekoṇa, in Śrījālandhara and Mālava,
in Kulūtā, Devikoṭa, Gokarṇa, and Marukeśvara.
At Aṭṭahāsa, at Viraja, at Rājagṛha on the great highway,
at Elāpura, at Kollagiri, at Sopāra, and at Jayantikā.
In Ujjayinī and Caritra, Kṣīrikā in Hastināpura,
Odukeśa, and the seat named Prayāga, as well as Māyāpurī;
On Mount Uras, on Malaya, and likewise on Bheruṇḍaka;
on Māhendra, Vāruṇa, and indeed on Hiraṇyapura.
Then Mahālakṣmī went there with her parasol of shade;
wherever the goddess went and wherever she looked, [there she remained].
There, O Mother of the Kula, having established the clusters of pilgrimage sites and divine shrines within the land of Bhārata, you have made your own fame known, O Mother of the Kula.
By him was created the Kaumārikākhaṇḍa, meritorious and purifying;
as it was said by the god Pūrvasantāna: "Go to Bhārata."
From that time forth, O Lord of Gods, a union was established here between both;
that which was performed by the Goddess was the awakening to the bliss of the Command (ājñānanda).
She returned there again, following her former form;
the god too was a disciple in his previous lineage, honored by the best of the gods.
Having performed [this] for the illustrious Oḍḍu Maheśāna, she shall then grant the command:
"From this time forward, [bestow] grace upon the land of Bhārata."
"Beginning from the city of Uḍupīṭha, perform the manifold creation," and so forth—

in the primordial descent (*ādyāvatāra*) of the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) measuring seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters,
on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimala-ṣaṭka*), in the *Kādi* division, in the Supreme Command of the Lord.
In the Svāminīmata, spoken in the tradition of the Mother (Avvākrama) as part of the venerable Caturviṃśatsahasrasaṃhitā,
this is the bliss named "The Pervasion of the Seat of the Command of the Venerable Lord."
The seventh bliss, Śrīnātha, said:
"What is this Western House (paścima-veśma), and what indeed is its authority?"
How is the seal of the divine body, and likewise the lineage transmission?
What is the root language, and likewise what is the family lineage (kulāgama)?
O Vakri, tell me everything that has been known through my instruction.
The venerable Vakrā said: I shall proclaim the compendium of the Bhairava division known as Manthāna,
the Kādibheda, the Sahasrajyeṣṭha-Kaulika.
O Śrīnātha, I shall proclaim to you the scripture of the Command (*ājñāśāstra*), the *Kramodaya*, which has been mastered through the lineage of Vakrikā and emerged from the path of Meru.
When the fourth age arrived,
that which was brought down from the original seat was indeed brought down into the western house during the Kali Yuga.
Its instruction for extraction, however, is the Kaulika tradition;
it is joined with the vowels and consonants and empowered by the mantra of universal withdrawal.
Above that is Bhairava together with Bhairavī, and above that is the Kulakrama,
which exists in twenty-seven divisions according to its various distinctions.
This "House" is the descent facing west, which is supreme;
its further instruction is the Lion descent.
Sixteen, and again sixteen, and another sixteen; thus, from the conjunction of these three groups, there are indeed twelve verses in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
First is Gajendra by name, and the sixfold Vidyākūṭa;
that is its color, that is the space of Śiva, that is its liṅga, and that is Śiva himself.
Then that seed-syllable of Āpa, as well as the self of the Goddess,
is said to consist of eight parts and twelve verses.

By the will of Candra, Sūrya, and Śiva, having performed the addition and subtraction of the phonemes through their mutual conjunction, this constitutes the enclosure of the field (*kṣetraparigraha*).
The sixteen rays, consisting of the kalās beginning with Amṛtā and ending with Visarga, form that horizontal line; the deity Vāmadeva is said to reside at its end.
Unnata, Raudrī, and the others ending with Thasāntā follow in sequence;
Jyeṣṭhā, Vāmā, and Raudrī correspond to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Because of the unification of these three, that place is the abode of the Yoginīs;
and those who live upon the nectar and other [substances] within the circle of the womb are the Liṅgas.
One should place the Siddhas and the Yoginīs one above the other;
the first line is the Mistress of the Wheel of Vowels, and the second extends from Ka to Ta.
The third [line] consists of three lines beginning with *thā* and ending with *disā*; it is the Mistress of the Gods (*sureśvarī*).
Regarding those fifty Siddhayoginīs mentioned here, I shall now speak of them.
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa: Ānanda, Vimala, Ciñci, Mitra, Moḍīśa, Caryaka,
the sixth deity, as well as Tūṣṇī, Kadamba, and he known by the name Maunī.
Advaita, Siṃhanātha, as well as Kandarpī, Krāḍaka, Varada, Kaulīśa, Garuḍa, Piṅgala, and Khaga.
The Pañcaka, the Kallola, and likewise the Khecara;
the Candragarbha, the Gajendra, the Kuṇḍala, and the Candrapuryaka.
And Śaṅkhanātha, Śavara, Vīradeva, and Vikrama; Pippalīśa, Pulinda, Goṣṭhīśa, and likewise Kamala.
Gajakarṇa, Mahendra, the one named Tārā, Varcakeśaka,
Akhaṇḍa, Kuraṅga, and likewise Vaiphala.
Ājñānātha, the one called Viśuddha, likewise Anāhata, Maṇipūrṇa, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Avatāra, and Kumāraka.
Śilāśekharanātha and Krūra after that;
thus, forty-eight [deities] are to be known as the retinue of the Siddhas.
Having explained the awakening of the verses according to the sequence of the *Gṛhasiddha*,
I shall hereafter explain that of the *Gṛhadevī* in due order.
Śarvarī, Śavarī, Śāvarī, and Pulindikā;
Klinnā, the goddess Kāmeśvarī, Śākinī, and Bhūtaḍāmarī.
Koṭarī, Śaṅkhinī, Kiṅkiṇī, Karaṅkiṇī,
Avvādevī, Samāyā, Suṣirā, and Ratnasundarī.
Raktākṣī, Agnijihvā, Ucchuṣmā, Nārājīvikā, Ambikā, Lambikā, and likewise Kadambinī.
Bhadrakālī, Siddhā, Śuṣkā, and Aparājitā; Ghorā, Aghorā, Thaghorā, and Bhagānanā.
Nandinī, Mālinī, Saṃhārī, and likewise Kapilā;
Vivvā, Vidyutpatākā, and likewise Kāpālinī.
Mahāmāyā, Peppiyī, Cchommā, Yogamāyikā; [from] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Kālikā, Mīna, Meṣā, and the supreme Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī.
Śivādūtī and Vicitrā are to be known as the goddesses in their respective order;
this is the assembly of the wives of the Siddhas, the pure retinue of the Goddess.
Just as there are castes, so too are there Siddhas in the maṇḍala of the divine womb;
this sequence of the Siddhas has indeed been illustrated at the beginning of the collection of verses.
Having first performed five *praṇavas* extending from the beginning to the end of the *āvāpa*,
O Lord, one should worship the western chamber according to this procedure.
Śiva: O fair-faced Maitreya, within the house are these two, Ha and Kṣa;
the illustrious one is named Kucandra, and the goddess is Kubjikā.
These two should be joined simultaneously in the pentad situated in the peak-abode (kūṭaveśman):
with the five at the beginning, with the five at the end, and with the Vidyā in between them.
And that command is the realization in the world, the great savior of the three realms;
whoever she gazes upon, even he goes to the supreme state.
"O God, when others have attained that state, they will then certainly obtain perfection.
Thus, the oral tradition of the Āśrama has been proclaimed in three divisions:
the sixteen Siddhas of the Upper Command (ūrdhva-ṣoḍaśa-siddhājñā) and the sixteen Siddhas in the North (uttare).
In the south there are sixteen, and Śiva is the deity in the center.
Seated within the *bhaga*, having pierced the womb, one should proceed to the supreme;
resting between the *svādhiṣṭhāna* and the *pūraka*, she has a horizontal form.
Such is the command of the Krama-cakra; the Brahma-knot is downward-facing.
The Unmanā energy, the power of Kaulinī, effects the supreme possession.
Above that is the wheel, which forms a semi-circular mandala;
within its interior is the Kadamba tree, the Kuṇḍagolaka of the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Within that, there is a subtle wick of the Command (ājñā) shaped like a plow;
it has entered the end of the vulva (bhaga), and the Command, resting there, faces downward.
That supreme Vakrikā is formidable; once she is known, piercing proceeds, resulting in shaking, possession, trembling, and horizontal, upward, and downward movements in an instant.
Or, by the mere recollection of the command, there is entry into Pātāla; thus,
the fifty Rudras beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha have been extracted from their cities.
The twelve verses of Meru are established within the half-circle;
in its center is the wheel of emanation (sṛṣṭicakra), from which the goddesses of the path have emerged.
O Maheśvara, I shall establish your authority;
together with you, Sadyojāta is located in the west among the seats beginning with the Yoga-pīṭha.
This city of Siddhālayapura, however, is the abode of the house of Yonimudrā;
this city is proclaimed to be differentiated by twelve verses.
There, in the center, the Vidyā has entered, formed into two groups of five;
O Kuleśvara, this is the path of the Goddess on the path of the Full Moon sequence.
I, who am turned face downwards, rest there in the primordial seat (ādyapīṭha) and exercises authority by revolving in a counter-clockwise direction.
And when the end of the ring finger (anāmā) is fully perfected, there is the attainment of the Command (ājñāsiddhi) in the Kula lineage;
[the letters] beginning with *bha* and ending with *ca* have spread downwards and upwards.
Then the knowledge of form shines forth, having the appearance of the flame of a spear-lamp; it is the light of the digit of the moon, garlanded by the lap of the crescent moon.
This moon of the full office has emerged from the center of Śiva.
Thus, these twelve verses of the Kumārikākhaṇḍa constitute that very deity of the Krama.
O Śambhu, O Mahādeva, through their union, the Kaulika [teaching], which is more excellent in its qualities, emerged in due order from the Meru-path of the lineage.
The city is said to be the support of power, and the city is the enclosure of the field. Within it resides the Goddess; I am Kubjikā, and she is the Moon.
She is the Liṅga, the support of the Kula, while Ciñciṇī is the authority.
Through the application of the field, the liṅga, and the hermitage, the house becomes Candrapura.
Starting from Candrapūrṇagṛha, the succession of the lineage will become manifest in the world of mortals through its descent in the Kali age.
In the mortal realm, the Uḷisiddha hermitage has emerged from Candrapurī;
there, the syllable *o* and the letter *ṣ*, as well as you who are named Mitra [reside].
That knowledge, which was sealed within them, was declared at the seat of Uḍa;
it was then brought down by nine disciples in Puṇḍravardhana.
There shall be authority by means of three [siddhas] in Koṅkaṇa and Pūrṇagiri;
by three siddhas in Pātāla, and again by three in Candrapūrṇapura in the intermediate space (antarikṣa). Therein is a tree named Ciñciṇī.
O Protector, that was broken by you; therefore, you are remembered as Ciñciṇī.
In that city of Candrapuryaka, there was one renowned as Kīrtideva;
he should bestow grace upon those sixteen sons of the Siddhas who reside there.
The lineage of their gurus is well-known in its successive order,
beginning with Unmanā and continuing down to the venerable Nātha Ciñciṇī.
O Śambhu, without knowing the Flower Convention (puṣpasaṃketaka), one does not possess liberation.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the lineage of gurus (gurvogha) beginning with Unmanā and ending with Ādinātha is designated as the "Flower."
In the Kali age, however, in Koṅkaṇa, that [tradition] was divided threefold starting from the Nātha;
there is no initiation, nor supreme state, nor indeed the sequence of the lineage, for there is no traversing of the Krama in that which is devoid of the convention of flowers.
Just as grain does not sprout in a field from which the seed has been discarded,
liberation is not found in those who lack the convention of the flower. The Primordial Lord, absorbed in the three, is renowned as Vṛkṣanātha.

To you, during the present Kali Yuga, nine sons were born in the mortal realm of Koṅkaṇa: three below and three above. Of these, six have passed away without lineage, while three remain with their lineages in Koṅkaṇa.
Their designations are found in the oral tradition within the Śrīdeśa, the maṇḍala of lineages.
Gagana, Kumuda, Padma, Deva, Bhairava, Kamala, Śivarāma, Kṛṣṇānanda, and Trilocana.
Thus they were born in succession, each individually by means of a convention:
the second, the fourth, and the fifth; and three below.
The seventh, eighth, and ninth—these three go upwards in succession;
they were all formerly sky-farers (*khecarāḥ*) by the power of the divine command (*divyājñā*).
Those who have gone to the netherworld (*pātāla*) are three [others], and yet others enjoy worldly pleasures (*bhoga*).
Three [stages] are established in authority: the first and the third.
The sixth [category], consisting of the nature of the Command (ājñā), is established in the sequence of authority.
From them, a lineage has arisen here among men, numbering sixteen. *The Kumārikākhaṇḍa:* 16.24–25ab.
I shall state their names by means of the convention of worship:
Sūra, Tīvra, Khecara, Garbhamukta, and Siṃhaka.
Then there are Jaya, Vijayamitra, Vīra, the fivefold Vimala, Ratnakeśava, Unmatta, and the stream of Mudrās.
Thus, these sixteen shall become perfected ones in the Kali age,
O observer of noble vows, excluding the fifth from the two groups of four mentioned previously.
The sons of Gadeva are to be known as the Jyeṣṭha-oligās;
however, the fifth son of Padeva is recorded among the Madhyama-oligās.
Those from the ninth up to the sixteenth should be known as the *bāla-olikā*;
they are to be known as the sons of Kadeva; thus are those sixteen Siddhas.
In the Kali age, first there will be the lineage of Parā, second the lineage of Vakrikā,
and after that, the lineage of Siddhā.
In the eldest [lineage] there will be fifty-two, and in the middle, twenty-seven.
In the lineage of the child, they will number eighty-four.
O Maheśvara, their lineage of perfected ones shall indeed be innumerable,
and their command shall be most fierce.
I shall now describe the nine and sixteen places of worship:
in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the first is between the eyebrows, and the second is in the foundation-mandala (ādhāramaṇḍala).
The third is in Maṇipūra, while the fourth and fifth are likewise;
having worshipped them again in Ādhāra, the sixth is indeed located in Svādhiṣṭhāna.
O God, one should worship the seventh, eighth, and ninth [deities] in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta).
Such is the sequence of worship for the bodies of those nine Siddhas.
O Mahādeva, hear now the determination of the locations for the sixteen:
eight are on the garland of skulls, the ninth is in the circle of the navel, and from the tenth up to the sixteenth, one should worship them on the garland of *bhagas*.
Their lineage has arisen within the cycle of existence on the path of the Kali age, up to the eleventh station; here, in this sequence, is the purity of the lineages,
for this is the succession of the tradition and likewise the transmission from teacher to disciple.

O Lord of the Clan, in the Kali age there will be nothing remaining [of the lineage]. He who worships the flood of his own clan’s gurus without seed (nirbīja) remains further in saṃsāra; he does not turn back from saṃsāra.
He who worships Śrīnātha without Vṛkṣanātha remains further in saṃsāra and does not turn back from it;
this has been told to you in the maṇḍala of the Mother of the Three Ols.
There is no unexplained matter here; the definitive conclusion has been declared in this compendium (*saṃhitā*).
Sixteen sons of the Siddhas were born from the wombs of Mitra; this is the first, the Jyeṣṭha-lineage, in brief, according to the division of the transmission (*krama*).
It is proclaimed to be in the center of the city; beginning from there, one performs the sequential worship.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
the second is Madhyamolī, located in the southern and northern corners;
the third is Bālolī, situated in the eastern corner, following that sequence.
Therein, that mudrā is described as the lineage-command within the wombs;
Oṣa, Mitrā, and the Siddhas are proclaimed to exist within the three lineages (oli).
O Lord, he who speaks otherwise regarding the lunar-city hermitage,
as well as the three lineages and the determination of the twelve verses, [is at fault].
O Lord of Gods, he who does not know the Yoga-pīṭha, the three Siddhas, the Krama, the Vidyā, and the Maṇḍala, shall not be worthy of worship.
He is not a disciple in the Kula or Kaula; he has no authority in this scripture.
This, however, is the "Sutra of the Promise" from the Sūtra of Candrapurya.
First, in this Kula scripture, and subsequently its very sequel,
there are the primary mudrās with their three divisions, as well as twelve verses.
Likewise, there are the goddesses who are household-siddhas, and the Vidyā-devī Pūrṇimā; the three persons who are lineage-siddhas, and the sixteen siddhas themselves.

"O God, having first known them, one should thereafter proclaim the sequence. Thus, in the primordial descent of the Great Manthānabhairava Sacrifice, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding a hundred thousand quarters, descended into the primary seat along the path of the Seat of Knowledge (Vidyāpīṭha), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (Vimala-Ṣaṭka), in the *Kā* division.
In the *Ājñāpārameśvarī*, the *Svāminīmata*, consisting of twenty-four thousand verses as spoken in the *Avvākrama*, within the description of the section on the illustrious *Candrapura*,
this is the bliss named *Kramodaya*.
Oṃ, may there be well-being!
Salutation to the sandals of Śrīnātha. Salutation to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
In the *Manthānabhairavatantra*, within the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*, Śrīnātha said:
O Goddess, you are my perfection, O Mistress, O Ādinātha born of the *akula* lineage!
Speak the instruction of knowledge which is the essence within the Western Tradition.
O Kaulīśā, reveal the eighth bliss, the supreme Meru-prastāra,
by the mere knowledge of which the path of Vidyā proceeds.
The illustrious Kubjikā said:
"Meru is established both externally and internally, in its gross and subtle forms;
the subtle form is the wheel of deities, while the gross form is the assumption of phonemes."
That which is both supreme and non-supreme, infinite, all-pervading, and situated within the cause— from that, the power of Will emerged as the goddess Vakrā, indeed facing downwards.
Having previously learned from the mouth of his guru that this hermitage of his is located in the fifty chambers of Meru, one should ascend its extraction.

The science, beginning from the full moon and consisting of six types within the divisions starting with 'ka', has been explained to you by the Siddha; now, however, a certain lineage [of it] shall be told.
This essence of the Western Tradition, which is the path to Meru as it was ordained, is contained in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa;
[it should be practiced] on a very pure plot of ground smeared with dust and cow dung.
In a place strewn with heaps of flowers, one should have three cubits prepared;
there, one should worship a maiden as well as the son of the preceptor.
In a solitary, secluded, and delightful place, not crowded with common folk,
one who has bathed, purified by mantras, and whose inner self is perfectly cleansed [should perform the rite].
His consciousness is the bliss of wine, his form is worshipped by heroes;
having first prepared a mandala there, he should worship the sandals of the Guru.
Having satisfied him with great devotion through gifts of gold, cows, clothing, and so forth,
one should thereafter worship the teacher of the Kula tradition while facing the east.
Like Mount Meru, it is the Meru-array, the auspicious abode of all mantras;
it is the pervasive authority over the Kula goddesses and the practitioners of mantra.
Having worshipped the ninefold chalk [deities], one then becomes a destroyer of the enemies of Dharma;
the field is twenty-seven finger-breadths in extent, measured with equal lines on all sides.
In that very place, one should draw Mount Meru; its sequential method is as follows:
O Lord, there are thirteen divisions, straight and clear, in due order.
One should draw horizontal and vertical lines in equal measure,
resulting in a total count of one hundred and four squares.
First, taking one in the middle, there are three below it horizontally;
below that, five, and again seven beneath that.
Nine below, and eleven below that again,
thirteen further below, and one syllable in the center.
Beginning from the primordial location, I shall describe the sequence of Meru;
first, taking the supreme and non-supreme abode situated upon the summit of Meru. (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
The Yogapīṭhas and the three Siddhas, below that the five jewels;
beneath those the seven Mothers, below them the nine deities;
below that the eleven Rudras, and the thirteen Divine Siddhas.
Below that, O Lord of Ciñciṇī, fifty divisions have been proclaimed.
This is the extraction of the sequence of worship for the Meru-prastāra diagram;
having first performed it according to the principle of emanation (sṛṣṭi), one should then erase the remaining [elements] on the outside.
Facing east and so forth, [one should place them] from west to west; facing east, with six, five, four, three, and one [respectively].
Likewise, by means of six [factors] in due order, one and two are reached by six, four by three,
and five and six by both the forward and reverse sequences.
The well-arranged array consists solely of the form of the *liṅga*:
one, thirteen, eleven, and likewise nine.
By means of seven, five, and three, there is only one Maheśvara;
from Śiva down to the power of the aperture (randhra-śakti), such is the sequence of the innate (sahaja).
One should worship with supreme devotion using the five types of offerings;
and one should write the fifty perfected syllables according to the sequence of the Mātṛkā.
In a counter-clockwise sequence, up to the western [position] in the center,
place that which is conjoined with the neuter below, having passed beyond the groups of consonants.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: one should extract the letters *aja*, *kāja*, and *jhaka*, as well as the vowel *ā*;
then the letters *cha* and *bha*, *ña*, *ma*, and the fifth, which is *i*.
And likewise *ca*, *ba*, *ka*, *ra*, *sa*, *ha*; *ya*, *ṭa*, the letter *ī* as the seventh; *ṅa*, *pha*, *ka*, *ra*, *ṣa*, *ka*, *ra*, *la*, *repha*.
The letter *ṭha* and the letter *u* are the ninth in the mandala of the Mothers;
likewise, *gha*, *pa*, *na*, *dha*, and *da*.
And likewise the syllable *ṭha* with the letter *ḍa*, and the letter *ū* as the tenth;
the letters *ga*, *kha*, and *ka*, as well as the syllables *aḥ* and *aṃ*.
The vowels *au*, *ai*, *e*, *lū*, *ḷ*, *ṛ*, and *ṝ* are declared to be thirteen; and the one called *kaṣa* is situated below.
Now listen, O Lord of Gods, as I speak of those [terms] established in the lexicon of sounds, from the letter 'a' to the letter 'kṣa', according to their application in ritual placement (nyāsa).
The arrangement in direct order and the description of syllables in reverse order;
the nectar, the son of the Sun, Māyā, Gaurī, and the piercer with a single arrow.
Lupta, Mahendra, Rāvaṇa with a frowning face,
Pudgala, Gajakarṇa, Goṣṭhī, and Tripadī as well.
Likewise, the Bindu, the end of the vowels, and thereafter the Arising of the Phonemes (varṇodaya); then Mahān, Vṛṣabha, Siṃha, Mātara, and Haṭṭakeśvara.
Jilaka, Śūlarāja, Unmatta, Vīrabāhuka,
Kapāla, Jaṭāhāra, Vāsuki, and Ṣoḍha— these are the grahas.
One should worship Nīlakaṇṭha, Parāvarta, Kuvera, Girijātmaja,
Tāra, Dvijapati, Rāva, as well as Śakti and Purandara.
Ekavīra, Haya, Agnidhāman, Pārthiva, Padmayoni, Mahāśaṅkha, and again Dhūmradhvaja.
The seed-syllable of emanation, Anaṅga, and the parasol of shadow; beyond this,
one should worship the Meru-prastāra together with chalk, according to the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.

And one should not forget anything here; one should extract the path of knowledge through the lion’s gaze, O Śambhu, by means of withdrawal according to its own nature. I am the mistress of the sacred seat, the goddess named the Yoginī Kubjikā.
And here, according to the distinction of the types of soil, the sequence for the Ajā and Māvāsika [offerings] is as follows.
Now, indeed, I shall proclaim the definitive extraction of the Vidyā:
it is the head of the very Rāva belonging to the city of Śakti.
The first auspicious syllable is indeed of two kinds and has one foot;
between Śaṅkha and Pārthiva lies Padmayoni, the abode of Śiva.
O Mahādeva, the second syllable is joined with Māyā;
it is the seat of the abode of Fire, pierced by the skull (kapāla) and the letter U.
The third syllable has been declared; I shall now tell you the fourth:
O God, the auspicious arising of the phonemes within Ananta-Hanuman.
O best of gods, one should extract the syllable joined with the end of Māyā;
the fifth syllable shall be that which is split by the first of the six and by Ṭa above.
The seat of the Lord of the Twice-born, adorned with a skull upon its head, is declared to be the sixth syllable; now hear the seventh from the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:
it is adorned above by the end of "horse" (*hayānta*).
For this supreme syllable, the Moon situated in the middle and end of Vāsuki, should be cast down from Hara in that same manner.
O Śambhu, between Śūla and Hāṭaka, differentiated by the end of Unmatta,
is the Saura [mantra] fashioned by Ekavīra, extracted from the eight syllables.
Both these, the moon and the sun, are adorned above by a skull;
appearing upon the crown of the head, they are the gate-arches of the rampart of knowledge.
