Siṃhaughahanūmān said: "O Lord, this city is enveloped by illusion;
this ninth syllable of Sarvakāminī has been struck down."
"The seed-syllable of Ananga, pierced by the Jaṭāhāra at its end—
this tenth syllable has been declared to you, O Bhairava."
One should place the abode of fire between the matted locks (jaṭā) and the king (pārthiva);
this letter, conjoined with the sun (ai), becomes the eleventh letter when divided.
Hanuman, the lion on the head, and the shadow adorned above—this is declared the twelfth syllable; "unmatte" (in the mad one) is the thirteenth.
O Lord of the Thirty-three, its seat is the "Single Hero," which is pierced by the seat of that [deity];
this is declared to be the fourteenth syllable.

The single syllable of the Star (tārakākṣara), which is at the end of Śiva—the Lord of the Twice-born—is declared to be the fifteenth; it was revealed by the Goddess of Gods. In the central city of the Sixteen-fold Nīlakaṇṭha, that is its seat.
The Kevala is known as sixteen-fold, and the Hayaśīrṣa is likewise unique.
The seventeenth is declared to begin with the letter *pha*, and the eighteenth consists of ten [letters].
There are four nasals (*anunāsika*); these are the perfected ones who pervade the mantra.
They are the four Yugas, and they are the seats (*pīṭhas*) on this earthly plane.
Then, O best of gods, the three seed-syllables should be known as the tongue of Vidyā.
The bodiless one (anaṅga) situated after "horse" (ha), conjoined with the end of "earth" (la),
pierced by the first of "Rāvaṇa" (ra), and struck by the head of "bodiless" (a).
This is the seed-syllable of Rudra, numbered as the nineteenth;
it is pierced by the end of the matted locks (jaṭā) situated between the syllables of Hara and Pārthiva.
The syllable *gau* joined with the end of *kapāla* (the letter *ha*) and pierced by the younger brother of Hara (*ra*),
this is the *piṇḍa* consisting of *māyā*; it enters the head of Viṣṇu.
The syllable *A* joined with the end of *Śaṃkha*, *Vīra*, *Antaga*, *Anaṅga*, *Jaṭāhāra*, and so forth;
the *Kūṭa* situated between *A* and *I*, struck on the head by the end of *Hara*.
This is proclaimed as the single syllable of Brahman, the twenty-first aggregate;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—these are the Siddhas endowed with the sequence.
Situated upon their head is the power (śakti) consisting of the letter *ka*, established in the throat;
it is conjoined with the arising of the vowels situated in the middle of the eyes.
This twenty-second letter shall become the twenty-third;
it is joined with the city of the power of emanation (Sṛṣṭiśaktipurā) and with the dust of Ha.
I am this horse-bodied one, pervaded by the skull-headed [deity].
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the first [vowel] of the person (pudgala) is situated upon the head of Vāsuki.
The twenty-fourth letter, which expresses the names of the mudrās,
has been declared by the illustrious Lord for the sake of your accomplishment, together with the Consort.
The twenty-fifth [letter] is known by the name of the vowel *ī*,
together with the syllable *aṅga* situated in a single word, preceded by the power (*śakti*) ending in *ra*.
Hanuman is at the end of the three syllables; joined with that, it is placed below.
Dhūmra-mātṛ is situated in the middle, and it is joined with the seat (āsana) itself.
The head-ornament, rich with jewels, and the mass [of the body] were stepped upon by him;
the peak was made blazing with commands—the leader of the six lineages and families.
By this, O God, one remembers and becomes a vessel for the Kaula;
the Command (ājñā) proceeds in the disciple through the practice of that Command.
And there is no doubt, O beautiful one, that you will attain the power of flight before long;
furthermore, O Supreme Lord, this peak of consciousness is sixfold.
The first seat, Khecara, is endowed with six seats;
when the mantrin beholds it, he falls— that is certain.
By reciting it twenty-seven hundred thousand times, one gains the power of moving through the sky;
[one sees the deity] blazing in the form of a lamp, situated in the center of the Krama-maṇḍala.
That tall liṅga and that tree are the Kramanāyaka according to the ritual rule. His garden is preceded by Agni and Jālandhara;
ending with Khāṇī is Pūrṇagiri, and ending with Ha is Koṅkaṇa.
And Ekapāda, known as Tisra, are established according to the sequence of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
This indeed is the sixfold Piṇḍa, the supreme hermitage of the Lord;
[from] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
This is that khecarīmudrā, by which the wondrous three worlds are swallowed up.
Within the triad of *olī*s, this is the command in the Kubjikā tradition;
its form is Aghorā, and its extraction is performed in reverse order.
The twenty-seventh letter is joined with the fire [Ra] at the beginning of Jaṭāhāra and below that [Ha];
it becomes the twenty-eighth.
Hanumān struck the head of the lion with a javelin;
the head of the lordly elephant, known by the name Nīlakaṇṭha, was then felled.
O handsome one, the twenty-ninth chapter concerning Māyā has been told to you;
I shall now speak again of the thirtieth, the Parāvartaśira.
The thirty-first is proclaimed as Kevala and Hanumādyam;
O God, the thirty-second is declared to be the very seat (āsana) of Śūla,
beginning with Ekavīra and so forth.
Up to the end of the *bhaga*, it is declared that the supreme body is Bhairava, while the goddess Bimbā resides in the sky.
One should perform the extraction in reverse order from the seats and then in direct order;
this is known as "the lion's gaze," so called because it is like a lion.
She is renowned as Ādipīṭheśvarī, distinguished by the three mudrās.
Śrīnātha said:
"O Goddess, this excellent city which blazes with a terrifying form—"
Tell me, however, the method for making [the poison] immortal (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), which is terrifying to the disciples;
by means of which it shall grant complete accomplishment to the disciples everywhere. *The Section on the Virgin (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)*: 16.109cd–110ab.
"I desire this auspicious lunar practice (cāndreya-karaṇa) as its application.
Śrīvakrā said:
"Therefore, this is the tradition that follows after the previous one."
O Śrīnātha, I shall proclaim to you the auspicious rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa): having first uttered five *praṇavas*, one should likewise utter them at the end in reverse order.
The Vidyā situated between those two is Pūrṇimā; there is no doubt about this.
There is nothing further to elaborate here; one should extract the five-syllabled Vidyā.
Merely by its utterance, great sovereignty is set in motion;
it is the fourth [consonant] from the letter of Vāyu, situated below, which was previously worshipped.
This is the Vidyā of Kauleśvarī, which pervades the crest of the topknot, blazes with the wick of the Command, and is distinguished by the letter 'O' at its end.
This divine lady is the Goddess Vahnivāsinī by name; O God, one should contemplate her as slightly red, situated in the center of the *ādhāra-maṇi*.
From one hundred thousand recitations, success is attained and the Great Piercing (mahāvedha) proceeds;
it is the fourth [vowel] beginning with Amṛta, which is the third below the letter *i*.
That which stands at the end of the vowel *yā*, situated within the *bindu* and *nāda*, struck by the head [of the letter *ha*] upon its own head—
this is indeed remembered as Mahāmāyā, the agitator of the three worlds.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
One should meditate on the fire, resembling a tawny-brown hue, within the maṇipūra;
through one hundred thousand recitations, there is subjugation, possession, and the attainment of prosperity.
The letter *ṣa* ending in *v*, mounted upon *ṭāsa* and pierced by *uśira*,
marked with the digit (*kalā*) and the point (*bindu*), is the Sound (*nāda*) at the crown of the head, which brings an end to Death (*kṛtānta*).
This is that goddess Śāṅkarī, who brings about the destruction of all suffering;
one should meditate upon her, resembling snow, the kunda flower, and the moon, within the Anāhata [cakra], O Lord.
By reciting it one hundred thousand times just once, a person shall obtain the Kaula knowledge;
he shall attain worldly enjoyments, good fortune, fame, and prosperity.
"The younger brother of Pāṇu, situated in the midst of the *khara*, pierced by the sound of *elīna*, and pervaded by the digit of the lunar drop— this is difficult to attain even for the gods."
This is that Khecarī-vidyā, dark-hued, red, and pure-limbed;
through the recitation of one hundred thousand [mantras], success is attained, and one becomes a recipient of boons from the Mothers.
Lightness, the cessation of karma, emergence within the lattice,
and the stabilization of the stream— it brings about supreme possession without a doubt.
The space situated within the letter *ya*, ending with *ha* and separated by *la*;
the head of *ṛ* and the head of *o* as one, marked by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and the sky-farer (*khaga*).
One should contemplate this Bhairavī Vidyā as white and red;
through one hundred thousand recitations of the *śalākā* at the station of the command (*ājñāsthāna*), there is the attainment of prosperity.
Having performed this, one brings about the destruction of anger; the army of Śakra is destroyed, there is no doubt.
This is the section on the Maiden (Kumārikākhaṇḍa), concerning the suppression of the wicked and the striking down of enemies.
There is no doubt in this matter: by the mere act of propitiating her, a human being attains the fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
The yogi who discovers this Kaulika Fivefold Knowledge (vidyā-pañcaka) also goes to the supreme reality, having gone to which he does not grieve.
Vāgbhava is the first seed-syllable; Māyā-bīja is the second.

The third is the seed-syllable of Śrī, the fourth is Khecara, and the fifth is named Bhairava; these should be known as the ornaments of the Kula. These five Praṇavas are declared to be the illuminators in the Kulakrama.
Furthermore, these are proclaimed as the primary seats of the Vidyā:
first is Kāmarūpa, and the second is Jālapīṭha.
Pūrṇagiri is the third, Oḍiyāna is the fourth, and the fifth is known as Tisrapīṭha; these are the five places where the Siddhas reside.
Maitrīśa, Caryadeva, Ṣaṣṭhīśa, Oḍa,
and Tūṣṇīśa— the Lord of the Gods of gods— these are the five Siddhas in their proper order.
Beginning from the first seat (pīṭha), one should indeed perform the sequential worship;
joined with the five praṇavas, it is accomplished—of this there is no doubt.
He who worships the Krama devoid of the five syllables of the Vidyā should be known as one established in non-Krama; he is not ordained for liberation.
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
the five-syllable sequence, the yoga, the five syllables of the sequence-mantra (vidyā),
the wheel that is the abode of the five elements, and likewise the self in five ways.
Having performed this placement (nyāsa) of the five syllables, agitation arises;
and those who are born into the family of the Yoginīs attain the pentad.
Having indeed gone to Kāmarūpa and likewise to Jālandhara,
and having gone to another, the fourth sacred seat (pīṭha), Pūrṇagiri.
Furthermore, having gone again to the place called Tisra, one should practice the fivefold knowledge;
they are accomplished through the previous sequence, and not otherwise, O you who are praised by heroes.
First, five hundred thousand recitations must be performed by the practitioner;
however, through the power of union, he should recite one hundred thousand for the Vidyā at the primary seat (pīṭha).
The practitioner shall become a partaker of accomplishment; there is no doubt that he will attain the power of moving through the sky.
In that sacred seat (pīṭha), a man shall obtain union with the Khecarī, heroic accomplishment, great pervasiveness, and, according to his will, the agitation of the city.
Atomicity, magnificence, lightness, and indeed reachability;
Furthermore, there are irresistible will, lordship, and mastery;
wherever one desires, by the power of one's wish, these eight perfections are attained in this very life.
The yogi shall attain the state of the immortals and become Rudra himself;
this is the five-syllabled vidyā, adorned with the five mudrās.
In the Kulakaula, the first [mudrā] should be known by those who contemplate the arousal;
it is the Yonimudrā, as well as the Śaṅkhinī and the Padmamudrā.
O Lord of Gods, [he who is] likewise devoid of the skull-mudrā and that which is known as the jar-mudrā,
being liberated from the five mudrās and bereft of the five vidyās, such a practitioner of mantra would not be a follower of the lineage, nor would he be a vessel for accomplishment.
Those who speak of them as Kaulikas do so for the sake of the attachment to the tongue and the organ of generation.

For them, there is no lineage of the Kula; otherwise, a fall would occur. [In the] Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the fivefold group consists of the Vidyās, the meditations (dhyānas), the sacred seats (pīṭhas), the Siddhas, and the Mudrās.
This indeed should be known according to its true nature, as well as the fivefold group of five syllables;
it has been indicated to you, O Siddha, and must be guarded like one's own body.
"This supreme secret must not be told to just anyone.

Thus [ends] the determination of the Pure Six Thousand, brought down to the first sacred seat (pīṭha) on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), emerged from the Meru-path within the lineage (anvaya) of the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, measuring seventy million verses and exceeding one hundred thousand quarters (lakṣapādādhika).

In the *Kādibheda*, within the *Ājñāpārameśvara* of the *Svāminīmata*, in the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the tradition of the Mother (*avvākrama*), in the determination of the layout of Meru,
this is the bliss named the Extraction of the Vidyā. Śrīnātha said:
O Goddess of the gods, I have heard the supreme extraction of the Vidyā;
yet, O Lord, the *kūṭa* of the Goddess has not been understood by me in detail.
"Now I wish to hear it; speak that now, O Lord.
Śrīvakrā said:
"The Ninth Bliss."
O Maheśvara, that single peak is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru.
Without that, there is no accomplishment; listen to this, O handsome one:
first is Jālapīṭha, and Pūrṇarya is the second.
The third is declared to be Koṅkaṇa, and Kāmarūpa is the fourth;
the fifth seat is Oṃkāra, and the sixth is the Lord of the Three Streams (Trisrotanāyaka).
Those six are known to have an object of focus within the body,
while those above them are without an object; I shall now explain these six in detail.
Now.
Indubindu, Svayamnātha, Śakti, and above them Vyāpinī;
above that, Samanā is to be known, and Unmanā likewise above her.
From the union of both of these, those twelve [levels] come into being.
Now, I shall presently explain the categories (padārthas) as a collection.
The form of fire, known as the "net," resides in the heart;
it resembles a pomegranate flower, is situated within a well, and belongs to Pūrṇagiri.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Koṅkaṇa is at the uvula, resembling the autumnal sky;
Kāmākhya is in the middle of the palate, as pure as snow, the kunda flower, and the moon.
Above that, one should know the syllable Oṃ, possessing the luster of a mirror;
it is called the triangle and should be meditated upon as rising up within the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
One should meditate on the Lord of the Seat named Tisra, resembling molten gold;
above that is the Wheel of Space (vyomacakra), possessing a radiance like a whirling firebrand.
Having thoroughly practiced the form of the Bindu, above that is the Half-moon;
it is declared to be the form of Light, with Ādinātha at its summit.
One should understand the Śiva-tattva as unmanifest; one should contemplate it like a wheel, beginning from the heart up to the top of the head.
That much is declared to be the "peak" (kūṭa), established in nine ways;
one should pierce it gradually, by means of the piercing of the suṣumnā channel.
Above that, I shall now describe the different types of *olīs* in three ways:
having left a space of four finger-breadths, the straight *śakti* is prescribed.
One should meditate upon her, resembling the flax flower, pervading the sky;
above that, she is said to be the Pervasive One (Vyāpinī), four finger-breadths higher.
She is a female ascetic by her very nature, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons;
above the Śiva-tattva, however, the three goddesses of the lineage (olidevyas) are traditionally taught.
(From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
Above that is the state of Unmanā; indeed, the state of Śambhu is the state of sound.
Having thoroughly practiced the one Void, wherein everything ceases.
When Unmanā is attained at the end of Śūnyā, who would not be liberated from bondage?
Now I shall further explain another, supreme, and secret cause.
The first is called Kāmarūpa, with a peak shaped like a śṛṅgāṭa;
the second is the seed-syllable of Māyā, while Guhā and Tūṣṇikā are the mudrās.
The third is the divine seed-syllable of Rudra, worshipped by the best of gods;
the fourth is the Khecarī-pīṭha, whose form is *khapharemi*.
The fifth is named Bhairava, marked with *hasarai*;
these are declared to be the five sacred seats (*pīṭha*) known by secret names in the Kula tradition.
The five symbolic conventions for these have been introduced in this treatise:
the vowel *ī*, the vowel *ā*, and the vowels *i*, *u*, and *o*—this is the pentad of vowels.
O Śambhu, these have arisen from the sequence of the principles (tattva) by the will of Kula:
the first seat (pīṭha) is the long vowel, and the fourth is the leader of the vowels.
In the second [chapter] of the Svarodaya, the third [chapter], and the third [chapter];
the fourth [chapter] is in the fourth, while the thirteenth is in the fifth.
These are remembered as the jewel-seats (ratnapīṭhas): O, Jā, Pū, and Kā, together with Satisrakā; their mistress is I, and the Vidyā is Mahāntārikā.
She is both with form and without form, adorned with the aspect of non-duality;
she is both gross and subtle, moving within the power of consciousness.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Mahāmāyā, whose nature is consciousness, though unwritable, appears in the form of that which is written;
the Supreme Goddess shall sport in the secret place, in the heart, and in the mouth.
When joined with the peak of the mudrā, it becomes sealed by that;
as long as one does not find the peak, the vidyā is not accomplished.
Thereafter, I shall explain the Kaulika [tradition], which is complete through the divisions beginning with *ka* and so forth, by means of its hidden meaning; it is the thirty-two-syllable Vidyā.
Just as she has been described by means of convention (*saṃketa*), she bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*) upon yogins;
first is the convention of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), and after that, the convention of the Blessed Lady (*bhagavatī*).
The third is the convention of form and consciousness;
beyond that, the fourth is declared to be [the convention of] name, and the fifth is ornamentation.
Then the sixth is the designation called Brahmā; the seventh is the seed-syllable [of Brahmā];
the eighth is the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu, and the ninth is said to be that of Rudra.
The fifth pair is called Karālā, and the eleventh is said to be Amṛtā;
the twelfth that has appeared is indeed Mahābhairavī.
The thirteenth is pervasion (vyāpti), and the fourteenth is the established state (saṃsthiti);
accomplishment (siddhi) is in the fifteenth place, and the command (ājñā) is in the sixteenth step.
The sixteen-fold convention was established for the purpose of instruction;
thereafter, the Goddess indeed appears in three ways within the successions and lineages.
I shall now explain that according to the instruction of Karṇa. In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the division of forms is declared to be threefold, in reverse order within the three sequences.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, two types of obstacles arise through perversion;
as long as the movement is not known, how can there be purity of the lineage (oli) in the sequence?
First is the cause of transformation, and immediately after that, O gentle one, is the Great Tree; furthermore, in this context, it is threefold by way of its instrumental function.
Having first understood the purification of the form, one should recollect the reality of the Command;
though liberated from consciousness, it continues to function even through negligence.
In that regard, the sequence of the void is without authority apart from the Guru;
however, the seed-syllable of Rudra, consisting of three segments, is distinct from Śakti.
Why is the burning away of impurities brought about by Śakti?
Having first recognized him as being endowed with Śakti, the destruction of impurities was then commanded.
When the nectar is devoid of the Yoginī and lacks the visarga, how could liberation arise from it? Nor does heaven proceed from it.
When [the mantra] ends with Bhairava and is elongated, why is the body divided?
From where would the power of Bhairavī arise, and from where would it exist in the circle of the Siddhas?
When the cage of the mandala is pervaded by that which is imperishable and empty,
liberation from that cycle of existence is not proclaimed here.
For all [of them], preceded by the word "namas" as an address to the Goddess, there is the loss of family and destruction; the loss of intellect occurs within one's own self at all times.
The increase of impurities occurs; from what would that increase arise?
Then, in this wheel of saṃsāra, it rises day by day.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
A lunar day devoid of a sacred seat (pīṭha) on the new moon does not bestow the fruit of accomplishment here;
moreover, being bereft of the Command (ājñā), it brings about the destruction of one's fortune at the end.
Knowledge becomes unfortunate; there is no doubt that it results in misfortune.
Furthermore, if the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) yoga is not applied at the beginning and the end, [the same result follows].
Then, by the power of the letter *ra*, the fire of Bhairava will blaze forth;
by that, she, whose form is terrifying, will become visibly drenched.
In that regard, there is a certain instrument which operates within the *hasa*;
having first performed the elision (*lopa*) of the sun (*ravi*), the *vāruṇī* digit resides therein.
By means of the movement of the moon, it then becomes a river of fullness;
because the moon's rays flow [therein], it is therefore called "Full" (Pūrṇā).
If both [mantras] are recited according to the rule, yet lacking five [syllables], they will still not bring success; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Excluding both sets of five, joined with the vocative "namo";
by reciting the vidyā thus on the new moon day even a hundred crores of times [one attains success].
O Hara, although it is said that in the Kali age, knowledge becomes averse to the mortal world even when taught on the lion-throne of mantra in the southern region.
The power to punish or favor, as well as the perception of things such as the splitting of trees, is the majesty of this sacred field; and that, moreover, arises from the power of the vidyā-mantra.
By the power of the Vaṭuka, external conditions are established;
the Vidyā becomes self-evident according to the sequence of the current.

O Khecarī, those who are devoid of the current (ogha) are not liberated from falling; therefore, this is the section on the Virgin (Kumārikākhaṇḍa). One should recite the five [syllables] in direct order at the beginning of the recitation and in reverse order at the end.

O God, O Lord of the Suras, having performed the coming and going in the center according to the sequence of emanation beginning with the letter *Bhā*, then that [day] becomes the full moon day (*pūrṇimā*).
When the Vidyā is uttered even once, the cage of the body trembles;
the mantra-practitioner becomes a portion of Rudra, and the Goddess Vidyā is the Full Moon.
Otherwise, O Lord, she would not have been introduced into this scripture;
for this is indeed the "Encasement" (saṃpuṭa) of the Yoga-vidyā, preceded by the body.
That which is renowned as the five-syllabled mantra—he who knows it attains perfection.
This pure vidyā is enclosed by the *saṃpuṭa*, yet when devoid of the *saṃpuṭa* it is likewise pure.
It is impure; of this there is no doubt. It bestows obstacles at every step.
Therefore, for the purpose of destroying those obstacles, the *saṃpuṭa* has been taught.
The new moon day shall become full; the dark [fortnight] will become thick.
That which is fierce becomes gentle when overcome by the Karaṇa.
O best of gods, those five seats which were previously mentioned should be formed in sequence beginning with the syllable *bha*, following the order starting from the Vāgbhava mantra.
Furthermore, one should join those same [syllables] in reverse order at the end of the letter *ca*;
first there are five *praṇavas*, and at the end, they too are dispersed.
I have entered into the midst of the Vidyā as you, Kaulinī, whose form consists of the thirty-two syllables; this is indeed by means of this very instrument.
That [mantra] consists of forty-two syllables; it belongs to his own mantra in the Western lineage.
O beloved of the Vaidikas, the *praṇava* (OM) should be given as its illuminator (*dīpana*).
Therefore, she is liberated and devoid of the six musical scales (ṣaḍjāti).
She is preceded by *oṃ* and *namaḥ*, and consists of *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*.
And likewise, ending with *svāhā* and excluding *rakṣa* and *phaṭ*,
by these mantra-words she becomes perfected and supreme once she has emerged there.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Even those who are preeminent in the tantras for the purpose of worship and fire-offerings (homakarma),
by performing [these rites] within the Kula tradition, a fall from yoga indeed occurs.
When knowledge is illuminated within its own nature and established in the circle of fire,
then it is perfected, having transcended even the tantras and mantras.
And there exists no knowledge equal to this within the three worlds;
it is found in this Kula scripture as the deity of the sacred seats (pīṭha) among the sacred seats.
There is no knowledge higher than this; there is nothing superior to the scripture of the Command (ājñā).
There is nothing higher than the sequence of the sacred seats (pīṭhakrama); there is nothing higher than the mouth of the Guru.

Thus, in the introduction to the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses emerged from the Path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primary seat on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (Vidyāpīṭha), in the determination of the Pure Six-Thousand, in the Kādi division, in the Svāminīmata which is the Supreme Lord’s Command, in the venerable twenty-four thousand [verse scripture]—

In the Saṃhitā spoken by Avvākrama, in the description of the chapter on consciousness consisting of the various divisions beginning with the Full Vidyā, this is the Bliss named Kramodaya. Śrīnātha said:
This is the Tenth Bliss.
"What is this that you have told regarding the *pūrṇakaraṇa* of the Vidyā—
the splendor of the *piṇḍa* of Bhairava that arises from the midst of the *auṣadha*?"
Because of the complete suppression of the two *repha*s situated at the beginning and the end, this is the process of curving;
it is never a full [vocal] production.
This is the thorn of knowledge; thus it becomes pinned down.
Tell me its unpinning, by which it may become full.
The venerable Vakrā said: This most excellent and secret question has been brought down by the God of gods;
there is no one other than you who possesses the intelligence to answer it, so listen to that.
In the *piṇḍa* of Bhairava, situated at the beginning and the end,
the "dart" (*śalya*) is located between the vowels and the consonants, possessing a radiance equal to the midday sun.
Having performed its elision there, that Vāruṇī digit,
having placed nectar at the beginning and the end, then the vidyā becomes perfected.

O God, by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, the power of flight shall be attained by the practitioner; this has been declared as the oral instruction, and no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
For one who is engaged in that sequence and devoted to the recitation of the Vidyā,
there is accomplishment in the final age, along with many signs of realization.
Through the practice of the knowledge of the lost and the peripheral consciousness, this very continuum of his arises; this was previously explained by Prastāra.
Having understood that the power of Rudra arises from Meru, one becomes a seeker of knowledge;
now, the complete Vidyā is declared according to the division of its parts.
The first word is *cceviṇikipada*, the second is *ṇikicchīṃcchā*,
the third is *khimurāgho*, and the fourth is *amenaṇa*.
The fifth is ña ṅa shrau~ śīṃ; the sixth should be sahā~ kebjiku;
śrī~ ha regho would be the seventh; and tivagabhapada is the eighth.
This Vidyā, consisting of eight words, is declared to be the great-bodied Aghorā;
it is preceded by five *praṇavas* and ends with five [syllables] in reverse order.
O Bhairava, this yoga of the fulfillment of the instruments has been told to you;
one should purify its six limbs through the placement on the hands (karanyāsa).
One should first perform the placement (vinyāsa) of the twelve divisions;
prior to that, one should perform the placement of the faces according to the method of emanation.
Beginning from the upper face up to the western face—the gentle one [is worshipped] by the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), and the fierce one by the other sequence.
First, having placed the western face, [one proceeds] up to the upper face in due order. This is the *Tukumārikākhaṇḍa*.
To that extent, the five limbs of the Siddha have been described as being precisely the process of withdrawal.
Through the process of withdrawal, however, it is partless; through the process of emanation, it is with parts.
Having understood the union of emanation and withdrawal, one should cause [the disciple] to enter the divine mouth.
One should place the syllables beginning with *bha* and ending with *ra* on the upward-facing mouth;
one should place the syllables beginning with the peak (*kūṭa*) of the Goddess and ending with her name on the head-mouth.
Having superimposed the three seed-syllables, one should first place the eastern face;
the syllables beginning with *ṅa* and ending with *śūnya* (the letter *ha*) should be known as the southern face;
and from *sūrya* (the letter *ra*) up to *soma* (the letter *sa*), one should place them on the northern face.
Having practiced the sequence beginning with *ka* and so forth, one should finally place this [syllable] in the mouth.
The goddesses belonging to those six groups are, in their respective order:
the Supreme Goddess (Parā), Mālinī, and Siddhayogeśvarī.
Likewise, the goddess named Kālikā is the fifth, having Tripurāmūrti;
and to its west, moreover, is Umākhecarī as the first.
Beginning from the western face, having joined the Vāgbhava [syllable] at the beginning and end,
and having again performed the six limbs by means of the Pīṭha-nyāsa and Anu-nyāsa;
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: Again, one should place the Heart mantra beginning with the letter *bha* and ending with the letter *ra*;
then, having extracted that which begins with the Peak of the Self (*ātmakūṭa*) and ends with the Name, one should place the Head.
In the *śikhā* [mantra] are three seed-syllables: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
and from *ṅa* up to the end of *śūnya*, they are placed in sequence within the armor-deity (*varmadevī*).
One should place these two, *cchā~* and *cchīṃ*, as the Moon upon the two eyes;
then one should place the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) preceded by *vicce kiṇikiṇi*.
O fortunate one, the limbs (*aṅga*) are thus joined with the *kaulikā* at the beginning and end.
And one should place them in a folded manner, O God, for they are supreme providers of all protection.
With those six limbs, one should worship the six deities in the sequence beginning with the heart;
likewise, the Goddess known as Hṛtkamalāmbā and Kuladīpā.
Barbarā, she who is called Bahurūpā, Mahantārī, and Koṅkaṇā—
thus this group of six deities is proclaimed as the limbs.
One should install the family deity (kuladevatā) by means of these twelve divisions;
those who are liberated from the injunctions of the tantras [should install] the limbs of the Siddhas in the two six-limbed [mantras].
One should place the limbs [of the mantra] in their proper order, beginning with *oṃ namaḥ* and ending with *svāhā*, followed by *vauṣaṭ*, *svasti*, *arṇava*, *vaṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*.
"O Śambhu, having been applied at the beginning and the end according to the sequence of the Yoga-pīṭhas,
the ritual deposition (nyāsa) is subsequently commenced as it has been declared in the Kulāgama. In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the group of six known as Vakramukha was previously determined in the Nirṇaya."
The six limbs are the six mudrās; in the sequence of the twelve,
they are the yoni-mudrā, the siṃhā, the dūtī-mudrā,
the ciñciṇī, the śūla-mudrā, and the vakriṇī— thus the group of six mudrās in order.
When the vidyā has been differentiated by these [syllables], one will then become a master of accomplishment;
when it is sealed with the yonimudrā, one should then practice the vidyā.
I shall describe the twelve meditations (dhyāna) individually upon the faces and limbs:
the face on the front is white, the head [face] is red, the eastern face is pale yellow,
the southern face is black, and the northern face is yellow.
The western face, however, is dark red and is worshipped by the thirty gods.
Resembling pure crystal, it is distinguished as being in the heart of the Goddess;
resembling molten gold, it is proclaimed to be the head of the Goddess.

One should visualize the fierce [deity] with a crest of lightning-tongues surrounded by garlands of flames; one should then place the armor-mantra, which is slightly dark and red, and possesses many colors.
The two eyes have a luster equal to the moon and sun, are circular and cool as snow;
and the weapon is like fire, the destroyer of all obstacles.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
This is the yoga transmitted through the lineage concerning the twelvefold ritual placement (nyāsa).
O Lord of Gods, by constantly performing these placements, the practitioner shall become a partaker of success (siddhi).
Whatever desires one wishes for, those one obtains, and not otherwise;
there would be only this single great fault arising from the practice of the vidyā.
Whomever the practitioner, overcome by anger, might look upon, he shall cause that person to fall;
of this there is no doubt, even if that person were equal to Śakra himself.
Having indeed constructed the vajra-penthouse by means of the *pīṭha-nyāsa* and *anunyāsa*,
the bursting of mudrās occurs, as well as movement and observation.
There is no doubt that a divine body, bodily luster, long life,
good fortune, radiance, and splendor arise; and from all sides, mastery over desire, strength, heroism, and all supernatural accomplishments (siddhis) come forth.
Thus, for one whose knowledge is purified by scripture and who follows the pure sequence, there is [liberation].
This power has been declared, characterized by the conviction of the perfected ones;
through the yoga of constant practice, it is accomplished in twelve years.
The mother of the gods, the mother of the world, the mother of the universe, she is firmly established; O God, the goddess of gods, whose body is vast, is the abode of all.
Moving through the sky by himself, he enjoys the depths of the netherworld;
just as I am and just as you are, so too is that supreme practitioner, [as described in] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
She who causes immediate possession, the terrible one, whose form is both non-terrible and terrible,
the sovereign of great vidyās, Māyā, Bhairavī, the supreme deity.
By the mere utterance of this, the destruction of all sins occurs:
even the killing of a Brahmin, innumerable killings of women, cows, and children.
Those who destroy land, those who steal gold, those who carry off the wives of others,
the treacherous toward their guru, the evil-minded, and especially those who betray their friends;
Those who commit acts of violence against fire, as well as those who betray trust,
those who act as thieves on the public road, and those who neglect their father and mother;
Even many [sins] committed, equal in measure to a heap of Mount Meru,
are reduced to ashes in that very instant by the recitation and placement (nyāsa) of the Vidyā.
O God, by reciting it even once, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords;
by remembering it, the yogi becomes pure and forever free from disease.

The merit of saving one who has come for refuge to a cow’s house is greater than that of a thousand horse-sacrifices or ten million gifts of cows and maidens; it is a merit that brings liberation through mere remembrance.

He who faces the enemy directly in battle, who gives up his life for the sake of cows, and likewise he who fasts unto death, falls from a precipice, or dies on the great highway; [all these attain the same merit].
Whatever fruit is obtained during an eclipse of the moon or the sun when they are seized by Rāhu,
that same fruit a hero shall obtain even from the mere recollection of this vidyā.
The Yoginīs who bestow boons upon him— whether born of the sacred seats (pīṭha), born of the fields (kṣetra), innate (sahaja), or born of the arts (kalaja)— worship him at every step.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
An unfortunate man becomes fortunate and attains the favor of the people;
he achieves victory in battle and gains renown at the royal court.
A sonless man obtains sons, as well as the perfection of long life and health;
and a woman whose children have died shall become one whose sons live.
O Lord of Gods, he who has this Vidyā residing in his mouth has accomplished all that is to be done.
O Lord, I am not able to describe [you] with but a single tongue.
Whatever desires one may wish for, all those shall be attained;
in the Kali age, this power has come within the range of human experience.
O Lord of the gods, this [mantra] has been accomplished by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the leaders;
by the power of this knowledge, men have attained divinity.
Those who constantly remember this, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, [attain their goals].
"Salvation is in his palm"—such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
O Maheśvara, she is honored by Brahmā and by Śakra,
as well as by Viṣṇu, Bhairava, and also by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras.
"This knowledge was honored by Māruta, Kuvera, the world-protectors of the ten directions, and even by all the gods."
"That [mantra] is not proclaimed as true knowledge, nor should it be recited if one is devoid of material offerings.
By doing so, one incurs a great curse; therefore, the Yoginīs who are the leaders of the wheel must be protected with effort—this is the command of the Supreme Lord."

In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*: thus, in the primordial descent (*ādyāvatāra*) of the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) comprising seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primary seat (*ādyapīṭha*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Sixfold Group (*vimalaṣaṭkanirṇaya*).

In the *Kādibheda*, within the *Ājñāpārameśvara* known as the *Svāminīmata*, which consists of twenty-four thousand verses and is spoken in the tradition of the Mother (*Avvākrama*), this is the bliss named "The Arising of the Sequence" (*Kramodaya*) in the description of the majesty of the Vidyā.
The venerable Vakrā said: "O Śambhu, I shall declare the sequence of the Goddess of the Letters (Varṇadevī) as it truly is; this is the eleventh bliss."
Likewise, the arrangement of the *kūṭa*, the number of recitations (*japa*), the *argha* offering, and the mandala.
Following the order of emanation, one should place the thirty-two goddesses beginning from the top;
then, having performed the placement of the Vidyā starting with the *vāgbhava* syllable, one performs the Kaulika placement.
One should place the first [syllable] on the head, the second in the circle of the fourth [state],
and both the third and the fourth on the two eyes.
One should place the fifth and likewise the sixth—these two being fixed—at the location of the command (ājñā); and the seventh at the tip of the nose, and likewise the eighth.
The ninth is in the three [joints] of the middle [finger], and the ten-syllable seed-mantra is in the mouth;
the twelfth is in the right ear, and likewise the thirteenth is in the left.
One should know that the fourteenth letter of the Goddess is located in the throat;
the fifteenth is on the right shoulder, and the sixteenth would be on the left.
The seventeenth [vow] is on the right arm-staff, the eighteenth on the left;
the nineteenth is on the heart, and the twentieth is on the circle of the navel.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:

the twenty-first [is located] in the two thighs; the twenty-second in the circle of the womb (yonimaṇḍala); the twenty-third in the center of the hub; and the twenty-fourth resides in the channels (nāḍī).
O Mahādeva, the twenty-fifth [digit] is on the buttock of Sūṣmaṇā;
that called Bhagīśa is on the right buttock, and the twenty-sixth is on the left buttock.
One should place these two, the twenty-seventh and the twenty-eighth, upon the knees;
the twenty-ninth and the thirtieth, one should place upon both shanks;
and the thirty-first and the thirty-second, likewise upon the right and left feet.
Now, O Bhairava, the deities of the letters are thirty-two auspicious ones.
Spread forth by means of the word-mantras distinguished by the letters of their own names,
they are Bhīmā, Gaganavegā, and Vīradevī as the fourth.
Ghorā, Raktākṣī, Kūṭamudrā, Śreya, as well as Kaivartī— the goddess of the fisherman— and Kubjikādevī, the goddess of Kubera and Hara.
Harī, Harānandā, Ṅaṇanañamaṭeśvarī,
the one called Nāgā, Mīnadevī, and likewise Ambikā.
Ghoramukhī, Rāvā, Musalāyudhakhecarī,
Cchāṃkārī, Chiṃcchā, and Kiṅkiṇī are the family deities (kuladevatās).
Karaṅkiṇī, Nārāyaṇī, Vimalā, and likewise Varcikā—
these thirty-two goddesses are to be known as the presiding authorities in their respective locations.
When these alone have been worshipped, there is no further bondage to birth;
this very thing was previously declared to be the Kaulika utterance of that [mantra].
And that is the single-syllable peak (kūṭa), the sevenfold command, and the sky-farer (khecara).
Its sixfold instrument is the Lion’s Sequence (siṃhakrama) therein. [In the] Kumārikākhaṇḍa: Oḍiyāṇa is between the eyebrows; Kāmākhya is at the birth of power (śakti).
In the center of the hexagon is the Void; it is filled by the Fullness of Sound.
The *tejas* is at Jālandhara in the navel; that called *tisra* is in the *viśuddhi*;
that called *candra* is in the middle of the palate; and in its center is the circle of the *bindu*.
That which is at the end of the sixteen is known as the *ājñā*; this is according to the sequence of Khecarī.
Those whose nature is to seek the state beyond the footprints, and those who are devoted to liberation while living.
O God, they do not fall; having reached the final stage and performed the union of the triad, they are cast into the mandala of the limit of command.
And one should visualize a cluster of flame-like rays facing downwards;
O God, by performing nine hundred thousand recitations, one may even accomplish the three worlds.
Listen to the description of the *argha*-maṇḍala as it is taught in the family tradition (*kulācāra*):
in a solitary, secluded, and beautiful place, in the western direction of the letter *E*.
On a site free from the gaze of cattle,
one should prepare a square mandala measuring one cubit, using cow dung.
In the center of that, fashion a circular mandala as the solar disc,
anointed with *alika*, sandalwood, and saffron, and consecrated with the five *praṇava* mantras.
Having cast that five-syllable vidyā onto the palm of the right hand,
one should raise it by means of conjunction through a counter-clockwise rotation.
Then, having formed the fist in the middle, [one draws] the mandala called Akhaṇḍa.
(Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
Having first performed the five praṇavas, one should then arrange the eight ramparts.
O Lord of Devas, beginning from the direction of Indra, one should ascend through the eight directions in sequence with their three seed-syllables; thereafter, one should raise up their hand.
One should cleanse the mirror there, measuring sixteen finger-breadths [in size];
it should be tripled with one finger-breadth [of thickness] and purified with ashes.
One should establish [the deity] with the weapon-mantra of the Goddess and veil it with the armor-mantra;
within the triangle, one should draw the power Kauleśī facing downwards.
Outside of that, one should cause a hexagon to be made, adorned with three girdles;
then, having placed the hero’s vessel, by means of this very procedure.
One should assign her six limbs, including the face, both externally and internally;
and one should offer the three-fold bali-oblation to the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapāla), Vaṭuka, and the Yoginīs.
Having first performed the preliminary rites, one should begin the worship; success is desired to be free from obstacles. One should bring a golden pitcher, or in its absence, one made of silver.
It should be made of copper or even of clay, free from cracks, perfectly level, auspicious,
with a neck as high as a conch shell, golden in color, and devoid of hair or sand.
Having washed it at the beginning and end, one should purify it with the King of Weapons (astra-rāja);
then, having veiled it with the Armor (varma), one should fill it with the substance of *ali*.
O Maheśvara, one should establish [the deity] at the front of the mandala with the Koṅkaṇa weapon;
likewise, the entry of the form occurs through the self by means of the enveloping armor-mantra.
Then one should perform the placement of the Vidyā (vidyānyāsa) according to the sequence beginning with the letter *bha*,
and thereafter perform the sequential worship (*kramārcana*) according to the order of the individual phonemes.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) within the triangle, one should scatter a handful of flowers with the Vidyā;
then, by means of the conjunction of the Vidyā, one should place the six seats (pīṭhaṣaṭka) on the outside.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
[the goddesses] are conjoined with the five praṇavas on the western petal of the Oṃkāra [lotus]: Jālapīṭha is in the southeast, while Pūrṇagiryaka is in the southwest.
In the east is the one called Kāmā; in the wind corner (northwest) is Tisraka;
in the northeast is the one named Koṅkaṇa, which is the refuge of the *ulī*-siddhas.
In the triangle, however, the one called Bhagīśa is to be worshipped in due order;
the five limbs of the Siddhas are in the center, while the six-limbed [mantra] is in the hexagon.
The heart is indeed at Kāmarūpa, while the head is remembered as Pūrṇagiri;
the crest-lock (śikhā) is at the seat of Jālandhara, and the armor (kavaca) is at the one known as Tisra.
One should worship the Eye at the Oṃkāra-pīṭha, and the Weapon-mantra at Koṅkaṇa;
outside of that, on the girdle, one should worship the twelve verses.
The girdle of the Mistress of the Wheel of Vowels consists of the letters from *a* to the final *visarga*;
the second girdle, which is external, consists of the sequence from *ka* to *bha*, and therein lies accomplishment.

The third [syllable] is followed by one like me (mādi-sānta); this indeed is the collection of phonemes. [One should worship] with white flowers scented with *malaya* sandalwood and smeared with saffron.
And formerly, [the image was worshipped] with pure mirrors, as well as with all medicinal herbs,
with fragrant incense, and with lamps made of wheat and other grains.
O God, [one should worship] with the three kinds of intoxicants, with milk-rice, jaggery-rice, and meat-rice; and with raw meat, mud, and the three [other substances].
Having worshipped this Kubjikākrama, one should present the offering;
thereafter, one should worship the jar with three handfuls of flowers dedicated to the Vidyā.
One should offer sandalwood, saffron, and so forth, as well as oneself;
then, one should also offer the argha and flowers thirty-two times, corresponding to the number of syllables.
Having placed both knees upon the ground and having offered the *argha* with the *vidyā*,
one should announce the number of recitations (*japa*) to the Great Wheel.
O Ambā, O Siddhā, likewise O Aghorā, O Supreme Goddess,
grant me my desired great siddhi, which brings about the fruit of all desires.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
thereafter, eight maidens should be worshipped; or six, or three, or even one.
Then, at the beginning of the ritual cycle, the practitioner of mantra will undoubtedly attain accomplishment (siddhi).
One should observe the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) and destroy desire, anger, and the like; from that, success follows without doubt, and through its practice, the desired goal is attained.
Listen now to the rule for the number of recitations, ranging from one thousand up to one hundred thousand;
the rosary for the left hand should be made of crystal or rudrākṣa beads.
A rosary made of lotus seeds should be prepared; one may have it made from whatever is available. In the absence of a rosary, one should begin the recitation using the hand.
O Maheśvara, by means of the procedure prescribed in the Āgamas, one should rotate counter-clockwise, beginning from the base of the left index finger.
One shall gradually attain perfection in recitation (*japa*) through the oral instruction of the guru;
whether it be gross or subtle, one must not overstep the *meru* with the hand.
Having avoided that [central] one, however, he should perform the four outer corners;
the recitation (*japya*) should be performed according to the number of joints (*parvan*), while avoiding both the middle ones.
In this manner, by means of the prescribed sequence and through the mental movement of going and returning while revolving counter-clockwise, perform the act of going.
One should visualize one's own mind as a water-pot through inhalation;
having then exhaled, there is accomplishment both in this world and in the next.
For as many syllables as there are in the count, for that long one should perform the *kumbhaka* (retention).

Together with the breath, by means of its force, it brings about the supreme possession (*āveśa*). According to this very procedure—neither too fast nor too slow—in the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*: [it is said].
Having understood the movement of the intermediate course, one should perform the recitation during the three junctions.
Thus, O Lord, recitation performed with the hands is proclaimed as the most excellent;
or else, listen now to its greatness when performed with a rosary.
When recited one thousand times, an approaching enemy is turned back;
with two thousand, spiritual power is activated; and with three thousand, the perfections of sovereignty are attained.
Through four [qualities], there is good fortune among people; through five, longevity and health;
through six, the attainment of knowledge; and through seven, the [proper] state [of practice] shall come to be.
With eight [months] one perceives some divine form consisting of the Kula; with nine, one attains the yoga of the Khecarakrama, which is Nirvāṇa.
Piercing occurs with ten [recitations], the bursting of seals with twenty,
killing with thirty, and immobilization with forty.
In battle, in the royal court, at a gambling match, in a dispute, or in the midst of enemies;
likewise, the shattering of rocks and the felling of trees—[all this is accomplished] by reciting [the mantra] fifty thousand times; of this there is no doubt.
Even Tilottamā, the celestial maiden, comes under one's control with sixty thousand [repetitions]; of this there is no doubt. What need is there to mention humans?
Kings, regional rulers, and those dwelling in the inner apartments likewise fall under one's power.
And whatever other men in the world are intent on obeying commands,
they may accomplish the Vetālas along with seventy thousand [of them] in the Kumārikā-khaṇḍa.
Likewise, O God, Brahmā himself, in his own embodied form, becomes the moving and unmoving world, including the Dānava Mahiṣāsura.
By reciting this eighty thousand times, one enjoys pleasures in the netherworld (pātāla) and sports with maidens; of this there is no doubt.
O beloved, by ninety [lakhs], one becomes Viṣṇu himself with a body of gold;
having become the lord of the earth, he enjoys sovereignty under a single umbrella.
By means of one hundred thousand [recitations], a human being himself becomes Rudra and dwells there;
a celestial chariot adorned with five chowries comes for him.
Accompanied by eight goddesses, surrounded by sixty-four [deities],
and encircled by many perfected ones (siddhas) like circles of stars and constellations.
In the Kali age, there shall be a great adept, a practitioner endowed with the Vidyā;
he travels by way of the sky to where Bhairavī herself resides.
Dwelling there in the midst, he becomes free from old age and death;
O Lord of the gods, that supreme practitioner is just as I am.
Assuming any form at will, the glorious one becomes a sky-walker through a hundred thousand recitations;
possessing great power and able to take any shape, he indeed sports throughout the three worlds.
In one moment he assumes the form of Śaṅkara, in another the form of Vaiṣṇava;
in a moment the form of Brahmā, and in an instant that of Indra, Sūrya, and Candra.
In one moment he takes the form of Nārāyaṇa, in another he becomes the Wind;
in a moment his form is blazing, and from moment to moment he becomes gross or subtle.
In one moment he was a bird in the sky, in another a lion in the great forest;
then a cat, a jackal, a dog, a camel, and a donkey.
A bull and likewise a ram, an owl and similarly a tiger, a bear and a deer, or else a great elephant.
And in an instant, he may assume various forms in the world of humans; thus,
O Kumārikā, perfection is born, and one becomes free from old age and death.
"By means of one hundred thousand recitations, the practitioner attains the power of flight;
wherever the mind goes, there he finds great glory."
Whatever desire he may conceive, that very thing proceeds for him in an instant;
no place is inaccessible to him, nor does he wander like a moth.
Just as even a single lion slays herds of rutting elephants,
so does this supreme practitioner slay the gods of worldly existence.
The supreme practitioner shall become equal to you through the practice of the Vidyā;
having gone to a solitary tree, a cremation ground, or a crossroads.
In a forest, in a secluded place, or in an empty temple—
these are the places where the infinite recitation of the vidyā should be performed.
O fortunate one, at the time of worship, the knower of the Kaula path,
whose mind has wandered through the night-walk and whose soul is detached from saṃsāra, [should proceed].
O Bhairava, this accomplishment has been declared for one engaged in the ritual service of the Vidyā; however, it is not for a householder who is shrouded in illusion.
Success is not attained in the home in such a way that one may obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
rather, in this very world of the living, one becomes liberated while alive—of this there is no doubt.
But those who are devoted to the worship of Vidyā, whose minds are fixed on it and who are intent upon that as their supreme goal,
having gone indeed to the primordial seat (Ādipīṭha) or to Pūrṇagiri;
O God, whether in the place called Jāla or likewise in the venerable Kāmarūpa, they attain accomplishment without a doubt; for them there is no further suffering.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
He in whose mouth this Great Vidyā resides constantly shall be liberated from all obstacles and attain victory everywhere.
In battle, in the royal court, in gambling, in the midst of enemies, in water and fire, in the forest, on uneven ground, in difficult passes, and likewise on the paths of thieves.
In the presence of scorpions, venomous serpents, intoxicated elephants, and bulls;
during the fall of meteors and when the quarters of the sky are ablaze; and in the midst of a host of Yoginīs—[one should remain].
In a tree frequented by night-stalkers, at a lightning strike, at a crossroads, in battle, at a sacred occasion, at a wheel, on a sacred seat (pīṭha), in a field (kṣetra), and so forth.

"And by the power of this Vidyā, the yogi shall attain auspiciousness. Thus, in the *Ādyāvatāra*, in the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) measuring seventy million [verses] emerged from the path of Meru,

exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the first sacred seat (*pīṭha*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimala-ṣaṭka*), in the *Kādi* division.

In the Ājñāpārameśvara, the Svāminīmata, the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the Avvākrama tradition, this is the bliss named the "Procedure for the Recitation of the Vidyā."
The twelfth bliss: the venerable Vakrā said: "Victory to you, O Lord of Gods, in whose heart this Vidyā resides!"
There shall be happiness, health, prosperity, long life, and a heroic livelihood."
Through the practice of this knowledge, radiance, brilliance, and beauty shall arise;
of this there is no doubt. What anxiety, then, regarding death or battle?
For whomsoever this rare and great vidyā should be perfected, success is held in his hand; he is a perfected one—of this there is no doubt.
A thousand killings of cows, a hundred thousand killings of Brahmins, as well as other sins born of ignorance—all these perish; there is no doubt about this.
This knowledge, as soon as it is remembered, destroys all that is inauspicious;
it is the enjoyment of sweet food and drink, divine luxury, and an elixir of immortality.
An excellent bed, a vehicle, clothing, and ornaments—
by the mere act of remembering once, these come forth through the penetration of the vidyā.

The knowledge of the meaning of categories, the entire wealth of understanding reality, sons and grandsons, the supreme ultimate truth, and the highest gnosis— all these proceed from the penetration of true knowledge.
The supreme reality, the supreme state, the supreme formless yoga,
and incomparable supreme fortune proceed from the penetration of the Vidyā.
The supreme command of Vāgbhava is the highest knowledge and the ultimate bliss;
by the mere act of remembering it once, one proceeds through the penetration of the Vidyā.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
the Śāmbhava [tradition], the knowledge of Śakti, the Vaiṣṇava, the Saurasaṃhitā,
the Buddhist and others, the Ārhata, and those devoted to the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
The six limbs are agitated by the penetration of the Vidyā and not otherwise;
[so too are] the Siddhāntas of the Śaivasiddha and others, as well as the Lākulas, Tumburas, and so forth.
Those such as the Nityātantra and others which proceed from the penetration of the Vidyā,
as well as the Vaidika, Gāruḍa, and Tantra systems characterized by the terminology of the Sutantras.
Yoga, which is supreme nirvāṇa, proceeds from the penetration of the vidyā;
it is that sattvic knowledge established by me in this world.
By the mere act of remembering it once, through the penetration of the vidyā,
all collections of scriptures— whether the Nityātantra and so forth— in every respect, proceed [into action].
O Lord of the gods of gods, O Supreme Lord, the Tantras such as the Svacchanda and others roar many times over until they are agitated by the Vidyā.
The powers of the thirty-two-syllable vidyā do not equal even a sixteenth part [of its power],
just as thousands of elephants turn their backs in the face of a lion.
Likewise, the sciences and mantras turn away from one who has attained true knowledge;
yet, just as the moon nourishes all things moving and unmoving during the night, so does he sustain the world.
In this way, through its complete differentiation, it becomes a source of nourishment,
just as a blazing lamp destroys the darkness.
And one should cut their terrible membrane; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, O fair-faced one, is the venerable Śrīkujā-vidyā of six types.
There is no doubt that it burns away the accumulation of sins residing in the body,
as well as whatever karma— whether auspicious or inauspicious— has been acquired over the course of seven lifetimes; [this is from] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
All that dissolves through the practice of vidyā; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever collections of scriptures there may be, and various mantras, vidyās, and so forth—[all these dissolve].
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of that power of knowledge.
Śrīnātha said: "What you have said is correct; this power arises from the practice of knowledge, and not otherwise."
But why is it that practitioners who are devoted to recitation do not achieve success? O Great Goddess, you should deign to sever this doubt.
The illustrious Vakrā said:
"O God, humans are unfortunate, arrogant with the pride of learning, devoid of noble birth and character, and intent upon approaching those who should not be approached."
Delighting in the consumption of forbidden food, they quarrel here and there; filled with great greed, they cause the destruction of living beings;
they are excessively attached to sensual desires and constantly contemplate the meaning of many scriptures.
They grasp at the meaning of speculative reasoning and dispute with one another.
Through the great delusion of Māyā, they perform evil deeds such as seizing wealth and the like; they engage in censure and act out of passion.
Those who violate the commands of their guru do not respect the samayas; O fair-faced one, they commit treachery against the guru and treachery against the samaya.
Therefore, those men who are devoid of accomplishment even through the practice of knowledge,
and those who have fallen away from austerity— their number is not known.

Satiated with wine and meat, yet longing for dalliance with the wives of others, there is neither worldly enjoyment nor liberation, O God, due to approaching those who should not be approached. (From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
They are known as Śvapacas;
they are vulgar people who drink liquor at will and eat meat at will.
Those shrouded by the veil of ignorance engage in forbidden sexual acts;
for them there is no liberation here, as liberation is held to arise from self-restraint.

From excessive drinking, from desire for enjoyment, likewise from the practice of approaching those who should not be approached, and from eating what should not be eaten— how can there be liberation?
How can there be liberation through improper action? How could it arise from greed for wealth?
These are the most sinful among those corrupted by pride, who revile the proponents of the Tantras.
For those who are attached to wrong paths, no success is found anywhere; they are devoid of the meaning of the scriptures and are transgressors of proper conduct.
There is no accomplishment in their practice, nor are they vessels for liberation;
such are the qualities of disciples, practitioners, and sons of the master.
For those who are habituated to the propitiation of knowledge, devoted to the guru, humble, and observers of the conduct of the samaya, become vessels for spiritual accomplishment.
Established in the state of dualistic conduct, yet free from the three "M" syllables;
devoid of greed, possessing true wealth, peaceful, and always delighting in eternal bliss;
devoted to the meaning of the Agamas, steadfast, and indifferent toward the treatises of logic.
They are devoted, faithful, and dedicated to compassion for all living beings.
Those who possess such distinguished qualities indeed achieve success without deliberation;
for them, the *vidyā* is accomplished, but for others, it is never accomplished at any time.

The knowledge transmitted through the lineage, along with the consecration of the *argha* offering and the maṇḍala, is fully manifest; as long as it has not been understood, how could one obtain accomplishment? (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
That which has emerged from another text and is joined with a different class of birth is not to be understood as a bestower of accomplishment within the Western Tradition (Anvaya) in the House.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice [this] from the mouth of the Guru. Thus,

in the primordial descent (*ādyāvatāra*) of the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) measuring seventy million [verses], emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding a hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primary seat (*ādyapīṭha*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Sixfold [System] (*vimalaṣaṭkanirṇaya*).

In the *Ājñāpārameśvara*, known as the *Svāminīmata*, belonging to the division beginning with *Ka* and comprising the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the *Avvākrama* tradition, this is the bliss named the Arising of the Sequence (*Kramodaya*), within the chapter describing the majesty of the Vidyā.
Śrīnātha said:
"It has been stated that the thirteenth bliss is 'Śiva'; how is that name understood by the world?"
Since it would be incomplete due to its deficiency, how could it attain the status of an agent?
Or how can one who relies on saṃsāra enjoy pleasures?
How can there be death for such a person? Tell me the definitive truth.
The illustrious Vakrā said:
It is the most excellent of all, supremely peaceful, resting upon the reality beyond syllables;
it is the nature of light, free from appearance, infinite, and eternally manifest.
This is to be known as beyond reasoning, self-liberated, and firmly established;
it is indivisible, impenetrable, untainted, and both transcendent and immanent.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the others are the immortal life-force residing therein;
it has the nature of supreme bliss and is devoted to eternal bliss.
It consists of supreme bliss, is peaceful, and is devoid of the eight causes;
it is liberated from the principles of the qualities (guṇatattva) and is free from both that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be accepted.
There is no birth from a womb for him; the all-pervasive Lord exists in every state.
There is no other whatsoever who is not an agent—the embodied Śiva, the Sovereign. From his will has emerged Power, whose form is Sound (nāda) and whose essence is consciousness. *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*
By her, he is led to reality through the concentration on the downward-facing form.
When it shines forth joined with the principles (tattvas), then, having attained identity with them,
it becomes embodied yet remains formless, being pure by its very nature.
Since he relies upon the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), therefore, though stainless, he is born through his actions and moves within the body joined with the principles (tattvas).
Then, through the principle of Māyā, he is indeed stained and experiences enjoyments;
when those objects of enjoyment are exhausted, there arises suffering, yet he continues to take delight, being presided over by his prior [condition].
"Arising from illusion (māyā) and arising from action (karman), as well as that which pertains to this world (aihika) based on the [lower] principles—
impurity (mala) is said to be threefold, impelled by the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas."
When the impure self has attained immersion in power through the will of Śiva, the innate being ascends [to the state] of Māyā.
Then, the attainment born of karma occurs within the city of consciousness established in its true state;
at that time, moreover, the great impurity pertaining to this world arises once again.
The knower of mantras should perform the burning of that very [object] by means of the descent of power (śaktipāta),
having ascended with the Śakti whose nature is supreme bliss, as before.
Overpowered by the prior cause and struck down below,
one should extract the power in the form of a lamp-flame as the state of bliss.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
there, Mahāmāyā is the impurity; she is led playfully along the path of purification upward by him, like the resonance of a spider's thread.
By means of the powerful resonance of Brahman, one may burn away former impurities;
above that is the Supreme Power, which abides together with Śiva.
It dissolves into the supreme void; one should cast it into the highest abode.
There, one should purify the worldly [impurity], for the dross leaves the gold behind.
In brief, this triad of impurities was acquired at the time of union with Śakti by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
When the interior of the self is rendered empty through the power of Rudra’s energy,
then his purification from impurity occurs, and he attains a state of stainlessness.
When one abiding in the primordial nature (prakṛti) is released from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra,
the self must first be purified by the self through the descent of power (śaktipāta) and its resulting conviction.
At that time, only his body remains,
possessed of the principles (tattvas), while merit and demerit have ceased to exist.
When the exhaustion of karma has been attained, there is liberation; of this there is no doubt.
It is just as pure gold, once freed from the naga-stone, is no longer destroyed.
Thus, one whose self is pure and tranquil perishes through attachment to illusion;
yet, by the mere act of initiation, the disciple may attain the supreme state.
Through the descent of power (śaktipāta), purification occurs and impurity abandons the gold;
this [descent] is, in brief, threefold according to Śiva, the Supreme Self.

It is abandoned through piercing (*vedha*), ripening (*pāka*), and the practice of mantra (*mantrābhyāsa*) with ease; this is declared to be the "ripening of impurity" (*malapāka*), which is threefold according to its three natures.
Having pierced through the gross, the subtle, and the supreme, one becomes pure in body;
through the yoga of constant practice, the three impurities are dissolved away.
Freed from the impurity of illusion by means of the eye of knowledge, this lord of yogis becomes liberated while living; when he moves about, he is Śiva himself.
Therefore, he is not stained by them, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water;
even when situated amidst the drops, one who is united with the principles (tattvas) is unstained by will alone.
Likewise, the knower of reality, through the practice of yoga, is not stained by Śiva himself.
For one who has been pierced by the very nature of the command of the Pratyaya, there is indeed the destruction of impurity.
Having reached the limit of saṃsāra, he will attain reality through the process of reversal:
earth dissolves into the earthly element, and water into the sphere of Varuṇa.
For fire indeed goes to dissolution in fire, wind in the circle of air, and the space element goes into the midst of the sky; thus do the five principles [merge].
Sound dissolves into space; touch indeed into the head of wind;
taste into the midst of water; form is offered into the mouth of fire;
and smell dissolves into the earth—thus is the group of five subtle elements (tanmātras).
Speech is in the principle of Vāgīśvara, and the hand is the instrument.
The two feet dissolve into the netherworld (pātāla), the anus into the sphere of wind, and the generative organ into the middle of the sky; such is this fivefold action. In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
through contact with the sense organs of cognition, their dissolution likewise occurs.
The ear dissolves into this sound, and likewise the skin into flesh.
The eye dissolves into the moon and sun; the tongue indeed into the mandala of Rāhu;
the nose into the principle of smell; and above that, the [remaining] fourfold [dissolves].
The mind dissolves into the *bindu*, and the intellect (*dhi*) again into the principle of *vidyā*;
egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) dissolves at the end of Śiva, and all things dissolve into primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The family consisting of twenty-fourfold elements, governed by dharma, kāma, and artha, dissolves into the vessel of the iḍā; liberation is the fourth.
Through the descent of power (śaktipāta) and its arrival, the disciple is liberated;
emptied of Māyā, he goes to Kailāsa, the summit of all.
Therefore, death exists here for that which consists of twenty-four principles;
but there is no death for the Śiva-principle, which has attained liberation.
When there is an absence of the production of illusion, through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and by means of realization,
that Śiva alone exists. Just as a face might enter into a mirror without moving,
so the Lord enters within the *kula*.
Liberated from old age and death, he attains liberation even within this very birth.

Just as one who knows reality through the practice of yoga perceives both the single and the manifold, so too is there the cognition of that which has been pierced, whose nature is the command of consciousness.
When the impurity has fallen away and one has attained mastery here in this lineage, there is liberation;
for one who is pierced [by grace], liberation does not abide through the doctrines of causal reasoning. (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
For one who is devoid of initiation and mantras and lacks the purification of impurities,
karma continues to bind him again and again due to the force of his previous [actions].
Impelled by itself through its own lack of self-mastery, it assumes a threefold impurity;
not knowing the supreme reality, one is bound therein and is not liberated.
Not from holy places such as those for fasting, nor when the self has been purified by vows, nor during a fast, nor during an eclipse of the moon or sun, nor even in battle.
In a relationship involving one who has sought refuge, or in the presence of cattle, water, or fire,
at the roots of a temple of the gods, in Vārāṇasī, or at Jaleśvara;
In Kedāra and all such places, or even in the battle at Kurukṣetra,
there is no liberation for living beings; those people suffer in vain, yet they merely attain heaven, where the eightfold qualities prevail.
A residue of debt persists within the mortal sphere of the world.
When the auspicious and inauspicious have been encountered, they experience pleasure and pain;
without the exhaustion of karma, how can their liberation be established?

Through initiation alone, even without practice, one attains purification from impurity by virtue of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), as determined by signs such as trembling, paralysis, and so forth.
In this world, experience is common to all; yet Prakṛti, by the will of Puruṣa,
is said here to be supported by Puruṣa through its own activity.
When one does not rely on emptiness within emptiness, being free from expectations and having ascended to the state where there is no existence, then the establishment of existence is grasping.
It would come to be.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
The knower of mantras should purify, according to the prescribed ritual, those very external rites that have indeed arisen spontaneously in direct perception.
Śrīnātha said:
Thus, there is an infinite accumulation of karma based on māyā;
how then, O piercer, does the seed of māyā exist within the three worlds?
By the mere recollection of that, what fruit accrues to human beings? [Tell me] the true nature of the body, which is a mixture of the seven constituent elements (dhātus).
Thus, the reality of the means of valid cognition consists of the apprehension of the channels of the bones;
how is it that this is likewise declared here in every body within the manifest city?
"O Umā, tell me everything in such a form.
Śrīvakrā said:
"In the beginning, the supreme goddess Tanvī is the one who wields the staff and is beautifully delighted."
One should meditate upon Mahāmāyā, devoid of vowels, blazing upon the seat of Śiva,
straight and clear with a great current, sealed by the Yoni-mudrā.
Resorting to the root of Khecarī, she converses with Śiva;
and at the end of the heart-lotus, she is led by one who possesses the luster of a Kadamba flower.
One should remember her with the moon of gnosis in the bindu-cakra at the crown of the head;
she, pure as snow, jasmine, and the moon, is led to the supreme void.
While [the breath] is waning, one should remember Vakrā; make it abide in the nose.
O Daughter of the Mountain, the great flood of eternal bliss indeed flows there.

Having correctly brought about the destruction of illusion through the maintenance of absorption in yoga, and having performed the dissolution, emergence, and transformation, one should become possessed of right conduct.
When the consciousness that was [formerly] veiled by illusion has been destroyed, it becomes as pure as clear crystal;
through constant practice by means of this instrument, one then attains the sleep of yoga (yoganidrā).

In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the connection regarding the performance of *māyā* has been taught for the sake of attaining perfection; and for the sake of the liberation of those seeking release, the divisions of power (*śakti*)— both supreme (*parā*) and non-supreme (*aparā*)— are explained.
Śrīnātha said:
How do they know the first rising and setting in due order within the Śākta, Āṇava,
and Śāmbhava sequences, as well as their restraint and grace?
The venerable Vakrā said:
One should purify the complete purification of suppression within the internal sacrifice—
that which was previously extracted from the Bhairava-āgama as consisting of the nature of Śiva.
"By her, through the sequential worship performed previously, the exhaustion of karma occurred within her own body.
Śrīnātha said:
"How was karma described at the beginning? What is the remedy for its exhaustion?"
"How is there purification for human beings? Tell me, what is the path to liberation? Śrīvakrā said:
"The Tantrikas do not find the complete purification of karma belonging to themselves."
Therefore, according to the Kula teaching, there is no liberation for them here;
[this concludes] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
And Śiva is the agent in sovereignty and in the fourfold collection of beings.
The Supreme Self is without space; it arises from that which possesses space. It is the self-existent cause in the world, yet it is insentient and of the nature of emptiness.
When the individual soul (jīva) is no longer independent, being devoid of right and wrong conduct,
it proceeds through the practice of yoga in this world with its essential nature become empty.
And for that [consciousness] as well, the cause is the upward-moving consciousness, the sun of knowledge;
it shines in the form of pure awareness, whether in its rising, its setting, or their unity.

The reflection of the moon and sun within the stainless [reality], which is the essence of the poison of desire and resides within the Nirañjana, is the partless [state] born from the son of the River (the Fire).
He who stands as the light-form himself, burning away darkness, is the Puruṣa common to all; he is Bhairava because he sustains all.
Stainless, complete, and all-pervading, like clarified butter within milk,
the reality of Śiva is the supreme bliss, hidden and untainted.
Ineffable, imperishable, tranquil, all-pervading, and facing every direction—
from Him emerged the Power (Śakti) as His Will, appearing as a straight line directed downwards.
