The terrible flame of fire, possessing great luster, resides in the midst of the visarga;
it pervades the path of emanation within the two states consisting of dharma and adharma.
The innate power is Māyā, arisen for the sake of creation;
she sustains the three qualities, is exceedingly fierce, has the form of sound, and is Manonmanī.
(Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
The deity Śiva is both staff-shaped and formless, yet possesses form;
this impurity of illusion is the karma that arises from the partless [Absolute].
Therefore, that entire yogin stands above the principle of *māyā*;
thus, previously, his bondage was designated by the name "the impurity of *māyā*."

In the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world], the bondage of karma exists regarding the state of being an agent. Brahmā and the others, composed of the five elements, are the incarnations for the sake of manifestation;
they are neither artificial nor innate, but are merely enveloped by material experience.
Afflicted by illusion and delusion, the Bindu is the Self beyond the world.
And that very [nature] pervades primordial matter (prakṛti) and consists of the bondage of karma;
that bound soul (paśu), overcome by the bond of fetters, exists within the three qualities (guṇatraya).
One performs action through the quality of goodness (sattva), while one abiding in passion (rajas) pursues desire;
one possessed by darkness (tamas) remembers sinful deeds, experiencing both pleasure and pain.
Without understanding heaven and hell, one does not find liberation;
one experiences the results of good and evil deeds—the desirable and undesirable that were wished for by the mind.
In this same way, honor and dishonor, as well as impurity,
are to be understood [as obstacles] even in the world of Brahmā, in the world of Viṣṇu, and in the world of Indra which possesses the luster of the moon.
O Bhairava, he experiences the fruits of his karma in the world of Yakṣas, among the Gandharvas, in the families of Rākṣasas and Piśācas, and in the eightfold heaven.
When an impure evil deed has been committed, one goes instantly to hell,
or likewise to the animal womb or as a wild beast in this most terrible world of mortals.
Bound by the noose of karma, he falls into terrible hells, even among mobile and immobile beings; thus does he experience [the results].
The auspicious and the inauspicious.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
By that [means], through the power of karma, the yogi becomes multiform like a gem;
and by cutting off karma through practice, he shall then enter into nirvāṇa.
Pervading the void, that Bhairava remains within the worlds;
having destroyed Māyā, he is known as the Jīva in the other, the Western City.
It arises on the peak of jewels; by that, liberation is ordained.
Knowing this, one should cause the removal of its impurity accordingly.
Śrīnātha said: Thus, his threefold impurity— consisting of that which is innate, that which is dependent on karma,
and that which is natural as well as mental— arises from the delusion of *māyā* within the ocean of worldly existence.
"How is their destruction proclaimed in this fierce sequence?
Śrīvakrā said:
"Having performed the act of cessation, [one should practice] the sequence of the mandala arising from the five."
Relying upon the Yoni-mudrā, joined with the Māyā of Bhairavī,
and presiding over the practice of Kumbhaka, by that means the jewel [of the bindu] shall ascend.
One should gradually come to rest until [the energy] reaches Raudrī at the crown of the head;
through that penetration, the destruction of the world's impurities occurs.
This indeed is the setting of illusion; it becomes stainless gold.
[The stages are: shaking, entering, trembling, sleep, reeling, and the ant-like sensation.
The dance of a single woman, the speech [of a child], the shedding of tears like a deer, the various leaps, and the roar of a lion— these are the eleven signs of recognition.
When the stage of Rudra’s portion is reached, having attained the state of dissolution above the Fourth (turyātīta),
all karmas perish once that which is both supreme and non-supreme (parāpara) is perceived.
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
being the very nature of supreme bliss (*parānanda*), is the embodiment of bliss;
by knowing this distinction between burning and nourishing, the destruction of karma occurs.
Having gradually made the body dependent upon liberated knowledge and performing worship in successive stages,
one who is completely freed from the bonds of Paśu falls into the circle of knowledge.
There is the experience of command, possession, and the frequent arising of horripilation.

One should constantly worship the lineage (*anvaya*), and repeatedly grasp the lineage as the foremost. Through the gradual practice of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajāpa*), one attains the power of moving through the sky (*khegati*).
In the southern region [is the abode] of Śiva, the lord who bears five forms.
"When the terrible Kali age arrives, one should then worship that [deity] in due order.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"This is the command; by the falling away of impurity, the Niṣkalā [form] becomes the Sakalā according to the Āgama."
It has been stated that [this] is not taught in other philosophical systems;
thus, I have brought down for you this "Five Stages" (Kramapañcaka) of the hermitage.
But today I have clearly understood the great ripening of karma;
how could there be burning for him who has dissolved [himself] into the Krama-maṇḍala?
The venerable Vakrā said:
Once again, by means of another sequence,
[I shall give] the determination of the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) in this sequence [known as] Vṛddhakaumāra, Siddhaguhyā, and Kulakandara.
The practitioner who fulfills the sequence is an adept possessed by the Vajra;
placing his own mudrā in the hand of the yoginī, he directs his mind downward.
The Mudrāmaṇḍala is circular, the hermitage of the Supreme Lord;
it is made of pure molten gold, and in its center is a circle. —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
The solar disc is slightly reddish due to its counter-clockwise rotation;
in its center is an unbroken wheel, slightly reddish and resembling light.
In the center of that is the supreme island, as white as cow's milk and tranquil like Varuṇa.
One should remember him wandering there within the teaching of the three lineages (olī).
O Lord of the World, within that wheel of birth is a circle of the bindu,
resembling a whirling firebrand due to its counter-clockwise rotation.
The supreme Vidyā, the highest Goddess, who is contained within that,
is Śakti in her formidable form, the light-form Manonmanī.
The flame of the lamp’s wick is terrible, blazing and free from smoke;
possessing the luster of thousands of millions of Rudras, she is the supreme and yet non-supreme power of Rudra.

The Śrīdevī, whose nature is consciousness, has been contemplated by the Lord of Śiva as having a curved form through the nature of the Command (ājñā), yet she is the expansion [of that consciousness]. The Bindu, bearing ten million Rudras, is the Power (śakti) that extends to the dissolution of the earth.
Her supreme power is Tejas, the Śakti of Rudra, Maheśvarī,
Kulakubjikā; she blazes with her own four rays within the Raudra-maṇḍala in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
In this way, one should recollect that stream of rays through concealed retention.
One should purify the body of the disciple with a single-minded exhalation;
trembling and horripilation occur when [the breath is held] with a firm fist.
And when the principle of Śakti has been reached, having raised [the breath] very slowly by means of the flow through the central channel, it should be brought to the end of the Suṣumnā as before.
One should cause it to enter the region of the navel, coiled like a serpent,
in the form of a whirling firebrand through a counter-clockwise rotation.
That digit (kalā), having been performed in four ways in counter-clockwise rotation, is led by way of the upper path as far as the fivefold space of the heart.
She is led to the supreme abode within the mandala of the Nameless Path;
and above that, she is being dissolved in the center of the Meru-mandala.
At the end of the fourfold sequence, one should cause the mere resonance (dhvanimātra) to enter;
one should raise the Power (śakti) in its stainless form from the sphere of the root-center (kandamaṇḍala).
Gradually, gradually, bring about the dissolution of that which has the form of sound into the upward path;
its arising is within the *bindu*, and likewise its setting again.
"In that very place, on the upward path, effect the dissolution of Śakti.
Thus, according to the various traditions of the Āgamas, the New Moon (Amāvāsyā) has been enjoined.
This is the ripening of karma; however, through the maintenance of the penetration of power, when the agitation of the body has occurred, there is the destruction of the impurities of the disciples.
When the Kumārikākhaṇḍa proceeds within the body, then the exhaustion of karma occurs;
this [process] of projection and burning is established in the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).
In the form of supreme bliss, it revolves through the determination of the sequence;
first is the gross sacrifice, and then follows the subtle method.
Henceforth, I shall again explain the *pūrṇabhedha* according to another sequence, as transmitted through the *āgama*, divided into eighteen divisions.
One should draw forth from the upper station, from the center of the *bindu*, that which is in the form of semen;
she who was previously diminished now rains down the nectar of fullness.
The crooked power (vakraśakti), whose self is infinite, is contemplated as having a gentle form;
at the arrival of dissolution, she is emanation (sṛṣṭi), the supreme digit (kalā) known as Ciciṇī.
And one should bring [the deity] at the end of the ring finger, resembling a drop of milk;
then the consecration occurs by that very [deity] in its prior form.
In the heart-cakra, which is the locus of fullness, she possesses a radiance equal to the full moon;
having thus visualized her with the mind, one should cause her to enter one's own cakra.
Laughing with supreme bliss, that power whose nature is consciousness, being joyfully celebrated, flows into the mandala of the Nameless and Nameless;
therefore, the full-moon night of satisfaction, filled with nectar, proceeds.
This is the consecration of the command, distinguished by the emanation of the scriptures.
Having purified [the path] through the movement of going and coming, one should thereafter perform the sequential worship. In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the first part of the Kriyāpāda, the "Possession by Power" (śaktyāveśa) is here described.
The true nature of the Heart and the nature of the Void, the distinctions of Yoga, both supreme and inferior,
and the sequence of existence— these are utterly sealed within the Primordial Seat.
Thus, in the great Bhairava sacrifice,
the sequence of the path to liberation was introduced by means of the scripture within the wheel.
Thus, whoever constantly practices this Devyākrama Sūtra, which is filled with the mental sacrifice, that yogi shall become a destroyer of bonds.
The illustrious one who possesses liberation while living is not tainted by prior sin;
through practice with a single group, he proceeds for two, three, or five [stages].
Merely by remembering [the Guru], even a slayer of a Brahmin shall attain perfection;
how much more so one whose soul is purified of rebirth and who observes the commands of the Guru!
Therefore, the subtle body is indeed composed of the six elements of primordial nature;
by reciting [the mantra] thirty-two hundred thousand times, one abides within the mandala of the mudrā.
The abandonment of the ground, agitation in the city, signs such as the bursting of the *mudrā*,
shaking and penetration through movement, or even the transition into another; indeed,
the eight [siddhis] beginning with *aṇimā* manifest as direct perceptible signs.
Through mere meditation upon her form as ten million flashes of lightning, union is attained.
One should perform all rites, including the immobilization of enemy armies,
as well as whatever concerns the past, the future, the present, the distant, or the near.
The cognition of hearing from afar, the employment of the Kaula language,
the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
and the supreme, subtle oral tradition of the Krama above the Krama— this becomes twofold.
The gross [body] arises from the subtle body through forty-two stages in sequence;
from its light, it emerges in the three mandalas for the sake of the sequential process.

Having understood the prior sequence of yoga, one should subsequently receive the consecration of the command; when accomplishment is attained through such conviction, then one is a worshiper of the sequence.

Thus ends the bliss named *Kramodaya*, in the introduction to the *Kādibheda* division, within the description of the chapter on the destruction of impurities (*malakṣaya*). The venerable Kaulīśa said:
"The hero who has been authorized and consecrated, desiring the state of a hero... This is the fourteenth bliss.
The practitioner of mantras should observe the vow of knowledge correctly, according to the prescribed ritual.
"Therefore, I wish to hear about that unsurpassed vow of the Vidyā.
Śrīvakrā said:
"Listen, O God, I shall proclaim the supreme vow of the Vidyā."
Whether one has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot— whether a graduate or a student—
one must perform the external vow, which is concealed within the Kaulika conduct.

Whether abiding in the stages (*krama*) or established in the vows (*vrata*), a yogi who wears the five seals (*pañcamudrā*), is devoted to ashes, and is naked as the directions, attains perfection in every state.
Whether wearing rags or bark garments, or adorned with all kinds of ornaments, or clad in red robes, or even assuming whatever attire he desires.
"In whatever dress the supreme practitioner conducts himself, that very thing is declared to be his vow; such is the certainty of the scripture."
Whatever ornament he wears, whatever he speaks with his voice,
and whatever action he performs through his conduct of concealment— all these follow in sequence.

This is the external vow (*bāhyavrata*), a practice known as the "vow of the end" (*antavratamanāmaka*). In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*, one should establish the mind like matted hair (*jaṭāvat*), because of the disregard for external activity.
One should yoke the mind as one and practice the circle of the self;
that is the matted hair, not the burden of matted locks—it is the purification of the body for those who observe vows.
By the mere recollection of the command, one falls like a tree with its roots severed;
one knows nothing at all, nor hears, nor sees.
Thus, one who has been shorn by the Command is truly shorn; one whose hair is merely shorn is not shorn. For him whose crest is like a lamp, I, the Great Arīkā, am his Vidyā.
That which is perceived by one established in samādhi is the crest-lock (śikhā); it is not merely a lock of hair, for it is the crest-lock [of realization].
Karma has been reduced to ashes by the rays within the maṇḍala.
Having meditated upon the destruction of impurity, this is liberation; this is ash, free from disease;
it is called the garment, the sky, the indivisible, and the circle of emptiness.
In the midst of that is the power of the sprout (aṅkurā-śakti), the abode of the worlds of the three times;
it is designated as "Naked" (digambara), for one who is merely naked is not truly digambara.
One who is purified by the *kula* practices the *para-brahma-kula* as a *kaula*; with all dualities completely exhausted, he becomes a practitioner of the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
That which is exceedingly smooth, supreme, and pure as the support of the Kadamba tree—by drinking that, purification occurs; this is the true bath, and not otherwise.
Between the *camara* and the *ciñciṇī*, it is differentiated in every city;
there, the movement of the utterance (*uccāra*) is to be known as the "delighting one" (*ramaṇī*) by the name of the Hero (*vīra*).
Free from the external sequence, the stream that rains down nectar—
the yogi, established in samādhi, becomes the sky within the sky of the sky.
That is declared to be *valkala*; it is not skin that is called *valkala*.
By means of this sequential distinction, the principles (*tattvas*) abide within the configuration of the locations.
This is declared to be true adornment; it is not merely an ornament of gold.
Having understood the entire family to be the gateway, it is called the "all-encompassing ornament."
The supreme power called Vidyā is established in two divisions:
it is the power of consciousness (cicchakti), which is the attainment (siddhi), and the auspicious Sāvitrī, who resides within the phonemes.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
He who would proceed upon the path of the Vidyā according to the ritual action seen in the scriptures [should perform] meditation,
worship, recitation, fire-oblation, as well as the observance of the pledges (samaya).

This is declared to be the vow of knowledge (vidyā-vrata), the unsurpassed external vow. Knowledge, however, should be known as residing in the navel; it moves as far as the end of the twelve [finger-breadths].
In all places of observance, by him the great vow of knowledge was undertaken;
[therein dwell] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
These are indeed the stations of the vow where that supreme [goddess] delights;
having known that supreme station, he is one who has practiced the vow of knowledge (*vidyā*).
Knowledge is a row of syllables, and that row is indeed downward-facing within the wheel.
Among them, however, it stands as the one established in the vow of blood, which cuts through the veil of ignorance.
The cloth is red within, not red on the outside;
he is one who wears the red garment and awakens beings through the six modes.
This is known as the Kaulika vow; it does not belong to those who observe external vows.
O God, the bearer of the five mudrās is therefore the cause of the fivefold [manifestation].
Adorned with these, Śiva, bearing the five mudrās, should abide in the heart; adorned with these, the mantra-practitioner, resorting to the sacred field (kṣetra), should wander about.
In a cremation ground, a forest, a well, a garden, an auspicious temple, an empty royal palace, a mountain, or at a crossroads, the mantra-practitioner [should dwell].
O sinless one, [one should practice] at a crossroads, on village streets, or on the shore of the great ocean; or on the bank of a river confluence, or beneath a solitary tree.
In a single-linga shrine, or in a grove, or in the eight sacred fields,
respectively, is the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Prayāgā, Varuṇā, Kollā, and Aṭṭahāsā are victorious!
Caritra, Ekāmraka, and likewise Devīkoṭṭa as the eighth—
among these, the mantra-practitioner who desires the accomplishment of the Yoginīs should wander.
Carrying a skull-topped staff and observing silence, he should always wander with speed.
Or [he holds] a hand-drum, a noose, and a sword, as well as a trident and a shield.
The iron arrow, the knife, the discus, the goad, the mace, the bow,
the club, the dagger, the spear, as well as the staff and the water-pot.
One should likewise carry these most excellent weapons even at the time of ritual practice;
this supreme vow consists of the number of weapons and the five daily rites.
The practitioner of mantra should practice for twelve days, or even for a fortnight or a month;
or else for six months, a year, two years, or even three.
Even a slayer of a Brahmin attains perfection by practicing the mantra for twelve years;
one whose inner self is purified becomes an awakener of the lineage.
One shall partake of accomplishment without delay and be liberated through the lineage;
O Lord of Gods, within a single year, one is honored by the members of the maṇḍala.
Together with the excellent women of the inner apartments, the king’s son, along with his retinue—
whether superior, inferior, or middling— will undoubtedly come under [his] control.
Twice a year, yakṣa maidens with eyes agitated by desire come to his city and instantly give up their lives.
Within three years, the seven netherworlds and the daughters of the gods and other celestial beings—
intoxicated with passion and their eyes wandering with lust— come under one's control.
Moving with the gait of rutting elephants, possessing inexhaustible youth,
they are agitated by the lord of practitioners and instantly surrender their lives.
One should accomplish the Brahma-worlds and so forth in four, five, and likewise six [years];
O lady of excellent hips, in the seventh year, the Rudras are established.
"They are accomplished for the best of practitioners"—this is the certainty of the scripture.
[This is] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa;
in the eighth [chapter] is that which is called Īśvara, and in the ninth is Sadāśiva.
Having become tenfold, the Great One sports in the sky;
by means of eleven, O Mahādeva, he attains the state of Rudra.

Endowed with the twelve qualities and possessed of the powers beginning with *aṇimā*, the mantra-practitioner who knows the sequence becomes a *vidyādhara* and goes to the state of moving through the sky;
for that auspicious yogi, imperishable and invincible, wanders everywhere at will.
Thus, O sinless one, the fruit of the vow has been told to you;
now I shall explain the path of yoga, the adoption of specific places and stages of life, and the purification of the body through practice as it was in former times.
What is called a "house" is actually a cremation ground; the body is the cremation ground within the house.
But it is proclaimed that one whose mind has departed wanders without rest.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa it is said:
"Ka is declared to be the body; at its end are the two eyes.
Through those two, the Self perceives the world consisting of speech, along with all that is moving and unmoving."
The forest is said by him to be situated at the end of the body;
the mind is designated as the well,
so it has been designated.
There, the field-possessor (kṣetrin) should proceed to the support; by that, it is known as a "well" (kūpa), for he forms many intentions.
The mind, when aroused, resides in the navel;
that which resides in the navel perceives [itself] within all living beings.
Because it leads one to the attainment of the state, it is called a "garden" (udyāna);
O Lord, it bestows that immortal state which resides in the sky.
The yogi moves within the family (kula) of the bonds consisting of dharma and adharma; therefore, O Lord, the embodied soul is always called the "family of the gods" (devakula).
The King is designated as the Self for those whose minds are united with the principles;
he abounds in qualities such as sound and is adorned by the collection of all principles.
Therefore, he performs action and goes along with that very same [action];
ever joined in the state beyond mind (*unmanatva*), the mind is declared to be empty. Because the "empty" is the royal palace, it is always dear to him in the state beyond mind.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
the mountain is the mouth of the Guru; one should rely upon its summit.
Standing there upon the mountain peak, he wanders through it all;
I shall now describe the crossroads: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrikā.
The wandering of a person who is joined with Ambikā is declared to be the "crossroads"; this is what has been described as that path.
O Maheśvara, the path is said to consist of three channels;
among them, Iḍā constantly moves along the triple-path, performing coming and going.
He who, established in a single state at the triple-path (tripatha), performs [the practice], attains success.
The village is said to be the body, and the self is remembered as the embodied one (dehin).
The ālaya is the support for all sentient beings' experiences of pleasure and pain, high and low;
it moves upward and downward like the foundation of a street, the Lord of the World.
Therefore, the channel (nāḍī) is remembered as the "street" (rathyā), for it belongs to the Self beginning with Brahmā;
likewise, the "bank" (taṭa) is fully explained as the "utterance of Śiva" (śivoccāra).
But the end of suffering is beyond the *rala* [vowels], known as the shore of the ocean;
there the all-pervading Lord Śiva, the supreme cause, moves.
The practitioner of mantra remains constantly, and his conduct is revealed at the end;
[this is from] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
That supreme Kuṇḍalinī, which is the support of the eternal sound, resounds.
That river, which is the form of yoga, flows eternally into the ocean of the void;
it is joined with the supreme confluence and is revealed at the end of the transmental state.
That confluence is fully described as being proclaimed by the river;
it is the support of power, both supreme and inferior, which flows everywhere.
By that [power], the all-pervading one is led; this is declared to be the bank of the river.
O Supreme God, there is one tree; the supreme Śakti is one, yet she is threefold.
The single channel born of the senses is revealed as being designated by the term *bindu*;
it wanders day and night without ceasing, yet again it attains dissolution in the supreme abode, which is beyond the mind and free from affliction.
Therefore, O Lord, I have declared that for practitioners there is but one tree;
the supreme reality is indeed one alone—the supreme nectar that is the support of the *liṅga*.
Furthermore, from the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: "O God, this is the Ekaliṅga; now, as for the other grove (ṣaṇḍa)..."
The heart is said to be a lake endowed with eight petals;

The seed-syllable of Śakti, known as Haṃsa and identified with Manonmanī, is served by the one whose heart is the lotus abiding within the person (pudgala); it rejoices there.
That is described in the scripture as the "Ṣaṇḍa"; from that, there are eight fields (*kṣetra*).

Those which are *pīṭhas* are indeed *kṣetras*, and those which are *kṣetras* are *pīṭhas* in sequence;

though seeing, he does not see, and though being seen, he is not seen.
The goddesses, whose characteristics are intermingled, cannot be discerned at all.

O lady of beautiful hips, they arise within the elemental coverings of earth, water, and fire through the specific support of their seats,

One performs the internal, the external, the vow, the conduct, and the practice.

In all the limbs, beginning with the head, and in the joints of the major and minor members.

Therefore, I shall explain in due order and according to the truth the ḍamaruka of the renowned wandering person (pudgala) who possesses the nature of impetus.

Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and likewise Raudrī, whose nature consists of will, knowledge, and action—

The iron arrow (*nārāca*) and the spear (*śakti*), which consist of the utterance of the instruments (*karaṇa*), remain established; indeed, it is through the power of cessation (*nirodhinī*) that one awakens these very five instruments.

like a wheel, she rotates eternally, with Parāparā stationed at the goad.
O King, though situated internally, she remains established through external means;
she constantly performs her activities while sitting as well as lying down.

O beloved, the resonance (nāda) situated in the state of the pestle (muṣala), moving upward in the form of a line, consists of running, leaping, obstructing, contracting, and expanding; this is the section concerning the maiden (kumārikākhaṇḍa).
Having pierced that, the movement upward is called *muṣala*, which is Sadāśiva;
it is the bow and the unnameable target by which one pierces the Supreme.
Having filled [the vessel] with the supreme mind-eye accompanied by emission,
one should wander about with the skull-cup as the instrument, facing downwards;
indeed, it is purified by the two seasons and situated within the causal source.
By this final instrument, the supreme Kaṭṭārikā is to be known.
O Three-eyed One, one attains union with reality through the mace;
for that single [channel] has entered the supreme aperture and bestows auspicious nectar.
Those who have gone with the mace do not return;

O Lord, that is the perfection of yoga and the power within the internal sound (nāda);

The washerwoman, the leather-worker, the outcaste woman, the brahmin woman, the Kaulinī, the Cakralolā, the Maithunī, and the Nārasiṃhakī—

The eating of sacrificial porridge (caru) together in one place by both the lowest castes and the twice-born.

In the Ājñāpārameśvara, the Svāminīmata, the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the Avvākrama tradition, this is the bliss named the Chapter on Conduct.

O Great Śambhu, out of my former affection, I shall declare the certainty:
she who is the supreme power (parā-śakti), O God, whose form is the womb of the universe.
For therein everything that consists of speech, as well as the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, has arisen; therefore she is the Mother, and she is the Supreme Goddess Śakti.
She is called *duhitṛ* because she arises (*udbhava*) from him, and she is called *duhitṛ* because she milks (*duhana*) the world;
furthermore, she is likewise called his second daughter and his sister.
The Supreme Goddess, whose form is the Bhaga, is subtle and Unmanā, together with the Self;

In that very same way, the sister residing within the self, whose form is the *bhaga*, is self-born, exceedingly subtle, and has spread forth within the center of the cave. —From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*—
Arising from herself, self-born, and called the innate (sahajā) digit,
she dwells within all living beings as the supreme one who abides at the limit.
Indeed, there is one Supreme Goddess who stands before you, born of the lowest caste;
being entirely free from passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas), she is known as Rajakī.
The entire world, both stationary and moving, is colored with its whole body;
it moves about because it has been colored by that secret passage within the skin.
She should be known as Carmakārī and is likewise called Mātaṅgī;

she is the foremost among all scriptures and has arisen as the leader.
Therein, nothing else whatsoever exists within the mind; it is *manonmanī*.
She is declared to be *unmanā*, for she is the supreme bearer of immortality.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
"O Ānanda, that state of equanimity belongs indeed to one whose mind is intoxicated with the bliss of wine;

But upon the completion of the yoga practice, immediately thereafter,
having abandoned the expansion of cyclic existence, [one abides] in the five [realms], such as Kāmarūpa and the others.

for that very great vow (*mahāvrata*) is Nirvāṇa throughout all the lineages (*oli*).
When beings attain dispassion, then the vow leading to Nirvāṇa is reached;
I shall describe the path of the Kaulikas, which has emerged as the sequence of the Sky-farers (Khecarī).
One should perform protection within the family of the vow; Piṅgalā, however, is nakedly clad.
With that very [mantra], one should cause the performance of the terrible [rite] joined with the Vidyā, both supreme and non-supreme.

His face is contracted, cutting through the impurities of saṃsāra;

Those who contemplate yoga should collect alms either five or seven times, or again eight or ten, or even thirty-two times.

Equipped with the five weapons— the iron arrow (nārāca), the knife (kṣurikā), the sword (khaḍga), the small dagger (kartarī), and the sickle (paṅkaṭī)— he is well-adorned with the weapons of the Kaulas.
He may wander over the entire earth as the foremost among the three lineages;

That which is called the "vow" (vrata) of the Vidyā should be known as the "Command-Paṭa.

just as before; and one should make twenty-seven alms-meals, or ten, or even four.
The terrible weapon of the five missiles has emerged from the primordial seat.

Having likewise colored a skull-cup made of copper with red ochre,
The practitioner of mantras, having taken up the five weapons as before and the weapon of Bhairava, should wander about; this is the auspicious vow of yoga.
The threefold vow has been shown for the Ulīns who have attained perfection through the lineage;
for these, the most excellent seat is a very soft deer-skin.
Among those three seats, for the eldest, the middle, and the youngest,
the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana) is first, and the lotus posture (padmāsana) is second.
In the third vow, known as the Svastika, preceded by the ritual of the mudrās,
the Lord of Yogins should always sleep in houses such as those at Prayāga.

The heroic conduct, the heroic vow, and the activities associated with the assembly of heroes consist of the messenger girls' going everywhere, both externally and internally.
In the practice of the night-walker, those who observe the vow must perform their conduct in three ways:
they should not restrain the mind; wherever the mind goes, there they should go, and they should practice the conduct of desire.
This sign has been declared as threefold, consisting of the manifest and the collection of vows.

One should always practice devotion toward the eight family goddesses (*kuladevī*) and should always worship the eight [goddesses], beginning with the courtesan (*veśyā*), according to the Kaula sequence.

Now, one who is free from [the regular] conduct but seeks the goal of *caru* may perform it even at home; by means of the night-practice (*niśācāra*), after the consumption [of the substance], the supreme state is attained.
One who observes this vow becomes equal in power to me in person, like Rudra;
by means of this unmanifest vow, one may assume any form at will.
— The Section on the Virgin: The characteristic of the Kaula,
which is established within the domain of those situated in the sequence of transmigratory existence.
The secret undertaking of the vows has been fully explained to the masters;
however, their conduct (*caryā*)—which is the union with the *sadhā*—has not been told to them.
Therefore, they call it the Unmanifest; one should practice the vow, joined with self-conduct, as the most secret vow.
Thus [is the teaching] for the Kaulika king who is purified by the scriptures.
The stage of conduct has been fully explained and concluded with its definitive resolution;
it includes the practice of the vow regarding what is not given, as well as the lineage transmission of what is not given.
There is nothing to be grasped, for there is no grasping of an object in another; by following the conduct prescribed in the scriptures of the gurus, one avoids falling.
Whatever vow, practice, or Kaulika union has been bestowed by that very [teacher], all of that becomes fruitful for the disciple; of this there is no doubt among those who observe the vows.
Otherwise, there is no vow, no practice, no renunciation, and nowhere any ritual sequence,
as long as one does not perceive the knowledge that is the pure Kaulika meaning of the Mata.

"As long as there is no destruction of delusion, one should therefore embrace the scripture. Thus, in the *Ādyavatāra*, within the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage measuring seventy million verses emerged from the path of Meru,

exceeding a hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primary seat (*ādyapīṭha*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimalaṣaṭka*).

In the *Kādibheda*, the *Ājñāpārameśvara*, the *Svāminīmata*, the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the *Avvākrama* tradition, this is the chapter on the section concerning Conduct (*Caryāpāda*), titled "Bliss. Śrīnātha said:
"The lord of yogis, peaceful and devoted to the conduct of the Kula, desires spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*)."
O Lord, how should one wander for alms, and how should one utter speech?
O Goddess, you have indicated that alms-gathering should be performed among eight families;
please, out of your grace, explain the determination of the conventions of speech.
The venerable Vakrā said:
The sixteenth bliss consists of Prayāga, Avaranā, Kollā, Aṭṭahāsa, and Jayantikā.
Caritra, Ekāmraka, and likewise Devikoṭṭa as the eighth.
O Lord of Gods, now hear as I describe that supreme convention of terminology within the eight houses, which brings about both spiritual accomplishment and liberation.
*Ku lā ī ā*, O *tribhuvanāvalī*, this is the instruction for practice in the Divine Tradition (*divyāmnāya*): "Give me the sacrificial pap (*caruka*), *ī ā*.

This syllabic conduct (*akṣarī caryā*) has been declared at Prayāga, O fair-faced one; it is called the letter *ku* in the house of a courtesan, having gone forth spontaneously during the night-wandering (*niśācāra*).
*Ku śā ī ā*, the instruction for practice in the *Kulāmnāya* concerning the entire series of worlds: "Give me the sacrificial pap (*caruka*), ī ā.
This second practice is said to be the one from Kāmarūpa, known as *Kunāmikā*;
the goddess *Śuṇḍinī* of Varaṇā has gone to the assembly of the covenant (*samayamelaka*).

*Ku ve ī ā*: In the tradition of the *Samayāmnāya*, this is the instruction on practice regarding the series of unbroken mandalas. "Give me the sacrificial pap (*caruka*)," *ī ā*. [From] the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*: The practice is said to be the *Kuṃkuṇḍī*; it is the third within the sphere of the *Samaya*.
In *Kaulle* is the goddess Kaivartinī, born from the name *Ku*, the mother of the world.

Ku-yā-ī-ā! This is the instruction on the practice within the Mudrāmnāya of the supreme lineage of Śiva-gurus. Give me the sacrificial pap (caruka), ī-ā! The conduct (caryā) called Kauśalī has been taught; it is the fourth, the Mahābalā.
The Goddess has gone to Aṭṭahāsa, she who is named Ku, in the house of the butcher woman.
*ku bhu ī ā*: "The lineage of supreme bliss; this is the instruction for practice in the *Ādyāmnāya*. Give me the sacrificial pap (*caruka*), *ā ī*!
The practice known as *Kāñcīmukhā* is remembered as the fifth, called 'Existence' (*bhava*).
It is always performed at Jayantī by the one named Kuṇḍukī in her house."
In the *Ṣaṭkāmnāya*, the instruction on practice (*pracāropadeśa*) is as follows: "O Mother, in the belly (*ku-kṣe*), [is] the *Āmātaṅgāvalī*; *carukaṃ* is for my body, *me ā ī*.
Vāgeśī is remembered as the practice (*caryā*); the sixth is the one who effects restraint (*nigrahakārikā*).
It is established eternally in the place called Caritra, in the house of the washerwoman named Ku."

Ku Ni Ā: This is the instruction on the practice within the *Pīṭhāmnāya* concerning the series of worlds of the night-stalkers (*niśācāra*). Give me the sacrificial pap (*caruka*), Ā Ī! This practice (*caryā*) taught by Śāṅkarī is the seventh, O lady of excellent complexion;
the goddess Śilpinī, known as Ku, has entered the pledge (*samaya*) at Ekāmra.
Kuma Ā! In the tradition of the lineage of the family of liberation (*mokṣakulāvalīpāramparya*), this is the instruction on practice: "Give me the sacrificial pap (*caruka*)," Āī!
This is the eighth practice taught by Bhairavī in the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*, which bestows liberation.
In Devikoṭṭa she is called Kunāmā, and in the house of Kauśaṭī.
The illustrious Vakrā said:
"The eightfold accomplishment (siddhyaṣṭaka) exists within the Kula tradition by the grace of the Mothers.
Brahmāṇī is known as a courtesan, and Śāṅkarī is remembered as a liquor-seller."
The maiden fisherwoman is known as Kaumārī; the butcher-woman is remembered as Vaiṣṇavī; the goddess Kaṇḍukī is Vārāhī; and the washerwoman is remembered as Indrāṇī.
Cāmuṇḍā should be known as the artisan, and Mahālakṣmī as the lowest-born;
having understood this according to the division of the field of practice, one should perform the accumulation.
Mā mā mā ya ḍi ā ho āva ho, O Prayāgabhairavī, ī ā, O you who are skillful in the conduct of the *samaya*, give me the *caruka*!
This practice is the Great Practice; one should perform it in the house of a courtesan. Having obtained the *caruka* from there, one then becomes a Lord of the Kaula.

O Mother, O Grandmother, O My Mother! Not "huṃ huṃ," nor "ā" nor "ho"! O Varaṇā-Bhairavī, in the bliss of the yoga of the conduct of the *samaya* of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), O you who are beautiful in the conduct of the *samaya*, give me the sacrificial pap (*caruka*)!
In Vārāṇasī, indeed, is Varaṇā, at the gathering of the conduct of the *samaya*.
O Great Adept, having performed the ritual in the tavern, [attain] the state of Vāgeśvarī.
O Jāgriṇī! Ma i di dvi ā ghug! Ghurumāla is coming! O Jambhaṇi Jambhaṇi! Ho! O Kollāpurabhairavī! Ī ā! O you who are skillful in the conduct of the *samaya*, give me the *caruka*!
In Kollāpura, the great practitioner Kaivarttī, though naked, attained the sovereignty of knowledge through the grace of the command of *caruka*; of this there is no doubt.
O you who dwell in the cremation ground, surrounded by the assembly, O Mother, my family-accomplishment! O Aṭṭahāsabhairavī, you who act according to the samaya, give me the sacrificial pap (caruka)!
Your conduct resides in the abode of the butcher, situated in the midst of the uproar of Aṭṭahāsa.
By the grace of the command of the samaya, she grants accomplishment through the caru offering.
Subhari, subhari! Āho! Kuḍi, kuḍi! Ho! O Māyā, Mahāmāyā! Come, come, O lowly one! Feed, feed! O Bhairavī, you who are skilled in the conduct of the *samaya*, give me the *caruka*!
Born in the temple of the ball, in the cave of the Jayantī lineage!
By the offering of that sacrificial pap (caru), one becomes a lord of heroes within the family of the Yoginīs.

"Lambe lambe na homāli lilivijje samara savak kahajantī, sā caritrabhairavī ā samayācāru dehi me carukam / jambukī ca parānande unmanānandacetasā //" "Lambe, Lambe, Na Homāli, Lilivijje, Samara, Savak, Kahajantī—she is Caritrabhairavī; O you who follow the conduct of the pledge (samayācāra), give me the sacrificial pap (caruka)! And Jambukī, in supreme bliss, with a mind of the bliss beyond the mind (unmanānanda)."
Having obtained her auspicious sacrificial pap (caru), Bhairava [resides] within the lineage of Bhairavī.
O Mother! O All! O Thou who dwellest in the *sala* tree! O Śatayojanaparamānanda! O Ākandukībhairavī! O Thou who art skillful in the conduct of the *samaya*! Grant me the *caruka*!
She who brings about union within the temple of the artisan—[to her I bow].
The yogi, desiring the sacrificial pap (caru), should bestow various kinds of accomplishments (siddhi).
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
O Mātaṅgī, of pure intellect, manifest Yoginī, Siddhi of the Samaya, O Māyā, within the wheel of the conduct of the Samaya;
O divine Yoginī worshipped by the three worlds, O Devikoṭṭabhairava, grant me the *caruka* according to the conduct of the Samaya!
Born in the lineage of the beginningless, stainless Mataṅgī, Mataṅginī,
having obtained the sacrificial pap (caru) with a mind of devotion, shall become a sky-walker (khecaro).
Thus ends the chapter on the Sūtra of the Conduct of the Eight Kulas and the Kula.
Śrīnātha said: All transgressions of the *samaya* rules are as numerous as an incalculable heap of Mount Meru;
for the sake of purifying them, this Vidyā has appeared.

O Kaulinī, this is how it occurs when the maṇḍala of the pledge (samaya-maṇḍala) has been accomplished, yet through negligence it has come to be omitted along with the hymn to the seats (pīṭha-stava).
The practitioner will suffer from illness, be afflicted by various obstacles,
and consequently face the fear of untimely death, as well as poverty and strife.
O Goddess of gods, what is the destiny of one who experiences bad dreams, loss of undertakings, and repeated hatred from the world? How may such a person attain complete purification?
The illustrious Vakrā said: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Śambhu! Listen to that which has been spoken by me;
I shall explain all of it to you in detail through many divisions."
By serving the seats (pīṭha), secondary seats (upapīṭha), meeting places (saṃdoha), fields (kṣetra), and secondary fields (upakṣetra),
as well as the locations of the gates (dvāra) and sub-gates (upadvāra), one becomes pure.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa: Now, one who is incapable or negligent attains complete purification through the service of the Vidyāpīṭha and the Oghas, provided that he recites [this] having risen in the morning.
Therefore, I shall fully explain this for the purification of violations of the commitments (*samaya*):
sixty-four wheels (*cakra*) are established through the divisions of the *kūṭas*.
I shall now describe the sixty-four seats (pīṭhas) in their proper sequence; according to the Western tradition, there are the five Praṇavas of the Śākta school.
Through the union with the Mātṛkūṭa, one should recite the Pīṭha-stava:
"At Aṭṭahāsa dwells she who resides in the Kadamba tree, gentle-faced and bearer of the vajra."
I bow to the bringer of auspiciousness, who is endowed with a great bell;
she resides in a Karañja tree at Caritrā, is known as Kṛṣṇā, and holds a spear.
Endowed with great power, I bow to her who bestows excellent accomplishment,
who is accompanied by Agnideva, who holds a staff in her hand, and who dwells in the mountains.
I bow to Mahālakṣmī of the Kaula lineage, the increaser of fortune;
to Jvālāmukhī, who dwells in the Nimba tree, who is victorious, and who bears a sword.
I bow to Mahāmāyā, who dwells in the Aśvattha tree at Ujjayinī, who is accompanied by great pretas, who bestows the accomplishment of all aims, and who holds a noose.
I bow to her who is joined with Mahākāla, who accomplishes all aims,
who dwells beneath an udumbara tree, who possesses the speed of the wind, and whose weapon is a banner.
At Prayāga, I bow to Pavanopetā, the destroyer of enemies;
in Vārāṇasī, however, she is Tālasthā, with upward-pointing hair and a mace as her weapon.
I bow my head to the Goddess Śāṅkarī, who is accompanied by Śaṅkara; to Karṇamoṭī, who dwells in the banyan tree, together with Śūla and Hetuka;
and to her at Śrīkoṭi, the bestower of fortune, whom I praise as the giver of sovereignty and prosperity.
In Virajā is the goddess Ambikā, who holds a mudrā and a paṭṭiśa.
I bow to the auspicious Jayāvahā, who is endowed with fire, whose face is like fire, and who holds a vajra and a spear.
Erūḍe! Agnivaktrā! Vajraśaktidharā! Śubhā! I bow to you.
I bow to her who destroys enemies, who is accompanied by the sound of a bell,
who holds a mace as a weapon in her hand, and who is endowed with great shanks.
I bow to Piṅgākṣī in Hastināpura for the sake of destroying enemies;
and to Kharāsyā in Elāpura, who is of great strength and holds a noose in her hand.
I bow to her who possesses ears like an elephant's, the crusher of the wicked;
and likewise to Kumārī at Gokarṇa, who bears a seal and a staff.
I bow to Indrāṇī, who possesses thighs like lightning, who crushes enemies,
resides in the Maru region, and effects the attraction of the three worlds.
I bow to her who is accompanied by Karāla, who holds a goad,
who is joined with Romajaṅgha, and who possesses the plow-weapon (Halāyudha) in the city.
I bow to Vakrā, who dwells in Gacchanivāsinī, for the sake of attaining the supreme siddhi—
she who is endowed with the kumbhaka breath and adorned with a khaṭvāṅga in her hand.
I bow to Cāmuṇḍā at Pauṇḍravardhana on the bank of the Puru for the sake of purifying my sins—
she who has a gracious countenance and bears the Vajraśṛṅkhala weapon.
I bow to her who is accompanied by Trijaṭā, who effects bondage and paralysis,
whose face is lightning, and who stands with her staff and spear raised as weapons.
I bow to her who is endowed with the sound of a bell, who causes the paralysis of the Daityas,
who is accompanied by Ulkāmukha, whose hair stands erect, and who possesses great strength. — From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
I bow to her who holds a seal and a staff in her hands, the breaker of the limbs of the wicked;
I bow to her who is accompanied by flesh-eaters and who brandishes a small sword.
I bow to Agnivaktrā at Sopāra, who slaughters all sacrificial animals; and at Kṣīrika, I bow to Lokamātā, who holds a sword in her hand.
I bow to her who is accompanied by Mahāsena, who cuts through the flood of misfortunes,
who holds a vajra and a goad, and who is joined by Bhīmasena.
One should worship the Goddess who causes paralysis and attraction, who makes the city of Māyā tremble,
and who is accompanied by Mahākrodha, at Pūtanāmrātikeśvara.
I bow to her who wields the mace and the plow as weapons, who effects striking and drawing,
whose nose was broken at Rājagṛha, and who is endowed with great ears.
I bow to the wielder of the vajra-śakti, the bestower of all fruits,
the Mistress of Secrets, possessed of great enjoyment, who is eternally united with Paśupati.
I bow to her who is established in Nepal, the remover of the terrible darkness of worldly existence;
and to Goddess Śāradā in Kashmir, accompanied by Vidyeśvara.
I bow to the Great Power who is endowed with the seat of knowledge, who bestows the wisdom of the Vidyās, who removes all obstacles, and who brings about the destruction of suffering.
[He worshipped] Pārvatī, who is accompanied by Mahāśara and resides on the mountain;
[he worshipped] Jayeśvarī of Kumārikākhaṇḍa in Kulūtā; and the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa) of those clad in nakedness.
Accompanied by Kapālīśa, she bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
at Siṃhuhāra, she is known as Kulālā, endowed with manifold enjoyments.
I bow to her who is accompanied by Bhairava, the destroyer of sins,
who resides in Bhojapurī and Mahācampā, the supreme *kalā* that quivers with grace.
I bow to Ambikādevī in Strīrājya, who is accompanied by Kailāsa, who destroys evil dreams, and who brings to an end the path of difficulties.
Joined with Naṭeśvara, I bow to her for the attainment of knowledge and wealth;
on Mount Mahendra, I salute Mahāmāyā, who holds a sword in her hand.
Equal to Mount Mahāmeru, she who cuts through great suffering,
intensely red within the sacrificial altar, and bestower of the flood of all gnosis.
I perpetually bow to Aparājitā, who is accompanied by Caṇḍeśvara,
who holds a mace in her hand, who is Mahāmāyā, and who is joined with the three-eyed Lord.
With cruel hands, she is Mahākālī, the destroyer of all dualities;
in the great cremation ground, she is Ghaṇṭālī, possessing the bell as her supreme weapon.
I bow to that Bhairavī who is endowed with the Ahinogha [river],
and to Ciñciṇī, the mistress of the Ciñciṇī tree, who dwells in the Kadamba tree.
I bow to her who is joined with Bhadreśvara, who brings about the destruction of great sins;
she is the terrifying Ūrdhvakeśī in the Karavīra cremation ground within the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
She is clothed in nakedness, holds a drinking vessel, and is auspicious;
she is known as Chinnamuṇḍā on Laṅguḍa and is accompanied by Krodharāja.
I bow to her who holds a scissor in her hand, the destroyer of sins;
she is the Goddess of Desire in the cremation ground, the sovereign of the world.
She is joined with Manmatha and situated in the form of a triangle;
in one corner called the cremation ground, she is triangular and clad in red garments.
Accompanied by Triśira, adorned with human skulls and hands,
she is the leader of the Mātaṅga clan in the Ekavīra cremation ground.
I bow to her who is accompanied by Mātaṅgīśa, who holds a hand-bell and anklets,
the messenger of Śiva in the *Ḍohara* [meter], and she who is worshipped by both Asuras and Suras.
Endowed with a horse-head, holding a bow and arrows, she is the supreme one;
the great Siddha on Śrīparvata who reveals the path of the Siddhas.
[One should meditate on her] endowed with a *jyotir-liṅga*, bearing auspicious great weapons;
in Oṇaka, she possesses a great spear (*mahāśakti*) that manifests liberation,
is united with supreme bliss (*parānanda*), and has a flower-bow raised in her hand.
One should worship Caṇḍinī under the shade of a parasol, as well as Ūrdhvakeśī and Mahaujasī.
She is endowed with hair standing erect, holding the Mantramātṛs in her hands;
on the back of the mountain, she is Trijaṭā, united with the King of Mountains.

I bow to the Rudra-śakti who holds a great ḍamaru drum in her hand, who removes the fear of those blinded by darkness, who utters the sounds "hakka" and "ḍokke," who is accompanied by Śrīkaṇṭha, and who is endowed with the digit of fiery flames.
The one called Bhagā possesses the latent impression of the Siddhas.
In Devīkoṭṭa, one should worship Mahāmāyā, who holds a bow and a noose in her hands.
She is endowed with a terrifying form, the destroyer of the fear of saṃsāra;
she is the auspicious Caṇḍakāpālinī in the dreadful forest of Mahāmāyā.
I bow to her who is joined with Pracaṇḍa, who holds a deer-horn aloft in her hand,
the one garlanded by the lineage of Ciñciṇī, in the beautiful and glorious city of Candrapura.
She is endowed with a protruding belly, her hands raised like ten million flashes of lightning,
the Great Mistress of Mantras in the region of Mahāmalaya.
In Mālava, one should worship Mahākālī, who is accompanied by Cakreśvara and holds a gourd (kūṣmāṇḍa) and a staff (ayudha) in her hands,
and who holds a skull (kāla-kaṅkāla) in her hand.
Accompanied by Meghanāda, she bestows both knowledge and higher realization;
she is the glorious Mālinī, residing in the abode of Kedāra, established within the [radiant] Aras.
I bow to Mahālakṣmī, who brings happiness to the world, who is accompanied by Sadāśiva, who holds a trident in her hand, and who dwells in the formidable Mahālakṣmī forest.

I bow to her who is joined with Tumburu and whose domain is the granting of boons and fearlessness. In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the sacred fields (kṣetra), subsidiary fields (upakṣetra), and assemblies (saṃdoha) are proclaimed to be fifty-four.
I shall proclaim to you ten other [sites], namely the *pīṭhas*, *upapīṭhas*, and *saṃdohas*;
I shall describe them in brief according to the procedure for the sequence of worship.
In Candradvīpa, I bow down to her who is named Kulālā, who is endowed with the Vidyārāja, and who holds a chisel and a hammer in her hands in the western direction.
I bow to Raktā, Karālā, Caṇḍākṣī, Mahocchuṣmā, and Bhairavī;
and at the syllable Oṃ, I praise Agnikā, who is intent upon holding a rosary for recitation.
I bow to the Goddess residing in Jālandhara, the Fortune of Desire, the light of the world,
who is accompanied by Phaleśvara and who destroys the affliction of misfortune.
At Pūrṇagiri, I bow to Sarvamaṅgalā, who has a large neck, who carries a shaven head and a skull-topped staff, and who is united with Pūrṇeśvara.
I perpetually bow to Aparājitā, who is born of the mind, who holds a skull-topped staff and an elephant-goad in her hands in Kāmarūpa, and who is ever united with Kāmeśvara.
At Tisrapīṭha is Tribhuvanā, the sovereign lady of the lords of the thirty gods,
who holds a skull and a staff in her hands, bestows boons, and possesses a universal form.
I bow to the goddess Cāmuṇḍā, who is clothed in a hide, who wears a severed head, who is established at Ekāmra, and who removes all inauspiciousness.
I bow to the Goddess Agnikā, who is endowed with fire and holds a razor-edged blade in her hand;
I bow to the Fortune of Liberation in Kāmakoṭṭa, the Great Goddess who is without vowels and eternally dwells in Arbuda, for the sake of the increase of prosperity. *Śrīvivṛddhyekumārikākhaṇḍa*.
I bow to her who is united with Arbudeśvara and who removes the affliction of obstacles.
Residing in Hiraṇyapura, she is supreme and united with Śiva;
holding a book of knowledge in her hand, she bestows the fruit of the ultimate reality.
The Mothers of the Wheel of the Earth are stationed in the multitude of fields and sub-fields.
Whoever, being composed in mind, should recite [this] together with the guardians of the field (kṣetrapāla).

Having risen in the morning, or at the time of sleep, the wise knower of mantras [should worship] at the first seat (ādyapīṭha), in the presence of the Krama, during yoga, in the maṇḍala of the rule (samaya).
Even one who is joined with terrible sins would become beloved by the goddesses—
even a killer of his father, a killer of his mother, a killer of a Brahmin, or even a killer of a cow.
A killer of an embryo, a slayer of animals, one who has committed the gravest sin by violating the teacher’s bed,
a thief of a hero’s property, and one who has fallen away from his vows through negligence;
One whose self has been depleted by neglecting the conduct of the mantra, even by merely reciting the names of the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*),
is liberated from all sins and shall never see an evil rebirth; moreover, one whose self is pure in disposition who recites them at the three times of day [attains the same].
One attains one's desired objects and becomes beloved by women,
whether at a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), a mandala, or before an image.
Or on a cloth,
or on a *liṅga* of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, or even while standing in the midst of water.
Whoever, being well-composed, recites this three times a day or at a single time,
shall be protected from poison, weapons, water, fire, as well as from diseases, malevolent spirits, and planetary influences.
Ajita: He shall live for a very long time, free from affliction;
he will accomplish his goal perfectly and fruitfully—of this there is no doubt.
Just as that which is sown in the wilderness without seed is fruitless,
so too is [the practice] with seed in the section on virgins.
Starting from Aṭṭahāsa up to the city of Hāṭaka.
"This indeed is the lineage of mantras that bestows fruits such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
Thus spoke Śrīnātha.
Extending as far as the edge of the golden pedestal.
Regarding the seats beginning with Aṭṭahāsa and all the other seats, since one is unable [to proceed] without the five seed-syllables,
tell me the means for that through the union with the Mātṛkūṭa.
The illustrious Vakrā said: Having established the five lamps in the sacred seats beginning with Aṭṭahāsa,
one should likewise utter the Heart of the Mothers of Hemakūṭa.

Through the application of reciting from beginning to end, all have entered the family of the Mother; this yoga of performing the beginning and the end is the supreme method for producing the seed-syllable.
This has now been declared for those who are incapable, in the context of the Śrīgṛha;
therefore, both worldly enjoyment and liberation arise from the recitation of the sacred seats (pīṭhas).
The bases of this King of Hymns are the *praṇavas* at the beginning and the end;
success is attained through their secret recitation by a yogi who is a knower of mantra.
When a great danger has arisen, one should have a circular maṇḍala constructed with the dung of a tawny cow according to the eightfold procedure.

Likewise, for other [practitioners], the jewel of Śiva [is attained] in a secluded place or a sacrificial temple through the service of the King of Hymns by the *sādhakas* and *putrakas* of the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
With fragrant white flowers, well-scented with saffron,
incense such as sandalwood and perfumes, and with *sumana* blossoms and *palāla* grass.
Having offered food offerings, edible items, drinks, and various auspicious lamps,
one should place a jar filled with heroic substances (vīradravya) in the center.
Having offered the seat consisting of the syllable *aiṃ*, which is marked by the *kanda* [of the body],
one should oneself perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the letters and the great *piṇḍa* upon the hands and the body.
One should perform the Pīṭhayāga with a body endowed with the *piṇḍa*;
having worshipped Hiraṇya in the center, [one worships] Paścima, which grants all desires.
Others [should proceed] by way of reverse order as far as Aṭṭahāsaka;
the Pīṭhayāga must be performed starting from Śrīpura and so forth.
The lords of the pīṭhas, upapīṭhas, saṃdohas, kṣetras, and upakṣetras—
all of them serve as gateways to the central Śiva-pīṭha.
Joined with the Lord of the Pretas through the pervasion of Śiva,
those auspicious mantras residing there— when worshipped and fully gratified with devotion by those who rely on the path of action— bestow knowledge upon all.
Therefore, O Hairaṇya, one should with all effort [worship] this supreme Hairaṇya-pīṭha.
If worship is performed there constantly, one shall obtain all desires. The seats (pīṭhas) located in the cardinal and intermediate directions are external to the central seat.
One should sequentially apply the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha) in the place of the womb;
one should rotate the sixty-four lamps and sacred seats.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Having fasted for a day and night, one should sleep alone, well-restrained,
established in the vow of celibacy, and avoiding meat and wine.
There, the recitation of the mantra should be performed for thirty measures;
at the clear dawn, the practitioner of mantra should partake of the heroic feast (vīrabhojya).
Then, having prostrated repeatedly before the seats, the mantra-practitioner should ask for forgiveness;
thus, free from obstacles, everything becomes a bestower of accomplishment, including afflictions, malevolent planets, and the like, as well as yakṣas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and guhyakas.
Especially when the king suffers a defeat in a region that is formidable for the enemy.
He is liberated from calamities and shall obtain wealth and grain;
[this applies] even regarding the rites of harming others, such as killing, eradication, and so forth.
For one is indeed released from the mire of evil and remains stainless like a clean cloth;
by the sequential application of the yogas of the seats (*pīṭha*), the evil-minded person shall not be reborn.
Even one who has become like a corpse shall obtain his desired objects;
by that consecration, she whose children have died becomes possessed of living sons.

One desiring a son obtains sons; one shall attain good fortune. One desiring knowledge obtains knowledge; one desiring wealth becomes wealthy. One desiring a wife obtains a wife, proud of her beauty and youth.
One who desires land obtains land; one who desires drink shall obtain drink.
One who seeks knowledge obtains knowledge; one who seeks the pledge (samaya) obtains the pledge;
and one whose habit is the propitiation of the mantra becomes free from affliction.
One who is constantly devoted to the practice of yoga, having attained perfection, shall proceed to the supreme state.
This is the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, revealed as a hymn of praise to the sacred seats (pīṭhas) in connection with the science of the feet (pādavidyā).
The attainment of both the collective and the individual [forms] arises from the recitation and retention of the mantra;
in this lineage, the recitation of the hymn is declared to be the collective form.
Thus, in the primordial descent of the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage measuring seventy million verses that has emerged from the path of Meru.

In the *Avvākrama*, belonging to the *Kādiveda* division brought down to the first seat (*ādyapīṭha*) in [this scripture] exceeding one hundred thousand quarters; within the section on the Praise of the Seats (*pīṭhastava*), following the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six-Thousand (*vimalaṣaṭka*), in the *Kādiveda* division, in the *Svāminīmata* which is the supreme command of the Lord and consists of twenty-four thousand [verses].
Thus ends the chapter on Knowledge, named Ānanda, within the spoken [text].
Oṃ, may there be well-being!
Salutation to the sandals of Śrīnātha. Salutation to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
In the Manthānabhairavatantra, within the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, this is the seventeenth bliss (saptadaśānanda).
The illustrious Vakrā said: Now I shall tell you the sixteenfold convention, which is the essence of the lineage revealed within the Divine Current (divyaugha).
The lineage on the path of Meru is the deity therein;
the emergence at Oṃkāra is proclaimed as the Siddhānvaya.
Tuṣṇīdevī, Guhāvāsī, the Kadambaka tree,
Siṃhasaṃketaka, and Avvā Guhavāsinī.
The house is said to be Candrapura; the division is Manthānabhairava;
the lineage is the goddess Amarikā, who is established on the path of the Left (vāmamārga).
The lineage has its essence in the Pratyaya [tradition], while its authority resides in Koṅkaṇa; its birthplace is Brahmaśilā, and its established seat of accomplishment is Kāmarūpa.
Fame is found in the ciñciṇī tree, and success indeed in the ocean;
O Lord of Gods, I am pleased with him who knows the lineage transmission (kulakrama).
But this, O Kaulika, is the essence that has emerged from the Kula lineage;
having known the convention consisting of sixteen aspects, one becomes a member of the spiritual succession.
Śrīnātha said:
O Mistress of the Gods, what is the path of Meru in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, and who is the deity here in this lineage?
Tell me of the emergence of the syllable Oṃ, and speak to me concerning its accomplishment as well.
However, reveal another cave-dwelling, the Kadamba tree, and the Siṃhaka; I do not know them, especially Candrapurī.

O Kaulinī, make manifest the lineage (*gotra*) and the piercing of the churning-stick (*manthānabhedam*); O Mother, what indeed is the sign (*pratyaya*) in the tradition, and likewise the authority (*adhikāra*)?
O Maheśvarī, tell me of the birth-place, the Brahma-stone, and the womb;
what is the state in Kāmarūpa? Tell me of the fame of Ciñciṇī.
"But how is there accomplishment in the ocean? This I ask, O Kaulinī;
tell me clearly, one by one, for you ought to sever my doubt."
The venerable Vakrā said:
"O Lord of Gods, the conventions established in the Kula tradition consist of the lineage of the sixteen-fold form of the lunar city's reflection."
O Śambhu, now hear the thread of its lineage and the sixfold sequence, which is a compendium of the essence of nectar.
At every step, I have explained this in detail, point by point;
yet this question, O God of gods, is one that has been brought down [to earth] in extreme secrecy.
I shall tell you that by which you may know it in its entirety:
Meru, renowned throughout the world, beautiful with the abodes of the deities.
Adorned with three peaks and presided over by the three gods—
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— these are established in the lineage of the Siddhas.
Ānanda, Vimala, and Ciñcā are the names of these three purities. Ānanda, the pervasive deity is established within all beings.
Creation, in its pure form, resides within the house of the command of the syllable *Cikā*;
by merely realizing these, human beings shall attain liberation.
And the Great Goddess Vyāpinī is established within each one;
the exceedingly fierce Taraṅgiṇī pervades every single body.
With her limbs adorned by the Three Jewels, she is illuminated by her very nature;
she reveals the path that is straight, clear, perfectly pure, and like nectar.
That digit named Amā has indeed come to the hermitage within the secret maṇḍala;
she is the supreme goddess, resembling the flower of the pomegranate tree.
Two forms of Māyā, Guhaka and Ṛtukāla, are seen;
she is renowned by the name Vicitrā, and by her everything is pervaded without exception.
O Lord, this is that very deity who was described by me as a deity;
having emerged from the cave-hermitage, she who was voiceless has now become possessed of a voice.
Resembling pure crystal, she stands together with the powers (śaktis);
having emerged through the tortoise-channel (kūrmanāḍī), she is joined with the lunar orb. In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, it is said:
"The two Siddhas are thus renowned; they adorn the circle of Meru."
They are the agents of creation and destruction, and they abide again in the state of dissolution.
O God, the emergence from the syllable Oṃ is celebrated as Sādākhya;
he is Brahmā, he is Viṣṇu, he is Rudra, and he is Maheśvara.
For this syllable Oṃ is sung as being composed of all the gods; it stands upon the highest peak in the center of Meru, having the ocean as its foundation.
Within the center of the cave of the triangle, the syllable Oṃ is seen;
she who dwells in the cave in the midst of nectar is indeed praised by means of the Bindu.
The convention-tree root is at the center of the womb, a *kadamba* tree;
by it this Meru is pervaded, the abode of all yogis.
The Goddess, established through the differentiation of designations by Hara using the designation "bindu," has proclaimed the seals of speech and their symbols by means of convention.

In the aforementioned *Sahitā*, however, the Lord Ādinātha first spoke the very sequence of mantras as a means of realization.
Accompanied by the mudrās of speech, Bhairava is the mass of sounds;
and that is the third path, the primordial seat (ādyapīṭha), O King of the lords of gods.
Furthermore, its extraction is just like that of the horse; indeed, according to the sequence of creation, one should know the Self to be like Rudra and maintain Rudra as being like the Self.
Having known [the self] both externally and internally, one should cause the mass of sounds to descend;
from Amṛta (A) to the end of Ha—this is the supreme of phonemes.
The lineage of the Mātṛkās is indeed one, yet it is the source of the Bhaga;
by applying its fifty divisions, agitation is produced.
This arrangement of syllables, refined by the impressions of previous practice— if the sequence of the seed-syllables is not understood at that time, one is not liberated.
Having placed the head of Anaṅga upon your forehead,
and likewise that of the letter Ña, there shall be that circle of faces.
Likewise, having placed the sixteen [syllables] of Tejas at the extremities in that same manner,
these two eyes of the God, O Lord, are the illuminators of the moon and the sun.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
it is likewise said that the Kalā is the head of Mahendra;
O God, these two ears are declared to be the right and the left.
At the end of two *kalās*, both [channels] joined with the nostrils are reversed;
one should cast down the pair beginning with Mahendra onto both the mouth and the cheeks.
The two syllables *rāvaṇāntau* are in reverse order at the bottom of the rows of teeth;
the first two syllables of *rājendra* are the *iṣṭau*, well-visualized below and above.
O Maheśvara, having raised the seat of Girijā to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
its first part, known as the Visarga, is prescribed at the root of the tongue.
The wheel of vowels is traditionally known as that which begins with the letter 'a' and ends with the visarga;
there, the deity Brahmāṇī resides within the maṇḍala of Śambhu.
Now, I shall describe the ancillary parts; listen to their true nature as it is.
Having placed the master upon the seat of the twice-born, one should [place] the right shoulder with that.
The lion’s seat, the arm-seat and so forth, the elbow, the jaw,
and the head should be placed, with the right hand upon it.
O God, from that [letter] ending in *siṃha* (sa), which is between the letters *gha*, the *ka*-group located at the tips of the nails of the right hand is fivefold and joined with Māheśvarī.
Just as the first and supreme limb of the Bimba of Śaktipura [was struck],
so too should its head be struck down, joined with the left arm.

In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: One should place *Bha* and *Śira* on the elbow; *Ā* and the rest on the back of the hand; *Māyā* and the rest on the fingers of the hand; and [the remaining letters] on the tips of the nails.
O Lord, the *ca*-group has been revealed by you as belonging to Kaumārī;
establish it firmly on the right side as the first constituent of Gaurī.
O Rudra, her seat is on the right side, below the knees and shanks;
it begins with the letter *ḍa* and extends to the foot, reaching the back of the right sole.
O Kaulika, by joining the fingers at that grasp and likewise the nails,
the essence of the Vaiṣṇavī, which is the Ṭa-group, shines forth on the right path.
The left buttock should rest upon the earth, and the right thigh should be below the water; this is known as the Mahāśaṅkha posture, in which the knee is placed upon the shank.
Likewise, below Dhūmradhvaja, the soles and backs of the feet are remembered; resting upon the head of Anaṅga are the toes, ending at the tips of the nails.
One should place the group presided over by Vārāhī according to the *Kramapaddhati*;
thus, in the arising of the phonemes (*varṇodaya*), it goes to the right side of the left hip.
Nor is he situated within the womb; others say he faces all directions. They know him to have six heads, his spinal column at the back, and his belly above the hips.
O Mahādeva, that which has reached its end is the Heart, the mass of sounds;
the group presided over by Indrāṇī is the Heart of the Kula-yoginī.
The skin, skull, and the blood located above them, as well as the matted hair and so forth;
the flesh situated immediately below [the skin], and the sinews located beneath the "limbless" [flesh].
Know that the four pervasive principles (tattvas) belonging to the fire element reside in the solar mandala; understand the *ya*-group as being joined with its own aggregate of digits (*kalā*).
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
likewise, the marrow ends with the letter *pha*, and below Hara is the sphere of semen (*śukramaṇḍala*).
In this way, the head of Kuvera is joined with its bones;
situated in the middle is the "middle vital breath," the downward-facing principle of the anus,
the group presided over by Cāmuṇḍā, which is the eighth in enumeration.
O God, they know that which transcends the groups, yet resides below, consisting of the self together with the *visarga*, as having entered the image and reached the place of wrath.
His ninth goddess is Mahālakṣmī,
who presides over the supreme collection of phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with *ha*.
The sequence of the *mātṛkā* itself, however, is the causal sign born from the womb;
thus, it proceeds in order through fifty divisions, beginning with 'A' and ending with 'Kṣa'.
This arrangement of syllables, refined by the impressions of previous practice,
does not release one who has not understood the sequential placement of the seed-syllables.

O Lord of the Gods, those who have mastered the syllables of the Śabdabrahman and whose rays are formed by refinement proceed toward the primordial flood of the sequence of fulfilled duties; yet this is merely the natural state.

The first creation of sounds, phonemes, and syllables is the emergence of their sequence; by that, for one who has attained perfection through the direct order, you are indeed the Mass of Sounds (Śabdarāśika).
Sound, however, resides within the earth; within the earth is Hara-mālinī.
By means of Mālinī, who is the mass of sounds (śabdarāśi), the three worlds are woven like warp and woof.
O Maheśvara, devoid of illumination, you are internally empty;
therefore, one should utter the illumination at the beginning of that mass of sounds.

The Heart of the Kulakhecarī is that which has the letter *ya* as its younger brother (*yānuja*), stands in the midst of *kha-ra*, is pierced by the arm of the lordly elephant (*gajendra-bhuja*), and is split by the moon-like radiance of the crest (*candrakānti-śikhā*).
Having first fashioned the form of the Hero separately for each seed-syllable, O God,
the placement becomes brilliantly radiant within the three *mālinī* and *praṇava* syllables.
Having formed a casket at the beginning and the end with this mass of sounds,
one should perform the deposition (nyāsa) thus encapsulated, joined with the faces and the limbs.
Having taken the bull situated in the center, established upon the seat of power (śakti),
and Mahākāla with the Pināka bow situated beneath that,
this is declared to be the peak; one should further fashion it in six ways.
It is to be differentiated by the six short vowels, adorned with the moon-bindu (anusvāra) above and above; likewise in the east, west, south, and north.
O Mahādeva, this is the placement of the faces, illuminated by the primordial seeds.
Tūṣṇīśa and Kulīśa, Śrīkaṇṭha and Aghorabhairava,
Uttareśa and Anantīśa, and Sadāśiva in the west.
— O fair-faced one, these perfected ones (siddhas) are to be assigned to the six faces;
now I shall speak of the limbs (aṅgas), which I will explain in brief.
Having placed the middle *vṛṣabha* (the letter Ṣa), which is conjoined with the seat of Hara (the letter Ha),
one should produce the son (*suta*) among the vowels (*atādi*), conjoined with the heart and the head (the letters Ha and Sa).
Having placed the head of Nīlakaṇṭha at the peak, one should extract this sixfold [mantra],
distinguished by the six long vowels and marked with Kalā, Bindu, and Śiva.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Aghora is conjoined with the heart; Amogha is the ornament of the head;
Nīlakaṇṭha is to be applied to the crest-lock; and Ekavīraka resides in the armor.
One should place Piṅgala in the eyes and Kapila on Bhairava;
thus, one should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅga) joined with these six Bhairavas.

Then, having performed the lighting and so forth, the placement (*nyāsa*) becomes encapsulated (*sampuṭa*). By means of this encapsulation, the limbs that were empty become filled; the rays, which were previously hollow within, remain as all-pervading and well-illuminated pervaders.
This indeed is the mass of sounds, endowed with well-illuminated limbs.
He who places [the sequence] at the beginning of the Krama is purified even if he is a slayer of a Brahmin;
he who constantly performs this placement becomes an enemy of the state of being liberated while living.
The wise one shall become free from affliction and is not defiled by committed sins;
by the power of the mass of sounds (Śabdarāśi), he becomes equal to a Siddha.
Where there is the unshakable command (*ājñākṣobha*), as well as the wave (*ghūrmi*) and repeated possession (*āveśa*),
and where the consciousness of another arises— that is where the Supreme (*parā*) delights.
The attainment of the state beyond all positions constitutes liberation from bondage;
this, O Person of Sound, is indeed presided over by the words of Brahman.
The empowerment of the Kaula, however, is the realization consisting of the mass of sounds;
within that mass are fifty divisions, and the single sound is proclaimed as the Vāgbhava.
Therefore, O Bhairava, the mass of sounds is remembered as the embodiment of Rudra-hood;
its form is Navātman, the lamp of the Kula in the teaching.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: I shall proclaim its extraction; listen with one-pointed attention, O handsome one!
Bhṛgu, Lākula, Saṃvarta, Mahākāla, and Pinākin.
Khaḍgīśa, the one called Bhujaṅga, Vālīśa, and Arghanāyaka;
marked with a digit and a bindu, the fourth is the resonance (nāda) in the form of light.
O God, among these [deities] is Navātman, Vṛkṣīśa, and Vṛkṣanāyaka;
and in Kalā is Paramānandabhairava, who has become incarnate.
His hermitage is the Brahma-tree, situated on the path beyond the three folds; there, within the mandala at the end of the fourth state, the Śākta bliss proceeds.
Therein, one should contemplate the *piṇḍa* as the illuminator consisting of the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*),
white as snow, jasmine, and the moon, and blazing with the brilliance of a hundred suns.
The goddess seated upon his lap was none other than I, Mālinī;
O Lord, I am the one who shares his nature and bears his auspicious form.
Empowered by the seed-syllable of Māyā and placed in the position of the offering water (argha),
she shines forth, resembling a pomegranate flower and rich in radiant emanations.
In the form of a sprout, the Brahma-knot indeed faces downward;
Kubjikā, in her supreme form, begins with the letter 'A' and extends as far as Śiva.
The repose of Śiva and Śakti occurs in the heart-maṇḍala through both direct and reverse orders;
Śiva is above and Śakti is below, while their expansion constitutes the intermediate plane.
And there, having repeatedly recognized the state of possession, the stage arises;
the mass of sounds abides in the fourth state, while Mālinī herself is established in the womb.
