Between those two is the mouth of the Guru, and Ānanda is downward-facing;
this is declared to be the Great Current (mahaugha) of Śiva and Śakti in their respective order.
In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:
I shall now proclaim the ritual placement of the forms (*mūrtinyāsa*) as it has been ordained in its proper sequence:
in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), on the forehead, on the face, and in the circle of the heart.
At the navel, the secret place, the two thighs, the two shanks, and the pair of feet—
thus is the ritual placement (nyāsa) described, empowered by the five jewels.
For thus, regarding the prescription of the limbs, listen now as I shall explain it:
"Resembling pure crystal, she shines within the heart of the Goddess."
The head is like madder-red,
while the crest is like a blazing meteor;
it is slightly reddish and pure white, and both eyes are likewise red.
And one should know the Astra-mantra to be like the Aghora-mantra, resembling the pure sky;
having understood this division of syllables, one becomes a slayer of enemies through accomplishment.
The Mālinī is the mass of sounds, augmented by the Rudras and Yoginīs;
it is conjoined with the illuminations and differentiated by the sequence of the six limbs.
O fair-faced one, this Umāmaheśvara-cakra, which is endowed with a hundred thousand locations and joined with meditations and dhāraṇīs, has been explained to you.
Those whose limbs are devoid of distinctions of caste should be understood in sequence as before;
[they are] Mālinī, the mass of sounds, which is the foundation of the Kula, Kaula, and Krama traditions.

O Maheśvara, the Kulasiddhānta has been told; the Path is to be known. Thus, in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, in the descent of the command (ājñāvatāra), in the sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage (anvaya) measuring seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru.

In the *Ājñāpārameśvara*, known as the *Svāminīmata*, which consists of twenty-four thousand verses, spoken in the tradition of the Mother (*Avvākrama*), belonging to the division beginning with the letter *Ka*, determined in the *Vimalaṣaṭka* on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*Vidyāpīṭha*) within the first descent of the Pīṭhas exceeding one hundred thousand quarters,
in the description of the chapter on the Mass of Sounds (*Śabdarāśi*).
The bliss named Kramodaya.
Śrīnātha said:
"The Viṃśānanda and the Mālinī Śabdarāśi— both of these have been heard by me."
Now I desire to hear about the supreme Kaulinī, who possesses the threefold knowledge.
The venerable Vakrā said: O Śambhu, now listen to the Kaulika triad of Vidyās, which pertains to another conceptualization of that which is well-established as the Mass of Sounds (Śabdarāśi).
There is the *parā*, the *aparā*, and likewise the *parāparā*;
O observer of noble vows, I shall now describe another extraction (*uddhāra*) of them.
The first [mantra] is Parāparā, consisting of forty-five syllables;
it is adorned with the initial nectar (A), the head of space (H), and the lord of elephants (M).
The head of that planet should be struck down, pierced by the seat of that planet;
having taken the head of Padmayoni, it is joined with the end of the Earth.
The first word consists of the skull-ending (kapālānta) with a bindu and is joined with the half-moon; this is how the second [word] should be.
The first [syllable] is Tārā, the first is Ṭha, likewise Anaṅgamastaka,
Pādra, Ekaśira, Bhadra, and Adhimastaka of that planet.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
the middle and Ananga, pierced by the abode of fire;
Khaśiras overpowered by Khaśiras, the mandala of the seat of the skull.
O Śambhu, that whose head is occupied by the piercing agent (vedhaka) starting from its color,
and which stands on a single foot, likewise resides in the center of Meru.
O Great Lord, the third foot, joined with its beloved, has been extracted;
it begins with *na*, ends with *ya*, and is situated below, illuminated by the rising sun.
The laughing one (Ha) seated upon a lotus (Ra), with the syllable Gha below it and joined with Māyā (I), is declared as the fourth word; now let the fifth follow.
The letter *m* joined with *Gaurī*, likewise that which goes to the end of *Bhānu*;
*Jāsana* occupied by *Īśvara*, the end of *Rāva*, and that which goes to *Rādhā*.
The musical instrument (vādya) and the Solitary Hero (ekavīra), with a double repetition for the sixth,
ending with the "thick" (ghanānta) together with Māyā, constitute the Anaṅgāsanamaṇḍala.
These two, through double repetition, constitute the seventh word;
the first ends with *sayā*, and the second is divided by the vowel *e*.
The eighth syllable is likewise thus: ending with *ṭha* and situated upon a lotus;
one should apply it as transcending the groups (*varga*), distinct, and divided into two parts.
The ninth step is declared to be the emission situated in the abode of fire;
the tenth step is extracted by repeating that alone twice.
But indeed, by the sequence of the *pada-krama* of the eleven vowels,
one should [recite] the Vāgbhava along with Māyā, as well as Prasādabhairava.
O God, that which was at the beginning was placed at the end; the Parāparā has been extracted and declared to consist of forty-six [syllables], within which is the seat of the wings.
For this knowledge is both supreme and non-supreme, having emerged from the support;
this is declared to be the seat of the Krama, not a deer-skin.
One who has mastered the self should practice the lower [mantra] established in the Vidyā;
it is the Māyā-piṇḍa together with the *phera*, placed above and below the *rāva*.
Thus, when this three-syllable vidyā is joined with the first [syllable],
and when that first [syllable] is at the end, then it becomes a half-verse.
The goddess Jvalikā is three-and-a-half [units] in extent; she is the Vidyā Aparabhairavī.
She indeed has emerged from the Unstruck (anāhata) as the side of the Form (mūrti).
Above that is the supreme wing of Śambhu, which is vast for the world;
and your single-syllable Vidyā is fivefold. In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
the flame from the pericarp of Meru pierces the summit of the conch.
Above the seat of Kuvera, it is traditionally taught that [the mantra] ends with the Visarga.
This is that Blessed Goddess, known by the name Vahnivāsinī;
she is the singular-formed, supreme Mother, established as the Mother of the Universe.
The Vidyā stands on the path of Śambhu in the form of the emanation of Śambhu;
below that is the seat of the path, subtle and dear to the heart.
O Lord, its supreme seat is that which is Śākta, according to the Kaulikas;
between the Śākta and the Śāmbhava, there is the branch known as Āṇava.
Having placed this root of the three thorns (trikaṇṭaka), agitation arises;
this is the triad of the sequence of vidyās belonging to Mālinī and the Assembly of Sounds (śabdarāśi).
Through practice for a single year, the supreme state arises;
for those born into the family of Yoginīs, I was indeed pleased in the past.
They will know the divisions within the Trika, endowed with the mass of sounds,
and the arrangement of places and phonemes fashioned by the fifty Rudras.
O Lord, this supreme secret *nyāsa*, worshipped by the thirty gods,
consists of the three Vidyās, the three Siddhas, the three Pīṭhas, and the three deities.
Having known the three trees, the three caves, the triple power that is radiant with the qualities (guṇas),
and that which moves through the path of the three channels, one should ascend the triad of Vidyās.

Thus, in the introduction to the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand, in the *Kā* division, in the *Svāminīmata* which is the supreme command of the Lord, in the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the tradition of the Goddess.
The Bliss named Trividyādhikāra, the Twenty-first Bliss. The venerable Vakrā said:
Now I shall proclaim another, the supreme Aghorāṣṭaka.
It should be performed with the movement of inhalation and exhalation, encapsulated by Śiva.
O Śambhu, I shall now explain the sequence of the division of the words:
first is the word *aghora*, and second is *aghorī*.
This is that first *ghorā*; and as for how the second would be, it is the word *paramaghorā*, which is the supreme *paramaghoryī*.
The third is declared to be Aghorikā, [consisting of] the syllable *havisarga* (the visarga of *havi*) which is of terrible form, and the syllable *ī* which goes to the end; now listen to the fourth.
Ghoramukhi, Ghoramukhā, differentiated by the vowel *ī*;
the next pair of words are Bhīmabhīṣaṇī and Bhīmabhīṣaṇā.
O Maheśvara, the fourth [syllable] belongs to Gaurī, and the fifth also belongs to Gaurī;
the words "vama piba heti" are joined with "hāyī vama piba."
This sixth is said to be Aghorā; the seventh shall be the other [Bhīṣaṇā].
The word *ruru* and *ra-ra*, and again the word *ruru* and *ra-ra*.
These *repha*s situated in the letter *a* are illuminated by the syllables of Gaurī;
she is that seventh Ghoṣī, and now the eighth shall be described.
Phetkārī and Phetkāryā, pierced by the fourth vowel—
this indeed is the Aghorī-aṣṭaka, through the sixteenfold division of its words.

The Ghorikāṣṭaka has been taught according to the sequence of two-footed steps; it is extracted from the eight [mantras] beginning with Aghorī, though it is devoid of the illuminating [syllables]. From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
But, O God, that which is devoid of seed-syllables does not bestow accomplishment; one should not practice it.
Therefore, O Bhairava, listen now to the method for making it possess a seed-syllable.
The sign of the sequence of the Mātṛkā, pierced by the fire of the full moon,
is pervaded by the union with Gaurī and blazes like the wick of the Command.
This is the seed-syllable of Mahendra; likewise, one should cast Prasādabhairava at its end, situated in the middle and pierced by the head of Mahendra.
O Maheśvara, the seed-syllable of space (Ha) is pervaded by the spear and the javelin, differentiated by the ocean of the presiding powers, situated in that state, and established in the visarga.
The fourth [syllable] is formed by reversing *ba* and joined with the head of *toraṇa*;
likewise, it is well-established upon a moon-seat both below and above it.
Above that, moreover, from the conjunction of the agitation, one should extract the seed-syllable of sound (rāva),
which consists of the letter *va*, the letter *ma*, and the semi-vowel (*antastha*).
Seated upon the throne of Kubera, above the Guru who is pierced by the *bindu*—
this indeed is the seed-syllable of Kaulinī, saluted by gods and perfected beings.
The fourth [vowel] from the first [consonant], pierced by the fire-piercer (the letter *ra*),
with a dot (*bindu*) marked above like the moon, is beneficial when offered as the sixth oblation in the seventh [day].
This is declared to be Kālāgnirudra, beloved by all people. [He is] the Lord in the center of Bha-la, struck by the primordial [sound], the cranial [vibration].
It is pervaded by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*, extracted from the city of Mahārudra;
it is the first of others, [the mantra] of Dhūmradhvaja, pierced by the seat of the archway (*toraṇa*).
The moon upon the crest of the archway, unbroken bliss,
the king of seed-syllables of the Yoginīs, the most excellent of the supreme states of sound.
One should form this group of eight seed-syllables for the eight [syllables] of Ghoryā;
then, divide the eight seed-syllables of the sixteen words into two parts each.
O Lord of Gods, at the conclusion of the words, those sixteen seeds are traditionally taught to be joined with Śiva at the beginning and the end.
Having made the fourteenth [vowel] the head of the *jīva* of *prasāda*,
O King Śiva, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and commence the practice.
In the two feet, the knees, the shanks, the foundation, the heart, the mandala, the two sides of the belly, the spinal column, and likewise in the two arms;
One should thus place the mandala of the faces in the eight locations,
having first performed the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhāra) and then again the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭi).

O Lord of Gods, I have described to you the *aghoryātmaka* placement (*nyāsa*), extracted from the enclosure of the three thorns (*trikaṇṭāvaraṇa*), which is joined with the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*).
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
together with mind, intellect, and ego— this is known as the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka).
The eight deities beginning with Brahmāṇī, numbering sixty-four,
should be installed in this manner according to the sequence of pervasion within the group of eight Aghorīs.
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa: Now follows the sequence of the Vidyā-nyāsa, joined with the limbs of the Siddhas,
which was previously explained by me according to the sequence of the hand-nyāsa.
Now, one should likewise perform the deposition of the seed-syllables and the five seats;
one should produce the great syllable beginning with the Visarga as a vowel in five ways.
"O God, having thus formed the Great Being (Mahadbhūta), pierced by a long lotus and marked with a digit and a bindu— this indeed is the pentad of seed-syllables."
Indeed, that which is joined with the five principles (tattvas) should be deposited for the Goddess:
Earth is the seed-syllable of Śakti, Water is the seed-syllable of Soma,
Fire is the seed-syllable of Sūrya, and Wind is the seed-syllable of Bindu.
Space, sound, and the seed-syllable—these indeed constitute the fivefold seed.
Their five locations are indeed established in the mouth of the Guru:
earth is in the *kanda-cakra*, while water is in the *yoni-maṇḍala*.
Fire indeed resides in the navel-wheel, air in the circle of the heart, and space between the eyebrows; these are the five seed-syllable locations.
Having formed the five seed-syllable abodes and joined them with the first [syllable],
one should perform the deposition of the five seeds after receiving the teacher’s instruction.
Otherwise, O handsome one, there would be no state devoid of seed;
and among the principles such as earth and the rest, there would be neither bondage nor dissolution.
(From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
Through constant practice in this Kaula [tradition], how could there be rebirth again?
This is the Unmanī-karaṇa; herein lies the deposition of the five seed-syllables.
O God, the pentad of principles (tattva) is established in the sequence of authority;
in the oral instruction it is indeed so, and in the ritual placement (nyāsa), it constitutes the five seats (pīṭha).
One should practice those five *praṇavas* which were previously mentioned;
having first established the seats (*pīṭhas*) before them, one should then commence the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
The northern eastern seat (pīṭha), however, is adorned with the fifth [vowel] at its beginning and end;
likewise, Jālandhara is located between the eyebrows and has the luster of the color black.
The form beginning with the second [vowel] and ending with the final one is slightly red in the heart-maṇḍala;
likewise, the one named Pūrṇagiri is established between the third [vowel] and the final one.

And the yellow-colored one is situated at the navel; likewise, there is another, Kāmarūpa, which resides at the beginning, end, and middle of the first [syllable], more secret than snow, the kunda flower, and the moon.
The fifth seat consists of three [syllables] joined at the beginning and end of the fourth;
it is green, extremely fierce, and is revealed in the location of the bulb (kanda).
Arising is at Kāmarūpa, persistence is at Pūrṇagiri;
withdrawal is at the southern seat, and nirvāṇa resides in the fifth.
O Bhairava, this is the deposition of the five seats, beginning with the first seat which is Viśrāma;
such is the visualization of these seats, starting with Kāmarūpa and the others.
In that manner, one should indeed perform the fivefold meditation on the principles (tattvas) in sequence;
just as the principles are the seeds, so too are the five seats (pīṭhas).
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Having known [the reality] both externally and internally, who would not be released from bondage?
O God, when the ritual placement of the sacred seats (pīṭhanyāsa) has been performed, the yogins perceive something.
O God, the maṇḍala of Akhaṇḍapura is unseen;
therein resides that Kaulinī Vidyā, which pierces the internal organ.
When there arises an authoritative conviction regarding the principles (tattvas),
then the supreme nyāsa is proclaimed, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.

This has been declared for you, the perfected one, as that which is well-established on the path of the perfected ones. Thus, in the primordial descent of the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primary seat on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (Vidyāpīṭha), in the determination of the Pure Six-Thousand (Vimala-ṣaṭka), in the Kādi division.
In the *Ājñāpārameśvara*, the *Svāminīmata*, the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the *Avvākrama* tradition,
this is the bliss named the Arising of the Sequence (*Kramodaya*), within the description of the Five Principles (*Tattvapañcaka*).
The twenty-second bliss.
The venerable Vakrā said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the ritual placement (nyāsa) worshipped by the thirty gods.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in six ways and with twelve divisions during the coming and going [of the breath].
The auspicious supreme single-syllabled Śakti is declared to be sixfold;
her seat is known as Ṣoḍhā, and one should enter the city of the Ṣoḍhā-Śakti.
"O handsome one, listen to its sixteen divisions according to the path:
having established Gauryā in twelve ways, O Jaṭāhāra, [one should proceed] again."
Having caused it to be pierced by the *bindu* and struck upon the heads of the moon and sun, its limbs are known as twelve; from that, the parasol of the shadow [arises] in due order.
The lion throne is the first, the primordial seat is the second;
the third is indeed the solitary hero, and the fourth is in the circle of Hara.
The fifth is the seed-syllable of Śakti; the sixth is the seat of the letter Ma;
the seventh is the portion of Ji-la; and the eighth is the head of Hara.
O God, one should place Haśira as the ninth, Tāraṇa-śiras as the tenth,
Rājya as the eleventh, and Tāraka as the twelfth.
One should pierce all those adorned with the Single Hero (ekavīra) by means of the Piercer (vedhaka);
they are purified by the digits of the moon and light, and differentiated by the twelve Rudras.
Furthermore, O Lord of Gods, through the union with the Rudra-śakti, my form performs the sixfold installation (ṣoḍhānyāsa) once again by means of the twelve Gaurīs.
There is no further illumination for her; she is Gaurī, illuminated by twelve [syllables].
She is indeed the power of Rudra, the sixfold power that is neuter. In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*: first, one should perform her twelvefold placement (*nyāsa*) according to the sequence of emanation.
Afterwards, one should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), which is traditionally known as "going and returning" (gamāgama).
And in the locus of anger, [one should contemplate] both eyes, both nostrils, the throat, the heart, the navel, the yoni, and the foundation-mandala (ādhāramaṇḍala).
The sequence of the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa) has been declared; it is remembered as the path beginning with Gaurī and the others.
At the beginning of the seed-syllable of emanation (sṛṣṭibīja), it is blossomed by the moon-point (indubindu).
O Lord of Gods, by always placing the two words for "going" and "coming" in the sequence beginning with the letter *ma*, in front of the mandala according to the proper order;
Through practice for one year, divine knowledge is fully activated;
when twelve years have been reached, one may pierce even stones.
By the power of the penetration of the Command, he can pulverize mountain peaks and cause numerous seals to burst apart; he performs various wonders.
O beloved, whatever being that person might behold as a cage of vajra-nooses, he should purify that by means of his power and accomplish it during the Kali age.
Having placed this upon the lion-throne of knowledge, the Śakti proceeds;
after some time, she certainly attains the arising of the qualities without delay.
The mouth of the Guru is Nirvāṇa, and likewise it consists of thirty-two syllables;
that is the Command (ājñā), and through that sequence, one should commence the authority of the Guru.

O God, having first understood the mandala conjoined with the three sciences (*vidyā*) and the sequence of deities, as well as the twelve verses that determine the three lineages (*oli*), one then subdues the manifold [world]. (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
And with one mantra-line, as well as half of a vidyā-line.
The mudrā consists of one-eighth part, designated as the "feet of the Guru";
when it is without parts and in a state of nirvāṇa, then a man shall attain accomplishment (siddhi).
Having understood this prior sequence, one should subsequently practice the sixfold [method];
and that, extracted from the Siṃhāsana, consists of twelve divisions.
His presiding Vidyā is the supreme single-syllabled one;
and Kauleśa resides in the center of Meru, seated upon a skull-throne.
But below, conjoined with the creation (sṛṣṭi) and adorned with thirteen [vowels],
this is indeed the supreme *visarga*, devoid of the protracted (*pluta*) vowel.
By means of the very word "neuter," he is neither female nor the preeminent male cause;
his authority has come to the house in the glorious city of Candra.
But its internal determination is through the traditional oral instruction;
at the beginning, that entire [teaching] was proclaimed as being in the form of a *kūṭa*, indeed facing downwards.
O God, one should place [the syllable] Manonmanā, white as snow, jasmine, and the moon, while it flows forth, at the end of the *kopa* according to the sequence of the lion-form.
Nor should an illumination be given for this [mantra], for it is illuminated by its very nature;
through a hundred thousand recitations, success shall arise, and from that, one goes to the supreme state.

Thus, in the *Avvākrama*— belonging to the *Svāminīmata*, the supreme command of the Lord, within the division beginning with the letter *Ka*, in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimala-ṣaṭka*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) exceeding a hundred thousand quarters, emerged from the path of Meru, in the lineage of the sacrifice of Manthānabhairava at the initial descent, measuring seventy million verses— [The text continues...]
In this discourse describing the sixfold authority, this is the bliss named the Arising of the Sequence.
The venerable Vakrā said:
Now I shall describe that abode, distinguished by the triad of Vidyās, which constitutes the twenty-third bliss.
By means of the arrangement of the eight groups of consonants, it has indeed emerged from the rootless source.
The first word is *a' ā na a*, the second is *ā tha gho tu*,
the third should be *i' ṝ re*, and the fourth is *ī ṝ hrīṃ*.
U, ḷ, pa, and pa shall be the fifth; ū, lṛ, and ra are recorded as the sixth; ṝ and ma are the seventh, and the eighth is ṝ, dha, and gha.
*Lṛ* *ṇa* *re* is given as the ninth; *lṛ* *u* *hrauṃ* is remembered as the tenth;
*e* *ū* *gho* is the eleventh, and *ai* *ī* *ram* is the twelfth.
The letter *au* is the thirteenth, and *ka* is the fourteenth;
*aṃ*, *kha*, and *haḥ* are the fifteenth, while *aḥ*, *ga*, and *gho* are the sixteenth.
Ka-gha-ra is the seventeenth; khaṅa-mu is the eighteenth;
ga-i-khi is the nineteenth; and gha-a~ bhī is the twentieth.
Ṅa, va, and ma are the twenty-first; ca and bha are the twenty-second;
cha, ya, and ṣa are the twenty-third; and ja, ḍha, and ṇi are the twenty-fourth.
Jha, ḍa, va, and pa are the twenty-fifth; ña, ṭha, ma, and ṣa are the twenty-sixth;
ṭa, jha, va, and sa are the twenty-seventh; and ṭha, ña, and ma are the twenty-eighth.

Ḍa, aḥ, pi, and ūnatriṃśa (twenty-nine) constitute the thirtieth word; ṇa, ra, pi, and ekatriṃśat (thirty-one) constitute the thirty-first, and ta, ja, va, and dvayatriṃśam (thirty-two) constitute the next.
*Tha-pa-he-ti* is the thirty-third; *de-sa-he* is the thirty-fourth;
*dhaha-ru* is the thirty-fifth; and *na-ccha-ru* is the thirty-sixth.
Pa-la-ra is thirty-seven, pha-ā-ra is thirty-eight;
ba-ṣa-vi is thirty-nine, and bhakṣa-cce is forty.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa: Ma Ma Aiṃ is the forty-first; Ya Śa Hrīṃ is the forty-second; Ra A Hūṃ is the forty-third; La Ta Hrīṃ is the forty-fourth.
VA E AIṂ is the forty-fifth; ŚA AI HRĪṂ is the forty-sixth;
ṢA O AIṂ is the forty-seventh; SA AU KṢAṂ is the forty-eighth.
HA DA HRĪṂ is the forty-ninth; PHA HASRAUṂ is the fiftieth.
Through the conjunction of these fifty words, that [mantra] is grasped in its entirety by way of summary.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) within that [mandala] according to the sequence of the mass of sounds (śabdarāśi);
by practicing this nyāsa, one becomes possessed of a divine body.
Success is attained by reciting [this] for six months, or certainly within a year;
the Vajrayoginī who is without flaw cannot be pierced even by the blows of weapons.
Having first placed the seed-syllable *rāva* at the beginning of the mantra-pada and likewise again at its end,
one should place it within the enclosure of the *rāva*-seed syllables, according to the distinctions of the threefold Vidyā.
Therefore, that intensely blazing grasping, devoid of seeds and turned away,
having emerged from the other's body, is a mass of yoginīs' faces.
Thus, that field of grasping is entirely according to the prescribed rule;
indeed, the movement of the family is thus established in the family practice.
He who possesses this placement upon the mouth also abides in the state of peace;
there is no doubt that he does not engage in any unrighteousness previously practiced.
The venerable Vakrā said: I shall further declare another [rite], the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the sequence of the commitments (*samaya*).
By means of the sequence of the division of the steps, the Vidyā becomes the Mistress of the Seat (*pīṭheśvarī*).
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: first is the word *cce vi ce*, and second is *ṇiki ṇiki*;
*ccha ra ī* with a half-moon, and *ccha ra ā* with a full moon.
The third *repha* from both [mantras] should be placed again at the beginning;
having placed *ū* with the moon (*sa*) at the throat, the fourth *pada* is extracted.
The sixth word is formed by the doubling of the syllable *kaha* due to conjunction;
the eight-word mantra of the deity is remembered as being formed by the doubling of the syllable *saha*.
Hara (ha) and the moon (u), situated in the void (zero), become two-fold; this is remembered as the ninth [letter].
Ni-ka-ko (ṇa) and two-fives (ten); ni-ka-ko (ṇa) is ten plus one (eleven).
Ha-śakti, the void (śūnya), the half-moon (candrārdha), the digit (kalā), the letter Ra, and the Moon;
with Gaurī, the void—in this sequence, there is thus one single aggregate, the twelfth.
This very word *menaṇañaṅa* is the thirteenth;
*haragaurī*, *śaśi*, *śūnya*, *harā*, *śūnya*, and *maulinī*.
The fourteenth word is known as *khimurāgho a*,
and the fifteenth is declared to be *rāva regho-a*, the sixteenth.
*Reghora* should be the seventeenth; *re rā rāḥ* is the eighteenth;
*kebjiku hasau* is the twentieth; and the twenty-first word is *śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ*.
It has been explained according to the lion-gait (siṃhakrama), beginning with the syllable Aiṃ in its proper sequence;
arising occurs by way of the solar path, and obstruction by way of the lunar path.
Following the sequence of the moon and the sun, and by means of the sixty-four phonemes,
the name called "Samaya" has been joined to the primordial Kula and Kaula.
Endowed with the beginning and the end, joined with the seed-syllable, she is Manonmanā;
she is Pīṭheśvarī, Māyā, Samayā, and Kulamālinī. She is Kumārikākhaṇḍa; she is radiant when conjoined with the seed-syllable, and devoid of the seed-syllable when not ignited.
He who is the great presiding authority over this succeeds when he is served.
With fourteen seed-syllables, Koṅkaṇā is said to be adorned with flames;
when recited one hundred thousand times, the power of Rudra is set in motion.
By this mere knowledge, even by reciting this vidyā just once, or simply by remembering it, or merely by its extraction, [one is liberated].
Even by remembering it, one gains good fortune and the destruction of great sins;
the sin committed over seven lifetimes perishes merely by reciting it.
At that very moment, the disciple is liberated within the wheel, or within another mandala,
at a seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) or a secondary seat (upapīṭha), and from the midst of the circle of yoginīs.
At a solitary tree, in a cremation ground, at a gathering, or at a crossroads—
by means of the libation that fills the vessel, [it is offered] into the skull-bowl of Viśvāmitra.
Alternatively, one may worship and offer libations in a human skull; thereby, one shall be released from the violation of the *samaya* and [attain] splendor, longevity, and valor.
The true nature of knowledge proceeds as the assembly of the Yoginī-kula;
one who is joined to the observance (samaya) likewise obtains the hero’s substance and the sacrificial pap (caru).
From consuming it, success is attained; otherwise, death would occur.
When the state free from doubt has been reached, one should partake of the sequence of the *samaya*.
Having consumed the *samaya* sacrificial porridge (*caruka*), which bestows the fruit of all accomplishments, [success follows].
Whether established in a vow or devoid of a vow, one who is not initiated becomes initiated.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
One who is uninitiated becomes initiated; the unfortunate becomes fortunate;
one of short life-span gains long life, and the poor man becomes wealthy.
The mantra-practitioner who is a holder of the vidyā of the samaya, relying upon heroic substances,
possesses incomparable authority in this scripture within the city of Kaulinī.
One who is devoid of the knowledge of the samaya, who has abandoned the conduct of the family (kula),
and whose practice of mantra has been ruined— even if initiated— remains a bound soul (paśu).
From the violation of commitments comes poverty; from transgressing against the Guru comes death.
When the command is broken, how can there be accomplishment? One will soon go to hell.

One should guard the family tradition, the lineage of gurus, and the Kula scripture; as well as the food offering, the sacrificial rice (caru), and whatever else is established according to the ritual sequence.
One who stands firm in the vows of knowledge should consume the guru’s remains— the *caru* oblation consecrated with ten thousand recitations of the *samaya* mantra—
having first performed a prostration with eight limbs before the mandala.
Having placed [them] in both hands, grant permission out of your grace.

When thus addressed by the disciple, through the grace of the Guru’s mouth, the Kaulika perfection is attained by consuming [the substance]; it is not otherwise for one who is free from conceptual construction.
Now I shall describe the Kaulika deposition according to the method of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāya).
One should perform the deposition of the first seven syllables, the letter *ra* (repha), and the third [syllable] for the eye, and [the syllable] *kopā*.
O God, *rārā* is assigned to both ears; *kubjikā* is remembered for the mouth; and *rā rā* is assigned to the two eyes.
The mistress of the family.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa it is said:
"One should place the trident at the tip of the nose in Aghora;
the seed-syllable of sound (rāva) is for the tongue, and Aghorā is in the three seats."
Having placed *mukhi* upon the two lips, *hrāṃ* and *hrīṃ* on both cheeks,
one should assign the letter *ṅa* to the chin and the letter *ña* to the neck and waist-belt.
The syllables *me*, *ṇa*, and *ca*— beginning with *kra*— are the essence of the heart.
Thus is the Necklace and Girdle;
the syllable HŪṂ is in the center of the vital breath.
One should place this triad upon the breasts: *Koṃkaṇi*.
Having placed *Koṃkaṇa* on the abdomen, one places the letter *i* in the navel-mandala;
*hrauṃ hrauṃ* on the two hands, and the sound *kahau hasa* on the back.
And one should place the syllable *kaha*, accompanied by the sound of laughter (*hasa*), upon the two shoulders.
In the pair of arms, one should say "kahānyam"; in the circle of the womb, "glauṃkāra"; with the two hands, "sahaśabda"; and with the fingers of the hands, "samaya".
One should place "Bhairavī" in Aghorā, "Chāṃ Chhaḥ" on the pair of thighs,
"Kiṇī" on the two knees and shanks, and "Kiṇi" on the two feet.
In this [mantra], the Vāgbhava syllable is at the tip of the big toe and in the middle of the face;
starting from whichever place [the ritual] begins, the placement (nyāsa) is performed with the Vidyā.
Furthermore, the utterance [of the mantra] occurs at the very end of the foot, where its dissolution takes place;
indeed, it is proclaimed that this constitutes both its rising and its setting.
This is that Samayā-vidyā who has emerged from the Apasavya;
she alone is the presiding authority over the field of that planet.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
one attains perfection through the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Vidyā by means of the Kūṭa itself, according to the prescribed rule,
during the worship with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) before the mandala in the presence of the Guru.

Or, in the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) or in the wheel (cakra), wherever it has been performed according to the sequence, there for him the Kaulika realization arises as the condition for the Great State (mahāvasthā).
He shows compassion to that [practitioner] and to the Goddess through a vision in a dream;
soon, being liberated from all dualities, he attains the state of moving through the sky.
Thus, in the introduction to the Great Sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses emerged from the Path of Meru,

exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (Vidyāpīṭha), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand, in the Kādi division, in the Svāminīmata which is the Supreme Lord’s Command,
in the venerable Compendium of Twenty-Four Thousand verses spoken in the Avvākrama tradition, this is the sequence describing the chapter on the Vidyā of the Observance of the Planets.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth bliss.
The venerable Lord said:
"O Mistress who shatters the maiden's [pride], I have heard your word from your mouth."
How is that *mātṛkā* known by the name "divided into twelve verses"?
"O Goddess, I do not understand; explain the meaning of the verse clearly.
Śrīvakrā said: "Since I have been questioned by you with the expansion of great bliss (mahānanda), [I shall explain it]."
I shall explain all of that— the determination of the sequence of the Mātṛkā—
He who is both supreme and non-supreme, infinite, all-pervading, and the imperishable cause.
O Maheśvara, the supreme state called Praśānta is beyond peace, free from ailment, and devoid of the forms previously fashioned by Bhairava.
In the succession of eons, even through hundreds of previous manvantaras and eighty-four yugas, she remained as firm as a stone.
For one day at the Bhairava sacrifice, you are Bhairava and I am Bhairavī;
yet neither the form of a woman nor the form of a man exists for us, nor is there any form whatsoever anywhere.
O Hara, I know only this little: that the mind, finding delight in the bliss of union within the state of emptiness where darkness is one, becomes like the tranquility of the Kula.
O Hara, neither by speech, nor by hearing and sight,
nor even by the intellect do I comprehend that which bestows the bliss of absolute liberation and which is the hundredfold delight.
His will is a mere slight consciousness, unmanifest yet possessing the form of manifestation.

Regarding this, she says—having fallen into amazement: "What is this void-like form? Thinking it to be a dense and terrible place, I spoke while terrified and with a mind as if asleep. *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
I have entered into the Bhairava sacrifice, abiding there in my supreme form.
O Lord, some form exists in the nature of atoms; it is like a lion, a destroyer of lions, turned away and agitated by darkness.
Akula, Ādikula, Vyākula, Kulakaulika, and Kalanā;
ending with Dhvanināda, that Nāda has thus come forth in five ways.
And that reality of the phonemes and so forth, the great arising of the *kalās*,
as well as the one enriched by the *kalās*, the peaceful one, and the unmoving one beginning with the *visarga*.
One should place the Mahogra, Kālika-rāva, and likewise the one called Rūpa,
following the sequence of the *Kulapaddhati* through the yoga of the *Kulāvalita*.
The supreme practitioner receives these twelve verses, passed from ear to ear, by means of constant practice of recitation.
O Bhairava, this knowledge should be given to him alone, and never otherwise; it is [conferred] by means of the five general clusters of praṇavas.
One should extract the twelve auspicious verses presided over by the six peaks, by means of the great divine [mantras] called *haṃsa*, which are presided over by the Supreme Form (*parāmūrti*).
There are four [groups] with sixteen divisions each, as well as six within the space of the sky;
those situated in the midst of emanation are located between *ha* and *kṣa*, according to their twofold division.
How is the pair called "Kathā," and how is Anaṅga joined with Sṛṣṭi?
Beneath that, O Lord, is Hanumān, accompanied by Rāvamārga.
In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*,

within the determination of the twelve verses, [the syllable] is described as being stepped upon by the head of the Lord of Elephants (*gajendra*), marked with the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*, and joined with the light of the *ājñā*.
The second syllable has been declared; now as for how the third should be:
it is pierced by the head of the bindu of space (vyomabindu) and joined with the digits of Nāda and Śakti; this is called Mahogra.
One should recite it while it flows as nectar and is joined with tranquility.
O Great Śambhu, there is a double repetition as far as the letters of the Mātṛkā, pierced by the fire-piercer (agnivedhaka).
This supreme knowledge of the ritual arrangement is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Having extracted the lineage method through the yoga of the family succession,
this truth, which is for the sake of the collective purpose and is otherwise unspeakable, has been shown to you.
That supreme-and-non-supreme deity Bhairava is the destroyer of worldly existence;
his will, indeed called the Nameless, is a slight consciousness that gathers [all things].
And she indeed, as the all-pervasive one, is the complete supreme Kaulinī;
she is the Amā, the subtle, the nameless, who has gone to dissolution in the bliss beyond bliss.
And that Bhairavī is indeed peaceful, differentiated by Ananta;
therefore, through the differentiation of Manthāna, she is divided into the higher and the lower.
Thus, O Haṃsa, the bodiless one who exists within creation is the destroyer of desire;
he is the Great Soul, born from the nectar of the blazing fire.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
These two, known as Śiva and Śakti, are woven warp and woof throughout the three worlds;
this secret has been declared under the name Mahāmanthāna.
Śrīnātha said: O Lord, what is my designation? From where did I arise, O stainless one?
I have become agitated; tell me without any doubt.
The venerable Vakrā said:
"O Lord of the Kula, your question has been answered along with its secret; O Amoghājñā, I shall tell you without doubt of the digit that is the wish-granting cow of desire."
O Hara, just as I, who was once a mass of consciousness and bliss, have now become a mere body of bliss,
by that [transformation] our former satisfaction has become the earth.
The Earth spoke: "You are the Great Sound (Mahac-chabda), the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), and the imperishable syllables;
she is known as the Will of Śiva-Śambhu, and her characteristic is perfect peace."
I am a certain art, Kālī, the incomplete one, the Śāmbhavī of the Kula;
for I am the Supreme Will, arisen from the Beyond, unmanifest yet possessing manifest form.
Kulālī is the mistress of the Kulakaula; she becomes pervasive from Akula.
Through union with her in the form of the Pervader (Vyāpaka), [the state] arises.
Through union, however, she who was without movement was set in motion;
first is that which is called Nameless, the eternal crest upon the head.
And Mahābhairavajyotis is pervasive in the western house.
Thus indeed is the sequence of the sixfold group (ṣaṭkakrama), you who are the Vidyā enveloped by the Void. In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
the arising is named Vimala, the Nectar, the Drop, and Bhairava.
Arising through conjunction, they are then recorded as twelve at the end.
Residing within my form, she should perform the indication of the cause of emanation.
I am she, and she is the one supreme [Parā] and the other [Aparā] in the ocean of accomplishments.
O Sāgara, O Manmatha, by name, you go to the end of the Kula and Akula.
The triple family, the three principles, the threefold mantra-practitioner, and the powers.
The three Siddhas, the three currents, the three principles, and the interior of the triple path—
that supreme and great station, as vast as the ocean, is pervaded by me.
The mandala is "unbroken" (akhaṇḍa), extending as far as the ocean, the moon, and the sun;
it is indeed unbroken, infinite, and likewise inexhaustible.
O Lord, Akula is the fifth, to be known as the ornament of the Kulas;
thus the Nāda has arisen, having come forth in five ways in succession.
In sequence, emanation is established in the womb; indeed, she alone is downward-facing.
She is the Great Form, whose nature is existence, whose form is light, and who is Manonmanī.
O Bhairava, the power Kuṇḍalinī is the Unmanā state, moving with the velocity of mind;
she is the digit named Amā, Kālī, who remains struck [in the center].
And her very seat is the vessel (pātra) which is celebrated by the name Iḍā;
that Iḍā is Bhairavī, the peaceful one, declared to be the vessel of power (śakti).
At the rising of the lunar disc, it emits the radiant sun;
and that [sun] is a dense and formidable drop (*bindu*) born from the gurgling nectar.
The Kaulinī, who is the nature of the fire situated within the *maphreka-saharāva*, manifests as the *kalā* through the sixfold division of the Śāmbhava state.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Abiding in the unity of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, she dwells within the limits of space;
from the aggregate of principles beginning with space, the phonemes were indeed born from that principle.
And those [notes] overcome by the *kalās* are to be known according to their nature as the pentads and so forth:
the five elements are the five vowels, which arise from the subtle *Śāmbhava*;
*Śāmbhava* is the secret [syllable] consisting of the letters *ra*, *kha*, *sa*, and *ha*.
Its very first face is conjoined with the nameless [vowel] and the nameless [consonant].
O Maheśvara, listen to how it was stated according to the order of emanation:
space conjoined with the individual soul (jīva), and fire conjoined with Ardhīśa.
O Bhairava, O Hara, you are the syllable (akṣara) who is presided over by the head of grace (anugraha), pierced by the subtle sound (nāda),
and presided over by the digit of the moon (candrakalā) within the point (bindu).
The Void is conjoined with the Sky-farer (Khecarī) and rests upon the limit of the Far-reaching (Pharamanta);
it is differentiated by a single foot and marked by the digits of Sound (Nāda) and the Drop (Bindu).
This is that supreme Khecarī-vidyā, which attracts the three worlds;
it is the deity situated in the middle of *ya* and again situated in the middle of *ha*.
Having grasped that which is situated in the midst of the Naṭa, they know it to be contained within that;
it rests upon the peak of Gaurī and is endowed with the digit of the lunar drop.
The third Vidyā of Śaṅkara has been declared, the Mistress of the Kula;
the fourth, named Māyā, O Hara, is situated on the seat of space (vyomāsana),
conjoined with the locus of fire (agnidhāma) and positioned between *i* and *u*.
Ambikā, who possesses the *bindu* and the half-measure (*ardhakalā*), is of fierce form.

She is the ineffable Mother, the Power (*śakti*) differentiated by the syllables *ha*, *sa*, *pha*, and *ka*; she is endowed with the measures of *nāda* and *bindu*, and her form is that of the Vāgbhava syllable.
The Kaulinī is the ground of knowledge for the Kulanāthas and the Siddhas;
the Śāmbhava Praṇavas are five, and the sixth is supreme consciousness.
The goddess Pūrṇā, who is both supreme and non-supreme, is endowed with six limbs and six faces;
one should utter her according to the sequence of the six seed-syllables, following the instruction of the Guru.
O Śambhu, he who knows this great twelve-fold arrangement of verses, joined with the words and meanings of the verses through the divine union of the two hexads;
He too shall become a bearer of the Kaulika command in a single lifetime;
whomever he touches with his hand and whomever he beholds with his eye.
Whatever one recollects with devotion, all that is accomplished in an instant—
even many wicked and cruel beings, such as earth-dwellers, serpents, and rākṣasas.
"By the mere sight of him, they flee in the ten directions;
this is the truth declared by me, the supreme intended meaning of the verse."
Those who perform this placement, knowing the three times, go to the supreme goal.
Śrīvakrā said: Now I shall describe another sequence, established in twelve verses.
Listen to those twelve Siddhayoginīs by their names:
[from] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Kālī, Karālī, and Vikṛtānanā.
Kroṣṭukī, Bhīmabhadrā, Vāyuvegā, Hayānanā,
Gambhīrā, and Ghoṣaṇī— these are remembered as the twelve Yoginīs.
Having first placed three *vāgbhava* syllables and those same [syllables] at the end in reverse order,
the goddesses are joined by the *saṃpuṭa* method for the sake of accomplishing the twelve limbs.
One should place Nandā on the head and the one called Bhadrā on the forehead.
And Jayā is in the right eye, and Kālī is in the left.
Karālī is on the right ear, and Vikṛtānanā on the left;
Kroṣṭukī is at the tip of the nose, and Bhīmarudrā likewise on the mouth.
Vāyuvegā is at the throat, Hayā is situated in the heart,
Gambhīrā is in the middle of the navel, and Ghoṣiṇī is in the middle of the secret place.
Thus is the supreme placement (*nyāsa*) of the goddesses, which bestows a divine body;
this placement of the enclosure is declared to have twelve limbs.
For the lion of the *samaya*, twelve yoginīs are traditionally taught;
having first performed their placement (*nyāsa*), wherever a man may go, [he shall succeed].
In each of those places, O Maheśvara, he obtains abundant knowledge and great gain, as well as a gathering of the secret Yoginīs.
Indeed, by the power of the twelve limbs, they proclaim knowledge;
being pleased, they grant divine sacrificial porridge and swift progress.
O Maheśvara, if the yogi who bears a divine form remains concealed, I shall further explain another sequence: the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for the appropriation of the sacred field (*kṣetra*).
From Amṛta (A) up to Jīva (Ha), conjoined with the designations Ha and Kṣa,
one should perform the nyāsa according to the sequence of the aggregate of sounds (śabdarāśi).
I shall proclaim the instruction regarding the supreme possession by the Goddess;
and the illumination must be performed separately for each and every letter.
The two designations are Hakṣa; the locations are Prāṇa, Krodha, and Khe-bala.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, no further kindling is to be given by those two, for they are kindled by their own inherent nature.
The aggregate whose nature is the radiance of the phonemes follows the sequence of the vowels and consonants;
indeed, the field of the sequence of vowels and consonants is the domain of the Supreme Goddess.
One should know the lamp, the yoga of bliss, and the grasping of power;
first indeed is the wheel of vowels, which is the determination of the sixteen principles (tattvas).

And those letters beginning with *ka* which have been taught as the life-force (*jīva*) of all embodied beings—their manifestation occurs through the *visarga*; this is the appropriation of the field (*kṣetra*).
Krodha is said to be the vital power (prāṇakalā), and she is enveloped by the energy of Rudra;
one should practice the union of these two through the mouth of the Guru.
By means of the method of emanation, one should perform the placement [of mantras] on the head and other parts to take possession of the field;
for without taking possession of the field, what is to be accomplished by mortals does not succeed.
For their sake, however, the means of accomplishment, the narrative, and the ritual acceptance have been taught;
by practicing this, O Lord, there is consecration within the command.
For through practice, realization arises within one month;
at that time, one neither hears nor sees the boundaries of the field.
Henceforth, I shall explain again the threefold authority,
by the mere knowledge of which authority proceeds.
O God, the lineage consists of a triad: the eldest, the middle, and the youngest;
namely, the Bāla-krama, the Kaumāra, and the Vṛddha—these are the three lineages.

O Śambhu, their three peaks have emerged from the body of Parā; they are the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the collection of the beginning and end of the nature of breath, and the nitamba situated at the beginning.
Likewise, [he places] the left breast, the throat, and the staff on the right shoulder;
again the vital breath (prāṇa) and again the staff—[all] milked together into a single mass.
In this way, the eleven Rudras are joined together;
this is declared to be the Rudrakūṭa, conjoined with the void (kha) and the half-moon.
This, extracted from the lineage of the elders, has been illuminated by Chinnamuṇḍa;
that very [essence] is devoid of milk and pierced by the nose.
O handsome one, this *kaumāra-krama-kūṭa* has been declared to you;
it is indeed that very [syllable] made empty by the nose and pierced by the left earring.
The third and the youngest are declared to be the Bālakrama;
the Guru should perform the placement of the three lineages (oli) and the three peaks (kūṭa).
One should place the eldest [wheel] in the circle of the brow-midpoint,
the middle one in the region of the navel, and the youngest from the form of desire.
For those disciples born in the lineage of the Siddhas through the three Aulī stages,
a threefold nyāsa has been declared, which is always beneficial for them.
"O Lord of Gods, by this sequence," such is the command of the Supreme Lord;
at that very moment, the lineage of that curse there became averted.
Those who worship the Guru as being equal to themselves, yet without the seed-syllable (nirbīja),
remain further within saṃsāra and do not turn back from saṃsāra.
There is no illumination whatsoever for them, as they are illuminated by the Śāmbhava-kūṭa;
therefore, the arrangement of the kūṭas, extracted through the sequence of mantras, is threefold.
Furthermore, those three are established by means of the reverse order:
the syllable *o*, the syllable *ṣa*, and the syllable *mi*—these are the three *ulikas*.
Having placed the leaders there according to their essential nature as a single mass,
one performs the placement through the instruction of the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, which brings about the supreme possession.
The youngest, the middle, and the eldest; the middle one from the center of the womb, and that other which is the youngest, the third one within the womb.
One should not perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) in this manner, nor otherwise;
O Śambhu, having understood the threefold authority, one should begin the sacrifice.
Hereafter, I shall describe the ritual placement of the five jewels (*ratnapañcaka*).
The pentad has been taught everywhere for the Siddhas who have mastered the secret signs of the Siddhas.
The third tooth of the Goddess is again her own self in the heart;
her hip is the *śikhā* [mantra] pierced by the right breast,
and it is filled with the left earring, pierced by *kha-śakti* and Śiva.
The Five Jewels have been declared, proclaimed as beloved by all people;
for those perfected in medicine, friendship, and spiritual attainments, the sequence of the Immortal (Amarikā) is indeed established.
By means of that, the hidden meaning is obtained—the Kulakaulika made manifest.
O Mahādeva, through the exhaustion of karma, this vidyā becomes fivefold; it should be constantly cultivated within one's lineage, and thereby one becomes a destroyer of karma.
That supreme aggregate which begins with the Jewel is located in the Foundation Mandala;
the fourth is in the region of the throat, and the fifth is in the Fourth Mandala. (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
One should place five Ekavīras; there is no illumination for them anywhere, as they have gone to dissolution in the center of the bhaga through union with the interior of the syllable Aiṃ.
One should place the five [syllables] in the fields, illuminated by their own nature;
merely by this placement of longevity, a person becomes free from defects.
By shaking the divine seats and cities, one shall attain the siddhi of the heroes;
together with fifty heroes, one obtains various enjoyments.
O Lord, if one turns [the wheel] through recollection or even by recitation,
then for that yogin, the abode of all accomplishments proceeds.
Through divine vision, there is agitation in the city; however, through reliance on the five, accomplishment is attained.
When ten hundred thousand recitations have been performed, the intense command comes forth.
Through the five jewels, complete accomplishment is attained; the state of nirvāṇa is reached after first understanding the intended meaning and the clear words of the mantra.
This indeed is the Kaulika Sūtra, encircled by the sixteenfold installation (ṣoḍhānyāsa);
it is the flood of mantras of the sixteen lineages, the transmission (krama) consisting of sixteen forms.
O Vimalavijñāna, this has emerged from the noble path;
the family consists of sixteen divisions, and the continuum likewise consists of sixteen.
The lineage born of the sixteen commands has been extracted from the *Nyāsamañjūṣaka*;
it must be guarded with great effort and should not be shown to practitioners of Tantra.

O beautiful one, thus has the power of the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa) been declared; it should be understood from the instruction of the guru as the compendium of the meaning of the Saṃhitā, from the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
The detailed account was previously explained in the *Mata* consisting of more than one hundred thousand quarters;
here, it is presented in brief as found in the twenty-four thousand [verse] version.
"The sūtra of the sixfold deposition has thus been declared to you, O handsome one.
Thus [ends the section] in the primordial descent of the Great Sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses emerged from the path of Meru,
exceeding a hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the first seat, on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (vimala-ṣaṭka).

In the *Ājñāpārameśvara* belonging to the *Kādibheda*, in the *Svāminīmata* consisting of twenty-four thousand verses as spoken in the *Avvākrama*, in the description of the sequence of the *Ṣoḍhānyāsamañjūṣā*,
this is the bliss named *Kramodaya*; the twenty-fifth bliss.
Śrīnātha said:
"O Maheśvarī, the Kula with its sixteen divisions has been understood by me;
but how is the other, natural Kula [to be known] through its reverse order?"
The six cakras, the sixteen supports, the three lakṣas, and the five voids—
these have not been clearly understood by me according to the sequence of the Kula path.
"Now, O Goddess, let it be told how the division of the Kula occurs.
The venerable Vakrā said: "This most excellent question has been brought down by the God of Gods."
I shall explain his reflection upon the sequence of the *Kulapañcāśikā*;
O Śambhu, O Bhairava, listen as I speak of the sequence of the root of the Kula.
First, the kanda-cakra, which arises from the stalk of the kanda, is downward-facing;
that secret kanda-cakra is situated with its face turned downwards.
Possessing four petals and a radiance equal to a ruby,
its four divisions are the lords of the wheels within the foundation.
The *piṇḍa* is his grace, stainless as snow, jasmine, and the moon;
above that is the second, the King of Yoga, facing downwards.
Resembling fire and tawny in color, with a body blazing with flames—
its six divisions are to be known as the Lord of the Wheel, Svādhiṣṭhāna.
Its mass is a great roar, slightly red and pure by nature.
In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:
above that is the third wheel, the fire of the navel.
The great jewel is greatly radiant; its divisions are indeed ten.
It is presided over by the sixth vowel and bears the moon situated within the bindu.
Resembling the flower of the pomegranate tree, it is a blazing, terrifying fire;
that is the certain conviction regarding the perfected *piṇḍa* of the *maṇipūra*.
Renowned as the leader of the wheels and honored by the gods and siddhas,
his fourth [wheel] is above that, in the heart, a downward-facing wheel.
Its color appears like its enemy; it has twelve divisions.
It is renowned as the Lord of the Wheel (*cakranāyaka*), and therein lies Anāhatabhairava.
His heart is the Khecarī-piṇḍa consisting of twelve syllables;
his meditation should be red, slightly mixed with dark blue.
Therefore, I shall now fully explain another determination of the wheels;
its divisions, white as snow, jasmine, and the moon, are sixteen.
There, the pure Bhairava is said to be the leader of the wheel;
its seed-syllable (piṇḍa) is the vehicle, differentiated by three feet.
Its color is green, resembling a dark blue cloud;
above that is the supreme wheel, vast and situated in the fourth state.
O Lord, bliss like cow’s milk, whose form is radiant energy and whose shape is that of a vulva—
two divisions of that have been proclaimed for the Sovereign of the Ājñā-cakra.
That seed-syllable of his is the Vāgbhava-piṇḍa, resembling the red glow of vermilion;
it is the seventh [letter] resulting from the abandonment of six, situated above in the void-mandala of space.
That is declared to be beyond the fourth (turyātīta); from that, the group of six has emerged.
Indeed, by way of the sequence of emanation, that flood of wheels is visualized from above.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the fourth wheel at the throat indeed has sixteen spokes;
the heart has twelve spokes, while the navel is known to have ten.
The six-spoked wheel is the womb-circle (yonicakra), while the four-spoked one is known as the anus-giver;
furthermore, their sequence of accomplishment follows the order beginning with purification.
Viśuddha is divided into sixteen parts, Anāhata into twelve,
Maṇi into ten, and Svādhiṣṭhāna consists of six.
They know there are four divisions in the Ādhāra and two divisions in the Ājñā;
the divisions beginning with the letter 'A' and ending with the Visarga are recorded as sixteen.
The twelve [vowels] beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha* reside in the *anāhata* [cakra];
the ten divisions beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *pha* reside in the *maṇi* [cakra].
O Mahādeva, listen now to how the sixfold division from the letter *ba* to the letter *la* resides respectively in the Svādhiṣṭhāna and the Ādhāra.
The four divisions beginning with the letter *va* and ending with the letter *sa* are the supports;
the sixth wheel, formed by the two letters *ha* and *kṣa*, is located between the eyebrows.
Excluding two syllables, twelve verses are traditionally taught;
through the abandonment of six, liberation occurs in the seventh—thus, O Ānanda, is it established therein.
Furthermore, there are sixteen supports and three hundred thousand [pores];
the sixteen supports of the *kalās* begin with Amṛtā and end with Visarga.
And for them, the Yoginīs and Siddhas are established within their own bodies:
Ananta, Ākāśa, Indu, and that which is named Īśvara.
Udaya, Ūrjanātha, Ṛkṣakarṇa, and Ṛṣabha;
Liptāṅga, Lūliha, Ekapāda, and Maheśvara.
Likewise, Rāvaṇa, Avalī,
Aumuni, Ambunātha, Ahvavāha, and Ādhāra— these are remembered as the sixteen [supports].
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
These very great Siddhas, joined with the syllable *aiṃ* at the beginning and the end, have pervaded the body;
their locations are sixteen.
In the first *ghaṇṭikā* [is] the second [element];
in the palate-circle [are] marrow, fat, and semen; and furthermore, Kuṇḍalī [consists of] sinew, bone, skin, hair, filaments, and likewise nectar.
Flesh and blood indeed become the submarine fire and the wind.
And space as well, O God—thus are the sixteen supports.
Among them, O God, are the three lineages (oli), which are the triad of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
In brief, the three characteristics are mind, intellect, and ego.

Of these, indeed, there are three perfected ones who are immovable; O friend, their dissolution occurs in this manner: Bhairava is in the five voids, in the support (ādhāra), in the heart, and likewise in the threshold (kapāṭaka) of Kula.
Having pierced the target situated in the five voids, one attains movement through the sky;
[one sees] another solar disc situated in the midst of the lunar disc.
Situated in the middle of the wind-maṇḍala is another, the space-maṇḍala;
space is said to be fivefold: below, in the middle, and at the top.
The pervaders of these are five, which differentiate the path of the bindu;
indeed, their "Five Siddhas" are joined with Śiva at the beginning and the end.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
these five great elements were fashioned as the agents of creation.
Śrīkaṇṭha, Śaṅkara, Ananta, Sādākhya, and Piṅgala—
these five are the creators of emanation, as well as the Siddhas within the Five Families (Pañcakula).
Śrīkaṇṭha is to be known as the earth; Śaṅkara is said to be the water.
Ananta is declared to be fire, and Sādākhya is said to be the wind.
Ākāśa is to be known as Piṅgala; these five are the creators of emanation.
This indeed is the secret path of Kula that has been explained to you in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Just as a woman of good family is kept hidden, so too is the lineage (kula) to be most carefully concealed.
Having first understood the extraction (uddhāra), one should thereafter begin the sacrifice.
This is the practice of the lineage transmission (kulakramācāra), distinguished by the Bindu-maṇḍala.
Having fixed the mind upon that target, the power of Rudra proceeds.
Whether below, in the middle, or above, one should establish authority equal to one's own self;
then, one should discipline the mind of one's own body.
Then, by way of being both external and internal, pleasure arises;
having taken up that which belongs to the families and the non-families, the body is divided into six parts.
Furthermore, the Navasaṃjñā becomes the ocean of the division of families;
Śaṅkha, Śakti, Yoga, and Mahāgṛha as the fourth.
The fifth is declared by the Lord to be the foot, while the sixth is called the *āvalī* of the past; the two following are proclaimed as the subsequent ones,
and the ninth family, O Mahādeva, is the supreme bliss.
The Kula, however, is renowned as being divided into nine types, facing in every direction.
O God, [these are] the Uḍḍāmara, Siddhakaula, Gaṇākhya, Khecarīmata, Candrākhya, Raurava, Vīrākhya, and Bhūtaḍāmara.

But the ninth is the Mahākaula, which provides direct realization and its own specific authority; by means of it, the Command was brought down into the doctrine exceeding one hundred thousand quarters.
Therefore, that is the Siddhakaula; at that time, it is the state of conviction for the Kaula, the transmental (unmanī) condition—this is the instruction of the Kaula.
That which is proclaimed as Kulakaula is without beginning or end and unstruck;
one should know that the single Kula is differentiated by the five voids.

The seat, their piercing, and the sequence of the Fifty Families of the Kula; thus, in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, in the primordial descent of the Great Sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primary seat on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (Vidyāpīṭha), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand, in the division beginning with 'Ka'.

In the Ājñāpārameśvara, the Svāminīmata, the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the Avvākrama tradition, this is the bliss named Kramodaya, occurring within the description of the chapter on the Kulapañcāśikā.
Śrīnātha said:
What is the Kula of the Twenty-sixth Bliss? What is the conduct of its lineage? And what is the worship in the Krama-maṇḍala?
Speak, O Great Goddess; by your grace, tell me, O Lord.
The venerable Vakrā said: "The Root Sūtra of the Krama consists of three and a half verses;
beginning from that, the emanation proceeds in sequence—thus [it is] the Khecarī."

That power called Bhaga, which possesses threefold movement, consists of three syllables and is of three types; within it, situated in the center, is the brilliantly radiant Śrī-Ṣoḍaśānta together with the supreme digit (kalā).
That which is known as Śrī-Jālandhara, whose abode is manifest, is located in the southern corner.

On the left is the venerable Pūrṇapīṭha, which causes fear to the fettered; then Kāmarūpa, and above that Tisrapīṭha, endowed with the supreme *kalā*. On the forehead, within the triangle, is the entire divine Candrapīṭha, agitated by the *kalā* of Supreme Śiva.

In the midst of that is the curved liṅga (*vakraliṅga*), which produces supreme bliss, is of the nature of the drop (*bindu*), is divided into three, and is the very essence of eternal bliss; from the churning above that arises the sixfold authority (*ṣaṭprakārādhikāra*).
Above that is the flood of the lineage of the ancient transmission (*pūrvāmnāyakramaugha*), and further still, the aged, the adolescent, and the child;
thus is everything pervaded by Rudra-Śakti, the mother of maintenance, dissolution, and generation, through her three divisions. (From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*)

The Command of Ciñcā, consisting of the divisions beginning with *ka*, bestows the bliss of both the non-dual (*akula*) and the dual (*kula*); the Command of the Guru, whose nature is consciousness, possesses six aspects and removes the fear of bound souls within the center of the lunar orb.

The eternally moist, intensely red Śrī Kujā— the supreme bliss-power (parānanda-śakti) who is joyful and fearless— is well-known for manifesting the divine liṅga of Śambhu, her beautiful body agitated with passion;
she has brought down for you this primordial thread facing downwards.
That power which is called Parā is the Goddess whose form is the *bhaga*.
At its center is that supreme Goddess, the deity of the seats among all seats;
she who is the power known as Bhaga, whose movement is again threefold.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara correspond to the letters beginning with *ā* and *tha*;
Jyeṣṭhā, Vāmā, and Raudrī are differentiated by the twelve verses.
That supreme power of Rudra is established in three locations:
in the forehead, the heart, and the womb; she flows through these three sites of action.
Semen and blood are located in the junctions of the three channels;
these three are Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā, which is the middle one.
Thus, O God, by means of the yoga of bliss, the triple power (triśakti) is under its own authority;
its sequence consists of the stages of childhood, youth, and old age.
In the three lineages, there is one sequence joined with the five seats:
Ānanda, Ānandabindu, Akṣara, and Paramā Kalā.
These five seats are established in sequence within the inner limb;
and in the outer limb, they are the peaks (kūṭas): O, JĀ, PŪ, KĀ, and TISRAKA. —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
The entire Kula and Kaula is enveloped by the digits of Śiva and Śakti;
it is a multitude enveloped in bliss, and it proceeds within bliss itself.
In one whose mind experiences the bliss of emergence, equanimity arises;
in the midst of that is the subtle *liṅga*, the divine *liṅga* facing downward.
Then, by means of the perceived inner self, one enters that hollow space situated within the orb of the moon in the midst of the supreme ether.
Established in samādhi, one beholds the form of the *bindu* in the expanse of the sky;
there, the arising of the bliss of consciousness and its intense immersion (*āveśa*) proceed.
"Both its form and its own nature"—this refers to the auditory cognition;
when consciousness and its mental factors have been churned, "the substratum of karma has been churned."
From the churning of the wheel as well, there is a repeated immersion into yoga;
that wheel within the lineage is slightly red, and situated therein is the circle of the bindu.
Because it has been split, melted, and churned by recollection,
it is divided into six types and further into twenty-eight divisions.
A group of four, a group of five, a group of six, a group of four, a group of five, and a group of four—this is indeed the sequence of six types; he who knows this is a Kaulika.
First, there is the group of four seats (pīṭha) and the four deities of the seats;
then, another group of five Siddhas, endowed with the sixfold knowledge.
The Mahantārīpañcaka and the Olitrayakulakrama are recorded as having six types, consisting of twenty-eight divisions. (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
By these, the self of the Kula is divided; then there is the continuous flow of bliss.
At the end of the Kali age, in Kāmākhya, there is also the pentad situated nearby.
And this state indeed arises in Kula and Kaula, which is called Tisra;
it is the twenty-eighth division, and it will come to pass in the future.
Thus, those five seats have been spread out in the previous sūtra;
likewise, the deities and so forth [are established] according to the principle of emanation—listen to this now.
Gajajihvā, Agnijihvā, Taḍijjihvā as the third,
Śukrajihvā, Amarā, and Rasajihvā as the fifth.
I shall now proclaim their five accomplishments in sequence:
the five groups [of deities] reside within the orbs of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, and within the Bindu.
Possession, trembling, bliss, heat, roaring, and drying—
this indeed is the sixfold knowledge residing in its natural state as the object of cognition.
Māyā is the power of Śambhu, as well as Will, Knowledge, and Action;
this is declared to be the tetrad, while Mahantārī constitutes the pentad.
Sound, touch, taste, the goddess [of sight], that which pervades form, and smell—these indeed are your products of ego-consciousness; they are proclaimed as the pentad.
The Vimalāntara and the Ātman—thus the Olitrika is remembered.
In this way, these twenty-eight divisions of the Krama have been told to you.
The Great Liṅga, known as the Divine Maṇḍala, is differentiated by these [energies].

Among them, that which belongs to the lineage of Vidyā is the Supreme, the highest Kalā; it is eternally manifest, extremely subtle, and is firmly established at the tip of the nose. —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Its form resembles a woolen thread, and it is as cool as cow’s milk or snow.
O Maheśvara, by that [power] this living soul lives; it is the divine liṅga.
Its entire lineage of perfected ones (siddhas) and its twenty-eight divisions are likewise [established].
As soon as it has been consumed by her, an internal state arises;
where the gross junction of the three channels remains concentrated in one place.
By that, Tripura is the seat (pīṭha) through which the three streams flow;
it is called Tisra and is located in the forehead. There, the Brahma-knot is downward-facing, and the wheel (cakra) at the aperture of the forehead consists of the rays of knowledge and realization.
In this way, the Yoginī pervades the Meru in sequence, facing downwards.
That supreme power, which brings rest, is situated there;
she is the Mother who moves within the city of the two sides, the right and the left.
Furthermore, there is dissolution at the tip of that middle peak of the *bhaga*;
thus, that power of Rudra is established through three divisions.
Established there in the primary abode by the will of Kula, the Goddess of gods,
whose limbs are curved, freely bestows the true essence of gnosis.
Then, having received the Command from the mouth of the Guru, the great festival of the path to liberation proceeds; the power of Rudra unfolds.
The command (ājñā) passed from mouth to mouth is the kinsman within the Kula lineage;
the perfection of speech arises through its manifestation in the Kula and Kaula traditions.
O you who are fond of devotion, when there is triple purity through action, mind, and speech,
the Command resides in that disciple; one devoid of such disposition does not attain success.
Otherwise, there will certainly be fear of the bonds of *paśu* for the disciple;
[she is] the power of Rudra, the Great Goddess, the unfailing one, and the mother of the world.
The nature of the Divine Command (divyājñā) is manifold in its perfected form;
it exists through the power of Nityaklinnā and by virtue of its exceedingly passionate nature.
The disciple attains the arising characterized by supreme bliss;
and that which is the corresponding power is well-known as the supreme one born from the shadow.
Performing the daily rites according to his own will like one who is wise,
he— abiding in the wheel of power and bearing the divine linga on his body— shall bring about liberation.
The shadow in the moon, the sun, and water, as well as in fire, the moon, the sun, and a mirror— likewise, that supreme goddess, moving in the most subtle way, resides within the tip of a star.
Just as one might see Paśudharā, who is crooked and faces downward,
so too am I that Goddess, the form Kubjikā, the Kulakaulinī.

One should behold its sequence of sūtras as it has been taught, emerging from the flood of the [spiritual] succession, which is perfectly endowed with the meaning of wisdom and serves as the instruction for the Root Sūtra.
O Hara, for the sake of destroying the very impurity of one who is purified by such scripture, I have here determined this compendium consisting of the thread of wisdom.
By this, the Sūtra has been indicated; however, the Root Sūtra is [to be understood] from its very root.
Whoever, being devoid of the thread of wisdom, should determine it otherwise, [is at fault].
For him there is no scripture, nor root-text, nor knowledge in the form of an object of cognition; there is neither lineage nor succession, neither preceptor nor spiritual son.
Therefore, with every effort, one should master the Root Sūtra.
Śrīnātha said:
"The Kramaugha Root Sūtra is awakened by the Prajñā Sūtra."
And from your mouth I have learned that I am perfected; there is no doubt in this.
This manifestation of divine bliss has arisen through your grace.
(From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
Aiṃ! Salutations to you, O Mahāmāyā, unconquered one whose form is splendor;
you who abide in the center of the lunar orb, whose nature is sound, and who are established in the void;
you who reside in the embodiment of the syllable Aiṃ, the divine Liṅga that is neuter.
I shall be born in the supreme mother, O Mother, at the end of the Kula lineage.
Born from the primordial seat, resting upon the fifty seats,
resembling fire and tawny in hue, it awakens the throbbing channels.
O Supreme Goddess, when the Vāgbhava [syllable] has arisen at the end of the emission (visarga),
resting upon the support of the half-measure of the letter *ha*, having become void, arisen in the sky,
situated in the point (*bindu*), established in the moon, and dependent upon the wheel of the Sky-farers (*khecarīcakra*).
O Gurumāmbā, O Kubjikā, O Supreme Goddess of the goddesses!
O Mother, within the Lord, distinct from the bliss of the Self,
O Goddess of the gods, you are established in the immutable Yogapīṭha.
In this terrible Kali age, within the circle of the mandala situated on a difficult path,
there is both the whirlpool and the absence of a whirlpool, which brings rest in the state of dissolution.
O Great Goddess, you are Maṅgalā, who has taken recourse to the seat of Oṃkāra;
O Goddess Māyā, you are in Jālandhara and face downward at Pūrṇapīṭha.
And you are Kāmeśvarī, O moist one, the Yoginī of the form of desire;
you are Māyā, Bhairavī, Śaktinī, and Nīyakī within the five sacred seats (pīṭhas).
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
You are Kālī; you are the sovereign mistress of the lords of the half-pīṭhas in Ujjayinī;
you reside in the pīṭhas and upapīṭhas; you are the primordial one in the maṇḍala of the Krama.

O Goddess, you who abide in the center of the five *praṇavas*, at the end of the full [syllable], O Mother of the Kula, you who reside within the wheel of the Mothers and are surrounded by the six Yoginīs.
And you are that ḍākinī Māyā, of immeasurable and supreme splendor,
with the sound of tinkling bells and blazing flames, and the resonance of lutes, cymbals, and drums.
In the union of the abodes of the three realms, resting upon the threefold course,
peaceful and having reached the three modes, O beloved whose body is the Mother-mantra!
O Goddess who has ascended the seat of the syllable *aiṃ*, who is the form of the *bindu* manifested in three ways;
O Mother of the syllable *hrīṃ*, O Dispeller of the divisions of the syllables *kṣāṃ kṣāṃ klīṃ*; O Pervasive One, who dwells within the pervasive letters *yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ*.

O Goddess Hemahemāvatī, O smiling one, O you who dwell in the midst of swans; O Sovereign of the cry of swans, O formidable one, O you whose body faces downward; O fortunate one, O stainless one, O peaceful one, O beloved of the knowledge of the knowable!
In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:

O beloved one, whose essential nature is the form of Brahman, who are surrounded by the *samaya*, who revolve with the three qualities of the syllable *hrīṃ*, you whose body is mantra, *hrīṃ hrīṃ*! *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ samayāvṛte hrīṃkāratriguṇāvarte hrī~ hrī~ mantratanu priye*.
O Goddess who assumes illusory forms, O Gajajihvā, O Gajeśvarī!
You alone are Vidyujjihvā; Hāṃ Hrīṃ Hūṃ, O you who are born from the womb of Bhaga!

O Mistress of the seventh [state], who has ascended to the state of supreme peace through the renunciation of the six, you who abide in the fourth beyond the fourth, at the summit of the fourth, arising from existence and transcending existence.
In the subtle and the extremely subtle, in the well-established state of the Lord of Gods, in bliss and the bliss beyond bliss, adorned by the sequence of the immortals.
By the syllable *glāṃ*, you are Brāhmī in the earthly realm; by the syllable *slūṃ*, you are indeed Vaiṣṇavī;
by the syllable *plāṃ*, you are Raudrī in the Kula; and by the syllable *mlāṃ*, you are Īśvarī.
O Nlūṃkāra, O Leader, O Nandā, you who delight in supreme eternal bliss; O Umā, you are Māyā, established as the foundation of all accomplishments and sacred seats.
O my Mother, O supreme Illusion, O my auspicious one, O Sarasvatī;
you are my mother, you are my wife, and you reside within the inner chamber of my life.
