O Mistress, you who possess divine power; O you who are deep red, clothed in reality; O you who are beautiful in every limb, moist, situated in the channel of life, and auspicious!
O Gaurī, through the mantras consisting of the syllables *hāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *hūṃ*, you move and cause the world to flow; you abide in the state of mantra-penetration at the end of Śakti.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
within the Kula-mātaṅginī-cakra, the Vidyā-devī is called Kubjā;
her form resembles the full moon, and her face is like a vulva filled with the moon.
O Mistress of the Wheel, born from the twenty-eight syllables through the divisions of twenty-seven words, O Kaulīśī, who has taken refuge in the lineage of the Sovereign (Īśvarī)!
O Mistress of the Lotus, you who possess the form of the fifty perfected ones;
O you who have arisen from Aṭṭahāsa, adorned by the circle of swans!
O Māyā, you abide in the center of the lunar orb; O Maheśvarī, you with the blazing tongue, you abide within the solar orb and within the fire orb.
O Wind, whose speed is like the breath within the mind, who pervades both the supreme and the non-supreme,
who abides in the void within the void, and who is served by the perfected ones!
O Goddess, when one has gone into the supportless, into the sky that is difficult to traverse,
into that which is profound with primordial wisdom and discernment, and into the solitary form of the object of knowledge;
O Goddess who brings about stability and dissolution, O Mother within the circle of the principles (tattvas),
you are the power that agitates the principles and pierces through the darkness of ignorance.
O Mother of all the gods, O Umā, who are dearer to me than life itself; O Sovereign of the Universe, Sustainer of the World, Bestower of the Tradition;
salutations to you, O Supreme Nirvāṇa, O Great Ambikā, the Womb of the World!
Remember your former pledge, made out of affection and with a devoted mind.
"Be pleased with us, O Supreme One; you are our mother, even by the thirty gods.
Thus has the hymn to Māyā been proclaimed, as it has come down through the lineage of the speech of yogins.
The goddess Vakrikā, the deity of the sacred seat (pīṭha), effects his descent; the man attains happiness, health, prosperity, and a stable state. —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
One becomes liberated from all evil even at that very moment;
by reciting this hymn, one shall not undergo rebirth again.
In this very life, he shall obtain enjoyments, gains, honor, fame, and prosperity; and for him who proceeds through the sequence of stages, these shall come about in succession.

For one who is engaged in the conduct of the *samaya*, the intense Command (*tīvrājñā*) comes forth. Thus, in the *Ādyāvatāra*, in the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage measuring seventy million verses emerged from the path of Meru,
exceeding a hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primary seat (*ādyapīṭha*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Sixfold [System].

In the *Kādibheda*, within the *Ājñāpārameśvara* according to the *Svāminīmata*, in the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the *Avvākrama* tradition, in the description of the section on the Root Sūtras, this is the bliss named the Section on the Hymn to Māyā.
The twenty-seventh bliss:
Śrīnātha said:
"O Goddess, Siddha, Mistress of the World, Ādinātha, born of the Kula!"
Speak, however, the instruction on knowledge which is the essence of the Western lineage.
"O Mistress of the Kaulas, reveal the mandala of the scripture of worship!
The venerable Vakrā said: "The essence of the world of Śiva is the mandala of the form of the worlds."
I shall now fully explain that circle of gurus (gurumaṇḍala), which exists externally, resides within one's own body, is internal, and consists of consciousness.
O Lord, that Śiva, who is beginningless, unmanifest, and the supreme cause,
has become embodied as Mantra for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds.
Having descended into the world of mortals as the supreme bestower of grace,
this deity Navātmanandabhairava is to be worshipped within the mandala.
The Lord, bearing five forms and endowed with sixteen limbs,
has descended in the Kali age, assuming ninefold manifestations.
Listen to how he, who resides in the forms of the fifty Rudras, is to be worshipped;
O Mahādeva, his extraction has been indicated by five verses.
In the middle of the four syllables beginning with *a*, there is likewise the fifth;
then *la-ka-yakṣa-ta-na-ra-ma-ḍa-kha*—thus they are reversed.
O God, that mandala which extends from ḍa, ḍha, ṭha, and ṭa down to da is known as having emerged from Meru through emanation; it is the second [mandala] of the two authorities.
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa: Indra, water, fire, wind, and space—this is knowledge, O fair-complexioned one; Kuṇḍalī is the third crore.
Hṛdaya, Samaya, Sarvajña, Kadambaka, Khagīśa, Gurunātha, and Ratnabīja as the fourth.
Having recited the mantra at the end of the *pādukā*— namely, *kadamba vimalaugha ca samayaṃ bhairavāvalī*— one should worship the circle of gurus.
O God, before the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), one should perform the worship of the maṇḍala of gurus,
according to the previously mentioned sequence, provided with the five seats.
One should worship the Guru fivefold, distinguished by the three types of grace,
beginning from the northeast corner up to the center as the fifth.
The maṇḍala, the authority, the Siddhas, the Samaya, and the Yoginī—
these five are divided into fivefold ways, joined with the fivefold Kaulinī.
The Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] together with Māyā, pierced by Lakṣmī and Prasāda,
joined with Navātman and Ānanda, constitutes the circle of the five Gurus.
O Mahādeva, one should constantly worship the excellent [deities] ending with Pādukā;
likewise, those residing within the inner circle should be worshipped within one's own self.
The first is said to be in the *ādhāra*, the second in the *yonimaṇḍala*,
the third in the *nābhicakra*, and the fourth in the *anāhata*.
The fifth is in the region of the throat, while Ādinātha is at the crown of the head;
from Śrīkaṇṭha to Piṅgala, five [deities] are thus conceived in five ways.
O handsome one, at dawn, at midday, and at twilight,
one should perform [the rite] five times before the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) and in the presence of the guru.
One must perform the propitiation so that it may be complete and grant success;
one should never leave the maṇḍala of the Guru empty.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Having performed the complete worship according to one's means,
[one should offer] the *ārātrī*, sandalwood paste, lamps, and the substances of the heroes (*vīradravya*).
The announcement should be made, and one should perform prostrations with the eight limbs;
the wise person should prostrate like a staff with the eight limbs three or five times.
Having performed a hundred circumambulations, one should worship the sandals of the Guru;
the wise person should constantly observe this rule of conduct.
Success arises from its observance; otherwise, one goes to hell—this applies to all the joints of the *oli*, as well as to the regular and occasional rites.
In the mandala-rite worship, everything shall reach complete perfection.
Hereafter, O Bhairava, I shall explain [it] according to reality; listen!
Then, having worshipped the Śrīkrama as prescribed in the venerable Kulāgama,
perform its descent constantly upon the ritual seat (paryaṅka) in brief.
Having prepared a seat of deerskin and the auspicious syllable of speech (*vāgbhava*),
one should consecrate pure *śrīkhaṇḍa* sandalwood and saffron mixed with water; then, having performed the recitation of the mantra (*vidyā*), one should write the threefold sequence.
The yogapīṭha of the ancient first sequence is declared to be threefold.
Outside of that, having drawn a hexagon, one should encircle it with the syllable *aiṃ*;
outside that, an eight-petaled lotus surrounded by three girdles.
Outside of that, having drawn a well-proportioned square with excellent lines,
one should write the sequence of Kaumāra, joined with a six-spoked wheel.
"Endowed with an eight-petaled lotus, this is the sequence of the Bālakrama.
Thus has this division of the sequences of the maṇḍala been revealed. O God, the division of the ritual placement (nyāsa) is likewise [found] in the Vṛddha, Kumāra, and Bālaka [traditions]."
The first is the mass of sounds (Śabdarāśi), and likewise the second is Mālinī.
Thus, there are the three Vidyās, and the fourth consists of their limbs;
likewise, there is the Aghorī group of eight and the five limbs of the Siddhas.
Having performed this sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa), one should thereafter begin the sacrifice;
this is the supreme placement and enclosure (nyāsāvaraṇa) of the eldest [deity] according to the lineage of the elders (vṛddhakrama).
Now, for the intermediate accomplishment of Kaumāra, in due order:
first is the field of its grasping, and second is the fivefold seed.
The third is the twelve-limbed [mantra], and the fourth is the perfected limb;
the fifth should be the six-limbed, while the sixth is the placement of the sacred seats (pīṭhanyāsa).
Having performed the seventh [rite] called Khecara, one should begin the sacrifice.
Now I shall again explain the third enclosure of the Krama.
The first is the *samaya-vidyā*, the second is the *siddhāṅga*,
the third is the *ṣaḍaṅga*, and the fourth consists of the verses (*śloka*).

The fifth chapter shall be on the empowerment (adhikāra), the sixth on the appropriation of the field (kṣetraparigraha), the seventh on the arrangement of jewels (ratnavinyāsa), and likewise the eighth on the arrangement of vidyās (vidyānyāsa).
Having thus performed the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should thereafter worship the sequence of the Child (*bālakrama*).
Having understood the mandala of the sequences, [one should do so] in the western *ekacakra*.
One should purify both the Siddhāṅga and the Ṣaḍaṅga; the Skull of Viśvāmitra is well-perfected and auspicious for yogins. (From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
At the front of the seat, the practitioner should purify the human skull-cup filled with substances using the Koṅkaṇa-weapon mantra and veil it with the armor mantra.
Having entered the form, one should bring the six-faced [deity] into the heart and the eyes;
the act of bringing about the presence [of the deity] is completed by means of the head.
In this way, one should apply the sixfold ritual action to the root-vidyā;
by means of that, one becomes sealed with the Yoni-mudrā and the Mahāmudrā.
Then, O God, one should employ the descent known as Karāla;
having recited the root-vidyā three times, [one attains] presence in the Krama-maṇḍala.
Furthermore, having placed a second vessel filled with sandalwood nectar before the five [deities] and so forth, he should consecrate it once again with that same mantra.
Then, having placed the third vessel upon the five jewels,
he should sacrifice there again from the south, north, and center.
Having thus first prepared the three vessels, one should commence the worship;
with sandalwood paste, one should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) of the Vidyā within one's own continuum.
One should perform the placement (vinyāsa) with the root mantra, fumigating oneself individually at each respective location from the letter *bha* to the letter *ca*.
Having commenced with the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) according to the sequence of one's own lineage,
one should illuminate eight lamps of sesame oil with the first five [mantras], in accordance with the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
Immediately after the consecration of the seat, [one should offer] sandalwood combined with incense, fragrance, saffron, and unbroken rice grains in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Once the root mantra has been mastered, one should perform acts of giving within one's lineage;
having first formed the three mudrās, one should then commence the worship.
The sequential worship residing within the body should be performed according to the previous procedure;
thereafter, one should perform the sequence that is both external and internal, situated upon the external seats (pīṭhas).
First, one should perform the sequential worship with sandalwood paste mixed with unbroken rice grains;
with those fragrant white flowers, the Kula lineage should be honored.
In the absence [of those], one may offer red flowers, as well as fragrant yellow ones,
*sumanās*, *campakas*, lotuses, and beautiful blue water-lilies (*nīlotpala*).
One should worship the lineage tradition with those [flowers] obtained according to local custom—
[namely] trees that are odorless, thorny, broken, or shriveled.
O Lord of the Gods, the sequential worship (kramapūjā) must not be performed even mentally;
likewise, the offering of incense and the separate sequence of commands (ājñākrama) are likewise forbidden.
Then the worship with honey (alipūjā) should be performed by means of the Vaiṣṇavī-pada alone;
there, a great roar arises, agitating the conviction.
With the root mantra of the Vidyā, he [placed] the rosary upon his left hand, which possesses incomparable presence and is fierce, bringing fear to the Paśus.
The rosary should be made of crystal or rudrākṣa seeds, consisting of one hundred and eight beads;
it may have two or three beads per inch, according to the preference of the wise.
Whether gross or subtle, no jewel whatsoever may ever transcend Meru; however,
in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, with the exception of the thumb, there is the fourfold [arrangement] as it is attained.
Likewise, one should avoid the two middle fingers by rotating counter-clockwise;
this [method] may be performed with the hands or with a rosary.
One should recognize that stainless, pure, and supreme crest situated above as Mount Meru by means of the rosary; by leaping over it, one shall go to hell.
In the counter-clockwise order, Sadyojāta is prescribed;
having ascended to that supreme meditation or the mantra which grants liberation,
one should [worship] within one's own lineage, on the seat of the self, or within the mandala of the self.
Either in the center of the triangle of the mantra, or within the full vidyā.
One should perform the recitation and meditation upon the forty-two-fold conception within the triangle;
that recitation should be mental, or else it may be the *ātma-kūṭa*.
In the beginning, one should worship Śiva, who is marked with the Yonimudrā and the Āmānāma [mudrā],
in the center of the fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) by means of that root-mantra (mūlavidyā).
One should make the meditation (dhyāna) reddish-black according to the specific rite;
furthermore, one should perform the refinement (saṃskāra) in the upper, middle, and lower parts accordingly.

"One should meditate on that which has entered my womb; one should not apply it externally"— thus [it is said] in the *Ādyāvatāra*, in the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) measuring seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters,
brought down to the primary seat (*ādyapīṭha*), in the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimalaṣaṭka*), in the *Kādi* division.

In the *Ājñāpārameśvarī*, the *Svāminīmata*, the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the *Avvākrama* tradition, within the description of the chapter on the Mandala of the Krama and the Mandala of the Gurus,
this is the bliss named the Arising of the Krama (*Kramodaya*). Śrīnātha said:
"O Goddess, I have heard the entire procedure for worship in its proper sequence;
now I wish to hear about the single sequence that is threefold—how is it so?"
The venerable Vakrā said:
"O Lord, listen; I shall explain the single *krama* in its threefold manner as the twenty-eighth bliss."
According to the division of the three stages of life—childhood, youth, and old age.
First is the lineage of the elders, which has come down through the succession of the Jyeṣṭha-oli;
then, O King, the determination of knowledge as it has been received by the practitioners of mantra.
The first letters of the seats are O, JĀ, PŪ, and KĀ—this quartet constitutes the four ages; these are the seats upon this earthly plane.
And those five great elements, conjoined with the four pervaders,
proceed in sequence from the principle of space (vyomatattva) onwards, beginning with the syllable Oṃ.
The syllable Oṃ is situated in the element of space; the syllable Jā resides in fire; the syllable Pū is situated in the element of water; and the syllable Kā is located in earth.
O Pārtha, one should place the power (śakti) below them; for those [energies],
it is situated below by means of the downward-pointing power (adhaḥśakti) residing within the limbs.
Āpa, Daṇḍa, and Mālinī.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Thus the seats (pīṭhas) are divided into four, marked by the moon and the sun;
this Command (ājñā) is established at the crown of the head, and it is known as the quartet of seats.
O beloved, I shall describe their fourfold meditation pertaining to the self.
The wise know the letter *dhā* to be like Aghora, and the letter *jā* to be Puruṣa.
The syllable *pū* is Vāmadeva, while the syllable *kā* has the form of Sadyojāta;
these goddesses reside within the inner limbs, located between the eyebrows, in the heart, and at the navel.
Within the center of the *yoni*, the fourfold group of goddesses is proclaimed;
among those beginning with the letter *ka*, there are four, distinguished as feminine and neuter.
The Lords of the Pīṭhas are fully described as being united with the meditation on the Pīṭhas;
among them, the four Siddhas are to be worshipped in the four Pīṭhas.
The word *hara* is for the fourfold placement (*caturnyāsa*);
the word *hara* is fourfold, differentiated by the first [vowel] and the four long [vowels], marked at the peak of the *ājñā*.
The four seed-syllables of the seats and their meditations are as before;
hereafter, I shall explain the determination of the five voids.
Having established the void (vyoma) in five ways beneath the Śakti, it is augmented by light,
permeated by the five long vowels, and adorned with the Bindu and Nāda.
This indeed is the meditation on the five voids, which for them is like that of Aghora;
O God, the transmission of the command (ājñā) constitutes its sequence of mantras.
And those five pervasive ones who have been described— the forms of fire and possessed of great power—
we shall now declare their five locations within this scripture.
In the ears, the nostrils, and the mouth, the fivefold space (vyomapañcaka) is to be known:
earth, the water principle, fire, wind, and that which is designated as space.
Likewise, the sixth is the principle of Power (śaktitattva), and below those is the Sun;
and likewise, that is the principle of Air (vāyutattva), differentiated by the syllable of Sound (nāda).
O Maheśvara, the peak-syllable of the Command (ājñākūṭa) resides in the drop (bindu), in the power of resonance (nādaśakti), and likewise in the anus,
the womb, the navel, the heart, the throat, and between the eyebrows.
This group of six has been described, and it is sixfold according to its symbolic convention:
the first wick is white, and the second is yellow in form.
The third is blue-colored, and the fourth should be green;
the fifth has the appearance of red ochre, and the sixth is reddish in color.
I shall now describe another fivefold [mantra], the great and enchanting Mahantāyī: having established the syllable *haṃsa* in five ways, it is endowed with *a*, *i*, *u*, *e*, and *o*.
One should perform the fivefold [practice] of Mahantārya, who is pervaded by the power of Nāda,
upon the two sides of the belly, between the breasts, and also on the back.
White, yellow, reddish, and green constitute the group of five;
their meditation is indeed fivefold, occurring in three ways within the middle.
It is declared as the "Three Thorns"; one should practice the triad of vidyās.
Their three locations are the foundation (ādhāra), the heart, and the fourth (turya).
The first dhyāna is red; the second should be yellow;
the third is pure white, consisting of the qualities of goodness, passion, and darkness.
The sequence of mantras has been extracted in twenty-seven divisions;
I shall now describe its sequential nomenclature—listen, O Bhairava!
The fourfold *ojāpūkā* is indeed the fourfold *kāpūjā-o*;
it is manifest as the deity of the seat (*pīṭha*) within the seat of mantra (*mantrapīṭha*) without interruption.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa: O God, their secret names are Avi, Me, Te, and Asaṃjñā; these are the four names of those mantra-deities.
One should worship the Goddess of the Seat (pīṭhadevī) according to the instruction, together with Samameti and Sākāra, as the retinue of the Goddess.
One should thus practice the five voids conjoined with the mantras;
we shall now describe their five deities at the time of worship.
One should divide the *vyoma* (the letter *ha*) into five parts; their fivefold authority consists of the fivefold conjunction of *kā*, *si*, *re*, *pha*, and *si*.
Then there is the Command (ājñā), which is the secret designation of the Krama;
one should apply it in its sixfold form, distinguished by the syllables *ā*, *jñā*, and *kukāra*.
The goddesses are gathered at their head, established in the sequence of their respective offices;
they are proclaimed as the six conventions, [consisting of] lava, ra, ha, ya, śa, and ṣa.
Likewise, there are four Siddhas joined with the previously mentioned sequence;
these five are in the lineage-less [tradition], and their names are kept secret.
The five fields beginning with the equinox and the solstice,
the three [groups] beginning with Trikaṇṭaka, adorned by the triad of Vidyās.
The letter *e*, the letter *a*, and the third, the letter *ka*—these are the secret designations for the triad of deities: Ku, Ku, Ku.
A group of four, a group of five, a group of six, a group of four, a group of five, and a group of three—
these are the twenty-seven varieties consisting of six types.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, first there are the four sacred seats (pīṭha) and the four deities of the seats;
then another five voids (vyoma), and likewise another six commands (ājñā).
Furthermore, there is the group of four Siddhas, and "beginningless" makes five;
likewise, the Trikaṇṭaka should be mentioned, extracted from the lineage of the Jyeṣṭha-oḷi.
This is declared to be the sequence of the elders, illuminated by the five praṇavas,
joined with the locations and mantras, and endowed with meditation and dhāraṇā.
He who worships that which resides within the body becomes a Kula-yogin;
the lineage of the Jyeṣṭha-oli, as it has been proclaimed, should be worshipped by the teachers.
Having begun from the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) and having worshipped the sequence according to its true meaning,
one should perform the sacrifice after having received [the teaching] from the mouth of the guru precisely through the power of the oral instruction.
Otherwise, it bestows obstacles; one must not transgress the command of the Guru regarding the wheel.
Now I shall describe the second [mandala], the Kaumāra, which has the *madhyamolika*.

In the lineage of the Elders (*vṛddhakrama*), the worship according to the sequence is taught step by step, beginning from Pūrṇapīṭha and proceeding through the Middle Lineage (*madhyamoli*) in due order.
The names and colors of those wise ones are endowed with the principles (tattvas);
four are presided over by Śakti and are seated upon the seat of Hara and Māyā.
Distinguished by the vowels Ā, Ī, Ū, and AIŚVARA, and marked with Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā—
thus are the four Pīṭhas, the quartet of the Goddesses of the Pīṭhas.
The first letter, the fourfold nyāsa, and likewise the triad of neuter vowels;
these are pervaded by the four long vowels and marked with the crest of Khaśakti.
U, ū, and śūnyakalā are the Moon; the seed-syllable of Śiva is fourfold.
O God, that [first] part of the Kumārikākhaṇḍa is one, while the second is doubled.
Having established the third as threefold, the fourth as fourfold,
and the fifth as fivefold— this indeed is the "fivefold family" (kulapañcaka).
That five-fold, radiant, auspicious, and imperishable grace becomes the hexad of Śambhu’s power; thus does the hexad of Vidyās come to be.
The six groups of *hara* and the six groups of *īṣat* form the head by means of the agitator (*kṣobhaka*). [With] *pha*, *ra*, *e*, and *ma*, make these two—the moon and the sun—sixfold.

At the end of those [syllables] stands the six-syllable Vidyā of Svayambhū, accompanied by the six [vowels] and endowed with the long [vowels], the bindu, and the śikhā; it is also known as the Ṣaṭka.
Now, regarding the names of the five voids (*vyomapañcaka*) and the fivefold pervasion (*vyāptipañcaka*):
having established earth and the other elements in three ways, they are differentiated by the Lord (*īśvara*).
The Ātmatattva is distinguished by the three long vowels and the triad of qualities;
the fourth, the Vāyutattva, is distinguished by the Triple Gem.
The fifth is the *vyoma-tattva*, distinguished by being marked with three *kalās*.
These five pervasive [principles] abide in a threefold manner, marked by the stages of *bindu* and *nāda*.
Then, first of all, there is the principle of the Bindu (the Point) and the seat of Earth;
these are distinguished by the syllables Ā, Ī, U, and Ū, and are marked by the crest of the Moon in the Sky.
Thus, those three are established as perfected in the form of gnosis;
the sequence of mantras has been extracted in this manner for one who is matured according to the proper order.
And O Mahādeva, the ritual procedure is just as it was for the Youthful and the Aged;
likewise are the conventional language and the indication of the conventions of names.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, there are the four: O, JĀ, PŪ, and KĀÑ; this is the quartet of KĀ-PŪ-JĀ-O.
Furthermore, MĀ, VI, SAJJA, and SAMU—this is the secret convention (saṃketa).
These pīṭhas are most secret, as are the deities of the pīṭhas;
and the four pīṭha-siddhas—their convention is extremely subtle.
Furthermore, his convention regarding the five families is fivefold:
Aku, Saku, Saku, Aṃku, and again Aku.
This is indeed the group of five families (kulapañcaka), and beyond that is the group of six vowels (ambhāṣaṭka);
one should make the vowel *aṃ* sixfold by dividing it with the four vowels.
In front of that, there should be six offices for the Elder Goddess (Vṛddhadevī):
Āpa, Iti, Ma, Aṃkāra, Ma, and Avvākrama.
Ma, Kha, A, Ce, D, and Bha— this is the group of six called Ambhāṣaṭka; indeed, this is declared in the Kaula language to be the sequence of mantras.
The convention for that [yoga] is fivefold, namely the five yogas themselves: *asā*, *sasa*, *vayoga*, *iti-saku*,
and *īsasaka*.
The secret [teaching] arises from the union with the manifest, conjoined with the previous sequence;
it is the triad of the Siddhas within the very triad, and among those, the convention is threefold.
If one is a *siddha*, may all those proclaimed in the sequence of mantras be successful;
having performed the various modes of conduct of the previous sequence, one should practice thoroughly.
By the power of the oral instruction alone, the sequence of the Youthful (Kaumāra-krama) has been extracted;
now, the sixfold sequence of the Middle Lineage (Madhyama-oli) shall likewise be presented.
It is taught that there are four, five, six, four, five, and three;
these are the six types of divisions, totaling twenty-seven.
First, there is the tetrad of seats and the four deities of the seats,
beginning with Pūrṇagiri, [located at] Udaya, Madhya, and Olikā; furthermore, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed Bālakrama.
I shall explain them in the previous sequence, starting from the mudrās and the seats in their proper order.
The primary liṅgas of the pīṭhas, endowed with the four jewels,
were all fashioned as the peaks (kūṭas) of the Self; subsequently, the fourfold pīṭhas and their four mantra-deities came into being.
The first is the seed-syllable Vāgbhava; the second is the seed-syllable Māyā.
The third is the seed-syllable of the Sun, and the fourth is the sky-farer;
the great peak-syllable is the essence of the Vidyā, the one God who is fourfold.
The fifth [category] is the ninefold aggregate, which arises from semen and the rest;
O Rudra, it is born from Śakti up to Ākāśa, and the Moon is the awakener of bliss.

The descent of power (śaktipāta) is the wave, whose form is the bliss of the ninefold self; it is the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, presided over by the head of the power of space (khaśakti), and it presides over the summit of the primordial sound (nāda).
Retention (*dhāraṇā*), however, is the penetration by power (*śakti-āveśa*);
this is taught in the lineage of Ādinātha in passages such as "in *ojā*, *apū*, and *ke*, etc."
The fifth is Siddhanāyaka.
Śrīnātha, the root Śrīguru, the determination of the lineage of the command,
common to all the sequences, the foundation— thus is Bhairava.
Merely by its utterance, one will become [the master] of all states;
indeed, the fivefold Siddhas are established within the four seats (catuḥpīṭha).
The fifth is the Supreme Lord, the Śrī Guru, the central leader; O one of noble vows, these two are renowned as the means for accomplishment in the primordial seat.
Furthermore, I shall describe another group of six knowledges that is the leader of the Kaula;
it is the cause of the Vidyā here, and it is indeed fourfold.
Innate, mounted upon Māyā, and differentiated by the family of bliss;
O Maheśvara, it resides within the aggregate of *ma*, *e*, *kha*, *pha*, and *ra*, situated in the Vāgbhava syllable.

The pervasive [reality] of the Kula-yogins is situated between the fourth arch and the Śakti; that is the Bindu, with the Daṇḍa below it, filled by the ocean of the vital breath (anila). —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Accompanied by the resonance of a bell and struck on the head with the thumb,
it is perfected at the arising of the swan-colored [state], proclaimed as the two neuters.
Likewise, another [letter] becomes pervasive when pervaded by both the *nāda* and the *varṇa*;
these four are pervasive within the space, and below them is the image of the *Śakti*.
The wise one [should contemplate] the pervasive Mahādevī residing in the Visarga, whose face is turned in all directions,
[extending] from the head downwards through the Ājñācakra and other centers according to the sequence of emanation.
This sixfold knowledge is the truth, difficult to obtain even for the gods;
furthermore, they now know the fivefold [knowledge] of Mahantāyī.
But for the second letter of the third group,
one should perform [the ritual] fivefold, differentiated by the five long vowels.
"O Maheśvara, standing in the center of the circle of command, perform three revolutions;
and you alone, being solitary, place yourself at the beginning of them."
And having accomplished the three oḷis, their triad should be as follows: the four nasalized [consonants] are indeed formed below by the bindu.
One should again join the threefold great peak as a single unity;
one should then differentiate the letter *ū*, the letter *ī*, and the letter *ā*, and so forth.

O God, one should place the Jyeṣṭha and Madhyama [mantras], which are inseparable from the powers of Nāda and Kalā; by means of these three, O Lord, the wheel of mantras is extracted in three ways within the olis.
This wheel of the sequence of mantras is proclaimed as its convention;
the four sacred seats (pīṭhas) are hidden by means of the first letter of each of the goddesses' names.
(Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
Likewise, by that very [method], the four goddesses of the seats (pīṭhas) are to be known:
Aṃkunātha, Ciṃ, and the one designated by the syllable Ka.
Thus the group of four is established; the pentad is designated as the "pair.
It is pervaded by the crest and the topknot, joined with *ku*, *i*, and *ava*.
One should indeed undertake this Siddhapañcaka in the sacred seats (pīṭhas);
O Lord, listen to this convention of the sixfold knowledge.
*Ākha*, *iti*, *visaṃ*, and likewise *avidyā*, as well as the supreme; *mama*, *ca*, *iti*, *svāsu*, and *āmei*—this is the hexad of knowledge.
Furthermore, there is the "Great One" (Mahantāyī), the indication of the pentad,
the non-conceited pervasion on one side, and that which is the face of the collection.
And that [occurs] through another sequence alone across all [the sites]; thus there are five groups of six. In this way, those divisions are twenty-seven;
first, there is the tetrad of seats, and then the four deities of the seats.
Furthermore, there is the Siddhapañcaka and likewise another, the Jñānaṣaṭka.
The Great Noble Ones: the group of five and the triad of Ols immediately following; this is called the sequence of the Child (bālakrama), differentiated by the five praṇavas.
It is remembered as being associated with the hermitage of Lakṣāśrama, [and] Vṛddhakaumāraka;
and Kaniṣṭholī is declared, starting from Kāmarūpa in due order.
The first is called the Eldest, the second is named the Middle, and the third is the Child;
thus, in the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), this single transmission is said to be threefold.
The sequential worship (kramapūjana) should be performed according to the distinction of one's own lineage (oli);
"one's own lineage" refers to the mandala, the wheel (cakra), and the transmission of the mantra-instruction.
Having understood the oral tradition of the lineage within the succession of the Siddha lineages—the Sūtra of the linguistic convention—authority proceeds. [In the] Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
thereafter, the Kula-krama is to be worshipped; otherwise, never.
The powder is one thing, the ritual action is another, and the employment of the mantra is yet another.
Furthermore, there is another procedure for worship, namely the mandala arranged in reverse order;
whether it be that of the Elder, the Youth, or the Child, or else the sequence of the Sky-farers (Khecarī).
For the Śrīkrama is impure if, despite being practiced, it does not bring success;
yet it succeeds when it has emerged from the mouth of the Guru, even if through negligence.
One should first remove obstacles for the disciple and purify that which is impure;
for he who worships what is impure or he who gives [initiation] while violating the scriptures [brings harm].
The teacher will surely kill that disciple at that very moment;
by accepting the disciple, death will come before long, and not otherwise.

O Lord, one should not cause a violation of the scriptures for one's own disciple who is a true devotee; however, such a thing may be done toward one who is undevoted, deceitful, or who causes the neglect of ritual practice.
One should not cause such a person to receive the knowledge, the ritual sequence, the mandala, and so forth;
likewise, one should conceal the command inherited from one's lineage and the oral instructions.
Whether out of fear, affection, greed for wealth, or a desire for a position of high status,
whoever bestows the Kramamoghā [initiations] will certainly go to hell.
And because there is no separation [from the body], death does not apply to the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) in this way;
one who knows the sequence should guard it with effort.
One should protect one's entire knowledge as one would wealth from thieves;
having worshipped the Kula tradition with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra-pūjā).
O observer of excellent vows, one should contemplate the primordial flood with the intellect through the inner sense;
when one performs it externally, one should show it to other people,
for there is no doubt that it constitutes a violation of the command, and from such proclamation, one goes to hell.
O you who are fond of devotion, may there be purity in action, mind, and speech.

One should bestow grace upon a humble person who is devoted to the True One and has been tested for twelve years; one should transmit the scripture to him. Otherwise, it must never be done for the sake of the tongue or the genitals. (From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*)

Those who proclaim the Śrīkrama for the sake of the signs of the tongue and the organ of generation, and who speak of the oral tradition (mukhāmnāya)— this Kula is the scripture of the command (ājñā)—
for them there is no accomplishment in this world, nor is it found in the next.
Out of greed or delusion, or puffed up with false ego,
one may improperly grasp the scripture— the oral Kaula tradition— without following the proper sequence.
All that [effort] of his is fruitless, like a water-lily in the sky;
likewise, activity becomes fruitless through the practice of non-sequential [action].
Those who delight in the sequential worship (kramapūjā), who are peaceful and free from passion and hatred—they are fit for the Kula and Kaula; the rest are of inferior birth.
O handsome one, he who grasps the scripture out of greed for the sake of worldly gain,
or for the sake of fame, or for the sake of renown, or even for the sake of his son;
If a minister grants authority for the sake of the Krama stage, O God, he destroys it; there is no doubt that this is a great betrayal.
Having become a worm in the midst of excrement, he lives upon impurity;
just as there is no means of escape for him, such is his lowest rebirth.
And the sequence is said to be threefold: gross, subtle, and likewise supreme;
namely, the Śākta, the Śāmbhava, and the Āṇava as the third.
The "three thorns" consist of the higher-lower, the lower, and the higher;
the wise know the single *oli*-sequence to be threefold through the division of these three triads.

The gross [level] is called the sequence of the elders (*vṛddhakrama*); it pertains to the authority of the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*). The subtle sequence is that of the youth (*kaumāra*), and it is proclaimed as the "very subtle" (*susūkṣma*).
Having meditated upon the supreme Bālakrama, which is the third [state] arising from the youngest, it is indeed one alone, yet divided threefold;
this single Krama is the Trikaṇṭaka.
The Śrīkrama is said to be threefold, and they know the Olikrama to be threefold as well; O beautiful one, these four Kramas have emerged from my body. —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.

The Khecarī, the Krama, and the primordial [Krama]—the Vṛddha, Kumāra, and Bālaka; for these, accomplishment occurs according to the four ages (*caturyuga*) and likewise through the sequence of one's own lineage.
In the Kṛta age, the Khecarakrama was proclaimed; likewise, the Vṛddhakrama in Tretā;
the Kumārakrama in Dvāpara; and the Bālakrama in the Kali age.
Thus, O Mahādeva, those four lineages were brought down at the end of the age; in the Kali Yuga, the lineage is to be known as fourfold.
I shall describe their rising and likewise their setting;
by means of this very rising and setting, the fourfold sequence is to be known.
Listen to the procedure for those [channels] that have emerged from my body:
O Sky-farer, the sequence within them is joined to the Nameless (anāmā) and the Nameless-less (anāma);
having emerged through the power of gnosis, it has gone to dissolution in the midst of the marrow.
Furthermore, that which has issued forth from my anger in a progressively increasing sequence.
O God, that which is within the sinews is known as *astamana*;
the *kaumāra* state resides in the navel-cakra, having emerged from that place.
Its dissolution is in the blood, and this is its rising and setting;
likewise, that which is called the "sequence of the child" has emerged from the wheel of the womb.
The threefold rising and setting is dissolved within the semen; it is joined with the three sequences and conjoined with rising and setting. (From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
He is the disciple; in the Western Tradition, the others are merely bearers of the name.
Listen, O Lord, I shall explain the single transmission as it exists in its threefold form.
At the time when everything undergoes dissolution within my body, there are no moons, suns, planets, or stars; there is neither the world nor even the mountains.
"O King, it is not that I am non-existent, nor are you, nor is this world of moving and unmoving beings empty; rather,
from that very formless [reality], the emergence of divine gnosis occurs."
The Power (Śakti) has emerged by the will of Śiva, taking the form of a sprout;
resembling a flash of lightning, it illuminates the expanse of the sky.
Having mastered her senses through divine command, she practiced fierce asceticism;
consequently, she became distracted in mind and reached old age.
The sprout is divided into two: that which possesses form and that which is stainless;
this union of Śiva and Śakti is proclaimed to exist within all living beings.
O God, you are Śiva, the Lord of Kaula; I am that supreme Kubjinī. By means of the Khecarī [practice], my threefold form has arisen.
At dawn I am a child, at midday I am a youth, and by the conduct of night I am an old woman; this is my threefold course.
Therefore, three types have been proclaimed: one in the Kula-krama, and in the Bāla-krama; when there is a Bālā-vā [Bālā-vidyā], then it becomes the Bāla-krama.
At midday, he is young and youthful; therefore, he is known as the "Middle" one. At the time of twilight, however, he assumes an aged form and becomes the "Aged" one.
By means of the three forms alone, a single sequence becomes threefold;
among those, I am indeed the Vidyā of the Goddess, endowed with six faces and limbs.
Likewise, the eight families are on the exterior, encircling the Krama-maṇḍala;
by them the Kumārikākhaṇḍa is adorned— the three worlds in their various forms, whose nature is like the sky.
Therefore, those mandalas have been described as being devoid of rising and setting;
all the mandalas that illuminate [the world] are entirely bound in three ways.
Indeed, this arising of the sequence is thus entirely bound in three ways.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the eightfold group of the family goddesses (kuladevī) as they are.

The eight letters of the eight groups (aṣṭavarga), differentiated by the syllable *aiṃ* at their end, pervaded by *nāda* and *bindu*, and residing in the navel, are the deities of the Kula. The three seed-syllables (*bīja*), the Prāsāda mantra, and the fifth, the Rāva seed-syllable.
Immediately thereafter, the eight goddesses of the [Varga] group are to be assigned at the end.
Brāhmī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Varāhikā,
Indrāṇī, Āgneyī, and Cāmuṇḍā as the eighth.
And the ninth is Mahālakṣmī, illuminated by the *visarga*;
having placed five *praṇavas* at the beginning, [one forms] nine combinations for each [syllable].
Having performed the ritual up to the sandals (pādukānta), one should begin the sacrifice;
this is the rule for the *olīs* by means of the vidyā conjoined with the rule (*samaya*).
Having known that which is declared as the obscuration of the sequence, one becomes a destroyer of the enemies of accomplishment;
there are twenty-seven divisions according to the threefold sequence.
O God, I have also told you their secret signs (saṃketaka) regarding the sandals and the seats, according to the lineage of the Siddhanāthas.
One should assign the word "Avvā" to all the deities in the lineage (krama), ending with "Pādukā"; thus, having worshipped the lineage in front according to the ritual rule.
Furthermore, O Lord of Gods, regarding the rising and setting of these sequences,
the rising of the first sequence occurs in the first sacred seat (pīṭha).
The dissolution of the primordial Khecarī indeed occurs at the Tisra-pīṭha;
likewise, the emergence of the Vṛddhakrama occurs at the Tisra-pīṭha within the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Furthermore, for that Kaumāra [pīṭha], there is dissolution in Kāmarūpa and likewise its emergence in Pūrṇagiri; its dissolution is in the primordial seat (Ādyapīṭha).
Likewise, the arising of the Bālākrama occurs in Kāmarūpa, while its dissolution is in the seat of Oṃkāra; such is the definitive determination of this sequence.
Having understood what was explained in this preceding sūtra, one should become a follower of the lineage;
and when the section on the sequence has been completed, there is the sūtra of the yogin’s command.
"From its single recitation, there is the accomplishment of his command and the destruction of impurities.
Thus, in the introduction to the Great Manthānabhairava Sacrifice, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses emerged from the Path of Meru,
exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primary seat on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (Vidyāpīṭha), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (Vimala-Ṣaṭka).

In the *Ājñāpārameśvara*, belonging to the division beginning with *Ka*, in the *Svāminīmata* consisting of twenty-four thousand verses as spoken in the *Avvākrama*, in the description of the threefold authority of the *Krama*,
this is the bliss named the Arising of the *Krama*.
The thirty-ninth bliss:
Śrīnātha said, "I am a disciple by my very nature; O Kaulinī, show me your grace."
O Goddess, whatever [is required] by your command, O Lord, let grace be bestowed.
I bow to the Supreme Nectar, who is without beginning or end, who is peaceful, the primordial Lord born of the Kula, and who dwells within the secret space of the kanda.
I bow to her who resides at the end of the twelve, situated in the triangle, arising from the foundation of the kanda, merged within the left, and supremely imperishable.
Fully endowed with all desires and presided over by the power of will (*icchā-śakti*),
you create by mere will the entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving.
O Kāmeśvarī, you who are known as Kāmā, who are self-born in Kāmarūpa,
and who abide within the sacred seat of Kāma— O you whose form is desire, I bow to you!
O Kāmeśvarī, you who have emerged from the center of the *bindu*,
whose abode is the *bhaga*, at the end of the secret *guhya* called Kāmākhya, adorned by the great Siddhas.
Inlaid with all kinds of jewels, adorned with great gems, decorated with pearls, corals, and other such things, it was most delightful.
Constructed of vajra and vaiḍūrya, variegated with indranīla gems,
illuminated by many jewels, and adorned with great precious ornaments.
Abounding with fragrant scents, smeared with saffron water,
perfumed with incense such as camphor and the like, and gladdened by the joy of wine.
Abounding in fragrant scents, charming with the five [offerings] and more,
it is presided over by various species of flowers of diverse colors.
"You are worshipped by hosts of Siddhas in the sky filled with the moon and clusters of stars; you reside in the center of the assembly of Khecarīs, situated upon Mount Mandara, in the neuter state."
O Great Mother, you who give birth to the fifty liṅgas in the form of the womb;
O Goddess, you who abide within the secret end, dwelling in the thicket of the cave.
It is neither female nor masculine, O Ānanda, nor is it neuter;
for you, O Goddess, shine forth within the form of the eleven jewels.
I am truly unable to describe you; what has been spoken by me in brief is the secret of the Great Jewel, which brings forth divine bliss.
Having offered praise, I ask you: listen, O beloved one of Kāmarūpa! Who am I, and who are you, O Goddess? And what is it that is sung here by name?
I do not know your true nature due to the power and majesty of your splendor, nor do I know your salutation, your color, your form, or your established lineage.
The sacred seats, the instruction of mantras, and the conduct of the Krama as it truly exists—all these are always dissolved and submerged within me; I do not know your state.
O Goddess, beloved of the God of gods, you who are dearer to me than my own life-breaths: I see nothing in this world of moving and unmoving beings that is devoid of you.
O Gaurī, O beautiful-eyed one, show favor to me, your devotee;
O Mistress of the Gods, there is a certain secret, the Kaula knowledge, which is very difficult to obtain.
I wish to hear that by the mere descent of which accomplishment is attained in the Kali age; tell it to me without any doubt.
The venerable Vakrā said:
Listen, O Lord, to the truth regarding the cause that is most excellent and secret;
it is more secret than the secret, a secret to be guarded with great effort.
The *Yoginīhṛdaya* is secret, most secret, and well-guarded; it must always be protected, O Śambhu, like wealth from thieves. [From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:
She has emerged from the supreme splendor, unmanifest yet possessing a manifest form.
Śambhu is said to be situated on the right side, and Viṣṇu on the left.
Brahmā, possessed of great power, stands situated in the center in the form of a bindu;
and I am established in his midst in the form of radiant energy.

She resides in the worlds beginning with Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; among all things stationary and moving; within the constellations, planets, and zodiac signs; and even among worms, insects, and the like.
And she, whose form consists of the letters of the Mātṛkā, resides within the interior of my womb;
likewise, there are the four [sites], namely the Pīṭhas, Upapīṭhas, and Kṣetras, as well as others.
O abode of the Yoginīs and Siddhas, whatever exists in the form of speech,
I create the entire universe, and I shall withdraw it again.
I abide as the supreme digit in the secret place, the heart, and likewise in the mouth;
hear now how my form exists through the division of the gross and the subtle.
I shall now fully describe to you that one which is of divine form and possesses great power;
it is declared to be the supreme single syllable, the ground of knowledge for the perfected ones.
Yogavidyā is the great lore (mahāvidyā) residing in the hearts of the Rudras;
in the section of the Rudras (rudrakhaṇḍa), she is the supreme [power] of the Rudras, following after knowledge.
At Kāmākhyā she is called Samayā, and at Pūrṇaka she is the Goddess of the Seat (Pīṭhadevī);
at Oṃkāra she is known as Yoginī, within the mandala of the three mudrās.
Endowed with the threefold knowledge, you manifest as an incarnation in age after age;
rule over this lineage-group of the *olīs*, beginning with Amarya.
O God, that supreme single-syllable mantra previously shown to you,
which is extremely subtle and resides within the *lakṣa*, I shall now explain correctly.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
she is first described as having short vowels; she appears slightly elevated,
dark like the petal of a blue lotus, and possessing a luster equal to the ashes of a hero.
She has six faces and six forms, moving within the power of consciousness;
she gazes with eighteen round eyes.
Endowed with twelve arms and adorned with various garlands of flowers,
seated upon a throne of a corpse and a lion, and beautified by diverse ornaments,
she has ascended the teaching of the family over thousands of millions of families.
The method for its *piṇḍa* as described is difficult to obtain even for the gods.
Ananta is her eternal anklet-ornament for the feet; Takṣaka shines as a girdle around her waist;
Karkoṭaka is on the goddess's ears; and Vāsuki, the Bhairava, is upon her neck.
The Kulika is on the crown, and the Gonāsa on the earrings.
Others [are indicated] by dates, rings, and fingers; the Nāga families likewise [are indicated] by these.
Padma is situated on the first eyebrow-staff, and Mahāpadma on the second.
He holds a khaṭvāṅga, a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, and a beautiful rosary;
he also holds a cluster of blossoms encrusted with jewels, possessing a radiance like a mass of lightning.
With his uppermost hand he holds a *koṭyāgama*, and likewise Śaṅkhapāla;
[he also holds] a skull-cup, the gesture of granting boons, a trident, and the mirror of karma.
And in the right hand of the goddess, the five divine substances shine,
along with a jar belonging to her who is ninety-two hundred years old.
Upon the head of the Goddess is a garland of vowels, and hanging as a necklace of letters,
her throat shines with a necklace of fifty scorpions.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
the face of the Supreme Goddess (Parādevī) shines auspiciously in the east, situated above,
white as cow’s milk, divine, and endowed with the seventeenth digit (kalā).
On the second head is the face named Gaganamālinī;
it has the luster of a conch, the moon, or snow, and is of gentle form and most beautiful.
The third face is the eastern one, pale white and overwhelmed with wrath;
it is known as Siddhayogeśvarī and is adorned with the form of the mantra.
To the right is the one called Kālikā, resembling a blue lotus;
it is fierce with formidable fangs and has slightly elongated, reddish eyes.
Resembling the flower of the pomegranate, gentle and bestowing bliss,
the fifth [wheel] named Tripurā is circular like the full moon.
Preceded by Umākhecarī, the western [form] is white in appearance;
it is divine, bestows grace upon all, and when meditated upon, grants the fruit of liberation.
His heart shines like a clear mirror,
and his head is radiant with splendor, resembling the rays of the rising sun.
The crest has the radiance of thousands of millions of lightning flashes and possesses a brilliant form; the armor is impenetrable by splendor, difficult to behold, and multiform.
His two eyes possess a luster equal to the moon and the sun; his third eye resembles fire;
and his weapon has the hue of the fire of time, licking [its prey] and being most difficult to endure.
One should indeed withdraw everything and permeate it with one's vital energy (*tejas*);
the earth is situated at the level of the knees, while the waters are established at the navel.
They know that fire is in the middle of the heart, wind is in the region of the throat, space is in the forehead, and Brahmā is located in the navel.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Viṣṇu is situated in the center of the heart; the one known as Rudra resides in the throat;
Īśvara is located in the forehead; and above that is the imperishable Śiva.
She who is the illustrious Viśvarūpā, whose nature is all-pervasive,
who is clothed in fire as her garment, and whose radiance is equal to a mass of splendor.
One should meditate upon this form of the Goddess; one should contemplate it as being filled.
She is that Unmanā, subtle, that digit (kalā) within the world.
In the Kali age, the Goddess of gods, the Mother of the World,
has arisen in the sky, in the mortal world, in the netherworld, and in Hāṭṭakera.
O Śambhu, having recognized this form of the Goddess— established in the group of labials (the *olivarga*) and in the form of the Command (*ājñā*) in Koṅkaṇa— one should begin the sacrifice.
Thus, in the primordial descent (*ādyāvatāra*) of the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) comprising seventy million verses emerged from the Path of Meru,

exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primary seat (*ādyapīṭha*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimala-ṣaṭka*), in the *Kādi* division,
in the Supreme Lord’s Command (*ājñāpārameśvara*), in the *Svāminīmata*, the glorious compendium of twenty-four thousand verses, in the *Avvākrama*—
Thus was spoken the Sūtra on the Instruction for Meditating on the Form of the Goddess.

"And at the time of writing the commentary, explain the procedure clearly.

In the Śrīmata, the king of doctrines, within the great lineage of the three sections,
hear how obstacles arise for one who is devoid of the prescribed ritual.
Portents arise, and obstacles manifest in many ways;
diseases break out, and kings [turn hostile] even toward their own kin.
In one's own home there is constant quarreling and most terrible anxiety;
members of one's own lineage become enraged and engage in mutual strife.
There is loss of wealth, lack of gain, separation from loved ones, and even the death of friends.
Pigeons constantly alight upon and enter the house;
vultures, crows, and ravens roam about the surroundings during the untimely twilight of the sun.
Pregnant women miscarry their fetuses; there is thunder, the falling of meteors, conflagrations in all directions, and the kindling of fires on the mountain peaks.
O dear one, he constantly sees terrible dreams at night;
due to the wrath of Candrasvāti, fearsome winds blow.
And extremely fierce, venomous serpents enter into the interior of his house;
such a thing happens to him who recites [this] with disrespect.

It should be above the house.

And it is born [there]. In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the accomplished yoginīs and the accomplished staff-bearers protect this great family of the Śrīmata, numbering in the tens of millions and beyond count.
With invisible forms, eternally perfected in yoga, and possessed of great power,
they protect the practitioners of the family (kulayogins) within the teaching of the illustrious Lord.
Terrifying cries of jackals resound in the ten directions,
and tawny-colored dogs constantly make dreadful sounds within the house.
O lady of beautiful hips, vultures and funeral pyres enter his house;
such great portents as these certainly befall one who acts contrary to the prescribed rules.
For one who violates the samaya, there is no limit to the number of obstacles;
therefore, the ritual procedure must be performed for that purpose, providing confidence while the [mantra] is being written.
"O Lord, I shall provide for you the destruction of all obstacles;
however, this book must be protected with effort from the touch of those who are excluded from it."
However, one must apply effort until the text is completed;
for, being devoid of its proper arrangement, it does not become clear at all.
O Lord, having reached the full lunar day (pūrṇatithi) conjoined with the Sun,
or on a Thursday, one should avoid malefic constellations.
On the eighth or the fourteenth [lunar day], in conjunction with an auspicious constellation,
one should go to a secluded, solitary, and pleasant place, free from the sight of cattle.
Having smeared it with cow dung and made it free from depressions and elevations,
one should construct a square mandala there on all sides.
Upon a beautiful svastika strewn with heaps of flowers,
lamps ignited with ghee should be placed there in the intermediate directions.
Having placed the jar, filled with *āli* [liquor], upon a *svastika*,
one should indeed worship the *trikhaṇḍa* [yantra], adorned with garlands of flowers.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: the seat consists of three sections—the section of the Mothers and the section of the Mantras; indeed, the center is filled by the Navātman.
Having placed a book there— whether written or unwritten—
one should wrap it in a pair of cloths and cause a golden interior to be made.
Having worshipped with the fivefold offerings, one should present the food offering;
the outer bali should be given by the preceptor according to the ritual injunctions.
Then, amidst the sounding of auspicious proclamations, one should cause the five verses to be written:
the Saṃvartī-maṇḍala and the introduction to the Krama.
One should explain it, or have it written down somewhere, according to the rule and in proper sequence,
for the initiates (samayī), the practitioners (sādhaka), the spiritual sons (putra), and the young yoginīs.
The *ārātrī* ceremony should be performed from the east; one should fill the vessels with honey, and then, having bowed with the head to the *kulakumbha*, one should do so once again.
One should summon eight maidens and cause perfumes and incense to be offered;
[one should invite] the lords of yogis who are present nearby, as well as yogis initiated into the Kula.
One should worship with the finest flowers and incense with the finest incense;
having heated everything with liquor, one should offer fish and meats.
At its conclusion, one should pray for the command of the Blessed Lady and for the lineage-initiates:
"I shall write the Śrīmata; may it be accomplished without obstacle."
Having received permission, the lord of yogins, having worshipped the lineage transmission (kulakrama) and having diligently worshipped the book there according to the prescribed rite, [proceeded].
Then, intent on devotion, one should satisfy all the deities residing within the body with auspicious sounds and the resonance of conch shells and musical instruments.
To the accompaniment of the beautiful songs of celestial maidens, one should draw the Saṃvartī maṇḍala;
thereafter, the scribe should be honored with garlands, garments, wine, and other offerings.
O Lord of Gods, on the first day, one should perform the worship of the Discus with auspicious sounds of musical instruments and the great resonance of hymns and lutes.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Relying upon the play of the wheel (cakrakrīḍā), the wise man should cast snow;
thus on the first day, and again every day according to his capacity.
And the wise who know the ritual rules perform the *bali* offering every night day after day;
one should continue this practice until the text is completed,
otherwise one will incur a great curse from the family of the Yoginīs.
It should be written with devotion for that purpose; otherwise, it will bring about obstacles.
And you [should protect] this one.
O Lord, one who lacks merit and is excluded from the womb of the Yoginīs cannot obtain this glorious Mahākula of such a kind.
This secret, which is my entire essence consisting of twenty-four thousand [verses],
must never be given to those who lack devotion, nor to the deceitful or those of cruel deeds.
It should not be given to Tantrikas, and especially not to logicians;
it should not be given to a hypocrite, nor to a fool, nor to one who is impotent or prone to anger.
O handsome one, those who possess the enjoyments of heaven and the underworld have indeed renounced the most wicked egoism, hypocrisy, and the life of a parasite.
One whose soul is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra should take refuge in the remembrance of the Guru;
it should be given to a disciple who is devoted to the Guru, but one should not cause it to be given to one who lacks devotion.
To one who is devoted to the guru, peaceful, indifferent to worldly conduct,
possessing profound knowledge and great tranquility, truthful, and having conquered the senses;
Those who, having renounced before their gurus until the end of this life,
follow the will of the guru through the actions of mind, speech, and body;
This secret should be given to one who has been tested for twelve years and who understands the convention as well as the annual sequence.
The root-sūtra, the sequence, and the lineage of the succession of gurus should be given;
likewise, the sixteenth chapter has indeed been indicated for you upon the surface of the earth.
The Kula-āgama should be given to him solely by virtue of the oral tradition;
there shall be no door-bolt, no key, and no vajra-joint for the two doors.
"To one who understands the conventions (saṃketa) here, the Kula-āgama should be given.
Śrīnātha said:
"I am your disciple; I am the delighted Siddha Bhairava Hara."
And having been authorized by the mantras, O Mistress of the Kula, how should I today perform the practice of the Kula lineage, the Kaula tradition, and the oral instruction?
"Speak, O one called Surendrā, regarding knowledge: how is the Vakrāmnāya and the Kula?
Śrīvakrā said; Śrīvakrā said:
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: the Wick at the Navel, the Serpent, the Tārkṣya, the Vidyā, and the Vajra in the two door-panels—
this is the eightfold knowledge, the Vaiṣṇava lineage of the West.
O lady of excellent limbs, he who knows this shall become an awakener of the doctrine.
Śrīnātha said:
O Goddess, what is the *nābhivartikā*, and what, moreover, is the *ahivṛkṣa*?
What is the vidyā, who is the one called Vajra, and how are the two door-panels? Tell me.
The root is the navel; the lineage is Meru; the wick is the Self and Mālinī;
the oral tradition is the primordial knowledge, the junction, and the arising of the lineage of command.
The tree is the vajra-family island called the hexagon, located between the two door-panels;
this is declared to be the illuminating consciousness in the division beginning with *ka*.
Listen again, O Bhairava, to its division according to the true principle (*tattva*):
in the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*, the navel is known as the sequence of Meru; the command of division consists of twenty-seven.
There are six steps and six mudrās; then four at the beginning, and again four;
likewise a group of five, then a group of six, and again a group of five consisting of four.

Thus, that which is the arising of the sequence, transmitted from ear to ear as oral instruction, is the ritual procedure for worship; it is not a matter of mere intellectual knowledge, but the lineage transmission of the Kula.
Within its triangle is the imperishable power (śakti) that is itself triangular;
she is the ground, the resting place of stability, and the oral tradition of the lineage.
The earth, the sky, and the ocean constitute the maṇḍala of dissolution;
having ascended by means of the sequence of instantaneous possession (*sadyāveśa*), one revolves counter-clockwise.
The wind-mandala is said to be situated in the fourth state under the name Mahi;
having fixed the *lakṣa* there, one should indeed grasp the Vaiṣṇava ground.
That digit (*kalā*), the moonlight of the nectar of the sphere (*golaka*), flows there.
This basis for meditative concentration is attained by the yoginīs.
O Rudra, having understood the course of conduct, one should practice the "Ahi" mantra;
likewise, the "Tāraṇa," the "Guru," the "Akṣi," the "Vidyārāja," and the "Navātmaka."
He alone is proclaimed as Bhairava, Ananta, Śukra, and so forth;
thus has Tākṣya been described, the supreme teacher among teachers.
The Queen of Vidyās, whose face is auspicious, begins with the letter *bha* and ends with the letter *ca*;
she rests upon the lap of the Guru, the Vidyā at the end of the five [vowels] and upon the fifth head.
Vidyā, Candrakalā, Jyotsnā, and Mahantāyī are proclaimed [as her names]. One whose self is purified by this [mantra] is said to have a ninefold self.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the instruction on the Vidyā has been declared, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
The Piṇḍa of the Vajra-nature is remembered as the sixfold Vajrapiṇḍa.
That lineage of all embodied beings is indeed said to be of six types;
it is the great ocean of six types, beginning from the support (ādhāra) and ending with the eyebrows.
The vajra-convention has been explained; no deliberation should be made here.
One’s own tree is its mass, and outside the tree is the sequence.
Its arising and dissolution are the coming and going of Śiva and Śakti. Śakti is the root; when the *kalās* are full, it is "complete," which is the *pūraka* (inhalation).
That which is the upward breath above that is "withdrawal," which is the *recaka* (exhalation).
That Śiva is the cause of the dissolution and emergence of the Kula-tree.
And these two, known as the "doors," are the very nature of prāṇa and apāna;
thus, having perceived this eightfold knowledge, one perceives the Western [tradition].
O Śambhu, those who have been purified by the Western Command and who expound the meaning of these verses, they alone know this stainless Pārameśvara.
This is the knowledge of the eightfold Śrīmata consisting of seventy million verses;
it is the oral tradition from the mouths of the deities, containing hidden meanings and serving as an instruction.
Rudrāṃśa knows that great, most difficult, and inaccessible western [teaching], yet mortals do not find the great medicine of the oral tradition (saṃpradāya). [In the] Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
[it teaches] the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākāraka-sambandha), case endings, and light suffixes.
Its divisions are concealed by groups of seven, like a woman of noble family.
One might be led astray by corrupted words; therefore, the wise person should abandon what is corrupted.
By means of those straightforward, though ungrammatical, words, the follower of Śiva is reached.
One should purify the phonemes of the convention through a single oral tradition,
and not by means of *laṭa* and *loṭa* [grammatical errors], nor by means of dry logic and the like.
O Lord, in the commentary on the Āgama, the divine speech resides independently;
having understood this [world] to be contrary [to that], the divine tradition proceeds.
Thus, having cast aside mere scholarship, one should listen to the simple Kaulika tradition,
which has come down from ear to ear as an oral transmission.
The teaching on the meaning of the syllables, the Kaulika tradition,
and the Nigarbha— these six alone are declared to be the traditions (saṃpradāyas).
O Bhairava, the essence and the instruction of the verses have been determined for you; there is nothing higher than the Kaulika command, and indeed nothing more supreme than the Śrīmata.
There is nothing superior to the oral tradition; everything else is to be discarded like straw.
Having reflected thus with diligence, one should practice the Kaula tradition of the mouth.
The wick of command, Śiva, the path, the shade of the tree, Soma, the Sun, the Supreme, the Paramahaṃsa, Kuvera, and the series of seats (pīṭhamāvalī).
Kumārī, Kartarī, Bhāṣā, Mātrātmā, and likewise Mātārī;
[these are located in] the east, west, center, and the northwestern and southeastern corners.
The six wombs, the peaks, and the Lord of the Kula from A to Kṣa—
he who knows this knowledge is Bhairava himself in person.
In this way, from the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the reality of the sequential meaning has emerged from the seventy million [verses].
He who, being of a bound soul (paśu), would destroy it, by him the Guru is destroyed.
By him Meru has been lost and by him it has been transgressed;
this is the doctrine, this is the yoga, this is the reality of the Ocean of Kula.
The lineage-current, the transmission-current, and likewise the supreme knowledge-current should be worshipped with diligence; they are never destroyed.
Within the Śaiva system consisting of five currents, this sixth, the *Kulaviniścaya*,
is the supreme, peaceful compendium of the essence derived from the mouth of Aja.
The Great Doctrine of the Glorious Khageśī, known by the name Kramodayajñāna, which is auspicious through the lineage of the Siddhas and proficient in the command of direct realization.

"The Kriyāpāda, likewise the Jñānapāda as the third,
and the Caryāpāda as the fourth— this is the Saṃhitā consisting of four quarters."
One should protect [the deity] with great effort, as if protecting a fawn or one's own son,
with white flowers, fragrant substances, and sandalwood that has been consecrated, along with bees, divine incense, lamps, and auspicious caru offerings.
For it must be constantly worshipped by those endowed with great devotion.
From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:
"If one's mind is distracted or agitated, the sequential worship (*kramapūjā*) will not succeed.
Having first fashioned the maṇḍala of the Guru, one should worship the five Gurus."
If this lion-throne is honored, the three worlds will be honored;
it must be protected like one's own life, and the word of the Guru must be observed.
One should certainly not show it to animals;
rather, one should show it in a secluded, solitary, and delightful place, free from wicked beings.
Abounding with fragrant scents, perfumed with sweet incense,
covered by the rising moon, and filled with the requisites for worship.
Having devoutly honored the Guru with lamps, water-offerings, and cooked rice, as well as with successive offerings of gold, garments, ornaments, and other such things, being full of affection;
The maiden yoginī should be honored with gifts of gold and other excellent offerings;
when she has been authorized and consecrated by those who have received initiation, my doctrine is considered to be without flaw.
"So be it," they said; thus honored, she asked about what is auspicious, having taken to heart the instruction of her guru for the illumination of those of dull intellect.
O Mahādeva, through hearing the Āgamas, a great penetration quickly arises; one must grasp the entire essence within the family of the Yoginīs.
In this illustrious lineage, the lamp of the Pārameśvara is difficult to obtain;
it should never be explained to one devoid of the prescribed rules, nor should it ever be written down.
It should not be written on the leaf of a barbarian tree, nor should it be written on palm-leaf;
it must be written on another material—on a very pure birch-bark free from knots.
O God, it shall bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*), and never otherwise;
and I shall now fully explain the ink with which the Maṭha is written.
Otherwise, O Lord, it would never produce obstacles;
therefore, O highly fortunate one, listen to that supreme method for preparing the ink.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: vermilion, lac-dye mixed with water, a messenger (dūtī) mixed with saffron,
a woman’s flower, and likewise the impure [substance] as well as the Vaiṣṇava fluid.
Following the instructions alone, the knower of mantras should mark it upon an iron slab; having taken up half of what remains, he should do so with the Aghora-weapon mantra.
And I shall fully declare to you that supreme mantra which utterly destroys obstacles:
*aiṃ hāṃ hrīṃ hūṃ prasphura prasphura ghora ghoratara tanurūpa caṭa caṭa pracaṭa pracaṭa kaha kaha vama vama ghāṭaya ghāṭaya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ*.
O God, this Aghora-weapon has emerged from my wrath.
By merely reciting it seven times, one obtains the fruit of the sixfold installation (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
Six types of ink have been declared; with that, this doctrine should be written.
Otherwise, O God, one should not write; for what is written in such a manner brings obstacles.
Just as the procedure for exposition is proclaimed, so too is the act of writing.
The scribe should be a pure devotee, expert in the lineage,
devoted to his guru, tranquil, and a worshiper of the Kula scriptures.
Devoted to the Kumārī-yoginīs, dedicated to celibacy,
delighting in the Kula scriptures, skillful, and free from hypocrisy and deceit.
Having bathed well, purified by mantras, and anointed with yakṣakardama,
he put on a pair of garments and was adorned with flower garlands.
Having perfumed [the image] with excellent incense,

and having satisfied one's own guru according to the extent of one's wealth— with a golden ring on the ring finger, with bracelets, bangles, and necklaces, and with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of gold and cows.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
one should subsequently perform the *ārātrī* ceremony and fill the *kulakumbha*.
Having worshipped the scripture situated there, adorned with divine garments,
and having worshipped the Krama preceded by the maṇḍala of the Guru;
O handsome one, a garland of lamps must be offered to the King of Mantras,
and the heroic feast (vīrabhojya) must be performed just as I previously described.
It should not be given to the disciple of another; it may be given only after receiving prior authorization.
He who gives it otherwise is overcome by obstacles.

"O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, having thoroughly examined them through action, mind, and speech, the instructions spoken in sequence for the female messengers (dūtīs) should be bestowed."
One should bestow this Śrīmata upon him, or else by the command of one's own guru;
otherwise, it must not be given to one who is devoid of purity regarding the guru.
Out of greed for wealth, out of fear, or out of affection, one should never fail to give this;
O Lord of Gods, this sacred rule has been diligently upheld by me.
In one who is devoid of devotion, deceitful, cruel, truthless, fond of quarreling,
a mere ritualist (tāntrika), corrupted by hatred, arrogant, and full of egoism;
One should never cause [the teaching] to be given out of greed to one who is devoid of the lineage,

nor to one who is devoid of purity in the *oli*, nor to one who is bereft of purity in the *krama*, nor to one who has fallen from the *samaya*, nor to a most wicked person, nor to a deceiver, nor to one who reviles the Guru.
When the Lord is most desired by the mind, and likewise when people are intent upon sin.

O lover of devotion, you who seek the welfare of others, [act] toward this disciple who subsists on knowledge, who is attached to the profession of a scribe, who argues with fallacious reasoning, and whose passion wavers like a flash of lightning.
To one who is non-devout, miserly, fickle, addicted to drink,
devoid of the worship of the gods, and lacking in purity and right conduct;
One should not cause the King of Mantras to be given to one who practices deceitful vows;
rather, it should be given to one whose mental state and physical being are steady, and who offers up all their possessions. —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
To you who are pure in deed, mind, and speech; who are affectionate toward your devotees; whose bodily limbs have been dissolved [in liberation]; and who are skilled in the lineage of the masters.
The King of Mantras should be bestowed upon one who has been tested for twelve years,
neither out of greed for wealth, nor out of fear, nor out of affection, nor through pressure, nor merely for the sake of the lore.
This jewel, the treasury of knowledge and the ancestral lineage, must not be given;
it must not be given even to one's own son, much less to other people.

O you who are devoted to those who love you, one should not bestow [this] specifically upon those who seek only their own ends in this most terrible Kali age, for they possess small minds and lack true consciousness.
O God, those who are initiated by teachers who are powerless, devoid of knowledge, and lacking in certainty, as well as those disciples who have not been properly examined; |||
Due to negligence, they may somehow experience sufferings;
for one who kisses [the consort] while devoid of devotion, devoid of ritual action, and devoid of meditative state is a mere magnetizer.
One whose knowledge is not stainless should never be granted the Kula-āgama;
his authorization must be revoked, and he should be avoided with great effort.
Then the practitioner of mantra attains accomplishment; otherwise, he is considered a doer of evil.
This is stated in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, in the Nirvāṇottara Yoga, and likewise in the supreme Kālottara.
And likewise in the *Ūrdhvasrotas-karaṇa*, as well as in the *Svacchandabhairava*,
the *Nityātantra*, the *Yāmala*, and the *Tripurārṇava*.
In the Yāmala, in the Rurubheda, and likewise in the Brahmayāmala,
in the Oḍāmara or the Ḍāmara, and indeed in the Carcikākrama;
O Mahādeva, [it is taught] in the Picu-named [tantra], or in the Kālikākrama, or in the Bhairava-tantra, or in the Somasiddhānta and Lākula,
or in the Tumburu, the Ekavīra, or the Jayā-tantra and the Vāsuka.
In the Mātaṅga, the Brahmatantra, and the Pratiṣṭhāpārameśvara;
In the Āṇava, in the Piṅgalā, likewise in the Rasasvacchandaka,
in the Vācaspate, in the first [scripture], in the Lakṣapāda, O beautiful one, in the Vāmamārga, and in the Siddhayogeśvarīmata of Gaurī;
In Mate, Picumate, and likewise in Devyāmata.
O God, [it is taught] in the Śivādūtīmata, in the Khecarīmatottara,
in the Ḍāmaradūtīmata, and likewise in the Sundarīmata.
And likewise in the view of Maṅgalā, in the continuous succession of the lineage of space,
in the womb of space, in Hṛṣīkeśa, and also in the profound abyss.
O God, those disciples who have been initiated into the Tantras and Āgamas during the Kali age do not attain perfection in this age; such are the "spiritual sons" (putrakas) in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
O King, as long as the Kulasiṃha has not risen,
there shall be no entry of the sons into the western house.
