For those who are destitute and devoid of the Kula lineage, from where can there be enjoyment, from where the Kaulika realization, and from where liberation?
Furthermore, O God, in the Kali age, during the final period known as Siṃhadarśana, all will become unworthy of initiation and will be devoid of the path of Meru;
having first abandoned their guru and discarded the sequence of their previous stage of life.
Then one should bestow grace, specifically in the western direction.
Otherwise, all those beasts have been deluded by me in the Kali age, according to the nature of the age, through each philosophical system that presents a vision of liberation.
Likewise, in the Tretā age it is the south;
in the Kṛta age it is called the upward-flowing west, and in the Kali age it is the west.
In the Dvāpara age, the leftward stream (vāmasrotas) prevails;

in the Kali age, however, the western stream (paścimasrotas), namely Sadyojāta, is the lineage transmission (kulakrama). Thus, the arising of the four [streams] is proclaimed in the Śaiva doctrine according to the ages (yugas).
For whichever age has indeed come to its disappearance, for that very one there shall be success; otherwise, it never occurs.
One yoke is one thing, another is the philosophical view, and likewise another is the guru;
all of that is fruitless for him, just like clarified butter poured into ashes.
Having understood this, [one knows] the western house of the first Kali age;
and the Guru said to Maheśvara regarding the meaning of the venerable [text] for those of the past:
O Maheśvara, my descent is indeed at Oṃkārapīṭha;
likewise, the authority of Siṃha is proclaimed in Dakṣiṇāpatha.
In that very place, the pure realization is established within the four quarters; and through the greatness of the sacred field, it abides in every house for the sake of the disciples.

The piercing [of the centers] through the bursting of mudrās and so forth occurs in Koṅkaṇa and Dakṣiṇāpatha; there, in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the Command (ājñā) was previously proclaimed by me in the place known as Pūrṇa.
The secret was not told by the Guru to Mānava in the Dakṣiṇāpatha;
however, this secret concerning the path to Meru has been told to you, O Siddha.
In the Pīṭhoghaṇa [tradition] of the Trimudrā, the maṇḍala and the Kula-āgama were extracted from the twenty-four thousand [verse] version consisting of one hundred thousand quarters.
I too have obtained this oral transmission from Khecarī on the Himalayas;
O Śambhu, it has been received in the Kali age during the reign of the Mleccha kings in the north.
During the descent of Madhumanthana, upon the encounter with Rāvaṇa,
and at that very Karavīraka cremation ground of the primordial seat (ādyapīṭha).
O Bhairava, authority should be granted to one who is a portion of Rudra, who has attained perfection, and whose mind is pierced; this is the *Siddhakulāgama*.
The Kaulika instruction, as it truly exists, is [revealed] through the practice of night-walking (*niśācāra*).
The meaning of the Saṃhitā is a great matter that must be explained, even though it is as if unseen.
One should bestow the tradition of the sequence of knowledge for the sake of renown in the southern region,
along with the specific Heart [Tantra] consisting of twenty-four thousand verses.
O handsome one, it should be given according to one's capacity within the city of wisdom (dhīpura), assuming a human form,
for the sake of a human disciple whose disposition is pure.
One may give it to him without fault; otherwise, one would incur blame.
By him alone was I previously propitiated in the assembly of the thirty gods.
O Śambhu, I am indeed pleased with him; he has been created from the mortal world in human form, and he is perfected—of this there is no doubt.
O Hara, because of practice throughout many successive births, I have been propitiated by him;
indeed, he who was previously a portion of Rudra shall obtain the Kula scripture. (From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
Having attained perfection and been manifested in human form from the world of mortals for the benefit of living beings, may he obtain the supreme state.
He knows the meaning of the *saṃhitā*, which is difficult to comprehend and hard for even the gods to attain;
he knows the meaning of the terminology and the language of the *sūtras*, as it has been transmitted through the lineage of succession.
There he says: "Abiding there in the form of the mantra, you are the supreme guru;
there, worship must be performed at the three times, and furthermore, the mandala."
As I am, so are you; such indeed is the sequence of the Sky-farer (khecara).
Just as the great knowledge of the scriptures is, so is he the awakener of the doctrine.
With the eyes of wisdom, one perceives no duality with the Guru;
one must never commit an insult, an act of hostility, or a transgression of his word, nor should one ever harbor hatred toward him.
Like a lamp in the darkness, or like the moon in the night.
Likewise, that minister Dīpaka [acted] within the lineage and family succession of the Oḷīs;
and whatever was performed by his sons for the sake of others was likewise done for him alone.
All that is my authority; I abide in his city, and his lion-throne of mantra holds authority over the three worlds.
The perfected one who awakens the mind has declared in the southern region that one sees,
with the eye of wisdom, that which is situated at a distance of a hundred yojanas.
There is no success for those with empty hands; one who has full hands possesses success.
This great mantra-practitioner of the Kumārikākhaṇḍa beholds the Guru as the manifest Bhairava.
One should never engage in discussion with a disciple of a different lineage;
even one who is younger is considered senior by virtue of being in the current of the Guru.
One's own lineage and the sequence of that [lineage] should be purified according to the Vakrāgama;
then success will arise for the disciple, otherwise never.
O God, in whose house this Śrīmata remains worshipped,
there I always abide within his city, bestowing prosperity upon him.
"Wherever there is any auspiciousness, there I am the presiding authority;
and whoever knows the reality recites it all, or half of it."
Whether it be a quarter-verse, a single verse, or even half a verse,
one who studies it shall obtain the fruit of knowledge and enjoy worldly prosperity in this life.
Furthermore, O Lord Ciñciṇī, that human being attains everything, including the four feet, in due order,
through direct perception in the form of an illusion.
Whichever living being is beheld— even by seeing, touching, speaking with, or associating with them— that one also goes to the supreme state.
Success arises for the sinful, and the initiation of gnosis proceeds for one who reads and hears this *Śrīmata*, the Kula scripture.
But he who perceives the extraction of the mantra, even if unawakened due to negligence, becomes initiated at that very moment; indeed, he has gone to the Western Abode.
The maṇḍala of the Guru should be performed before the Guru according to the tradition,
preceded by three circumambulations and prostrations with the eight limbs.
Having prostrated again and again with great devotion, the mantra-knower should once more pay homage to him.
Those disciples are progressive and pure by whom this Śrīmata has been seen;
they are liberated even while living, whereas others, though living, are as good as dead.
Perfect accomplishment proceeds.
In this section on the Virgin (Kumārikākhaṇḍa):
Having attained birth in this world, if one has not practiced the Śrīmata nor listened to it with devotion, then that person's life is indeed in vain.
If one does not recognize this great jewel of the ancestral lineage,
it will be difficult for them to find again in birth after birth;
like a person who has obtained a pure moonstone gem and yet casts it away.
Furthermore, for those men, such a [teaching] of the illustrious Śrīśrīmata is likewise difficult to obtain.
Whoever should hate the illustrious teacher who awakens one to the Mata,
that person goes to a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings.
One should utter "Śrīnātha," "Bhairava," and "pādukām" either in front or behind, following the sequence before one's own guru.
Wherever the practitioner of mantra goes, he should recite this triad;
however, one should not say "to Śiva"—this is the six-syllabled mantra.
On the Kaulika path, one should not utter the word "pādukā";
rather, one should cause the mandala and the extraction of the sequence (kramoddhāra) to be performed in the presence of the Mata.
Alternatively, one should perform the worship of the maṇḍala of the gurus with devotion;
having first performed the sequential worship (kramapūjā) with flowers, incense, and so forth, in due order.
One should smear [the image] with sandalwood, saffron, and musk,
and having lit a beautiful lamp combined with honey and meat.
A fragrant heap of flowers, perfumed with sweet scents, should be prepared;
then a single maiden should worship [the deity], as well as the son of the preceptor.
First, having bowed to the mantras, the mudrās, the maṇḍala of the five gurus,
and my *Vidyāmūlasūtra*, one should meditate upon the *Kulāgama*.
In a solitary, secluded, and delightful place, free from wicked creatures,
[one should worship] the teacher, or one's own guru, or even the mother of the guru.
Having requested their command, one should say:
"May it be for our benefit; likewise, may there be Kaulika accomplishment."
Then, O Maheśvara, it should be recited according to such a procedure;
the Kumārikākhaṇḍa is exceedingly captivating.
One should establish the final conclusion therein;
the speech is exceedingly charming and diverse, consisting of many musical modes (*gāndharva*).
With a voice that is internally pure through refined speech and the like,
yet possessing a slight *kākali* tone, a person should recite that very *samaya* with faith.
Otherwise, there would be a loss of accomplishment for the practitioner; therefore, it must be so.
One should cause it to be performed according to the Kulācāra as explained by Niśācāra;
O fair-faced one, the procedure for that explanation was previously told to you.
Having performed [this], one should indeed listen [to the teaching] in no other way whatsoever,
in a divine and delightful place that is free from the sight of common cattle.
In a place strewn with heaps of flowers, well-protected, consecrated,
and richly perfumed with great incense, the preceptor should face the east.
The disciples, facing westward, should listen to the Kula-āgama;
they should reveal it in secret to the disciple, and the Mukha-āgama should be bestowed upon him.
Likewise, there shall be the realization of the hidden meaning before long,
as well as the root-stage vidyā and the wondrous sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
Having written [the mantra] with *ali* and *kuṅkuma* and having performed worship, one should cause it to be given.
Having received it, the disciple should ask for forgiveness; then, purified by the *ali*, he should drink it.
Thereafter, the pledge (samaya) should be proclaimed in brief, as follows:
"One should not revile yogis or yoginīs; one should not look upon the naked wife of another."
One should never speak disparagingly, nor should one desire a woman who does not wish for it—
be she the wife of a teacher, the wife of a hero, or likewise one who is humpbacked or dwarfed.
One should not desire a maiden, nor a woman from a cow-pen, nor one whose nose has been cut off;
these, O fair-faced one, are the rules that must be proclaimed in brief.
I shall first explain the sixty-four traditions (*samaya*) as follows:
"The section on the Virgin (*kumārikākhaṇḍa*) must not transgress the command of the Guru; by transgressing it, one will fall into hell."
Through its protection, success arises and one attains the eternal state,
O Lord— even when staying in a wretched house, among base people, or in a contemptible place.
One should not disclose the oral tradition regarding the meaning of the scriptures in the midst of the uninitiated;
one should not give it away impulsively, nor should one reveal it to those who are not yet fit vessels.
Having restrained himself and remained silent, he should then observe the vow of silence;
for he who knows the succession of the lineage of gurus as well as the sequence of the years.
"The mandala and the root-sūtra should be given to him through oral instruction;
otherwise, having recognized the disciple as being devoid of merit despite being endowed with devotion,"
Having first made one's own disciple [worthy], then the oral transmission (mukhāgama) should be given;
otherwise, to a disciple who is likely to act contrary to it, one should never give the oral transmission.
He who, preceded by the realization of the Command (ājñā), knows the state of *unmanībhāva* and the signs born of the body, is a disciple in the Kula tradition.
O Śambhu, he whose state of meditative cultivation remains and in whom the state of realization throbs, may he become a vessel for the doctrine through the innate union.
O Lord, one should show [the teaching] before those who are devoted to the sequential path and intent upon the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭha), but one should avoid those who lack devotion.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
One should not converse with those who subsist upon their guru or who maintain vows of hypocrisy; one should not reveal the Śrīmata to them.
O God, one should reveal this single essential doctrine by the command of the Goddess; those men who understand it, O Lord, are liberated—of this there is no doubt.
Thus, in the introduction to the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses emerged from the path of Meru,

exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand, in the *Kādi* division, in the *Svāminīmata* which is the supreme command of the Lord,
in the venerable *Kulāgama* accompanied by twenty-four thousand verses as spoken in the tradition of the Mother (*avvākrama*).
The bliss named the method of writing and explaining the description of the majesty [of the Lord].
Oṃ, may there be well-being!
Salutation to the sandals of the venerable Lord. Salutation to the venerable Gaṇeśa.
In the Manthānabhairavatantra, within the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, this is the thirty-first bliss.
Śrīnātha said:
O Maheśvarī, the ritual procedure of the Kulāgama has been understood by me;
now I wish to hear the procedure for initiation (dīkṣā) according to its proper sequence.
Therefore, I wish to hear that which is the essence of the Western Tradition (paścimānvaya):
everything concerning initiation, worship, the scriptures, and the mandala.
"What is meant by the word *dīkṣā*? By your grace, you should explain it.
The venerable Vakrā said:
"Listen, O Lord; I shall speak. I will proclaim *dīkṣā* to you."
The true essence of knowledge is bestowed, and the cage of bonds is destroyed;
because it possesses the nature of both bestowing and destroying, it is therefore celebrated here as *dīkṣā*.
Śrīnātha said:
"Of how many kinds is the piercing (vedha), and in what place should one employ it?
How does the power of the Command (ājñā) effect the purification of the impurity of bound souls (paśu)?"
How does one become a *samayin*, a *putraka*, and a *sādhaka*?
[Explain] briefly the status of an *ācārya* and the determination of the four stages of life (*caturāśrama*).
"Tell me everything, O Mistress of the Gods, if you are pleased, O Vakrikā! Śrīvakrā said:
"Now, from the sprinkling of the argha vessel and from the observation of the Krama worship... (Kumārikākhaṇḍa).
By hearing the samayas, a person may attain the status of a *samayin*;
by conversing with them using a tooth-stick, one attains the status of a *putraka*.
Pierced and consecrated in the teaching of the Siddhas,
he has transferred his knowledge and realization and is highly proficient in the flood of the Krama.
The consecrated one, who knows liberation, is appointed as the instructor;
now follows the supreme secret, the most excellent knowledge of piercing.
Now, the sequence of piercing (vedhakrama) according to the division of downward and upward is described here: the piercing by mantra is called nāda, and beyond that is the piercing by bindu.
The piercing by the serpent of power (*śākta-bhujaṅgavedha*) is declared to be the supreme piercing;
the piercing by mantra (*mantravedha*) occurs through the recitation of the mantra and the visualization of the wheels (*cakras*) and so forth.
One should meditate upon the supreme six-spoked wheel, filled with garlands of flames;
or else, there is pervasion in the twelve-spoked wheel through the yoga of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*).
The supreme mind is to be awakened; this is declared to be the piercing by mantra (*mantravedha*). O Maheśāna, in the heart-cakra there is a radiance filled with the flames of the *bindu*.
By that one should awaken the disciple; this is declared to be the Piercing of the Bindu (bindu-vedha).
O handsome one, having uttered the Śakti-mantra with the upward movement, it is the Śākta [piercing].
Kubjikā, whose form is crooked, resides upon a seat shaped like a śṛṅgāṭaka;
she is to be uttered along with the Ādhāra and other [cakras], having the appearance of a lamp and resembling a crest-lock (śikhā).
With the state of a steady mind and body, one should pierce the entire universe;
this is declared to be the Śāktavedha, possessing the great momentum of a whirling staff.
This is that supreme power, which causes supreme bliss to blossom;
adorned with five groups of five, she goes beyond the place of birth.
These same five kalās, from the supreme reality (paratattva) onwards, are on the right:
Vyomā, Śāntā, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Nivṛtti.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, Pūrṇā, Sūkṣmā, and Parāmṛtā;
she is conjoined with the five families and adorned by the five voids.
Joined with the five Brahmās and joined with the five causes,
she thus emerges from the abode of Brahmā in fivefold form.
Resting in the station of Brahmā, she shines in the form of lightning;
as the *pratiṣṭhā*, she pierces the body and awakens the supreme self.
Thus has the Bhujaṅgavedha been described in the Kula scripture;
as for the Saṃsphurakādivedha, it is illustrated in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa as the path of the quarters of the Kalās.
O Lord, this must not be told to anyone; it should be guarded with great effort as a secret more secret than the secret, to be protected like one's own body.
O Lord of the Gods, when the mind has ceased, that which is proclaimed as supreme bliss is neither the senses, nor the vital breath, nor within the domain of the internal organ.
There is no mind, nor is there anything to be thought, nor does any thinker exist at all;
when all states of being have utterly ceased, that which is supreme is called penetration.
All this has been told to you by me with supreme devotion;
it must be guarded with effort, just as one would guard wealth from thieves.
By means of the middle movement alone, there is entry at the end of the middle;
the middle Rudra-śakti, however, should press down and up.
Then, one should join the vital breath, in the form of a drop, to the tip of the power;
the self should perceive that subtle form, resembling a firefly.

Beginning from the big toe, one should cause [the breath] to enter unperceived by the unperceiving until it reaches the region of the navel; there, one should join it with the power of Rudra within the city that has the shape of a *śṛṅgāṭaka*,
whose form is coiled like a serpent.
Extremely subtle, whirling, and possessing a radiance equal to a garland of flames.
One should contemplate her blazing through all the apertures in the central region;
as long as the power remains within the body, it abides having entered the apertures for the duration of a muhūrta.
And then, a swoon arises whose nature is all-pervasive;
it trembles, of this there is no doubt, like a tree whose roots have been severed.
Fearless yet agitated, he falls to the ground like a piece of wood;
for that power called Amṛtā has the nature of the full moon.
Merely by being pervaded by her, one then becomes possessed of consciousness.
This is declared to be the downward piercing (*adhovedha*); now hear about the upward piercing (*ūrdhvavedha*). *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
Having fixed the mind at the limit of the Unmanā state, she who is the supreme essence of the Sāman fills the entire universe as far as the seven worlds.
At its end, at the peak of the triangle of Meru, resides the pervasive power (Vyāpinī);
she herself, situated in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), is as pure as snow, the kunda flower, and the moon.
At the point of contact between the moon and the sun, she who has the form of the seat of the elements (the earth) emerged,
having struck and pierced the center of the navel-lotus.
O God, one should meditate on the supreme [energy], extremely subtle, within the interior of the throat-pipe,
coiled like a serpent, as far as it has reached the aperture of Brahma.
Having brought about dissolution there by means of the self, one should pierce the door of Brahmā;
the full moon proceeds as the form of desire, and the new moon proceeds [thereafter].
From the element of earth up to Śiva, Vidyunjihvā, the great flame,
should emerge through the upper aperture until it reaches the head of the target.
Having the appearance of twelve suns and the radiance of the fire of universal destruction,
this is declared to be the "Middle Attraction," which reveals all knowledge.
The supreme energy (parā kalā), shimmering within the six chakras and the sixteen supports, resides in the hollow of the crow’s beak; she brings about the destruction of the wings of the senses.
In the center of the palate, at the end of the resonance (nāda), the Supreme (Parā) pierces the Bindu; she is Kākinī in the form of a crow, Haṃsinī with the body of a swan. —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
O Lord of the Universe, the destroyer of the universe, the swan in the lake of worldly existence—
she is that subtle Unmanā, who cuts asunder all dualities.
The Yoginī exists as past, future, and indeed present;
she becomes the commonality of the wheel of Khecarīs by her own will.
Thereupon, O one honored by heroes, the accomplishment of Khecarī arises above that.
Khagamā, Khagati, and indeed Khagatikhamadhyagā.

She whose nature is space (kha), the Mistress of the Sky (khageśī), Kubjikā, she who moves through the sky (khagamā), and the Supreme (parā)—that Mistress of the Sky is sixfold; she is Suṣumṇā, whose form is the void (vyoma).
There the yogi perceives various kinds of perfected beings;
and above that, having clearly burst through the abode of liberation.
Through diligent effort, the lord of divine yogis should fill the supreme power and enter the stainless, all-pervading, and transcendent reality that is beyond all qualities.
Omniscience, perfect contentment, and the primordial ground of beginningless awakening;
independent, eternal, undecaying, infinite, everlasting, and firm.
Pervasive, having the nature of space as its limit, it is resorted to by Anantanātha;
it is extremely subtle, supreme, peaceful, and devoid of coming and going.
One whose self is constantly disciplined should meditate upon that which is dense like the sky,
stainless, supreme, peaceful, nirvana, and changeless.
The Kula born from Kula is Kaula, while Akula is both supreme and non-supreme;
that which is called Raudrī has been described by me like the sun released from Rāhu.

One whose self is constantly disciplined should meditate upon her— who resembles ten million suns and possesses a radiance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction— until, through the power of absorption, one has reached dissolution. In that state, he always beholds the feet of the Rudras there.
Practicing in this manner, the yogi should perceive [the goal] right there.
A crest of light, resembling the flame of a lamp, issues forth from the center of the navel;
there in the middle, one beholds it in the form of a spark of fire.
That [light], throbbing with its own brilliance, spreads from the drop;
upon entering, it abides within the heart, having performed the visualization of that very [drop].
From that point, it moves upward like the wick of a glistening lamp;
one should pierce the thread which resembles a throbbing *liṅga* and is of subtle form.
And I am that Goddess there, appearing in the form of Kubjikā.
Having reached the cavity of the throat, she ceases, taking on a subtle form.
And having emerged upwards, it reaches the range of the cavity of the palate,
through the gateway of the uvula, into the sphere of the *bindu* known as *Krama*.
One should perceive within the center of the *bindu* a sound of various forms;
that digit (*kalā*) which has emerged above the *bindu* is Kālakarṣaṇī.
She is the very nature of the form of light, possessing the brilliance of smokeless embers;
she is called Nirvāṇā and Śāntarūpā, appearing as a sleeping serpent.
Free from appearances, perfectly luminous, and resting at the end of the twelve,
she has the form of the space of sound and is devoid of inhalation and exhalation.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
The supreme reality is soundless; it is called the unmanifest locus.
Having reached that very locus, the yogi becomes endowed with divine qualities.
Possessing divine knowledge, the divine eye, and divine splendor, he has entered a divine body with a form like the sky, his mind having abandoned the cycle of worldly existence.
He is the knower of the three times, the embodiment of knowledge of the unseen;
he is himself the agent, he is himself the destroyer, and he assumes whatever form he desires.
The knower of yoga, always observing the vows, performs divine action;
having emerged through the three apertures, he beholds [the world] like the orb of the sun.
One should perceive the subtle crest-lock (*śikhā*) as having the shape of a *kadamba* bud, throbbing and radiant with splendor, emerging from the three gateways.
It dissolves into that mandala, a sphere shaped like a kadamba flower,
having pierced through the sun, the moon, and the third, the mandala of fire.
Therein reside Will, Knowledge, and Action; there are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
and there all the hosts of gods dwell, together with the mountains, forests, and groves.
Then one should behold three lines at the junction of the tip of the great nose;
and one should apply the Knowledge-Spear (jñānaśūla) either upon ashes or even upon water.
By the mere discovery of that, one obtains direct vision of the Goddess;
at that very moment, she effects the piercing (*vedha*) of the entire world, both the stationary and the moving.
Whether manifest or hidden, within the conch, the handful of flowers, or the water-pot, there is the movement,
the possession, the trembling, and the range of flickering like lightning.
By the power of yoga, he performs those actions;
then that human being, having become a Siddha in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, attains unbroken perfection.
And divine splendor arises, as well as the eight qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā); likewise, the spirits, vetālas, yoginīs, guhyakas, and mātṛkās [come under one's control].
O fair-faced one, he who has mastered the ritual attains success from these:
in a lotus leaf, in fruit, in water, and among both stationary and moving beings.
The yogi is a penetrator everywhere—in wood, in clods of earth, and in stone;
there is nothing superior to this to be found in the three worlds.
O God, having understood the sequence of piercing— which is difficult to find in the three worlds—
one should pierce the mantras and tantras through the vision of the supreme reality.
The power known as Amṛtā, having emerged from the womb of the Moon and reached the aperture of Brahmā, pierces through the interior of the worlds.
One should contemplate the piercing (*vedha*) in every world and the piercing in every form;
in the form [of the deity], however, there is the great piercing (*mahāvedha*), which causes trembling in every form.

O Maheśvara, you have explained to me that in the smokeless [fire] one knows the piercing born of smoke, and with the sun, the piercing born of the sun; and in the unnameable [fire], the intense piercing.
The great piercing by means of the firefly, likewise the form of light;
the piercing of the drop, and similarly the third [piercing] in the resonance and in the digit.
O Great Lord, there is the piercing of the jar (*ghaṭavedha*), likewise the piercing of space (*khavedha*),
and similarly the fierce piercing of power (*śaktivedha*), which brings about various wonders.
Likewise, the syllable *Ha*, containing the power (*śakti*) within its womb, proceeds in the wheel of space (*vyomacakra*);
one should meditate upon that all-pervading mass of phonemes situated within sound.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: One should diligently expand the mind, intellect, and ego through all the apertures into the supreme abode, [located] from the heart, the throat, and the middle of the palate.
At the end of the nose, perform whatever action has been attained according to your desire;
O fair-faced one, one may pierce wood, stone, and trees.
Piercing wood with wood, however, is devoid of true knowledge.
Thus, O God, in the practice of yoga, the knower of yoga becomes one who has attained the target.
O Mahādeva, wherever she is applied, she makes everything directly manifest; one who has attained perfection in yoga becomes Bhairava himself.
By the power of my command, he who was ever devoted to the family lineage received his consecration in the house at the glorious Candrapura.
The one named Kucandraśekhara is an executor of commands and possesses great power;
this Śrīkaṇṭha, known as the friend of Śrīnātha, is indicated by the sign of silence.
This sixth teacher, Oḍīśācārya, beheld the great Piṅgala, who is called Sadāśiva and is known by nine names, as the Nātha [seated] beneath a tamarind tree.
The ninefold reality has been declared as the abode of the earth and the temple of the deities;
he who shall command the gods by name and by the designation of the instruments.
For these shall indeed come into being in the eastern region, and they shall indeed come into being in the southern region;
in the form of a single mother, they consist of five, seven, and nine syllables.
The end of the sixteen and the end of the sequence have arrived in the Kramapaddhati;
the Kramapaddhati is said to consist of eighteen divisions in pairs.
O God, he who thus discovers the path of piercing (*vedha*) within the Kula tradition is not burned by fire, nor is he pierced even by weapons.
O Lord, he does not die in water, nor is he harmed by living beings;
he enjoys various pleasures among gods, asuras, and humans.
Possessing a divine form and great luster, he becomes a knower of the three times;
this is declared in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa as being pierced according to reality, O God, until one reaches the state free from affliction.

He should display to all the world his power, which is like a lotus in form and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns, as well as his illusory manifestation, which is a complex array of magical creations.
Thousands of millions of moons, hundreds of millions of lightning flashes,
many fires, and even numerous gusts of wind.
Having reflected thus, one should enter the form of Śakti in an instant;
and by the power of divine Śakti, one should pierce the entire universe.
Of all meditations without exception, the meditation of power (śākta-dhyāna) is distinguished;
O God, he who knows this is the Lord Kaulīśa.
And that Self is the essence of all worlds; it alone is the eternal state.
It is indeed Brahmā, it is Śakra, it is both the Moon and the Sun, and it is indeed the Fire.
He is indeed Yama, he is Dharma, and he is indeed Maruta;
that all-pervading one, whose self is liberated, abides by himself like a swan.
Having become one who seeks to deliver [beings], you have descended into the Kali age;
just as I am and just as you are, so too is that most excellent practitioner.
And he who understands this very [truth] regarding saṃsāra, O Śambhu— this first-born [son] is the essence of essences, capable of delivering others across [the ocean of existence].
That is called [the "one who has entered"].
O Lord of Gods, he who knows the sequence of piercing (vedhakrama) is a true teacher;
for the piercing that seizes the bound soul (paśu) brings about immediate realization.
O Bhairava, by the grace of his command, he acts through the differentiation of the Kulas;
there is one supreme, subtle Śakti who produces manifold cognitions.
It must be guarded with effort if one desires long life.
Thus spoke Śrīnātha in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Such is the science of piercing (vedha), which produces great wonder.
"O Lord, tell me what kind of instrument is used for the piercing of the sacrificial animal (paśu).
The venerable Vakrā said: Listen, O Lord, I shall proclaim that which is the supreme essence of essences."
From the support of thirty-six finger-breadths, the heart is twelve finger-breadths from the throat;
the bound soul (paśu), facing forward, is enveloped by the upward movement of power (śakti).
Then, having grasped that which has become liquefied, one should bring it to one's own city;
having rested with the exhaling breath (recaka), one should pierce [the path] with the retention breath (kumbhaka).
Purification occurs through that very tranquil state which fulfills all formative impressions (saṃskāra),
within the partless, stainless, peaceful, non-conceptual, and disease-free [reality].
Having drawn up [the breath] by means of *recaka*, one should deposit it by means of *pūraka*;
during *kumbhaka*, one should remain like a jar, and the nectar of the sphere (*golaka*) arises. Having joined her, whose form is like coral, to each and every *tattva*.
Śakti, in her curved form, is the bestower of all accomplishments and their purposes.
Śrīnātha said:
"O Lord, this initiation by piercing (*vedhadīkṣā*) has been indicated as being devoid of external means.
O Goddess of gods, tell me of the Śāmbhava [initiation], wherein there is no rebirth from a womb."
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa: The venerable Vakrā said:
"O Bhairava, listen clearly to the question that has been posed along with its secret meaning."
Listen to the supreme knowledge, which is direct perception and all-encompassing.
Just as the seed of the yoginīs must always be kept secret by you,
so too is the place consisting of the crow’s beak, devoid of above and below.
Situated in the center of the circle of the palate is a sixteen-spoked [wheel] of great luster;
there dwells a certain woman known as Sarvakāmikā.
When there is contact in that place, then one pierces the fetters (paśus);
one attains the supreme state and should meditate upon Śiva, who is omnipresent.
This piercing has been told to you in the most excellent doctrine known as the Śrīmata;
the deities are pleased with whoever understands it according to its true nature.
In the sixty-four great wheels, O leader of the wheel of the sky-farers (khecarī),
there dwell those who reside in the sky, on earth, and in the netherworld, as well as the Guhyakas and the outcastes.
O beloved, those born of the same family and those born of noble lineages are satisfied at every step by your eyes—
eyes that have the form of tender lotus petals, with pupils bright and tremulous, reaching to the ears, full of passion, and graceful.
They behold the practitioner who is born of the Yoginīs; of this there is no doubt.
Established therein, being well-composed, he shall indeed obtain [his goal] according to the prescribed rule;
for whether it be restraint or grace, it is accomplished without hesitation. (From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
One should apply the practice to the six cakras through the division of the moving wheel;
having moved it again and entered it again, one who is clear-minded should move it once more.
Through both shaking and penetration, one then pierces the bound souls;
by means of yoga, one should pierce the *piṇḍa* enclosed within the cavity of the *piṇḍa*.
One should pierce the aggregate with the aggregate; one should accomplish the aggregate by means of the aggregate.
One's own self and the external self are both established together in one place.
"O Bhairava, O God, out of devotion to you, I have told you this: first, the knower of reality must purify himself by means of the descent of power (śaktipāta)."
At the end of the age, when the kingdom of the Mlecchas arises, those born from all castes will speak without lineage and will become outcasts.
Men will have short lifespans and little intelligence; they will have gray hair while still in their youth, engage in forbidden sexual acts, and be devoid of virtuous conduct.
Because they are excessively greedy and addicted to various vices,
they do not attend upon their teachers, nor do they serve their mothers and fathers.
At the end of the Kali age, there will be practitioners established in the Kaula tradition;
they will belong to all four castes, and especially to the Brahmins.

The most excellent ones who are knowers of the Vedas, as well as others who are outcastes— there will be a single meal of sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for both the outcastes and the twice-born together. This has been told to you in its entirety regarding what will happen at the end of the Kali age in the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
By that means, his comprehension will undoubtedly become much slower.

Thus, in the introduction to the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), in the determination of the Sixfold Subsequent Pure Division, in the *Kādi* division, in the *Ājñāpārameśvara*, the *Svāminīmata*, the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses, as spoken in the *Avvākrama*.
In the description of the authority for the initiation of piercing, this is the bliss named the Arising of the Sequence (Kramodaya).
The venerable Vakrā said:
Now I shall fully explain the great arising from the center of Meru.
By the mere knowledge of which, entry proceeds.
Sumanta is the foremost prosperity; Sumukha is the powerful treasure; Pratāpin is the pride; Pramada is the great joy; and Vijaya is the devoted one.
Sudhanya, Dhanavān, Dhārī, Kāla, Śravaṇa, Yama, Marīci, Viraja, Vāgmī, Vipula, and Kulīpati.
Indrajit, Himavat, Maulī, Kāmada, Śaṅkha, Bodhaka,
Viśvāṅgī, Śubhada, Krūra, Acintya, Vijayī, and Pati.
Sumālī, Śarvara, Kānta, Śuci, Vādī, Śucivrata, Kulajihva, Sama, Śakra, Sumantrī, Vanavān, and Madhu.
Gāndhārī, Ṭaṅkavṛt, Śārva, Śūra, Bhaṭṭa, Vikrama,
Udghoṣa, Bhṛgu, Śrīvatsa, Kaustubha, Malaya, and Rathī.
Vikaṭa, Śaṃkara, Garva, Sunanda, Hanumantaka,
Viśvāṅga, Viśvajit, Vāgmī, Kaśmala, and likewise Amala.
Bhīmasena, Subhīma, Bhīmarūpa, and Mahābala; Vasu, Vasubhṛta, Dhātṛ, the Vasus, Vāsava, and Guru.
Tejasvin, Sarvadarśin, Sarvātman, Priyavādin,
A, Pretavāsa, Priya, Svāti, Viśāla, and Abhaya.
Śṛṅgārī, Sundara, Ratna, Vicitra, Bhogaḍambhaka,
Śaśi, Mahāharṣa, Mahājihva, Krakaca, and Śūladaṇḍin— [these belong to] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Śatakratu and Dakṣa constitute this century of Śatakratu;
this is declared to be the emergence of a year, beginning from Sumantu and ending with Dakṣa.
They revolve like a wheel; from Sumanta, there shall be a rising, and when destruction has reached the end of Dakṣa, it proceeds again from Sumanta.
The rising and setting [of the ages] in the Kṛta and the others should be known as follows:
Dakṣa [lives] for one hundred years after [the passing of] one hundred [ages].
Then, when the portion of Dakṣa remained, on the eighth day of Śiva in the month of Śiva,
the western rising occurred, consecrated by Siddhanātha.
Thus, that which is called the "arising of the year" (abdodaya) has been declared as divine;
the preeminent teacher who knows this is the one authorized in the Kula lineage.
Śrīnātha said: Regarding the liberation of bound souls (*paśu*) from sin, both in this world and the next,
how is the Guru— who has reached the further shore of the knowledge of piercing (*vedha*)— to be examined?
Many teachers wander upon this surface of the earth;
tell me the characteristics of a true guru, for I wish to hear them according to their true nature.
O Goddess of gods, please state again, with clear meaning, the characteristics of disciples according to their true nature, in accordance with the procedure for initiation.
"Tell me about the practice of the observance (*samayācaraṇa*) and also about *nirvāṇa*.
The illustrious Vakrā said: 'Excellent, excellent, O Great Śambhu! You ask me very extensively.'"
I shall explain everything in its proper sequence; listen now, so that the great pervasion of yogis may proceed everywhere.
O Lord, those masters on the surface of the earth who assume illusory forms and subsist by relying on the conduct of a teacher belong to the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Fallen from their lineage, devoid of compassion, always delighting in what is contemptible,
addicted to liquor and meat, fickle, and full of hypocrisy.
They are devoted to backbiting, always engaged in base actions,
full of egoism, deceitful, cruel, and speakers of false instructions and knowledge.
They will be makers of strife, intoxicated with pride, constantly reviling others,
attached to greed, full of delusion, and ever intent on deception.
Those who engage in artificial worldly dealings seek instruction from others;
yet they possess these very same qualities and merely bear the title of "Teacher."
Those who are constantly devoted to the non-duality of food, who covet the property of their gurus, and who consume the belongings of yoginīs, are not to be honored on this earth.
For they are fierce and indeed harmful, especially the Kāpālikas,
who long for the substances of the heroes and are devoid of worship and ritual refinement.
Those who perform penance for improper conduct, those who eat what is unfit to be eaten, and those devoted to drinking what should not be drunk— these must be avoided with great effort.
Indeed, he who violates the command of the Guru does not return from the hells;
those disciples initiated by such [Gurus] are not vessels for auspiciousness,
for they initiate out of greed and with a mind corrupted by delusion.
And those who are devoid of the initiation of piercing (vedhadīkṣā), yet are kissers [of the Guru] and lie upon the bed of the Krama.
O God, those who are devoid of worship fall into the ocean of hell;
as a tree carries one across a river, a stone does not carry even another stone.
In the same way, a teacher devoid of qualities cannot deliver one from the ocean of existence;
he who stands outside the doctrine must be avoided with great effort.
"O lotus-faced one, listen to [the account of] the teachers among the four castes:
whether they be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra who drinks liquor."
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, I have described the characteristics of the four castes and those of the teachers as follows:
they are endowed with the awakening of the intense Command and are the illustrious ones who bring about the realization of the ultimate meaning.
Endowed with both primordial wisdom and discerning consciousness, they carry out the commands of their guru;
they are stainless and free from conceptual proliferation, devoid of the sense of "mine," and without possessions.
Free from agitation, always blissful, untainted, and dwelling in the state beyond conceptual construction;
endowed with forbearance, possessed of compassion, truthful in speech, and having conquered the senses.
All were devoted to non-violence, intent on compassion for all living beings;
they possessed peaceful minds, practiced virtuous conduct, had abandoned dualities, and were firm in their vows.
They were not lustful toward women nor cruel; they turned their backs on mean actions, were satisfied by divine knowledge, noble, and possessed serene intellects.
Those who possess affection for their spiritual lineage, are endowed with true devotion, remain indifferent toward royal wealth,
are authorized for the festivals of the Guru, are intent upon the Command, and possess great strength.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
[The teacher] is a speaker of pleasant words, a giver, an enjoyer, and one who does not beg;
he may be a follower of Vedānta, or Siddhānta, or likewise other traditions such as Vāma or Dakṣiṇa.
He does not defile the scriptures, nor the true devotees, nor the young maidens;
he is a seer of the lands of the yogis, yoginīs, and vīras, and is no petty man.
He is a steadfast knower of the three times, capable of both cursing and bestowing grace.
Whether [the disciple is] perceptible or imperceptible, he is skilled in the initiation of piercing.
Devoted to the performance of rites, tranquil, eating sparingly, and well-restrained,
he is constantly delighted by divine bliss, ever pure and sanctified.
Having attained the glory of Kulakaula, he has reached the further shore of the Western lineage;
free from revulsion, a knower of all things, he is an indifferent seeker of the supreme state.
Those who know how to protect the conduct of the samaya, who are proficient in the oral lineage,
who understand the secret conventions, who are learned, and who always maintain their unmanifest signs;
Having entered the path of the virtuous, he is indifferent toward the path of the wicked; though engaged with the worldly ways, he observes the proper timing and remains free from possessiveness.
He was devoted to the ritual section [of the Veda], peaceful, solitary, and a resident of the city;
he was a great scholar, possessed of honor, and had reached the further shore of the meaning of all the scriptures.
Always joyful in mind, generous, beloved by all people,
skilled in initiation and consecration, and a master of those respective subjects.

He is a renunciant, a knower of the protector of Dharma, one who serves at the proper time, and is non-violent; his soul has entered the path of heroes, and he disregards the company of those addicted to liquor.
The pure Bhaṭṭabhārya, however, disregards the path of the bound soul (paśu);

he is in the state of Unmanā beyond passion, free from the tantric conduct (tantrācāra), liberated from [the rites of] consecration and so forth, and always devoted to truth and purity. —From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
He knows how to examine the class of disciples; he is liberated and possesses a pure mind.
Clad in white garments, with disheveled hair and naked as the sky,
he is fortunate, handsome, eloquent, and indifferent to various religious observances.
Alternatively, he may assume a guise at his own will, or be one who is well-washed yet greedy for wealth;
he may be attached to passion and hatred, or even be of wicked conduct.
One should avoid from afar a teacher who dwells in a border region; rather, one should seek one born in a land of the virtuous, who is capable of both restraint and favor.
Such a teacher has been described in this lineage as one who bestows auspiciousness;
having obtained such a guru, who would not be liberated from bondage?
The characteristics of the teacher have been declared; now hear those of the disciples.
In the Western Tradition, there is no fitness for disciples who have not been examined.
He was a devoted and humble son who honored his father and mother;
he was always delighted by dharma, peaceful, generous, and ever-observant of proper conduct.
Devoted to the worship of the Guru’s feet, honoring the gods, the sacred fire, and the Guru,
his soul terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, he yearns for the path to liberation.
Free from deceit, wise, and peaceful, he disregards the science of logic;
he is ever devoted to the Yoginīs and a worshiper of young maidens.
Free from anger and free from backbiting, thoroughly examined with effort, discerning the noble meaning, never deceitful, and always truthful in speech.

One who offers his body—the very essence of his life—to the Guru, being pure in three ways through action, mind, and speech, and who is devoted to devotion; one who is free from deceit and envy, and who disregards the wives of others—[this is the disciple]. (From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*)
And this disciple, who desires the knowledge of liberation, is a lamp for his lineage.
He is free from dispute, never hostile, and always humble toward his elders; he knows how to observe the conventions of conduct and honors the sequence of auspicious signs.
Constantly devoted to the worship of the gods and intent on affection for his kin—
a disciple endowed with such qualities should be examined through various means.
For he indeed becomes worthy of initiation through the glance of the intense Command;
otherwise, if the disciple is initiated while possessed of contrary meanings, [the result is adverse].
That teacher and that disciple shall go to the Raurava hell,
whether they be Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Śūdras, or others of the lowest castes.
All those who are pure in their disposition and devotion, and who are detached from the surface of the earth, should be made disciples; there is no need for deliberation in this matter.
One should not take their birth into account, but should examine their devotion;
for a Brahmin who lacks devotion is declared to be a Caṇḍāla.
If even a Caṇḍāla possesses devotion, he is ordained as a Brāhmaṇa; what does it matter to him that his birth is different? Devotion alone is the cause in this matter.
Even a learned man who lacks discernment is equal to a fool on this earth;
for even a fool, if he is discerning, pure, and devoted to devotion, is truly wise.
He should be known as a wise man, fit for the continuation of his lineage—
[provided he is] not an unworthy recipient, nor one who is contemptible, foolish, devoid of devotion, or associated with the wicked.
One should not practice the Kaula way with one who is deceitful or a slanderer;
nor indeed should one who, deluded by greed for material wealth, practices it [with such a person]. (From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
The yoginīs become angry with him and devour his fat and flesh;
therefore, one should by all means not undergo initiation out of greed.

Thus, in the primordial descent (*ādyāvatāra*) of the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) measuring seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru, in the section exceeding one hundred thousand quarters,

brought down to the first sacred seat (*ādyapīṭha*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimalaṣaṭkanirṇaya*), in the *Kādi* division, in the *Svāminīmata* which is the supreme command of the Lord, concerning the teacher and the disciple...
In the description of the section on characteristics, this is the bliss named "The Arising of the Sequence."
The illustrious Vakrā said: This is the thirty-third bliss;
I shall now declare the Kula initiation for a disciple who has been thoroughly tested.
Initiation is traditionally held to be of two kinds: that which bestows yoga and that which bestows enjoyment.
It is said that when performed out of sight it bestows yoga, but when performed in the presence [of the deity] it bestows enjoyment;
O Bhairava, out of devotion to you, I shall explain both of these to you.
The heart vibrates with force as if with a flame of fire within itself;
it quickly moves toward the cavity of the palate, and then the sound of a crackling burst occurs.
Know that mind to be flickering; through the steadiness of the mind, it attains immobility.
Like a lamp, it is seen [to be steady] upon the completion of the swan’s movement.
By that he perceives power and attains the state of upward-leaping;
the vision of reality arises, and it becomes the third eye.
Then the attainment of Nirvana is perceived in the form of a drop;
the realization of the state of non-duality occurs when one has reached immovability.
Having abandoned the pairs of opposites and the knots of time, one becomes dissolved in the supreme state;
possessing a firm aim and freedom from dullness, one embraces the circle of the Mothers.
The past, the future, and the present lead to one's welfare; likewise, in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the stream of water falls swiftly, and there is the contraction of the *nīḍī*.
Furthermore, he beholds his own entry into fire within meditative absorption;
he converses with vetālas, and their blessings are heard.
One shall behold divine knowledge and divine splendor arises;
thus are those eighty-four states according to the sequence.
For as it is with one, so it is with all; this is the sign in the lineage succession, taught for those sons of disciples who are vessels for liberation.
Those disciples who lack the [proper] stages and who attempt to leap over the sequence will not attain liberation even in hundreds of millions of eons.
One should know them to be devoid of seed; for them, there is never any rebirth. Furthermore, all those who lack initiation are destitute of the destruction of impurity.
O Maheśvara, through the descent of power (śaktipāta) there arises the intense knowledge of piercing;
O God, without this state of knowledge, no conviction whatsoever is born.
Those who are devoid of the [inner] condition (pratyaya) are proclaimed to be like cattle;
O Lord of Gods, the piercing performed in the absence of direct perception (parokṣavedha) will now be fully explained.
"Even those animals who have undergone the purificatory rites of the six paths and are free from worldly states are proclaimed as 'initiated' (dīkṣita) in the teaching of the Siddhas."
The state of those pierced by the piercing of the imperceptible [reality] indeed manifests;
then, the impurities are destroyed, and "it has arisen"—such is the supreme command of the Lord.

Initiation by means of yoga is said to be [effective] even from hundreds of leagues away through the Command (ājñā). In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, initiation by means of the principles (tattvadīkṣā) consists of the principles, mantras, and words within the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
Endowed with the colors and the worlds, and adorned with circles of dust-pits,
initiation is declared to be of two kinds in this lineage of Śrīkula.
According to the division into Tantra and Kaulika, she is both the Hotrī and the Vedhavatī;
for those intent on the recitation of mantras, she is everywhere shown as the Hotrī.
The initiation by piercing (*vedhadīkṣā*), which is preceded by [the Guru’s] command and bestows yoga, is very difficult to obtain;
yet by meditating on the sandals of one's own guru, the cage of the body trembles.
I shall now describe the procedure for the initiation by piercing (vedhadīkṣā);
one should employ the piercings at the time of initiation upon a human disciple.
The flower initiation, the conch initiation, the empowerment, the sign of the scales, as well as the stimulation and the protection— initiation is thus remembered as being fivefold.
Having filled his joined palms with flowers and placed them upon his own head,
he then performs the consecration with flowers through the power of the mantra's energy.
When the conch-vessel held in the hand, filled with flowers and unbroken rice grains,
is gradually raised to the crown of the head, that is the conch-consecration (śaṅkhābhiṣecana).
Immediately after that, one should initiate a disciple who has been purified by the balance.
For lightness resulting from the cutting away of karma is known as the sign of the balance. [From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:
Having drawn a six-petalled lotus with a vajra-maṇḍala on the outside...]
In the midst of that, one should place the disciple, provided with the substances for the Yoginīs.
Having worshipped the assembly of yoginīs with perfumes, incense, garlands, and so forth,
there then arises, through their glance, a pervasive sensation throughout all the limbs and a trembling.
Pierced [by the arrow], he falls unconscious; there is no need for deliberation here.
In this way, the rite of initiation (dīkṣā) should be understood as it has come down through the lineage of succession.
Initiation is said to be threefold: Āṇava, Śākta, and Śāmbhava.
The Āṇava is said to be for those with direct perception, while that which is Śākta pertains to the five [senses].
Initiation that effects purification through the six paths is known as Śāmbhavī;
by means of any mantra whatsoever, the paralysis of the bonds (*pāśastobha*) is produced.
The *āṇava* [initiation] is revealed as pertaining to the past, having occurred at another time;
likewise, there are the vocal and mental [initiations], arising from seeing and touching.
Thus, that individual (āṇava) initiation is prescribed as being of four kinds,
by means of touching [the disciple] with a staff, a patched garment, a cloth, a bowl, and so forth.
Or, O fair-faced one, even by touching a limb, that is called "piercing by touch," [effective] even across five hundred yojanas.
O you who are fond of devotion, the command [of the Guru] proceeds even from afar through the threefold purity;
the power of that Guru’s command becomes a deity out of compassion.
That very attainment of qualities is called mental piercing (*mānasīvedha*). O Śambhu, mental piercing is the first; tactile piercing (*sparśavedha*) is the second. *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
The piercing of vision is the third, while the piercing of the difficult [obstacles] is the fourth;
thus is the fourfold initiation of knowledge established.
One should initiate a disciple born within [the lineage]; that is called "piercing by sight" (dṛṣṭivedha).
Thus has been described the Great Initiation (mahādīkṣā), which produces immediate realization.
The disciple who has obtained the knowledge of the guru through the procedure for the initiation of wisdom should bring all the requisites for the initiation into the presence of the guru.
Fragrant unbroken grains, flowers, incense, lamps, and likewise sacrificial oblations (caru);
as well as food, edibles, drink, garments, and so forth, together with gold.
Having fully prepared all the materials and implements, such as elephants, horses, and vehicles, and having offered them all before the Guru,
one should worship the assembly of Yoginīs and the virgins with devotion.
Likewise, with divine ornaments such as bracelets, bangles, garments, and so forth.
Having performed all the preliminary rites for the Guru according to one's capacity,
one should thereafter offer one's own body to the venerable Gurus.
Alternatively, if he is destitute of wealth and intent on causing distress to his teacher,
he should perform prostrations with a staff and offer all his possessions.

O you who are devoted to those with devotion, whether one is wealthy or destitute, the teacher, having understood and examined them, should look upon them with compassion through the threefold purity.
When his vision finds rest, he is pierced and falls in an instant;
he should then quickly proclaim the ineffable reality of gnosis.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: bliss, the arising [of energy], trembling, sleep, and the fifth, which is whirling—
these five states come upon the disciple who has realized the reality.
The abandonment of the grounds, the agitation of the city, and the piercing of the mudrās in manifold ways;
the cognition of hearing from afar and the setting forth of the Kaula speech.
The intoxication of the mind through all mantras, as well as singing and laughing,
dancing and the initial turning, proceed according to one's own will; indeed, all the previously mentioned qualities arise without a doubt.
From resting in that, there is a thousandfold [expansion], and when that is dissolved, there is indeed a hundred-thousandfold.
In that very state beyond dissolution, through the power of intense command,
one attains the supreme abode, free from old age and death.
"Thus, O leader of yoga, the procedure for initiation is threefold:
the first occurs through recollection, and the third through a mere glance."
Thus, that various initiation brings about the five states.
Śrī Bhairava said: "Today my birth has become fruitful, since you have become a granter of boons to me."
The initiation of yoga, which produces immediate conviction and is free from the six paths— that which was known by me through your grace has now been understood by me.
But I ask you, O Goddess, who have come through the lineage of the tradition of reality: tell me, according to the ultimate truth, the specific distinctions of the initiation of the six paths.
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa: The venerable Vakrā said: "Listen, O Lord, I shall explain that which you have asked."
O Lord, Leader of Sages, all that is indeed true and subtle;
initiation, refined through the six paths, bestows yoga by means of the expansion of reality.
Since it exists within the Kula tradition, I shall speak of it to you today.
First, one who is expert in the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā) should examine the ground;
he should have it excavated to a depth of seven cubits and then fill the excavation back up again.
Where the soil is rich with dust, that ground bestows all desires;
one should diligently cleanse it, removing husks and thorns.
One should diligently prepare that [mixture] with thorns, charcoal, hair, and so forth;
likewise, it should contain ghee from the middle [of the cow], milk, buttermilk, and the bark of the five trees.

Having prepared a water mixture with triphalā, the heartwood of the bījavṛkṣa, and khadira, one should sprinkle it [upon the site] again and again. Then, in the northeast, one should construct a mandala that grants all desires.
And that [was done] by them according to the very sequence previously established by the root sūtra.
It may be on the eighth, or the one called Bhūta (the fourteenth), or the full moon, or the seventh; it may be the tenth, the ninth, the third, or the twelfth.
One should cause an auspicious maṇḍala to be prepared during the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight,
in summer, spring, winter, or even autumn;
[therein] great heroes, full of devotion and pure in their vows, have approached.
The examination by which one has completely crossed over, as demonstrated in the treatise.
A Śūdra [should be examined] in twelve years, a Vaiśya in nine,
a Kṣatriya in six years, and a Brāhmaṇa in half of that;
I shall now explain how one should examine them by means of contrary actions.
The lowest [practitioner] in a superior rite, and the highest [practitioner] in an inferior rite;
thus, in various ways, they should be thoroughly examined with great effort in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Having passed the examination, those who are highly qualified and well-disciplined should be favored with rewards appropriate to their merit;
however, one should diligently avoid those who act contrary [to the rules], for they are not fit vessels for the lineage.
Those born outside the family of Yoginīs do not obtain initiation in the teaching; yet, if one should initiate unworthy disciples out of greed or delusion, [the fault lies with the teacher].
An obstacle will arise for both of them before long; there is no doubt about this.
Having understood this, the great mantra-practitioner, possessed of great intelligence, should remain humble.
Then the preceptor should command: "Let the gathering of the ritual materials be prepared without hesitation; thereafter, the young maiden is to be honored."
There, in the great and glorious sacrificial pavilion, one should worship the Lord of Gods,
accompanied by the world-protectors and endowed with the gatekeepers.
It was covered with mango sprouts and hung with garlands and wreaths;
eight jars were placed in the cardinal and intermediate directions, with a *kulakumbha* in the northeast,
accompanied by a *vardhanī* vessel for the weapon-mantra, and well-honored with flower garlands.
There, one should worship the Lord of Gods, Navātmānandabhairava.
O God, one should have a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed, purified according to the detailed ritual procedure;
it should be one cubit deep, triangular in shape, and provided with three tiers (mekhalā).
Having done this, O Lord of Gods, one should thereafter begin the sacrifice;
first, however, being well-composed, one should perform worship in the mandala.
One should worship the God of the gods, Navātman, of great splendor.
The Goddess, who is the supreme single syllable, resides upon his lap.
Holding a lotus in her hand, possessing a massive body, peaceful in appearance, and bestowing boons;
she drinks divine wine, laughing with intoxication overflowing.
Likewise, one should worship the Mother located externally as previously described;
one should offer two kinds of food offerings (naivedya) accompanied by wine and spirits.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
In this manner, the worship should be performed after worshipping the Krama with devotion;
that which was previously indicated to you, consisting of divine provisions, [should be employed].
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods and petitioned the Supreme Lord,
O Protector, he makes [the ritual] free from defects within this glorious sacrificial pavilion.
Likewise, O God, by your grace, success shall be attained;
having gone near the fire, one should proceed according to the sequence of the ritual.
Indeed, the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and ending with the funeral (śiva-anta) must be performed without hesitation, offering oblations by groups of five.
And having performed the oblation, thereafter perform the worship as before;
one should satisfy those residing within the maṇḍala with the thirty-two-syllable vidyā.

O lady of beautiful hips, worship should always be performed according to the rules for one situated on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and especially for one situated within oneself; this practice should always be carried out in solitude.

Having offered the bali-oblation to Vaṭuka, the deity, the Kṣetrapālas, and so forth, as well as to the Yoginīs, and having presented and consecrated [the offering] at the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) of the Krama;
Then, one should cause the well-restrained disciple, with flowers in his hands, to enter;
thereafter, one should have him release the flower in the western part of the deity's [mandala].
Having prostrated before Mahādeva, one should go near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);

having meditated upon the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) with the mind, one should place them within the body. O observer of good vows, this libation (tarpaṇa) is for the purpose of bringing [the deity] into proximity, from the letter 'A' to the letter 'Kṣa'. —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
The practitioner of mantra should always consume the caru oblation with milk as if it were nectar.
O Lord, with *śyāmāka* sprouts, or with *śāli* rice, or with *priyaṅgu*;
and with *masūra*, *yava*, as well as *godhūma* and *vrīhi* grains, O Lord.
In a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay— one that is unblemished, smooth, and free from fine dust or sand—
one should purify it with the Astra-mantra and then ignite it with the Mūla-vidyā.
Having taken a firebrand from the auspicious fire, one should kindle it both outside and inside;
then, having performed the protection ritual and being of serene mind, one should place it there in the fire.
Then, having prepared a vessel filled with milk and [anointed] with clarified butter and other substances, one should proceed.
One should place [the deity] in the midst of the fire so that she becomes motionless;
the movement is performed with the root mantra, the thirty-two-syllable vidyā.
One should perform the covering with white and black cloths using the root-mantra;
the wise should constantly perform the sprinkling and the moving [of the vessel].
Having placed it upon the vessel of accomplishment, one should divide it into ten portions.
First, it should be placed upon the sacrificial ground; second, in the northern direction.
The third [offering] is for Agni, and the fourth is for the Self;
having offered the sacrificial food (naivedya) at these three locations, one should present the bali offering outside.
Having thus satisfied the guardians, the Mothers, and those who protect the fields, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) afterwards.
Then, having prostrated before the Lord and praised him in brief,
one should offer a tooth-stick that is provided with milky sap and free from knots.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
A palm leaf should be made one span in length, straight, smooth, and very beautiful;
it may be from a mango tree, an arjuna tree, or even from an aśvattha tree.
Then, having consecrated with mantras the aśvattha tree and other offerings along with flowers and the like as prescribed for the deity, one who bestows the fruit of all desires should present them.
The fall of that [object] would be observed as either auspicious or inauspicious;
in the western direction it becomes excellent, and facing the east it would be most sublime.
One should know that the northern direction is auspicious, and likewise the northeastern direction is most excellent;
however, O Mahādeva, in the other directions it is the reverse.
The preceptor, being well-composed, should observe with effort;
if it is auspicious, he attains success, but if it is inauspicious, he should perform a fire-oblation (homa).
Having summoned Janī with the mantra "saṃsvaya indra," he, standing together with his companions,
should bestow the dream-mantra upon those disciples.

At dawn, when the sky is clear, having gone to perform the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) and having paid homage to the gods and ancestors, the disciple should return to the presence of the guru and disclose his dream, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.
One attains success in what is auspicious; in what is inauspicious, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*).
When this is done, success will arise and there will be the pacification of obstacles.
O dear one, having fashioned figures of flour and cow-dung, [one should offer them] to Śrī Varāyana.
One should diligently offer it with *unmatta*, leaves, *bilva*, and so forth;
having taken a *karaṇī* made from cotton.
One should cause chalk to be taken; one should procure pure and white [chalk].
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
one should place the thread reaching the Brahma-position in the eastern direction.
O Lord, the laying of the cord is likewise distinguished from the south;
one should accomplish that with effort through the application of the northern portion.
Then, having divided [the line] into four parts based on the eastern sūtra,
there will be two fish-marks by means of that which is the fourth part;
one should establish the eight directions by drawing lines from east to west.
It should indeed be oriented toward the south and north; thereafter, one should establish the intermediate corners.
In the southeast, southwest, and likewise up to the northwest, one should proceed in due order;
thus, when the field has been prepared, one should establish a square.
Once the field has been made square, one should subsequently fashion a lotus;
one should draw the supreme lotus, measuring twenty-four finger-breadths in length.
One should fashion [the lotus] with eight petals, radiant with a pericarp and filaments:
the portion of the pericarp is in the first [layer], the filaments in the second,
the joints of the petals in the third, and the tips of the petals in the fourth.
One should draw a line of obstruction outside the lotus.
The leaf-pattern (patraka) should be placed on the outside with a measurement of four finger-breadths;
outside of those, a pathway (vīthī) of one cubit's measure [should be made]; the door is said to be the size of a lotus, or else half of that.
Having thus laid out the lines with the thread, one should then scatter the colored powders.
They are declared to be red, yellow, white, and black;
the lines should be drawn evenly, unbroken, and very beautiful.
One should determine the interval between the lines to be the measure of a barley grain (*yava*).

The pericarp (*karṇikā*) should be made yellow, and the lotus-petal (*puṣkara*) red in color. In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*, the filaments (*kesara*) should be made rich in red and yellow, and white as well.
They were beautifully adorned.
The petals should be made white and adorned on all sides; O lady of excellent hips, the practitioner who performs this according to the ritual in brief,
being devoted to it, O Mahādeva, shall not undergo birth again.
One wanders in saṃsāra as long as one does not find reality;
when the mind has attained the state of oneness, one is neither bound nor liberated.
I shall explain the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan) in brief; listen to that.
O wise one, the agent of universal dissolution is located on the soles of one's own feet.
One should worship the god Bhairava as he resides in the wheel of space (vyomacakra),
with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, excellent incense, and other auspicious items.
Having worshipped with diligence, the knower of reality should subsequently consecrate the disciple;
he should cause him to tremble by means of the ritual application of the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
The collection of sounds beginning with the letter *kṣa* and ending with the letter *a* should be employed;
the analytical expansion of the letter *kṣa* is to be known on the path of the deposition of the principles (*tattva-nyāsa*).
This Mātṛkā-nyāsa, encapsulated by the principle of withdrawal (saṃhāra-tattva), has been described;
when the principles have been meditated upon and deposited, then initiation bestows auspiciousness.
Just as with oneself, so should the knower of yoga apply the *tattvamātṛkā* to the disciple; then, having performed the paralysis of the bonds (*pāśastobha*) through the application of the *kalās*.
Having joined [the disciple] face-to-face, one should then pierce the disciple.
Śrīnātha said:
"The initiation by means of the phonemes (varṇadīkṣā) is the supreme essence, capable of delivering one across the ocean of worldly existence."
"Now I wish to hear about the initiation into the principles (*tattvadīkṣā*) according to the truth.
The venerable Vakrā said:
"I shall explain the initiation into the principles; listen, O long-eyed one!"
Kumārikākhaṇḍa: Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well—
by these, when purified, one is purified in six ways, O fair-faced one.
Sound alone is declared to be the [first] of the organs of action; likewise, there are five organs of cognition.
The five subtle elements (tanmātras) are to be known [as the objects]; hereafter follows their defining characteristics.
Touch, taste, form, smell, and sound constitute the five subtle elements (tanmātras);
the ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose constitute the five organs of action (karaṇas).
The organs of cognition have been described; now hear about that which consists of fivefold [organs]:
speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals as the fifth.
O Three-eyed One, this group of five known as karma has been described to you:
mind, intellect, and ego, ending with primordial nature (prakṛti), in their proper order;
as well as rajas and tamas, which arise from the qualities of the Pradhāna.
Sattva and the unmanifest (avyakta) are thus described; the twenty-fifth is proclaimed.
The twenty-sixth principle is to be known as the Puruṣa, the experiencer of pleasure and pain;
he is the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), bound by karma that has been acquired through Prakṛti.
That which remains as the residual impression of karma is declared to be the object of experience;
by that knowledge, the seeds of existence are purified without exception.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa: All the remaining [principles] that exist sequentially along the path,
above that is known as Niyati (Restriction), situated on the path of the Restrictor.
O beautiful one, Time and Number are the two agents; that which has been created by them is pervaded by a digit (kalā), while the reality (tattva) remains as it is, being thus measured.
Therefore, this *kalā* is said to belong to one whose mind is shattered by passion (*rāga*).
For the self (*ātman*) is colored by passion and becomes enveloped by *māyā*.
*Vidyā* should be known as that which causes perception; *vidyā* perceives the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Those who understand the meaning of the supreme knowledge shall attain the pure path.
Impelled by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), one may again undergo birth and death,
or attain either liberation or worldly enjoyment, as directed by the Lord (Īśvara).
Sadāśiva is indeed the knower and the liberator of the bound souls (paśus).
Having abandoned the state of the seed of Māyā and having fully enjoyed all worldly enjoyments,
Śakti— pervasive, subtle, and following the dharma of Śiva— [remains].
But Śiva is declared to be all things, established in a peaceful form.
Thus, O God, the path to be purified according to the number of principles consists of thirty-six steps; these are indeed to be purified by the wise.
O lady of excellent hips, the mental enjoyments of individual souls are to be purified according to the nature of the nine principles in the sequence beginning with *prakṛti*. Furthermore,
the triad of principles known as *ātman*, *vidyā*, and *śiva* has been proclaimed.
These are declared to be the primary ones; they are to be purified by the teachers.
O Three-eyed One, by these pure [principles], the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) are purified;
likewise, all those [beings] should be perceived through these rays of light,
O Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
But now, O observer of noble vows, I shall explain to you the path of the *kalās*.
The reality (*tattva*) is pervaded by the *kalās*, and that reality indeed has the form of the *kalās*.
Mahādeva, the omniscient Supreme Lord, is himself the form of the *kalās*.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti.
Śāntyātītā is to be known as the supreme; the elements beginning with earth are remembered [as her aspects]. And Sūkṣmā and Susūkṣmā belong to the pervasive Vyāpinī of the Lord of Gods.
Pervasive, of the nature of space, and infinite, she is supported by the Lord;
O sinless one, the path of the kalās has thus been described to you in brief.
Therefore, the highly intelligent and supreme teacher should purify one of these;
having purified the path of mantra by means of both the higher and lower *vidyā*.
O Great Lord, the contemplator of reality should awaken the path of the worlds,
beginning from Kalā and so forth, all the way up to Śiva.
O Mahādeva, this sixfold procedure regarding the phonemes and their meanings must be performed according to the rites seen in the scriptures, in their proper sequence.
Therefore, O God, one among these should be diligently purified by the Guru, who knows the paths, having established the limit of cyclic existence.
O God, you should bestow grace upon the bound souls (paśus) according to your will,
having understood [their nature] through the distinction between creation and withdrawal, in accordance with their karma.
The transmigrating being is said to be a mere beast, presided over by merit and demerit;
he dwells within the cage of fetters in a bond consisting of primordial illusion.
(Kumārikākhaṇḍa)

But that which is the single primordial impurity, O observer of noble vows, which remains established as the seed, attains the state of sprouting by depending upon the field of phenomena— that is, by depending upon the field.
The field (*kṣetra*) would be the impurity (*mala*) of that innate (*sahaja*) perceiver;
just as the seed of a *aśvattha* tree, once fallen, sprouts with thousands of branches and trunks through its connection with the support of the soil.
Thus, the self (ātman) is considered to be eternally based on *māyā* and of the nature of *māyā*.
For that *māyā* proceeds from the atom (*aṇu*) because it has a real cause;
