O Lord of Gods, *māyā* does not proceed at all for one who is without a cause.
Sometimes, even for those destined for liberation, the pure path does not proceed;
O God, Śiva is not found, for Māyā alone exists,
and she is bondage by her very nature— liberation is not found anywhere.
then it would be so.
That is known as the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti), and it is said to be present in the yoga of liberation.
Liberation does not occur for them as long as the signless state has not arisen;
it is just as a king, though bound by his own fault, remains engaged in that very bondage.

For those men whose innate impurity is identical with the true nature of reality, there is neither liberation nor bondage; rather, that [impurity] which is the support [of experience] is forcibly overcome.
Then, his illusion, awakened by the continuity [of consciousness], would proceed,
for there is indeed one continuous stream.
Consciousness, which is enveloped by the *kalās* and whose sphere of experience is revealed by *vidyā*, is colored by *rāga* and joined with the instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*).
From awakening, through illusion, one attains detachment from reality;
[otherwise] bondage ensues. Good and evil, the qualities based upon that, non-dharma, and its dharma—in brief, [these are the consequences]. *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
The two bonds are traditionally held to be of the very nature of illusion; bound by them, the soul remains [in bondage].
Having understood their separation from the Self, from Māyā, and from Śiva, however...
Listen now to how it happens later and later through the loosening of the noose: an insentient being, bitten by a snake through negligence, has its life departed.
It moves and vibrates, and indeed it makes requests at the sacred site;
the power of the mantra is clearly seen—why is it not investigated?
The shaking, the trembling, the paralysis, and the coming and going of stones—
these, O fair-faced one, are indeed the most excellent and supreme signs among them.
Bondage consists of merit and demerit; it does not belong to the Self in any other way.
O Supreme Lord, its destruction is not to be achieved through initiation.
Whatever actions have been performed in the past and those which he performs now are exhausted by initiation; through the practice of alms-gathering, he shall go to Śiva.
O Lord of Gods, when the noose whose nature is dharma has been exhausted, those who are established in adharma have no other means by which they might remain on that path.
When the self is indeed released from its bonds and remains without support,
it falls and trembles like a tree whose roots have been severed;
just as a tree, once cut down by external blows, quivers upon the ground.
And there is no doubt that the soul is like a potato freed from its husk;
likewise, the wise should effect the separation from the fetters through initiation (*dīkṣā*).
When this separation has occurred, then there is undoubtedly a state of paralysis (*stobha*). —From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*
What is designated as "paralysis" (stobha) consists of trembling and falling;
for anyone situated therein, the yoga is indeed free from affliction.
Thus, the paralysis of the fetters occurs, and one is liberated from the bonds of dharma and the rest.
"Liberation indeed comes to him"—such is the injunction of the scriptures.
From the paralysis of the noose, accomplishment arises; he too is fully perfected within the *saṃvara*.
That which is called *saṃvara* is indeed the mind, for it is undoubtedly liberation.
"Therefore, this auspicious liberation is manifest; it bestows yoga and bestows enjoyment.

O Great Lord, he who knows this is liberated and shall liberate the bound souls (paśus). Thus [ends] the introduction to the Mahāmanthānabhairava Sacrifice, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru.

In the *Svāminīmata*, which consists of twenty-four thousand verses, spoken in the *Avvākrama* tradition, belonging to the *Ājñāpārameśvara* within the *Kādibheda*, which determines the Pure Six Thousand (*vimala-ṣaṭka*) on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) exceeding one hundred thousand quarters,
this is the chapter on Initiation with Seed (*sabīja-dīkṣā*).
His name was Ānanda.
Śrīnātha said:
In the thirty-fourth bliss,
how is the fire-oblation (homa) prescribed for an initiated disciple?
For one who is engaged in the obligatory rites, how can there be success in the occasional rites?
The venerable Vakrā said:
For those who live off others and whose minds are afflicted by passion—
for them, the rites of oblation are not prescribed, nor is the recitation of mantras (vidyājāpa) recommended.

But for those householders who are devoted to the life of a householder and who worship the gods, the sacred fires, and their teachers—for such householders, this established rule applies: the performance of sacrifice accompanied by knowledge is highly praised.
Then, in a solitary, secluded, and beautiful place, one should purify the ground;
having performed the Vāstuyāga and other rites, one should have a sacrificial pavilion constructed.

On the southern ground, one should fashion a wheel and a *triratra* [fire-pit] for the *triratra* rite; the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) is said to possess the proper characteristics, and its excavation should be made equal to that. In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:
one should construct an altar (*vedī*) in six parts, circular in shape and resembling the form of the world.
One should arrange three seats above, and perform the worship of Kāpūjā in due order.
Briefly stated, there are one hundred and five finger-breadths at the beginning;
however, this is not prescribed for those who are ignorant or for those of great stature among the people.
The collection of three triangles is common to all and bestows all accomplishments;
it is for the sake of liberation for those seeking release during the ancestral rite of fire-oblation.
One should perform the sprinkling with the *ājñā* weapons and the veiling with the *kavaca*. Then, one should perform the uprooting with the *netra* mantra, followed by the *mahantāyī*.
Filling the wheel of the sky-farer (khecarīcakra) by equalizing it with the Vāgbhava syllables,
sprinkling with the essence of the moon, and pounding according to the will of Bhairava.
One should perform the cleansing with supreme joys, the smearing with the seed-syllables of knowledge, and the sprinkling and invocation; one should perform the drying with the five seats.
Sprinkling, veiling, uprooting, filling, leveling,
sprinkling [again], pounding, and sweeping.
Smearing, sprinkling, and drying—these are what is called [the process of] purification.
Thus, these eleven consecrations, when performed with the proper instruments, bestow fearlessness.
In this case, the fourfold correct form of the pit is set forth;
because it is made without ritual refinement, that pit does not bestow accomplishment.
There, one should fashion the seat as the Aghorāstra-mantra within the center of the image;

the three-cornered world of the peak-syllable (kūṭa) should be raised by means of the needle-weapon (śalākāstra). [This occurs] in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, produced from the luster of the sun, or else in the hall of fire-offerings (homaśālā).
One should summon the fire, tawny and reddish-brown, by means of the King of Mantras.
First, having raised the Śakti, whose form is that of the Vāgbhava syllable,
one of clear intellect should apply the Parā-mudrā with the exhaling breath (recaka).
O Goddess of the Gods, the Blessed Lady first brought down the lineage of Kulavāgīśvarī, which stands from the beginning up to the end of the *vicce* mantra;
she is the complete Vāgīśī within the mandala of knowledge, together with the limbs beginning with the heart.
Then, having performed the purification of the site, one should place the *liṅga* in its center.
Having first formed a single peak (kūṭa), then immediately following it with the seed-syllable,
and having performed the emanation pertaining to emanation, one should meditate upon the wheel situated within the womb.
In the center of that, however, is consciousness; according to the previous sequence, from its limb arises emanation, which then becomes its follower.
Having thus performed the complete worship, one should afterwards perform the ritual actions of the fire-oblation (homa),
meditating upon oneself as consisting of radiant energy within the circle of fire like semen.
The seed-syllable bearing the form of radiant energy proceeds within his womb;
it is fashioned within the Bhairava known as Kālāgnirudra, together with all things.
And when one is born into the supreme reality adorned with supreme bliss, produced within the Womb of the Moon, the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) occurs. In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:
one should offer three oblations into the fire and worship with the Heart mantra.
Then, by means of the Heart-peak (hṛtkūṭa), there is the emission of that [mantra] from the face turned away.
Having performed three oblations, one should worship with the binding of the topknot;
for the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), one should perform it according to one's capacity, joined with the syllable *ī*.
Having worshipped the head with oblations, the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) should take place;
its facing toward [the deity] occurs through four oblations at the four stages.
One should perform worship with the Kavaca mantra; then, with the Nivṛtti-pañca mantras, one should briefly offer oblations and worship with the Netra mantra.

Then, O large-eyed one, the wise consider that the bracelet should be placed on the hair in the left hand; thereafter follows the definitive determination of reality by means of the weapon-mantra of knowledge.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space,
as well as sound, touch, taste, form, and smell— these are the five subtle elements (tanmātras).
Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ constitute the five organs of action;
the ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose constitute the five organs of perception.
The mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), passion (rāga), knowledge (vidyā), and likewise limited power (kalā);
the principle of illusion (māyā), the principle of the Mistress of Desire (kāmeśvarī), pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā), and that which is called Śiva.

The Goddess of Command is the supreme state, the determination of the thirty-two principles; in the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*, the Vidyā joined with the Bindu is at the beginning within the maṇḍala of Kālāgnirudra.
The meaning of *vā* is the union with *rūṇa*; the divine sound (*nāda*) together with the bindu is the great seed-maker seed, that flood of seeds again and again.
Then, the purification from birth-impurity, as well as the oblation with the Vidyā and Astra mantras,
is taught in three stages for the liberation of those seeking release.
Having removed the hair-tassel and ring, one should offer oblations with liquor infused with the *bhāva* of a bee;
by that very act, one attains purity, which is then called the "Name-consecration."
In the Kali age he is known as Kucandra; in the Dvāpara age by the name Ṣaṣṭha; in the Tretā age he is Vahni, the bearer of the practice; and in the Kṛta age he is ordained as Mitra.
In this very way, through the fourfold group of perfected ones, you attain the state of fire;
and through the fourfold mantra of the Self, by means of three oblations each.
The four designations are established at the beginning of the first group of four;
the emergence of the teeth is purified fivefold by means of the *ka*-group.
O Lord of the gods, three oblations should be offered with drops;
one should perform the fire-sacrifice with the three-syllable mantra used for the first feeding of solid food.
Relying upon the name beginning with Vāgbhava, one should offer three oblations;
by means of these three other oblations, the Vidyujjihvā [mantra] becomes most powerful.
The tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇa), which is difficult even for the gods to obtain, has been described.
Hereafter, I shall explain the binding of the girdle-thread (mekhalāsūtratabandhana) in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Having offered the fourfold [mantras] beginning with Vyāpaka, conjoined with the *saṃhāra* and the *bindu*,
five times with the mantra for the sake of the Yoginī’s presence,
one should purify the entire essence of the initiation (*upanayana*) on the path within that city.
But the binding of the vow occurs in the heart-cakra, within the third seed-syllable of fire.

Having performed the oblation, the preceptor, as a practitioner of mantras, should offer to Navātmānandabhairava; for the sake of perfecting the observance and attaining accomplishment, O Lord of Yoga, he should purify [the disciple].
First, having bound Māyāpurī with a long bindu,
one should perform the rites of purification, beginning with the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) and so forth, for the sake of the ritual action.
The practitioner of mantra, surrounded by the Rudras and adorned with the five-syllable [mantra], should perform all that with four or eight oblations using the dhyāna-mantra.
Having ascended to the supportless state above by the command of the Sky-farer,
the glorious bearer of the Brahma-vidyā should perform the fire-oblation with the Brahma-vidyā.
First, by means of the assembly of powers (śakti) in sequence up to the End of the Sky-goers (khecarānta),
one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the Vidyā-krama and its purificatory rites (saṃskāra) as they have been handed down.
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—these five are the creators of the universe; one should worship them with the five-syllable mantra."
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Brahmā is in the southern face, Viṣṇu is situated in the north,
Rudra is in the western direction, and Īśvara is in the eastern direction.
Sadāśiva is indeed the single mass at the end of the vulva, which is fivefold;
for the Brahmin, the seat is dry cow-dung spread upon a layer of grass.
With a ball of sesame seeds, one attains the seat of Viṣṇu;
here, the head belongs to Īśvara, while the substance belongs to Sadāśiva.
Having first placed [the deities] upon the seats, one should assume the form of the fivefold embodiment;
and externally, one should worship the world-protectors, beginning from the east and ending with Īśāna.
One should worship [the guardians] according to the ritual for weapons once the protection-pit has been consecrated:
Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, and Vāyu.
From Kuvera up to Īśa, they are to be worshipped in due order:
the vajra, the spear-weapon, the staff, the lord of serpents, the earring, and the banner.
The mallet and the trident are proclaimed as the eighth;
having first placed the *māyā-śrī*, the foot is then recited.
Above is Brahmā and below is Viṣṇu, with their two weapons, the lotus and the disc;
having thus worshipped with diligence, there is the removal of all obstacles.
Blazing, kindling, piercing, supreme terrifying, purifying, nourishing, consecrating, and facing the presence [of the deity].
In the former teaching, those whose ritual preparations are by nature effortless offer oblations with these eight;
thus the five-faced fire is generated.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the group of Uḍḍiyāna individually within each division of the *uli* according to the previous rule; the placement on the tongue, however, is fivefold.
Kapālī, Kāpālī, Kākinī, Kumārikā,
and Kubjikā— these, in sequence, are the tongues [of the goddesses] by means of the three seed-syllables.
Then one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the Yoga-pīṭha and subsequently assign the eight kalās;
[one should worship] the fifty deities of the rosary by means of the collection of letters beginning with *na* and ending with *pha*.
Then, having recollected [the deity] with supreme devotion, one should first perform the five limbs of the Siddha according to the previous rule, beginning with the *trikaṇṭaka* and the others.

Having performed the entire ritual of placement (*nyāsa*) according to the prescribed method, one should indicate the sign of success (*pratyaya*), having purified the self within its primordial nature (*prakṛti*) through the successive order of the sacrificial rite.
The rite of Uḍanātha should be performed by means of the collection beginning with fire;
one should meditate upon the fire above and below in brief, situated in the center of the sun.
Having placed the three-footed [mantra] below, well-composed within the group of emanations (sṛṣṭivarga),
that which is called "Jvala" is declared, endowed with the sixfold wind.
The letter *ra* situated between these two, resting upon the *bindu*, becomes the illuminator (*dīpana*).
Having placed the group of six within the power (*śakti*), it is joined with the downward power (*adhaḥśakti*).
That is designated as piercing; the terrifying consists of the fivefold roar. [From] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
one should cause the descent of the Vidyā-deity; one should cause the descent of the Vidyā-deity.

One should perform the sprinkling with the *āpyāyana* mantra from the *Candragarbha* [tantra] and the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) according to the command (*ājñā*). One should cause [the deity] to face forward with the *astra* mantra; one should not act otherwise than in this sequence.
The realization of the entire Lord Uḍana and of Cakrakālānala was brought about by the eight purificatory rites beginning with *jvalana*.
Having thus completed in every respect this unsurpassed Vidyā-homa,
which is the very essence of ritual action according to the *Homapaddhati*,
there can be no oblation or realization, nor any independence, for one who does not understand this.
Whoever should perform a fire-oblation (homa) devoid of the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa-saṃskāra), [that act is fruitless].
He who remains in improper action should be known as such; he is not ordained for liberation.
Having raised up the supreme, vibrating Kuṇḍalinī from the center of the navel—
Through the resonance (nāda), one should awaken the innate (sahaja) within the citpura at the end of the triangle;
having recollected the Peak Syllable (kūṭākṣara), which is slightly red and possesses the brilliance of fire.
And that goddess, O Lord, when remembered by me, shall indeed enter into me;
having fixed my mind upon her, she has likewise been brought into myself.
O Great Lord of the Krama-vidyā, having meditated upon the mantra and performed the oblation ten times with barley and sesame seeds, accomplishment is attained in accordance with the ritual action.
A rosary made of crystal, moving both in the natural and reverse directions, is for the rite of oblation; this is the summary determination of the ten-fold portion.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: Through a single oblation, possession arises within the body;
through a second oblation, the attainment of the state of total peace is achieved.
With three measures, the wise man attains excellence; with four, he attains prosperity;
when the homa is performed with five measures, good fortune and happiness prevail.
When the homa is performed with six measures, stability of the body arises;
with seven, fame is attained; and with eight, the realization of gnosis is reached.
When a homa of nine mātrās is performed, mastery of speech (vāgīśatva) arises;
when a homa of ten mātrās is performed, the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), free from all ailment, is attained.
When two thousand oblations have been performed, the piercing of the animal occurs even when out of sight;
by means of the root-vidyā, immobilization takes place within jars, wood, and other such objects.
One should accomplish all tasks, such as the bursting of seals, the piercing [of obstacles] with three vidyās, the felling of trees with four, and the shattering of houses.
With five [recitations], there is the drying up of mountains and even the ocean;
with six, the pillars of the rows of gates [are moved] and gray hair is warded off;
with seven, one brings the deities under control—this is not otherwise.
What need is there to mention men and maidens, let alone yakṣa maidens?
Having accomplished the eight superknowledges (*aṣṭābhijñā*), one should assume the form of Brahmā;
with nine [faces], the form of Bhairava; and with ten, the form of Rudra.
Regarding the power of flight (*khegati*): one shall fly up toward the western quarter; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, in the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*, the procedure for the tenth part is established according to the divisions of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Vīrabhadra should perform the unsurpassed Vidyā-homa;
he should have it performed by one belonging to the Vāyu-group.
One should accomplish success at the tip of the liṅga by means of the division of the fire-oblation (homa).
For the sake of pacification during daily rites, or on the eighth or fourteenth lunar day.
A wise person should perform the *mātrā-homa* either at the time of initiation or otherwise;
one should offer eight hundred oblations, for then they become vessels of accomplishment.
In this manner, one should always worship exactly eight hundred [offerings] on occasions such as Śivarātri, or during the Pavitraka rite, or at other festival times.
Having attained heroism, one achieves perfection and reaches the world of Rudra;
[this is equal to] thousands of sacrifices and hundreds of horse-sacrifices.
Whatever fruit the mantra-practitioner may obtain [from other rites], he shall receive a hundredfold more from performing the daily fire-oblation;
the mantra-practitioner who performs the daily homa obtains the fruit of bathing in the Ganges.
When an oblation is performed on the eighth lunar day at Vārāṇasī, it is equal to that [at Kedāra];
when an oblation is performed on the fourteenth lunar day at Kedāra, the fruit is the same.
When all the fire-offerings have been performed, there is the consecration by all holy fords, the purifying rite of the king of oblations, and the sovereignty over all mantras.
By the offering of the *siddhi-homa*, one becomes a destroyer of all obstacles to accomplishment.
In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*,
the ritual of the *vidyā-homa* is prescribed as the constant conduct for householders.
On the right of the sequence, one should offer oblations with liquor purified by the Mūrtis. With white *arka* flowers, *hayāri* [white mustard], and beautiful white blossoms,
as well as with great substances for occasional rites, one attains the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*.
Whatever belongs to the past or the future functions within the present.
Śrīnātha said:

How is the measurement of the substances here determined, along with the ritual procedure and its definitive conclusion? Furthermore, how is the measure of the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) prescribed according to its proportions?
The illustrious Vakrā said:
"Beyond this is the measurement for the contemplation of substances;
it grants all desires and serves for the pacification of those intent upon their daily rites."
Having prepared white arka flowers together with sesame seeds, one partakes of them;
by means of clarified butter and the seed-syllable of fire, the fires achieve their fulfillment.
It is well known that with the knowledge of the Self, a pellet of guggulu resin, the size of a wild bird's egg, is excellent when held in the right hand.
Having smeared and rubbed [the substance] with sesame oil, one should offer one *pala* of clarified butter;
in a city, these oblations for auspicious rites grant all accomplishments.
In the mouths of the Vidyās, one should offer five oblations of cooked food into the sacred seats (pīṭhas);
then, in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, one should offer five palas of meat and a pill into the fire.
Through the measurement of the *mātrā*, there is accomplishment; the fruit of the daily fire-oblation is great.
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations by means of the power of Rudra and may move about as he pleases.
He becomes the protector of the supernatural powers, such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and the rest, and not otherwise;
having performed the fire-oblation consisting of the measures (*mātrā*), he thereafter becomes one who possesses the lineage (*anvayin*).
Therefore, the ritual procedure for this occasion is prescribed here:
one should offer eight hundred handfuls of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter.
Having prepared a pill according to the measure of the fruit of the sun and moon (arkenduphala),
the wise practitioner should first prepare it with guggulu and then perform the fire-oblation (homa).
In this manner, one should not perform the fire-oblation for a month with an unlimited measure;
rather, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of red cow's milk and clarified butter.
One should offer flowers of four colors according to the prescribed rite; first, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the three thorns within the sacrificial pit as well as upon oneself.
In the same way here, one should perform the deposition of the Vidyās, as well as the other, the Pañcasiddhas;
having performed the Mālinī-ṣaḍaṅga, [one places them] on the mouth and tongue in due order.
One should offer the oblations into the sacrificial pit according to the distinct divisions of their forms;
[this is] Uḍḍiyāṇa, the great mouth, frequented by the accomplished yoginīs.
One should meditate on the deity in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), Jālavaktra to the south,
Pūrṇagiri to the north, and Kāmarūpa in front of that.
Above that is a single fifth seat (pīṭha) known by the name Tisra;
these are the five faces of the seats. Within them, the tongues [of fire] are, in order: the group of four beginning with Vyāpakā, and Saṃhāra conjoined with Bindu. *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*
It is pervaded by the letter *ra* as the sixth, according to the division of the previous name.
One should indeed install the family goddess Kubjeśī in the central seat;
as for Vaṭuka and the Yoginīs, one should cast their offering outside.
Furthermore, one should worship there the Great Sequence (mahākrama) of the Knowledge Goddess (vidyādevī),
together with her faces and limbs, as well as the four seats (pīṭha).
One should likewise worship the four deities and the eight Kula goddesses.
Or, O God, the wise one should cause it to blaze with the king of weapons.
Having kindled [the fire], O Maheśāna, one should veil it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*).

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—these three cities (*puratraya*) are indeed present upon the *darbha* grass; there, one should place the large and small ladles (*śru* and *sruva*) facing forward with the seed-syllable of the Vidyā.
Having filled the *śruva* ladle with clarified butter, the Vidyā-deity is worshipped.
The *yonimudrā* is without support; one should perform the fire offering (*homa*) by means of inhalation (*pūraka*).
All that must be done in the rite of *homa* is performed with the left hand.
Then, having placed the *vidyā* within a handful of flowers, one of clear intellect [should proceed].
Having performed the completion of the faces and limbs, the wise one should offer oblations;
having offered with the six limbs complete, he should offer to the four tongues and likewise to the eight family goddesses, beginning with the first oblation.
Thus are the five oblations; having offered the five, the fire-sacrifice proceeds with the movement [of the beads] by means of the rosary held in the left hand.
One should perform the sattvic oblation (*sāttvika-homa*), which grants all desires through knowledge.
In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:
no one should overstep Meru, nor should one overstep the shadow of Meru.
Sesame seeds should be consecrated with clarified butter and ignited by the fire-seed mantra;
one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) at a tenth part of the total number of recitations.

When joined with *puṣpa*, it bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*) upon one who has conquered the sense of touch (*tilāta*). O Śārdūla, [the seeds of] *apāmārga*, *somarājā*, and *pippala* likewise [bestow success].
Īśvara, as well as Brahmā, Jīva, and Meghavāhana—these eight are declared to be the fuel-sticks; one should offer them along with clarified butter.
With sesame-smeared and beautiful flowers, three thousand [offerings] are prescribed;
two hundred, O fair-hipped lady, or half of that; or briefly, a fourth part for all the faces; less than that does not grant success.
O Viśālākṣa, [one should likewise apply] the Ājñā-vidyā to the face and the limbs.
Immediately after [the offerings] to the Jihvās, the Kuladevīs, and the Lokeshas,
one should perform an additional fire-oblation, and thereafter the Aghora-weapon oblation.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, he should afterwards offer five oblations each to the faces,
the six limbs, the tongues, and the family goddesses.
With a round *māṣa* bean, one should offer a beautiful oblation to satisfy the deity;
thereafter, the practitioner who is the patron should also offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
When the gurus have been honored, there shall be the grace of all accomplishments;
one should offer gifts according to one's means and even dedicate one's own body.

Through the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), your success shall arise; then you will obtain the fruit of the sacrifice. Through stinginess regarding wealth, hell is created; that which was performed becomes as if unperformed. — *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*
Thus, in the primordial descent of the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses emerged from the Path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters,
brought down to the first sacred seat (*ādyapīṭha*) via the Path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six-Thousand [Verse Section],
in the *Kādi* division, in the *Svāminīmata* belonging to the Supreme Lord’s Command, contained within the venerable twenty-four thousand [verse] collection.
In the Avvākrama tradition, this is the bliss titled "The Determination of the Fire Offering."
The thirty-fifth bliss:
Śrīnātha said:
"I have heard the Tantra of Division (*Bhedatantra*) regarding the compendium of the Left (*vāma*) and the Right (*dakṣiṇa*)."
The division into triads exists within all [the systems], such as the Yāmalas and others.
There are many Nityatantras, Āgamas, Gahvaras, and so forth;
now I wish to hear how the Trika division of the Kula is.
"By the mere knowledge of which the division of the triad proceeds.
Śrīvakrā said: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Śambhu! You have now asked correctly."
Thus I shall speak to you out of devotion, O fair-faced one;
it has not been told by me to anyone else, yet out of love for you, I speak it now.
O Lord, even for me, this was previously spoken by the bodiless Īśa:
regarding that which is formless, void-like, and yet consists of the moving and the unmoving.
The infinite gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas; neither the moon nor the sun, nor the planets, nor the constellations; neither the hermitages nor the sages [could perceive it].
Neither I, O King, nor you, nor the hosts, nor the mountains and forests exist within that formless,
non-dual, and most terrible ocean.
From the state beyond bliss, the divine command has proceeded forth;
the power (śakti) has emerged by the will of Śiva, and she is indeed myself, Śivā.
This is the non-dual Śiva-Śakti; I have indeed become the Crooked One (Kuṭilā).
Because this was emitted by Him in three ways, my form has the shape of a triangle.
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Pervading this entire universe through its lower, upper, and middle parts,
the Goddess, who dwells on the path of Kula, contemplates the unmanifest state.
By him creation was revealed;
mutual affection arose.
The Unmanifest in the form of the Manifest,
and the Unmanifest-Unmanifest whose nature is Sound—
these two are the Command of the Lord; by them this world was created.
By his will, the entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is created.
The seats (pīṭha), sub-seats (upapīṭha), and fields (kṣetra); the moons, gods, and dānavas;
the hosts (gaṇa), nāgas, planets (graha), yakṣas, siddhas, gandharvas, and humans.
The mountains and the oceans were likewise fashioned;
having proceeded with three portions, the Goddess creates the three worlds in an instant.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—these three gods were created;
and the triad of seats (pīṭhatraya), O Lord of Gods, was likewise created in brief.
And where the Goddess of gods resides, both as a single entity and in manifold forms—
by her this entire world, consisting of the stationary and the moving, was created.
Performing creation and dissolution as a mere sport for diversion,
she creates the universe in three ways from her supreme city of Śṛṅgā.
Therein, the three gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara were born;
thus the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) was fashioned in the form of a triangle.
In the center of that is Kaulinī, who is accessible through easy means for the qualified practitioner;
in the eastern corner is Kāmākhya, and likewise Pūrṇagiri in the north.
Jālapīṭha is in the south, while Uḍḍiyāṇa is in the west;
there are many secondary seats (upapīṭhas), fields (kṣetras), and gathering places (saṃdohas) in manifold ways.
Established here in the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and in the center—
Śrīnātha said,
[this is] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
O Lord, you previously described the three seats (pīṭha) of the Goddess that are located outside.
"Now I wish to hear; tell it to me in brief.
The venerable Vakrā said:
"O Lord Bhairava, out of great affection, I shall tell it to you."
That which was not taught to anyone before has indeed been revealed to me by the Lord: that the city of the three seats resides within the body.
O Lord of Gods, the lords of the seats (pīṭhādhipas) and likewise the goddesses of the seats reside within the body; the three auspicious seats are situated in the lower, upper, and middle portions.
Existing in the form of a triangle, she is established in three locations:
namely, Kāmākhya in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, and Uḍḍiyāṇa in the Anāhata.
The nose is to be known as Pūrṇagiri; Ujjainī is situated at the point (bindu).
Śakti consists of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) and the third is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).
The goddesses, each established in their own place, are accompanied by their retinues;
the power of will (icchā-śakti) resides in Kāmākhya, while Uḍḍiyāna is the nature of action (kriyā).
O Lord of Gods, the third [power], Jñānaśakti, resides in Pūrṇapīṭha;
this division is proclaimed according to the differentiation of the six cakras and their foundations.
Endowed with the sixfold division beginning with Ḍa, Ra, La, Ka, Sa,
and Ha, those who do not know their distinctions are deluded by the darkness of ignorance.
Śrīnātha said:
"O Goddess, bestower of realization and knowledge, a great doubt has arisen and my heart is distressed; I do not know [the answer], O Goddess."
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
O Bhairavī, Goddess of the lords of gods, omniscient Supreme Sovereign!
How was the Goddess, together with her retinue, born within the three seats (pīṭhas)?
In the six cakras, there are six goddesses, distinguished as one and many;
divided into three ways, they are differentiated and established in six modes.
The illustrious Vakrā said:
"O Lord of the Gods, you have asked a most secret question;
O Śambhu, you must protect the Nāyikās born of the sacred seats."
Though she is one, she is divided into many; she abides both externally and internally.
The Goddess is established in every field and stationed in every sacred seat (pīṭha).
O God, listen to how your name and sign are to be understood:
though it is but one, it is pervasive and subtle; it is the unstruck rain of the *kalās*.
It is to be known as Candrapūrṇā, which rests upon that which transcends the fourth state (*turyātīta*).
White as snow, jasmine, and the moon, it is one-hundredth part of the tip of a hair.
And that Śravantī is proclaimed in the syllable Oṃ in her own form;
she is the measure situated below the letter *ha*, located in the middle of the position of the half-moon.
That which is called Uḍḍiyāṇa has emerged from the half-moon;
the Power, in its stainless form, has issued forth by the will of the Command.
Having reached the cavity of the palate by piercing the *suṣumnā* channel,
she fills [the space] on all sides through union with the submarine fire (*vāḍavānala*).
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
This is his supreme, divine seat, which is exceedingly difficult to attain.
From its vicinity, indeed, the straight line has arisen, facing downwards.
Drawing everything toward herself, she is the soul of all, formidable with garlands of flames;
having reached the unstruck state (*anāhata*), she is that which causes the swan to blossom.
She is known as Jvālāmukhī in the sacred seat named Jāla;
she is the digit (kalā) in the form of Time, Kākinī, whose body is that of a swan (haṃsa).
Filled with jewels, great blue in color, having the form of the full moon,
wearing divine yellow garments, she is the serpent Kuṇḍalī who lies asleep.
Agitating the entire world, she herself resides at Pūrṇapīṭha;
situated in the center of the Maṇinābhi, her form is triangular in shape.
Resembling a Kadamba bud, she is Bhairavī of knowledge and realization.
That goddess, self-arisen, is endowed with the letters beginning with A and the rest.
That [syllable] beginning with the letter *tha* is divided; that stone is pure and perfected.
She is the mother of all goddesses, including gods, asuras, and humans.
But when she has arisen in the realm of desire and form, she is the passionate one who removes impurity;
the six seats have been fully described, so now hear likewise of the six wheels.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: The first wheel is the Foundation (ādhāra), provided with four petals;
the deity there is the Ḍākinī named Siddhakoṭīśvara.
The second is the Svādhiṣṭhāna, endowed with six petals;
there the Lord, the supreme among millions of mudrās, and Rākinī manifest.
The third [center] has ten petals and is filled with jewels due to its cessation;
its lord is Mantrakoṭīśvara, and its mother is Lākinī.
The fourth wheel has twelve spokes and is known by the name Anāhata;
there resides Vidyākoṭīśvara, accompanied by Kākinī.
The fifth is named Viśuddha, and it is beautiful with sixteen spokes.
O Lord Samayakoṭīśvara, Sākī is the embodiment of consciousness.
The two words *śiva* and *śakti* constitute the sixth *āja* by their very nature; there, the syllable *hā* is the Lord of the Point (*bindu*), whose form is the Command (*ājñā*).
Renowned as Haṃseśvarī, she is the agent of both creation and dissolution;
though one, all-pervasive, and subtle, she stands oriented toward the act of creation.
Above that, however, the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) emerges with three divisions:
the power of will (icchāśakti), the power of action (kriyāśakti), and the power of knowledge as the third.
The power of will (icchā-śakti) is on the left, while the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is on the right;
the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), which follows divine knowledge, is between the two.
The Goddess, abiding in the state of Raudrī, is called Rudra-śakti;
there, O God, the three seats (pīṭhas) are established as supreme.
On the left is the one called Kāmarūpa, and Pūrṇagiri is on the right;
Uḍḍiyāṇa is between those two, while Ujjainī is situated at the Bindu.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—these are proclaimed by name;
from them the nine Śaktis were born, as well as the Mothers beginning with Brahmāṇī.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
Śrīnātha said: "The ninefold division of energies, as well as the tetrad beginning with Jayā..."
She who is the eleventh of the Rudras, and she who is Rudrāṇī, the Great Goddess Maheśvarī.
Why then has this been stated again? You have led me astray with such detail. Be gracious, O Goddess of the lords of gods, O you known as Śrī Kujā, [explain] according to the sequence.
How is it that the Goddess, though she is one, is established through manifold divisions?
How is her retinue? Be gracious and tell me.
The venerable Vakrā said:
"I shall speak to you, being well-pleased, of the most excellent questions and various statements; listen attentively with a focused mind."
Listen, O Lord, I shall explain its divisions as they truly exist;
O Supreme Lord, all these are indeed its divisions.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—thus she is established in a threefold manner.
Now, hear again how these divisions of hers are situated.
The command (ājñā) which resides in the place of the bindu, situated above the half-moon,
is the digit (kalā) that abides as the bindu for all beings and rains down nectar.
At the end it stands in the form of light, and likewise above that in the form of a star;
above that is the mouth of the Guru, which is called the Unborn and is free from all affliction.
O God, situated at the end of Īśvara is the eternal, auspicious, and immutable [state];
from that, the ninefold cage of the body was born for the Navātman.
Likewise, O beloved, the supreme Śakti has arisen; she is established in nine states, is the tenfold cause of Yoga, and manifests as a twofold division.
The entire universe, both external and internal, is bound in three ways;
both of those have come under the sway of Manmatha and have emerged from the *dvādaśānta*.
Having attained the state of Raudrī through that very sequence,
she resides in the city of the support of the *kanda* and is known as the one who causes trembling and possession.
The company is known as Raudrī; Ghūrmaṇī is of the nature of arising;
she is called Ekāṅganartanī, Aśrupātī, and Kuraṅgī.
Siṃhaśabdī and Pulindī are proclaimed as the eleventh;
these indeed reside in the portion of Rudra and attain dissolution at the end of the twelve.
"The sequence of the sacred seats (pīṭhakrama) has been declared by means of the triad beginning with Vāmā.
Śrī Bhairava said: "Am I of little intelligence? Do you consider me to be almost like a dullard?"
"O Goddess, why do you cause me to wander, and for what purpose, O Sovereign of the Gods?
I am all-pervading and the agent, yet I remain subject to the limit of your command."
"Therefore, O Goddess, out of compassion, speak the knowledge of great exaltation.
Śrīvakrā said:
"Excellent, excellent, O fortunate one, you who are a vessel for unfailing knowledge!"
I shall speak without doubt, O beloved, that secret and hidden Kaulinī doctrine which destroys delusion regarding knowledge and is proclaimed through mantras.
That which has not been told to anyone, that I shall now relate to you:
O God, in the first age, in the beginning, there was the emergence of the Divine Command within the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Having arisen there, that goddess took on a form shaped like a sprout;
by her divine command, she performed austerities with her senses subdued.
Then, having assumed a hunchbacked form, crooked and clad in rags,
I became threefold in nature and reached the state of old age.
The union of Śiva and Śakti is proclaimed as the all-pervasive Śāmbhava state.
Śakti is manifested on the left, while Śiva is traditionally held to be on the right;
likewise, Brahmāṇī is on the left and Raudrī is on the right.
It is proclaimed as being present in all living beings in the form of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* [nādīs].
The Moon is born from the left,
and the Sun is indeed born from Raudrī;
O fair-faced one, the entire world is divided into two, interwoven like warp and woof.
But it shall be explained as divided into three types; listen now.
O Lord of the World, the assembly of beings, both moving and unmoving, is divided in three ways.
Moving through the course of the Suṣumnā, she is renowned by the name Vicitrā;
she is variegated by the threefold nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—the Goddess is established in three ways;
she is eternally absorbed at the end of Puṣkara, resting upon the station of the Great Path.
She is renowned by the name Śivā, always absorbed in Śiva;
O God, I shall now describe another way in which she is established through her divisions.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Śivā— also known as Anāmayā—
are the threefold powers (śaktis) such as Will (icchā) and the rest, which arise from the qualities (guṇas) beginning with Sattva.
In this very manner, O God, he who consists of three aspects is established;
now the supreme fourfold division is being proclaimed.
O Kuleśvara, that beloved of yours who is indeed divided by the distinctions of the hollows and so forth must be known by the Kaulika alone as the four within the Kula.
By way of the left and right channels, she is remembered as fourfold and eightfold;
Vāmā and the goddess Jayā are on the left, and likewise Vijayā is on the right.
Through these very divisions, this [tradition] is indeed eightfold;
furthermore, the eighteen-fold lineage emerged from the command of Unmanā.
Endowed with four modes, five, six, and threefold in nature—
this very [system] has been proclaimed by me as the arising of the eighteen-fold sequence.
O God of beautiful countenance, through the division of the moon and sun and their conjunction on the left and right, there is rising and setting in four ways.
Furthermore, through the application of emanation and the arising of the five Brahmās,
there are five states belonging to the Kula-born, known by the names beginning with Vimalā.
Thus, indeed, I exist as the source of the world in fivefold form;
listen, O God, for I shall proclaim the supreme teaching that follows in six ways.

I shall tell you that which has not been told to anyone; O Lord of Gods, in former times I heard it from the mouth of Himavat. In the Kumārikā-khaṇḍa, I have arisen as sixfold, and in three ways I take the form of a *śṛṅgāṭa*.
The sacred seats (pīṭhas) have been fully described to you in their various divisions, O beloved.
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā as the third—
these three goddesses are to be known as the triad of seats (pīṭha).
From these goddesses, each pair has arisen;
indeed, through a sixfold division, they are established within the six cakras.
Two by two, they are renowned as being born upon the sacred seats (pīṭhas), the ornaments of their families;
I shall state their names according to the seats upon which they reside.
Hākinī and Śākinī have emerged from Oḍḍiyāṇa;
Kākinī and Lākinī have emerged from Pūrṇagiri.
Rākinī and Ḍākinī emerged from Kāmarūpa;
thus were the goddesses born, capable of both restraint and grace.
In every land, there exist those renowned in the teachings of the Siddhas;
they are seven times seven oceans [in number], both born of lineage (*kulaja*) and born together (*sahaja*).
These are the *khecarī*, the *bhūcarī*, and likewise the *sahajā* and the *kulajā*.
But the retinue of the Lord of Gods consists of many forms and types:
the four groups beginning with Vāmā, those four who have Śiva as their foundation,
the sixty-four goddesses, and the thirty-two Prajātikās.
These are endowed with sixteen digits; there are twelve born of the Sun,
eight goddesses born of the Kula, as well as a group of four and a group of three.

Indeed, O Lord of Gods, all this has thus emerged from the venerable Kubjā. In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*, in the primordial descent of the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses that has issued forth on the path of Meru,

exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primary seat (*ādyapīṭha*) on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimalaṣaṭka*).

In the *Kādibheda*, within the *Ājñāpārameśvara* of the *Svāminīmata*, in the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the *Avvākrama*, in the description of the authority over the emanation of the *Trikabhedas*, this is the bliss named the Arising of the Sequence (*Kramodaya*).
Śrīnātha said:
"O Maheśvarī, all of this has been understood by me through your grace;
now I wish to hear how the knowledge of the ritual practice (anuṣṭhāna) comes to be."
O Goddess, bestower of enjoyment and liberation, ground of higher realization and knowledge,
I wish to hear about Nirvāṇa, the unmanifest, and that which is both supreme and non-supreme.
The venerable Vakrā said: "Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom, you who are capable of crossing over saṃsāra! This is the thirty-sixth bliss."
I shall speak, without doubt, so that the command of Nirvāṇa may be realized.
I shall explain the supreme and inferior reality; listen, O lotus-faced one, according to the path of the conduct of the observance (samaya), as it has come down from the mouth of the Guru.
The reality that has passed from ear to ear is eternally arisen and undivided;
it is the perpetually arisen great bliss, uninterrupted and continuous.
O God, that which bestows all bliss upon practitioners desiring accomplishment is situated within the mouth of the Guru; this scripture is merely a brief summary of it.
O mind, you who are always of the nature of constant practice, you are eternally one; thus you are that self-consciousness by which the person is perceived as an object of thought.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
He whose command is full, who is eternally blissful, independent, and free from doubt;
he who moves within the Kula as partless—he has neither sleep, nor hunger, nor thirst.
There is neither mind nor perception, and he who possesses the self is always dispassionate;
there is neither exertion nor delight, and likewise neither cold nor heat.
He does not perceive anything at all, such as pleasure or pain,
nor does he ever experience singing, laughter, or the playing of musical instruments.
Running and leaping also proceed according to one's own will;
such various types of actions occur in whatever manner they may.
In that very way, one should not fear; one should play according to one's own will.
Thus, O Supreme Bliss, the Transmental (*unmanā*) is ever-arisen.
O God Bhairava, this state of yours is said to be difficult to attain;
those bound souls (paśus) who are excluded from divine knowledge will mock it, just as a fool mocks the path of the scriptures, or as one might mock the pleasure of a maiden.
In that same way, those who mock the path of yoga do not find reality.
The path of the Vedas is described in one way, that which is known through the Āgamas in another,
the Kaulika path in yet another, and the ultimate reality in still another.
Therefore, one should indeed abandon delusion and practice the non-conceptual state;
one is oneself the Guru, oneself the disciple, oneself the Shakti, and oneself Shiva.
Being himself gross, himself subtle, and himself both the higher and the lower,
one whose self is peaceful should indeed sustain the higher and the lower within his own body.

Those by whom [the state] ending with Unmanā has been attained are the Siddhas of the Śākta and Śāmbhava [traditions]. However, on this earth, the propitiation of all of them is performed within the Maṇḍala.
One should not leave the mandala empty of the lineage of Gurus, Siddhas, and Ācāryas, nor of Vṛkṣanātha within the teaching, if one desires accomplishment for oneself.
When the deluded soul, out of greed, has emptied the mandala of the Guru,
then whence can he have the Command (ājñā), and whence the Kaulika realization?
Deceitful, treacherous, and cruel, those who revile the yoginīs have gone to a terrible hell and are bound within the Great Belly.
Fourteen eons, difficult to traverse and most terrible, have passed;
having offered the food-offering (piṇḍa) endowed with great devotion, his mind became serene.
One who is destitute of wealth must again serve the Guru like a slave;
the Supreme Power, arising from pure being, is established within the center of the body.
Having abandoned the body, hear this supreme, subtle form of the Command;
always contemplate the meditation on reality, the great arising of the Yoginīs.
And Kubjikā is the supreme goddess who brings about immediate realization;
one should pay homage to the supreme goddess, whose nature is the sustaining of Bhairava.
I pay homage to her who is accompanied by Bhairava, the bestower of the accomplishment of the Command,
to Yogeśī, Siddhamātṛ, Khecarī, and likewise Bhūcarī.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Having paid homage to Kuṭilā and meditated upon her sandals at the head,
one should commence the supreme yoga after bowing to the sandals of the Guru.
Situated in the center of the *ādhāra-cakra*, between the moon, the sun, and the fire,
is the circle of fire in the middle, having the form of the flame of a pure lamp.
The yogi begins the meditation; before long, he shall become a partaker of accomplishment, [visualizing it] resembling a circle of lightning and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Resembling molten gold, arising from consciousness in the form of flames,
it fills the entire universe with its rays as far as the realm of Brahmā.
Having fixed the mind within that center and become firm,
the wise one should meditate upon the most wonderful yoga, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
Before long, one attains accomplishment and achieves whatever one desires by will.
Possession occurs for that person, evidenced by trembling, paralysis, and so forth;
whirling, shaking, paralysis, and great gyrating set in.
He too shall be constantly possessed by the assembly of yoginīs.
As well as the past and the future, entering another's body,
moving an image, causing explosions, and likewise the paralyzing of an army.
He may travel to great foreign lands as far as the ocean-bound earth;
he performs all actions, whether they ought to be done or not, like one who has attained spiritual perfection.
When the self has attained the state of reality, it acts; of this there is no doubt.
This great knowledge is difficult to obtain and should not be given to just anyone.
One should bestow it upon a disciple who is devoted to the guru and possesses faith.
They are always devoted to the Kādyāgama, truthful, and firm in their vows.
To them this knowledge, difficult even for the gods to attain, should be given. O God, this which pertains to the ground of the Root Chakra has been told to you in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Listen, O Lord, Master of the World, to another definitive teaching on knowledge:
that which resides in the center of one's own *adhicakra*, pervaded by both [the individual and the universal].
The Kuṇḍalinī, who is the supreme power (parā śakti), resides in the Maṇipūra;
like a sleeping serpent, O Goddess of Gods, she has the form of a coil.
The Goddess Mahāmudrā always awakens those who are unawakened;
having fixed the mind right there, one should strike it with the staff of the vital breath.
There is no doubt that one trembles and experiences horripilation again and again;
by means of this yoga of practice, [one attains] a radiance equal to a ruby.
Through meditation, the yogi attains the power of moving through the sky; of this there is no doubt.
[He perceives] that which has the shape of a *kadamba* flower bud, adorned with ten million points (*bindu*).
One of steady mind should meditate on that reality residing within the Śakti-sūtra;
having risen from the locus of the navel, cause it to dissolve into the heart.
The yogi should draw [the breath] from the heart and deposit it in the pit of the throat;
having flooded the uvula, he should slowly drink the nectar of knowledge.
Above that, one should take refuge in the Brahma-randhra, the upward-reaching sky;
there, O Lord of Gods, one experiences a supreme, cool touch that bestows yoga.
Returning again, O Lord of Gods, bring about dissolution in Maṇipūrṇa;
this is the yoga for the perception of touch, which effects the resolution of the knot at the navel.
Bound by Śiva and Śakti, he abides in the supreme yoga;
and through the practice of these very states, he proceeds to Sadāśiva.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Moving through the divisions of below and above in the form of vital breath (prāṇa),
that energy (śakti) is declared to be supreme, difficult to attain even for the gods.
Thus, O Lord, has this yoga, which is most difficult to attain, been explained to you;
it must not be given to those who are not devoted, nor to those who harbor hatred for the samaya.
He was a speaker of truth and firm in his vows toward those who were true devotees, excellent disciples,
those who offered him all their possessions, and those who longed for the knowledge of reality.
This supreme heart-essence of knowledge should be given to those yogins;
however, he who would speak of it otherwise would become the most wicked of sinners.
Śrīnātha said: Śrīvakrā said:
"I have heard the true nature of reality, the definitive teaching on Maṇipūrṇa."
Now I wish to hear about the supreme, unstruck sound of yoga.
Listen with a single-minded focus, O Lord, to that which is difficult to attain—the true essence of gnosis.
That which is the all-pervading *haṃsa*, O God, the carrier within the heart, certainly reaches the manifest, eternal state; that *ātman* is the *haṃsa*, it is the *pudgala*.
The stainless Śiva is all-pervasive, the sustainer of the bodies of embodied beings.
O Śrīkaṇṭha, what is the use of speaking at length? His names are indeed innumerable, numbering in the tens of millions;
I shall describe his true nature so that practitioners may realize it.
Having the appearance of a firefly or lightning, with the luster of pure crystal,
that supreme reality flashes forth, gladdened by the movement of power (śakti).
Seated in the center of the lotus-throne of the heart, having dissolved into the tip of the lotus,
the swan— the Lord Sadāśiva— resounds "Haṃsa, Haṃsa."
It strikes with the staff of power (śakti-daṇḍa) by way of the nature of inhalation and exhalation;
because it is struck by power (śakti), it is therefore called "Unstruck" (anāhata).
This is from the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Struck by the staff of power, it produces ten kinds of sound:
first the sound "ciṇi," and secondly "ciñciṇi."
The third is the long-lasting sound, while the fourth is the sound of a conch;
the fifth is the resonance of stringed instruments, and likewise the sixth is the sound of the flute.
The seventh is called the sound of bronze cymbals, the eighth is like the roar of clouds,
the ninth is the sound of a conflagration, and the tenth is the resonance of a drum.
O fortunate one, by abandoning the nine syllables and knowing that tenth which bestows liberation, one shall attain perfection before long.
One should constantly meditate and recite with pure mental flowers endowed with dhyāna; then, O God, one shall soon obtain realization.
Śrīnātha said:
"The scriptures are so extensive that they cannot be fully mastered;
yet what you have spoken, O Great Goddess, known as the Haṃsa, is exceedingly difficult to attain."
"In truth, this has not been understood by me; tell it to me in its pure form.
The venerable Vakrā said: "Listen, O Lord of great wisdom, to the definitive teaching on pure gnosis."
One should meditate upon the eternal Haṃsa situated in the center of the seat of the heart-lotus,
established in the form of a star, shaped like a cluster of Kadamba flowers.
One should meditate [on him] with a network of one's own rays, possessing the splendor of ten thousand suns;
like a lamp situated in a windless place, remaining steady and motionless, having made the mind immovable, [one should contemplate him] blazing with intensely radiant flames.
For one who practices in this manner, accomplishment is not far off:
the power of hearing from afar, the knowledge of others' bodies, entering another's body,
shattering statues, verbal mastery, and likewise the paralyzing of armies.
A divine possession shall arise, and accomplishment is desired before long.
This knowledge, O God, which is extremely difficult to attain, has been told to you in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
This pure [teaching] brings immediate accomplishment; what else do you wish to ask?
It is the Unstruck, the Nameless, O Śrīnātha, who takes the form of a swan.
"The union of Śiva and Śakti must be known by those who desire accomplishment.
Śrīnātha said:
"I have heard the true nature of reality, which is pure, stainless, and immaculate."
"Furthermore, I wish to hear about that which is pure from the pure, both supreme and non-supreme.
The venerable Vakrā said: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Śambhu! Out of a desire for the welfare of the Kaulas,"
You inquire about the supreme reality, the consciousness that is the highest nectar.
Brahmā and the others, all the asuras, the siddhas, and the supreme yogis— having fully accomplished this knowledge, they have attained the state of immortality.
Bring about dissolution in the eternal, supreme, and divine place at the throat.
The eternal yoga, the supreme state of immortalization, is attained—
that power whose essence is Rudra, which has gone to dissolution at the end of the twelve.
O God, one should meditate upon that [deity] with the mind as steady as the flame of a lamp;
by means of that very [meditation], the Self itself [perceives] the Lord, the Sovereign, within the wheel of the heart.
O God, one attains *sāvitrī* even before long; it is not otherwise.
O Lord, listen to the supreme division, the unsurpassed knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) from the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
Śiva, the innate, three-eyed one, seated in the center of the lotus-throne of the heart,
mounted upon the solar disc, and as pure as clear crystal.
It revolves at the edge of the wheel, moving individually upon each petal;
thus the yogi practices for six months, O Three-eyed One.
Before long, the unbroken Great Pervasion (mahāvyāpti) is accomplished for him;
having performed the contraction of the tongue, he should meditate until the limit of the "āvahala" is reached.
The yogi who practices in this manner becomes free from all diseases;
having pierced him with the spear of power (śakti-śūla), he should drink the supreme nectar.
The yogi shall possess a divine body and become beloved by the *khecarīs*;
whatever desires he may long for, whether they be in heaven or upon the earth, [he shall attain them].
The lord of yogis attains each of those states before long; there is no doubt about this.
O God, I have thus explained to you this realization which is like nectar.
"What else do you ask, O Lord? I shall tell you that very thing.
Śrīnātha said:
"O Mother of the Gaṇas, by your grace I have heard the Pure Principle (śuddhatattva)."
"Now I wish to hear the reality of the Command (*ājñātattva*), which is very difficult to attain.
The venerable Vakrā said: "O Śambhu, you have asked clearly; [I shall explain] the supreme knowledge whose nature is that which is to be known (*jñeya*)."
I shall speak without doubt of the great arising of the realized reality,
which consists of Bhairava— the light of the digits of Nāda and Bindu, and bliss. (The Section on the Virgin)
When all of them have entered the sequence of the six cakras at the station of Dhruva,
the cage of the body trembles by the mere recollection of these.
Between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, in the midst of the enclosure of the moon and sun,
the yogin situated therein should contemplate that Raudrikā—
Rudrāṇī in her fierce form, the Raudrī who has arisen from the dissolution of *kalā*.
Raudrī, possessing the brilliance of a thousand fires, [pierces] with the probe of knowledge.
Emerging from the aperture of form, possessing a radiance equal to the fire of time,
she utters the supreme sound, which is beyond the written and the nameless.
Raising [the breath] from the cavity of the palate, she drinks the supreme nectar;
flowing as *nāda* and *bindu*, she takes the form of the submarine fire (*vāḍavānala*).
In the Kali age, she has arisen at the station of the Command (ājñā) with a brilliantly radiant luster;
there, within the wheel, resides the infinite Śakti known as Śāntā, clothed in pure raiment.
Once the station of the Command has been attained, one may perform whatever action one desires.
By means of movement, one should cause all beings—including gods, asuras, and humans—to move.
The yogi, with his mind fixed upon that [state], should pierce Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Rudra, along with the mountains, forests, and groves, at the station of Dhruva.
In that place is a great wheel, perfectly circular with thirty-two spokes,
possessing a brilliance equal to ten thousand suns and a radiance like ten million moons.
Shining with the brilliance of ten million or a hundred million fires and filled with garlands of flames,
the Goddess resides there together with Bhairava.
Where the Goddess is established in the form of Ādinātha,
that is proclaimed as the Great Wheel (Mahācakra), which is designated as the Command (Ājñā).
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Śrīnātha, Bhairavī, Śāntā, Kālikā, and she who is Vakrikā; Bhīmā, Khageśī, Citrā, Vicitrā, and Kuṭilānanā.
Nandā, Bhadrā, the one named Jayantī, Vijayā, Aparājitā,
Mohanī, Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, Hemā, Kūṣmāṇḍī, and Carcikā.
Taraṅgā, Nirmalā, Caṇḍā, Vidyujjihvā, Bhayāvahā,
Śavarī, Śāvarī, Śarvarī, and Pulindikā.
"Nityaklinnā and Suraktā are the deities within the various sequences;
they are established in the great wheel of thirty-two spokes within the sphere of space."
Whether with form or formless, one should recollect the deities of the wheels;
for him who knows these infinite natures, the command possesses a flashing radiance.
The power Vakrā is known as Virūpā, the one called Kūṭā, the supreme and imperishable;
expanding through Śakti, she is the tranquil one, the radiant one whose face is the Bhaga.
One should repeatedly contemplate the Kulakaulinī in the great wheel at the station of the command (ājñā), which repeatedly inflames all things with the flame of reality.
At that very moment, he achieves fame in the Śrīkrama within the abode of Varuṇa;
[he perceives] the abandonment of land, the agitation of cities, and the signs of departure from one's dwelling,
as well as the past, the future, the present, and the supreme and the non-supreme.
And it produces the cognition of hearing from a distance according to one's wish.
O Śambhu, this supreme [teaching], which is more essential than the essence itself, has been previously told to you;

it brings about the Great Pervasion, consists of six peaks, and is sixfold in nature. This yoga of the support and the supported should be practiced within the division of the Six Groups (*ṣaṭkabheda*) in the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
Through the renunciation of the six, liberation occurs in the seventh stage by means of the powers of the unchanging and the changing.
The practice of the sequence of mantra and vidyā has emerged from the end of the seven;
at the end of the seventh, there is dissolution therein, together with the organs of action.
Just as the vital winds (*vāta*) residing within the body formerly impel the mind and the limbs,
so too does that power (*śakti*), which is both supreme and non-supreme (*parāparā*), reside within the body.
She is one, yet she exists through manifold divisions; she is that very one with six faces.
She is the bliss of Bhairava, the form of the mind, and the state beyond the mind (Manonmanā).
The Goddess of the gods delights there in the multitude of sense-objects and families,
O Bhairava, as long as the Śrīmata has not been heard according to the division of the lineages;
as long as there is no compassion from the Guru, how can there be accomplishment in the Kula?
Therefore, one should abandon everything else and take refuge in the wheel of command (ājñācakra).
By remembering [this], the yogi is liberated from the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra,
even from the most terrible crimes of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, or killing a woman.
At that very moment, the yogi is liberated through the practice of the sequence of the six cakras.
The yoginīs— both those dwelling in non-divine and divine bodies, as well as the sahajā and kulajā— become pleased with him, and the yogis also attain accomplishment.
Thus, this transmission of the command is not to be given to just anyone.
Now, if [the mantra] is given through negligence, one is purified by one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajāpa*).

Thus, in the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*, in the introduction to the Great Sacrifice (*mahāmanthānabhairavayajña*) of the lineage (*anvaya*), which consists of seventy million verses and has emerged from the Path of Meru.

In the [text] exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the first seat (*ādyapīṭha*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimalaṣaṭka*), in the *Kādibheda*,

in the *Svāminīmata* which is the supreme command of the Lord, in the description of the chapter on the knowledge of consciousness within the glorious *Caturviṃśatsahasra*, this is the bliss named the Arising of the Sequence (*kramodaya*).
Śrīnātha said: O Bhairavī, by your grace, the initiation (dīkṣā) arising from the Kula has been understood,
as well as the ritual procedure for the sacrificial fire-pit (homakuṇḍa) and the instruction according to its proper sequence.

"Now I wish to hear the characteristics of the conduct of the observance (samayācāra). The venerable Vakrā said: [I shall explain] the proper conduct for disciples as it is enjoined by the scriptures."
O Lord of Gods, listen now to all that in due order.
[This is] the thirty-seventh bliss: formerly, after many births, the exhaustion of one's own karma was attained.
Through initiation, perfection is attained; O Bhava, it is the supreme goal.
Yet for one who has been initiated, if the bond of karma is not swiftly severed, [perfection does not follow].
"He possesses neither great compassion nor adherence to the conduct of the samaya;
yet, having obtained the guru’s great compassion, he becomes a protector of the conduct of the samaya."
"One is liberated from the bonds of karma"—this is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Even one who has been purified by initiation is [liberated] despite having violated the rules of conduct.
He is not liberated from his bonds if he does not possess proper conduct;
he should constantly honor the maṇḍala of the Guru with perfumes, incense, unbroken rice grains, and other offerings.
One should perform the purification of the maṇḍala preceded by the worship of the Guru and the deity;
first, having worshipped the book in a solitary and secluded place— this is from the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
One should listen to the Kula-āgama conjoined with that instruction;
and having heard the meaning of the scriptural teaching, one should honor the guru like a servant.
And the disciple who desires liberation must observe the rules of conduct;
he should be illustrious, a knower of the scriptures, and born of a noble family.
One should perform the eight-limbed prostration in the presence of a Guru who knows reality;
excessive laughter, haughtiness, and stretching out the limbs in a playful manner [are to be avoided].
One should not engage in amusement, idle chatter, or debate in the presence of the guru; nor should one blow the nose, make fraudulent sounds, or clean the teeth.
One should not assume a cross-legged posture at will in the presence of the Guru;
nor should one perform an improper act that is contrary to the rules, even if it has not been explicitly forbidden by the Guru.
For the guru alone knows [the truth]; he himself should deliberate upon the tantra, as well as the seat, the bed, the parasol, the ornaments, and the vehicle.
One who desires accomplishment should not treat the guru with indifference;
for these are the guru’s seat, his cloth, his meditation band, and his sandals.
Indeed, the bowl, the rosary, the loincloth garment,
the weapon, the scripture, the great secret, and whatever divine implements there may be—
Endowed with devotion, they should be worshipped by you and protected with great effort;
[offer] perfumes, incense, betel, and whatever food, drink, and so forth there may be.
Having offered everything to the Guru, it should be received according to his instruction.
Thus, having performed devotion to the Guru, the disciple becomes one whose devotion is unwavering. *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
He shall obtain the compassion of the Guru, and the consecration is performed;
by receiving the Guru’s command, the disciple’s own authority constantly proceeds.

One who constantly desires spiritual accomplishment moves about in the world according to their own will; if this Caryāvadhūta should move through the sacred seats (pīṭha) and fields (kṣetra) in due order, [he attains success].
The Lord of Yogis, desiring spiritual accomplishment, should take up a skull-bowl along with its accessories for the purpose of eating, on account of the intensity of his observance of the command.
The lord of yogis should always dwell eternally in an empty temple,
regarding friend and foe, pleasure and pain, the desirable and the undesirable, and the auspicious and the inauspicious as equal.
Likewise, honor and dishonor, as well as blame and praise;
stone and gold are equal to him, and vegetables are like rice and boiled grain.
If a yogin abides in equanimity while desiring accomplishment,
he may at times be a priest, at times an actor, and at times a renunciant man.
Assuming various forms, the yogin should wander upon the surface of the earth;
he should possess devotion toward the guru, as well as toward his elders and the family tradition.
One should always worship the Yoginīs and the Kumārīs with devotion,
[avoiding] greed, delusion, laziness, violation of the command, and possessiveness.
One who desires spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*) should not harbor greed or attachment to sense objects.
[He should revere] the mantra, the rudrākṣa rosary, the sandals, the circle of gurus (*gurumaṇḍala*),
the mirror, as well as the *liṅga*, the ritual gestures (*mudrā*), and the *Kulāgama*.
And likewise, one should not bestow the knowledge of Śavarī upon just anyone.
One should always destroy these: passion, hatred, egoism, slander accompanied by hypocrisy, anger, greed, and likewise laziness.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
one should never in any way disparage the conventional conduct of others, the assembly of Kumārīs and Yoginīs, the substances of accomplishment, or the sacred seats (pīṭhas).
The lineage of the conduct of the Yoginīs and Siddhas, the Kula tradition transmitted through succession,
the unseen and unprecedented secret scripture, and the deity itself.
One should offer praise to all and avoid treachery against one's guru; one should also avoid gambling, sorcery, and the slaughter or restraint of animals.
A family practitioner of yoga should not watch a fight between wrestlers and cocks, nor a naked girl with exposed breasts, nor the genitals of a woman, nor animal play.
One should not feel disgust toward a fool, one afflicted with leprosy, one lacking limbs, one who is deaf, or even one who is blind;
nor should one feel disgust toward the smell of flesh, feces, or urine, nor likewise toward liquor.
Trees, shrubs, creepers, vines, grasses, and all other stationary plants should not be uprooted, nor should they be cut, nor pierced, nor should one cause them any injury.
Whatever there may be— scents, flowers, and so forth, as well as the substances of the Yoginīs—
and whatever is obtained unasked, with that one should worship the Kula tradition.
By means of this practice, the yogi intent on accomplishment should always worship the sandals of the Guru with the flowers of mindfulness.
One who desires spiritual accomplishment should not revile the school of Kauṭilya, nor the assembly for debate, nor the gathering of cattle out of envy, nor wooden or stone deities.
One should not engage in worldly affairs, and especially not in assemblies of cattle;
one should avoid the third, the drinking assembly—these three are indeed sins.
One should always attend assemblies of the lineage, and especially assemblies concerning the sacred succession.
And the third is the sacrificial assembly; one should protect these three.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
A wise man should not consume poison, nor should he play with serpents;
one who desires spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*) should not perform acts of extreme recklessness.

One should not dwell upon the ways of women, nor upon violence, nor upon sense-objects that transcend the self; having attained this, one should avoid what is to be abandoned, and therefore one should be a master of the senses.
A lord of yogis should always reside in the house of a Prajāpati or among Vaiśyas.
Wherever there is cultivation, let it proceed right there.
One who desires unbroken success must not obstruct the mind;
one should constantly wander the earth following the path of non-dual conduct.
"Do not touch me! I am full of faults"—thus people would always say. A lord of yogins desiring accomplishment should wander for alms among the eight families;
he must not utter the word "Rere," nor likewise the word "Hehe."
One should not utter the word "Gaurī" and then perform [the rite] for Kālikā.
One who observes the samaya should not utter the word "khañjī," nor likewise the word "kumārikā. One should not practice [in such a manner].
One should not say "Śākinī," nor should one utter "Sehārī," nor indeed should one utter it.
One who desires accomplishment in the teaching should not practice the village-dharma;
namely, [the rites involving] a ewe, a hen, a peahen, a goose, and likewise a sow.
The buffalo, the owl, the yak, the vulture,
the goat, the doe, and likewise the bird— these and other living beings are also of the feminine gender.
Having been approached by them, I have forbidden it:
"I shall not eat meat, nor even [consume] the practitioner or the preceptor."
O lady of beautiful hips, one should never revile those who are worthy of worship and salutation:
the fisherman, the ball-player, the barbarian, the banner-bearer, the butcher, and the soldier.
One who is misshapen, deformed, impotent, or insane, as well as one who is diseased;
a wrestler, a bard, one rich in treasure, a craftsman, or a leather-worker.
One should never show contempt, nor should one act with arrogance by means of the syllable *hūṃ*.
In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:
one must never harbor enmity, nor should one engage in reckless violence.
The ritual bed should be prepared at a solitary tree, a crossroads, a field-site, or a cremation ground; however, one should not perform a lowly rite (*kṣudrakarman*) in such places.
One should sleep in a secluded place and should not cause physical distress;
[one should do so] in a temple, on a riverbank, or amidst ashes and cow dung.
One should not engage in lying down together, nor in sexual intercourse with another's wife; one must not speak of one's own kinsmen’s wives, especially within one's own circle.
The leg of a bed, a millstone, a full water-jar,
likewise a grinding stone, a mortar, a hearth, a pestle, and a threshold.
O beloved, one should never touch with the foot, nor ever step over, a bow, a shield, a sword, or any other weapons.
O handsome one, one should not eat food at an improper time, nor with the left hand;
one should not give [food] with the left hand, but should give it with the right hand.
O Bhairava, one should receive what is given by another with the left hand;
one should not give medicine, nor should one perform the recitation of mantras or the protection of vidyās.
One should not engage in idle chatter with one another regarding the Śiva scriptures, nor should one ever find fault with the Śiva scriptures; rather, one should always preserve them.
O Lord, your own teaching must be heard with diligent effort;
it should always be protected and worshipped, for it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should never speak what is unspeakable, nor should one perform anything contradictory;
