one should address all places of Rudra as being preceded by "Śrī."
One should utter the name of the Guru preceded by "Śrī" and followed by "namaskāra";
one should not undertake pilgrimages, but should practice yoga.
One should not speak excessively; one should keep in mind the words of the Guru. Taking up the unmanifested *liṅga*, one should never make it manifest. (From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
O Lord of Gods, those born of the Kula who desire to attain spiritual perfection and liberation must not share a meal of sacrificial oblation (caru) in one place with practitioners of Tantra.
One should not criticize the actions of others, whether they be compassionate or contemptible;
nor should one share a single vessel even with the Lord of the Family himself.
The mantras turn away and obstacles arise at every step;
therefore, with every effort, one should not use a single vessel.
The maṇḍala of the Guru should be prepared before the scripture and in the presence of the Guru;
having worshipped the Śrīkrama located upon the head, it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus, in the primordial descent (*ādyāvatāra*) of the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) measuring seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the first seat (*ādyāpīṭha*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the pure determination of the six groups (*ṣaṭkanirṇaya*),
in the division beginning with *ka*, in the supreme command of the Lord (*ājñāpārameśvara*), in the *Svāminīmata* accompanied by the venerable twenty-four thousand [verses].
This is the bliss named Kramodaya, within the description of the conduct of the samaya, in the division beginning with *ka* spoken by Abbākrama.
Śrīnātha said:
I have not heard what the root of the lineage is;
tell me the root of the *kula*, which is the instruction of the *kulāmnāya*.
Tell me, O Supreme Goddess, the great power of the Kula-yoni.
The illustrious Vakrā said: That power known as the Yoni (bhaga), which possesses a threefold movement, consists of three syllables and is of three types; this is the thirty-eighth bliss.
In its center is the brilliantly radiant Śrī-Uḍḍiyāṇa, together with the supreme *kalā*;
in the southern corner is that which is called the illustrious Jālandhara, whose abode is manifest;
and in the left corner is the illustrious Pūrṇapīṭha, which causes fear to the ignorant and by which the universe is filled.

In front of that is Kāmarūpa, endowed with the digit of passion (*madanakalā*) and the abode of all accomplishments; there is another, Tisrapīṭha, and above that, another, Candrapīṭha, on the forehead.
Above that is the wheel of the Mothers (*mātṛcakra*), encircled by three rings; Koṅkaṇa is above the point (*bindu*).
There are six seats; the principles of the seats are sixfold, and their manifestation occurs through six by means of six within each of the six.
The Siddhas are the goddesses of the six cakras; thereafter follows another group of six trees, and six creepers.
There are also the six mudrās of the goddesses, endowed with the threefold movement, and the Yoni in the corner of the Mothers.
At the end of the Yoni is the mass of phonemes (varṇarāśi), the cause of the sixfold process of manifestation, described in six verses.
And among the six dharmas, there is one verse of instruction consisting of three lines, encircled by three circles.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, she is the Mudrā; within her three wheels is the divine Liṅga, the Kuliśa of the three excellent faces.
At its end is the single world, situated in both Akula and Kula, the Lord whose form is Ciñciṇī.
In front of that [syllable], the three worlds are arranged according to rule; with six worlds on the right, and another collection of letters whose abode is manifest in the region of its left side.
Thus, having meditated upon that Liṅga of the Mothers, the Śiva-Sakala, the sixfold Oṃkāranātha, and the Vyomaliṅga located in the city of Tripura; and [meditated upon] the primordial seat Uḍḍiyāṇa,
the secret seat of the Mothers situated at the station of the triple path, which is the foot of the single-syllabled [mantras].
Among the liṅgas in the wheel of the Mothers, which is the abode of the stages of the Krama, is the liṅga of the space of the primordial abode (ālayākāśa).
O Lord of the mudrās, the joyful Master of the Word, residing in the hollow of the *saṃvartī* [lotus],
you who are divided by the six cakras; O host of yogis adorned with the digit of Supreme Śiva, you have dissolved into the left path of the supreme nectar within the triangle.
In the center of that is the divine liṅga, which produces supreme bliss, having the form of the bindu and the nature of the void (kha).
From the churning of that which has the nature of eternal bliss, it is divided into six types.
The authority over knowledge and enjoyment, born of the innate family, is the triple command on the forehead;
there is the Lord Klinna at Kadamba, placed within the excellent fold, and the Lord Siddha-Kauḍāra at the end of the drop;
and he is Kapāda, the Bhairava of the joyful digit, the image of radiant energy.
Thus, the power of Rudra, the mother of maintenance and dissolution, pervades the entire universe through her three divisions;
experience the expansion of the twenty-seven divisions as the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] through its five divisions,
established in the middle of the island of Āmnāya at the station of Krama in Candrapura through its three divisions.
Abiding there, she is the Goddess of gods, consisting of both Akula and Kula, the giver of bliss, and autonomous.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
the Command of the Guru, who has given birth to the six [streams], who removes the fear of the bound souls (paśu), whose form is the divine lineage of the Siddhas,
and whose essential nature is Nityaklinnā.
The power of supreme bliss, delighted by the *bhaga*, is well-known.

Among the Siddhas, it is one with six; through the six rays of joy, the *piṅgala* is the peak (*kūṭa*) of the Mothers, the mass of seed-syllables (*bījarāśi*) of the peaks. In the city of the lotus-moon, its form is the Lord of the Sky-farer of the Command (*ājñā*).

The Khasaṃjñā creates the world-vigor along with the six divisions; the peak of the bindu, situated in the field of the phonemes and syllables, arises from the churning of the moon and sun as a single flower.
From that flower, another flower arises—this is the Śiva-paramaguru—and its flower is the Śākta.
Two flowers and another flower arise in the ocean: the divine goddess Kumārī.
That other flower of agitation arises from the midst of the world, belonging to both the *akula* and *kula* lineages.
Thus, these five flowers of the *kula*, together with the stages of the sequence (*kramapada*), have become the very form of the lineage.
O best of gods, this instruction on the tradition of the flowers is a pair consisting of a single authority.
The two flowers are the primary [path] of the ancient way, manifested through the sequence of the Mūrti and Liṅga.
Indeed, Agni and Soma are present face-to-face through the single state of the union of Śiva and Śakti, both red and friendly; there is bliss and a kiss, and above that,
the pair of divine Siddhas known as Kubjīśa and Kubjikā— the flood of the transmission of Mantra and Vidyā, both fully unfolded.
At the end of the Liṅga, in the Kali age, both Kulaśikhī and Sukalā shall be eternally blissful.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
These two, Hari and Hara, are supreme in Candrapūrya; [therein is] the radiance of the bliss of the central channel (madhyamānandaraśmi).
By its will, this [radiance] arises as *ra-ri-ra-ra-ru-bhiḥ*, and the emergence of the path of Meru occurs.
The Goddess Vakrikā alone, the source of the lineage, is the entirety of the deities;
having come from Tūṣṇinātha, she is fashioned in a mountain cave and illumined by the one named Anala.
At the end of the Maṇḍala of the two Siddhas, both Śiva and Śakti are perfectly accomplished through the seed-syllable of the flower.
In the midst of a solitary tree, both remaining silent within a cave,

they brought about another creation; above that, there arose the sacred seat (pīṭha) which is the primordial lord of the lineage-streams, Karavīra, the cremation ground that removes the impurities of the Kali age.
Therein reside five Siddhas, and following that, the pure five Siddha-devis; this very creation of the digit of the moon of the world has arisen from its primordial origin.
The sacred seats (pīṭhas) and so forth, the fields (kṣetra) and lingas, which burn away the impurities of the Kali age, are well-known on the path of wisdom.
All remain upon the seat, born from the command of the lineage originating from the slopes of the Mountain of Sunrise.
The fifty divine Rudras have entered into Akula and Kula; they are of one flavor in Oḍḍiyāṇa.

In the southern direction, their heroes reside in caves and in the waters of that very place. On the path of accomplishment, the fifty [letters] of the Mātṛpiṇḍa syllables possess unobstructed power within the lineage, the path of the perfected ones.
Or others, in the left corner, are the Bhairavas, situated on the path of the three steps and filled with lingas.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,

within the lineage of the tradition, these fifty Siddhas— renowned in the lineage of the Siddhas and honored by the best of gods— are established on the singular path of the Pūrṇapīṭha through the attainment of direct experience.
They too, having thus attained the supreme state in Kāmarūpa, are independent masters who bestow the bliss of exultant power upon the lineage of the Siddhas, their Liṅgas, and the women.
The fifty Rudras are established at the beginning in the Vīramārga;
those Bhairavas are indeed on the left in the city of the womb (bhaga) known as Uḍḍiyāṇa, which bears the name Rudra.
This is the path of the Siddhas alone, joined with the city of Śiva—the Siddhamārga of the Kula.
It has arisen at the Mūlapīṭha in the place called Vakrikā, together with the four yugas, and remains there in silence.
This lineage is the continuum, delightful through experience, this divine flood of the gods;
all this remains silent, its fortune arisen, just as the source is the single-flood mantra.
It is renowned in the tradition called Kubjikā, revealed by Śavarī in the silent god Khageśī.
The goddess moves like a bird within the divine wheel of space at the end of the circle of speech.
In this way, the lineage of the Goddess spreads through her rays; in the single tree at the center of the sacred seat (pīṭha),
two Siddhas are celebrated, while in the supreme city of Aparapura,
there is the sole Lord of the Silent Wheel (tūṣṇicakra).

Having remained silent for an eon, he creates a *kadamba* tree at the end of the "entering another's city" (*parapura-viśana*)— an ocean of intense bliss— and within that tree, he creates the supreme power (*śakti*) on the left-hand path (*vāmamārga*).
The *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:

through immediate immersion (*sadyāveśa*), Vāmā vomits forth the primordial nectar; that is this Kadamba, wherein resides Siṃhaka, born of the letters Ḍa, Ra, La, Ka, Sa, and Ha, which is the instruction on the command of realization.
Through the lion’s gaze, Raudrī is the treasury of the expanding Kula; she is the conviction of restraint and the fierce command.
By means of the state of union with the power of accomplishment, the teaching is indeed the Lion itself.
There is another divine mass of colors; the threefold Bhagavatī is in this house of Candrapurī, and that very Candradvīpa is the house named Pūrṇa, saluted by the best of gods.
Therein is the goddess Pūrṇā, who is well-gone on the path of Krama within the lineage, she whose syllable is *ku*.
In every division and every division, her power shines forth in the sky, like a mass of clouds released from the firmament.
Churning with the churning-stick, endowed with the art of passion, within the mass of the churning-stick of differentiation—
may Bhairava, together with Bhairavī, grant the supreme lineage of Bharatī as the instruction;
may that Śiva, situated in the center of the mandala, bestow the command of realization in the hermitage.
And that command, established by those who have broken through the seats, spreads forth with certainty within the jurisdiction of Koṅkaṇa.
His birth was in the central channel (*madhyacakra*), where he attained perfection upon the stone of Bhadrakūṭa with unimpeded movement;
he is the one of perfected vigor who, from the crushing of the sun and moon, [attained] the *kadamba* at the root of the bulb (*kandamūla*).
His abode is eternally in that very place, consisting of the six [colors/forms] through the experience of movement.

Her fame, the command of the Kula, swiftly bestows [its fruit] in the midst of the tamarind tree. From that, in the lineage of the Kula, accomplishment arises; the mass of gnosis is stirred by the rays of the sun and moon.
Thus, situated in the middle of that, on the path of the arisen Bhaga, it is divided into sixteen divisions;

the other twenty-seven divisions are those that move upon the earth—namely the infant, the youth, and the old—and another is the sky-farer (*khecara*) which is firmly established above them; this is the well-known lineage.
This mandala of the yogis, bowed to by the three worlds, is renowned in the center of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
In the Root Sūtra, it is the Mudraka that removes the darkness of the chapter and bestows liberation upon those who know it.
And in this lineage, the Root Sūtra known as Kujā, which has come from the mouth of Śivaguru, has been proclaimed.
For she, the illustrious Kujā, with her beautiful body agitated by desire, bestows all desires as a divine linga.
The instruction on the form of the Sūtra, proclaimed as the state of Śiva, is the Kaulika; differentiated by the divisions of Śakti and the gateways of the Pīṭhas,
it arises as the lordship over the Pīṭhas of the world.

I salute the Lord of Siddhas, the supreme master, the wheel of existence, dissolution, and manifestation, who by his name is the Lord of the Goddesses; he whose form is the syllable *Aiṃ* prevails over the earth, which is endowed with the various distinctions of the principles (*tattvas*).

The Yoga-pīṭha has been declared, manifest on the earth in Koṅkaṇa through various lineages (oli-bheda). At its center is the Root-Vidyā, the digit of the sun and moon; it is renowned as the Kūṭa-vidyā.
Arising from the upward breath (uccāra) of exhalation, it removes the fear of worldly existence; in the bright fortnight, it is full.
In the domain of the sacred seats and fields, at the manifest abode known by the name Śrīcandrapura.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
in her auspicious southern region, she is Aghorā, intent on the method of devouring and joined with Ghorā.

To the left is Śrīnāthasiddha; Kāmarāja is made manifest by the moon before him. Above that is she who is called Parā, the crusher of Madhu, well-absorbed in the half-moon. In the center of her churning-stick (manthāna) is the burner of the impurities of the Kali age; therein is born the Triple Power (triśakti).
Known as Will, Knowledge, and Action, she is the supreme, the intermediate, and the lower, born from the lineage of the Command (ājñā).
Therein, the Command moves between the left and the middle; it is hidden within the Knot of Brahmā.
Having pierced the assembly of chakras, it proceeds into the sky by way of the exit of the Suṣumṇā.
Having pierced the aperture of Brahmā, it wanders through the path of the sky by means of the three divine paths.
The Śakti, moving counter-clockwise and following a curved path, is the triangular power of Rudra;
she fills the six chakras, delights in the destruction of intoxication, and carries the wind through its five divisions.
She bears the two wings—both deficient and full—and the final wind filled with affection.
O independent one, at midnight, perform the withdrawal and the various emanations within the orbs of the sun and moon.

She indeed dwells in the heart, within the center of silence, in the Kadamba tree; she is known as Śrī-Kubjikā, the supreme divine power (parā-śakti) who eternally bestows satisfaction and pacifies the fear of bound souls (paśu).
Sporting with the six wheels, moving through the body of another, she wanders in the form of the imperishable syllable (akṣara).
Blooming and concentrated in a single mass, she is the digit of the nectar-moon, perfectly merged within the center of the *liṅga*.

She is to be known as the Kumārikā-khaṇḍa, the embodiment of the Liṅga; may that Guhyaśakti, the triangular one, the Divine Command (Divyājñā), the Mother of the World, who creates this universe and abides in the Āgamas as Lakṣmī, remove all fear.
This flood of aphorisms, known in the Kali Age as the first sūtra of the lineage,
is divided into various sections; it is composed of sequential words and famous metrical compositions,
equal to the Lord of Kula, and provides instruction on the path of Śakti which dissolves the impurities of the bound souls (paśus).
In the *Sūtrākāropasūtra*, it is stated: "In the Kali age, this Kula reveals the *Mūlasūtra*.

Thus, in the introduction to the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) measuring seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primordial seat (*ādyāpīṭha*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Sixfold Group (*vimala-ṣaṭka*).

In the *Kādibheda*, within the *Ājñāpārameśvara* known as the *Svāminīmata*, in the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the *Avvākrama*, in the section concerning the language of the *kulacaryā*, in the description of the chapter on the root-sūtras which are the source of the ocean of the *kulāmnāya*, this is the bliss named the Arising of the Sequence (*kramodaya*).
Śrīnātha said:
I bow to Śrīnātha, the teacher of the world, the lineage of the Siddhas, who has come down through the succession of tradition and is spoken of as the pinnacle of the Command (ājñā).
Together with sages, kinnaras, bhūtas, vetālas, and pannagas;
with rākṣasas, hosts of yakṣas, and the Maruts along with their throngs.
[He was worshipped] by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and others, as well as by the hosts of stars and the *bindu*;
likewise by Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, and others, by the Vasus, and by the Earth and the rest.
He was surrounded by his entire retinue, including Nandikeśvara, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, Caṇḍa, Vināyaka, Vīrabhadra, and other principal attendants.
He was surrounded by his sons, those who knew the covenant, by practitioners, teachers, and yogis, as well as by many other yogis who were knowers of reality.

Together with the entire assembly of yoginīs— those born of the kula, those born of the yoga of gnosis, those endowed with knowledge and realization, those who are innate, and those born of mantra and tantra.

[They arise] from those born of sacred seats (pīṭha), those born from the womb (garbha), those born of the field (kṣetra), and likewise those born of the womb (yoni), as well as from those born of the assembly of commitments (samayasandoha) among the Ḍākinīs and Rākinīs.
It was surrounded by Lākinīs and Kākinīs, as well as Śākinīs and Hākinīs,
and by other divine, stainless rites.
The divine assembly pavilion was adorned by Guhyakas, Pūtanās, and Yoginīs; it was variegated and exceedingly beautiful.
Adorned with various colorful paintings and embellished with garlands of jewels, it was covered with many cloths and surrounded by diverse trees and creepers.
The section on the Virgin Goddess (Kumārikākhaṇḍa), the thirty-ninth [chapter], consisting of bliss, endowed with walls and archways, and adorned with many jewels.
It was fashioned by Viśvakarman, richly adorned with magnificent great jewels.
Having seen the Goddess of the gods, the Mistress of the Kula, abiding there in a state of bliss, Śrīnātha, filled with humility, questioned her.
O Śrī Kujeśānī, in that which is called Bhaga, O Supreme Goddess, in the Inexplicable (Anākhyā),
this doubt of mine still remains today, O Goddess, within this ocean of the Kula.
O Mistress of the Kula, I ask you about that which has come down through the lineage of succession— the tradition of the Sadyojāta sequence within the lineage of the yoga of the perfected command.
The *Gṛhabheda*, however, is pure, extensive in its manifold meanings and details,
endowed with all conventions, secret, and extremely difficult to obtain.
"How does the mouth of the Guru abide, endowed with the language of direct command?
Śrīvakrā said:
"O Goddess, speak thus to him in this manner of entreaty; tell me without any doubt."
O Goddess Śilāśekharabhairavī, show compassion to me!
Well said, O Śambhu; I shall explain the arising of the sequence (kramodaya) according to each direction, the vast ocean of the meaning of the conventions and the lineage of the letter *ku*.
This division of the Northern Sixfold [Tantra] is just as it was previously obtained by me.
"I shall tell you that; listen, O long-eyed one.
Śrīnātha said:
"O Goddess, today my practice of austerity within this lineage has become fruitful."
Today, O Great Lord, through your grace, I have attained liberation;
tell me again in truth how you previously obtained it.
The venerable Vakrā said: [In] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Akula and Kula, and the definitive determination of Kulākula.
Above that, distinct from the [energies] beginning with Vikalā, is the multitude of moonlight.

The nature of the left-hand practice (vāmācāra) consists of the Kula, whose form begins with *ka* and ends with *bha*; the womb that has reached [the letters] from *ma* to *kṣa* is the right-hand womb (*dakṣayoni*), which is not a Yoginī.
The wheel marked with the three measures (trimātra) consists of the four syllables PŪṂ, KĀṂ, OṂ, and JĀṂ;
outside of that is the sixfold [arrangement], beginning from ĀDHĀRA and ending with ĀJÑĀ.
This Kaula is of six kinds, arising from the family of the six sheaths;
it is supreme, both higher than the supreme and non-supreme, the family of the heart, and the sphere of the family.
Akula is situated in the center of the womb, a sphere shaped like the letter *ṭha*;
at its end is the remainder of the digits (*kalā*), and above that is the "half-cart" (*śakaṭārdhaka*).
Its lower half is like the flickering light of a lamp;
situated there is the supreme power, which is threefold and located at the crown of the head.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—she is to be known as threefold.
Jyeṣṭhā has emerged on the right, and Vāmā follows the northern path.
Situated between those two, Raudrī has emerged from the remainder of the digits;
she is to be known as threefold by means of her movement up to the sun.
The portion remaining as a fraction in the center is pervaded by that [energy] in the form of a vulva;
she is the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the stainless Yoni, and Māyā, and she is the double-folded girdle.
One should know Śakaṭā as Jyotirīśvarabhairava;
he is the renowned cause celebrated in yoga, Bhairava whose nature is that of sustaining.
Situated in the midst of the power of bliss, impelled by knowledge and discernment,
it is the pure bliss of the sequence, delighted by the self of the bliss of the command.
Having known the bliss that produces eternal bliss, the bliss of the Western lineage, and the succession of bliss, who would not be liberated from bondage?
Or rather, when the eternal and stainless state of bliss has been attained,
that bliss which is itself beyond bliss illuminates the three worlds.
The expansion of all beings is known by the name of the "cavern of the womb";
the Goddess, seated upon the lap of bliss, is the ninefold deity consisting of the nine gods.
The state [arises] from the bliss of emergence; likewise, the bliss of consciousness resides within the self.
It is renowned as the three principles of the cart, the cavity, and the reality, consisting of the three qualities.
O Śambhu, sattva is the consciousness known as Kāmākhya, tamas is declared to be Jālandhara, and rajas is Pūrṇagiri; such is the determination of the family of the three seats.
The *piṇḍa* exists in the sequence of the elements as Uḍḍiyāṇa within the three worlds;
that indeed is the God, formless, in the midst of the sky, whose nature is the *kula*.
That is the object of knowledge, consisting of both theoretical and realized wisdom; it is that liberation which is the perfected Kaulika reality.
It is Kaulīśa, the Lord who moves through the sky, situated in the center of the navel-cavity.
That power is supreme, infinite, and Kaulinī by the will of Bhairava;
her Kula is divided threefold as the triple dot and the triple crest.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
there, situated in the center, is that Liṅga Bhairava, who consists of nine aspects;
he is endowed with the Kalās, yet transcends the Kalās, joined with Parā, and perfectly united.
This very form of a swan, situated in the sky, is perceived;
she indeed desires the *piṇḍa* known by the name Piṅgalabhairava.
The moon-bliss (Candrānanda) situated within the sun-bliss (Sūryānanda) is the *kulākula*;
its increase is that very state situated in the center, which has entered into the interval between the supreme lines (*parā-rekhā*).
That which is merged in the moonlight of Śiva is the manifest state of the sky-farer (*khecara*).
In this way, the wheel situated in yoga is divided into three measures.
One should know the Udaya-mātṛkā-yoga and the other, Jālandharodaya;
the Pūrṇakrama is on the left, while the Siṃha-śāsana is on the right.
And that which is called Kāma is situated at its tip, adorned with the letter *ī* as the womb;
having emerged from the center of space, it gradually arises through expansion.
Thus, the knowledge of the arising of the Bhaga, transmitted through the lineage of succession, is divided into twenty-seven sections; its hidden meaning is sixfold.
In this way, one should differentiate the secret maṇḍala through its sequential divisions;
the girdle, however, divided by its own distinctions, is known by the name of the Kaumāra sequence.
This Kaula [teaching], being sprinkled as far as the world of Brahmā, is white; this Kāmadeva is at the forefront, skilled in the act of emanation.
On the left is Viṣṇu, wearing yellow garments, who rests upon the principle of maintenance (sthiti);
on the right is Rudra, the great lord, wearing red garments, the performer of dissolution (laya).
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Thus, this triple-natured one is the infinite Kula lineage.
This Kula lineage, the Kaula, is proclaimed in Koṅkaṇa.
In the beautiful house of Candrapūra, which is surrounded by Meru-liṅgas,
he who drinks the nectar there certainly receives the command.
O God, the nectar of the tradition is the union of Śiva and Śakti;
those two, known as Pradhāna, consist of both the Flower (Puṣpa) and the Mother-Lord (Ambānātha).
The threefold creation arises from their union; she is called Avarṇā.
The Command of the Ocean, the Mother of the World, is established in eight abodes.
O God, Lakṣmī, whose nature is liberation, resides in Brahmāṇī and the other [deities];
she is further divided into many varieties, distinguished by the eight groups of eight.
And therefore, that which was taught as being of one kind has been purified through a sixfold sequence;
its lineage emerged with a measure of seventy million verses.
The Manthānabhairava Āgama exceeds a hundred thousand times ten million verses;
from its midst, this essence has been extracted, consisting of seventy million verses of the lineage.
This secret, supreme teaching of Śiva is like clarified butter— pure and essential— extracted from the scripture that is entwined by the creepers of ritual networks.
This is the determination of the path of emanation regarding the distinction of the first descent; [from] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Now I shall proclaim the Yoga that has emerged from the mouth of the Yoginī.
Speech, gesture, and gaze, along with the rows of letters of the alphabet;
the locations, the arrangement upon the body, and the sequence of the lineage masters—these are the threefold [categories].
He who indeed knows these six types is truly a follower of the Western Tradition:
the Maṭha-mudrā, the Guhā-mudrā, and the Yoni-mudrā as the third.
Karālā and Padminī, as well as Siddhi—these three are declared in the Bheda [Tantra];
likewise, the three Siddhavallīs and the three Kulavṛkṣas.
And the sequence is threefold yoga: that of the infant, the youth, and the sky-farer;
this lineage is further divided into three types: gross, subtle, and supreme.
The sequence of the five jewels consists of the five [deities] beginning with Brahmā who abide in the world;
the supreme knowledge of the three mudrās is conceived as the path of the monastery.
Having joined the form of spring to the sixfold monastery-house,
this great divine knowledge of verses is remembered as more divine than the divine.
It is traditionally taught that [the lineage] begins at the letter *ṭha* and extends westward as far as Kailāsa;
furthermore, the monastic community (*maṭhikā*) should be understood through its various divisions, beginning with Ānanda.
Having thus correctly understood from the Guru, one should begin the worship of the monastery (maṭha),
as well as the world (bhuvana), the great site (mahāsthāna), and each individual place that has arisen in bliss.
In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*,
the distinction between the monasteries (*maṭha*), the mudrās, and the sequences (*krama*) has been determined among the seventy million [verses].
He who knows this supreme secret of the divisions is a true teacher (*deśika*).
Ānanda, Āvali, Prabhū, Yogin,
likewise Atīta, and Pāda— these are the sixfold Kulakrama.
The sixteen-spoked wheel is called Great Bliss; the twelve-spoked is the Garland;
the ten-spoked is said to be Radiance; and the six-spoked is known as the Yogin.
Transcending the four objects of attachment and consisting of two parts by way of designation,
this sixfold knowledge brings about the awakening to the meaning of the verse.
He who knows this and is skilled in reciting the verses shall attain perfection within his lineage;
[namely,] the group of four, the group of five, and the group of three, accompanied by Ambā.
This Kaula tradition is of three kinds, descended through the lineage of succession;
O Śambhu, this Bālakrama was formerly concealed by me.
He who knows the sixfold [categories]— the tetrads, the pentads, the hexad, the tetrads, the pentads, and the triads— along with their external and internal aspects, [is a knower].
He should be known as a worthy practitioner of the Krama; otherwise, he is merely a bearer of the name.
O God, this is the Kaumāra-krama, beloved by the Yoginīs.
I have already explained the sequence in its youthful form:
four tetrads and five pentads.
O God, O fair-limbed one, there are six groups of six and likewise three groups of three;
this fearless sequence of the Khecarīs consists of these six types.
Today I have revealed the lineage of the Sky-faring Siddhas (Khecarasiddhasantāna).
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
there are four groups of four and a group of five that has come forth in five ways.
The group of six is divided into six kinds; the group of four is of four types;
the group of five is divided into five ways; and beyond that, the triad is threefold.
This is the gross method of the elders, practiced by accomplished yogis;
O God, I have likewise made manifest this state of the elders.
The lineage of the Supreme Lord, which is to be performed with the utmost secrecy,
and the Kula tradition in its sixfold nature, must be understood according to its essential form.
Thus, he who knows this fourfold knowledge, which proceeds in sequence according to its causal conditions,
and understands the unity of the external and internal, is a true teacher.
Thus, O God, the three stages have been declared for the sake of the *Saṃhitā*;
he who knows the *Śrīmata*, O God, by means of its secret symbolic terminology, [attains the goal].
He shall attain union with the Lord, O handsome one, as the knower of the Śrīkulāgama,
when the great sacred seat at the end of the letter *Ṭha* arrives in the Kali age.
It was concealed within the Śrīguhā, in the temple of Kanakamañjarī,
having been established according to the secret convention and preceded by the formal pledge (samaya).
To one who understands the secret signs here— the *nābhivarti*, the *ahīkā*, and the *vajrasandhi* of the two door-panels— to him the *Kulāgama* should be given.

Śrīnātha said: O you who possess the great secret of the convention, which is difficult to understand and hard for even the gods to attain, explain it out of compassion according to the ultimate truth, so that we may be free from fear.
The venerable Vakrā said:
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the root is the navel; Kula is Meru, and the wick is the Self and Mālinī.
The knowledge of the earth transmitted through the lineage, the emergence of the sequence of the command and the secret union.
Likewise: the three Siddhas, the three lineages, the heart-essence,
the three incarnations, as one, through four divisions, as fourfold, and again as threefold.
He who knows the division of the Kula shall be a guardian of the Krama;
he knows the three peaks, the three seeds, the seed of Śakti, and that which is both supreme and non-supreme.
The group of eight, the ninefold self, the sixfold, and the twelvefold division; the Khecarī path of the sky-farer, as well as the sequence of the commitment (samayakrama).
The tree is the Vajra family, and the island is that which is called the hexagon between the two door-panels;
this is declared to be the "illumination of consciousness" (dīpanavijñāna) in the division beginning with *ka*.
He who truly understands the lineage succession, the vidyā, the samaya, and the sequence of the maṇḍala, shall become an awakener of the Mata.
The three principles, the three seeds, the group of four, and the group of six,
as well as another group of six and a group of eight, are obtained from the mouth of the Guru.
The wise know that what is called "the descent into reality" (tattvāvatāra) is the sequence [of deities] received from the mouth of the Guru:
five, five, the supreme five, and the non-supreme five.
A group of six, again a group of six, another group of six, and likewise yet another;
a group of four joined with four, and a pair considered to be of two kinds.
O Sundara, I have proclaimed the ten-fold Krama-Kaumāra:
five, five, and likewise five, and furthermore, a group of six.
But the division of the Vimalakrama has come down through the lineage of succession;
there are four sections of the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, as well as four others, and likewise four more.
Furthermore, O God, there is another triad consisting of the Vidyās and the twelve Bījas; thus is the sequence of the Pīṭhas, which has come down through the lineage of succession.
He who understands this method is honored by the heroes in the sequence;
these twelve verses constitute the mandala of the mudrā-samaya.
It should be recited with great effort and not written down; these twelve verses, O fair-faced one, must be kept strictly secret.
If, through negligence, it is not transmitted from ear to ear, one should recognize that;
for by its mere utterance, perfection arises.
He knows the sixfold subject matter, is adorned with the five jewels,
is a knower of the twelve recitations of the Mother, and is devoted to the seed-syllable of Śakti.
He who has not seen the Khecarīmudrā, nor likewise the three Vidyās, and [has not received] the Guru—
only he who understands in this way may be a teacher of the Mata.
Having obtained such a guru, who would not be liberated from bondage? Indeed, the Great Āryā is likewise endowed with the two vidyās.
O Great Śambhu, the six peaks and the garland of eight stars—
he who knows this is a knower of reality, a guru who bestows liberation.
First, there is the tetrad of seats (pīṭha), then the four deities of the seats;
next is the pentad known as the Jewels (ratna), and likewise another, the hexad of yogas.
By the command of Vimalā, there are four Siddhas and another group of five;
there is also another Trika of Siddhas, as well as Ambā and Nātha.
Endowed with six aspects, transmitted through the lineage of succession,
and joined with the ritual of placement (nyāsa), it is the fourfold primordial flower.

It is sprinkled here; of this there is no doubt. One must not cause a violation of the command. Thus, O God, has been declared the most wonderful secret known as the Matā, as well as the convention of the seat-mandala and the collection of phonemes.
The Liṅga, Mālinī, the eight [mantras], and likewise the four weapons.
O God, he who knows the five roots, as well as the application, the four determinations regarding the house, and these nine divisions, is a true preceptor.
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa: The houses, the fields, the seats (pīṭhas), the four gates of the seats,
the secondary seats (upapīṭhas), and the gathering places (saṃdohas)— this sixfold [system] is the characteristic of liberation.
The convention of the three mudrās, and likewise the convention of the pīṭhas.
KHA KA.
The secret signs of places and likewise the secret signs of flowers.
The three authorities, as well as the collection of letters, and likewise Kha:ka.
O Maheśāna, this maṇḍala is known by the name of my mudrā.
Whoever knows these nine conventions and their sequence, for him there are four ribbons and indeed the state of an Ārāvi-teacher.
Having performed prostrations with the staff-like body, one should offer everything as an oblation;
having performed a hundred circumambulations, one should pay homage with the eight-limbed prostration.
If one does not recognize [the deity] in this way, then one should certainly not offer salutation;
if salutation is not performed, the removal of the divine command will occur.
One who lacks the command should recite a hundred thousand times, and then the intense command will proceed;
otherwise, if one does not recite a hundred thousand times, a flaw arises for him.
O God, one dies before long in a difficult family lineage,
in the presence of the Śrīkrama and likewise in the proximity of one's own guru, O God.
Likewise, for those who are well-known, as well as for the eldest, who are free from hypocrisy and deceit, the mandala should be prepared; for others, it would produce the opposite result.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
there is one peak-syllable (kūṭa), a pair of two, and likewise the five flowers;
the sequence of the Peak-syllables of the designations is obtained from the mouth of the Guru.
Therefore, in the Kula lineage, there is the command that there is nothing higher than the Guru;
now I shall speak of that which bestows the various divisions of other sequences, which is threefold.
The Śākta, the Śāmbhava, and the third, the Āṇava;
the six Siddhas, the six Yugas, the six Pīṭhas, and the six Mudrās— he who knows these belongs to the Kulakrama.
The six yoginīs, the six yoginīs, those who traverse the six paths.
At the end of the womb and within the lineage, there are the remaining reciters of the book; the four Siddhas adorned by the gods with the five jewels,
as well as the five Mahantārīs and likewise the four Pīṭhas.
Furthermore, this sequence consists of four and six types;
thus, the division of the Śākteya has been previously described by me to you.
The remaining others are "āṇava"; thus, all this division of the āṇava exists within the four ages.
The fifty Siddhas have been proclaimed as the Kaulikas;
this is declared in the *Yonyārṇava*, and this very *Kramodaya* has been spoken,
endowed with the three mudrās and renowned as the *Manthānamaṭha*.
The Yakṣiṇī, abiding in the midst of form, is the secret designation before her;
from that, the command issues forth, and the sign is the authoritative one.
There is Śaṅkhinī, and there is Śaṅkhinī; the second is the Śaṅkha-mudrā.
Kāmarūpa is well-known, and the lineage of the Gurus is very well known.
Endowed with the three mudrās, it is extracted by means of the conch, the hut, and the mudrā;
the Cave of the Goddess, the Cave of the Siddhas, and the third, called Kadamba.
O God, the *yonimudrā* is likewise obtained only rarely through your grace;
the *devīmudrā*, moreover, was previously revealed to you in three ways.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Kucukula and Akulī, as well as the Goddess, form the Trika; likewise, Mi, O, and Ṣa are the names of the Carya, known by the designation of the lineage of the Siddhas.

O fair-faced one, Śṛṅgāṭakeśvaranātha is proclaimed as the triple jewel; likewise, there are the sacred seats (pīṭha) and the subsidiary seats (upapīṭha), as well as those perfected in the seats (pīṭhasiddha).
The lineage of the Siddhas is fourfold, and that [is established] in the three lineages (oli) in sequence;
now, the supreme Siddha is Bindubhairava, whose garment is nectar.
At the end of the Kali age, one should worship Mataṅgīśa, the lord of the fifth seat;
situated there is the distinction of the couple, while in the Kula lineage there is but a single mudrā.
There shall be a Liṅga known by the name Bālā;
thus, at the end of the Kali age, there will be the descent of the sacred seats (pīṭha), of this there is no doubt.
The conch, the spear, as well as yoga, and the great house as the fourth;
the station is declared to be Candrapura, and the sixfold [set] is indeed Virāmaṇa.
The past lineage and the two subsequent ones have been proclaimed;
O lady of beautiful hips, the ninth house, Ānanda, is the most excellent among them.
He who knows the clans and the houses shall become a partaker of success in the Kula;
[this is] the Uḍḍāmara Siddhakaula, known as the Gaṇa, the Khecarīmata.
Caṇḍākhya, Raurava, Ghorākhya, Bhūtaḍāmara,
and the ninth, Mahākaula— therein the Command (ājñā) was revealed; thus the Kaula tradition stands established, arranged in ninefold succession.
Having known [the Self] both externally and internally, who would not be released from bondage?
The single root is the reliance on the command of the Guru; the five sacred seats (pīṭhas) are indeed the secret division. O God, the three offices are Sṛṣṭinātha and Sadāśiva.
The mass of sounds (śabdarāśi), Aghora, the eight [deities], their grasping, and likewise their burning;
the Mālinī-Ṣoḍhā convention from the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, which is sixfold and divided into twelve parts.

She is the sixfold, the sixth, the supreme, the sixfold, the sixfold, the possessor of the sixfold, the Kaulinī, the Śavarī, the sixfold, the sixfold one; she is eightfold by the designation of the sixfold.
Thus, the eightfold [deity] has been revealed through a sixfold hidden meaning;
he who understands this sixfold arrangement shall be a delighter of the Kula.
The Supreme is the single-syllabled, sixfold, and the sixfold one known as Vyomā;
she is endowed with the fourteen worlds and is the crest-jewel of the family of the Bindu of the letter *Ṭha*.
That Goddess, the Mother of the World, resides between Śakti and Kuṇḍalinī;
she is Parā, the supreme Kālī, the very digit (kalā) of the Supreme Lord.
Since she has been manifested in such a manner, how could there be a return?
This is indeed known as the Jīvamudrā; it has been definitively established among the seventy million [tantras].
The mouth of the Guru is the lamp of the Guru, the abode of the Supreme Lord;
for knowledge is obtained from that mouth, since it cannot be attained otherwise by merely hearing it.
Now, regarding those nine conventions: listen to them according to the meaning of the sūtra.
The mudrā is threefold and one; it is indeed secret within the five seats (pīṭha).
The sixfold group concerning the fatigue of the perception of places, the pair composed by Puṣpadeva,
the three topics of authority, the secret meaning of the verses, and the collection of phonemes.
The maṇḍala is said to be threefold; the mudrā is indeed the Supreme Goddess. Tāraka is the essence of the pledge (samaya), and Saṃjñā is indeed the Great Saviouress.
All these are obtained from the breath of the Guru in a most secret manner;
indeed, he who reflects in this way shall be one perfected in the teaching.
Now, in the form of the group of six, there is Nigrahā;
Ḍakā is Raktodarā, Rakā is Karālā,
Lakā is Kumbhā, Bhagodarā, and Kakā is indeed Kṛśodarā.
The syllable *kha* is the Yakṣa-gut, the Terrible; the syllable *ha* is the Rākṣasa-gut, the Family.
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa is defined as follows: what?
Thus, she is sixfold in her functions; she is renowned as Ciñcāmātā and Lambodarā.
And one should perform worship of these deities within one's own lineage.
The venerable Vakrā said:
A garment of light, a lamp, a skull resting upon Bhairava,
flowers, meat, the divine, and the gazing toward the ten directions.
In this very manner it should be performed; from that, success proceeds:
namely, striking, seizing, deluding, bursting, and likewise yawning.
Stambhana, uccāṭana, and even māraṇa as desired—
many such signs of efficacy arise simply from the propitiation of the Ṣaṭka.
Śrīnātha said:
O Goddess, by your grace, please explain the sixfold method according to the inner self (adhyātma),
by the mere knowledge of which there arises compassion for all living beings.
Knowledge consists of six aspects; Śiva consists of six aspects;
Vidyā consists of six aspects; and the Kula consists of six aspects.
The Kaulika worship consists of six types according to the sixfold sequence;
the root-sūtra is sixfold within the sixfold sequence of the Kaumāra-krama.
In the *Ṣaṭkrama*, the path of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) consists of six groups of six in sequence;
through the *Ṣaṭkrama*, the purifications (*saṃskāra*) and one's own spheres of authority (*svādhikāra*) are established within the *Ṣaṭkrama*.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: the path of the observance (samayāmārga) is in the Ṣaṭkrama; the jewel of the Kula is in the Ṣaṭkrama;
the host of Yoginīs is in the Ṣaṭkrama; and the single peak-syllable (kūṭa) is in the Ṣaṭkrama.

O Lord of Gods, in the *Ṣaṭkrama*, for the sake of the stainless meaning, there are six mandalas; furthermore, by means of the purpose of the *Ṣaṭkrama*, there is the arising of the lineage of the Jewel of the Kula.

He who understands the meaning of the *mata* is the teacher, the Lord of the Family (*kuleśvara*). Everything, beginning with that which is to be accomplished, becomes perfected through the command in the *Kula* lineage.
Thus, for those who are devoid of the goal and excluded from the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya),
there is no initiation, nor does the status of a teacher exist for them.
He who is devoid of the Kulārṇava has no authority in the Śiva-āgama;
those disciples who have been initiated into such [texts] are not vessels for auspiciousness.
O God, one should not write down this meaning of the Krama, which has emerged from the mouth [of the Guru], in a public place.
It resides eternally within the mouth of the Guru, and it is obtained from the mouth of the Guru.
Thus, endowed with awakening, one should become a bearer of the Kaulika command;
one should not associate with the wicked, nor should one abandon association with the virtuous.
If even the Lord of the Family himself were to perish through association with the wicked, then just as one perishes from such association,
so too does that which is the cause of purification perish.
In this way, even he who is pure perishes through association with the unrefined (paśu),
except by the renunciation of all dualities and by compassion for all living beings.
One attains liberation through equanimity toward enemy and friend, and not otherwise;
this applies to those householders who have been consecrated to the rank of family preceptor (kulācārya).
Even those who have mastered the conduct of the observance (samaya) may fall away through negligence;
there can be no liberation from the violation of the observance—such is the command of the Supreme Lord.

In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa; thus, in the primordial descent of the Great Manthānabhairava Sacrifice, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primary seat on the path of the Vidyāpīṭha, in the determination of the Pure Six-Thousand, in the Kādi division.
In the Ājñāpārameśvara, the Svāminīmata, this is the bliss named the Chapter on the Pure Division.
Śrīnātha said:
O Goddess, I have heard this forty-fold bliss, the secret that is hidden and within the sphere of the profound, exactly as it is.
But regarding the lineage, O Lord, I ask you again; even now, my confusion persists.
O Mistress of the Gods, the paths of the left and the right, as well as the Siddhāntas, are endowed with illusion and deceit, and are divided into ten, eight, and eighteen types.
In this matter, the excellent teachers should be known as those who are proficient in the knowledge of yoga;
for this *dhāraṇā* is both "with seed" (*sabīja*) and "without seed" (*nirbīja*), each distinct from the other.
Indeed, through the application of manifold means, there is a union directed toward the Self;
it resides in the *nāda*, is conjoined with the *bindu*, and is established in its own state, situated within the heart.
O God, it is unseen and devoid of form;
it abides at the end of emission, situated between the eyebrows within the Brahma-nāḍī.
Abiding within the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), likewise reaching as far as the door of Brahman;
this yoga stands in emergence (udbhava), while O Wielder of the Trident, it stands in separation (viśleṣa).
O Goddess of the Gods, that seed-syllable which abides in dissolution yet transcends dissolution, which is established from the beginning,
which dwells within all things, O Queen of the Gods, is the cause of accomplishment.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa: For what reason, O Goddess, most excellent of goddesses, have all those [teachings] previously mentioned by you— the Vāma and the Dakṣiṇa— been concealed?

There are seven times ten million incalculable [mantras] for the sake of bestowing grace upon the bound souls (paśus); for what reason do they not attain success, even when the ritual procedure (kalpa) has been performed until the end of the aeon?
O Lord of the World, O beautiful one, human beings undergo extreme suffering for the sake of liberation; why is it that they do not attain either liberation or spiritual accomplishment?
The illustrious Vakrā said:
O God, I shall indeed explain this which you have asked:
she who is the mother of mantras is the imperishable power known as Vāmā.
"O Lord of Gods, protected by that Kuṇḍalī, they have attained dissolution;
how is that subtle, supreme power, whose form is light, to be known?"
Just as the power of fire to burn, having reached the state of being the burner itself,
is likewise metaphorically designated as a property of Śiva.
All those by whom that has been realized have themselves accomplished their task;
indeed, through the empowerment of Śakti, they attain perfection even if they possess dull intellects.
This wisdom, which provides every means and produces immediate conviction,
is the joy of the Yoginī’s heart, transmitted through the lineage of succession.
I shall speak in brief out of affection for you, O leader of the gods:
the *bindu* is declared to be the self (*ātman*), and the self is remembered as the *bindu*.
The pervasive [Bindu] is beyond the other [Bindus], established in that which transcends dissolution;
having understood the two Bindus from that, one is liberated from saṃsāra.
Endowed with four digits, having the form of a spark of fire,
the Blessed Lord Īśa, the leader of the gods, resides in the heart-lotus.
It remains within the belly of Māyā like a flash of lightning in its brilliance;
Māyā, known as the "sleeping serpent," is situated in the form of a coil.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
she is called Kuṇḍalinī because she is the form of consciousness of the Self;
by her, O handsome one, this individual soul (jīva) is led both downward and upward.
That illusion is fully described as Vāmāvatī Kuṇḍalī;
the second, named Jyeṣṭhā, is remembered as the straight line (Ṛjurekhā).
Raudrī, whose form resembles a lotus fiber, is proclaimed to be on the path of emanation;
she who is Nirodhī is sung of as having the form of a śṛṅgāṭaka.
Icchā, Jñānī, Kriyā, and Viśvī—this tetrad is described to you.
The fifth is Śiva-śakti, who effects coming and going.
One draws the vital breath upward, and the second [power] draws it downward;
from the union of these two, O beloved, the wheel-less [state] arises.
This is to be known as the seventeenth, Desire, which performs volition (saṃkalpa).
And that [power] is to be known as threefold—sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa;
likewise, the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) exists as non-detached from knowledge. Knowledge, moreover, performs and transforms itself into eight forms.

In the performance of actions for the sake of worldly convention, that beast [of a person] performs the action consisting of merit and demerit through both conceptualization and discursive thought. (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
Vivī should be known as the awakener, the one that awakens the power of consciousness (cicchakti);
the fifth power, which is remembered as such, is established as the support (ādhārā).
The Supreme Power is indeed one alone, yet she exists through the differentiation of her activities;
by her power, O Beloved, one enjoys virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
And this mental creation is composed of the qualities of goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas);
it consists of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth.
The mind, the intellect, and the ego are known as the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka),
along with prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
The great wind called Prāṇa consists of Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya; its supports are the channels (nāḍīs).
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā as the third,
Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā, and likewise Pūṣā.
Alambuṣā, Kuhu, and Śaṅkhinī is recorded as the tenth;
together with these, O Mahāśambhu, the bindu of the heart remains there.
The deities beginning with Brahmā are denoted by the syllable *akāra*;
having become twofold, the *akāra* performs its function therein.
Will dissolves into knowledge through the activity known as knowledge;
activity, in turn, dissolves into the Bindu, and the Bindu dissolves into the nature of Śiva.
Established by their respective portions of Brahman, they all go to dissolution in their own respective places;
and Brahmā also, having withdrawn his own activities, departs.
The place ending in the vowel *i* is where Viṣṇu resides; even Viṣṇu, having withdrawn everything, goes to the region of the throat. (From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
One should know that the supreme place where the letter *U* resides is the end of the palate, the meeting point of all [the phonemes]. Rudra,
the Lord, also goes to where the letter *M* resides.
This has been taught by you in the Vāmadakṣiṇayāmala Tantra.
In that regard, O Leader of the Gods, all those who were there as inquirers— concerning conduct, ritual action, yoga, and gnosis— were entirely deluded by you.
In that state, there is no fully manifest gnosis that bestows divine bliss;
O one honored by heroes, having understood this, it was said that they lack such fitness.

O beloved, [it is attained] through mudrās, maṇḍalas, and mantras, through vows such as the cāndrāyaṇa, and likewise through yogic practices of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka).
I have been led astray by the ritual sections (karmakāṇḍa), and the knowledge [of the Self] was not spoken of by me;
yet, due to their pride in that knowledge, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra and the others, and Śakra and the other world-protectors, did not question me out of contempt.
All the hosts of Skanda and Nandi, the sages, the yakṣas, and the kinnaras.
By virtue of their inseparable connection, [the two] are figuratively designated as such in all cases:
there is no Śakti without Śiva, nor is there a Śiva devoid of Śakti.
No separation would ever be seen, just as between the wind and the sky;
that which is of the nature of power (śakti) is metaphorically designated by all [terms for] instruments (karaṇa), because by means of it he performs his function.
"And no other mantra is declared to be auspicious; she is called the imperishable power (avyayā śakti),
who is the mother of the universe and whose form is mantra."
How is she of the nature of mantra?
How indeed is she [described] in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa?
That cessation (nirodhī) is designated as being situated at the end of the uvula; by means of Raudrī, who obstructs the upward path, one enters [it].
At its end, where the letter *ma* resides, is the mark born from the end of the *nāda*.
That indeed is declared to be the abode of Śiva at the end of emission (visarga);
that indeed is declared to be the Great Void (mahāśūnya) at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta).
It is remembered as ending with the *kalā*, ending with the vowels, and ending with the *manas*;
therein sound arises when Raudrī becomes divided.
O God, Nāda also goes to where Kuṇḍalinī resides; one should know that to be the end of Nāda, which occurs above the Visarga.
Above that is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), renowned as the upward-flowing (ūrdhva-śrotas);
at the end of Vyāpinī, O Lord of Gods, the ninth is remembered as Samanā.
There, the *sphoṭa* arises; from that, the mouth of the Guru comes into being.
At its end, however, that which transcends dissolution (*layātīta*) is taught—of this there is no doubt.
O fair-faced one, this is the movement of the *bindu* for those who are awakened;
that which is above the mouth of the Guru is known as the station of Brahmā.
And that which is called *laya* is also that;
it reaches the end of power (*śaktyanta*), O God, for those who are unawakened by Nirodhinī.
For them, the animal realm is declared; this is proclaimed as the utterance of saṃsāra,
which has been brought to cessation.
Furthermore, I shall explain the binding and the grasping, by which there will be relinquishment;
it is always thus engaged.
Having abandoned the five causes, one shall attain the state of moving according to one's own will.
Thus, the yogi who has realized the Self should practice the meditation on Śakti;
then, O God, the eightfold qualities beginning with *aṇimā* shall arise for him.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
When, through the severing of the Brahma-knot, she becomes upward-facing,
then one attains oneness with Brahmā and proceeds to sound and touch.
Having abandoned those two, he goes upward; however, at the region of the throat, there is a cause.
There, Brahmā exists in the form of the effect where Viṣṇu is established.
When he is freed from the worldly states consisting of primordial nature (prakṛti), he is liberated, without a doubt.

Keśava, too, whose mind was abandoned by worldly activity while stationed on the forehead, has ceased his office; this Keśava is the teacher who makes [the truth] known. Where Rudra himself resides, endowed with the activity of a teacher.
"Even Rudra goes, O Lord of Gods, to the Lord who is the form of splendor.
That is declared to be the station of the Bindu; one should point out the mass of splendor, as well as the division consisting of splendor and the very activity of the vital breath."
Having abandoned those two, the functions of Rudra’s qualities proceed upward;
likewise, Īśvara [proceeds] into Nāda, and Sadāśiva into Śabda and the rest,
joined with the instruments such as the intellect and endowed with the qualities of ego.
And as he proceeds, the Lord likewise withdraws his activity;
there resides the god Sadāśiva, who is the substratum of the qualities of Śiva-knowledge.
Right there, the Lord, the knower of wisdom, remains deposited;
having withdrawn his own activity, he goes once again to dissolution. (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
That state where no activity exists is beyond dissolution;
it arises from its own nature through the intellect acting according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures.
Having attained the state that transcends all, one is liberated from the bonds of existence;
[these are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara as the fourth.
All of them assume the form of action where the *bindu* resides;
likewise, emergence, union, and dissolution each exist separately.
O Lord of the Gods, that supreme power which transcends all substrates is the Bindu whose essence is Śiva; within that support, they move in successive stages.
Even Sadāśiva, the Lord who acts according to his own will, O lady of excellent hips, performs the withdrawal at the end of Unmanā.
The knower [of reality] stands like a log of wood upon the Great Path as soon as that [state] is recollected;
at that moment, the bonds consisting of merit and demerit are destroyed, without a doubt.
O Lord of the God of Gods, as long as the body is not liberated from its great fetters, it does not go to the supreme state even when those [impurities] have been destroyed;
how then can there be liberation for him, even though the sixfold object has been purified?
Thus, O King, has renunciation been proclaimed by me through your knowledge.
By means of which [path], one endowed with all qualities attains the state of Śiva;
therein resides that Kuṇḍalinī power, called Anāmā, who is Manonmanī.
Endowed with the three powers, she is the awakener and the restrainer;
she should be known as the downward-moving obstructress and the upward-moving awakener.
Indeed, one [power] is directed toward dualistic existence, while later it becomes divided into many forms.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
She creates the entire universe, as far as the world of Brahmā.
O Bhairava, there is no doubt that it is perceived through the differentiation of its functions:
Vāmā is known as subtle emanation, while Jyeṣṭhā is intent upon preservation.
Raudrī is declared to be the power of withdrawal; though she is indeed one, she becomes threefold.
She is further said to be fivefold, then eightfold and ninefold, divided into fifty varieties, and reaching a state of infinite infinity.
She alone is to be known by means of another form as the Leader of Heroes (vīranāyikā).
Indeed, whatever world of speech exists is entirely pervaded by her;
therefore she is called Māyā, the embodiment of knowledge, and Kuṇḍalinī.
Having attained that, O God, he becomes *unmana* (beyond the mind), free from the fluctuations of the mind,
endowed with the eight qualities, and possessed of omniscience and other attributes.
With those very attributes which exist in the instrument (*karaṇa*), O God, he sports.
Afterwards, having brought about dissolution, it goes to rest and becomes the void whose nature is Śiva.
But that state transcends the mind; it is a hollow space located at the end of the twelve.
When one is joined with that void, one's own activity is withdrawn.
Above that, however, is remembered the all-pervading one, who is both devoid of qualities and yet endowed with qualities;
he is both insentient and sentient, transcending the qualities and untainted.
He is infinite, eternal, subtle, beyond conceptual construction, and supreme;
he is known as the source of all bliss, being neither merit nor demerit.
One is oneself the doer and oneself the destroyer, established within the ocean of saṃsāra; in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the Self is bound again by the self, and the Self is liberated by the self.
By this sequential yoga, one becomes the essence of the *yogabindu*;
however, it should be understood in brief that one must always practice while established in the *bindu*.
Henceforth I shall explain that which resides in *nāda*; listen now. *Nādakuṇḍalinī* is to be known as being situated in the center of the navel.
Having abandoned the five causes, it emerges through the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra);
having pierced everything from Brahmā up to Śiva, it proceeds on the upward path,
having grasped the bindu of the mind and indeed pierced the five voids (vyomapañcaka).
Resembling the beautiful autumn moon, she blazes like ten million flashes of lightning.
Shining like the rays of the rising sun, resembling coral sprouts,
and having a form like a fiber of a lotus stalk, it emerges from the lotus filament.
Resembling the rays of the cool moon and like the steady flame of a lamp,
at its end there is then a drop (bindu) in the form of a spark of fire.
When, having thus grasped the *bindu*, it is filled by the resonance (*dhvani*),
one abandons the five causes and remains established in the *śaṅkhabandha*.
Then, by means of emission, she is drawn upward very slowly; just as water in a lotus stalk is pulled up, or as one situated in the sky might draw [water] down,
or as a lamp in a windless place would have an uninterrupted flame.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
"Then, O auspicious-eyed one, there are two [factors] subject to variation, and the two fixed ones."
Having drawn [the breath] from the path of distraction, one should contract the two "caskets" (*saṃpuṭa*);
the trident (*triśūla*) situated within the *khecarī* should be performed by one who desires liberation.
One should direct [the breath] toward the tip of the *śakti* in the form of a drop of frost;
then, by means of the flow through the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), one should abandon the causal [bodies].
By means of exhalations (recaka), inhalations (pūraka), and expanded retentions (kumbhaka),
when one has abandoned the causal [states] and becomes equal to Śakti;
Then his perfection shall arise— the eightfold qualities beginning with *aṇiman*,
as well as knowledge of the past, the future, and likewise the present.
One attains [this] here, there is no doubt, through the power of Rudra’s Śakti;
O God, that which resides in Nāda has already been explained, as well as that which resides in Bindu.
Now listen to how it is established within Śakti,
just as it is described in the *Kulayonyārṇava* through the union of letters and vowels.
O God, that which was previously told to you in its extent of seventy million has now been revealed again, with its colors and forms concealed.
Therefore, those mantras do not succeed even if recited hundreds of millions of times;
for they are devoid of that imperishable power which, as the life-force of mantras, abides within them.
O lady of beautiful hips, lacking that power, they are as fruitless as autumn clouds.
O God, that Mātṛkā indeed is endowed with both the supreme and the non-supreme.

The entire universe, reaching as far as the world of Brahmā, is pervaded by her; O God, when she who is endowed with both the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā) resides therein—this is from the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
"Just as that which is not established in letters is established as letters and is omnipresent upon the earth,
so shall I, O Great Lord, declare the definitive conclusion."
That power which is supreme, subtle, and proclaimed as being beyond ritual conduct,
having coiled around the bindu of the heart, remains in a state of deep sleep in the form of a serpent.
There, the great yogi who has fallen asleep perceives nothing, O Lord;
she, whose nature is supreme bliss, awakens by that sound.
When she is stirred by the *bindu*, Kuṇḍalī becomes a straight line;
she should be known as Rekhinī when she resides within the enclosure of two *bindus*.

She is proclaimed as the three-pathed one and is sung of by the name Raudrī; she is designated as the Obstructress, blocking the path to liberation. She should be known as Ambikā, the digit of the half-moon, the moonlight in the center.
The one supreme power alone is born in a threefold manner.
From these [elements], joined and disjoined, the nine-group-born [alphabet] arises;
it is ninefold and threefold, and that is the rosary of the nine groups.
O God, leader of the gods, that [mudrā] should be known as fivefold, consisting of Sadyojāta and the others in their respective order, according to the five mantras.
O God, she who moves through the twelve vowels is said to reside in twelve places;
from the letter 'A' to the letter 'KṢa', she is established in fifty divisions.
The single-syllable [mantra] is located in the region of the heart; that which consists of two syllables is to be known as being in the throat;
and that which consists of three syllables should be understood as residing at the root of the tongue.
The production of phonemes is established in nine divisions, beginning from the tip of the tongue.
In this way, the arising of sound indeed unfolds for everything.
For as one is, so are all these sixteen of great power; then,
after the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
there are twenty-five, and above that, likewise nine.
By this sequential method, the emergence of the fifty [phonemes] has occurred;
they were created by me for the sake of conventional usage and for the purpose of analyzing words.
And manifestation never occurs without them;
therefore, O Lord, one should know that all this originates from the Mātṛkā.
There is no mantra higher than the Mātṛkā; there is no state higher than Unmanī.
There is no deity higher than the Guru; there is no Mudrā higher than Khecarī.
There is no knowledge higher than the Mātṛkā, nor is there meditation higher than the Mātṛkā; the supreme is beyond the Mātṛkā.
All this, through its division into gross and subtle, arises from the Mātṛkā.
Therefore, everything arises from that, and everything dissolves back into that very place;
O Lord, just as a drop of water [arises and vanishes], so too are arising and destruction.
In this very way, the elemental self (bhūtātman) dissolves into the drop of the mind (manobindu);
having abandoned Raudrī at the head, Jyeṣṭhā remains in the form of a weapon.
O fair-faced one, Vāmā, Kuṇḍalinī, and Ambikā are the Śaktis;
he who possesses them becomes a hero endowed with power and my beloved— of this there is no doubt— and he is worshipped by the best of practitioners.
Bhairava is Brahmā, O God, residing in Vāmā; Viṣṇu is proclaimed as Jyeṣṭhā; Rudra is Raudrī, O Maheśāna; and they know Ambikā to be Īśvara.
O God, from conjunction arises the auspicious sound whose essence is *nāda*;
indeed, it is established as all-pervasive through the five causes.
It is supreme. (From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*)
Jyeṣṭhā is declared for sunrise and is remembered for midday.
The twilight is to be known as Raudrī, at which time the setting of the sun occurs;
recaka is said to be performed with Vāmā, while pūraka is remembered as being performed with Jyeṣṭhā.
Kumbhaka is indicated by Raudrī; likewise, Ambikā abides in her own nature.
Iḍā is declared to be Vāmā, while Piṅgalā is remembered as Jyeṣṭhā.
Raudrī, however, abiding within Suṣumnā, is said to reside in the equinox (viṣuva);
Kuṇḍalī is to be known as being in the emergence (udbhava), and she is proclaimed as Vāmā.
Likewise, Jyeṣṭhā is said to abide in separation, while Raudrī is declared to be in dissolution; and Ambā, O leader of the gods, is to be known as that which transcends dissolution.
Kuṇḍalī, situated at the navel, should be known as sleeping in the form of a serpent;
and Raudrī is located in the throat, where Rudra, the Lord of the Universe, resides.
Jyeṣṭhikā is in the flow, Ambikā is situated in the middle within the enclosure of two dots at the aperture of Brahmā; these should be known by those who know the principles (tattva).
Kuṇḍalī, abiding in the mind, is to be known as that which is proclaimed as the waking state.
Impelled by Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī brings about the state beyond mind (unmanā). O Mahādeva, she who is called "asleep" has gone to dissolution at the end of the state beyond mind.
Ambikā, however, has transcended the mind; she resides in the state of the Fourth (turya).
Kuṇḍalī is to be known as the first, Vāmā as the second, and Raudrikā as the third, O God; the world is permeated by these three powers.
Manifestation, separation, and dissolution should be known as the third;
the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti), which transcends dissolution, is the one that unfolds the path to liberation.
Having realized that which is free from action and cause, devoid of causal reasoning,
and beyond what is to be abandoned or acquired, one is no longer bound by existence.
O dear one, just as a bird situated in the sky sees meat and swiftly draws it down through its swoop, O handsome one, so too [should one act] through possession (*āveśa*).
In that very same way, the lord of yogis should draw up the mind-bindu;
it remains dissolved through the fierce [power] until the completion of the mantra's recitation.
Likewise, O lady of excellent hips, the *bindu* follows along with the upward breath (*uccāra*).
Having performed the emptying of the void (*khakaraṇa*), one should join it to the place of the void, making the void stable.
One should join the *kūrma* [vāyu] with Maṅgala (Mars), and at the end of the vowels, joined with two;
one should impel it with the *udāna*, and then it shall go to the mouth of space (*khamukha*).
The *Kūrmasūtra* is auspicious; purification is performed solely for the sake of others.
There is no doubt that it is purified here; one should purify by means of the path of the twice-born (*dvija*).
By this very path, one should observe the seizing (*grahaṇa*).
Trembling located at the navel is to be known as yawning through the path of the mouth.
There is the falling of tears, the knitting of the eyebrows, and indeed the agitation of the mind;
the voice, residing in the throat, is shaken and released in many ways.
One who is intent on the culmination of yoga should recognize the shaking of the head, incoherent speech, the sound "hūṃ," and great roaring as the station of Rudra.
Furthermore, I shall describe the state of non-existence; listen to how that occurs.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
there is neither cessation, nor utterance, nor meditation, [but] the "lakṣayojana."
Then, having known [the Self] as abiding in its own nature, one is liberated;
there is no doubt in this.
Furthermore, volitional thought (*saṃkalpa*) is a great bondage, the cause of both destruction and arising.

"Having abandoned that, the yogi is liberated; he is not liberated as long as there is conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*). Neither the mind, nor the object of thought, nor the thinker is perceived."
O Lord, as long as there is volitional thought (saṃkalpa), so long does [the world] proceed;
there is neither the drop (bindu), nor the sound (nāda), nor power (śakti), nor even Śiva himself.
For this is the latent impression of ignorance, the very bond of saṃsāra;
it is formless, and there is no conceptualization [to oppose it]. Who is the savior? What can one do?
Having abandoned that, abandon everything—the snares of hope—without remainder.
Hope itself is the great bond; by it the entire world is bound.
As long as that [notion] is not abandoned, how indeed can there be liberation?
For those who speak of bondage and liberation, there is no such thing where everything has gone to dissolution.
He who has no longing even for liberation attains liberation;
in liberation, there is no postulated place, nor meditation, nor mental retention.

Vision is spread everywhere, characterized by pervading all things; for that which is without characteristics, how can there be a characteristic? For that which is without mind, how can there be a mind?
How could the wise conceive of a location for that which is non-existent?
One should cause the mind to dwell upon non-existence and abandon existence.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
When one ascends to the state of non-existence, one should then contemplate that "it exists.
Having abandoned the states of existence and non-existence, one should contemplate the all-empty.
The knowledge of the self, whether moving or unmoving, depends upon the fluctuations of the mind;
having known it as both with parts and without parts, one is then liberated from bondage.
As long as one cultivates that knowledge which is solely the support of consciousness,
having become solitary through the vital breath, one shall abandon the latent impressions of ignorance.
Free from the afflictions of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and the like, as well as mental cognitions,
one should perform that which is partless (niṣkala) at other times, relying upon that;
for having thus understood the void nature of all that moves and is stationary.
Like the space within a broken jar, that reality pervades all things yet remains undivided.
In the state of liberation, the entire world is delusion, which is the cause of bondage;
if delusion is stilled, liberation remains as one's natural state.
Thus, in the introduction to the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters,
on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (vimala-ṣaṭka), in the Kādi division, in the Svāminīmata which is the supreme command of the Lord,
in the venerable Compendium of Twenty-Four Thousand verses spoken in the tradition of the Mother (avvākrama).
In the description of the chapter on the sovereignty of wisdom, this is the bliss named the Arising of the Sequence (Kramodaya).
Śrīnātha said:
"O my beloved, there is a great and divine curiosity in me:
since that which does not exist there has no mark (lakṣa), how can there be a dwelling (bhavana) in the unmarked (alakṣa)?"
Forty-first [chapter], Ānanda:
Meditation is the mother of dualities; it is devoid of conceptualization and free from affliction.
Dhyāna, worship, recitation, and yoga—meditation indeed takes many forms.
"For what purpose, O Goddess, Supreme Sovereign, was she indicated by you?
Śrīvakrā said:
"There are various forms, colors, and numerous types of lakṣa-dhyānas."
Indeed, these have been revealed by me for the sake of purifying the mind;
for the mind is eternally restless, negligent, and powerful.
How can that be grasped, whose movement exceeds even the wind?
For as soon as one thing is contemplated, another has already appeared.
There is no meditation, nor a target, nor ever any volitional thought;
for this reason, O Lord, everything must be abandoned without remainder.
Just as someone with a torch in hand might discard it after seeing an object, so too,
having seen the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should then relinquish that knowledge.

O God, whatever hundred-thousand-fold [recitation] arises from the mind, or whatever meditation consists of conceptual construction—all that perishes; one should cultivate the realization: "I am not."
"I do not exist, nor does another exist; I am devoted to the practice of non-duality.
Thus, one who is liberated does not think "I am free," nor has he ever been bound.
Whether established in a vow or as a householder, one should abandon the latent impressions of ignorance;
one should not think, "I am a Brahmin," nor "I am of the lowest caste," nor "I am a deity."
Neither youth nor old age, nor even childhood, is the characteristic of one who is well-absorbed in meditation;
such a person does not think "I am in heaven," nor "I am in the underworld," nor "I am in the atmosphere."
"I am not," nor "this exists"—such is the characteristic of one who is well-absorbed;
he is neither a yogi nor a non-yogi, free from desire and without possessions.
Omniscience and freedom from egoism are the characteristics of one who is well-absorbed; the omniscient one thinks neither "I am," nor "I am a fool," nor "I am a scholar."
As long as one does not indeed abandon it, so long is there nothing for that person;
the state of "I am" is always bound within the three qualities (guṇas).
O Lord, as long as he does not abandon [these things], he will be restrained— he for whom pleasure and pain, friend and foe, and the auspicious and the inauspicious are equal.
