He is liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra; of this there is no doubt.
Just as a calf turns away from its mother when her milk is exhausted, so does he turn away from worldly existence.
Likewise, through the destruction of the mind, men attain Nirvana, the supreme state;
yet this entire world remains attached to sons, wives, and family.
Having abandoned those [states] and becoming free from the qualities (nirguṇa), one proceeds toward nirvāṇa—
even those who have reached the peak of existence (bhavāgra) and are devoted to that yoga [attain it].
Seized by craving and egoism, they fall into the ocean of existence.
Having abandoned egoism, one should abandon the sense of "mine. In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
having cast off all the snares of hope without exception, one should practice yoga.
Even a twice-born man who is a killer of a fetus or one who violates the teacher’s bed, though he may be a knower of the four Vedas.
One is not released from evils so long as one does not practice yoga;
once the self is liberated, it perceives everything, for the self alone is omnipresent.
Just as I am, so does he see everything with a single nature;
though existing in many states, it is one, like a thousand threads of wool.
One who is equal toward honor and dishonor, and equal toward the factions of friend and foe—he is liberated and shall liberate all; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
When one is established in one's own true nature, free from conceptual construction, indescribable, transcending the mind, and supreme, one is liberated;
of this there is no doubt. When the Lord is situated within oneself, for one who is established in the movement of the intrinsic nature, [liberation occurs].
No conceptualization is taught for him who is free from all meditative cultivations;
he should be known as Hiraṇyagarbha, by whom this entire world is pervaded.
Thus spoke Śrīnātha.
It is completely liberated from all dualities and devoid of all marks.
"In non-duality there is no second; how can it remain motionless?
Śrīvakrā said:
"O God, without the union of the moving and the unmoving, there is neither movement nor stillness."
The knowledge of the self, which is both moving and unmoving, depends upon the fluctuations of the mind;
that by which all this is moved is worshipped by the yogis.
O God, these five subtle elements— sound, touch, taste, form, and smell— are known as the attachments that possess great power for embodied beings.
And because of their grasping, those who are devoted to the yoga of peace are bound by the fault of attachment to conceptualization;
for from attachment, desire is born.
Śrīnātha said:
Therefore, one should abandon association;
for from bad company come worldly affairs as well as the study of the scriptures.
By renouncing all attachments, he shall go to the supreme goal; [this is] from the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
the acquisition of wealth through desire.
It is situated in the Bindu, situated in the Nāda, situated in the Śakti, and established in the heart.
O Goddess, that which was spoken by you— that [the Power] resides in the heart, is established in its own nature, and especially so— has all been understood by me.
"Now, regarding the abiding in the castes and the instruction—how is that?
The venerable Vakrā said:
'I shall explain the abiding in the castes.'"
O God, the method of grasping situated at the region of the navel has been explained to you as before; furthermore, there is dissolution into that which is free from affliction.
Listen, O long-eyed one!
Having understood this, O Lord of Gods, one should unite [the self] with the supreme state:
the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) is situated in the heart, while the principle of Knowledge (vidyātattva) is in the uvula.

The Śiva-principle resides at the place of dissolution, having reached the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). As previously stated in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, it is situated within Śakti; such is the path as it exists.
Now, O beloved, I shall tell you how you, established as the Lord of the World, become situated within each individual phoneme through Śakti.
For those desiring victory, the accomplishment of mantra comes swiftly through the sequence of the wheel-mālā.
The wheels beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha and ending with Saṃvartī are said to be fifty in their order; by them the entire world is pervaded.
O Three-eyed One, all of them should be known as standing in the midst of power.
Without them, the mantra would not be effective in accomplishing visible or invisible goals;
one should pronounce each individual syllable, differentiated by the twelve vowels.
One should contemplate the Self, Power, and Śiva there as having the form of light, conjoined with fire and wind, and marked by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*.
Make this [universe], which has become liquefied, dissolve into the abode of all powers—
[an abode] resembling shimmering rays and blazing like ten million flashes of lightning.
When that [knowledge] reaches a state of absorption and one becomes a knower of time, then,
established in the state of Sadāśiva, one perceives with the divine eye.
O observer of the vow of reality, one should see that which is eternally arisen as separated by various states;
through the power of this wheel, one sees everything situated within.
Within six months one will quickly fly up; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
This is the most secret of secrets; it must be concealed with great effort.
It must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who has no son; nor to those who delight in other scriptures, nor to those who maintain hypocritical vows,
nor to those devoted to other deities, nor to the deceitful at any time.
Devoted to hypocrisy and crookedness, they are revilers of the practice of non-duality.
O jewel, you must not give the Kula-āgama, which is a treasury of knowledge;
O one honored by the gods, if you should give this instruction to those [unworthy] out of negligence, [it will bring harm]. —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
The yoginīs become angry with him and dry up his fat and flesh—
[those who are] deeply devoted to their guru and the deity, and who are intent upon the fire-ritual (agnikārya).

At the time of initiation, one should examine those who are devoted to the Kumārī and to yoga, and who are intent upon pure observances, by means of signs such as the paralysis of their bonds (pāśastobha).
Wherever that power, the Manonmanī, is dissolved in the Amanaska state,
there the practitioner should lead himself and unite him with that [state] by means of the thread of power (śaktisūtra).
At that time, there will quickly be a manifestation of power (*stobha*) through various types of mudrā-bindings. When one is empowered by the *śakti*, one will chant the scriptures;
and when questioned, one will speak of both the past and the future.
He may leap up or fall to the ground, and he may be possessed again and again.
Thus it has been told to you, O Lord; now hear how the division occurs:
having set aside the group of neuter vowels, the twelve-spoked [cakra] is proclaimed.
Through the combination of the thirty-two phonemes, the Great Wheel (mahācakra) is proclaimed.
Thus, all the Mātṛkās are established within the tradition of the wheels; they are born from the western house and abide both externally and internally.
In the palate, however, is a sixteen-spoked [lotus], where that digit which brings nectar resides.
O God, when one abides in the emission (*visarga*), one experiences a touch resembling the peak of a snow mountain; at that time, O God, one hears from afar.
Satiated by the nectar of the *lambikā*, one speaks everything consisting of speech.
It brings about the deception of Death and likewise the destruction of diseases.
Established in power, one indeed acts in this manner and is liberated from sense objects and the like;
the attainment of qualities such as *aṇimā* occurs, without a doubt.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
O handsome one, if that dissolution becomes firmly established right there, then one quickly rises up; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
That which resides in the apertures is to be known as "with parts" (sakala), while that which transcends it is all-pervasive (vyāpaka).
Just as space within a jar appears to be limited, [so does the former appear].
Thus, the pervasive nature [of the Self], though separated from the body, is experienced:
"O Lord, just as when a jar is broken, the space remains situated therein."
In that same way, the living being (jīva), by virtue of its internal and external states, is like space;
just as a lamp situated inside a jar illuminates only one region.
And so, O Lord, just as the Self residing in the subtle body (liṅga), skillful in the operations of the mind,
is the illuminator everywhere even when the physical body is broken,
so too is the pervasive Supreme Lord liberated from all fetters.
Thus has pervasion been fully explained to you out of devotion, O observer of noble vows.
For as it is with one, so it is with all; [this is] the fifty-fold Bhairava of the Wheel, conjoined with fire and wind, and marked by the digits of Nāda and Bindu.
He is declared to be the performer of all rites, equalized according to his capacity;
this is from the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, in the primordial descent of the Great Sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava.

In the *Śrīcaturviṃśatisahasra*, the *Svāminīmata* belonging to the command of the Supreme Lord (*Ājñāpārameśvara*), within the division beginning with the letter *Ka*, which is the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*Vimalaṣaṭka*), brought down to the primary seat (*Ādyapīṭha*) along the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*Vidyāpīṭha*), exceeding one hundred thousand quarters and emerged from the path of Meru measuring seventy million lineages.
In the Sahitā, spoken by the Mother (Avvā), this is the bliss named Kramodaya, in the description of the section on Yoga.
Śrīnātha said:
O Kaulinī, tell me exactly as you know it in truth: the descent of the Root Power (mūlaśakti) within the Root Lineage (mūlānvaya) that has come down through the transmission (krama).
The venerable Vakrā said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the determination of the lineage of the syllable Ku. This is the forty-second bliss.
The knowledge consisting of three and a half verses is the Root Sūtra in the Kula lineage;
one who knows the expansion of the Ritual Sūtra is capable of attracting the three worlds.
That power known as Bhaga, which possesses a threefold path, consists of three syllables and has three aspects; of that [power],
situated in the center and brilliantly radiant together with the supreme digit (kala) of Śrī-Ūḍḍiyāṇa is that which is called Śrī-Jālandhara,
its abode manifest in the southern corner.
On the left is the venerable Pūrṇapīṭha, which causes fear to the fettered beings and by which the universe is filled.

In front of him is the one capable of assuming any form at will (*kāmarūpa*), endowed with the arts of love (*madanaka-laya*), the abode of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi-ālaya*), and the entire assembly of yogis adorned with the digits of Supreme Śiva (*paramaśiva-kalā*) within the triangle.
In its center is the divine liṅga, which bestows supreme bliss, having the nature of the drop (*bindu*) and the nature of space (*khara*).
From the churning of that which has the nature of eternal bliss, it becomes divided into six types.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:

Constantly experience the enjoyment of the Vidyā for the sake of the Krama; thus, the entire universe is pervaded by Rudra-śakti, the mother of maintenance and dissolution, through her three divisions at the forehead of the Command (ājñā).

The Goddess who dwells in the center—the God of gods—is the bestower of bliss consisting of both Akula and Kula; she is autonomous, her command is the Bindu, the remover of fear for bound souls, the giver of perfection, and the very form of consciousness.

I bow to the one named Śrī Kubjikā, who is eternally moist, intensely red, the supreme power of bliss rejoicing in the *bhaga*, who fulfills desires therein, and whose beautiful body is agitated; by her,
the Root Sūtra has been revealed in its threefold nature.
The four principal seats (*pīṭhas*), joined with the shade-trees, bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation; she is the Supreme Goddess known as Bhaga.
She is the power of the triple triangle, united with Akula and Kula, who causes the sixfold group to flow forth.
In the center is the Oṃkāra-pīṭha, joined with Madanaka; Kāmarūpa is at its front. On the right side is the one named Jāla, consisting of supreme nectar; in the left corner is Pūrṇa;
on the left is Śrīśailagiri; and on the right is Bhogamāhendra, the abode of the bliss of Rati.
At the beginning is Kailāsapūrṇa together with the three worlds; this is the Yoga-Kailāsa.
At the end of Vāmā is another pentad joined with the pure *kalā*, and the four Siddhas are in the east.
In the hexagon is the group of six Yogis; thereafter, in the sixfold manner, is the group consisting of the *kalās*.
At the end of Dakṣa is another pentad situated in the supreme state in the west, in the Olinātha-Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
At its beginning is Ekapuṣpa; beyond that is Akula; and at the end of Olinātha are the Pīṭhas.
These belong to the Goddess of the Pīṭhas, whose power consists of her attendants, divided into three groups of three in three locations.
Surrounded by eight Dakṣas and Yoginīs, as well as practitioners preceded by their sons, [is] Oḍḍāvvā, the primordial Śakti endowed with all qualities; at the end of that is the sixfold face.
Outside of that is the group of six limbs; thereafter, outside the *kula*, there are twenty-one maṇḍalas.
In the center is that which begins with the letter *ka*, a treasury of all qualities—the arrangement of these maṇḍalas.
There, on the outer side, are sixty-four [squares] distributed in the directions through the application of the *astra* mantra.

The four pillars at the corners, established in the intermediate directions according to the primary families—thus one should perform the sequence of worship for the primordial families; this is the first sūtra of the Śrīkrama.
O Śambhu, this Kriyāsūtra is recited in the Ṣaṭkrama;
by worshipping in this manner according to the prescribed rule, one shall become stainless in the hereafter.
As long as these two are not known, how can those two come to be?
Without compassion, how can there be liberation in the Śrīkrama?

Kāmarūpa is situated in the Bindu; thereafter, in the midst of the digit of the moon (the crescent), is the seat of Oḍḍiyāṇa; at the end of the Nāda is Jālapīṭha; and located on the path below that, within the triangle, is Mantrapīṭha.
This is the origin of the seats within the Kula-ogha, the mother of maintenance, dissolution, and birth; that realization is in the forehead.
I bow to the divine power known as Bhaga, who has attained the supreme state and is accompanied by the Siddhas.
Furthermore, I shall speak on the meaning of the Sṛṣṭikramasūtra, together with its commentary:
the Kumārikākhaṇḍa is the first, the form of Śakti, which is the sphere of both the unmanifest and the manifest.
The unmanifest Bhairava is indeed the Self; he is proclaimed as the bliss of the Self, born within the triangle, in the midst of the void, within the interior of space.
The wind, having the form of a bird, becomes the *udyāṇaka* by that [process];
from the midst of that *udyāṇaka*, the *bindu* falls into the mouth (*āgroke*).
There, the place called Kāmākhya has arisen and is remembered as the abode of all siddhas; it is the radiance that has emerged from the *bindu* on the right side of the *bhaga*.
Therein arises that which is called the Net, an intense radiance extremely difficult to endure;
by its brilliance, the light is cast off toward the left side in Kulottara.
Therefore, Pūrṇagiri said: "Thus the four seats have been described according to the path of emanation, as they have come down through the lineage of succession."
I shall state their secret names by means of a convention:
situated in the center of the Yoga-tantra is the Māyā-pīṭha within the womb.
One should know that the bestower of the path to liberation proceeds from the unmanifest;
the Vidyāpīṭha is situated in the south, located within the solar principle (sūryatattva). —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
But one should [meditate on] the bestower of the accomplishment of knowledge, who has emerged from the midst of the *nāda*,
within the radiance of the principle of the Moon, and likewise the seat of the mantra in the north.

One should know that the seat of the *mudrā*, which bestows the accomplishment of gnosis (*jñānasiddhi*) and proceeds from the midst of splendor, is the reality of Brahman (*brahmatattva*). That which stands before it,
which bestows the accomplishment of the body (*piṇḍasiddhi*) and proceeds from the body of the drop (*bindudeha*), is the seat of the *piṇḍa*.
This secret symbolic convention is proclaimed as the beginning of the Krama.

Indeed, by means of the names, there is the sequence of sacred seats (pīṭhāvalī) and the characteristics of the signs of the Yoginīs; through the power of the secret convention (saṃketa), one becomes a lineage-holder within the spiritual lineage (anvaya).
Thus has the meaning of the Sūtra been indicated and determined within the seven crores [of verses].
Now, O God, I shall declare the sequence of the Bhāṣā-kula.
Kula, kuśā, kuve, kuryā, kubhu, kukṣi, kuni, and kumā—
this is the treasury of conventions devised for the path of reality.
The understanding of the meaning of its language is obtained from the mouth of the Guru. Having spoken thus regarding the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa* and the *Kulāvalī*, [the text mentions] Kuśā and Śākinī.
Ku is the name of Veśyāvalī; Kuya is Yākinībhairavī;
Kubhu is Bhuktivatī; and Kukṣe is Kṣemaṃkarī.
Kunī, Niṣkramaṇā, Devī, Kumārī, and Maṅgalā—
thus, Kubjikā, the household deity, is eightfold.
She previously performed her practice at the eight sites of Advaitagṛha:
Prayāga, Varuṇā, Kolā, Aṭṭahāsa, and Jayantikā.
Caritra, Ekāmraka, and likewise Devīkoṭṭa as the eighth—
this is declared to be the group of eight shrines (gṛhāṣṭaka) that produces immediate conviction.
The divine authority shall bestow both knowledge and enjoyment upon all;
and the past [deities], as well as the Goddess herself, reside within the eight houses beginning with the courtesan.
The prostitute, the female elephant-keeper, the fisherwoman, the butcher, the bodice-maker, as well as the washerwoman, the artisan, and eighthly, the owl-woman.
These eight are declared to be the inciters of the household:
the prostitute residing at Prayāga and the liquor-seller at Vārāṇasī.
At Kaulagiri she is Kaivartī; at Aṭṭahāsa she is Khaṭṭikī;
at Jayantī she is said to be Kañcukī; and likewise at Caritra she is Rajakī.
At Ekāmra there is Śilpikā, O Lord, and at Devakoṭaka there is Kauśikī;
thus the eightfold Bhāṣā and the eightfold Kukārā are remembered.
That which is born of mantra, that which is innate, that which is born of yoga, and likewise that which is born of tantra;
that which is born of the family, that which is born of knowledge, that which is born of the womb, and likewise that which is born of space.
Power (śakti) is said to be of eight kinds, as proclaimed by [the teachers] beginning with Veśyā; that born of mantra (mantrajā) is called Sakalā, while the innate (sahajā) is Raudrikā.

The one born of yoga is characterized by ritual action; the one born of tantra is engaged in minor rites; the one born of the family (kula) is a companion to her beloved; and the one born of knowledge seeks the sacred pledge (samaya).
One born from a womb deludes living beings, while one born from space certainly kills.
Thus, in the eight fields (*kṣetra*), the group of eight beginning with Brahmāṇī is to be known; so the wise understand. *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
These eight should be understood and honored with great effort;
they should be known as bringers of welfare, for by insulting them, death may occur.
This divine octad of languages has been revealed in the Kula tradition;
it must be guarded with great effort and should not be given to one who is not a disciple.
Ākahā and hākahā, kukahā and likewise ḍākahā; rākahā and lākahā, kākahā and likewise sākahā.
Hāka-hā and kukaha are perfected in the four ages of the world;
that which causes knowledge to shine forth is called by the word *kahā*.
The Kula language has been declared by me according to the essential nature of gnosis; and those ten languages of mine have also been explained as they are joined with the meaning of the *Kaha*.
O Lord, by this language that family has been revealed;
he who does not know this language is not fit for the lineage.
Kai, kakha, mā, āgaja, ādi, and kuśadīpī— this group of six is the twelvefold language revealed by the Primordial Goddess.
This is indeed the sequence of the language of yoga, which bestows the rank of an Ācārya;
it is the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
O Lord of the Samaya, [consisting of] Kailāsa, Kamala, Bindu, and Kha in the center.
The Mātaṅga Kaula is non-dual, the dissolution and emergence of the universe,
perfected by the primordial Śiva beginning with the letter A, and sealed by the womb of Yākinī.
The vision of the lineage of the letter *ku* ending with the sacrificial sandals,
the section on Śavarī, the lamp-wick, and Mālinī.
Beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and from the sacred seat (*pīṭha*), the perfected state of the Lord of Yoga is attained;
this twelvefold terminology has been definitively established in the *Śrīkulāgama*.
And that teacher who knows the distinction between languages within the Kula lineage—namely the four languages: khe, khaka, kaukhaśika, and kuṣā—is truly such a one.
Ga, vi, sa, ga, pa, tri, mā, vi, mā, ma, and the fifth is ca;
ḍā, ho, ga, me, la, dhū, tri, ni, kā, hi, sā, hā, and khecarī.
The *kākumātṛkā* is declared to have a division into seven groups of six; the four languages consist of *ojā*, *pū*, *kā*, and *ā*; the fourfold set consists of *o*, *ca*, *ṣa*, and *mi*;
*avi* and *yavi* are two [groups] of three; and *mavi*, *ya*, and *vi* constitute the fifth.
The fourfold *ocaṣa* mantra.
Akusi, aku, three kavimuṣas, and four catuṣṭayas.
These six protected languages have been declared by me;
these sixty-eight languages are recited in the lineage.
He who thus knows these questions shall belong to the Western House;
such is the sequence of the Bhāṣā-krama, a knowledge of vast and extremely profound meaning.
O Mahādeva, how can one who does not know the sixty-eight divisions and the languages within the Kula lineage be called a teacher?
One should apply oneself to the path of the lineage (*gotramārga*) for the sake of determining the path to liberation.
Now, listen to how the conjunction of the *melaka* occurs, in the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
One should say "welcome" to the ministers with the forefinger extended;
likewise, one says "a very warm welcome" with two fingers, and "well-being" by pressing the thumb.
When the gaze is fixed upon the sky, one has arrived at the house of perfect security;
thus are the four kinds of mudrās remembered as the conventions of the *gotra*.
The gaze directed toward Indra (the east) is flickering; the gaze toward Yama (the south) is terrifying;
likewise, that toward Soma (the north) should be known as gentle; and the gaze fixed upon the intermediate space is motionless.
The fourfold eye-seal is proclaimed on the path of the seats;
it is divided by the sixteen vowels, while the Brahma-measure resides at the crown of the head.
O God, the measure of Viṣṇu has thus gone to the north, consisting of the letters from *ka* to *ta*;
while the measure of Rudra is on the south, distinguished by the letters from *tha* to *sa*.
Thus, these three lines have been proclaimed as the array of the letters of the Mātṛkā;
it is indeed the divine installation (nyāsa) within one's own body, known by the name Varṇarāśika.
I shall explain the six locations in detail for the purpose of instruction:
the Viśuddha is divided by sixteen, and the Anāhata by twelve.
The Svādhiṣṭhāna consists of six parts divided by ten jewels;
they know there are four divisions in the Ādhāra and two divisions in the Ājñā.
The tenfold essence of the Guru’s command within the ocean of saṃsāra,
[is found] in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa; indeed, the Khecarī [tradition] and likewise the lineage of the Self (ātma-oli) belong to the Kṛta Yuga.
In the Tretā Yuga, it is known as the Vṛddhakrama; in the Dvāpara, it is the Madhyamakrama; and in the Kali Yuga, it becomes the Bālakrama, transmitted through the lineage of the eldest.
The threefold sequence consists of the infant, the youth, and the aged;
the fourth is the pervasive and subtle—thus the single sequence is threefold.
O God, those men who understand this verse, which is the essence thus revealed by the command of the Goddess, are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Those who understand the meaning of this verse shall not be stained by auspicious or inauspicious deeds, nor by sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; they shall become stainless.
Without the meaning of the treatise, how can delusion be pacified in the final stage?
Therefore, the realization of the Śrīmata is like stainless gold.
By seeing or by touching these sacrificial animals, one becomes a destroyer of sin;
he shall become a master of the lineage (kulācārya), proficient in the knowledge of piercing (vedha).
Then, one who upholds the command and maintains the vows of the instruction shines in the family, O God, as an awakener of the glorious meaning.
Furthermore, whichever teacher, having examined the meaning of the doctrine, speaks falsely along with his disciples, shall go to the Raurava hell.
Otherwise, one does not understand the meaning of the scriptures according to reality;
if one were to produce a meaning for oneself, one would certainly go to hell.
And he who strikes on his own initiative is most wicked; he shall certainly not be a slayer of bonds.
For the knowledge presided over by Bhairavī dissolves into that of Bhairava.
Through Bhairavī, worldly enjoyment is attained; through Bhairava, liberation indeed occurs.
This is the speech of Bhairava from the Kumārikākhaṇḍa; it is of hidden meaning and supremely pure.
The entire continuum of bliss proceeds from Bhairava;
and those who, possessing the great vow, are pierced by the awakening of that consciousness-bliss, [attain it].
"They are liberated; there is no doubt that they arise within the three ages.

Thus, in the primordial descent (*ādyāvatāra*) of the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) measuring seventy million verses emerged from the Path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimalaṣaṭka*), in the *Kādi* division of the Supreme Lord’s Command (*ājñāpārameśvara*).
In the Svāminīmata, consisting of twenty-four thousand verses, as spoken in the Avvākrama tradition,
this is the bliss named Kramodaya, occurring in the description of the chapter on the Sūtras of the Sequence of Emanation.
The forty-third [chapter], Bliss:
Śrīnātha said:
"In age after age, the conduct is crowded with perfected yoginīs."
O you who are worshipped by Śaṅkara, tell me of the descent [of the Lord] and his state during the Yugas.
The illustrious Vakrā said: "Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom, O Ādinātha, Lord of the World!
I shall explain without any doubt that which you have asked."
O God, I shall now speak briefly of the descent [of the teaching] through the four ages, according to the sequence of tradition as it was previously taught by me.
The Siddha named Sādākhyā was the authority during the Kṛta Yuga;
he arrived at the house of the venerable lady Uttarānandadevī.
Four sons were born to him, leaders of their respective lineages;
I shall state their names individually, one by one.
The first is named Amara, the second is Ajara;
the third shall be Oṃkāra, and the fourth is Amṛtodbhava.
The gods were initiated by the immortal women; hear their number, O Lord of Umā:
seventy-seven crores were initiated by each one of them.
"O God, through the power of my command, they have all attained the state of moving through the air (khecaratva);
thus, in the Kṛta Yuga, that number of Siddhas has been declared."

Therefore, O one honored by the gods, I shall describe the true nature of the second age— the divine body, greatly radiant, born from the source of nectar situated within the center of the false staff, which bestows grace upon the deities— from the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
That which was previously spoken by me has come down precisely through the sequence of oral tradition.
He whose name is Śaṃkara, the perfected one and bestower of boons,
shall go along the southern path to his household for the sake of auspiciousness.
O Lord, four sons were born to him, illuminators of their lineage,
who were devoted to spiritual practice through the yoga and meditative absorption of mantra.
O handsome one, I shall state their names individually and in due order:
Aruṇa, Varuṇa, and Varada as the third.
O you of noble vows, the fourth, named Saṃcara, has been described to you.
O Maheśvara, hear now the number of the perfected ones (siddhas) who have been well-initiated as your sons.
By each one, nine hundred and ninety million were initiated;
his form was like the rising morning sun, with the luster of well-refined gold.
The seat situated within the cave stands to the north of the Trident-bearer;
when the second age has arrived, it bestows grace upon the Siddhas.
And as for the sequence of authority in the Dvāpara age, O God, I shall describe it out of affection for you; listen with a single-minded heart, my dear.
“Piṅgala came to the home of the goddess of the Western Tradition;
sons were born to him, each bestowing a boon.”
Vijaya, Vindhyanātha, Mārtaṇḍa, and Meṣa—
O handsome one, I shall describe to you others who have been initiated by these.
The world-protectors, the constellations, and the fixed circle of stars—
twelve crores in number— are initiated one by one.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the third [chapter] indicates the divine, blazing yellow color;
and by the grace of the Supreme Lord, the constellations and the world-protectors [are likewise revealed].
And in the fourth age, O God, hear the sequence of authority;
O Śaṅkara, I shall tell you by whom an incarnation was made.
The Goddess Avvā, who abides in the Eastern Tradition and possesses the form of Bhairava,
has a perfected one (siddha) named Śrīkaṇṭha who has come to her house.
O handsome one, hear also in truth what was done by him for others:
those who knew the reality of the Vedantic conclusions, who were initiated and possessed of great strength,
and who were the perfected ones (siddhas) authorized in the ancient tradition throughout the four ages.
All those Siddhas were initiated into the lineage of Śrīkaṇṭha’s Western Tradition: Khagendra, Kūrma, Mīna, and Macchendra as the fourth.
By these [four], sixteen Siddhas beginning with Kā were initiated, sixteen by each.
Thus has all this been told to you regarding the forms [of the teachings] in each successive age:
how the gods were initiated in the Kṛta age, and likewise how the Siddhas [were initiated] in the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age, O God, there were Gaṇas and Gandharvas; but in the fourth great age, the Kali, there are indeed innumerable human beings who have been initiated.
And when the final age has arrived, possessing a luster like that of black bees or collyrium—
the most terrible Kali Yuga, overwhelmed by sin—
The descent of the Siddhas has been brought down for the sake of the various meanings;
Oḍḍīśa, Tūṣṇīciñcīśa, and the fourth, known as Sthānu.
And at every step, O Śambhu, there is the great, supreme secret, renowned in form according to each successive age, illuminated by the intense Command.
How can one who does not know in truth the descent through the four ages, the divine stream, and the circle of gurus, be considered a member of the lineage?
In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*,
in the primordial descent (*ādyāvatāra*) of the great sacrifice of Mahānthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) comprising seventy million verses emerged from the path of Meru,

exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primary seat (*ādyapīṭha*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Sixfold Group (*vimalaṣaṭka*).
In the *Ājñāpārameśvarasvāminīmata*, belonging to the *Kādibheda* and consisting of twenty-four thousand verses,
this is the bliss (*ānanda*) named "The Description of the Sūtra on the Incarnation in the Four Ages."
The venerable Vakrā said:
Now I shall describe another [teaching], the pure *Kramodaya*, which is difficult to obtain. This is the forty-fourth bliss (*ānanda*).
O God, that Bindu which is all-pervading is the imperishable cause.
His will emerged as the power (*śakti*) from the conscious potter;
she is the possessor of his attributes, yet she is ungraspable, consisting of supreme consciousness and qualities.
And the Kundalī is the straight line itself, flashing as the light of reality; she is known as Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī, consisting of six aspects.
Below, due to the cessation of the *nāda*, there is the imperishable state called *unmanā* known as Peace (*śānti*).
Situated there in the Great Seat (*mahāpīṭha*), she is the one who brings about the descent of *Kulakaula*.
Form transcends form; the word and the aggregate follow in sequence.
The aggregate is proclaimed as the power Kuṇḍalinī, and the word is Haṃsa.
Form is said to consist of the drop (bindu), while that which transcends form is free from affliction;
therein, the four seats (pīṭhas) have arisen by the will of Kula.
That which transcends form is called Kāmarūpa; the great Pūrṇagiri is form (rūpa); the station called Jālandhara is proclaimed as the body (piṇḍa).
The fourfold *kā-pū-jā-o* has come down through the lineage of the Mūlakaula;
it is the Great Siddha called Sādākhya, established in the state of Sadāśiva. (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
And that very Self is further divided into three;
Śiva, Śakti, and Ātman—that which is one alone exists in a threefold state.
O Lord, Aghora is the supreme; that which is called Ghora is said to be Śakti;
and Śrīkaṇṭha is likewise the Self (Ātman); thus he is fourfold.
He who is indeed named Mitra is that god, the Lord of Umā;
this is declared to be the pervasion (vyāpti), while Oḍḍīśa becomes the sphere (golaka).
The sixth is declared to be Nāda; Caryā is said to be Ānanda.
Furthermore, Piṇḍa, Pada, Rūpa, and the fourth, Rūpātīta.
The Kaulika [tradition] arises from the sequence born of the divine sequence through the flow of emanation;
that power which is supreme bliss is established in the form of emanation.
White, yellow, red, and dark blue— thus the Goddess, whose nature is the Kula,
has arisen in these colors as the seats (pīṭhas) in the form of the vowels.
The letter *a*, the letter *i*, the letters *o* and *ai*,
and that which is designated as *oṃ*— from her, their emanation has issued forth.
Following the sequence beginning with Earth, there are the four seats O, JĀ, PŪ, and KĀ;
that which is declared as the fifth seat is known by the name Mātaṅga.
It is all-pervading, supremely subtle, and inaccessible to those devoid of a guru;
it is indeed the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda.
"Oṃ" is declared to be Sadāśiva; the letter "e" is known as Mitra;
the letter "o" is named Oḍḍīśa; and the letter "i" is called the sixth.
By the syllable *A*, those known as the Caryāpāda are the introducers of the Siddha tradition;
Mitra becomes a follower of the Ṛgveda, and Uḍḍama likewise a follower of the Yajurveda.
The sixth would be a follower of the Sāmaveda, and Caryānātha indeed belongs to the Atharvaveda;
likewise, O fair-faced one, the four sacred seats (pīṭhas) have come into being.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: the letter *ṛ*, the letter *ṝ*, as well as *ḷ* and *ḹ*;
Kāmarūpa is in *ṛ*, while Pūrṇapīṭha is in *ṝ*.
In the letter *la* is the one named Jāla, and in the letter *la* is Uḍḍiyāṇaka;
in the letter *ṛ* and in the letter *ṛ*, as well as *lṛ* and *lū*, are indeed the Saṃbhavas.
Oli is indeed proclaimed as E, AU, and Ātman itself;
OṂ, Maṣa, Yāmala, Vidyā, and Kubjā—these are the eight Śāmbhava [seeds].
That which is called Sādākhya is indeed known as Visargākhya; thus is the sequence of emanation remembered.
They say that the four neuter principles consist of the Yoginīs beginning with the Pīṭhas.
I shall explain according to the divisions of Vimalā and the others in the Śrīmata:
Vimalā is said to be in the letter *e*, while Pulindikā is in the letter *o*.
In the syllable *ī*, the Yogivimalās are located; in the syllable *a*, the Campakās;
and in the syllable *oṃ*, the Samayas are said to be, from which emanation proceeds.
The letter *e* is the division of the Ādhāra; the letter *o* is the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
the letter *i* is said to be the Maṇi; and the letter *a* is the Anāhata in the heart.
By the syllable *ukāra* it becomes purified; the Command (*ājñā*) is proclaimed as the Visarga.
This sixfold emanation exists within the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) in the Kula lineage.
Indeed, yours alone is the single Kaulinī, established in the form of emanation:
in the letter *va* she is known as Ḍākinī; in the letter *śa*, by the name Rākinī;
in the letter *ṣa*, Lākinī is to be known; and in the letter *sa*, they recognize her as Kākinī.
Sākinī is said to be in the syllable KṢA, and Hākinī is considered to be in the syllable HA.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa: The Origin of Yākī;
likewise, in the great multitude beginning with Ḍā, [it is] in the emission (visarga).
The Yoginīṣaṭka has been proclaimed; it bestows divine knowledge.
In the syllable *pa*, she is named Gaganā; in the syllable *pha*, she is Svargasaṃbhavā;
in the syllable *ba*, she is Pavanākhyā; and in the syllable *bha*, she is Matyasaṃbhavā.
In the syllable *ma*, the world of the Nāgas is indeed proclaimed as the five jewels;
the stone known as Śekhara is established within the syllable *ma*.
The notion of the Saṅgha is in the letter *na*, while in the letter *ka* is the Youth;
this has been fully explained according to the sequence of the differentiation of syllables for Śrīmātā.
He who understands the twenty-eight divisions attains success:
Brāhmī resides in the *ava* group, while Maheśvarī resides in the *ka* group.
Kaumārī resides in the *ca*-group, Vaiṣṇavī is remembered as being in the *ṭa*-group,
Vārāhī resides in the *ta*-group, and Aindrāṇī belongs to the *pa*-group.
The goddess Śuṣkā is proclaimed to reside in the *ya*-group, while Mahārāvā is likewise situated there;
Mahālakṣmī resides in the *śa*-group—these are the eight Mothers.
Śrīkujā is indeed one who is renowned as eightfold, the deity of the sacred seat (pīṭha);
thus is the emanation from the West: Saṃvartī and Mālinī herself.
The source of the universe is one; from that, creation proceeds in manifold ways.
All mantras, deities, mudrās, and vidyās are indeed beyond numbering.
O Kubjīśa, she who is the source of existence is known as Parā; her nature is that of consciousness, and her form is emanation.
Kubjinī is the mother, while Mālinī is bound to the body.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
O God, the head is formed by the *ava* group; the right arm by the *ka* group;
the left arm by the *ca* group; and the right shank is born from the *ṭa* group.
The left calf is remembered as the *tavarga*, and the two sides of the belly as the *pavarga*;
likewise, the back, the heart, the navel, the thighs, and the hips [are assigned to the remaining classes].
O God, by means of the *śavarga*, the body of the deity becomes radiant;
it consists of skin, blood, flesh, sinews, and the complete collection of bones.
Prāṇa, semen, and likewise anger are situated within the midst of decay;
and the body of Kujīśa has emerged from supreme tranquility.
The Great Mother, whose form is emanation, is renowned as the "Womb of the World";
she is that womb of all beings, established in the form of the [social] classes (*varṇa*).
All those deities of the syllables, as well as the heroes, the Bhairavas, the Rudras,
and the Siddhas, likewise emerged in the form of the syllables.
And that womb (yoni) is established throughout the entire range from Kālāgni up to Śiva.
Thus, it is divine, the Great Divine, beyond the reach of those who are both divine and non-divine.
Such is the lineage-tattva, the confluence of the field of experience and conduct.
O Great Śambhu, this secret, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain, has been told to you.
O God, those men who find this pure, divine knowledge extracted from the seventy million [verses] are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Whoever bestows initiation and instruction without the Vimalabheda, that is neither initiation nor instruction; it is as futile as offerings of oblations made without clarified butter.
For this Mātṛkā is indeed known, conjoined with the knowledge of the Siddhas;
it should not be given to anyone, O God, especially to one who is devoid of devotion.
O God, this should be given to those who delight in the sequential worship, who are tranquil, and who are free from passion and hatred; but never to others.
The most wicked, slanderers, cruel, and possessed by passion and hatred— those lowest of men, who wander through the Kula and Kaula traditions, are not worthy [of them].
They do not go to the supreme state; they were forbidden by me long ago.
But just as a dog sees another dog, so does the Buddha act.
And thus, the efforts of those men on earth who are submerged in the deep ocean of saṃsāra are fruitless, being shrouded by the darkness of ignorance.
Even those who have been initiated are not liberated if they are devoted to anger and greed;
they are like a worm in the midst of excrement that subsists on filth.
Thus, those fallen from their lineage fall into the ocean of hell;
they who follow the sway of egoism find no support in me.

For those who have been initiated into the teaching of the Siddhas and have ascended through the successive stages of the lineage, there is no lack of accomplishment in this world, nor is it absent in the next.
Likewise, O Śambhu, those who have been consecrated but are devoid of discipline and lacking in right conduct do not attain success, neither in this world nor in the next.
Everything is obtained from discipline; therefore, one should practice discipline.
Thus, those who are devoid of discipline are the most wicked on earth and are full of pride.
Those devoid of knowledge are not fit for the Kula or Kaula [traditions].
[This is from] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
[it concerns those] who are satisfied by the nectar of discipline and are devoted to peaceful conduct.
Even the accomplishment of those who possess [only] mouths is not that of one who is conceitedly learned.
This, O Lord of the God of Gods, which is called the Arising of Knowledge (*jñānodaya*), the essence of Śiva and the Kaula tradition, has been told by me to you in truth.
That celebrated Section on Knowledge has destroyed the enemy Kali and annihilated the mass of sins;
having seized [the seed] within the womb, it moves day and night with speed by means of the phoneme of the twilight (sandhyākṣara) of the principles (tattva).
Bow down constantly to that Nāda, whose nature is consciousness, which is worthy of the worship of the gods.
Bow down to the supreme Guru, the illustrious Mahānādinātha, the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

In this manifested abode for the sake of liberation and as the cause of knowledge, stands the stainless, unborn, and storehouse of all auspiciousness, known by the name Siddha— unfailing and skilled in destroying obstacles;
it is attained through states of wisdom, yielding manifold fruits, divine, and consisting of bliss.
I bow at the lotus feet of the illustrious Oḍīśanātha, who is free from all impurity.

O Infinite One, for whom there is neither distance nor day and night, nor any division of time; who is beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; who is as vast as the sky, devoted to liberation, and intent on the welfare of beings;
who delivers them from the fear of existence and firmly upholds the intense Command—[to you I bow].
Bow down to the excellent Guru, the venerable Mahātūṣṇinātha, who has taken refuge in states of divine play.
He is satiated by divine drinks—such as Amṛtā and others—which are accomplished through command and remove the impurities of the Kali age;

whether seen or unseen in form, that [nectar] falls, and he becomes one of pure body. Afterwards, becoming the very nature of play and devoted to the method of perfect equanimity, he arises as a divine yogin.
Victorious is that Blessed One, worthy of homage from all; may Caryanātha protect me—
he who has revealed this path of accomplishment in the world, and whose fame [resides] in Kollāpura within the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Having caused the Bilva tree to burst open, he departed once more and settled in Candrapurī;
there his fame became renowned throughout the three worlds after he beheld the Ciñcā tree.
I bow to the Lord of Trees, the supreme one of intense command, who removes the impurities of the Kali age.

Thus, in the introduction to the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses emerged from the Path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primordial seat on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand, in the *Kādi* division, in the *Ājñāpārameśvara*, in the *Svāminīmata* consisting of twenty-four thousand verses, as spoken in the *Avvākrama*.
The bliss named the Chapter on the Emanation of the Śrīkrama.
The forty-fifth [chapter], Ānanda:
Śrīvakrā said:
"Henceforth, I shall proclaim the definitive determination of the divisions of the Trika."
The supreme among the higher and lower.
Furthermore, that which resides in the seed is indeed the seedless, the supreme state;
it is non-dual, supreme knowledge, beyond mantra, and outside the range of sensory perception.
Thus, there may be a threefold division;
he by whom the great practice has been performed has manifested the causal condition.
Liberation arises from realization; for one who is liberated, bondage does not exist.
Thus has been declared the sequence of emanation, which is the definitive determination of the division of the Trika.
O Supreme Lord, in the Western tradition born from the sequence of the divine transmission,
the secret convention of the first descent has been declared as the arising of the Kula lineage.
And whoever, being illustrious, should comprehend this great doctrine known as the Śrīkula, he is liberated; he is a Kulācārya, delighted by supreme bliss.
Thus, I declare this unmanifest (avyakta) to be of the very nature of power (śakti);
from the unmanifest is born the Lion, and from the Lion comes the delusion of the cosmic dissolution (saṃvarta).
From *vibhrama* arises *śakti*; from *śakti*, *Kiñjalkabhairava*;
from *Bhairava*, *Akula* is born; and likewise from *Akula*, *Vikula*.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
from Vikula comes Puṃkula, and from Puṃkula again comes Khakula;
from Khakula, indeed, the Self is fivefold, and from Akula comes the lineage of Kula.
O one of great austerity, there is no doubt that at the end of the Kali age,
this divine knowledge of the Siddhas, proclaimed as the Kula tradition, will exist.
He who knows the primordial descent is a follower in the Kula teaching;
this is the knowledge of the sequence of emanation, the definitive conclusion of the lineage of the Siddhas.
O Supreme Lord, I have not explained this to anyone except you;
it must be guarded with effort and practiced without being disclosed.
O lady of excellent hips, he who understands this introductory sūtra concerning the determination of the lineage possesses the command within the fourfold [mandala].
First is the Kula tradition, second is the Krama tradition,
third is the Dvīpa tradition, and fourth is the Pīṭha tradition.
The fifth is the Siddha tradition, and the sixth is the Devī tradition;
this group of six traditions is proclaimed within the lineage.
First is the divine flower, and after that, the one known as the pair;
thus, this secret fivefold convention of flowers is complete.
This indeed is the Five Flowers (puṣpapañcaka), made manifest within the Kula;
whoever holds this divine [mantra] residing in the head, originating from the Youthful One (Kaumāra).
The Kaulika says: He should be known as one who awakens others to the teachings of the Ācāryas;

he attains the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*), and for him, spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*) rests in the palm of his hand. This is the definitive conclusion regarding the flower of the poets' mouths in the Western [Tradition], from the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
This divine arising of the Kula has come down through the succession of the lineage.
For he who remembers [this] from beginning to end in his youth, in that supreme state, shall attain family-perfection (kulasiddhi) and the power of moving through the sky; of this there is no doubt.
O you who move through space, O Khecarī, saluted by the heroes who traverse the sky:
one attains here, without a doubt, bliss that is one's own domain.
*Khecara* refers to the attainment of *khecarī*; it is so called because of moving through the sky (*kha*).
For one who has attained the perfection of *khecarī*, that very perfection is indeed *khecarī*.
This is your path of the sky-farer; it is divine command, there is no doubt in this.
For this is the Kula tradition, and this is declared to be the Kaula language.
Now, therefore, [I shall explain] the variation in sequence established in the Kula tradition:
the tetrad of O-JĀ-PŪ-KĀ, adorned by the four goddesses.
Endowed with the equality of space, together with the fourfold Vidyās;
Mi, Oṣa, and Ca—these four are each joined with all the Vidyās.
Within the intermediate state of the body (gasapamana), there is the perception of the jewel and the fivefold jewel;
endowed with the five arising from the jewel, it is designated as "vinivivi-sa."
The six [syllables] beginning with the letter *ḍa*, joined with the seventh,
along with the *aparakartarī* vidyā, are likewise [to be applied] among all seven.
In the midst of the *asaṃyo* [mantra], there is the pentad joined with the *vidyā*;
the triple pair, the triple peak, the unanointed, and that which is known as the triad.
O God, this is the Kramabhāṣā of the Kumārikākhaṇḍa; there are twenty-seven divisions which,
when meditated upon, bring success through the path of Yoga in the four ages.
Thus, O Lord, this sequence has been illuminated by the Lord of the Couple;
and the single-syllable mantra, which was indeed previously proclaimed, is the Vidyā.
Ka-kha is one's own guru, as well as the Tattvamālā and the sequence of the Pañcāśikā.
The Samaya, Mālinī, Vidyā, and likewise the Bhairavāṣṭaka.
Then follows the divine group of eight families, accompanied by the eight groups of eight;
thus has the sequence of worship of the Kaumāra [Tantra] been declared for every age.
In the tradition, in the Western Tradition, this is the divine Kula lineage;
it appeared in the South after more than a hundred [ages], specifically after a thousand years.
Therefore, O God, at the end of Dakṣa, one should not write this supreme flood of the Krama, spoken by the Lord of all Siddhis, in a book.
The sequence of the pure meaning of the doctrine, transmitted from ear to ear, should be known;
through worship, liberation is attained, which grants release from seven births.
This is the divine transmission of the Krama, according to the command of the twenty-seven families;
indeed, he who realizes it in this way shall become a worthy vessel for the Kaula.
Released from all sins, having gone to that divine western abode upon Kailāsa, he shall roam at his pleasure.
Freed from old age and death, such a person becomes equal to a Siddha;
even Yama is deceived by him who has fully honored the sacred tradition (Āmnāya).
And that [attainment] is to be known as gradual, occurring in the final house of the Yoginīs;
he is the one authorized in Kulakaula, and he is designated as the teacher (deśika).
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
For he who perceives the divisions of the sequence as separate in any other way is not liberated from all sins and does not turn back from hell.
His poverty increases and his lifespan becomes very short;
otherwise, however, [one should follow] the ritual conduct, the mudrās, and the maṇḍala as prescribed.
Whoever would speak of the seat and the sandals of the Goddess according to the ocean of the syllables of the *saṃjñā-mantra* within the lineage of the Siddhas, he shall become most sinful.
O God, this divine sequence bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
O God, this definitive teaching on the Kaumāra sequence has been declared to you.
Śrīnātha said:
O auspicious lady, this indeed is the Kramakaumāra, endowed with the divine language; it is clearly to be accomplished through knowledge. How, then, does the lineage of the seats (pīṭha) come to be?
"O Vakrikā, if you are pleased with me, tell it to me in detail.
Śrīvakrā said:
"Now, [I shall explain] another instruction on the sequence, its stainless meaning, exactly as it exists."
The fourfold sequence beginning with the *pīṭhas*, as well as the arising of the *bālakrama*;
through the conjunction of the *bālakrama*, the *kaumāra* has been explained to you.

Through the conjunction with the Youthful Sequence (kaumārakrama), the Sky-farer Sequence (khecarakrama) comes into being; through the conjunction with the Sky-farer Sequence, the Elderly Sequence (vṛddhakrama) clearly manifests.
This sixfold Kaula tradition is a sequence of secret conventions;
it consists of the lineage of the Gurus, the Navātman together with the Māyā-cakra,
the sequence of the eight Goddesses, and the internal doctrine of the sixty-four [deities].
Having thus understood the sequence step by step, as well as the sequence of the Khecarī [mudrā], indeed.
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
the Siddhakrama, the Nirācāra, the Mālinīkramarāja,
another, the Śabdarāśikrama, and likewise the Vīrāvalīkrama.
The lineage of the heroes (vīrāvalīkrama), the determination of the sequence of the Mothers (mātṛkākramanirṇaya),
the primordial lineage of the Yoginīs (yoginīkramamādya), and likewise the lineage of the pledges (samayākrama).
The divine sequence of the Jewel Garland, the determination of the sequence of the mandala,
another sequence for the classification of the abodes, and beyond that, the supreme divine sequence.
The auspicious Merukrama arises through these twenty-seven stages;
having thus understood that which is born of the sequence, there is liberation without a doubt.
Therefore, the abode of the Mothers of the mantras is called Kramottara;
it consists of the east, west, and center, as well as the left, right, and Kaulika.
The sixfold womb and the triangle are the Lord of the Kula, from *A* to *Kṣa*;
he who truly knows this is Bhairava himself.
Thus, by way of the meaning of the sequence, this reality has emerged from the seventy million [verses].
This is the doctrine; this is to be known; this is the reality of the Ocean of Kulas.
This lineage, the Kramaugha and the supreme Jñānaugha,
must be worshipped with diligence and should never be disparaged.
"In the Śaiva tradition consisting of five currents, this Krama transmission— the compendium of its essence— is declared in the sixth, the Kulaviniścaya."
The lineage of the Siddhas is auspicious, skilled in the command of conditions;
this knowledge known by the name *Kramodaya* is the great doctrine of Śrī Kujeśī.
This Kaula is "Sadyojāta" (the newly born), the immediate arising of the sequence of emanation;
it is remembered as the primordial source, the cause of the birth of that which was previously non-existent.

It immediately effects the power of moving through the sky; it is the immediate determination of the Kaula. It immediately effects the power of moving through the sky; this is the teaching spoken by the Śekhara-saṃgha.
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Truth is the supreme hermitage of Kula, the western abode of the Yoginīs;
it is known as the immediate source of all bliss.
Indeed, it is immediately seven crores.
This is the tradition that immediately [effects] grace and restraint;
it is the immediate sequence of transmission and the immediate determination of the Śaiva [path].
For immediately one becomes the abode of all glory, the Western House of the Mata;
whereas those who are thus bereft of the Immediate [Sadyah] are devoid of the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya).
They do not possess the consecration, nor does the status of a teacher exist for them; one who is devoid of the lineage of the family has no authority in the Śiva-āgama.
O God, those who have been initiated by him are not vessels for liberation;
O God, one should not openly write this meaning of the Krama, which has issued from the mouth [of the teacher].
It resides eternally in the mouth of the Guru and is obtained from the mouth of the Guru;
thus, when one is immediately joined [to it], one becomes a Kaulika.
If even Sadāśiva himself were to perish through association with the ignorant,
one must never associate with the wicked; for through association with the wicked,
even pure gold is ruined, just as it is ruined by contact with a serpent.
In this way, even one who is pure perishes through association with the wicked.
There is no liberation from association with cattle; one is not liberated by consecration.

[This is from] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, in the primordial descent (*ādyāvatāra*) of the Great Manthānabhairava Sacrifice, in the lineage (*anvaya*) comprising seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru.

In the *Caturviṃśatisahasra-saṃhitā*, spoken by the Mother (Avvā) in the tradition of the *Avvākrama*, belonging to the *Kādi* division, which consists of more than one hundred thousand quarters, within the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimala-ṣaṭka*), in the *Svāminīmata* which is the supreme command of the Lord,
in the description of the chapter on the Casket of the Sequence (*kramamañjūṣā*), this is the bliss named the Arising of the Sequence (*kramodaya*).
The venerable Vakrā said:
Now I shall proclaim the auspicious arising of the seats of the principles (tattva-pīṭha). This is the forty-sixth bliss.
Earth is to be known at Kāmākhyā, and fire at the southern seat.
Water is situated in Pūrṇagiri; Vāyu is established in Oṃkāra;
Ākāśa is in all the seats (pīṭhas); these are remembered by me as the constituent elements of the seats.
One should perceive sound, and touch right before it;
taste on the subsequent path, and form in the southern corner.
Within Kailāśa, however, there is the pentad beginning with the subtle element of smell;
and Sadāśiva is always stationed in the space in front of the hand.
The two feet are on the southern seat, while the anus is located in the northern corner;
the generative organ is in the middle of the three [central seats]; these, O [Lord], are my five organs of action.
The ear is in the Jālandhara seat, while the skin is said to be in Pūrṇagiri;
one should know the eye is in the center, and the tongue is in the Kāmākhyā maṇḍala.
The nose is located on the Tisra seat; thus are the organs of knowledge [situated].
The mind is said to be in Kāmākhya, while the intellect is in the circle of Udyāṇa.
They know that egoity (ahaṃkāra) resides in the south and primordial nature (prakṛti) in the west;
the person (puruṣa) is in the central seat. These five are the ornaments of the Kula. In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, it is declared that the twenty-five principles (tattvas) are situated upon the Yoga-pīṭha.
But those endowed with the three qualities should be known with diligent effort.
One should recognize *sattva* in the front, *rajas* in the northern mandala, and *tamas* on the southern path; now hear concerning the five jewels.
Brahmā resides in Kāmarūpa, Viṣṇu in the northern seat (Uttarapīṭhaka),
Rudra in the one named Jāla, and Īśvara in the Tisra-pīṭha.
Sadāśiva is between those two; these five are the agents of creation.
I shall declare their secret designations as they are stated in the seventy million [verses].
Śakara, Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Piṅgala as the fourth;
Sādākhya is the fifth, O Lord—these five are the makers of the immortals.
They are to be constantly worshipped as the bestowers of accomplishment and supernatural powers;
the wise know that Yonimudrā is at Kāmākhya and Karālā is in the south.
Padminī is at Pūrṇagiri within the space between the Ghaṭa and Mudrā; Kadambinī is at Tisrapīṭha; [these constitute] the arising of the five mudrās.
Dhyāna is said to be fourfold: Śyāmavarṇa is Oḍḍiyāṇaka;
Rakta is declared to be Jālandhara; and Pīta is indeed Vāmagocara.
Know that the northern meditation is white in the region called Kāma;
the middle meditation is immovable, while that situated to the south is mobile.
In the north, however, meditation on the two natures is foremost and very stable; O God, the Kṛta Yuga is in the center, and the Tretā Yuga is located in the southern corner.
In the north, Dvāpara is to be known; in front, Kali is said to be located.
Thus, O Maheśvara, the four yugas have been described within the mudrā-cakra.
They know that three trees are situated in a triangle: the Kadamba is known to be at the front, the Bilva is said to be on the right, and the one called Ciñcā is likewise on the north.
Thus, the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha) has been described according to the classification of reality;
O handsome one, I shall now explain the three family trees (kulavṛkṣa) by way of the path of the families (kulamārga).

Both the intellect (*buddhi*) situated within the light and the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) are established as threefold in each of the three ways when there is the latent impression of non-duality (*advaitavāsanā*).

Therein, the state of equal flavor (samarasa) is found through the bliss of the vulva (bhaga); having reached the mind where only a fraction remains, the Kadamba-like cluster of energies whirls about.
In the support of the *maṇipūrṇakalā*, one is always born and dies;
the Self speaks eternally, while the *kadamba* cluster resounds.
And the *bilva* arises as a drop (*bindu*) from the upward friction [of the breath];
through the distinction between the seen and the unseen, it is designated by the name of the *ciñciṇī* tree.
O Mahādeva, the instruction on the trees—the three family trees—is declared to be outside; he who knows this is said to be a seeker of the goal.
Śrīnātha said:

"O Goddess, you have told me the glorification and the knowledge of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) by which practitioners attain perfection; yet there is another doubt of mine—please explain it out of your grace."
The venerable Vakrā said:
"O God, I have not told this to anyone; I am telling it to you. (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
I have not revealed [this] to Brahmā, the primordial deities, and the others.
I shall relate to you that which was brought down by that supreme deity, Parameṣṭhin, as the cause for the attainment of self-knowledge.
I shall relate to you exactly what occurred previously:
Śrīkaṇṭha, Śaṅkara, Ananta, Sādākhya, and likewise Piṅgala—
these five are the pervasive ones in the world among the fourfold collection of beings.
Śrīkaṇṭha is to be known as the earth, and Śaṅkara is said to be the waters.
Tejas is known as Ananta, while Vāyu is called Sādākhya;
Ākāśa should be known as Piṅgala—these five are the creators of the universe.
Thus, this Lord Ciñciṇīnātha, whose great austerity has attained the perfection of the Command, stands ready to exercise both restraint and grace over the fivefold deity.
One should know that with a mind that has become fluid through the state of omniscience,
one moves thus through the world of the moving and the non-moving by means of the practice of mad conduct.
As it has been said: "The one named Piṅgala, the Lord of Siddhas, who is free from ailment, omniscient, all-pervading, and eternal, has descended upon the surface of the earth."
On the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, in that most excellent land composed of gold and jewels,
richly adorned with the splendor of various gems, and auspicious with its peaks of precious stones.
On the surface of the great Ocean of Milk, where the waves are its constant washing of the rocky floor,
and which is frequented by hosts of perfected sages, gandharvas, gods, and asuras;
In the Kumārikā-khaṇḍa,
Umā, the daughter of Dakṣa, having bestowed her grace there,
manifested an incarnation in four forms within the land of Bhārata.
In the city of the three worlds, you are the supreme savior of all people; O beloved one who effects the distinction of lineages for those submerged in the ocean of existence!
The first is Mitrānātha; Caryānātha is the second;
the third is known by the name Ṣaṣṭha; and the fourth is named Oḍḍīśa.
O lotus-faced one, this first tetrad descended in the beginning of the four ages for the sake of authority over the four seats, O best of days.
This venerable Oḍḍīśanātha is renowned by the name Tūṣṇīśa;
having assumed that single body by his own will, he [manifests] again in nine ways.
O Lord, in the Kali age, he will himself become his own disciple;
this distinction in names is mentioned here for the sake of favoring the world.
Gaganendra, Mahākubja, Ratneśa, Padmabhāskara, Devavaktrāmṛta, and another, Bhairavābja, is the fifth.
Kamalārka, Śivāmbhoja, Rāmatattvātman,
and Kṛṣṇamārtaṇḍanātha— these nine are the leaders of the Siddhas.
In the city called Pauṇḍra, in Ahicchatra, in Śrībhogavardhana,
in the delightful city of Pāṭalī, and in Māyāpurī, O fair-faced one!
In Kanyakubja, Alampura, Ayodhyā, and Vardhamānaka—
in these places, O Lord of Gods, those born of divine and human wombs [attain perfection].
Endowed with the power of the yoga of knowledge, she is self-supported within the Kaulika lineage;
she has been graced, O Lord of Gods, by the God born from the solar orb of the Command— [as described] in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
O Lord,
through the five full days of the months of Śrāvaṇa, Āṣāḍha, Vaiśākha, Caitra, and Kārttika,
you shall manifest your descent in succession by means of three kinds of divine rays that bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The reality of the five Lords, beginning with Gaganeśa and Ādinātha, has thus been declared.
Likewise, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Kaumāra, Mṛga, and Caitra;
on the twelfth, the seventh of the Sun (Sunday), and the fourteenth of Phālguna.
This secret, which is difficult to find on earth, has been proclaimed as belonging to the four lords of accomplishment, Kamala and the others; it must not be disclosed hastily.
The first, the second, and likewise the eighth in reverse order—
these three have merged into the supreme abode, free from the continuity of rebirth.
So too are the third, the fifth, and the sixth, as well as the other.
They were instructed by the Lord of Munis out of compassion for the sake of grace.
For these three eminent ones, whose vital energy is drawn upward, have gone to Kalpagrāma;
those [fires] are the ninth, the seventh, or the fourth, as before.
In the illustrious Santāna lineage, three— the eldest, the middle, and the youngest—
are proclaimed in order as the lords of emanation (sṛṣṭinātha) and other leaders of the Siddhas.
Possessing sharp command, they are easily managed when attentive, yet they delight in both punishment and favor;
they bestow the nectar of worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the entire universe of moving and unmoving beings.
Intoxicated by the pride of the intoxicant of knowledge, with eyes playful with bliss,
and satisfied by the bliss of their own true nature, they are remembered as those who accomplish the power of the Command.
With minds that have become unified through the state of omniscience,
all [beings] on the surface of the earth engage in the difficult practice known as the conduct of a madman.
In age after age, they shall be appointed to the land of action;
having arrived there, they will wander in the auspicious and excellent island of Candra,
which is endowed with every kind of wealth such as jewels, gems, and gold.
In that city of supreme bliss (Parānandapura), within the Kumārikā-khaṇḍa, which extends for seven yojanas;
In the triangle, three monasteries stand, possessing auspicious characteristics;
they are enriched by the splendor of the sun at midday and are replete with knowledge and realization.
In the direction of Nalāśā, the Saumya-rakṣās are to be known as imperishable in their sequence;
in them dwell those Siddhas who are preeminent in the power of knowledge and yoga.
For one hundred and one years, they remained intent upon their divine practice;
during this interval of time, the arrival of the flowers occurred.
In the past, during the great festival of Hara’s beloved, which brings the joy of the winter season,
on the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, he was adorned with the practice of non-duality.
Having assumed a fierce form for himself at the time of twilight within the entirety of the city of Śrīnagara,
the Supreme Lord established himself in the form of a madman for the sake of sport.
Known by the name Gaganendra, he was renowned as Vṛkṣanātha;
in this world, he was called Kūrma and reached the limits of the royal palace.
The daughter of King Śrīcandrabimba was Gaganāvatī.
The maiden, sixteen years of age, is endowed with beauty and youth.
Surrounded on all sides by men, women, eunuchs, children, maidens, and the most excellent of beings, that girl mocked him, saying, "Who is this who has come here?"
In the practice of the Piśāca and Ucchuṣma, there is unprecedented hair-raising terror.
Upon hearing that, he laughed at the eightfold terrifying [sight] there,
which was [accompanied by] a hundred thousand and more than a portion.
Having let out a cry, he vanished once more in half a moment.
The daughter of that tiger among kings, along with the city folk, was struck with wonder;
she lost consciousness, trembling with fear, her eyes agitated by confusion.
As the night drew to a close, the tremulous, tremulous-eyed woman was sleeping in the inner apartments;
she received this command: "Arise, for that Lord of the World has arrived."
This glorious Mūlanātha has manifested directly within the world of moving and unmoving beings for the sake of bestowing grace upon all creatures; go to him alone for refuge.
The Lord, who consists of eternal bliss, always dwells in the midst of the moon's radiance;
when he is worshipped by that [moon], the desired eternal accomplishment comes to be.
With garlands intense with divine fragrance, with incense, perfumes, and ointments;
with various foods of diverse flavors, with abundant divine sweetmeats, with many kinds of candied sweets, and with various liquors of the six tastes.
With divine offerings of wine, meat, and choice flavors, and with manifold hymns and praises;
Having praised the god of invisible form, she should pass that night;
then, having adorned herself, she rises from her bed, filled with the bliss of the heart. —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Endowed with every requisite and accompanied by her maidservant,
the maiden went to that hermitage where Siddheśvara was staying.
Having approached with humility according to the prescribed rite, she, together with her retinue,
worshipped the Protector, the Omniscient One, the Lord of Causes, with perfect offerings.
Being pleased with them, he indeed taught them the sequence of the Khecarī;
gazed upon by the command of the venerable Lord, they all attained the power of moving through the sky.
Then all the hosts of gods, their eyes wide with wonder, looked at one another and spoke to each other.
Rudra, Upendra, Viriñca, and the others, filled with great wonder,

[realized] that neither through recitations, nor austerities, nor various fire-offerings, nor through any spiritual practices, nor through any manifold rituals, [is this attained], but rather effortlessly by the mere command.
Through the grace of Siddhinātha, the supreme state has been attained.
Then all those gods— the Vasus and the Maruts— eager for the bliss of the lineage-knowledge (*kulājñāna*), were endowed with supreme devotion; such was the case in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Sages accompanied by their sons, by their wives, and by their observances of vows—
Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Marīci, and likewise Nārada.
Viśvāmitra, Yājñavalkya, Mānava, and others born of them;
the lords of the Dānavas, other planets, Gandharvas, and leaders of the birds.
Likewise, there were sixteen crores of other supreme gods headed by Rudra,
as well as Jamadagni, Bhṛgu, Dakṣa, Bharadvāja, and Kaśyapa.
The Kinnaras, Apsarases, Nāgas, and other lords of the world born from their portions,
along with seven crores of gods headed by Viṣṇu, together with their wives.
Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Pulaha, Gautama, and the Pracetasas,
as well as the ten classes of Brahmā and others numbering in the tens of millions, are the leaders of the gods.
Thus, these beings, as previously described, situated at the beginning, middle, and end,
arrived in succession at the feet of the Lord of Siddhas; thereafter, the best of gods likewise approached his lotus-like feet.
The supreme drink, which generates ultimate bliss, has been brought.
Various [liquors] produced from palm trees, as well as those from leaf-trees and flowers;
those arising from grapes and sugarcane juice; and those made from honey, molasses, and flour.
There are those made from dates, those from flour, those from *lodhra*, as well as those from *śāli* rice and so forth;
for they are indeed innumerable and manifold—who is capable of describing them all?
And various names of many kinds with delicious colors,
as well as many types of meat, were brought with devotion in diverse ways.
And there were delicious, divine foods to be chewed and eaten, O observer of noble vows, as well as things to be licked, drunk, and sucked, along with perfumes, incense, and garlands.
Having bowed with their heads to the ground according to the prescribed rite, they offered these [oblations];
then, from the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, [the worship proceeds] with songs, great musical instruments, and the most excellent hymns of praise.
Then, having been properly propitiated by the gods who were endowed with faith and humility,
he was served the supreme drink from divine vessels by the excellent Siddhas.
O Leader of the Thirty-three Gods, having first lifted the vessel with your hands while standing on the path of the recipient, you yourself drank the remnant of that drink.
O handsome one, [this] was given by the lords who were pleased, who abide in the state of yoga,
whose forms are naturally clear, and whose eyes were rolling.
Having gathered it together, the best of the gods, the guardians of the world, and those whose wealth is asceticism—
bowing with humility and rejoicing— drank that nectar which surpassed even ambrosia.
By the power of the command of Śrīnātha, all those with impaired senses became possessed of moving eyes, and all were gladdened by supreme bliss.
Therefore, O God, that which is known as the drinking of wine (surāpāna) is indeed proclaimed to be the consumption of that drink; those by whom it has not been tasted are gods, asuras, and rākṣasas.

Then, seeing that Śrīnātha had granted a boon to Śrī Vīrapāna— while the Yātudhānas, who were of a tamasic nature and bereft of their own forms and powers, remained satisfied— the Goddess Pārvatī experienced great joy.
O gods, this becomes the establishment of imperishable supreme bliss.
By yogis, however, [this should be done] everywhere during the worship of mantras and sacrifices,
at a fire-offering (yajña), a funeral rite (śrāddha), a wedding, and during consecrations and auspicious ceremonies.

During the time of the transmission of knowledge and realization, amidst the great battle of the army, [the rite was performed] by the yoginīs, ṛṣis, and siddhas, through the satiation of the gods, the fire, and the guru.
For indeed, there can be no accomplishment where wine is not found;
in the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*,
wine is eternally present and should be worshipped by him.
For those devoid of ritual action and knowledge, lacking devotion and sincerity,
whose conduct is divided for the sake of greed— for them, wine becomes undrinkable.

[One should avoid] those who are nihilists, devoid of truth, lacking in devotion, and merciless; those who are bereft of the purificatory rites of mantras pertaining to the Guru, the Devas, the Fire, and the Yoginīs.
By the drinking of the hero's draught (*vīrapāna*) which I have prescribed, men fall into the Raurava hell;
by that action, these cattle surely fall into hell.
Indeed, by that very means, those who are devoted to the gods, fire, and the guru, and who have been purified by the subtle elements (aṇu), arise as possessors of knowledge who know the three times.
This true *āsava* will always bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is renowned as a perfected substance (*siddhadravya*), known as *aliphalgu* and belonging to the Kaula tradition.
Whenever he goes among those who revile him, O Lord of Gods, he shall remain in the intense hell for as long as the eight kalpas beginning with Brahmā endure.
Viṣṇu is the essence, Brahmā is the support, and Maheśvara is the formless; the goddess Kubjikā is bliss, eternally established in the state of equal flavor (samarasa).
Since the Root Lord indeed exists in a state of manifestation, you must therefore attain the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*).
As long as one does not achieve this unity, how can there be spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*)?
O God, for those who have not performed the Śrīkrama, nor offered libations to the Yoginīs,
but instead drink together with the uninitiated (paśus), there will be hell for the heroes (vīras).
Surā is Śakti; Madya is Śiva; bliss is said to be liberation.
This entire universe, including all that moves and is immobile, extends from Ananta up to Śiva.
The entirety of the sixfold object— whether gross, subtle, or supreme—
becomes satiated by the offering of even a mere drop of the honeyed nectar.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: sacrifices, sacred fords, austerities, gifts, vows, and ritual observances,
as well as hundreds of thousands of millions of recitations, fire-offerings, and worship.
"All of them are not worth even a sixteenth part of Harṣadeva," so spoke the Supreme Lord, having previously bestowed his grace.
Out of compassion and by their own will, those lords vanished right there;
when they had departed, the gods returned to their own city,
and because they were completely satiated with supreme nectar (*amṛta*), they are known as *amaras*.
Then, in the Kali age, for those who have been diminished by eight times eight [sixty-four years], there are four [ages] according to one's own will.
When the years of the worldly era had passed, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the months of Caitra, Āśvina, and Kārttika, they were again [established] by me through my command.
Having made their descent upon Śrīśaila, Pāripātra, and likewise Arbuda,
those supreme men of fierce vajras appeared in succession among the excellent Nāgas.

Having maintained silence for as many years as there are suns (twelve), and having performed the excellent Kula-sacrifice for the sake of worshipping the Śrīkrama, one returns once more to the city of supreme bliss.
Having set out there, they indeed remain in their own respective positions of authority;
the bliss of the name together with its secret is [experienced] in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, arising from the mouth.
