O Piṅgeśa, those born in the lineage of one's own sons— whether superior, middling, or inferior—
will exist in the Kali age according to the distinction between the divine and the non-divine; likewise, O Śvetanātha, there will be the delusion of the mind regarding cruel clouds.
The half-moon, the sun for the Kaulas intoxicated by passion, the solar orb of the Kula.
Kauleśa, Kulamātaṅga, Rudra, Mārtaṇḍa,
Aghora, Caṇḍavega, and the sixth is Ānanda Khageśvara.
Kumuda and Coḍadeva are established as the forms of the rays;
abiding in the division of the three seed-syllables, they are omniscient, all-pervading, and imperishable.
(From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
They have entered the path of the sixteen supports of the universe of moving and non-moving beings;
for these divine ones of great heroism are renowned as the supports.
These very ones, through another division, are declared to be the knowers of the Śrīkrama;
they possess the power of the divine command in the human world, which is non-divine.
These men, in the form of the sun, shall indeed remove the darkness of ignorance for mortals;
understand their names from me.
The Moon, the Lotus, Vatsagulma, and the Sun; the Pillar, Power, and Fire; the Monkey, the Embryo, the Elephant, the Banyan Tree, and the Sole Valour of the Lion.
Trailokyaviraja is the sixth; Śrīpūpātmā is Jayāhnaka; Kāṃsāla is Abhayānanda; and Śrībhogaraleśa is Śobhavān.
Śrībimbavimalānanda, the one named Tīkṣṇa, Vijaya,
Varāṅgarudra, Vīreśa, Śrīdhāra, and Keśaveśvara.
The one called Sahasāmalamudrā, Vaṅka, Vibuddha, and Ḍāmara;
the one called Bhoja, and the sixteenth, which is the first of the groups, consisting of the second, third, and fourth [vowels].
The sixth, the eleventh, and another, these seven are the leaders of the Siddhas;
they abide in authority within the Jyeṣṭha-lineage, as do the seventh, eighth, and ninth,
as well as the tenth, the twelfth, another, and the thirteenth, which is Koṭipūrva.
These seven are proclaimed to reside in the office of the Bāla (Child) [state];
and this pair, numbering five, O fair-faced one,
resides in the office of the Madhyama (Middle), possessing the luster of the sun and fire of the Bāla.
Many others as well, such as Candrabimba and the rest, having gone outside that city, [bestowed] upon the wise a flood of the nectar of the Command for the sake of providing a causal sign.

Thus, by these perfected beings (siddhas) who have emerged from the three lineages, the divine authority has been established through various excellent hermitages in diverse locations. [End of] Kumārikākhaṇḍa.

The lineages of their sons, grandsons, and so forth— though of three kinds— will be innumerable, both divine and non-divine, each distinct from the other. Thus, this creation of Gaganīśa and the others occurs within the Kula lineage.
Having been born from the body of the illustrious Mūlanātha, the thirty-two-syllable deity of manifold forms,
they are declared to be thirty-five in number.
"Even those such as Kubja, whose forms are the void of consciousness (cidvyoma), are likewise absorbed; indeed, the venerable Lords (Śrīnāthas) bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
The Yoginīs are the imperishable ones born of the Kula; they are here called the consorts of the Siddhanāthas in their respective order.
Jñānāmbā, Śrīkujāmbā, Raudrāmbā— who is designated as Vāmā—
Jyeṣṭhāmbā, Ambikāmbā, and Kāmāmbā is remembered as the seventh;
Jālāmbā, known as Pūrṇā, and Oḍḍāmbā they know as the tenth.
Gaganāmbā, Mahāsiddharatnāmbā, and Padmacampakā.
Suravaktrāmṛtāmbā, likewise Lalitabhairavī,
Kamalāmbā, Śivāmbā, Rāmāmbā, and Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā.
Candrāmbā, Kalpaviśvāmbā, Vaṭāmbā, Gulmaśekharā,
Stambhāmbā, Virajāmbā, Raktākṣī, and Kulaśāsanā.
O sinless one, Lakṣmyambā, Sundarākhyā, Kuṭilāmbā,
Vikarāmbā, Vegāmbā, Unmanyāmbā— who grants all desired objects— and Mohinyāmbā, who delights the mind: these are thus proclaimed.

Possessing the supreme awakening to the nectar of immortality and omniscience, they are intent on illuminating [the world] and are capable of destroying the flood of the great noose of death consisting of the three types of suffering;
now follows their sequential description as previously indicated by the venerable lords.
I shall fully proclaim the secret concerning the basis for the distinctions among designations,
by the mere understanding of which and by the recitation of which [the goal is attained].
The accomplishment of the Command proceeds perpetually before the Śrīkrama;
all the deities [are present] with the divine rays that are the sons of Śrīvimalā.
I bow with devotion to that primordial Śrīnātha-Bhāskara, by whom those who have traveled the path beyond peace were initiated into the Kula teaching.
I bow to the preeminent Guru known as Sādākhya, who consists of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman) and bestows grace upon those who tread the path of peace.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
I bow to Ananta Rudra, who is infinite and imperishable, who abides in compassion and grace, and who has not entered the cycle of worldly knowledge.
"I salute that Lord Śaṅkara, O Rudra, who constantly performs auspicious deeds for those dwelling within the sacred seats and for the host of Heroic Mothers."
I bow to that Śrīkaṇṭha, who, having entered the path of cessation, burned away the impurity of illusion by manifesting in various forms.

I bow to that omnipresent Lord Piṅgala, who, having himself drunk the divine command— the nectarine wine— bestowed it [upon others], and who resides within the path of the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).

I bow down to that glorious Guru, the Lord of Friends (Mitrānātha), who out of affection attained friendship with the Śrīdevī at the Eastern Seat (Pūrvapīṭha) and who is sought after by those desiring knowledge.
I bow to Caryānātha, by whom authority was attained through the vow of Kulacaryā at the lotus of the illustrious Southern Seat (Dakṣiṇapīṭha).
I bow to the illustrious Ṣaṣṭhanātha, who, having recognized the group of five [disciples] at the hermitage of Pūrṇagiri, established the sixth chapter.
Having assumed a form of great and terrifying majesty that brings forth the world,
I bow to that Oḍḍīśa who rests upon the lotus of the glorious central seat.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: By him, through the swallowing of the nectar of moonlight, having entered the supreme path,
the restraint and grace of the fire, moon, and sun— which bear the net— were performed.
I bow to that tree of the sky, who holds dominion through intense power within the hermitage of the mind— the moon-lotus in the shade of the wish-fulfilling tree of the lineage.
I bow to that tree of the sky.
For he whose mental continuum consists of true resolve and who possesses pure power is the one by whom the entire universe was made crooked and the vision of the nāgas was [overturned].
I bow to the eternal Ratneśa, who is fivefold in nature, the great hunchback,
and the mother of all the heroic yakṣas in the Great Lotus Grove.
I bow to the illustrious Padmabhāskara,
by whom authority was established in the hermitage of the sage, where he [confronted] the Rākṣasa along with the Guhyakas.
I bow to that Śrī Guru, the mouth of the God, who was initiated;
likewise, [I bow] to the eight Kṣetrapālas at the sacrifice of Śrī Bhairava in Kāśī.
I bow down to that glorious Guru, by whom the sages and yakṣas at Naimiṣa were gazed upon with wrath, and who possesses a fierce lotus-face of terrifying commands.
O secret one, in former times, having consecrated Śatakratu in the Mahendra-kamala garden, he departed for the abode of Mahālakṣmī.
There, in a playful sequence, he performed the drying up, burning,
and tearing apart of all the trees, and then their supreme restoration once more for the sake of his fame.
I bow down to the illustrious Lord named Kamalākīkha,
by whom the two fires of the full time were indeed quenched with divine nectar.
I salute that Śrīnātha, the imperishable lotus of Śiva,
who has been initiated at the junction of the three and four paths at the feet of all embodied beings.
I bow down to that glorious Guru Rāma, the Lord of Jewels, by whose compassion he delights and who has bestowed his grace.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Kāma at Kubjāmraka, Kṛṣṇa at Dvārakā, Kṣitīśvara at Śrīnagarī, Gaṇādhyakṣa in Strīrājya, and [the Lord] on Mount Malaya.

I bow with devotion to that Lord Kṛṣṇa, the sun for the distressed, who is like a fire to the darkness of worldly existence, and before whom even the two self-controlled ones (Nara and Nārāyaṇa) have become his servants.
I bow to him who resides eternally in the primordial support, whose beard and eyes are tawny,
who is intoxicated by the wine of gnosis, and who is the moon-lotus.
I bow to Gulmanātha, who dwells in the midst of the second stage of life, whose radiance is equal to ten million moons, and who assumes the form of a youth.
I bow to that Śakti-fire, which resembles the autumnal sky, with fierce eyebrows and lotus-like eyes, who is the pillar established in the third state of the Self.

I bow to the one named Śrīkapīśa, who shines within the lotus of the fourth power, the foundation (ādhāra-śakti), dispelling the delusions of the intellect and appearing as the slight radiance of bliss.
I bow to that Vaṭasiṃha, who is eternally arisen in the form of rays within the sun-lotus at the fifth foundation, and who is known as Ardhenduvadana.
I bow to Virajeśa, the sun of the Kaula tradition who has ascended to the summit of the five voids within the sixth lotus of the six families, the intoxicated one.
I bow down to that Śrīpūpātmājyānandanātha, the Sun of the Kula, who is eternally arisen within the seventh support.
I bow to that Kaulīśa, the Lord of Sound, Splendor, Fearlessness, and Bliss, who resides in the eighth abode of Lakṣmī, the state where the digits of the three realms are consumed.
I bow to Ratneśa, the elephant of the Kula, whose senses are impaired by the intoxication of tasting the flavor of the expanse of consciousness, residing in the ninth hermitage.
In the tenth [chapter], I bow to that Śrī Guru, Rudramārtaṇḍa, who possesses the brilliance of the vast fire of time, and who is known as Śrībimba Vimala.
I bow to the one called Vijaya-khaḍga in the eleventh stage, the non-terrible one who severs the bonds of karma within the terrible cycle of saṃsāra.
Having entered the state of twelvefold bliss,
he has brought under his control the protector of the field (kṣetrapāla), who is Caṇḍavega in essence and possesses a fierce form.
I bow down to Śrīnātha, the Lord of the Heroes Rudra and Varāṅga,
who shines with a brilliance exceeding gold in the supportless state within the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
I bow to the one called Keśava, whose mouth is the void, the glorious Sixteenth Bliss;
who possesses the luster of sapphire, the thousandfold Self, the Lord of Birds.
I bow to the fire of all mudrās, which has fourteen bases;
it is like a white water-lily in the lotus of the self-abode, possessing the brilliance of the sun, and is numbered by the lunar days.
Or rather, O Lord of the lineage of the gods, I bow to Śrīnātha-Ḍāmara,
who is established in the bliss of the Command (ājñānanda) within the supreme support known as the Visarga.

For the sake of favoring the world, the ancient [teaching] known as the Bhujabalanirvāṇa, which has eyes like the fire at the end of time, is infinite and imperishable; it was formerly proclaimed by Bhojadeva.
With devotion, I bow to that glorious Guru, Ānandaraśmi;
[I offer] four, five, six, eight, half, five, and four added together.
Sustained by the principal [deities] of the three groups of six and eight, it is gradually held within the Śrīpīṭha by the command of the Vimalajñāna-siddharatnakula.
Through the grace and restraint of the world by means of Ānanda and the others,
the primordial source, together with Brāhmī and the rest, is the imperishable, all-pervading Kubjāmbā.

I perpetually salute the immovable Śrīnātha, who bestows all desires such as omniscience and other qualities; he resides in the primary authority of the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the world-teacher whose nature is pure consciousness.
Thus, this supreme secret, which increases the radiance of all commands,
should be recited by one endowed with mental focus,
either in the presence of the Glorious One or according to the sequence of the perfected maṇḍala.
His intense command flashes forth, [destroying] the great fears arising from the flood of misdeeds.
Diseases go to their destruction and enemies remain under one's control,
provided one always keeps the head-joined palms in reverence.
Having enjoyed glorious and abundant pleasures, one may fall into the state of being common with others.
"Because of his resolve in the practice of the Vidyā according to the tradition consisting of nine hundred thousand [verses],
this truth was proclaimed of old by the Unborn One of unmanifest form.
And that which is called the Śrīṣaṣṭha was brought down by him, Siddhanātha."
And their measure is said to be beyond conceptualization;
formerly, five siddhas were brought down at Śilāśekharaka,
and others at Kadambaguhyaka, as well as five at Śrīpura.
Fifty were favored in Śrī Kulūtā;
seven in Anandapura; and fourteen in the glorious Kāmarūpa.

One should know there are three [sites] in Jālandhara; in the West (Paścima), however, they are equal in number to the stars (twenty-seven); likewise, those at the Maṇibhadravaṭa hermitage are known to be equal in number to the lunar days (fifteen);
in Virajā there are four, while at Haṃsadvāra there are seventy.
The number of years in Mahāvāṭa is three hundred in Siṃhala.
There are one hundred and fifty million at Aṭṭahāsa, fifty million at Devīkota, sixty-four million at Pūrṇagiri, and thirty-two million at Pūrṇapāda.
In the illustrious Kollāpura, fifteen others were initiated;
forty in Satādeṣṭa; seventy-five in Gokarṇa;
and likewise, O Lord, in Bālukā and on the auspicious Candrabimba mountain.
Grace was bestowed by the Lord, who is numbered as the eleventh sun.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
"She who was beheld by the four [goddesses] on the western shore at Kālāra,
where destruction prevails, [is the one who grants] fifty hundred [years of life] through compassion for the intense command."
There are thirteen at Badarī, twenty-one at Śāligrāma, eight hundred at Kurukṣetra, and likewise [eight hundred] at Naimiṣa.
In Kanyakubja there are fifty-three; in Surālaya, seven heroes;
at the great tīrtha of Tattvasaṃkhyā, [there are] two hundred; and at Citrakūṭa, [two hundred].
Eighty-one [tīrthas] are fully enumerated at the confluence of the Tripathā and the Vindhya;
twenty-four are proclaimed at the meeting of the Sindhu and the ocean.
O Lord, one hundred and eight [images] were installed at Setubandha;
seven in the field of Godāvarī, and [seven each] in the region of Kaccha and Koṅkaṇa.
In sequence, eighty-four, twenty-four, seventy,
thirty-seven, forty-six are proclaimed in their respective places;
sixteen at Rudrakoṭi, and the same number at Ayodhyā.
In Kāmakoṭi there are sixty-four [yojanas], and likewise in Arbuda it is double that.
In Pauṇḍravardhana, in Kāśī, in both Parā and Aparā, in the land of Oḍra, in Gāndhāra, in Pañcanada, and in Puṣkara.
Likewise, at Urasāyā, Kaliṅga, and Vardhamānapura,
as well as on the bank of the Pampā river, [the practice] moves from seven at the beginning to seven times increased.
In these places, grace was bestowed by the Lord of the Siddhas:
in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
at the ninety-sixth [site] on the bank of the Gaṅgā, and at the glorious Mahodadhi.
In Śvetadvīpa there are thirty-three; likewise, two on Mount Mahendra;
twenty-eight indeed on Malaya; and six hundred on Himālaya.
Likewise, there are forty-five [sites] on Śrīgiri at Caṇḍikāśrama;
and in Dvārikā, O Lord of the Gods, there are one hundred and eighty-one.
In the kingdom of women, in the land called Barbar, in the desert region, and in the abode of the gods,
there are thirteen, ten, eight, and one hundred and one [yojanas] respectively.
Ninety-nine [deities] were correctly beheld on the banks of the Ganges by the great-souled Śrīnātha, out of his supreme compassion.
Thus all these have been described, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
according to the distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest, and by way of the sequence of the divine and the non-divine.
"Indeed, those who have transcended their duties (kṛtyātītāḥ) reside in the supreme Śiva, possessing the authority over the threefold command (trividhājñādhikāraḥ).
Śrīnātha said:
"O lady of excellent complexion, this has been indicated in the tantras for those who are lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhikānām)."
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and pride residing in the mind—
these are the four mortal sins (pātaka), and association with such persons is the fifth.
O Goddess, if one drinks intoxicants, one becomes a denizen of hell;
by even a drop as small as the tip of a blade of kusha grass, one will fall into the Raurava hell.
"O Goddess, the drinking of liquor is declared to be equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
For what reason, O Great Goddess, O Supreme Mother, was it drunk by you?"
In this supreme scriptural tradition of Tantra, O Maheśānī, wine is indeed determined to be the source of the arising of great merit within the Kula teaching.
This doubt of mine remains even today; you should resolve it now.
O Goddess, what is called *madya*, and what is called *surā*? [Kumārikākhaṇḍa]
"Tell me this in its true essence, O Vakrikā, if you are pleased with me.
Śrīvakrā said:
"O Lord of the Gods, my primordial nature is characterized by supreme bliss."
Therefore, O Lord, liquor has been described and revealed to you;
it is called a elixir (rasāyaṇa), filled with supreme bliss.
"Born from the body of Umā and beautiful from the center of the moon,
the God is all-pervading within the state of equal flavor (samarasa), characterized by supreme bliss."
That which produces the bliss of intoxication is then called *madya*;
that which is called the beautiful *surā* is known as *kuṇḍalinī*.
In the uvula she is eternally present as Vāruṇī, that supreme digit;
she is declared to be the spirituous liquor (surā) consisting of the self, abiding within the bodies of the heroes.
That which is intoxication is supreme heroism; that which is heroism is the king of heroes.
Having drunk it, he who follows the conduct of a hero shall attain union with the gods.
Therefore, the "hero’s drink" (vīrapāna) is remembered as that which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In ancient times, on the divine and most excellent mountain Kailāsa, the foremost of peaks, the Cakra was worshipped during the festival of Madana.
O Lord of Gods, the Great Power of the Eight-Eights was [revealed] by the Primordial Lord.
In that divine, supreme wheel, during the great festival of ultimate bliss,
sixty-four names were proclaimed for each individual.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Having drunk [the nectar], all the deities of the sixty-four wheels,
gladdened and individually delighted, bestowed their names upon it as Ānandanandita.
Vīrapāna, ali, khārjūra, water from a water-jar,
kādambarī, Rudra, Siddhi, the beautiful Kaustubha gem,
a vessel filled [with offerings], Puṇḍarīka, the Lord’s banner, and likewise gorocana.
The lord of yogins, the lord of serpents, Karpara, and Giri are the subjects to be proven.
The liberated lunar digit, the light that brings peace to the world and its stars, shines as liberation within the vessel of wine; this is the mudrā by means of the probe of gnosis.
The state, the unmanī, the disposition, the mantra, the vessel, the Lord of the Kula,
the pure, the five nights, the substance, and likewise the host of gods.
Samaya, Pītarāga, Aghora, and likewise Tumburu;
Siddhānta residing in the form of Rudra, Gandharva, and Śaṅkhaśuktika.
The great jewel of authority, the great lineage of the Lord of Yoga,
Naṭeśa, the Bindu, the Savior, and the lotus-faced Yoginī.
O God, Ghaṭaka, Uḍḍāmara, and Bhūti—these sixty-four Rudras are proclaimed; they are known in the circle of yogis as clearly defined designations.
O God, having understood these within the pure sphere of the Kula, one should drink;
for as long as this distinction of the play of the bees is not clearly known.
For that long, wine must not be drunk, as it results in the violation of the command.
Dark, red, rich in beauty, and adorned with the fragrance of perfumes—
such is the drinking of wine which is established in the world as nectar.
But this was perceived by those gods, sages, siddhas, yoginīs, yogins, and kinnaras who have realized the beautiful state of equal flavor (samarasa).
What I have revealed today was done previously; drinking the remainder of wine is mere mockery.
At the time of the arrival of the gods, she arose as one who was menstruating;
therefore, that goddess became renowned, being celebrated by the gods and the siddhas.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
the complete observance (samaya). One who drinks the empowered vidyā situated in a vessel at the front of the mandala, in the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), before the guru—[attains the goal].
He goes to the supreme abode and shall deliver a hundred generations of his lineage,
when he is endowed with incense, service, and libations.
Endowed with devotion, he shall deliver a hundred of his lineage;
O God, when one has not performed the Śrīkrama and has not offered the libation (tarpaṇa).
By drinking according to the ritual of animal-sacrifice, heroes go to hell;
by drinking according to the internal sequence, the state of Rudra is attained.
O God, he who drinks it openly goes certainly to hell;
one must not disclose its source to him, for it will constitute a great betrayal.
The teacher of the lineage should not engage in conversation with that very person; otherwise, there occurs an offense against the Yoginīs and a violation of the Command.
O God, that which is called *madya* is declared to be the supreme commitment (*samaya*) of the Supreme Lord; this must be guarded with great effort from those who do not observe the commitment.
Poverty results from breaking the commitments; death from transgressing against the Guru;
how can there be accomplishment when the Command is violated? By such transgression, one goes to hell.
Having performed the three-fold turning and having asked for forgiveness from the circle of bees,
the mantra-practitioner [should join] the index finger of the left hand with the little finger.
Having formed a fist there, one should then drink the medicinal substance;
having partaken of the lamp, the sacrificial pap, and the food, one should then drink the beverage.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Having offered flowers and incense, O handsome one, one should prepare the vessel of the samaya together with those of one's own lineage, free from conceptual construction.
Ekata: "All the castes are always present within the wheel;
yet all of them have emerged separately from outside the wheel."
The Vaṇī:

having performed the libation with the index finger in the intermediate space within the circle of the earth, those who are satisfied at the junction proceed to fulfillment; being satisfied, they bestow accomplishment.
Having performed the moderate libation in the intermediate space within the circle of the sky, O God, the ancestors are fully satisfied; being satiated, they go to the supreme goal.
Having performed the satiation of the Nameless One, the sequence, and the circle of gurus, all that— along with the three worlds of the moving and the unmoving— is thereby satisfied by him.
"Having performed the libation with the little finger, the Siddhas and the Mothers of Bhairava—the Vīras, Yoginīs, and Ācāryas—depart satisfied; of this there is no doubt."
All humans who have attained perfection in the mortal world are satisfied;
by performing the libation with the thumb, the Rudras are satisfied, and not otherwise.
The deities as well are satisfied, together with the Mothers.
They depart satisfied, of this there is no doubt; perform the libation in five ways.

Movement through the sky, the accomplishment of Rudra, the state of being ageless and immortal, the eightfold supernatural powers, the shaking of the city [of the body], and the attainment of one's desires and wishes are obtained.
By the sprinkling of drops and by the performance of the libation (tarpaṇa),
one obtains the fruit of ten million times ten million [merits] both in this world and in the next.
In this world, one attains fame, renown, and excellence, as well as a distinguished status; moreover, there is radiance in the body and the perfection of the power of subjugation.
Indeed, his time passes in the diversion of amorous play;
O son, whatever desires he may long for, those very desires he obtains. [This is from] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
The practitioner goes to the stainless world beyond, which is liberation;
this is the procedure for the sequence of falsehood (*alika*), including the libations to the deities and so forth.
Having prepared it, one should drink it; O Lord of Gods, one shall attain supreme accomplishment (*parā siddhi*).
Without the substance of the heroes (*vīradravya*), accomplishment is not seen in the Western [Tradition].
Therefore, one should not entertain doubt regarding this Siddhamārga, even if one’s life-breaths have reached the throat.
By means of *ali*, the western path is accomplished; there is no doubt in this.
*Ali* and *phalgu* have been thus explained.
He is not a disciple in the *Kulakrama*; he is a beast in the family of the Yoginīs.
Thus, he who recites the final sequence devoid of joy will become averse [to the practice], and there will be a terrible ruin of his lineage.
His worship becomes fruitless; there is no doubt in this matter.
Ignorance reveals itself to him, and neither the mantra nor the maṇḍala is effective for him.
One should not conceal the sequence, the lineage, or the Kaula secret;
one should never grant entry to the sacrificial ground.
One should avoid it with great effort, shunning it like a mosquito.
The lineage of its transmission was never revealed at any time;
one who is completely free from all doubts and delights in the drinking of heroes attains fitness in the final Kula-shāna.
The state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*) is traditionally defined as doubt; a bound soul is never found among living beings [who lack it].
Having abandoned the state of a bound soul, one should practice the Kulakaula according to the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
When the state of Kulakaula is attained, whence can there be doubt, and whence can there be impurity?
The practitioner of mantra may wander according to his own will; there is no fear in the ocean of existence.
"One should not use a single vessel if [the Guru] is the Lord of the Family (Kuleśvara) in person;
otherwise, the mantras turn away and obstacles arise at every step."

The slender one, situated in the center of the moon, whose mind is transcendent and who carries the flow of *manas*, is merged in the state beyond bliss; she is the true *surā*, not the intoxicating liquor.
And by me this path has been guarded and not revealed to the outside world;
humans do not know it at all, and for that reason they are considered like beasts.
It is [guarded] by the assemblies of all the gods and ṛṣis, as well as by the guhyakas, siddhas, and kinnaras.
It was worn by me around the neck, as well as by the excellent hosts of nāgas;
it is the wine of the gods, the bliss of the gods, born from the one called Kāmākhya.
At the time of sexual union, the wine is indeed the excellent wheel where the Yoginīs reside.
And that which is on the left of the pericarp, carrying the supreme nectar,
is the wine born of the body— excellent, auspicious, and the producer of eternal bliss.
By worshipping with that mudrā of the blissful knowledge of the Krama-kaula, the Supreme Brahman is satisfied; one should not perform this in the midst of the uninitiated (paśus).

That secret must always be concealed; through concealment, one who is joined with the Kaulinī-siddhi, the Vidyā, and the Samaya, and who drinks [the nectar] accompanied by the Mudrā, [attains success].
Having drunk that from the mandala in front of the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha),
he goes to the supreme abode and shall deliver a hundred of his lineages.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Having well understood the sequence of the Self (ātmakrama), one should then perform the drinking.
One should meditate on the vessel as the rising sun and drink the mantra as the rising moon.
In the center of that, one should contemplate a drop (bindu) with a luster equal to a ruby;
one should drink the seventeenth digit, which is perfectly filled with supreme nectar.
O Lord of the God of Gods, that wine which does not originate from grapes or sugarcane is indeed the great, terrifying splendor— the nectar flowing from its very essence.
The yogi should drink wine as the yoga-drink, engage in sexual union as the supreme state,
and consume meat through yoga as the supreme *nāda-bindu*.
The churning of the ocean of one's own intellect by means of sound and a mind of bliss—
this excellence of the "eye of emptiness" (śūnyanetra) is the elixir of purification.
O beloved, one should perform the mental offering of the drink of bliss;
one should know Śrī Bindubhairavī in the field between the eyebrows of the lotus-browed one.
O Lord, this supreme bliss of mental distraction has been explained to you— the arising of the Tilaka of the consciousness of others within tens of millions of mantras.

"O God, having known that which brings about all accomplishments, one should perform everything. Thus [ends] the section concerning the determination of the Pure Sixfold [System] (*vimala-ṣaṭka-nirṇaya*) within the *Kādi* division of the *Ājñāpārameśvara*, belonging to the lineage of the *Mahāmanthānabhairava-yajña*, which emerged from the path of Meru, measures seventy million verses, exceeds one hundred thousand quarters, and follows the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*). This is the introduction.

In the *Svāminīmata*, the *Śrīcaturviṃśatsahasrasaṃhitā* spoken in the *Avvākrama*, this is the bliss named the Arising of the Sequence (*Kramodaya*), within the description of the majesty of the chapter on Projection (*Vikṣepādhikāra*).
Śrīnātha said:
"O auspicious lady, the majesty and the ritual procedure of Harṣadeva have been clearly understood by me today in their proper sequence; however, the [procedure] for Vaṭuka has not been heard by me."
What indeed is his status as a *vaṭuka*, and from where does it arise? What is the purpose of worshipping him, and how is the offering (*bali*) presented?
"Tell me this, O Goddess of Gods: the meditation and worship according to their sequence.
Śrīvakrā said:
[This is] the forty-seventh bliss.
The six-faced lord of the Vaṭukas is my son of great strength.
I have granted authority over the entire Kula tradition;
and the high-souled Lord receives his share of the offerings.
As long as it has not been offered to Vaṭuka, so long is there no [attainment] in the Kula tradition;
[he is] of great form like Kapila-Ugra, wearing a mass of matted hair.
One should visualize before oneself the Lord with tawny eyes, staff in hand, adorned with ornaments of serpents, and surrounded by a multitude of various obstacles.
Śrīnātha said:
O Kuleśvarī, the ritual procedure for Vaṭuka has been understood by me;
I now wish to hear the further tradition concerning the Kṣetrapālas.
The venerable Vakrā said:
"Now listen, O one honored by the great lords of heroes; I shall speak. [End of] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
I shall explain the collection of phonemes so that they may understand it.
I shall state their names individually, one by one:
now there is Āsuri, and another is Indragarbha.
Īśvara, Ugratejas, Ūṣmākara, Ripughnaka, Nirīha, and likewise Deva, Liptāṅga, and Līnamastaka.
Likewise Ekāmra, Aindra, Oghavāha, and another,
Auṣadhi, Tamravarṇa, and the one called Visarga, O sinless one, is the last.
Kanṭhakāra, Gopāla, and another, Apasmara; Vyoma, Vakranāman, Chedaka, and Janmadāhaka.
And the Ṛṣis were Auttara, Ṭaṅkaṭha, Aṇḍadeha, Caṇḍavara, Dṛḍhakarṇa, Uttāna, Pāṇḍu, and Dāmama.
Dharmārambha, Nala, Palitānta, Puṃskṛta, Bṛhadvakṣas, Bhavāṇḍa, Ahlāda, and Yamāntaka are considered [the forms of Śiva].
Raktākṣa, Lambabāhu, Vakṣāyata, Śaśin, Ṣaṭha, Samādhi, the one named Hasa, and another, Kṣapāntaka.
These indeed are the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas), proclaimed by the name Kaulas;
they are innumerable, O Lord of Gods, and should be known by the best of practitioners.
All of them resemble blue collyrium, with long eyes whose corners are red;
intoxicated and agitated, they all drink the liquor of fermented honey.
Adorned with variegated skull-cups and garlands of severed heads, wearing wreaths of the lotus-like heads of great corpses, they are beloved by the yoginīs.
Mounted upon the aggregates of the deceased, these lords of heroes are praised by heroes;
in the offering of oblations and in worship, they all are bestowers of boons.
O Lord, as long as the ritual procedure for the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) is not known, obstacles will undoubtedly arise for practitioners; of this there is no doubt.
Śrīnātha said:
"O Bhairavī, by your grace, the Kṣetrapālas have been known by me in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa."
"Now, indeed, I wish to hear [this] for the benefit of the disciples."
"Tell me, how is the garland of names for an initiated and excellent disciple [bestowed]?
The venerable Vakrā said:
For those disciples who have been initiated into the teaching and are devoted to it..."
Listen now to how they are to be designated and what must be done for them. From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:
A is the bliss of the unborn; Ā is the bliss of the eyes; I is the bliss of the heart; Ī is the bliss of the image.
U is Udayānanda; Ū is Utpannānanda; Ṛ is Śaktyānanda; Ṝ is Līlānanda;
LṚ is Lalitānanda; LŪ is Raudrānanda; E is Somānanda;
AI is Candrānanda; O is Padmānanda; AU is Vijayānanda; AṂ is Kṣobhānanda.
A: Śeṣānanda; Ka: Kulānanda; Kha: Suṣirānanda; Ga: Bhāvānanda; Gha:
Pūrṇānanda; Ṅa: Śikhānanda; Ca: Pātrānanda; Cha: Bhūmyānanda; Ja: Parānanda; Jha: Raktānanda; Ña: Nāgānanda; Ṭa: Vāsānanda.
Ṭha is Rudrānanda; ṇa is Umānanda; ta is Nityānanda; tha is Bhairavānanda;
da is Devānanda; dha is Sukhānanda;
na is Iṣṭānanda; pa is Sūkṣmānanda.
Pha is Vipulānanda; ba is Śivānanda; bha is Bhogānanda; ma is Vīrānanda; ya is Pravarānanda; ra is Vicitrānanda; la is Rupānanda; va is Ātmānanda;
śa is Śobhānanda; ṣa is Vajrānanda.
O Lord, those names, designations, and syllables have been told by me to you.
"O Lord, these [mantras], which are normally unspeakable and cannot be given away, have been revealed by me out of affection for you;
they were not spoken by me but heard from the mouth of Himavat.
They should be known as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and granting boons to disciples."
Śrīnātha said:
"Vajrānanda; that is Netrānanda; Ha is Ājñānanda; Kṣa is Jvālānanda.
Śrīvakrā said:
"O Goddess, I have heard everything regarding the consecration of the disciples."
Now I wish to hear from you the characteristics of their commitments (samaya).
Listen, O God, I shall explain how the practice of the commitments is to be performed.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the garland of names for the initiated disciple has been revealed;
afterwards, one should cause him to hear the rules of conduct (samaya), just as I shall now declare them to you.

Thus, in the primordial descent (*ādyāvatāra*) of the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, measuring seventy million [verses], emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding a hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the first seat (*ādyapīṭha*), in the determination of the six subsequent divisions of the Pure Division (*vimalabheda*) within the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*),
in the *Kādi* division, in the *Svāminīmata*, which is the supreme command of the Lord, accompanied by the venerable twenty-four thousand [verses].
The chapter titled "Description of the Conduct of the Samaya" from the *Avvākrama-bhāṣita*.
Oṃ, may there be well-being!
Homage to the sandals of Śrīnātha! Homage to Śrīgaṇeśa!
In the Manthānabhairavatantra, within the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, Śrīnātha said:
"O Goddess, I have heard everything regarding the meaning of the stages in their entirety;
now I wish to hear the definitive explanation of the *Pūjāsūtra*."
The venerable Vakrā said:
"O Lord, listen; I shall explain the procedure for the Sūtra of Worship. This is the forty-eighth bliss."
By which mere consciousness the lineage of the family is set in motion.
In a solitary, secluded, and delightful place, free from wicked beings,
strewn with heaps of flowers, well-concealed, and perfumed with incense.
When the lord of the tenth house is absent and devoid of the aspect of a quadruped,
in such a great place, O Lord of the Gods, one should face the east.
One should draw the Varuṇa maṇḍala following the procedure for those born of the earth;
first, one should fashion a fourfold grid using well-strung, unbroken lines.
One should draw the mandala with the mantra consisting of five *praṇavas*;
having recited it for the Pervasive One (*vyāpaka*), one should offer a flower in the center.
O Shaven-headed One, O Mine of Jewels, having cast into the center of the mandala three times camphor, sandalwood, and musk consecrated with the five seed-syllables;
First the Guru should cause it to revolve; then the Guru should cause it to pierce;
then the Guru should establish it there—for the Guru alone is indeed fivefold.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: Now, having joined these two, one should cast them along with the five common [substances].
One should place a flower in the middle of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) with the hand facing westward.
Accompanied by the left hand, through a counter-clockwise rotation,
one should utter the five *praṇavas* and place five flowers in the center of that.
One who knows the ritual procedure should worship the five [deities] in sequence, beginning with Akhaṇḍa, on the seat through the general [mantras], and the thumb at the front of the fist.
In the west, however, one should perform the placement ninefold according to the divisions beginning with Amṛta;
in the north, one should place Soma in the circle of Īśāna and Sūrya.
One should place the peak-syllable (kūṭa) in the southwest and the circle of the bindu (binducakra) in the south;
Purandara, the god, in the east, and Varuṇa in the western direction.
One should place the fire [mudrā] in the southeast corner and place the wind [mudrā] in the northwest corner;
then, having raised the hand, [one should join] the little finger, the thumb, and the middle finger.
Through the application of the three mudrās, one should sequentially fashion the three girdles below the hands; the ninth is the presiding seed-syllable.
One should worship Śrīnātha in the center with five handfuls of flowers;
likewise, one should worship the two mandalas on the right and the left with liquor.
It should be performed in a counter-clockwise direction; one should place two seed-syllables at the navel.
One should place the seed-syllable of breath on the left, and place it on the right side of the navel.
The seat has been fully described, O Vaṭukeśvara and Yoginī;
it is before the mudrā-maṇḍala, and the maṇḍalas are each distinct.
One should always perform the ritual of offering by placing the seed-syllables starting from the fifth;
specifically, on that very western path, within a mandala measuring five finger-breadths.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
one should place the peak-syllable known as Śakti together with the Bindu in the center;
thus, it is adorned with the nine maṇḍalas by means of that which rests upon the tortoise-throne.
Thus indeed has the maṇḍala of the Guru been described in the three lineages:
water, perfume, food, flowers, meat, and incense for the argha offering.
O sinless one, one should cause the vessel to be filled with the right hand;
and with the right hand, one should form the staff-mudrā for Kṣetrapāla on the right side.
Furthermore, O handsome one, the Yoginīs [should place] the vessel with their left hands,
holding it in the right hand and placing it in the center of the mandala.

Having offered these three oblations and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) once more, he should sit down, perform the hand-gesture (mudrā), and then install the power of Śambhu (Śambhu-śakti).
Having performed the fivefold placement with both hands for the sake of purification, as well as the burning [of impurities],
one should form the hollowed palms in the form of lightning and flashes of light.
One should perform the nourishment (*āpyāyana*) with both hands turned upward;
one should do so with the first quarter of the mantra, accompanied by the moon (*candra*) and the *visarga*.
One should then brandish the weapon [mudrā], which resembles the fire of cosmic destruction;
this is the Āgneyī Ciñciṇīmudrā, the bearer of the command of Ciñciṇī.
Having abandoned both merit and demerit, one should press down upon the lower [lotus];
one should then visualize that red lotus facing downwards and fully blossomed.
There, in the center, is Mahālakṣa, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons,
with a form like coral, resembling the great crest of a flame.
— From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
By means of the flow in the central channel, she is led upward by the Power (śakti) into the Supreme,
being gradually consumed until the state of equal flavor (samarasa) is reached.
First, burning has been described; when the body is burnt, it goes to dissolution.
Then there is the re-nourishment from the top until the end of the pacification; this is the supreme *kalā*.
One should contemplate the supreme, most subtle channel, which has the form of a lotus fiber,
situated in the center [of the body] as far as the circle of birth.
O Śambhu, having first performed the nourishment (āpyāyana), thereafter one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa):
in the case of the Mūrti-pakṣa, one should place the Command (ājñā) in the middle of the hands, and in the case of the fist-form (muṣṭi), one should place it on both fists.
At the tip of the hand, one should place the thumb upon the upward-facing [palm] at the top;
the index finger faces forward, while the middle finger faces south.
One should place the heart on the ring finger, the back [of the hand] on the little finger, the head on the thumb, and the crown of the head on the index finger.
The *śikhā* [mantra] is indeed on the middle finger, while the *kavaca* is on the ring finger;
the *netra* is on the little finger, and the *astra* is on the back of the hand.
This is declared to be the ritual placement (*karanyāsa*) in sequence, beginning from the perspective of the [five] forms (*mūrti*).
One should place the Mūrti-mantra in the heart, extending from the head down to the feet.
This is declared to be the Ājñā-tattva, which faces upward and ends at Śakti.
One should place the Mūrdhavakā-mantra on the head, and the Pūrvavaktrā-mantra on the face.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the southern [face] is in the center of the heart, the northern in the secret circle,
and the western face is in the two feet; this is proclaimed as the placement of the staff (daṇḍanyāsa).
One should place the upper face upon the upper part, and the root [syllable] upon the crown of the head;
the eastern face in the east, and the southern face in the south.
Having placed the northern [syllable] in the north, one should place the western [syllable] in the west;
having placed the heart [syllable] in the heart, one should assign the head [syllable] to the head.
Having assigned the crest-mantra to the crest, the armor to all the limbs,
the eye-mantra to the two eyes, and the weapon-mantra to the backs of the hands;
Having performed this placement on the knees, one should subsequently place the vessel;
likewise, the incense and the water for honor (*argha*) should be placed upon the support in the Śrīkāra maṇḍala.
Through *prasāda*, there shall be fragrance; and through *rāva*, flowers.
One should utter *sauṃkāra* within the circle of Varuṇa.
One should purify everything with the Astra-mantra and envelop it with the Kavaca-mantra;
one should perform the nourishment (āpyāyana) with the Netra-mantra and the Dhenu-mudrā.
Listen now to how one should subsequently assign Mālinī and the others:
Mālinī, Śabdarāśi, Trividyā, and the Aṣṭaka of Aghorikā.
The twelve-verse garland, arising from the twelve limbs, consists of six parts and five jewels; it extends from the feet up to the crest-lock.
O God, one should place [the mantras] upon the girdle in reverse order according to the instruction;
O Śambhu, she is radiant with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra), and both her shoulders are endowed with those [mantric] graspings (grahas). —From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Endowed with sixteen knots, gladdened by the bliss of the Navātman,
the placement of the "mouth-casket" (mukhakośa) and the desired "bolt of the cloth" (paṭārgala) [are performed].
The sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa) has been fully described as existing through sixteen divisions;
having performed this sixfold deposition, one should extract the Krama maṇḍala.
Thus indeed has the mandala of the Guru been declared in the Western Tradition.
Śrīvakrā said:
One who is himself liberated from the mandala of the Guru should cause the mandala of the Guru to be made.
There, at the three times, one should ascend the fivefold [path] with the Lord of Kūṭa;
then, O Lord, one should deposit the division of the couple within the internal limbs.
One should extract the two offerings empowered by great strength;
joined with the binding of the mudrās, may your favor be restored from what was broken.
Having attained the arising of compassion and subsequently taken possession of a body, he is pierced by the inner thread— the thread of gnosis.
Freed from the knowledge of the sūtras, one should pierce the maṇḍala of the peak-syllable;
having recited the peak-syllable one hundred thousand times, being fully concentrated on the mantra-recitation.
Then, after the entry into the city, there is the abiding within the Gahvara in the body;
that Gahvara should likewise be brought forth from one's own self externally in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Having emerged from the supreme body, one should extract [the syllables] from the supreme body;
in the embodied and supreme reality, there is a pair of steps for each step.
Having repeatedly divided the triad, the triad, the tetrad, the tetrad, the hexad, and another hexad, each into their respective individual places;
Having first assumed the Kuṭilā [mudrā] with five fingers,
and having performed the throbbing of the final finger of Pūrṇimā, Amāvasyā proceeds.
The first lunar day (pratipadā) is remembered as being in the middle, free from both sides;
one whose body has been made complete by the flow of the nectar of realization (ājñā).
Having indeed abandoned the five wheels and attained the sixth, which is primordial and free from affliction, one should install it; these five are its pervasive [aspects].

By means of the process of emanation for [ordinary beings], but by means of withdrawal for yogins, one should constantly cast off the primary limbs (aṅga) therein and instead apply the secondary limbs (upāṅga).
One should place the three mudrās according to the division of the three lineages; having first placed the triad of mudrās, one should extract the sequential maṇḍala.
One should draw the *gahvara* in the east and likewise pierce it with the *gahvara*.
One should surround it from above with a circular line, even within the deep cavity.
Then, one should have it constructed, filled with the twenty-four principles (tattvas),
with eight petals arranged in order in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should arrange three girdles on the exterior in sequence; having first made a square city and subsequently divided it, this is the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
"Having established the sky-flower in the center according to the instruction on the abyss—
O Lord, having thus described the mandala, one should extract Lakṣmī therein."
O God, one should subsequently bring forth the three vessels in the place in front; first, one should arrange them on the left according to the division of the five Brahmans.
In that regard, the instruction according to the division of the churning-stick is fivefold;
there, one should place its commitment (samaya) in the center of Ānandapura.
Then, having produced joy and satisfaction, [he places] the arghya vessel on the right;
thereafter, it is separated from the arghya vessel and permeated by the Gāyatrī mantra.
One should worship with the *arghya* offering using the supreme seed-syllable together with Śiva,
as well as whatever flowers, incense, and so forth are prescribed according to the sequence in one's own ritual rules.
One should indeed extract this entire collection within the internal sacrifice;
one should remember the flood of the Guru, the *olipīṭha*, and the secret sign of the flower.
Among them, one should worship the Self below, starting from the *oli* and the *pīṭhas* in sequence,
up to the four *pīṭhas*, which constitute their four locations.
There are four leaders: the Siddhas [arise] in sequence from the *oli* and the seats (*pīṭha*) onwards;
at the syllable *Oṃ*, the fifth Lord [is reached], according to the sequence of the sixfold command (*ājñā*).
Beginning from the front corner and proceeding clockwise to the center,
there are again four Siddhas in sequence, starting from the eastern seat (pīṭha).
One should indeed worship the host of yoginīs in this manner in the seats of the Siddhas;
one should worship the triad in the three corners according to the oral instruction.
There are twenty-seven divisions according to the sequence of the six faces. In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*, the upper face is in the middle of the peak, and the root is from the mere upward direction.
First, in the northeast corner, there is the face of Dakṣa;
on the south is the right face; on the north should be the left face; and in the center is the western face.
The heart is in Kāmarūpa, while the head is said to be in Pūrṇagiri;
the crest-lock (śikhā) is in the sacred seat of Jālandhara, and the armor (kavaca) is in the sacred seat of Tisra.
The Eye is indeed in the half-moon, while the Weapon is in the circle of the bindu;
in the center, Ājñā, the thirty-two-syllabled one of hideous form, is to be worshipped.
On the petals, beginning from the east and proceeding counter-clockwise, are the eight Kulas;
on the girdle are twenty-five divisions according to the streams of the Puruṣas;
and by means of oral instruction, one should know the twenty-eight mandalas.
On the third girdle, however, there are sixty-four deities.
The Current of the Embodiments (sarvogha) is the first essence; the Current of the Sequence (kramaugha) is the second;
the Current of Knowledge (vidyaugha) would be the third; and the Current of the Family (kulaugha) is the fourth.
Having understood that the fifth is the stream of persons (*puruṣaugha*) and the sixth is the supreme divine stream (*divyaugha*),
which is divided into six types of knowledge (*vidyā*), one should begin the sacrifice.
O God, one should worship the eight fields in sequence, starting from the east, as the eight directions— namely, the floods (oghas)— beginning with Prayāga.
One should worship the Samaya [deities] with three divisions in the three corners;

the Mothers are at the front of the praise, while the Mantrakhaṇḍa is on the right and the Uttara [is on the left]. Having reached the three corners of the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, there are two hundred and ninety-two [deities].
O Maheśvara, one should worship the goddess Trikhaṇḍābhairavī with diligence.
Having pierced through the three instructions, the eightfold accomplishment is sought;
in their midst, the deity's sign and the arising of the lunar days proceed.
O Bhairava, one whose mind and self are absorbed in that should perform sacrifice according to the principle of emanation.
Whichever Vidyā belongs to whom, that is his Śrī in Oḍḍiyāṇaka.
One should purify the city until it reaches the number thirty-two;
when the city is purified, all is purified—this is the command of the Supreme Lord.
All violations of the samaya are purified throughout the four ages;
having understood this at the three corners and at their end, those seeking knowledge should exercise great authority in the house of the illustrious Candrapura.
O Śambhu, this is the internal sacrifice within the teaching of the three lineages (oli).
"He who knows that which has emerged from the command of Śambhu is a yogin"—
this is the thread of instruction for those who have cultivated their minds at every step.
The command of the deity produces the conviction of the paralysis of the fetters and so forth for whoever introduces the sequence here, even if it is devoid of the instruction of the Sūtra.
It shall turn its back upon him and does not follow him in the next world;
O Lord of the World, it is not to be revealed, for it brings joy to the heart.
The task, which reveals the command of Śambhu, must be performed more secretly than a secret.
Thus ends the section on the Krama-sūtras within the twenty-four thousand [verse] scripture of the primordial descent.
The forty-ninth bliss:
Śrī Kaulīśa said:
"I do not know the internal sacrifice, which is established as mental."
His meditation consists of the entire divine body together with its characteristic marks.
"Out of compassion, speak, O Mistress of the Gods, if you are pleased, O Kubjikā!
Śrī Kubjikā said:
"O Lord of the Gods, this question has been sung by you, yet it is most secret."
O Rudra, one should guard everything that is to be protected with great effort, as if it were one's own life;
one should assume the *samaya-mudrā* and take the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) or the auspicious posture (*svastikāsana*).
At the time of dawn, having bathed and standing facing west,
one should sit upon a soft seat with a single-pointed mind, composed in meditation.
Having stepped upon the region of Sutala and struck below,
one should perform exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), and then restrain the mind during retention (kumbhaka).
Having recollected one's own seat, [one should meditate on] the circle of power (śaktimaṇḍala) in its center,
which resembles a mass of splendor and illuminates the vault of the sky.
In the center of that, one should pierce the drop (bindu), which resembles a blazing flame,
having the form of an unbroken circle and being permeated by the five winds.
One perceives one's own form as a reflection, circular like the orb of the moon;
therein, worship should be performed through the internal experience.
Having raised the supreme Spanda-kuṇḍalinī from the seat of the *kanda* by means of the innate *nāda*, the maiden should be awakened within the solar orb at the foundation (*ādhāra*).
Resembling blazing gold, it destroys and annihilates darkness;
its nature is that of a circle of lightning-garlands, emerging from iron filings.
The knower of mantra should enter the lunar orb with the anusvāra;
for Māyā, Bindu, Ātman, Nāda, Śakti, and likewise Śiva [are present there].
It should be applied gradually, step by step; for by breaking through the sequence in due order, the extremely subtle sound, once perceived, proceeds without interruption.
Having gone there, the yogi delights in Kaulinī, the mistress of the Kula;
there, in the center, resides the divine Supreme Lord known as Haṃsa.
Although bodiless, it resides within the body, presided over by the power of consciousness (cicchakti) in a sequential manner;
through the mere perception of that [power], the differentiation of the sequence proceeds.
The sound of broken bell-metal is heard by the ear of wisdom;
it is proclaimed as the sound of the bell within the solar mandala.
The bell is the pledge (samaya) of the Mistress, fashioned by Viśvakarman.
Within the inner circle, the bell is remembered as the messenger (dūtī) who grants all desires.
Outside, a messenger made of bell-metal has arrived for the sake of stability;
the state of the lamp, the eye, and the mind is the cognition of "existence."
The water remembered at the dvādaśānta falls into the circle of the yoni;
it is known as Malaya, Kailāsa, and Sandalwood (Candana) which brings about tranquility.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: That digit which is filled with semen within the mandala known as the triangle, O God, she is afflicted by desire; one should pierce her with tranquility.
By means of that nectar, the mental yogis become intoxicated and ecstatic;
having tasted that nectar of wine, there is no longer any semblance of ordinary wine.
From cowherds and women to barbarians, Śūdras, and those who are commoners—
all were intoxicated and maddened on every side by that very yellow liquor.
But the liquor is artificial and external, common to all living beings;
it shines upon the three-cornered cloth with a ruby-red hue.
That very flesh is declared to be what should be accepted in the sequential worship;
it is known by the name Juṣṭacaṇḍālinī, and it is the Vidyā within your lineage.
One should perform the entire meditation using the true insignia of the Vidyā;
for that Vidyā which has been described to you, O handsome one, is mine.
Within the three circles at the end of the triangle, hanging down toward the lower region,
I, Kubjikā, should indeed be meditated upon in the form of the Vāḍava fire.
She has three eyes, six arms, and six faces, and possesses great strength;
she is dark green, red, and curved, and is adorned with all kinds of jewels.
She was most enchanting with bracelets, armlets, and necklaces, as well as with earrings; she had moon-like ear-ornaments and wore the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
Her head-ornament was the Śakti, beautifully adorned with garlands of jewels;
she had thick, curly locks of hair, slender limbs, and lovely eyes.
The goddess is naked, with her hair loosened; she is clothed in nakedness, sky-clad, fickle, full as the moon, and has round faces from both eyes.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
She whose face blazes with three triangles, whose radiance is like a mass of lightning,
who is perfectly filled with buttocks as firm as mountains, and who is worn thin yet adored by the Siddhas.
Her feet are adorned with anklets, her waist is fully decorated with a girdle,
and a flower-cluster inlaid with jewels rests in her left hand.
In the south, she holds a trident in her right hand and a skull-cup in her left;
this Vidyā of the Sword is eternally manifest in her right hand.
Adorned with all ornaments and wearing a multitude of Vāsuki serpents as necklaces,
she had a red face, was short in stature, and roared like the sound of thunderclouds.
With a wrathful gaze like that of a great lion, seated upon a lion throne,
her face uttering loud, boisterous laughter, she dances within a circle of fire.
With all her limbs complete and adorned with various ornaments,
she was crooked-limbed, stiff, misshapen, and terrifying.
One should contemplate Mātaṅgī, who delights in wine, who is intoxicated with passion and exceedingly languid, who rains down infallible and abundant [grace], and whose nature is nectar.
Completely merged in the great void, flowing through the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra),
Bhairavī— who is by nature the sustainer— nourishes all living beings;
her hips, neck, and buttocks are her limbs, and her eyes are slightly contracted.
One should pierce the target at the end of the *śakti* and gaze into the great void (*mahāvyoman*).
There the goddess, naked and dwelling [there], perfectly complete and most beautiful, surrounded by gods, is situated within the Great Womb.
Beholding the heroic practitioners and bestowing the fruit upon all, she is called Kaulinī; she is extremely secret and equal to the Guru.
Whatever desired object there may be, all that has been told by me;
this is the *Divyaughasūtra* from the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*, the definitive teaching concerning the Goddess of the Sacred Seat (*pīṭhadevī*).
This is the mudrā; with the six seats, one should apply the characteristic of meditation.
Afterwards, there is the sixfold ritual placement (vinyāsa) and the sixfold thread of meditation.
Immediately after worshipping the yoga conjoined with the sequence of the names,
my own oral tradition (kramāmnāya) has been directly indicated, not merely deliberated upon.
With various golden flowers, well-prepared fragrant offerings, sandalwood, vessels of honey, and food offerings such as *phalgu* and other fruits.
Having offered, according to the rules and with devotion, various types of lamps made from wheat and other grains before the Goddess, she who was well-concentrated [performed the rite].

Alternatively, one should fashion a parasol out of barley flour according to the number [of deities], with a height of two finger-breadths and a diameter of two finger-breadths, for the sake of the family deity.
The lamps should be fashioned in the shape of vulvas according to the prescribed measurement;
having done so, one should recite the auspicious *Mālinīdaṇḍaka* hymn at night.
Whether it be the eightfold enclosure of the Goddesses or likewise by means of the three lineages (oli),
one should perform the salutation according to the prescribed rule at the conclusion of the worship.

One should perform the three-fold triple-limbed [salutation] encapsulated by three *praṇavas*, then, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with five *praṇavas*, one should pay homage with the five-limbed [formula].
Then, having arranged the groups [of syllables], one should perform the prostration with eight limbs;
likewise, the three-limbed, the five-limbed, and the third, the eight-limbed prostration.

Having performed three prostrations, one should repeatedly bow down like a staff; having recited the family mantra (*kulavidyā*) eight times, four times, twice, or once, one should offer the food oblation (*naivedya*).
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
having performed the sequence of the forehead mark (tilaka), one should present the food offering (naivedya).
Having dismissed Bhairavī by means of the binding of mudrās, one should worship the Samayā;
having worshipped her, O God, the devoted practitioner should pay homage with the Root Sūtra.
Having applied the *tilaka* marks in sequence within one's own lineage according to the tradition,
and while seated upon the tortoise-posture (*kūrmāsana*) with both hands bound in the ritual mudrās;
The *caruka* of the Kaula tradition is supreme and difficult even for the gods to obtain;
first come the lamps of the *kula*, and after that, the substance of honey.
One should consume the sacrificial oblation mixed with meat with a mind free from conceptual construction;
this great spell of seven syllables is known as the bringer of all accomplishments.
Recited seven times, this Vaṭuka becomes purified and bestows success;
there is no duality with fellow practitioners, and great non-duality with the Guru.
One who is at odds with elder brothers, at odds with those previously initiated,
and who seeks to understand the opinions of the senior ministers and counselors— even if they are well-versed— [is not to be trusted].
One should not give the remains of the sacrificial porridge (caru) or a flower even to one who is the eldest;
otherwise, O God, a violation of the command occurs.
Having caused [the disciple] to consume the sacrificial porridge (caru) and the meat-wine according to the ritual injunctions,
and having sipped water (ācamana) to become pure, one should worship the Vidyā and the Samaya.
Whatever else besides that is purified here, of this there is no doubt;
having placed the floral remains upon one's head, one should dismiss the mandala.
Thereafter, one should attract [the deity] by means of the root-vidyā in reverse order;
this is declared to be the sequential worship, which one should perform during the time of a festival.
Those born into the family of the Yoginīs attain the eternal state. In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa it is said:
"Birth is one thing, ritual action is another; time is different, and even the mantra is otherwise."
He who speaks otherwise regarding the mandala, the sandals of the Goddess, her worship,
or the scripture within the lineage of the Siddhas, shall become the most sinful of all.
Truth, truth, and again truth—this triple truth has been spoken by me. It must not be given to one who is not a disciple, nor even to one's own son, O Bhairava.
It should not be given even to one's own brother, especially if he is not a devotee;
it should not be given out of pressure, nor indeed out of greed for wealth.
Devoted to the guru, devoted to the lineage, and observers of the conduct of the pledges—
to them this sūtra should be given, indeed to one for whom [the teacher] is pleased.
Those who give and those who receive the Guru’s command out of sequence shall both go to hell for as long as the dissolution of ten thousand aeons.
Thus ends the Sūtra on the Meditation on the Form of the Inner Sacrifice within the glorious Caturviṃśatisāhasra. The venerable Vakrā said:
"One should perform meditation according to one's state; one should practice with the Yonimudrā. (This is the fifty-first bliss.)
Having worshipped in sequence that which resides within the body, as it has been revealed in the Sūtra.
Śrī Kaulīśa said: O Great Goddess, [explain] how the sequential worship (kramapūjā) occurs within one's own body,
and in which specific locations it is accompanied by the extraction of mantras (mantroddhāra).
O Goddess, likewise, the fourfold Vidyā has been well-concealed and not revealed;
out of compassion, O Bhairavī, Mistress of the Gods, speak it for me, your devotee.
The venerable Vakrā said:
Then the entire sequence of worship proceeds according to its proper order;
one should worship the lineage of gurus on the head and Kāmarūpa in front.
The seat called Ātman is situated in the heart; the lineage of seats (pīṭhaugha) is located on the head, in the front corner, on the left, on the right, and in the center, in due order.
One should worship the four seats within the mandala of the faces;
[specifically] in the middle of the face, in the left eye, in the middle of the eyebrows, and in the right eye.
Having likewise worshipped at the tip of the nose, thereafter one should worship the sixfold knowledge;
in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, [one worships] in the heart, on the left path, on the left shoulder, and likewise elsewhere.
Between the eyebrows, on the right shoulder, and on the right path—these three constitute the group;
this wheel of the Goddess consists of six [deities], which one should worship according to the principle of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāya).
Then one should worship the four Siddhas below that;
indeed, in the wheel of birth (*janmacakra*), one should worship the group of five Yoginīs.
O Maheśvara, the Upadeśa is indeed to be honored upon its own seat;
it consists of twenty-eight divisions established through the lineage of succession.
One should worship the six syllables according to the sequence of the command-wheel (ājñācakra);
from the feet up to the knees, the teaching is both collective and individual.
Having performed sacrifices for all desires and many proofs,
when the hermitage is thus well-established, one should then install the side of the embodied form.
But there, for the sake of the realized reality (*ājñātattva*), one should likewise fashion the faces and limbs;
having worshipped the faces with the faces, one should worship the limbs with the limbs.
O Great Śambhu, one should worship the eight families in sequence, beginning from the feet:
Brahmāṇī is to be worshipped at the two feet, and Maheśvarī at the region of the knees.
Kaumārī is in the secret place, Vaiṣṇavī is situated at the navel;
Vārāhī is to be worshipped in the stomach, and Indrāṇī in the circle of the heart.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
one should worship the third in Maṇipūra, the fourth and likewise the fifth;
having worshipped them again in Ādhāra, one should worship the sixth indeed in Svādhiṣṭhāna.
One should worship [the deities] from the seventh up to the ninth within the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). Nine Siddhas have been thus described; now listen to the sixteen as well.
One should worship the garland of skulls up to the eighth, the ninth in the navel-maṇḍala,
and the sixteen-fold garland of vulvas.
O Lord, just as the maṇḍalas are situated within one's own body,
so too should one practice the pronunciation [of the mantras] *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ* according to the preceding sequence.
First on the right eye, then on the cheek and the ear;
then on the crown of the head, the right shoulder, the upper arm, and likewise on the middle of the hand.
In the belly, the buttocks, the knees, the shanks, and the right foot;
in the left foot, the left knee, the left buttock, and the left eye.
One should place [the syllables] on the right hand, in the middle of the arms, on the left shoulder, at the ear,
as well as on the cheek, the mouth, the forehead, and the nape of the neck.
"In the middle of the back, likewise in the support, the heart, and the circle of the face—
within these, mandalas numbering twenty-eight are to be worshipped."
O God, one should worship the eight groups of eight in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
one should worship the sixty-four great goddesses according to the prescribed ritual.
This has been told to you, O Śambhu; now I shall describe the sacred fields (kṣetras).
A sacred field is that which is supremely peaceful within the body and is conjoined with the principles (tattvas).
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) moves therein, established in the course of the eight abodes;
therefore, O Lord of the Gods of gods, this is proclaimed as the "Eight Fields" (kṣetrāṣṭaka).
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Those which are pīṭhas are indeed kṣetras, and those which are kṣetras are declared to be pīṭhas;
these are synonyms for them, [differing] in each respective scripture.
Prayāga is located at the region of the navel, while Varuṇā is situated in the heart;
Kaullagiri is indeed in the throat, and Bhīmanāda is in the palate.
In the station of the Bindu is that called Jayantī, while in the station of Nāda is Caritraka;
within the Śakti is Ekā—this should be known by those who have realized the Self.
That which has come from the mouth of the Guru is declared to be the eighth [type], Koṭivarṣa;
these places have been described by me as situated along the path of wandering and pilgrimage.
Having thus explained it, one should worship the God with the three divisions in their proper sequence:
the celebrated Stutikhaṇḍa on the head, and one should worship the Mātṛkhaṇḍa in the heart.
O God Maheśvara, one should indeed worship in the secret section of mantras;
this instruction on the sequence bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"Therefore, nothing exists beyond this"—this is the ultimate truth.
Whatever collections of scriptures there may be, they have all come down through a succession of tradition.
O Goddess of the Gods, other scriptures do not equal even a sixteenth part of this one.
Having understood the sixfold Kramaugha residing within the body, one should worship it constantly.

Having thus worshipped the one situated in the maṇḍala according to the prescribed sequence, [the ritual continues]. Thus ends the chapter on the Śrīkrama-sūtra within the lineage of the Great Manthānabhairava Sacrifice, which comprises seventy million verses; this is the fifty-first bliss.
In the Siddhānta there are five, the essence is fourfold, and in the Vāma tradition there is the sphere of the four.
They say that in the southern tradition,
as well as in the eastern and western lineages of the Krama, the Guru alone is the authority within the Kula lineage.
The sixth ends with the letter *ṇ*, the seventh ends with *m*, and the eighth belongs to Rudra, ending with *l*.
O God, the first, third, and fourth [vowels] of the Pervasive One (Vyāpaka),
along with the second and the first of Cañcala— these are the five subtle ones known as Nāda.
In the teaching of Navātmānandayogīndra, there is Vṛkṣanāyaka,
the Lord of the Tamarind Tree, who abides in three divisions and is endowed with eighty-one words.
It is radiant with sixteen digits and divided by the sixteen perfections;
it is illuminated by the five Praṇavas through both direct and reverse order.
Pervaded by the threefold knowledge and joined with the science of words (padavidyā),
it is white, reddish, black, and tawny, and endowed with the three junctions of the day.
O God, wearing the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) and endowed with a girdle and anklets,
you are mounted upon the five [vowels] within the central point (*bindu*), accompanied by the eleven stages of conduct (*caryā*).
Endowed with twelve dances and endowed with twelve musical instruments,
O Hero who maintains the vow of knowledge, you whose sphere of activity consists of the twelve threads.
The glorious holder of the ninefold command is the Lord of the Sequence within the Teaching;
situated within the seventeen kalās of the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, he is differentiated by the short and long vowels.
O Lord, within the three lineages of gurus, one should worship Ādinātha in the three lineages; he who knows how to perform the sequential worship together with him is a true teacher.
Otherwise, one does not know at all; one should not even engage in conversation, O Lord of Gods, nor [perform] the sequence of conduct, eating, or sleeping.
One should not practice the observance (samaya) with anyone other than the mouth of the Guru;
for one who follows the lineage of Ādinātha, there is the sequence of the circle of Gurus.
He who understands this according to reality shall be a delight to his family;
he should pay homage three times to the Eldest and take refuge in the Child in the throat.
One should place the *dhātṛ* [mudrā] at the heart, and the two hands with those born of the lineage;
whoever performs it otherwise will certainly be subject to penance.
Through one hundred thousand recitations, one becomes a purified soul and is reborn within the lineage;
this [teaching] of Vṛkṣanātha has come down through the succession of oral tradition.
The definitive teaching of Guhyāyā, emerging from Candradvīpa:
the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
Kāmarūpa, Haṣkaḍḍoka, Nepāla, and Puṇḍravardhana.
Purastīra, Kanyākubja, Pūrṇagiri, as well as Arbuda, Āmrākeraka, Ekāmravana, and Kāmakoṭṭika.
Kailāsa, Bhṛgunagara, Kedāra, Candrapūryaka,
Śrīpīṭha, Ekoṇa, Jālandhara, and Mālava.
Kulūta, Devikoṭṭa, Gokarṇa, Marukeśara,
Aṭṭahāsa, Viraja, Rājaveśma, and Mahāpatha.
Kollagiri, Kollāpura, Sopāra, Jayantikā, Caritra from Ujjayinī, Kṣīrikā, and Hastināpura.
The sacred seat named Prayāga in Udakeśa, as well as Māyāpurī;
likewise Urasā, Malaya, and the mountain Bheruṇḍaka.
Mahendra, Varuṇa, and Hiraṇyapura,
as well as Mahālakṣmī, the garden, and thereafter the parasol of shade.
These seats (pīṭhas) have been fully described; they are proclaimed to be fifty in number, produced according to the principle of emanation through a counter-clockwise rotation.
In the center of the mandala of the three peaks (traikūṭa), amidst the nine powers beginning with Vāmā,
the arising of the vowels and consonants is said to be the form of the sacred seat (pīṭha).
In the center of the maṇḍala of mudrās, it is made profound through illusion;
it is the division of vowels and consonants, the sequence of the Meruśrīgahvara.
The primary arrangement has been declared in the lineage of the Siddha teachings:
below is Kālāgnirudra, and above that are thirteen.
And those beginning with Bhaga, up to Ūdhvaga, are declared to be Daṇḍayas; in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
there are eleven Rudras above the city who hold authority in the lineage (santāna).
Above those are the nine Siddhas, and below them are the seven Yoginīs;
thus, in the mandala above, they are arranged in order beginning with Akhaṇḍā.
Above those three powers, however, is Nāthaciñciṇī;
indeed, the sequence of Gahvara has been declared as beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Nātha.

"That which is devoid of the placement of the Gahvara and lacks the lineage of the Siddhas is not to be worshipped by the teachers of the Western tradition"— thus was it stated regarding the Kādi division.
Thus ends the sequence of the Gahvara.
Thus concludes the Sūtra on the Array of Meru of the Fifty Seats in the *Śrīkādibheda*. [This is] the fifty-second bliss:
"The Lord, who is manifested in nine ways, is to be worshipped individually."
The Lord of the Family is named Ananta, as is Kandarpa and Vimala.
The ninth is proclaimed as the Lord Śāmbhavājñāvara, who is non-dual, silent, and the crest-jewel of the Samaya.
"The Self, through the nine lords, becomes the bearer of the nine forms.
Thus ends the Sūtra of Ādinātha from the *Kādibheda* in the venerable *Caturviṃśatisāhasra*. The venerable Vakrā said:
[This is] the fifty-third bliss.
I proclaim the *Sūtrasantānaka-prajñā* with its hidden meaning;
the second *Santāna*, the *Puṣpameru-vijñānabhairava*.
The path is known as beginning with *nā* and ending with *pha*; there are six deities in the lineage.
Twelve jewels have emerged from the two flowers of space.
Having emerged from the cave into the empty Saṃvartamaṇḍala garden, O Mi,
the Siddha remained there in the caves absorbed in the samādhis of silence.
In that case, there shall be the command of the *pratyaya*; the tree is indeed the *kadambaka*. The Vidyā stands like a lion, a lion capable of both cursing and bestowing grace.
The crooked command in the downward path is the sixfold house of Śakti;
through twenty-seven divisions, it is the division known as Manthānabhairava.
The conduct of Śiva and Śakti, which belongs to the lineage of the immortal non-dual [reality].
In Vakrikā, the abode of grace,
the house is Candrapurodaya.
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa consists of Siddhā, Śuṣkā, and Mahācchāyā in the other state of Trikūṭa;
that which is fashioned by conceptualization is indeed fashioned by the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāya).
The wise know the upper power and the lower power;
that is the union of the realization-seed of *Haṃsa* and *Mālinī*.
There are three perfected ones who possess the authority for the practice of Koṇā;
however, through the abandonment of the fluctuations of the mind, one gains authority in Kaṇa.
The divine sevenfold stone is pure, manifesting name and form at birth;
Brahmā, however, through a purified mind, possesses the latent impressions of the Kaulika tradition.
Through the abandonment of dualities, there is clarity; the auspicious stone of Brahma is birth itself.
O fair-faced one, wherever the desire of one established in samādhi may go, [there it remains].
Abiding is the union with yoga; abiding indeed occurs in Kāmarūpa. Having fixed the mind in the center of the bhaga, one should enter while reciting.
Delight of the mind and satisfaction of the intellect; fame [is found] in the *Ciñciṇīvṛkṣaka*;
in the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*, the great purpose is accomplished, which is indeed a great ocean of six types.
O God, through the abandonment of deluded cognition, success is indeed achieved in the ocean; for I am truly pleased with him who knows the lineage transmission.
Having understood this thread of wisdom, who would not be liberated from bondage?
[This occurs] precisely through the sequence beginning with the Transmental (unmanā) up to the venerable Lord Ciciṇī.
"O Lord, in the *Punarnava* sequence, the accomplishment (*siddhi*) is in the *Gahvara* sequence.
Thus ends the chapter on the Lineage Sutra (*santānasūtra*), divided into fifty sections, within the twenty-four thousand [verse] *Kādibheda*. The venerable Vakrā said:
[This is] the fifty-fourth bliss.
