One should contemplate the Vāgbhava, known as Praṇava, which is as pure as snow, the kunda flower, and the moon, yet resembles a flickering fire, situated in the center of the yoni.
The great seat of Kāmarūpa existed in the beginning during the Kṛta Yuga;
through one hundred thousand recitations, the sign of attainment shall enter as an agitation within the body.
And the second *praṇava*, O Hara, is on the seat of Jālandhara;
having meditated upon it as the rising morning sun, served by *siddhas* and *gandharvas*.
At night, under a solitary tree, one should recite [the mantra] two hundred thousand times;
this quickly effects the paralysis of fetters and brings about a great assembly of goddesses.
One attains heroic accomplishment and the power of entering the bodies of others;
such, O Ānanda, is the Great Seed, the third Praṇava.
O Great Beloved of yellow form, you are situated in the center of the navel;
Pūrṇagiri is the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha), worshipped by both gods and asuras.
By reciting the mantra three hundred thousand times at a crossroads during the night practice,
the practitioner attains the experiential realization of *ghūrmi*.
Without doubt, the agitation of the city is accomplished for one who is free from conceptual construction.
One should contemplate [the deity] in the middle of the throat— terrible, resembling crushed collyrium— from the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
In the future, at the end of the Kali age, one should perform four hundred thousand recitations at night in the empty temple of Tisrapīṭha.
Eternal bliss is always produced in the disciple, as well as invisibility; there is also the accomplishment of attracting material objects, and unsurpassed power over others and possession.
One should recognize this Bhairavarāja, resembling red lac, between the eyebrows; one should then conceive of it as the sacred seat (pīṭha) and the garden (udyāna).
To the east of the Svayambhū-liṅga, through five hundred thousand recitations performed by a night-walker, the realization of yogic sleep (yoganidrā) arises from that.
The past and the future indeed proceed within the present;
if one recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times through the utterance of the five *praṇavas*, [this occurs].
In an empty temple at night, the eight qualities beginning with *aṇimā* [are attained];
thus are those five *praṇavas* in the lineage of Śrī Kujā, first of all.
In the beginning of the mantra they follow the regular order, and at the end they are likewise in reverse order;
on the new moon day this becomes full, and in the Kali age it bestows liberation.
Thus ends the Pañcapraṇavasūtra within the glorious Caturviṃśatisāhasra.
The venerable Vakrā said: [This is] the fifty-fifth bliss;
in the intermediate space, in supreme bliss, in the Unmanā state, within the pentad of the void.
The supreme goddess is in the supreme body, within the mandala of pure nirvāṇa.
The five voids have arisen within the world of the supreme goddess,
in the heart, in the maṇḍala of the womb, within the pure wheel known as the *bindu*.
O Leader of the Sky, within the fivefold [group] of those [elements] at the base of the bulb (kandādhāra),
that Vyomapañca resides in the center of the Sky-wheel (vyomacakra).
Thus, when the Kṛta Yuga had begun, the Supreme Goddess manifested as the voids;
having understood the secret convention of the places, he then became the eldest brother.
Alternatively, he may be the deity of the ancestors, or the grandfather,
or indeed known as the great-grandfather, according to whichever elder he may be.
Having prepared their mandala, one should pay homage with the eight-limbed prostration;
one who desires accomplishment for oneself should not leave the mandala empty.
Having offered himself with a state of contemplation and a serene mind,
he should also construct a mandala there, provided with a tortoise-seat (kūrmāsana).
On the south, however, is the hero’s substance; the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is in the middle and the north.
One should cause a fourfold [area] to be made, excellent, with fine threads and very beautiful.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Having first obtained a vessel endowed with all auspicious marks—
possessing a neck like a conch shell, elevated, golden-hued, and free from hair or sand.
Even with the left hand joined [in mudrā], the sandals of Śrīnātha are to be placed in the center;
by means of the Vāgbhava syllable, the triad of trees is to be fashioned in the north.
Ciciṇī is to be known as being in the east, the second is Kadambaka,
and the third they call Bilva, accompanied by Vīgbhava.
First, the group of six Mothers, beginning with the letter *ḍa*, according to the prescribed rule;
by this sequence there shall be a group of six, and their seed-syllable (*bīja*) is likewise sixfold.
Having combined it with its own source and adorned it with the Vāgbhava syllable,
one should place the Lord of the Lineage (Olinātha) at the end of "Ambā's feet" in the respective positions of all.

In that place, O beautiful one, the lineage of the Guru is established according to the principle of emanation; then, beginning with the Vāgbhava syllable, one should ascend through the five [syllables] starting from the upper corner.
Then, having established it in the central place as well as in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
this is called the "Jyeṣṭha-maṇḍala" for the sake of the spiritual accomplishments of the gurus.
But for one who has failed to follow such a procedure and does not honor [the deities] after propitiating them, the yoginīs become despondent and devour his fat and flesh.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
One who has strayed from the meaning of "here" will not achieve success elsewhere;
therefore, with every effort, one should honor the elders.
And for those observing vows, for ascetics, and especially for lords of yogis—
whether they be men or women, or even teachers— at the command of their guru.
Those who were born in Koṅkaṇa in the past, and those who remain there and cause decay—
for them one should prepare a mandala that is deficient in materials, which yields no accomplishment.
"One should not perform [this] for one's sons during the gathering of the conduct of the *samaya*.
Thus ends the *Ārādhyamaṇḍalavidhānasūtra* in the *Śrīkādiccheda*. Through the yoga of universal attraction, everything is perfectly free from affliction;
it is one's own bliss and one's own true nature, known by the name *Śrīcandrapūrī*.
Arising from the unstruck sound, one should go to the Void, the abode of the Void;
having pierced the supreme supportless state, O Śrī Gulmanātha, this is the second.
O Śrīstambhadeva, the third [deity] is the consciousness arising from one's own sequence, partially obscured by the moon produced from one's own feet.
The fifty-sixth bliss:
merged within the triangular wheel, it has arisen through the single channel;
equal in brilliance to twelve suns, it is the fourth, known as Śrīkapīsa.
When the fluid is dissolved within the uvula and merged into the circle of fire,
the glorious city of Śrīpura— the supreme abode of the wheel of consciousness— comes into being.
Having indeed reached the two divisions, he has gone to dissolution at the end of the twelve; O God, the sixth [deity] is the stainless one situated in the middle between the heart and the ether.
One should illuminate the sky-mouth of the mudrā of the five families;
having pierced the locus of the bindu, the glorious Prayāga is the seventh.
The sky-faced one would cause the sound of the great dissolution to shake the universe;
and likewise, the eighth is the blazing one known as Śrīkāṃsa for all beings.
Established in the great void, he who bears the limbs of the Viṣṇu-liṅga is merged in the state of the Great Vajra under the name Bhogadeva.
When the supreme state has been attained and the fire and sun have dissolved therein,
his command becomes the fivefold pair of deities of the Bimba.
Having drawn in the sound of the letter *a* (avarṇa), one should take refuge in the empty sky;
having entered the Great Sound (*mahānāda*), one attains perfection as the glorious deity Khaḍga.
Having disregarded and set aside the deception of the world,
and having performed the cessation of the mind, one should likewise [worship] the twelve Rudras.
With the self awakened in the bliss of rasa and having attained dissolution into the reality of Brahman,
the stream that has reached the state of Nirvana is designated by the name Śiva.
Having entered the Great Sound (Mahānāda), he abides in the state of Śambhu; by way of his single-formed essential nature, the fourteenth is the glorious Mudrāsphoṭa.
The form of light and the sound have both attained oneness in the supreme void of the awakened one,
known by the name Śrīvaṅkāpura.
"Having gone to the abode of the Great Void, he remains established in the state of equal flavor (samarasa).
Awakened, he stays there as Bhurjadeva, the sixteenth.
Thus is the aphorism of the sixteen Siddhas. The venerable Vakrā said:
O Fifty-Seventh Bliss, it is explained according to the meaning of the stages (*bhūmikā*) of the eighteenfold lineage transmission (*kramāmnāya*):
the bliss born of the *Kula* in the wheel of space, the bliss of space, impelled by space.
Established in the void, her form withdrawn, she is therefore the supreme Unmanā;
she is called Unmanā and Anākhyā, arisen from the state that has no support.
O Maheśvara, the Goddess of Liberation is waveless and free from appearances;
she is all-pervading, the sovereign of all, subtle, beyond the principles (tattvas), and whose abode is the ultimate reality.
Unmanā is the stainless one for the class of the creation of Ālaya;
she is the great knower of all mantras, Mātaṅgī, in the family of the outcaste.
Having made the mind one-pointed, one should complete the Mālinī, which is filled with twelve flames,
through the Meghanāda [mantra] in the Parakaulika.
She is to be known as moving without hesitation in the state of Manonmanī,
within the expansion of the sky of consciousness at the end of the sixteen, in the secret maṇḍala.
In that [Kumārikākhaṇḍa], she who shines from of old with rays of blissful consciousness is the subtle,
eternal, and ever-awakened digit known as Samanā, whose form is pure awareness.

One should recognize the Command of Śambhu in its true nature at the end of the samana; it is devoid of objective categories, uninterrupted, and an ocean of ornaments consisting of the mass of consciousness.
Abiding above, she pervades the Lord of the Kula through the Self-born One;
therefore, having emerged from the supreme body, she is called Vyāpinī (the Pervasive One).
O Maheśvara, she is the purifier of the Śiva-principle, the uniter with the internal organ,
more vast than ten million sacrifices, and eternal bliss.
The Antyajā resides within the maṇḍala; she is subtle, unmanifest, supreme, and immutable. She has neither origin nor dissolution; she moves along the great path.
In the waveless sky, the pervasion of Nandinī is Kulakaulinī;
she is the seventy million mantras that have been proclaimed in the Prastāra.
Emerging from the center of Meru, the mantra becomes sevenfold;
it begins with Manthāna, Śiva, and Śakti, and by both the Sun and the Moon.
That great-souled one consists of three syllables; Manthāna becomes sevenfold.
From the abandonment of the six, in the seventh part—the Kumārikākhaṇḍa—there is liberation, a smokeless and stainless radiance.
That womb is called Tryākhya in the supreme space in the west;
it exists in play, in the cause of sport, and in contact, respectively.
She whose mind and consciousness are pure awareness is Heruka, possessing a subtle form;
she has the edge of a razor and a hundred aspects, yet is the letter A, augmented by sixteen.
“Emerging from the command of Samanā, pure as snow, jasmine, and the moon,
she dwells within the station of the divine realm, originating from the end of Aṭṭahāsa.”
She whose knowledge is the awakening of constant bliss is called Samayākṣī; she is the Sovereign of the Cintāmaṇi family, situated between the imperishable and the perishable.
That supreme digit which shines, dissolved within the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
is intensely fierce at the end of the Śāmbhava state, a flickering garland of flames.
Her form resembles a spark, with a radiance like the rising sun;
she is the Mother (Ambikā) of the divine jewel-trees in the ten and one incarnations.
In the abode of all the Siddhas, in the western house of Trikūṭa,
in the Kumārikā section: beginning from one house, Kālakarṣī is the deity.
Born in the abode of the Himavat, Saṃvartī has gone to the western quarter;
Maheśvarī, whose form is according to her will, returns once more to him who has departed.
Above the moon and sun, that lunar light (candrikā) of the Lord, which severs worldly existence,
shines like blue collyrium at the end of the twelve.
That which is the desire for the family of conduct and vigor is directly perceived in the Kali age;
this "Excellent Dawn of the Three Worlds," though most secret, has been made manifest.
Situated between the two poles of union, it is the emergence of the three peaks and the triple path;
it is the triple Kaula, pervaded by the three energies (kalās), the triple-segmented embodiment of Kula.
The mandala of the seat of Kālikā, which is the support of the half-digit of the belly,
is called Candrapūrya, situated within the peak of light.
Having known the movement of the moon's course, at the end of the dissolution,
the light-sun resounds within the five families called Nāda, situated above the Fourth State (turya).
O Lord, in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the arising of the path of mantra and the determination of the sequence of the Khecaras have been told to you, O Master— the most wonderful secret.
One should constantly meditate on non-existence within the teaching on the arising of intrinsic nature;
that reality, which is the essence of consciousness, [transcends] the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
Rudras, Bhairavas, Vīras, and others who are unawakened and deluded do not find this secret, the definitive teaching on the sequence of the Divine Current (divyaugha).
Accomplishment comes from serving the divine stream; accomplishment does not come from one who clings to existence.
This sword of the knowledge of non-existence has its cavernous base in the three voids.
One who is enraged by the strife of the Kali age shall destroy the heap of evil;
one sees with the eye of wisdom in the lamp of stainless non-existence.
The complete liberation from the self-nature of delusion, folly, and the bonds of the fettered beings is that which is grasped by one's own nature through the cultivation of non-existence.
For him whose sun of the light of command shines continuously and without interruption,
a stainless vision of knowledge arises toward the Supreme.
The mass of the darkness of ignorance perishes even through the mere remembrance of that blissful flood which is the domain of the Transmental (unmanā).
Filled with the lineage of Khañjīnātha, it is the arising and dissolution at the end of the triple void;
it has the form of a coiled triple creeper, the singular Trika, exceeding sixteen.
Through three [stages], one becomes glorious; this is the determination of the sequence of the three lineages (*tri-ūlya-krama*).
By way of eighteen modes, there is the determination of the Divine Current (*divyaugha*) doctrine, which is non-existence, the great bliss of space, and the determination of the [lineage] system.
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa is the cause for the arising of one's own nature.
And [he saw] Abhāva, who was like Mount Meru, dwelling in the cave of Durgandara.
The perfected one strides with ease through the divine lineage of transmission by means of contemplation;
this knowledge, born of its own nature, is all-pervading, eternal, and unborn.

Having attained through the divine sequence of digestion the stainless state that transcends all qualities, who would not be liberated from bondage by means of the path of the sky— the path of the sequence of the three purities?
And before long, by the command of the Guru, [he departed].
Vakrā brings about both bondage and liberation;
she is with support, yet she abides in the middle between both expansion and contraction; she is the Goddess of gods, both supreme and non-supreme, and she is without support.
Flow forth from its very root, resting upon the tree of the gradual stages:
the tree of the command-stage (*ājñākrama*), which has three branches originating from the navel,
covered by the sprouts of the lamps of gnosis, and entwined by the creepers of the *abhimātrās*.
Richly adorned with various shadow-bindus, decorated with petals like the rays of the moon, this single flower is called Anaṅga; its fragrance is the light whose essence is consciousness.
Its fruit is bliss, its nectar is the command, its satisfaction is the deception of time.
The yoga that produces delight, an ocean of liberation, command, and spiritual accomplishments.

With the eye of knowledge, one perceives that state of consciousness which has gone there— the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*)— where the mind has dissolved all objective existents. In the unity of the internal and external, she moves through the cavity of the *kanda* below and above.
When the blissless state has arisen, liberation occurs within the teaching of the divine stream.
The Kaula, arising from the yoga of the innate (*sahaja*), is the body of the lineage (*kulapiṇḍa*) consisting of three natures;
it is the determination of the sequence as one, three, five, six, and three.
O Śrīnātha, the form of the unseen family has been told to you;
the number of flowers is now declared according to the division into seventeen and one.
I perpetually revere the Guru, the knower of mantras, who begins with the Siddhas and is that supreme Khañjī; who is Bhairava in his nine masculine forms;
who is joined with the principles of the qualities (guṇatattva); and who reveals the command of Śambhu.
In the west, the arising occurs in the sequence of Kā, Pū, Jā, and O.
Arising from Akula and the others, the division of Kula exists in three ways;
yet the sequence of Kalās is divine, beginningless, and imperishable.
The *unmanā* is beyond the *mānā*; through it, knowledge proceeds.
Freed from the impurity of *māyā*, one beholds that which is both supreme and non-supreme (*parāpara*).
[It is the state] of the mind regarding its coming and going, and of one who delights in moving through the sky.
And there is no doubt regarding movement through the sky by means of practicing the sequence of the divine currents.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the Divine Power (divyaśakti) is the support of the Kula; she is the form of consciousness (cidrūpā), consisting of consciousness (cinmayā), and supreme (parā).
She who gathers the bliss of consciousness (cidānanda) is proclaimed as Vakrā.
Through the union with the bliss of expansion, she is eternally devoted to that expansion;
Śāmbhavī, the ground of knowledge, is the supreme nectar and liberation.
The ground of the sequence beginning with Unmanā, which extends to the end of the worlds,
has emerged from the divine current of the Kula through the power of the command inherent in that [ground].

The divine state of *sāmarasya* consists of the consciousness of the bliss of one's own bliss; it is ineffable and has the form of pure consciousness. Here, the *unmanā* state dissolves. By means of this [consciousness], one pervades everything within the sphere from Śiva down to the earth.
Abiding in both the non-divine and the divine, one perceives Manonmana.

The Kaulika [reality] is the refuge of rest, consisting of the supreme joy of one's own unfolding, arising from the conceptualization of Manonmanā, which is equal to and beyond the consciousness that has transcended tranquility.
The pervasive state of the sky-farer (khecarī) awakens one to the plane of non-existence;
it is formless, the supreme support, and the bestower of the knowledge of the state.

The pervasive power is unmanifest, yet it is manifest in both the manifest and the unmanifest. By means of its uninterrupted influence, that Śāmbhavī power gathers [all things]; this is the command of Śambhu. Within Kula, the digit of consciousness (citkalā), which is Manonmanī, resounds.
In the placement of the steps of Nandinī, one should meditate upon the stainless Self.
Then, through the practice of churning the middle, the fire of gnosis blazes forth;
and she, both supreme and non-supreme, stirs within, moving through the lower state while oriented toward bliss.
Blazing upward from the latent impressions of others,
that Kālī is indeed the Sovereign of the Sky (Khecarājñā) and Heruka, without interval.
By the power of the command of the *samaya*, it bestows equanimity;
consciousness, arising from its own nature, is the *samaya* in which all impurities have been destroyed.
The speech that agitates the world, devoid of both dissolution and origination,
abiding in the sky within the abode of emptiness— that state becomes Jambhalā.
Kalā is the ender of the parts [of time], Kālī, beyond all marks yet within the range of perception; she who attracts the supreme reality is called Kālakarṣī. (From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
At the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], in the supportless state, is Caṇḍarāvā, free from fear;
I am the flickering one, incomparable, solely intent on devouring the universe.
I am Aghorā, the supreme power of Śarva, abiding as Bhīmā within the path of the mind;
the mind arises through speech, and through speech it dissolves right there.
This destruction of the three worlds, which has fashioned a cage of despair,
shall remain within the penetration of my command, impelled throughout the entire range of the Kula.
The will of Viṣavaḥniśiva, which consists of the stainless state (*nirañjanapada*),
should be contemplated in the Nayakaula as the Linga of Space (*khaliṅga*) by way of leading [the disciple].
Residing in the midst of the void of the cavity of the cleft (*kandarandhrakha*), she is the "Solitary Heroine" (*ekavīrā*), possessed of great power.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Karaṅkiṇī and Kuraṅgīśa have spread forth within the center of the bulb (kanda).

In the three worlds, including all that moves and is immobile, she is the one who causes the expansion of the light of consciousness; she is the mantra-command of consciousness and matter, Carcikā, manifesting throughout the four ages.
Abiding within the state that is without support, her movement becomes supported;
O Śrīnātha, by your power she has descended in the Kali age.
Indeed, throughout the four ages, you and I are the investigators of knowledge and the object of knowledge,
within this beautiful and supreme Kula, the divine current, the state of Śambhu.
"There is accomplishment, there is no doubt"—this is the command of Kulakhecarī.
That Khecarī has the Kula as her support; with a mind that is by nature *unmanā*, she is merged in the great unmanifest syllable, free from qualities, and moving as the *haṃsa*.
One should demonstrate the time-moment (kālavelā) by means of the expansion of the form of Umanā.
The vision that has reached the state of *unmanā* is indeed downward-facing in the form of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
The pervasive power (*vyāpti*) within the *kula* is the *anāśritā*; she is the *kaulinī*, the *bhairavī* energy.
Having assumed the form of Bhairava, she vomits forth that which was previously accumulated.
Bhairavī rejoiced with him in ten and eight ways; therefore, he is Bhairava.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa: "When one's state of being has attained oneness through a mind absorbed in the Will,
you are Śrīnātha and I am Kubjā, born from the Churning One (Manthāna)."

The stringed instrument (*tantrīkalā*), the support of the *kula*, the churning *suṣumṇā*, the *amā*; the *vajra*, the bald one (*khalvāṭaka*), the flame (*jvāla*), the lame one (*khañjī*), and the radiant churning (*manthānabhāsvara*).
Therein, the entire world was first produced from the descent of the Protector;
he was the glorious one, perfected in the City of the Moon, consisting of consciousness and having the form of mind.
I am indeed the mind, the vital breath, and the Self within the circle of the Bindu; I am the sky-farer, the portion of Madana, the totality, and Vaḍavāmukha.
From that very [source], emission has flowed forth as something whose form consists of a modicum of consciousness;
O Great Lord, you are the ocean, whose nature is like a fierce submarine fire.
Saṃvartī has the form of universal dissolution; she extends from the nectar at the top to the earth below.
She is Vakrā by nature, whose form is the umbrella of Śiva’s shadow.
With the mind transcendent (*unmanā*) through the force of *manas*, one should again bring about the state of the five elements (*pañcatva*).

Having established time within the tortoise posture (*kūrmāsana*), one should unite the serpent that is one's own essential nature from Śiva down to the earth within the single principle (*ekatattva*).
This should be understood by the Great-souled One at the conclusion of the Saṃvartī-maṇḍala.
The *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*:
That *manthāna* (churning) is to be known as the ocean of the *mātṛkā*s, O Hara;
the *kalā*s are the water, the *tattva*s are the waves, and the phonemes (*varṇa*) are the fish.
That which was to be churned out for the sake of the fisherman has been attained; the glorious *Rājakam*, the meaning of the *Saṃhitā*, has been demonstrated by the hero Navātmānātha.
Those of great intelligence who, with minds entered into the divine stream, understand this treasury of knowledge called the twenty-four thousand, which possesses great meaning.
They go to the supreme abode where the Lord of the Family of Devas dwells; they are indeed ageless and immortal, and for them no further birth exists.
The divine current is Śāmbhava, O Śambhu; the divine current is the Kula-path;
the divine current is Nirālamba; and the divine current is Nirāmaya.
The knowledge of liberation is the divine flow; in the divine flow, there is movement through the sky.
Those whose minds are fixed here upon the divine flow have reached the ultimate state.
As long as Śrīnātha and Ciciṇī remain in uninterrupted and continuous union,
so long does the state of Unmanā exist through that condition of supreme vibration.
Śabdarāśi and Saṃvarta are known as Ananta Khecara;
Amogha and Bindunātha are designated by the name Anādi Śukra.
Ajātānanda, the one called Rakta, likewise Krīḍānātha,
Āśānandaughanātha, Rasānanda, and Dhvaja.
Jvālādeva, as well as Nagna and Kubjānanda—these are proclaimed as the eighteen Nāthas to be known; they have come down through the lineage beginning with Unmanā.
(From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*)
As far as the limit of Carcikā, extending through the Unmanā and Amanā states, so long are they to be worshipped in pairs according to the tradition of the Nāthas.
All those gods are sky-farers whose forms and lineages are unseen;
O Śrīnātha, the command of your Siddhas begins with Unmanā and follows in due order.
First, you should worship the couple together with yourself,
O Ciñciṇī;
by a single utterance, one becomes a pure soul, free from desire and without possessions.

One whose self is purified of existence and non-existence should practice that Kaula vow. O Lord, through the service of the command (*ājñā*) of the flower of the *kula* of the *khalolī*, one attains success by means of the upward gaze, the supportless state, and the attainment of bliss within oneself.
The identity with the fluctuations of the mind [is attained] from flower to flower within the lineage.
In the supportless intermediate space, during the worship of the sequence of the divine flood,
by means of the mere sound of resonance, one awakens to the reality of the waves; having contracted that which is purely conscious and unconscious, one then becomes a sky-farer (khecara).
In this compendium of the Khañjinī doctrine, which has attained the sequence of the Khecarīs.
Then liberation occurs, without a doubt; such is the command in the state of Śambhu.
Those disciples who are liberated from the command of Śambhu within the lineage of the Siddhas [are lost].

"They do not attain liberation"— this is the command of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarī ājñā*). In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*, in the primordial descent (*ādyāvatāra*) of the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) comprising seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters,

on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭhamārga*), in the determination of the Pure Six Thousand (*vimalaṣaṭkanirṇaya*), in the division beginning with 'Ka' (*kādibheda*), in the command of the Supreme Lord.
In the *Svāminīmata*, as spoken in the *Avvākrama* tradition within the *Śrīcaturviṃśatsahasra*,
this is the bliss named *Kramodaya*, occurring in the description of the chapter on the stages of the divine current beginning with *Unmanā*. Śrīnātha said:
Fifty-eighth Bliss:
"Now I wish to hear the supreme knowledge of the stages (bhūmikā);
O Mistress of the Gods, please graciously explain it according to the Root Sūtra."
The venerable Vakrā said: "The source of the ocean of the Kula tradition is proclaimed as the Root Sūtra.
Now hear the true nature of the stages of the Root Sūtra."
The single source of the sixfold root is the source characterized by the sixfold liṅga;
the cause of the sixfold seat is the pure consciousness consisting of the bliss of the source.
O Mahendra, listen now to the first seat of the lords of the gods,
renowned in this place called Kubjikā, which is intensely black like the black sky.
The Ālaya, beginning with the mass of seeds and adorned with the five *praṇavas*,
becomes the Viśrāmagarbhabhairava for the purpose of destruction.
When the embryo situated in the sky has emerged from the divine body,
that is the *liṅga* called Bhagīśa, the cause arising from the expansion [of emanation].
Situated in the form of a circle around the lofty Meru-mountain, within the Kumārikā-khaṇḍa,
above the half-moon, is the great cave of the space of the Liṅga, Āsīnā.
The Lord of the Cave (Guhanātha) is in the cave, situated within the cave at the end of the moon;
he is the master residing above the point (bindu), free from blemish, at the limit of the lunar orb.
For from that indeed arises the one supreme power of the Great Lord, the vehicle of all living beings;
it is the great void, the great seat, whose limbs consist of the seats, the liṅgas, and the thrones.
The virgin who is the supreme syllable of the great space-mind is also the embodiment of the bliss of emergence for the specific *liṅga*.
And that is the root, the great island, the leader of islands, all-pervading;
he is Śiva, the bestower of desires, whose linga is the skull of Kapāla.
The mind is situated on Meru; Meru has emerged from the center of Meru. And that is the root of the entire thread, the abode of its unfolding.
Having understood the power of the Sūtra through its threefold division based on the Maṇḍala— the Root Sūtra and that which is beyond it— one becomes a Lord of Heroes (Vīreśvara).
Akula stands in the midst of Kula; Kula is the single triangle.
Within the triangle is the power (śakti) Koṭarā, the stainless wheel of emanation.
Its triple seat and current have come down through the sequence of the six hexads; Meru is known as the abode of the lineage deity, transmitted through the succession.
Because he brings about the arising [of consciousness] from the path below the center of Meru, through the cessation of Śiva and Śakti, he is therefore Ciñciṇī-Bhairava.
Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Thus the Root, the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), is established within the three mandalas;
she is the power that agitates the universe, situated upon the highest peak.
The Yoginī Bhaga is renowned as having the nature of the space of existence;
she is common to all beings and is the limit of both their origin and dissolution.
She whose measure is the vowels, who is joined with the vowels, and who arises from the wheel of vowels—
she is indeed the goddess Brahmāṇī, in the form of the Mother of Vowels.
Five, five, and likewise five, four, and five in sequence—
this is the *liṅga*, the Supreme Mother, the deity Vāma residing within the *liṅga*.
Vaiṣṇavī resides in the center of Viṣṇu; she is Vaiṣṇavī, the mother of Viṣṇu.
She is the subtle will of Śiva, which has emerged forth, causing expansion and nourishment.
In the hexagon is that great liṅga, joined with both [halves] situated within; Raudrī, joined with both the liṅgas of Ha and Kṣa, arises from the differentiated kalā.
And she, indeed, on the southern path, was created by the Self-Existent One as the measure of Rudra;
for she is the divider, the obstructer, and the bringer about of the world's dissolution.
O God, that which is the measure of the vowel is Jyeṣṭhā, situated above;
from her, by means of the word "the other," Vāmā always arises.
Vāmā emits the universe from her own body; she is the pervasive power (vyāpti) of Śaṅkara.
Because of the non-difference between duality and non-duality, Raudrī is born as the Mother.
"In this way, one should behold the wheel of the three powers (śaktitraya), filled with fifty liṅgas, which is the abode of the deity; he shall become a true son of the Kula.
— *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*
The one called Śakti, the one called Śāmbhava, and the third called Āṇava—
by churning these three powers, there arises the single tree and the Liṅga.

Then, situated in the midst of the group of six, the family (kula) born from the ocean of the womb is proclaimed as the Island of the Moon; it is joined with the six initial [syllables] beginning with Vāgbhava,
and this Meru is indeed adorned above by the half-measure (ardhamātrā).
The power of the lunar light (candrikā-śakti) is one alone within the resonance (nāda), and likewise above it.
Thus, the syllable of the womb is named Kaulinī by the designation of Rudra;
she is the power of Rudra, and through her three divisions, she is the auspicious cause of Rudra’s command.
Śiva, who contemplates the entire wheel of the Mothers without exception,
having become the tasting of the essence in an instant, is proclaimed as Vāgbhava.
At the end of the speech of Saṃvartī is the Golaka, the circle of the sacrificial pit;
it is elevated for those who partake of Śiva, like a lofty ocean of lotuses.
In its center is the orb of the pericarp and a downward-facing lotus;
it is called the divine hermitage and the state beyond the mind, the supreme syllable in which only the subtle energy remains.
In the midst of that is the great space, adorned with the sixteen vowels; that Śakti, whose heart is the visarga and who resides within it, dwells in the center of the lotus.
She is the leader of the pericarp, and he is the *liṅga* whose nature is Śiva;
[he is] the nectar of all yoginīs, Kubjīśa, and Bindubhairava.
It is Bhairava, known as Bindu and Nāda, resembling the folds of a three-fold wrinkle;
in its center is the bliss of the *bhaga*, the great bliss born from the *bhaga*.
The Udbhavakaulika Yoga, the Liṅgodhāṇa, and the Devatākumārikākhaṇḍa belong to the self-arisen (svayambhū) side of the Mothers; they abide both externally and internally.
Located both externally and within one's own body, it is divided into sixteen distinctions;
the sixfold power is known as the supreme purity in Kāmarūpa.
Within the hexad is the sequential stage, the fierce Mātṛbhairava;
it is known as the Peak of Mudrās, the unique peak that is the peak of the single mudrā.
The peak of the mudrā is the supreme abode, which is that space, the highest state;
situated in the southern corner is Ambarīśaka, the lord of the field.
One should contemplate the radiant digit of the moon and the sun;
the Vidyā of the Karaṇakṣetra-liṅga is Mahantārikā.
The vulva and the phallus are fully described; the skull is the moon-crested Lord;
the universe is the belly, the navel is the abode of the deity Bhairava.
And Ahi, Paramā Kīrti, Sandhidevī, and then Kaulinī;
shaped like a vajra, a horn, or a jhaṭaka, it is situated facing downwards.
Its rising and setting, as well as the Mother-seal (mātṛmudrā) and the deity—
both are to be known in the middle of the Ākāśa-pīṭha within the sequence of the Goddess (devyākrama).
The syllable *vāgbhava* is at the beginning and the end; it is the arising of the Heart of the Yoginīs.
This is the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
The Supreme Lord Ānanda, situated in the center of the four seats.
By the power of his splendor, there is a fiery linga to the south;
and by the will of Śiva, that linga is known as Jāla, the deity of form.
Satiated by the constant flow of nectar, the lunar digit of immortality has arisen there;
at that moment of emergence, the Goddess Vāmadevatā has appeared.
Therefore, the sequence of the left-hand liṅga (vāmaliṅga) is established in the Left Path (vāmamārga).
The third is the space-liṅga (ākāśaliṅga), the full liṅga (pūrṇaliṅga) in the Kula tradition.
Then, the bliss filled with nectar flows within the sphere of space (vyomamaṇḍala).
For first, from the bindu, Kāmarāja, the source of existence, arises.
It is proclaimed as Kāmaliṅga by virtue of the power of Kāmeśvara;
having approached Kāmarūpa, both the Moon and the Sun were churned, and the Three-eyed Lord [manifested] within the three oceans.
For the sake of liberation of the Kula-yogins.
The bliss arising from the emergence of the *liṅga* is born as the vital breath (*māruta*) through its threefold nature.
Above that is the pure *prasa*, which is Nirvāṇa within the circle of the *bindu*;
it is the domain of authority and the place of rest, born as soon as it arises in Koṅkaṇa.
Then there is Koṅkaṇaliṅga; these six are the forms of the Liṅgas. They are to be worshipped within the mandala in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa as the sixfold Maṅgalaliṅga.
Through the sustenance of the mind and through the service of the knowledge of one's own mantra,
that manifest sign, Kīrtideva, appeared in Koṅkaṇa.
And [there is] the Krauḍora located in the hollow, conjoined with the power called Kroḍā;
and two [deities] situated between both are Kubjīśa and the body of Kubjikā.
The subtle body is indeed Kaulinī Māyā, and she consists of the fifty deities; through the distinctions of the nameless syllables, the supreme syllable is born.
Therefore, the supreme syllable is traditionally known as the first Kula, Vāgbhava;
its resonance has become threefold, adorned above by the letter Kha.
Having understood the heart of the gods and goddesses— the ocean of the Kula, difficult to comprehend, the secret instruction of the deity— liberation is not far off.
The lineage is characterized by sixteen divisions; that lineage consists of sixteen aspects.
The sixteenth is the sixteenth power (*śakti*); the lineage possesses sixteen limbs.
The lineage, Śekharānanda, Meruliṅga, and the sixfold [system]—
having first established the *lakṣa* therein, one attains the state of a sky-walker (*khecara*) at that very moment.

Then the infinite circle of power (śaktimaṇḍala) emerges from Meru, and Mātṛkā, with her three divisions, constitutes the lineage of the paths of Meru. Therein the lineage is born; therefore, one should emit the three flowers.

The goddess residing in the center of the left and right channels, the Kulakaulinī, Ambikā, named Herukā, is the supreme deity of the lineage; she is the goddess known as Kukārā, joined with the three *ī* vowels. *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*
Having emerged from the seat of the syllable Oṃ, the lineage of Siddhas became established;
there, the two great Siddhas, Maunī and Tūṣṇī, reside within the Kadamba trees.
Both great Siddhas reside in the tree; both Siddhas have been made manifest in the hermitage of the Supreme Lord, which dwells in the cave of emptiness.
There I shall establish fame, a cave, a linga, and a tree,
by means of the counter-clockwise application, where the deity is established.
The left path is called the *kadamba* tree; from that comes the *kadambaka*.
From the center of that, by the supreme command, arises the power of resonance (*nāda-śakti*), which is bliss.
Having first established the *bindu* extracted through the lion-signal (*siṃhasaṃketaka*),
its repetition is metaphorically designated by the word "supreme" (*parā*);
and that goddess, named Kubjikā, is indeed called "Supreme" (*parā*).
Dwelling in the cave [of the heart],
she is the stainless shadow of the moon, which assumes a body composed of digits.
This house is known as Candrapūrya within the lineage of the Kula;
from the churning of the form of differentiation, the Kula-deity is fashioned.
The drop (bindu), pierced at the end of the twelve, gives rise to passion;
from that piercing and friction, satisfaction and bliss are inferred.
The *Manthānabhedatantra* has been declared, and the *Binducakra* has been revealed.
Then the lineage (*gotra*) born of the five arises as the pericarp of Meru;
[therein dwell] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:

Having first firmly established the target (*lakṣa*), one should bring about the arousal within oneself; this is the repose in the bliss of emergence (*udbhavānanda*) that has arisen from taking recourse in the means of realization (*pratyaya*).
The arising of conditions, piercing, and the purification of bonds within the body.
The authority proceeds precisely through the sequence of the *olikula*;
Unmanī, whose nature is the power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*), is established in the supreme station.
Therein, meditation and concentration constitute the fivefold worship;
the Supreme Brahman is the supreme pervasion, and the stone itself arises from the emergence of the *kalās*.
Having beheld the crescent-moon *kalā*, one becomes the birth-stone of Brahman (*janmabrahmaśilā*).
Having made the mind steady and established therein within the Supreme Self.
When that which is called the "moon-segment" becomes straight and established in the state of libation (tarpaṇa),
then the state arises and the body-mass (piṇḍa) is instantly agitated.
The place of supreme savor is Ciñciṇī, through the bliss of the *bhaga*; by churning these together in one place, the mind, the consciousness, and the supreme intellect [are unified].
Having broken the bolt of the door of Brahmā, she is seen through her glories;
and thus, by means of sixteen divisions, there are exactly sixteen conventions.
The sixteen-fold one is called Ākula, arising from the Root Sūtra and free from blemish;
unify the root of the lineage with that one.
And then knowledge arises immediately, without a doubt:
in the space where the earth has become darkness, O excellent woman, there is the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the arising of power.
Having understood all secrets, one should move about; power proceeds for those beings born of devotion. The single *lakṣa* consists of seven *piṇḍakas*.
Having meditated upon the unborn and immortal state, one becomes free from doubt;
having abandoned all suspicion, drink the nectar of secret knowledge.
But having drunk [it], one will become very firm and a partaker of the sequence (*krama*).
Having performed all that is supreme and non-supreme, one belongs solely to the family of the lineage of the sequence.
Whatever desire the yogi may obtain, he then attains that which belongs to the Knower of the Self:
the space of the Self, which is the seed, beyond space, and higher than the supreme.
Having performed the closing and opening [of the eyes] and having worshipped Bhagīśa at that very moment,
one should worship the *bhaga* situated within one's own body and the deity in the aperture of power (*śakti-randhra*).
And there, the state that precedes the bliss of the female organ arises;
one attains supreme bliss, the power that is the deity of bliss.
From the friction of both, that which arises is liberation, the supreme austerity;
and that natural mudrā, through its threefold nature as the triple-seal (trimudrā), becomes the supreme Lord of Mudrās, the Tree; from their union, the state [of liberation] is born.
Five, three, four, five, twenty-seven, and likewise sixty-six.
Then that pure Bhaga, joined with the digit of emission (visargakalā), dissolves into the supreme abode through its upward resonance (uccāra) upon the surface of the earth.
The yogi should fully attain the auspicious ocean of space; in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, it is the mandala of the twelve vowels, which consists of the nature of the phonemes and is liberation itself.
The foundation for the mass and for the western house is the sky,
a great jewel filled with many jewels.
The heart of the Yoginīs is their meeting place at the crossroads;
that supreme location at the crossroads is the cremation ground, which is Kaulika.
Therein should abide the twelve-syllabled Vāgbhava, the unfolding [mantra],
which is the supreme syllable, the ether, and the teacher of the knowledge of the form.
And that lineage of the Kula transmission is presided over by the fourfold *uli* of the sixfold *kula* and the twenty-seven-fold sequence.
This seat of the yoga of tradition exists in every house of the Yoginīs;
it is called the Seal of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara-mudrā), employed through the fourfold [arrangement] and so forth.
O Lord of Gods, O fortunate one, within that wheel belonging to the sixfold supreme lineage of the Western Tradition, there is a deliberation consisting of seventy million verses.
And the Śrīmata, with its three divisions, as well as the Anvayakulārṇava,
which is the true essence of the knowledge of hidden meanings, have been brought down into the world of mortals.
