The deities of the Siddhas are three, and the command of the three divisions is designated by the name "Tri."
She who dwells on Trikūṭa, who dwells on Triśṛṅga, whose form is the bliss of the three syllables;
she is the cave and the peak of Meru, the lineage of the three Yoginīs,
the lineage of perpetual bliss, and the uninterrupted succession.
The waveless Śakti has gone;
she is the deity of the syllable *kukāra*.
The goddess named Kumudā resides in the northwest as a maiden;
by the will of Śiva, she remains a youthful goddess among the Vāyavas.
Formerly created by will, she was both terrible and non-terrible; born from the ocean of knowledge, she is the body of the waves and ripples of the sea, and she abides in the principle of Śiva.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
regarding the power of reality (tattvaśakti): She who is the Supreme Will (parā icchā) and the Knower (jñānī), consisting of consciousness (cinmayā),
is celebrated as the supreme [power] of cessation and separation.
Kīrti, known by the name Kātyāyanī, is the singular deity of the arts;
in the family of reversal, she is the deity named Kujā, who is devoted to passion.
And this goddess is the deity established in the intellect, named Intellect;
she is the power within the family of coming and going, and she is distinct even from consciousness.
The power that presides over all divisions is considered nameless and supreme;
she is the stainless self-purifier for one who has performed actions in the past.
She is the purifier of all the Siddhas, the one named Kuna, and the letter;
she is the manifest Mātṛbhairavī of the left-hand letter.
For those whose minds are absorbed in meditation upon that form consisting of the syllables of Bhairava,
she then appears in the ocean of Kubjikā as a whirlpool of virtuous forms; she stands in the mire of the principles of Śiva for the heroes.
The three mudrās of the space of the liṅga are for the sake of the triple accomplishment of the form-liṅga.
One form belongs to Śiva who possesses form; likewise, both possess form and are formless.
The Kaulika distinction is formless; that is then proclaimed as the Liṅga.
Illumination:
the cessation of all sentient beings is one's own domain.
In the agency of the arts and the instruments, the body, the subtle body (liṅga), and the mind are certainly [the agents].
Thus, that Śāmbhava Yoga, which has its internal abode in the midst of power, arises from the union of nectar and death; it is the supreme-non-supreme born of yoga.
And the triad, possessing three parts,
is the upper circle of Saṃvarta;
the Linga arises from the ocean as the "serpent-umbrella" through a sequence of six divisions.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
That Power which is the Supreme Will, known as the *bhaga*, is sixfold by way of its divisions;
she is the Yoginī in manifold forms, Indrāṇī, and the deity Brahmā.
And that [form], following the sequence of the tree, becomes perfectly still at the end of the tree;
because of its reversal, the form is recognized in an instant.
And Kāmadeva is the lord of yogis because he dwells within desire;
through desire, there is the enjoyment of pleasures, and those enjoyments arise from the determination of the void.
The determination of all mantras is the supreme goal consisting of the measure of Rudrī; above that goal is the beginningless, formless state, which is remembered as fivefold.
Through the ritual procedure of churning with the Command, the sixfold energy (kalā) becomes threefold;
the conceptualization of thought shines forth as the supreme Lord’s consciousness.
And this is the ripening of the three worlds through the investigation of the introductory exposition;
it relies upon the supreme mantra, which transcends mantra, being both the higher and the lower.
O Bhairava, she who is beyond [the womb], residing within the womb, the guest, and the cage of the self, is called by the name Ramaṇānandakā for you. In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
he who is liberated from the knowledge of the stages (bhūmikās), yet is a scholar who corrupts the true meaning;
"One who reviles those who produce self-arisen knowledge shall go to hell.

Thus, in the *Ādyāvatāra*, in the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) measuring seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the Seat of Command (*ājñāpīṭha*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the determination of the six subsequent divisions of the Pure Division (*vimalabheda*).

In the *Ājñāpārameśvara*, the *Svāminīmata*, the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the tradition of the Mother (*ambākrama*), within the description of the section on the stages of the Five Triads,
this is the bliss named the Arising of the Sequence (*kramodaya*).
The venerable Vakrā said: The sixty-fifth bliss is Parāgarbha, Vimala, Atithi, and Ātmapañjara.
The western house is the hermitage of Kailāsa, the bliss of Rāmaṇa.
When those seven future births have come to an end in that next life,
the jewel-casket of manifest knowledge will appear, resembling a flower in the sky.
Illusion, resembling a flower, flows from the cavity of the navel;
it is like an oblation poured into the consciousness of the mind, serving as the means for realizing the Self.
The sacrificial rite (*adhvara*) is the form to be purified, while the deity is named *adhvara*; having known the lineage of the field of the Meru path, it is called "liberation" (*santāna*).
The continuum of the physical jar remains stable like the jar itself;
having first recognized its persistence, it is then called a "continuum."
By means of the entities in the east and west, and in the north and south respectively,
the mind and intellect of one free from desire then possess the luster of the wish-fulfilling gem.
Having realized that this is the arising of that splendor and its final state is its setting, one enters the conduct; thus, one in the stage of conduct becomes a sky-clad ascetic (digambara).
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
the letter A, the letter Ā, the letter I, and the letter Ī are the Half-moon;
they are the Vidyā that opens the eyes, which is the purification of consciousness and the mind.
Having attained the seventh through the renunciation of the six, one reaches the eighth, imperishable state—
the state that is free from affliction, beginningless, and which transcends both sound and the end of sound.
For one whose five senses are restrained, the restraint of the [mental] state occurs by the supreme command;
the mind, with its waves and ripples, becomes the ocean—the supreme state.
Śakti is the ocean of the three principles; she is the perfected liṅga and the triple-striding one. She is the triad of forms, the Kula tradition, and the transcendent Bhairava of the sacred seats.
The yogi who effects the unification of the triad and the one is proclaimed as a possessor of the stages (bhūmika). This proclamation is common to all; the last [treatise] is the Kulārṇava.
Through the awakening to the sequence of the six steps, there are twenty-seven divisions;
having extracted [the essence] for the sake of the stages and knowing that supreme state, [one attains it].
Furthermore, for yogins, this instruction on the meaning of the stages is supreme for the unambiguous removal of delusion; indeed, one is not liberated without knowing it.
This is the essence of the Kaumāra sequence and the cutting through delusion,
which exists as the root-lineage family transmitted through the Kaula tradition.
The Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
The meaning of the stages, which is difficult for even yogins to discern, has been declared to you;
having understood it through the flood of the sequence of the hundred sūtras, one enters upon the conduct.
For one whose meaning of the stages is purified and who delights in the succession,
there occurs the attainment of the supreme state— the supreme, peaceful, and stainless.
Even if someone is a bearer of the command, if he is deluded, he is not a liberator;
for when the teacher is deluded regarding the sequence and the mandala, [he cannot grant liberation].
Then the disciple would not be liberated from the difficult-to-cross ocean of saṃsāra;
therefore, having abandoned delusion, one should thoroughly practice the Kaula knowledge.
The initiation of explanation must be performed; otherwise, it should never be done.
O Goddess, he who exercises authority without understanding the meaning of the *Saṃhitā* is himself a traitor and shall find his path cut off at the root.
In the first lineage of the Kaula and of the Western House.
Having understood this for the sake of the *saṃhitā*, one who is a vessel for liberation shall be liberated;
O Mahādeva, such a person is truly qualified, otherwise he is merely a bearer of the name.
That which gathers within the mind the consciousness-space, the dense bliss of consciousness—
that form of the Supreme Brahman is called the self-consciousness (ātma-caitanya).
Through constant practice, the yoga of the sky-born arises eternally for yogis;
having attained that supreme Brahman, he proceeds upon the path of liberation.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
[The yogin] goes to the supreme station called the *bhaga*, which, through its reversal,
[bestows] complete sovereignty, virtue, fame, and fortune.
The sixfold nature of dispassion and liberation is traditionally remembered as *bhaga*,
as is the stabilization of the cessation of mental fluctuations.
O Lord of Yogins, the one whose nature is certainty proceeds as a sixfold self;
this [proceeds] also from the churning of the three channels, which possess the three deities of the triad.
Having understood the course of the great path, who would not be liberated from bondage— that triple-folded pit of the moon, the sun, and fire?
The seat known as Bhaga, the seat known as Śaktibimba, and Uḍḍiyāṇa—
on the path of great liberation, these are remembered as the supreme attainment and the highest digit.
She who, by the resonance of sound, is called Amṛtā and is the Nameless (Anāmikā),
she is the Mother of the World known as Kṣobhā, the well-blazing Kulakaulinī.
Having the form of a great flame of light, she resides on the web-throne (jālapīṭha) to the right;
she is Rudrāṇī in her fierce form, renowned as the embodiment of liberation.
Satiated by the filling of nectar from the left [hand], she is established in the left corner;
she is proclaimed as Pūrṇagiryā, the mother of the full orb.
"Of her, whose ancestors are the constant instigators for the sake of liberation,
the hermitage of Bhairava is established as the fulfillment of the complete mental creation."
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, recitation, meditation, and worship are performed in the Void (śūnya); libation (tarpaṇa) is prescribed for the North (śiśira).
The path of the gods (devayāna) is in the North, while the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna) is in the South.
In the center is the bridge, the supreme command (parājñā), for it is remembered as such through its activity;
and there indeed is the sacred seat (pīṭha) called Kāmākhya, worshipped by the best of gods.
Having realized the power to perform restraint and grace,
the yogin becomes the destroyer of the impurities of bound souls and attains pervasion throughout the entire universe.
The practitioner of mantras who abides in the arising and maintenance of the state of absorption is the cause for the persistence of saṃsāra;
she is the universal pervasion within the supreme wheel, appearing in the form of a *liṅga* from its center.
That Kālī, who delights in supreme bliss, is deficient in the moon;
she is the power (śakti) arisen from the foundation of the kanda, the Kaulinī in the form of a coil.
Having meditated upon those imperishable [energies] with the mind, the wise one should slowly arise and perceive them with the mind within the Bindu and Nāda in the supreme abode.
Gradually, in the wheel of space (khe-cakra), Khecarī resides in the sky, having the nature of the lunar orb;
she becomes the single state of equal flavor (samarasa) of these three: Śiva, Ātman, and Śakti.
When the movement of the power whose nature is auspiciousness arises in the wheel of space (khecakra), there occurs a state of stability that functions for the sake of the stages (bhūmikā).
Then it attains a state of oneness characterized by supreme bliss;
this is the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Therefore, that which is the supreme power is the imperishable cause of happiness.
It is said that [the state] situated above transcends the path of *bindu* and *nāda*.
One should know that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva are of the nature of the five Brahmas; I shall now describe their locations.
Viṣṇu is situated in the heart of Brahmā, established in his throat.
Rudra is situated in the region of the palate, and Īśvara is at the end of Nirodhinī; there, above the uvula, on the upper path, one is obstructed.
That very place is said to be the station of the Bindu; above that is the station of the Nāda.
Residing there is the divine Śiva, who transcends the qualities (guṇa) and is both supreme and non-supreme.
By virtue of her nature as eternal bliss, she stands above the churning;
within that power (śakti), she is known as the one who obstructs from above, called Bhaga.
When, through practice, one has realized the sixfold great arising— consisting of Will, Knowledge, and Action, and endowed with the power of the Self— then [one attains liberation].
Filled with essence, she remains there, shimmering like nectar;
her form is curved like a serpent, and she is characterized by supreme bliss.
And by that [practice], this [world] dissolves into its own essential nature in six ways;
the non-supreme states come to an end, and the supreme state of the yogis is attained.
Where, having indeed shattered the door-panel of Brahmā, one enters the city of the supreme enemy;
having attained the path of Nirvāṇa, Sadāśiva becomes all-pervasive— thus [ends] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Moving stealthily, she strikes with her feet; she is Jayantī, the remover of impurity, the fickle one, the supreme Vidyā, garlanded with points in the sky.
One should drink that digit of the moon, which is a drop of nectar, with the mouth;
likewise, for the sake of liberation, one should draw it back in again through both nostrils.
The yogi who has attained dissolution through constant practice shall conquer old age and death;
he achieves the pacification of all diseases and the destruction of pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman).
Even when his [karmic] destruction is exhausted, the lord of yogins, remaining fixed in the instrument,
attains [realization] in the navel-lotus, the heart-lotus, and indeed the third, the face-lotus.
That power dwells eternally, established together with the individual soul (jīva),
in a single place where the abundance of enjoyments is present and adorned as pure consciousness alone.
Having firmly fixed [the mind] upon the heart-lotus, one should contemplate one's own true nature,
situated within the cavity of the lotus-bud because it has dissolved into the space of the heart.
One should cultivate a state of mind free from distraction; thus one shall attain the supreme state.
O mind, hold fast within your heart that imperishable, highest abode.
There, at all times, one should [maintain] the immovable flame of the crest according to one's strength;
there, within the fire-drill of the vital breath, one should [concentrate] with the mind again and again.
Then, O God, he shines like the sun released from the clouds;
that supreme, divine *kalā* which resides pervasively within the channels (*vartman*)— this is the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Knowing that, the yogi is liberated from the cycle of existence so difficult to transcend;
O wise one, the yogi should gaze at the lower part of the cavity of the palate.
When the mind is thus obstructed and remains for even a moment,
then, as if stepped upon by ants, such is the sensation that arises.
Once a state born of contact has been attained, one should not again move the mind;
it attains a subtle opening, a hundredth part of the tip of a hair.
Having emerged through that aperture, one should enter the state of Śākta;
in the ever-arisen station of Śākta, extending up to eleven finger-breadths, there above is the supreme, pure [state], resembling the fire of universal dissolution.
It was filled with rows of waves, surges, billows, and crests of waves.
The practitioner of mantra should contemplate the eternal [deity] descending into the heart-lotus of his own body;
from that, the yogi is born, freed from old age and death.
Transcending power, it goes to the Supreme; transcending space, it is all-pervading.
Then all agitations dissolve into that supreme state.
And it is known beyond doubt that one gains strength at every step;
my conviction is firm that the knowledge of reality resides within one's own body.
The knot in the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away,
and all evils are destroyed when that which is both transcendent and immanent is seen.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
One should gradually pierce [the centers] by means of the nature of supreme bliss;
having pierced the supreme station with an intellect held by fortitude.
One should contemplate the self as the power of consciousness, subtle and without support;
those whose minds are fixed on that which is without support are well-established—of this there is no doubt.
Abiding by itself within the body, and by itself within the range of the Self,
it arises for those who are awakened, but ceases for the unawakened.

Thus, in the introduction to the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses emerged from the Path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primordial seat on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), in the determination of the Sixfold Subsequent Division of the Vimalabheda,
in the Kādivarṇa division, in the Svāminīmata which is the supreme command of the Lord, accompanied by the glorious twenty-four thousand [verses].
In the description of the chapter on the divisions of the Self spoken in the Ambākrama,
this is the bliss named Kramodaya.
Śrīvakrama said: [This is] the sixty-sixth bliss,
concerning the Lord of the Ādhāra-cakra, within the leader of the Kaumāra-krama.
The two wings, situated in the sky, have manifested as the ocean.
The meaning of the mandala, which has been revealed in its entirety through its sixfold divisions,
is pure and consists of six types residing within the support.

Bhairava, who is the very essence of the remaining sequence of the womb (yoni) and its functional capacity, shines stainless within the wheel; having reached the end of the three sides, he has attained dissolution.
Always engaged in yoga through the sequence of the stages (*bhūmikrama*) in the hermitage, he is a contemplator of yoga;
he is bliss without beginning or end, the awakener of the heart-lotus from darkness.
The Lord of the Sun of the Full Wheel, the Bhairava who is the Mother of the Kula,
the destroyer of all things, the Vāgbhava-mantra, the crusher of enemies.
Āmoda is the supreme relish; Vijñāna is the hollow; Hara is manifest in vision as beauty, having abandoned all partisan attachment.
He is indeed the Lord Kaustubha of the mantra of the Ākāśacakra;
for seven births, he is truly equal in his capacity to bestow both prosperity and nourishment.
In this Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the accumulation of this impurity of the body born of birth, of poison, and of wind— which is burning— is destroyed; it is free from sin and unstruck (anāhata).
The Lord of Śrī is the half-moon of the wheel of the pure junction for those who apply themselves to unfolding [the reality] and desire to conquer the path to liberation.
For one who is liberated liberates the self; indeed, the self is traditionally held to be the liberator.
A yogi who is never unliberated attains the state of perfection through liberation.
From the churning of the wheel of the surging command, rays of awakening emerge;
through the power of the exhaustion of karma, the mandala is made manifest.
But by effortlessly piercing the sphere of the single Kadamba-lineage that has remained silent in its primordial nature,
the supreme cause is attained.
The sixty-four wheels are known as rays whose nature is awakening;
their leader stands within them, consisting of six syllables and free from the mind.
Having ascended through the central channel, enveloped by the six syllables,
they then emerge from the aperture as witnesses of the Lord of the Kula.
The single opening is called the cave (guhā), consisting of the *kādamba* and composed of awakened consciousness;
situated there, it provides the means of subsistence through the thorough knowledge of the six wheels (*cakras*).
Furthermore, the wheel of space, the wheel of earth, and the universal wheel are the abode of consciousness;
that is the great pervasion of the three wheels, and that pervasion occurs through the command of Kula.
In the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*,
within the world of the hexagon, is the Wheel of Space (*khacakra*) beginning with *kha* and *parā*.
It is the very nature of the knowledge of yoga for those whose minds have been exhausted by wandering.
The earth-wheel belongs to those who move on earth; it is the earth-mover that pierces the womb.
Because the fluctuations of the mind have dissolved, he remains established at the arising of the cessation of mental activity.
He who moves through the sky, the destroyer of the guardians of the quarters,
that Supreme Self is worshipped as Space and Time.
Thus, O Lord of Mantras, the threefold wheel within the sphere of space consists of all mantras abiding in emptiness; it is the "wheel of emptiness" in its three aspects.
The wheel devoid of the three qualities is devoid of the sixteen vowels;
that wheel would be without sound, and its deities are the lords of the zodiac signs.
The leader, the creator of emanation, who reaches the end of the city of the wheel of command, is born from the heroic power of the goddesses, the wheels, the siddhas, and the mantras.
Then, by means of the awakening to the bliss of the Self, the Moon and the Sun sequentially illuminate that [reality];
they are the illuminators of the shadow and of the shadow's shadow.
Having filled all bodies with darkness for those who dwell within them,
he is the knower of self-arisen wisdom and the illuminator of the lamp of primordial knowledge.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, there are two digits (kalā) of Anala and three digits of Ravi;
the supreme Mother is the Dhruvayoni, just as she is the womb for both Anala and Ravi.
Analārcita, Bhānu, and Śaśiprabhā within the Bhanu-manvantara—
these three are the Mothers of the Cakras of Space, Earth, and the Directions.
The single abode of the Mothers is the stainless Command of Fire;
she should abide in the partless Supreme, and then the Kalā arises.
In the dual nature, within its own form, there would be action characterized by movement;
however, in the Kula-knowledge of yoga, the command here is motionless in the center.
"That which is the supreme wheel, immovable due to cessation, bearing the form of gnosis— the assembly of the Mothers at night in the Ājñā-cakra, in the supreme state."
When the wheel and the measure of the Mothers have passed into the middle of the night,
sexual pleasure and delight increase through union devoid of the male organ.

The wheel of space situated in the center of space, adorned with the five spaces—this is the meditation of the liberated ones. Therein, O Lord, is the bliss of the sky-clad; that wheel is then the supreme heart of the yogi.
And the heart of space, together with the wheel of space, assumes the form of bliss while being flooded [with light].
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Then, the bliss arising from the wheel is the bliss of the supreme and the non-supreme;
having first purified the ocean and so forth, [one realizes] the supreme Kula within the heart.
O Bhairava, you are the supreme syllable, the source of the arising of all mantras, as well as of the Kula-jewel, of existence, and of the knowledge of existence.
The great lord named Akṣarabhairava is the nameless one;
the source of power, the bliss of dissolution, the Lord of Kula, the master rejoices.
Between the two, Prabhā and Kānti, and between the two paths, Meru and Mārga,
having understood both in reverse order, the movement of conduct becomes clear.
Having made it manifest, the bridge is manifest; the *kūṭaka* consists of four syllables.
It is the self of the supreme four *kalās*, an expansion abiding in the void.
Situated there is the assembly of the gods and goddesses, the ultimate limit of union;
it is the inexpressible wheel called the Sound of Śiva, which is the body of Śāmbhavī.
There, the Goddess Kṛṣṇā resides; she who stands in the conch is Śaṅkhanī.
For embodied beings whose bodies have been tasted by her essence, the [objects] such as flavors are to be grasped through their inner state (bhāva).
One should purify the base of the pericarp of the ocean through the distinction of the two *visargas*, as well as the wheel of both the *kalā* and the *nāda* at the *ghaṇṭikā*.
This purification consists of the reversal of all activities that are contrary [to the natural order].
Abiding in the syllable that pierces the bindu, it is the purification of the universal form.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
For one who possesses the yoga of sustaining [the breath], for one who has tamed the mind,
and for one established in the vow with firm devotion, purification is the cleansing of the *bindu*.
This is the practice for the Lord of the Immortals, the sovereign of various destinies;
it is the purification of reality for the sake of accomplishing reality.
O Lord of Ciñciṇī, knower of the three times, one should meditate upon the fivefold path and non-path of the principles, consisting of action, at the root of the ear.
Then the yogi should hold the life-force and the constituent parts by means of primordial nature;
from the root, the drop flows forth—the wheel worshipped by the hosts of gods.
From the root arises the one supreme *haṃsa*, consisting of the consciousness of Bhairava-bliss;
it is the power of the lamp of repose, according to the divisions of movement and utterance.
The "remainder of the digit" (kalāśeṣa) is known as the Root (mūla), and that Root is of the nature of Kula.
Because it is the remainder of the digit, it is the goddess Ṭaṅkiṇī, the deity of the Bhava [family].
The mistress of the lords of the wheels is in an aged state and holds a skull;
the skull has the form of the full moon, and she is the deity there at the new moon.
When the skull is dissolved above in the cremation ground of Karandhama,
the Karavīra,
having first broken through the city, it is then born as Samanā. (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
Having known the Self, whose form is the totality and who is taught as being accessible to the intellect,
the knower of the unstruck mantra easily attains the conduct of the moon.
By ceasing the coming and going [of the breath], one should strike [the vital centers] below and above;
having made the mind one-pointed, [one experiences] bliss in the city of the Unstruck (anāhata).
Then a great ocean of wind arises like a wheel,
and at that time, a beautiful *karavīra* tree emerges.
The power of Hara is Parā, the pericarp of the lotus;
situated on the path of the heart, she is the first [ground], known by the name Viśrāmabhūmikā.
When the unstruck (*anāhata*) wheel arises, one should effect the state that bestows nirvāṇa;
it is the abode of all yogins, the unstruck state within the embodied.
The king of mantras named Trikūṭa consists of the form of sound ending in the letter *ka*, encapsulated by the letter *sa*, and joined with the digit of the half-moon.
The king of mantras is the sovereign of the unstruck chakra (anāhata-cakra);
having performed the earthly instrument, he makes the instrument the abode of earth.
And that fire, situated in the middle of the sixteen and marked by the digit of the moon, bestows happiness upon all yogins; it is the cause arising from the expansion [of consciousness].

The Bhairava of the principle of consciousness (*vijñānatattva-bhairava*), whose very self is the mind that delights in the lotus, is known by those of heroic conduct within the unstruck wheel (*anāhata-cakra*). Having performed the movement of day and night, he causes the circle of vowels to blossom. *—From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.*
Having meditated on [the deity] dwelling in the cave at the end of the heart, one attains the state of pure consciousness.
Having understood the mantra of movement, the knowledge of going, and indeed both going and returning,
there is a radiance resembling the full moon between the jewel and the person.
This wheel, filled with the jewel, consists of both Śiva and Śakti;
because the sun and moon have dissolved therein, fire is then produced.
And that [space] is infinite and born from the digestive fire of primordial nature;
having bound the city of Śiva-Śakti, it then becomes full of jewels (maṇipūrṇa).
And that power belongs to the syllables and the signs;
it is the flood of powers of the emission of both Kaulas, the deity consisting of the six faces.
When one remains established there, absorbed in that state while the left and right [channels] persist,
then the station of the Moon arises within the nourishing channels (*āpyāyananāḍī*).
Step by step, through the differentiation of the channels, they are proclaimed as a single stalk.
The mental reflection upon all entities is experienced as awakening.
There, the contraction of the tone is the "all-channel" (sarvanāḍika);
the expansion of all the signs is the "jewel-filled" (maṇipūrṇa), possessing great luster.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
From *tejas* arises *nāda*; from *nāda*, sound (*śabda*) is born;
and it is also produced through the channels (*nāḍī*) by the striking together of the teeth, lips, palate, and tongue.
And then there arises the syllable, the desired deity of the eight groups,
the full moon that is the abode of all the deities.
The Koṅkaṇa wheel is situated in Maṇipūra and is illuminated by the thirty [gods];
the presiding deity there is Kiṅkiṇī, the dark-colored goddess.
This cave is a divine temple among the temples of the gods of gods;
it is the abode of all the Mothers, and this wheel belongs to the Supreme Lord.

Within that very [space], there is the abode of the Yoginīs, situated between the navel and the *ādhāra*. That is the stride of the Sun and Moon; it is called the "Space" (*kha*) consisting of three measures (*trimātra*), established within the Three Powers (*triśakti*).
Endowed with the arts of the three goals of life, it is differentiated by fifty lingas.
The wheel is the sovereign of the wheel of sounds, and Koṅkaṇa is its locus;
it establishes the divine authority of the goddesses within their own respective domains.
The consciousness of the purity of one’s own body is situated there, established in reality;
it is joined with the four seats and is the wheel of the letter *E* of the fire.
Thus, the wheel well-remembered within oneself, situated between both triangles, is declared to be the Adhiṣṭhāna, the Wheel of the Yoni, which is both supreme and non-supreme. In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
the wheel is between the anus and the genitals, beautifully adorned by fire and moon.
The Supreme Lord Khageśa, pervaded by drops of nectar.
The jewel known as the "kanda-wheel" pierces the vital points (*marmas*) of the channels;
it is each one of these that is the supreme power, designated by the name Nādamālinī.
That [goddess], however, has five aspects and three forms, her shape being that of the *bhaga*;
she indeed has the faces of Fire, Moon, and Sun at the end of the mantra-wheel.
The hermitage of all yogis has a summit shaped like a triangle;
it resembles a moving bracelet, being impenetrable and difficult to overcome.
The wind flows with power and speed like [the currents] of the sky;
therein the sixth is remembered as the yogin, and he exists by virtue of his non-dual nature.
His sixth power is remembered as the deity named Raudrī.

By the mere blocking of that [channel], everything situated within the *bhaga* is completely abandoned; through this renunciation, when the Lord of Birds (the Sun) resides in the seventh station, whose form is the void (*vyoma*), the unmanifest power (*avyākṛta-śakti*) comes to exist within the Śākta power for the sake of restraint and grace.
Then, joy arises for the living being from the *maṇi* person;
it is the support of the knot of life (*jīvagranthi*) located below at the birth-angle.
O Kaulīśa, when the mass of sounds arises within the waves and ripples of the mind,
there [is] Haṃsabhairava, the teacher of the Kaula.
That [syllable] resides within the letters of the skull, situated on the wheel at the door of the skull;
Dharitrī is in the city-wheel, and Mahālakṣmī is in the ether-wheel.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
By means of the restraint of the ten winds, the ten channels are pierced;
thus is the Foundation Wheel (ādhāracakra), the city of the arising of the perfected mantra.
Its power, called Maunā, resides in Malaya and is downward-facing;
since the Siddha is upward-facing, therefore that [power] becomes the means of realization (*pratyaya*).
The wheel is known to consist of conditions;
by moving through that wheel, and with all pervasive fears dissolved, one shall attain liberation upward.
And thus, O noble one, the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*) is sixfold; this is the brief teaching on the sixfold sequence of command, the great self-consecration family (*svādhiṣṭhānakula*).
Because the family (*kula*) is the purification for the sake of the stages (*bhūmi*),
[this] verse concerning the meaning of the stages [is called] *Vijñānakulabhāskara*.

"Revealed for those who desire to conquer ignorance, abiding in the abode of liberation"— thus [ends] the determination of the *Vimalabheda-uttaraṣaṭka*, brought down to the first sacred seat (*pīṭha*), within the lineage (*anvaya*) of the great sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, which consists of seventy million verses, emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, and belonging to the *Kādi* division.

In the *Ājñāpārameśvara*, the *Svāminīmata*, the venerable compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the tradition of the Mother (*ambākrama*), within the description of the chapter on the Eight Kulas of the Vakrāmnāya,
this is the bliss named the Arising of the Sequence (*kramodaya*).
The sixty-seventh blissful Śrīnātha said:
"Therefore, through the unfolding of the mudrās and mantras within the maṇḍala of the senses..."
And indeed, the various divisions of the sequence have been taught by you in the cave of Akula.
For them, the arising of reality is correctly preceded by the thorough mental cultivation of the self;
likewise, the section on reality is situated within the three sequences of the Yoga-pīṭha.
The venerable Vakrā said:
Beginning from the seat of emanation (sṛṣṭipīṭha) up until I, whose body is the Crooked One (Vakratanu),
I shall here describe in brief the arising of the principles (tattva).
In Kāmarūpa, Indra is present; desire is said to be creation.
Āpaḥ is declared to be Pūrṇagiri, and Tejas is remembered as Jālandhara.
The syllable Oṃ becomes Vāyu; that single principle becomes threefold. Therein, Ākāśa becomes Icchā, and he is proclaimed as Kumāra.
Above that is Kāminī, the mistress of the subtle element of smell;
she consists of taste and form, and is Pūrṇā, the blazing one of the subtle element of light.
The Oḍḍā consists of the form of sound; she is established as being threefold. Viṣṇu is the subtle element of touch, and he resides in the Siṃha-krama.
Śrīkaṇṭha is the embodiment of speech by virtue of his ordaining of words; the high-minded one is the essence of the hands; the self of Īśvara is in the feet; and Nandirudraka is in the anus.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
the generative organ (upastha) should be of the form of Bhairava and consist of Sadyojāta;
the ear belongs to the nature of Anāhata, while the skin-nature is Maṇipūraka.
The eye is sovereign gnosis, the breath is the tongue within the circle of the sense organs;
the nose is to be known as pure, and the mind is said to be their support.
Intellect is the Matangi woman, ego is Pulindika,
primordial nature is named Shavari, and the Purusha is called Vijaya.
He is Brahmā and he is non-dual, the creator of the three worlds; his portion, however, is the manifest [universe], which is the domain of the location of the physical body.
The external self and the internal self, both mobile and immobile, effect the combination and transformation of the parts and limbs of the *liṅga*.
Impelled by time through necessity amidst the various divisions and sub-divisions,
that power of Śiva, whose form is pure, has arisen.
She is a *samanā* by her very nature, the *unmanā* Mahantārī;
filled with the bliss of her own inherent joy, she creates the three worlds.
I am Kubjikā, whose very nature is the command of Śiva; though neuter, by virtue of having conquered my senses, I hold authority over the ascetic office.
For through the *saṃpuṭa* [mantra], the Vidyā is indeed divided according to the letters beginning with *bha*;
I am neither woman nor man, but rather that supreme power of will (*icchāśakti*).

The person (*puruṣa*) is merely like a seed; he is called the "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*). Consisting of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, as an agent, he is bound by attachment to karma. [In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa it is said:
"I am not the agent; I consider Śiva to be the one who will act because of his nature as the Person."
And that which begins with Earth (Dharitrī) and ends with Śiva is called the aggregate of the principles (tattvapiṇḍa).
In the fourfold creation of beings, he indeed becomes a bound soul (paśu);
in the eighth, the mental creation, he attains birth and enters the eighth stage of life (āśrama).
That state which begins from Kāmarūpa and the other seats is with substrate (sālaya),
as long as I, Śivā, have not been worshipped by millions of ritual acts.
How, then, can attainment be achieved by mortals in the Śrīkrama, which is most excellent in its qualities,
by means of which sacrifice there is the purification of the threefold impurity?
The principles and the twenty-seven steps proceed out of their proper order;
the sequential path has been shown for the sake of their destruction.
Sacrifice with the maṇḍala, recitation, and the great vow of the Śiva-vidyā—
all this becomes perfectly elevated, according to the established state of the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable].
Furthermore, I shall explain to you again the division of the principles (tattvas).
The earth is Kāmarūpa, and water is known as Pūrṇagiri.
Jālandhara is the great splendor, the mandala of Vāyu and Oṃkāra;
Ākāśa is the seat of Tisra, while the house is the glorious Candrapura.

The five great elements (mahābhūtas) are traditionally taught; from them arises the pentad of subtle elements (tanmātras). Fragrance resides in the earth principle (pārthiva-tattva), while taste resides in the water principle (āpas-tattva).
From fire comes form; from that, wind arises as touch.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, space is the great sound; these constitute the fivefold activity of the senses.
Speech is remembered as being in the principle of smell; the two hands in the principle of touch;
likewise, the feet in the midst of sound; and the anus arises in the fire element.

The generative organ arises from the *svāda* [tattva]; these constitute the fivefold group of the organs of action (*karmendriya*). Now, they speak of the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) in the same manner as the organs of action.
This ear is situated in the generative organ; likewise, the skin is located in the hand;
the great eye is the reality of the anus; and the tongue is in the circle of the feet.

The nose is traditionally held to reside in the principle of speech (vāktattva), and those [elements] beginning with earth are situated there; for that beginningless, immutable Śiva stands at the summit of them all.
The intellect (buddhi), appearing in whatever form it desires according to its past actions, is present;
the mind (manas) itself, by the power of the intellect, is situated in the sacred seat of Jālandhara.
Having first understood the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) through the speed of the mind,
one should know that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is established on the left path at Pūrṇagiri.
The Puruṣa, existing as mere seed within the abode of the lunar city,
has his hermitage in the resonance (nāda) which is the inner self, the moon.
Thus, the mark of the Blessed One (bhagavataḥ) is established in the form of the bhaga;
it is called the Great Mass (mahāpiṇḍa), whose nature consists of the causal principle (pratyaya) that is the power of action (kriyāśakti).
O Lord, I am that very one who has been protected and established on the path of mantra;
she is indeed the measure of Śiva, endowed with the quality of differentiation.
The bliss arising from the three streams is the bliss that garlands existence;
she is the mother of all living beings, according to the divisions of earth and the other elements.
In the center is that which is without beginning or end, devoid of dissolution and origination.
Space is something; even of the hundredth part of the most subtle [atom], there is a thousandth.
That void which is mere contemplation is called the auspicious consciousness (caitanya);
in this way, by its essential nature as reality, it is proclaimed as the Śākta-liṅga. (Kumārikākhaṇḍa)
That very reality, which was condensed into the essence of the *piṇḍī*, arose as Kīrtideva in the city of Śrīmacandrapura under the *ciñciṇī* tree in the vault of the sky.
He alone is the natural lord of the worlds; this entire universe, from Ananta up to Śiva, is dissolved within that Great Abode (Mahālaya).
Persistence, arising, and decline—these four gates also exist;
the noose, established in its predominance, is born from the waves of the ocean of Māyā.
Thus, while the entire path proceeds through activities such as sexual enjoyment and the like,
its cessation is proclaimed through metaphorical instruction.
The *piṇḍa* is its substratum, and she is proclaimed as such;
like a bird of bewildered mind caught in a snare of nooses.
Afterwards, once it has been abandoned, it rises up into the midst of the sky;
in the same way, the Self remains as the "abiding-in-the-body" (piṇḍastha) for one whose mind is deluded.
This mantra, residing in the *piṇḍa*, is the state [of being] characterized by form and so forth;
it transcends form, is all-pervading, and stands above all things.

"O Lord, I have correctly explained to you the Fifty Verses on Reality (Tattvapañcāśikā), consisting of the states of the mass (piṇḍastha), the state of the word (padastha), the state of form (rūpastha), and that which is devoid of form (rūpavarjita). — Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
O Lord of Gods, the practice of the Pīṭha-piṇḍa and the sequence of the Tattvapañcāśikā have been explained to you in the form of a sūtra, according to the sūtras.

Thus, in the introduction to the great sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses, in the glorious twenty-four thousand [verse] [Tantra], this is the Sūtra on the Chapter Concerning the Sequence of Principles (Tattvakrama).
The sixty-eighth bliss: the venerable Vakrā said:
"She who has six forms, whose body is great, whose nature is light, and who is clothed in yoga."
With its remainder and its latent impressions, it exists in all states as the most great.
Ciñciṇī is supremely formidable, radiant with dark, red, and crimson hues;
she is Kulamātaṅginī, the fierce Raudrī, the goddess Kujā, who possesses six faces.
She has the luster of ten or eight eyes, is languid with the bliss of wine,
has a face like the female organ, has the form of the female organ, and is endowed with six female organs.
Situated in the center of the *bhaga*, formidable, enclosed within the hollow of the womb of the *bhaga*,
Kubjikā, the mistress of the *kula*, consists of the collection of the thirty-two syllables.
Pervading the mandala in the sky through eighty-four arrangements,
she is indeed the goddess Khageśvarī, the immortal Śuddhakālikā.
The goddess Bhairavī, the supreme Tripurā, resides as the three-part [mantra];
she stands upon the path of the Mālinīkula, she is Kujā, and she dwells within the heart-lotus.
She is indeed Śrīkuladīpābhā, Barbarā, and Bahurūpiṇī; she is the mother of Rudra, the mother of the Siddhas, and the mother of Mahābhairava.
The Mother of Heroes, the Mother of Yogis, the Mother of the Sacred Seats, and the Daughter of the World;
endowed with six aspects, she is the Terrible One whose range extends across eighteen arms.
The trident, the knife, the sword, the iron arrow, and likewise the terrifying [weapon];
the noose, the hand-drum, the shield, and the sacrificial pap of the Kaulikas— [these are] from the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
These nine are on the right path, and likewise nine on the left path:
the skull-bowl, the khaṭvāṅga staff, the jewel-garland, and the bow.
One should contemplate the goddess together with her retinue, possessing eighteen mudrās: the goad, the seat-mudrā, the shield, and the book-throne.
She is endowed with five feet, naked and without clothing;
she has eyes like the bimba fruit, her face is turned downward, and she wears a serpent as a sacred thread.
Adorned with sacrificial threads born of the tongue and embellished by the five mudrās,
she possesses eighteen arms and utters the mudrās from her seat.
With the garland of vowels bound upon her head, she hangs from the necklace of letters;
she is adorned by the divine ether and by twelve million Ḍāmaras.
With a garland of jewels bound around her neck, adorned with divine gems,
the Supreme Goddess is beautified by great clusters of jasmine flowers.
Delighted by the fragrance of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor,
she is clothed in the directions perfumed with sweet scents and dressed in the fragrant smoke of incense.
The Supreme Goddess is clothed in divine jewels and magnificent garments;
she transcends all parts, is omnipresent, and stands above all.
The goddess Kujā is of six aspects and has the supreme unchanging as her form;
bearing such a form, the Command consists of forty-two syllables.
By her very nature she is humpbacked in form; in the division of the Vidyā, she is Kujāmbikā.
In Candradvīpa resides Mahākubjā, through the threefold grace of Śrīkaṇṭha. One should pierce the hundred thousand [syllables] of Kujā by means of the path.
Having thus understood meditation in the past, one should practice it within one's own body.
In this body, one should perform the sequential worship, recitation, and yoga belonging to the Kumārikākhaṇḍa;
one should meditate until reaching the state that transcends the internal organ (antakaraṇa).
He who worships the Krama anywhere while being devoid of meditation on Kujā and abandoned by the oral tradition (āmnāya) of Kujā is a bound soul (paśu), one whose self is impure.
His knowledge of the sequential maṇḍalas and all else will be useless;
he will not have a clear understanding of the next world as long as he does not worship the *kula*.
"In that case, how can there be any pervasion for him within the Śāmbhava Kula?
Śrī Kaulīśa said:
"O Goddess of the lords of gods, I have heard the meaning of the Āgamas in its entirety."
Now I wish to hear the instruction on the Sūtra of Liberation,
by the mere understanding of which one is released from the bondage of existence.
The illustrious Kubjikā said: "O Lord of Gods, I shall explain the path to liberation clearly;
you must keep it strictly secret and not give it to just anyone."
The Picumata Tantra, the Siddhayogeśvarīmata,
the Śivādūtīmata Tantra, and the Vāmeśvarīmata Tantra.
The Sundarī Tantra, the Ratnasundarikā-mata,
the Mātṛmata Tantra, and indeed the Rūpikā-mata Tantra.
The Sārasvata Tantra is considered [the first], then the Maṅgalāmata Tantra,
the Śikhottara Tantra, the Sutantra, and the Mālinīmata.
The Ambāmata Mahātantra, the Khecarīmata Tantra, the Bhairavīmata Tantra, and the Śrīkulālikāmata Tantra.
It is held that in the three lineages there are six [sections]; in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
there are clearly five authorities concerning the Krama that are without support.
The five causes are situated above; thus, according to your teaching, there are sixteen [levels].
Beginning from the first up to the end of Samanā, they are pervasive within their respective principles (tattvas).
O Śambhu, they remain established up to the limit of Samanā throughout the entire covering (āvaraṇa) of the Sakala state.
The Mahacchabdamata is first, followed by the Vimala and the Ṣaṭkanirṇaya.
But the descent into the six supreme [stages] indeed transcends the sixfold birth;
it always stands above the tantra, having passed beyond the belly of the Great Illusion.
The lineage of the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya) is the arising of the sequence (kramodaya), which is its own authority;
it transcends Māyā and arises first within the portion above Samanā.
In former times, there was an incarnation born within the division of Manthānabhairava,
from which emerged the Kādi division along with the ocean of Tārās, issued forth by the command of Śambhu;
by the mere knowledge of which, omniscience is attained in age after age.

One who knows the threefold division of the sections, who understands the ritual action of the four quarters, and who is disciplined in the sequence of the divisions beginning with *ka*, shall be an awakener of the doctrine; yet one devoid of the mantra-maṇḍala should be known as fallen from yoga.
Like a flower in the sky,
one who is devoid of the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*) and stripped of the sixfold power (*ṣoḍhāśakti*) wanders further in saṃsāra and does not turn back from it.
Having not given according to the rule, one is turned away from the command of the pledge.
He who constantly eats [forbidden food] eats the three hells;
he who, devoid of the three ablutions, worships the Krama, [is likewise lost]. —From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*—
The great fool who is devoid of the self of the samaya, being excluded from the three Gāyatrīs and bereft of that Vidyā and its grasping, experiences the three hells.

One who has transcended the sixfold maṇḍala does not turn back from *saṃsāra*. But he who worships the supreme secret of the Guru without seed (*nirbīja*) remains further in *saṃsāra*; he does not turn back from *saṃsāra*.
In the sequence of the divisions beginning with *ka*, it is not joined [with the others] and is devoid of the door of the chalk (*khaṭikā*).
One who has transcended the sixteen-fold grid (prastāra) is not released from their office;
[this applies] by the sequence beginning with Unmanā, up to Śrīnātha and Ciñciṇī.
"O Śambhu, without knowing the convention of the flowers, one does not possess liberation.
Śrīnātha said: [This is] the Sūtra on the Performance of the Observance (Samayānuṣṭhāna).
O Lord of Gods, how is it in the Buddhist [tradition], and how, how is it in the Ārhanta [tradition]?
But how is there liberation in the Vaiṣṇava, the Saura, and the Śaiva [traditions];
and how is it in the Vāma and Dakṣiṇa paths, and in the Mālinīkula?
O Goddess, how is the path to liberation in the Trika, and how in the Nityākrama? How is liberation in that which is called the Trikhaṇḍa, and how in the Krama of Kālikā?
Liberation indeed [is found] in the Amarikāmnāya as well as in the Śrīvakrikāmata;
for above that, there exists no mudrā, maṇḍala, or krama.
That eternal will is proclaimed to have a limited scope;
therein, from the Āgamas down to the Buddhist philosophy, [is its extent].
Since that reality of the intellect (buddhitattva) is not liberation, it is limited;
however, for those established in the tranquil Self, it is said to be limitless.
But those who have perished through lack of contentment and are arrogant with egoism—
for them there is rebirth once more, and saṃsāra does not cease.
"In this way, one should always meditate upon [the deity] at the end of Kujā in the form of liberation.
Thus has been briefly declared the consecration for the yoga of the embodied being.
Śrīkaulinī said:
From the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
I shall explain to you, out of affection, this secret of the Kaula tradition— the answer to the ultimate question— which is difficult even for the thirty gods to obtain and is free from doubt.
From the principle of earth up to the Puruṣa, Māyā should be known as being above;
she has the nature of the pure self of Sattva and is situated in the sequence of the eight groups.
Above that is the principle of Īśvara, and above that is Sadāśiva;
above him is Śiva, who is the stainless one pervading the sky.
Thus ends the great staff of the ocean, extending from Śiva down to the earth;
above that, the Śākta [energy] is fivefold, beginning with the form of resonance (dhvani) in due order.
The staff of great manifestation extends as far as the limit of the Samanā-ādhāra;
the third leader of the staff is the supreme bliss beyond the Kalās, belonging to the Kumārikākhaṇḍa.
Because it sustains all, the staff of Śambhu is said to have a terrifying form;
having thus understood the staff, one finds the state free from affliction above it.
Thus it exists as all-pervading, peaceful, omniscient, omnipresent, and supreme.
However, liberation is said to be of two kinds: that with a limit for those who know the objects of knowledge.
But liberation for those who know action and knowledge of the self is otherwise, being without limit:
the first [liberation] is the principle of *puruṣa*, and the second is the principle of *māyā*.
The third is Śuddhavidyā, and the fourth is above Īśvara;
the fifth is at the end of Sadāśiva, the sixth is liberation culminating in Śiva,
the seventh is said to be at the end of Śakti, and likewise the eighth is at the end of Samanā.
The eleventh is liberation; the twelfth is at the end of Klinnā and at the end of Trikhaṇḍā.
The thirteenth [day] is at the end of the eon, while the fourteenth is at the beginning and the end;
the fifteenth is at the end of Mars in the city of forty-two.
That which is partless, supreme knowledge, incomparable, and six-syllabled is declared as the sixteenfold [vidyā] when possessed of parts; this is proclaimed as liberation.
Established through sixteen divisions, she is situated in the state of the limitless.

At its end is that supreme liberation; having reached dissolution at the end of the void, the power whose nature is the internal void has attained voidness within the void. —From the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
When nothing whatsoever exists, that is proclaimed to be the limit.
Above that is the supreme state, the highest plane beyond all states of being,
which is free from mantra and meditation and devoid of the sequence of mudrās.
But the ultimate limit is supportless, devoid of all meditation,
transcending the performance of sacrifice, and free from the differentiation of the *bindu*.
Free from the three instruments of action, devoid of that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be accepted,
liberated from existence and non-existence, and free from any state of abiding.
Waveless, supremely peaceful, beyond bliss, without support,
the supreme void, the great void, the ultimate limit— this is the state of Śambhu.
The path to liberation is divided into two: with form (*sākāra*) and the stainless (*nirañjana*).
For that which is situated higher and higher, there is no certainty regarding the state with form.
When there is no limit to emptiness, then it would be non-independent;
how could it maintain supreme liberation as long as the limit of emptiness does not exist?
When the limit of the sequence has been reached at the end of the Void, in the supreme state free from affliction,
and when the subsequent sixfold [set] has been accomplished by relying upon the knowledge of the sequence.
O Maheśvara, as long as one remains in the path of mantra in future births above,
so long is eternal liberation proclaimed to have this limit.

Thus, the nature of liberation consists of the principle of Śūnya and so forth, which is of the nature of the Person (pauruṣa). That which is of the nature of the Person is declared to be Śūnya; Māyā is the very emptiness (śūnyatā) of that [Person].
In that way, Īśvara is void; from that, Sadāśiva is void;
Śiva, who is omnipresent, is void; and the end of sound (nādānta) is said to be void.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Vyāpinī is the cause, Śūnyā is the Equal One (Samanā), and her state is emptiness.
That which ends with Bhairava is known as emptiness; indeed, the state of Bhairavī is emptiness itself.
The state of the Vīrāvalī is emptiness; the Kālikākrama is emptiness;
the tradition of Amarikā is emptiness;
and the forty-two [deities] ending with Kujā are emptiness. Indeed, it is established at the end of the movement.
There, above that, is the supreme void, the waveless state of Śambhu.
For whom emptiness [is the nature].
"Completely free from mantra and vidyā, and devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted—the limit of the [mantra] Kujā has been declared; for mantras, there is no further collection."
Below that is the infinite, the most excellent of connections;
when it arises for the mantras, the sixfold great supreme command is born.
The desire for peace is the cause; this is clearly the tradition of the Void (Śūnyāmnāya).
It abides in sixteen divisions, and there is no end to it.
When the state consisting of meditative absorption is distinguished by mantra and mudrā,

and one is constantly devoted to recitation and worship, this liberation remains infinite; it persists from the principles of the Person (puruṣatattva) and so forth, as long as the cause of peaceful desire exists.
That which is designated as "non-independent" perishes upon the abandonment of meditative absorption.
For those seeking liberation, however, that peaceful state is difficult to attain without the abandonment of mantra—
that which is peaceful, supreme, empty, and devoid of all limbs.

That which is the meditation on the place and the lineage, wherein the mudrās and mantras have attained dissolution; [this is] the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, consisting of the fivefold practice of worship, recitation, ritual procedure, and substances.

Wherein lies the dissolution through the unshakable command, the eightfold qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā), the piercing of the meditative concentration on the abandonment of worldly prosperity, and the signs of attainment such as the bursting of the seals (mudrā).
When neither the past, the future, nor the present—nor even long life—is found therein, that is liberation: eternal and unborn.
But that which they desire is certainly the eternal peace, wherein all have gone to dissolution;
that is declared to be the limit, the independent [reality] facing in all directions.
When there is no abandonment of what has been attained and nothing else exists, there is sovereignty over all beings; this is the pair of syllables known as "Peace."
As long as the ritual actions of the philosophical systems proceed at every step,
so long is the application of the ritual of mantras prescribed by means of forceful suppression.
But when the supreme state has been attained, the one who possesses both action and knowledge ceases [from worldly activity];
until then, the pervasion of knowledge and action is proclaimed to be without end.
Until it reaches its limit and attains the state of peace— that Śāmbhava state which is devoid of ritual action and knowledge and ends with the dissolution of the body.
Likewise, knowledge free from internal conceptualization exists through the path of action;
yet peaceful knowledge devoid of action— wherein worship and meditation do not exist— is [the ultimate state].
Through the knowledge of action (*kriyājñāna*), one proceeds beyond desire through practice;
for those who have entered the path of accomplishment, that [state] is known to have a limit at the end:
this is the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
And that power of the ladder is realized at the end of the unborn;
without the ladder, liberation is difficult to attain on the path of emptiness.
Having reached its limit at the end of the sequence, she indeed attains dissolution at the end of the void;
just as a ball, when struck by a fist, would fly upward.
Because the sky is profound, the practitioner, through false conduct,
likewise remains in the state beyond conduct at the end of liberation with limits.
Just as a gall-nut creeps upward from the root all the way to the branch,
so too, having attained the Śrī-Śrīkrama, one proceeds until the ultimate end.
The practitioner, knowing the nature of all phenomena, shall gradually ascend from the Buddhist path onwards,
step by step, even over the course of many future births, until reaching the summit.
Having attained the state of the Kujāmnāya, one shall go to dissolution at the ultimate limit;
for such a person, there is no return again to birth after birth in the lower realms.
From the Buddhist scriptures up to the Kulālikāmnāya,
the ritual action of whichever [text] proceeds through the mutual application of qualities [is to be understood].
But having reached the goal of its limit, his activity ceases;
meanwhile, the practitioner remains mounted upon that activity, like a crab on a tree.
Having attained the state that transcends mantra, one should then abandon the scriptures;
for there is the destruction of the formalized form through the sequence of the five mudrās.
One should abandon these two syllables: "liberation" for that which is formless and tranquil.
Having known the entire essence,
however, the Kumārikākhaṇḍa,
there would be pervasion in the supreme, peaceful, and stainless state, not in a single birth.
Therefore, hereafter follows the path to liberation according to the method of pervasion as taught in the scriptures.
Having understood this through the correct procedure, one shall then attain the upward course—
the state of Buddha-consciousness, liberation, and the transcendence of the three qualities.
It is the Pradhāna for the proponents of the Vedas who know the self of the four Vedas;
it is the Puruṣa for the proponents of Sūrya; and it is the supreme state for the Sāṃkhyas.
The supreme state for those who hold the club-weapon in hand is the reality of Māyā;
for the Vaimalas, the supreme state is the Vidyā consisting of pure knowledge.
Those who know the eight measures and the Vedas, and are experts in the meaning of the Lākula [teachings],
attain the supreme state of Īśvara through the Pāśupata vow.
Those who know the scripture of the nine Nityās [attain] the supreme state, the Śiva-tattva;
having abandoned the five causes above that, one reaches Bhairava above even that.
The supreme state of eternal bliss belongs to the Tantrikas who follow the eight systems; it transcends the levels from *samanā* down to *kalā*, and is established in both the left and the right.
Liberation exists according to the sequence of the lineages; this is true, there is no doubt about it.
Above that is the group of six supreme [lineages], situated one above the other.
The first division is the Six-Spoked [Wheel] (Ṣaḍāra); the second is called Bhairava;
the third is Vīrāvalī; and the fourth is Kālikākula.
Then, following that first descent, above it is the Unstruck (anāhata);
now, according to the division of castes, there is the Kumārikākhaṇḍa known as the venerable Kulālikā.
Among those, that [first] division is devoid of the three sequences;
above that is the division beginning with *ka*, which measures seven crores.
The compendium of sūtras is declared to have been brought down by the Primordial Lord;
it is the foremost of all tantras, having emerged from seventy million [verses].
The core of that [work] consists of four koṭis, and from that, it exceeds one hundred thousand pādas;
this is the measure of all the scriptures, specifically in the Western lineage.
I have brought down for you this Mahākulālikāmata,
the Arising of the Sequence (Kramodaya), in brief, situated upon the seat of the mudrās.
Transcending the knowledge of mantras, devoid of distinctions of caste,
liberated from the dust of the maṇḍala, and free from all meditative absorptions.
Free from the conduct of the tantras, it possesses authority within the three lineages;
therefore, it is extracted as the essence of essences, like clarified butter from milk.
The source of the tradition is the number of the Jinas, transmitted through the lineage of the root;
it consists of three sections and six supreme parts, established by the command of Viśeṣa.
The teaching of the Great Sequence belongs to the one who resembles the lineage of the Siddhas,
the perfected one whose nature is pure, and who abides at the end of the full moon.
Transcending the sixteen grids (prastāra), that which is extracted at the first seat is the Śāmbhava [tradition], along with its secret; it is declared to be neuter.
The supreme [teaching] of all seekers, from the Buddhist scriptures onwards in sequence,
having mastered the *Mālinīvijaya* up to the neuter scripture, is the *Kumārikākhaṇḍa*.
For them, however, those [lineages] arise separately for each division;
liberation occurs in one's own place within the lineage of the sages.
Even for one intent on the Great Transmission (mahākrama), there is supreme dissolution at the end of the stages;
when this tradition of Kujā is accomplished, it is the path of liberation within this limit.
The Buddhist, the Māhārha, the Vedic, the Saura, the Sāṃkhya, and the Vaiṣṇava; as well as the pure Yoga-vow and the great Pāśupata.
The specific Śaiva [tradition] consists of the determination of the eight Bhairavas and the six Parās ending with Kujā, which are situated one above the other.
The Buddhist scripture is superior to that of the Arhat; from that, the Vedic system;
the Saura is superior to the Veda-scripture; and the Sāṃkhya and Vaiṣṇava are superior to the Saura.
From that, the Yogaśāstra arose in many ways, and from it the Mahāvrata;
from that, the Vaimala, the Sāra, the eight Pramāṇas, and the Lākula [arose].
From that, the Pāśupata was proclaimed; from that, the Śaiva in its many forms.
Beyond that, however, is the Svacchanda, both partless (niṣkala) and with parts (sakala).
Bahurūpa, Aghorīśa, Vyādhibhakṣa, Bhairava,
Candragarbha-vijñāna, Tumburu, and Amṛteśvara.
Even in sequence, the lineage of the *Mālinīvijaya* is sixfold;
above that is the Yoga of the *Klinnā* tradition, which is the supreme state beyond it.
The lineage tradition of the Vīrāvalī, another Kālikākrama,
then the Kulakapāṭa, which is the primordial teaching on the paths.
From that very [source], for the benefit of others, is this pure Kaula tradition of Kujā;
above that, however, are the two syllables "Śāntam" (Peace), which constitute Nirānanda.
Having attained the eternal Śāmbhava liberation, which is devoid of the web of ritual actions and free from the instruction of mantras,
one will exist in all states.
Starting from the Buddhist scriptures up to the neuter *kādyam*.
One should always follow the ultimate limit by means of the abandonment of mantra;
in this [system], liberation is characterized as non-dual, both externally and internally.
In the *Muktisaṃgrahasūtra*, it is stated that there is nothing superior to this [knowledge] through its divisions beginning with "I" (ida);
liberation is known by means of the scriptural tradition (*śāstrāmnāya*), and not otherwise.
Established in the Vedas, above the animal (paśu), and further upward on the left;
having heard [it] on the path of the left and right, in the determination of the Mother (Ambikā) of the South,
that light which is dissolved for the sake of attaining union is in the venerable Vakrikāmata.
"There is nothing higher than this"—such is the command of the Supreme Lord.

Thus, in the introduction to the Great Sacrifice of Mahāmanthānabhairava, in the lineage comprising seventy million verses emerged from the path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primordial seat along the path of the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), in the Vimalabhedottara, in the determination of the Six Thousand, in the Kādivarṇa division, in the Svāminīmata which is the supreme command of the Lord;
In the *Śrīcaturviṃśatsahasrasaṃhitā*, spoken in the tradition of the Mother (*ambākrama*), this is the bliss titled "The Chapter on the Sūtra of the Compendium of Liberation. Śrīnātha said:
[This is] the sixty-ninth bliss.
"You are my guru, O Mistress of the Gods; I am yours for deliberation.
This is the command of Rudra, Bhairava, and the Vīras; it belongs to no one else."
"Out of my state of friendship and compassion, it has been revealed.
Śrīvakrā said: "Then the Lord was commanded regarding the undertaking of the command."
O Great Elder, Śrīkaṇṭha bestowed this transmission in the Kṛta Yuga,
in the year Prabhu, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
Then, in the Tretā Yuga, there was the descent of Bālaśauli; O Lord of Gods, there was also the grace bestowed upon Durvāsas and Oḍḍīśa.

The *Moḍāmara* was bestowed upon him; the lineage of heroes (*vīrāvalī*) is clearly manifest in the year *Hita*, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, during the *Pramoda* [yoga].
In the Dvāpara age, he granted the favor of a command even to the six-faced one;
the vow known as Kaumāra was bestowed upon Śrīvatsa on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
In every age, the descent [of the teaching] occurs in the month of Caitra through the central channel;
this is known by the Lord of the Sixth. Then, moreover, in the Kali Age, that command of Nandirudra and the grace of Caryānātha [are bestowed].
He himself correctly carries out the command according to the sequence of seniority.
The descent into Jyeṣṭholī is thus the sequence of the Olikrama;
the fourth is common to all, established in the state beyond parts.
O Lord, such is the sequence of the Vīrāvalī; thus there are four sequences.
There will be a fifth sequence, O Lord, at the end of the Kali age; of this there is no doubt.
When the Kṣaya year had arrived, on the fourteenth day of Śivarātri,
[the consecration was performed] for the illustrious Piṅgalarudra and for Mataṅgīśa.
Having performed the transmission of the command, he gave him also that Khecarī,
the essence of the Root-Lineage (mūlānvaya), which has emerged from the divine Liṅga.
At the end of the age, the entire lineage of Liṅgolyā will come into being;
among the five Lords of the Age, Bhairava is indeed the Primordial Lord (Ādinātha).
O Navātmānandadeveśa, Lord of the Sovereigns of Vidyārāja,
Śrīkujeśa, the Great-Souled One born from the will of Śrīkuja!
Named Kucandraśekhara, he emerged from the level of Samanā;
thus, O Mother of the Kula, is the descent into the lap [of the Goddess] in Candradvīpa.
Indeed, Icchānātha stands alone, accompanied by the five who have attained the power of command (ājñāsiddha);
from among them, three stand in authority over the three lineages (oli).
This Lord Śrīkaṇṭha has gone here for the sake of cultivating a spirit of friendliness;
for he resides in Kāmarūpa for the purpose of delivering all living beings.
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa:
Purandara; that Blessed One, Oḍunātha, who resides in Jālandhara during the Tretā Yuga, is indeed the bestower of siddhi upon the heroes.
In the Dvāpara age, that Blessed Lord Śrīkumāra is indeed the Lord of the Sixth;
he who resides at Pūrṇagiri bestows the perfection of yoga upon yogins.
O Lord of Gods, he is Nandirudra Caryānātha in the Kali age;
he who resides at Śrī Oṃkāra is indeed the bestower of both enjoyment and liberation.
He who has gone to the southern direction, in the city of Śrīcandrapura,
is the one named Piṅgala at the end of the age, the lord of Mataṅgīs, possessed of great power.
For the sake of command, at the seat of Tisra, there is the fifth, the Lord of Siddhas;
he is the pervasive Navātman, established from beginningless time.
The World-Teacher, the joy of Kucandraśekhara, emerged from Candradvīpa on the lunar seat (candrapīṭha) as the lineage of accomplished masters (siddhaugha) beginning with Śrīmitranātha.
In the western [direction] is the lineage of the Siddhas, devoid of the eastern lineage;
O God, it is in the western age and in the northern kingdom of the Mlecchas.
But when the other two— the teacher and the disciple— have fallen under the sway of greed and delusion,
when their immersion in the Command has vanished, and when their authority has come to an end;
I shall effect my descent in the fifth leader of the seats;
there in the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the venerable Mataṅgīśa is perfected together with Śrīmātangī.
Beginning from that point, there will be a great fourfold worship;
this truth has been proclaimed by me in the [text] of twenty-four thousand [verses].
In the venerable Kumārikākhaṇḍa, within the six-thousand-verse Matottama,
the first is the Kumārikākhaṇḍa and the second is the Siddhakhaṇḍa.
O Lord, the third primary section consists of four quarters in sequence;
this *Vṛkṣa* of the goddess Kubjikā comprises twenty-four thousand verses.
It was placed in the hand of Śeṣarāja for a specific purpose.
Then the Goddess spoke these words: "Whoever knows this in its true essence..."
To him who is endowed with the command of the Creator and is a servant for bestowing grace,
this scripture should be given once his competence has been manifested.
O Bhairava, it was previously held upon his head by the Naga King according to command;
thereafter, it was [received] from Viśvadeva, the Lord of Siddhas.
He was brought for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees and for their protection,
at the great seat (pīṭha) of Oṃkāra, which is adorned by perfected yoginīs.
And the yoginī named Kanakamañjarī, who possesses great power,
established that knowledge in his house, having first performed the ritual commitment (samaya).
In the Kumārikākhaṇḍa, the wick of the navel, the serpent, the vajra-joint, and the two door-panels—
whosoever understands the secret signs (*saṃketa*) herein, to him the Kula scripture should be given.

"Otherwise, it must not be given at all"— this is the command of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvarī). Thus, in the primordial descent (*ādyāvatāra*) of the Great Sacrifice of Manthānabhairava, in the lineage (*anvaya*) measuring seventy million verses, emerged from the Path of Meru, exceeding one hundred thousand quarters, brought down to the primary seat (*ādyapīṭha*), on the path of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the Vimalabheda-Uttara—
In the determination of the hexad, in the Kādibheda, in the Svāminīmata which belongs to the Supreme Lord’s command, in the compendium of twenty-four thousand verses spoken in the Āmbākrama,
the venerable Kumārikākhaṇḍa is completed.
The Pārameśvara is considered to be one hundred million verses in extent;
from this, the essence was extracted in a measure of seventy million verses.
From that [text] of seven crores, the one of one hundred thousand and four hundred verses is more essential;
from this, the twenty-four thousand verse version is even more essential.
Revealed by Mitrā herself in three sections from the northeast of Kujā,
may the *kulayoginīs* rejoice, and may the sons of the *kula* rejoice!
May the venerable Kula-teachers and all others who have received Kula-initiation rejoice!
